By the 1850s, Jewish people had established a synagogue in the gold-producing country town of Bendigo.
During the mid-nineteenth century, Bendigo became an important center of gold prospecting and attracted numerous Jews from the German-speaking world.
A congregation or synagogue was formed during the Victorian Gold Rush period.
M. V. Lazarus of Bendigo, known as 'Bendigo Lazarus', was noted as a Jewish business pioneer who did much to open up new parts in the back country of Victoria.
Earliest documented Jewish presence: A letter by Charles Hodges noted the presence of a 'synagogue' (a gathered Jewish community for worship) among the religious sects on the Bendigo goldfields.
George Mackay's 1891 history of Bendigo placed the earliest organised gatherings for Jewish worship in 1854.
Local newspaper advertisements indicated that an organized Hebrew congregation with an acting committee had formed in Bendigo by 1855.
On 13 July 1856, following a concerted fundraising campaign, the community laid the foundation stone for a synagogue.
On July 13, 1856, the Bendigo Hebrew congregation celebrated the opening of their first synagogue, built of wood and located in Dowling Street, with an address by Israel Moses.
In late 1859, the Bendigo Hebrew congregation employed their first Jewish minister, Isaac Friedman, who led worship, advised on shehitah, and conducted marriages.
A synagogue existed in Sandhurst (now Bendigo) from 1862 to approximately 1910, indicating an organized Jewish community.
Jewish minister Isaac Friedman served the Bendigo Hebrew congregation until 1868, when he moved to Melbourne.
In the early 1870s, Bendigo built an impressive new synagogue in the Byzantine and Moorish styles and hired a new Jewish minister, Isaac Stone.
A footnote referencing The Bendigo Advertiser from September 4, 1872 relates to the commissioning and construction of the new synagogue by the Hebrew congregation.
In the 1880s, the Bendigo Hebrew Congregation hired Jewish minister Isidore Myers and later D. H. Harris.
In the 1890s, the Bendigo Hebrew Congregation hired Jewish minister J. Goldstein.

First Jewish settlers in Amstetten "in the mid-1860s" (page text: "Mitte der 1860er Jahre"); 1865 is a conventional mid-decade year. About two decades later Amstetten became seat of a district-wide Israelite Kultusgemeinde (IKG; Wikipedia: first founded at Kemmelbach 1861, renamed IKG Amstetten in 1897; prayer room in Amstetten consecrated 18 Aug 1896).
Page table "Juden in Amstetten": 1890 = 40 Jews (in 9 families); source cited by the page: J. Freihammer, Das Schicksal der Amstettner Juden (1989). Town count, not the district community.

Same page table: 1923 = 20 Jews (in 9 families). (1900 = 45 in the same table.) The table gives c. 350 for 1934 but marks it "gesamte Kultusgemeinde" (whole IKG district), so it is not used as a town count.

Table: 1938 = 29 Jews. After the Anschluss the Jews were boycotted and had to leave; on 10 Nov 1938 SS men set fire to the Jewish prayer room (Betraum) in the Ardaggerstraße and wrecked Jewish homes and shops (page text; same fact in Lind, doew.at gum_lind.pdf).

Table: May 1939 = 3 Jews; Sept 1939 "keine" (none). The text adds that the last Jewish family left in Aug 1939 but one resident was overlooked and survived unnoticed until autumn 1941, so no 0-row is entered.

In the 1860s the Orthodox wine merchant Simon Hacker (born 1830 in Kobersdorf) settled with his wife in Erlach; he bought Erlach no. 69 in 1875. Earlier, at the end of the 18th century, Erlach had a warehouse for Jewish itinerant traders; in 1867 the Jewish industrialist Leopold Abeles bought the local spinning mill (he lived in Vienna). 1865 is a conventional year for "the 1860s" (TU Wien diploma thesis by T. Koplmüller 2023, section 2-3).

Private synagogue (prayer room, ca. 30 seats plus ca. 15 in the women's gallery) built by Simon Hacker: the thesis dates it 1895/96 in chapter 3, but 1885/86 in chapter 2.1 (citing Lind 2004) - sources conflict. Orthodox Jews from Erlach and neighbouring villages attended; the synagogue was looted after the Anschluss in March 1938; Leopold Hacker and his wife were murdered in 1942 (Theresienstadt / Treblinka). Hacker-Haus museum for contemporary history opened 2019.

In June 1855 the stillborn child of a Jewish mother taking the cure at Bad Gleichenberg was refused burial in the Catholic cemetery of Trautmannsdorf (parish of the spa) - earliest dated trace of Jewish spa guests (Wikipedia, Jüdischer Friedhof Trautmannsdorf in Oststeiermark). No local Jewish Kultusgemeinde developed; the spa was visited mainly by Jewish guests from Vienna and Hungary/Transylvania.

In 1880 the IKG Graz laid out a Jewish cemetery at Trautmannsdorf (Bad Gleichenberg) because of the steadily growing number of Jewish spa guests; hall built 1887; 94 Jewish people were buried there up to 1938. After 1867 a Jewish infrastructure (kosher restaurants and bakeries, pensions, Israelite hospital, ritual bath) developed in Bad Gleichenberg (Graz page of jüdische-gemeinden.de).

After the Anschluss of March 1938 Jewish life in Bad Gleichenberg was ended abruptly; the cemetery was desecrated in the November pogrom (Graz page of jüdische-gemeinden.de, section Bad Gleichenberg).

A small Jewish community developed in the spa town of Bad Ischl from the middle of the 19th century; because of the distance to the Linz Kultusgemeinde it kept a certain independence without becoming an official community (Linz page of jüdische-gemeinden.de, section Bad Ischl). 1850 is a conventional mid-century year.
In 1934 about 60 resident Jewish citizens were counted in the spa town; the number of Jewish visitors was considerably larger (page text).

After the Anschluss (March 1938) Jewish shops were looted and Jewish-owned houses and villas had to be sold under pressure ("Arisierung" driven by Wilhelm Haenel); in Nov 1938 many resident Jewish men were arrested. A small Jewish community re-formed briefly after 1945 (DP camp).

Jewish cemetery laid out about 1879 as a walled section of the village cemetery; burials were of members of the Jewish families resident in Bad Pirawarth; last burial 1938; 10 gravestones remain (Wikipedia, Jüdischer Friedhof Bad Pirawarth). Pirawarth belonged to the IKG Gänserndorf district (1907/08).

Jewish cemetery laid out in 1908 by the Chewra Kadischa of Mattersburg for the burial of spa guests (Wikipedia, Jüdischer Friedhof Bad Sauerbrunn). Wikipedia (Bad Sauerbrunn): with the spa a small permanent Jewish community arose, a branch of the Mattersburg Kultusgemeinde; about two thirds of spa guests were Jewish.
After the Anschluss the Sauerbrunn Jews were expelled and forced to sell their property at a loss or had it "aryanised" (Wikipedia, Bad Sauerbrunn); only a few survivors returned after 1945.

Regesten Band 2, Nr. 468 and 469 (28/29 Jan 1340): the Jew Scheblein "aus Schwanberg" appears as a moneylender/creditor together with Scheblein of Cilli, Zarach and Mendlein of Graz (the annotations to Nr. 496, 503, 506 and 520, dated 1342-1344, discuss whether the Scheblein named there is the one of Schwanberg or of Cilli); the Wikipedia article on Jews in Styria lists Bad Schwanberg among the towns with Jews. Identification with Schwanberg (Deutschlandsberg district) rests on the Cilli/Graz context. Expelled with all Styrian Jews in 1496/97.

The Israelite Bethausverein Vöslau bought a house in the Petzgasse in 1911 and installed a synagogue (men's room 60 m2, women's room 20 m2) with its own teacher and shochet; the association existed until 1938 and was swelled by Jewish spa guests in summer. The prayer room was wrecked in the 1938 pogrom.

comment: Jews of Bruck an der Leitha in 1377. On 30 July 1377, in Vienna, the Jewess Zema, widow of Mosche of Bruck an der Leitha, and her cousin Scheftlein 'aus Bruck an der Leitha' sold a vineyard, for 60 pounds, to Michael Geukramer of the Vienna city council, with the consent of the lord of the land, Provost Berthold von Wehingen of St Stephen's cathedral; the charter says Zema had bought the vineyard 'um ir aigenhaffts ledigs gut' (with her own free money). Brugger p. 83 uses it to show that Jews could own property outside Vienna's Jewish quarter on the same terms as Christians. The map has Bruck rows for 1300 (synagogue), 1351 and 1420; this adds a dated 1377 presence, with a Jewish widow acting as owner. No population. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:766/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 3, 2015), no. 1538 on PDF p. 241]

source: https://tyche.univie.ac.at/index.php/tyche/article/view/4942 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnuntum | Grüll, T., 'Jewish Presence in the Danubian Provinces of the Roman Empire', in: M. Hrbácsek (ed.), Židovský kultúrny fenomén v stredoeurópskom kontexte / Zsidó kultúra közép-európai kontextusban, UKF Nitra 2016 (ISBN 978-80-558-1092-8), pp. 9-18, here pp. 14-15 (PDF pp. 10-11)
comment: Tombstone fragment (local limestone, 60 x 89 x 20.5 cm, found 2009 in the canabae of the Roman town) of [M.] Mulvius[...], styled 'domo Iudaeus' ('by home a Jew/Judaean') and 'negotians' (trader); Grüll calls him the only Jewish tradesman of the Danubian provinces attested by an epitaph. The name Mulvius is common in north-east Italy and especially Aquileia, so he may have come with legio XV Apollinaris (back at Carnuntum from 71 AD) after the First Jewish War, as a trader or as a soldier's slave. DISPUTED: 'domo Iudaeus' can mean origin from Iudaea or adherence to Judaism; the editors (Beutler and Kremer, Tyche 28, 2013) date both new Carnuntum stones to the end of the 1st or the beginning of the 2nd century and conclude that they probably do not name Jews; Grüll (pp. 14-15) leaves both readings open (if 'Judaean' is meant, 135/6 AD is a terminus ante quem). Year 100 = midpoint of 'end of 1st / beginning of 2nd century' (period only). Confidence low. No population. An undated menorah oil lamp is also known from Carnuntum (AMC VI 3 329/54, Dávid 2014, cited by Grüll p. 15); not written as its own row because it has no date. Carnuntum (modern Petronell-Carnuntum and Bad Deutsch-Altenburg) has no marker on the map yet; coordinates from the Wikipedia article 'Carnuntum'.

comment: Epitaph (three non-joining fragments; above the text field a volute krater with ivy flanked by date palms, gable above) of P. Aemilius [...] Verecundus (aged 75) and his son P. Aemilius [...]vus (aged 50), set up by a P. Aemilius [...]; line 6 reads 'do(mo) Iud(a)ei[...]'. Found 2009 re-used in the late-antique water-main south of the civil town of Carnuntum; now in the Archaeological Museum Carnuntinum, Bad Deutsch-Altenburg. EDH dates it 71-150 AD (midpoint 110); the editors' abstract (Tyche 28, 2013) says end of the 1st / beginning of the 2nd century, used here as year 100 (period only). Grüll (p. 12) uses the Roman-style name as an example of a probable descendant of a freed Jewish slave who was adopted by a Roman citizen. DISPUTED: the editors read 'domo Iudaeus' as possibly 'from Iudaea' and conclude the deceased probably are not named as Jews. Confidence low. Names are Notes only; no population. A second, unpublished Carnuntum epitaph for a slave-girl of the soldier L. Varius Verecundus (Varia Margale) is mentioned by Grüll (n. 2) but nothing shows she was Jewish; not written.

Following ritual murder trials in other areas (such as Trento in 1475), all Jews were expelled from the town of Feldkirch.

On January 7, 1943, 14 Jewish refugees from Slovakia attempting to escape to Switzerland were discovered hiding in a coal train at the Feldkirch railway station. They were detained in the Feldkirch prison before being deported; this represents a group of transit refugees, not a resident population.

comment: On 31 August 1361 the Gurk bishop John II (chancellor of Duke Rudolf IV) assigned part of his revenues, to raise money for Rudolf's Friuli campaign against Patriarch Ludovico della Torre, to the Straßburg burghers Hans Vetter and Hans Payer, who had borrowed 500 florins for him "bei dem Juden Häslein (Heaslein) aus Friesach" (regest Nr. 996; Wiedl p. 69). The debt was still open in 1367: Häslein had been paid 160 florins and held a new bond for the other 340 (regest Nr. 1221 of 5 November 1367; Wiedl pp. 70-71). Wiedl (p. 71) calls Häslein "second to none" among the moneylenders at the height of his activity; his brother Isserlein of Friesach is also named. The map has Friesach rows for 1124, 1255, 1346, 1349 and 1498 only. No population. Confidence high. [Source detail: (Brugger and Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 2: 1339-1365, Innsbruck 2010, Nr. 996, p. 265); (Brugger and Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 3: 1366-1386, Innsbruck 2015, Nr. 1221)]

comment: In the arbitration of 28 October 1365 between Bishop Paul of Freising (earlier of Gurk) and the Dukes Albrecht III and Leopold III the dukes promised to press "den Juden Abrech (Afrechen) aus Friesach" for a deferral, payment in instalments and moderate interest on the bishop's debt (regest Nr. 1140/1141, pp. 334-335). Wiedl (p. 67 and n.56) notes that Abrech, as an inhabitant of Friesach, was a subject of the Archbishop of Salzburg, lord of Friesach, whereas Mosche of Maribor was a subject of the dukes and Chatschim of Celje a fief of the Counts of Cilli. The regests show Abrech (son of Perusch/Izchak) as the leading Jewish moneylender of Friesach in the 1350s. The map has no Friesach row between 1349 and 1498. No population. Confidence high. [Source detail: (Brugger and Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 2: 1339-1365, Innsbruck 2010, Nr. 1140-1141, pp. 334-335)]

comment: Event: forced baptism of a Jewish child of Herzogenburg in the Viennese Geserah. After the Geserah the boy Matthias, born in Herzogenburg and baptised, was placed with the Augustinian canons of St Andrä an der Traisen (Herzogenburg): Provost Erhart confirmed receipt of 50 pounds of Viennese pennies from Duke Albrecht V, which Matthias was to receive when he came of age (HHStA Vienna, Familienurkunden no. 43, dated 21 March 1422 in Keil's footnote 39; the body text says March 1421). In January 1430 (footnote 40: 15 Jan 1431) Matthias, 'New Christian born in Herzogenburg', confirmed that the provosts had lovingly looked after him, educated him in the Christian faith and let him attend school, that he had used the 50 pounds and was owed nothing more. Keil pp. 106-107: Albrecht V, who presumably murdered the boy's parents, supported baptised children (Brugger: he took away 'their only child, their property and their home country'). The map has Herzogenburg 1421 (all Jews expelled under the edict); this adds the baptised child. Year of Data 1422 follows the dated footnote (see conflicts file for the 1421/1422 discrepancy inside the paper). Wiedl (p. 58) writes that Plume, one of the most prestigious Jewish moneylenders of early 14th-century Austria, had settled in Klosterneuburg around 1320, so the local community "definitely had the financial capacity" to (co-)finance a major church rebuilding; she nevertheless judges the rumour of 1331 (Small Chronicle of Klosterneuburg, regest Nr. 351) that Provost Stephen of Sierndorf had pawned the Verdun altar panels to Jews most probably unfounded (no pawning ever took place). The map has Klosterneuburg rows for 1275, 1295, 1302 and 1330 but none for the 1320s (1321 is the earliest dated mention of Plume). No population. Confidence high. On 8 April 1380 Heinrich Flötzer, ducal steward (Amtmann auf dem Herzogsgut) in Klosterneuburg, heard a complaint of the Augustinian monastery's revenue office (Oblei) about a Jewish house on the Hundskehle 'neben der Judenschule und auch neben dem Obleihaus' (next to the synagogue and the Obleihaus): a latrine too close to the Obleihaus wall and rainwater running through the wall into its courtyard. The house belonged to David Steuss, a Viennese Jew, 'Sohn des Hendlein aus Klosterneuburg'; he came to court with 'die gesamte Judengemeinde von Klosterneuburg' (Brugger p. 90: probably all the community's representatives). Six arbiters, all from Klosterneuburg, were named, among them the town's Jewish judge Nikolaus von Mosletzberg (Brugger: the Jewish side chose the current Jewish judge of Klosterneuburg and his predecessor, and as third arbiter the monastery's cellarer). Verdict: the Jews may keep the latrine but must wall it in by 24 June; rainwater may run through, but no filth, kitchen scraps or blood may be poured into it (Brugger p. 91: the mention of blood suggests that the house served the community for kosher slaughter). Brugger p. 90: Klosterneuburg housed 'a small, but prosperous Jewish community with close ties to Vienna'. The map has Klosterneuburg rows for 1371 (synagogue first mentioned) and 1420; this adds a dated 1380 court case naming synagogue, community and Jewish judge. No population. comment: Jewish households at the Niedermarkt of Klosterneuburg in 1388-89. On 8 March 1389 Brother Thomas, steward of the canons' hospital (Chorherrenspital) in Klosterneuburg, heard the Jew Isachar Tiem, acting for the children of David Steuss (his sons Hendlein and Jona), who sued to take over a garden at the Niedermarkt that the late Conrad Schaffer had pledged for a debt of 80 pounds plus interest; the garden bordered the house of the Jew Hetschlein, the heirs and all other claimants, 'Christians and Jews', were asked whether anyone wished to redeem it, nobody did, and the garden was handed to Tiem (Regest IV no. 1913). A year earlier (15 June 1388) the Jew Manusch is described as living with a house at Klosterneuburg ('mit haws gesezzen ze Newnburg klosterhalben', Regest IV no. 1893); he is probably the son of Lea Scheblin, who owned a house in Klosterneuburg. Keil p. 103 n. 27 cites Lohrmann (1992), p. 219, for a house owned by Jews in 1389 on the 'nidern Markt', and n. 26 for Manusch, son of Scheblein, who granted numerous small loans of about 10 pounds around 1400. No population. The Kleine Klosterneuburger Chronik (written after 1428) tells of 'ein judin zu Closterneuburg' who accepted baptism and was named Barbara; she had been married to the Jew Schebelein, then married Niclas den Lueger, son of a burgher, and after his death Niclas den Lister, son of a burgher of Pressburg. Duke Albrecht V gave Barbara and her three baptised children (Thomas, Kathrei and the minor Jakob) half a house on the Nidern Markt that had belonged to the Jew Lewein, 'immediately after all four of us had received holy baptism'; they sold it on 12 Nov 1430 (Klosterneuburg Stiftsarchiv, Urk. 1430 XI 12). Keil pp. 103-104: she was integrated immediately into Christian society, socially and topographically; whether her baptism was forced or voluntary is irrelevant in a context of violence and fear of death. comment: Jewish houses in Krems and the clerical ban on selling to Jews (1368-1374). On 11 Feb 1368 Friedlieb, dean of Krems and canon of Passau, confirmed that Jans Rotter and his wife Anna had bought their house 'in dem langen hofe', next to the house of the Jew Nachim, on condition that they never sell, pawn or give it to a Jew (Regest III no. 1229). The regest note quotes Kerschbaumer for an older list in the parish land register of 1360 of dues the Jews had to pay on St Michael's Day for houses at the Helltor, in the Kirchengasse, in the Langenhof, at the daily market and at the Schupfen, i.e. several Jewish houses in Krems by 1360. Similar clauses (resale only to Christians, not to Jews) appear in leases of Admont (11 Nov 1370, nos. 1320-1321, steward of the Admont court in Krems), Reichersberg (15 June 1373, no. 1412), Gleink (3 Feb 1374, no. 1433) and Lambach (19 Feb 1374, no. 1435). Brugger p. 84: Krems 'housed the second largest Jewish community after Vienna'; the clauses are documented only for clergymen and monasteries, never laypeople, and seem specific to the Krems region; none is known for Vienna. The map has Krems rows for 1355 (return after the Black Death) and 1392; this adds the 1360-1374 house and discrimination evidence. No population. comment: Event: a forcibly baptised Jew of Krems imprisoned for planning to return to Judaism. On 27 Sept 1421 Jakob of Krems, 'etwann genant ytsekl Jud' (formerly called Jew Isak), declared that he had been jailed in Krems because he admitted, without torture, that he planned to leave the Christian faith and return to the 'Jewish and heretical faith', for which he had 'forfeited life and soul'; 'with God's mercy', also towards his wife and children, the judge and council of Krems released him after he swore an Urfehde to remain a Christian (Stadtarchiv Krems, StAKr-0203; printed Franz Kurz 1835, pp. 364-365 no. 2; the Regesta misreads 'etwan' as a surname). Keil pp. 113-114: this charter is a solid basis for the Kleine Klosterneuburger Chronik's report that numerous reconverts were burnt, and the council of Krems probably knew Isak-Jakob's family, since Krems, with Vienna and Wiener Neustadt, held one of the three oldest Jewish communities in Austria. No online source found: the monasterium.net page cited by Keil is blocked to scripts (Cloudflare 403) and the other online pages checked (de.wikipedia Wiener Gesera, JE) do not mention Jakob/Isak; source is a scholarly volume. comment: Jewish residents of Perchtoldsdorf in the 1370s. On 21 April 1372 the Jew Freudel, son of Patusch of Perchtoldsdorf, sold a small vineyard in Perchtoldsdorf (an der Soss, near the Krautgaerten) for 12 pounds to Nikolaus Gegelein of Perchtoldsdorf, in a German-language charter; he declared that the vineyard owed one and a half buckets of wine 'zu Seelgerät' (rent charge donated for a Christian's soul) to the nuns of St Theobald in Vienna (Regest III no. 1379; Brugger p. 85). The regest note records another sale by a Perchtoldsdorf Jew (Thoerl) on 8 Nov 1375, and Albrecht V's privilege of 4 May 1417 to the 'Jews of Perchtoldsdorf and Mödling' (Regest V no. 2620) shows the community continued until the Geserah; the map's only Perchtoldsdorf row is 1420 (Jewish women's suicide). No population. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:766/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 3, 2015), no. 1379 on PDF p. 147]

The editors call Merchlin the first known Jew of Pulkau and think he is the Marquard/Merchlin in front of whose house the alleged bleeding host was found on the eve of St Vitalis, 27 April 1338 (Regesten 1, no. 436), the incident that started the Pulkau persecutions (the map has a Pulkau 1338 row; this 1329 row is earlier). de.wikipedia (Pulkauer Verfolgungen) says he "seit zehn Jahren in Pulkau lebte"; Brugger 2013 (p. 193 n. 16) says he had lived in Pulkau for at least a decade by 1338 and cites the same charter. Legend holds that around the 15th century Jewish migrants eventually sojourned in Rechnitz under Count Batthyany's permission; the Rechnitzer family assumed their name here.
A document from before 1527 (Baumkircher-Urbar) mentioned two Jewish families, Spiegel and Grünwald, in connection with the fiefdom of Rechnitz; Estimate based on families.
Assumption that a synagogue or prayer house stood in Rechnitz as early as this year; a Torah curtain dates from this year.
Oldest written reference to the Jewish community, establishing it as the oldest in Southern Burgenland.
A synagogue, commissioned by the Batthyány family, was bought by the Jewish Community.
An impressive baroque rebuilding of the synagogue was finished, with room for 400 people.
A 'Chewra Kadischa' ('Devout Brotherhood') Burial Society was established to arrange funerals and welfare.
In the 18th century, Jews constituted 10% of the farmers in Rechnitz.
Rabbi Eleazar Kalir, previously Rabbi in Amsterdam and Berlin, began teaching in Rechnitz.
Rabbi Eleazar Kalir concluded his ten-year tenure as head of the local Jeschiwa.
The Jewish community of Körmend remained under the jurisdiction of the Rohonc (Rechnitz) community until the end of the 18th century.
Gabriel Engelsmann became Rabbi, serving strictly Orthodox and presiding over a popular Jeschiwa.
At its height in the first half of the 19th century, the Jewish community had around 850 members.
Gustav Pick, the son of a Jewish merchant and future composer, was born in Rechnitz on December 20.
Date of the Memorial Book of the 'Chewra Kadischa' Rechnitz.
The synagogue was once more enlarged.
Jews were allowed by law to become residents and take up trades; 89 Jewish stores and factories were active.
Gustav Pick's family moved from Rechnitz to Vienna.
Rabbi Gabriel Engelsmann concluded his tenure.

The Jewish school was closed due to a lack of pupils.
Two Jewish doctors had their offices in Rechnitz in the 1930s.
A local chapter of the Union of Jewish Frontline Soldiers was founded.
A local chapter of the Austrian Zionist Organization was founded.
Jewish men and women were still living in Rechnitz; all were expelled or deported by the Nazis.
From autumn, Jewish forced laborers were billeted in the cellars and stables of Castle Batthyány.
On March 24-25, 200 Hungarian Jewish forced laborers were murdered on the grounds of Schloss Rechnitz.
The Rechnitz Massacre occurred on the eve of the Russian army's arrival, where 200 Hungarian Jews were murdered.
The Rechnitz Massacre occurred on the eve of the Russian army's arrival, where 200 Hungarian Jews were murdered.
Hundreds of Hungarian Jews were murdered by the Nazis during forced marches; a memorial site marks the location.
Only a single Jewish family (Netti Blau and her two adult children) returned to settle after 1945.
Theresia (Riza) Blau, a returned Jewish resident, died and was buried in Vienna.
The town council had a memorial plaque attached to commemorate the Jewish community.
A memorial plaque for the Jewish community was ceremoniously unveiled in November.
Three glass plates were installed to symbolize the demise of the Jewish community.

Shortly after the Anschluss the state police ordered their names to be reported; during the Reichspogromnacht (Nov 1938) the Jews living in Ried were arrested and after their release emigrated; a plaque at the Charlotte-Taitl-Haus (Roßmarkt 29) remembers the last Jewish resident, murdered in Auschwitz.

The first references to Jews in the city of Salzburg itself dates from 1282.
Oldest documented Jewish settlement in Salzburg (aelteste urkundliche Erwaehnung 1284); Judengasse was centre of settlement until expulsion; synagogue in house Judengasse 15 until 1415.

Jews functioned as moneylenders in the city of Salzburg, including among their customers members of the city administration; in 1285 a Jewish banker, Isaac, is noted among those who lent money to the treasury of the archbishop.

source: https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/o:55 | Wiedl, "Sacred Objects in Jewish Hands. Two Case Studies", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 64 n. 36
comment: On 9 September 1338 Bishop Albrecht II of Passau, lord of St. Pölten, granted the town a charter with provisions for the Jews (regest Nr. 444, art. 66-67): no Jew may lend to the burghers on houses, mass vestments ("messgewannt"), unthreshed grain or bloodied garments, only on good pledges or on letters under the town judge's seal, and the Jews must present their bonds and pledges three times a year at the court days before the judge and burghers. Wiedl (p. 64 n.36) lists it among the Austrian town statutes that ban sacred objects as pawns, which appear (with the exception of Feldkirch) only in towns under ecclesiastical lords (Villach, St. Pölten, Pettau). The map has St. Pölten rows for c. 1300 (first reports of Jews) and for the pogroms of 1306 and 1338; the charter is a separate act of the same year. No population. Confidence high. [Source detail: (Brugger and Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 1: bis 1338, Innsbruck 2005, Nr. 444, p. 341)]

comment: The atlas has 'Vindobona' (identified here with Vienna; the atlas label is ancient or alternative) labelled on the map 'Distribution of Jews, middle of the sixth century' (that map has no separate legend, so every labelled place is read as a place with Jewish evidence). In 905 decrees were issued fixing the toll to be paid by Jewish merchants in Austria; this proves only that Jews traveled in that country.
Jews began settling in Vienna and in the area that was to become Judenplatz around 1150, coinciding with the settlement of the House of Babenberg.
As early as 1194 Duke Leopold VI of Austria placed a Jew named Shlom (Solomon) at the head of the mint.
Event: Two years later (1196) the Crusaders reached Vienna, rushed to the house of Solomon and murdered him and fifteen other Jews; the duke executed two ringleaders.
Quantitative estimates of the number of Jews in Vienna between the thirteenth and eighteenth centuries are in the range of 500 to 4,000.

In 1235 the Jew Teka (Tecanus) is mentioned as living in Vienna; he acted as state banker for Austria, and had far-flung financial interests.

In Aug. 1238 Emperor Frederick II took the Jews of Vienna under his protection (servi camerae); the charter of Duke Frederick II of July 1, 1244 became the model for the status of the Jews of Bohemia, Moravia, Hungary, Silesia and Poland.
The rich Jew Techau of Vienna was bondsman of Duke Leopold VI in 1255 for a debt of 2,000 pounds of silver; in 1257 the brothers Lublin and Nekelo were treasury agents (Kammergrafen).

Event: At the time of the Black Death persecutions of 1348–49, the community of Vienna was spared and even served as a refuge for Jews from other places; it developed rapidly during the reign of Rudolf iv (1339–65).

comment: Plague year in Vienna: the Jewish community was large, died heavily and enlarged its cemetery. Konrad von Megenberg's Buch der Natur (the Regesten editors date the passage [1349]) says that there were as many Jews in Vienna as in any city he knew in the German lands, and that they died so heavily in the plague that they had to enlarge their cemetery considerably and buy two houses for it ("daz si irn freithof vil weitern muesten und zwai haueser dar zuo chauften"); he adds that he does not know whether any Jews poisoned wells, but that it would have been folly to poison themselves. Brugger p. 92 (n. 52) quotes this as one of the Church-side refutations of the well-poisoning charge for Austria. So in 1349 Vienna's Jews were not attacked (compare the Krems pogrom of 29 Sept 1349); the map has Vienna 1348 (spared) and 1350 rows but not the cemetery enlargement. No population stated. Confidence high for the fact, medium for the exact year. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:58/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 2, 2010), no. 650 on PDF pp. 101-102]

Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 87
comment: The Jewish court (Judengericht) of Vienna was an existing institution in 1361. On 20 July 1361 Duke Rudolf IV granted the city a series of privileges; one provision exempts the Judengericht, alongside the Hofgericht, the Stadtgericht and the Münzgericht, from the abolition of the ecclesiastical and secular courts in Vienna and its suburbs, so that it keeps its rights (Regest 992). Brugger p. 87 (n. 32): the Judengericht is a 'mixed' municipal court of Christian and Jewish assessors presided by the Jewish judge; sources for such courts are extremely rare in Austria, and this charter explicitly names the Viennese one. The regest note adds that similar privileges exist for Wiener Neustadt (no. 1006), Bruck an der Leitha (no. 1047) and Tulln (no. 1072). Evidence of a self-administering Jewish community in Vienna in 1361; the map has no Vienna row between 1350 and 1369. No population. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:58/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 2, 2010), no. 992 on PDF pp. 264-265]
Event: The Jews of Vienna appear to have suffered in the persecutions following the Black Death (1369); in 1370 they were seized, deprived of their possessions and expelled, but soon returned.

comment: On 1 September 1370 the dukes Albrecht III and Leopold III annulled the debts of their chancellor, Bishop Johann of Brixen (earlier bishop of Gurk), to "ihrem Juden David Steuss aus Wien": two promissory notes of 500 and 100 pounds of Viennese pfennig, capital and interest; the chancellor's Vienna houses and other pledges were freed of the claim (regest Nr. 1315; original Diözesanarchiv Brixen, Oberes Archiv 447, shown as Fig. 1 in Wiedl p. 70). Wiedl (p. 69) names David Steuss as the bishop's closest business partner, to whom he had pawned houses and jewellery; the regest calls him a Jew "aus Wien". It shows a leading Viennese Jewish financier still lending to the Church and protected by the dukes in 1370. The map's Vienna row of 1369 (Jewish Encyclopedia) says the Jews were seized and expelled in 1370 but soon returned; the regest does not mention that, so the two statements are not contradictory, but the owner may want to compare them. No population. Confidence high. [Source detail: (Brugger and Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 3: 1366-1386, Innsbruck 2015, Nr. 1315, p. 106)]

comment: Street-level topography of Vienna's Jewish quarter in 1373. On 23 Aug 1373 two members of the city council decided a complaint by Jakob Poll, chaplain of the Ottenheim chapel in the City Hall, against the Jew Merchlein, whose house lay 'unter den Juden zu Wien bei dem Judentürlein in der Wipplingerstraße' (among the Jews of Vienna, at the little Jews' gate in the Wipplingerstrasse): Merchlein had built a kitchen in his courtyard and a chimney so low that smoke and 'unrainer gesmach' (unclean smell) reached Jakob's house and the chapel during early mass. After an inspection the council ordered him to raise the chimney and remove the kitchen. Brugger pp. 88-89: the charter treats it as an ordinary neighbour dispute, with no religious language except the smell remark, which may echo the odor iudaicus stereotype. Merchlein is traceable since 1349 as son of Nachman from Friesach/Salzburg (Regest note); in 1351 he was already involved in a case with the same chaplain, then decided by a court of city judge and Jewish judge (Brugger p. 87). No population. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:766/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 3, 2015), no. 1421 on PDF p. 174]

comment: Event: violence against the Jews of Vienna in the 1370s, evidenced by a burnt Jewish house. In a charter of 26 April 1376 (priest Andreas von Muthmannsdorf and the Viennese burgher Berthold, for a Mass foundation) a rent charge of four pounds on a Jewish house in Vienna was worth little because the house had burnt down completely 'ze der zeit do man di juden gemainlich angegriffen het' (at the time when the Jews were universally attacked) and then fallen into ruin, so that Heinrich Huber got only 24 pounds for it (Brugger: half the usual redemption sum); the loss was proved by a document sealed by the Viennese Jewish judge. Brugger pp. 92-93: no general persecution of Vienna's Jews is known for this period, but several Christian chronicles report that the Austrian dukes seized wealthy Jews and extorted ransom in the 1370s (dated 1370, 1371 or 1377), and this charter is a rare indicator that these seizures were accompanied by massive physical violence. The regest note (Schwarz) links the attack to the dukes' capture of the Austrian Jews. Year of Data 1376 is the charter date; the attack itself was earlier (1370s, exact year uncertain). See the proposed event 1370-1371 and the conflicts file. No population. Confidence medium. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:766/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 3, 2015), no. 1493 (and nos. 1330, 1368, 1550 for the chronicle dates) on PDF p. 214]

T. Utterback and M. L. Price (eds.), Jews in Medieval Christendom: "Slay Them Not" (Brill, Leiden 2013), pp. 189-200, p. 199 n. 39 (PDF p. 14)
comment: Event: in 1383 Duke Albrecht III had the Viennese Jewish banker David Steuss arrested and held in Mödling castle until he paid a ransom of about 50,000 pounds (de.wikipedia "David Steuss", citing the Wiener Annalen: "Erst nach einer Zahlung von etwa 50 000 Pfund wurde er freigelassen"). Brugger 2013 (p. 199 with n. 39) gives the same: 50,000 pounds in 1383 to regain his freedom, as the best-known case of the dukes' practice, from the 1370s, of holding rich Jewish financiers captive until they paid large ransoms. The Wien Geschichte Wiki (Jüdische Geschichte) gives the same arrest and place but a ransom of only "1.000 Pfund Pfennig": the online sources disagree on the sum (see conflicts file); the de.wikipedia and Brugger figure is used. Named person only in Notes; no population stated. Confidence medium (amount).

comment: Event: persecutions in Styria and Carinthia in 1397 drove more than a thousand Jews to Vienna. The Wiener Annalen (printed in Regesten 4 no. 2143, dated April-September 1397) say "Do komen dew juden gen Wienn (Wien) geflochen, mer denn tausent, von Steyr und Kernden" and that the refugees promised the dukes "XVI M tl." (16,000 tl.) by Michaelmas (29 September) for securing peace, because they feared the Viennese mob; the duke and the council of Vienna then forbade any wrong against a Jew. The dukes William and Albrecht IV ordered their Landmarschall on 3 September 1397 to protect all their Jews in Vienna, Wiener Neustadt and Neunkirchen (no. 2141) and issued a new privilege on 13 December 1397 (no. 2147). The Wien Geschichte Wiki likewise says more than 1,000 Jews fled to Vienna and offered the dukes 16,000 Gulden for restoring peace. Brugger 2013 (p. 198) gives 16,000 marks, says the duke prevented violence in Vienna in return for the promise, and names Dukes Leopold IV and Wilhelm as granters of the 1397 privilege (the Regesten name Wilhelm and Albrecht IV): currency and ruler differ between the sources (see conflicts file). The refugees are not Vienna's own Jewish population, so Population is blank. Confidence high for the event, low for the sum. [Source detail: (open-access PDF https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/api/object/o:1229/download, fetched: Brugger/Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter 4, 2013), nos. 2141, 2143 and 2147 on PDF pp. 187-191]

The 'Viennese Geserah' of 1420/21 and the Forced Baptism of the Jews", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 100, 102-103
comment: Event: start of the Viennese Geserah. On 23 May 1420, on the orders of Duke Albrecht V, the Jews of Vienna and Lower Austria (de.wikipedia and JE: all Jews of Austria) were arrested and under threat of death urged to convert; some were baptised, and according to the Kleine Klosterneuburger Chronik some of those who then returned to Judaism were burnt as renegades. The poor were expelled and driven down the Danube in boats (de.wikipedia: about a month later, some sources say 21 June 1420; Keil p. 100: in September 1420 800 destitute Jews were put on rafts and left to drift downstream, received partly in Hungary and partly in Pressburg); the wealthy were kept in prison and tortured to reveal hidden treasure and to accept baptism after the Duke's return from the Hussite War (Winer gesere, Ebendorfer). Aug 1420: Hanna, widow of Peltl of Salzburg and a Viennese moneylender, still confirmed the payment of a Viennese burgher's debt on 14 Aug 1420 'during the imprisonment of the wealthy Jews of Vienna' (Keil p. 102-103 n. 23). The Winer gesere also describes a collective suicide of prisoners in the synagogue. Keil p. 100 gives the financial and political background (Hussite War costs, the Duke's wedding). The burning of 12 March 1421 is covered by other rows (Vienna 1421). The map's existing Vienna rows begin the Geserah only with 1421 (exile). No population (800 = expelled, not the community).

source: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_Gesera | https://www.jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/2152-austria | Keil, "What Happened to the 'New Christians'? The 'Viennese Geserah' of 1420/21 and the Forced Baptism of the Jews", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 101-102, 105-106, 108-109, 113
comment: Event: forced baptism of Jewish children and adults in the Viennese Geserah, and the fate of the baptised. De.wikipedia: forced baptism was ordered for children under 15, although Pope Martin V's bull Licet Iudeorum omnium (1 Jan 1421) forbade baptising children under 12 against their own or their parents' will (JE 'Austria' dates the bull Dec 1420; Keil p. 105 n. 32 cites Simonsohn no. 606, letter of 1 Jan 1421). The children were spared the burning of 12 March 1421: the abbot Martin von Leibitz (Senatorium) writes that some were given to monasteries and that two of them were later prioresses of the nunneries of Himmelpforte (St Agnes) and St Magdalena vor dem Schottentor in Vienna (Keil pp. 105-106). Keil found 28 New Christians by name in the sources (17 men, 4 women, 7 children or youths; 22 certainly baptised in the Geserah): e.g. Lea/Elspeth, daughter of the moneylender Hanna 'Peltlin', received in April 1422 the house at Wildbercherstrasse (today Wipplingerstrasse 12) that had belonged to Rabbi Meisterl, tortured in the Geserah (Keil p. 102); master Gabriel the New Christian bought a house in Aug 1422 and Nicodemus the New Christian one in Dec 1435 (p. 108); Paul of Melk, a convert, was several times rector of the university (1451, 1457, 1461, 1471; p. 109). Keil's conclusion (p. 113): the Austrian converts were neither stigmatised nor excluded and enjoyed Albrecht V's protection. The burning of the c. 200 remaining Jews on 12 March 1421 is in other agents' pending Vienna 1421 rows. No population.
The Jewish community of Vienna was exiled.

The oldest tombstone in the Rossau Cemetery (9 Seegasse Cemetery), the site of the medieval Jewish community, dates from 1450.

In 1528 Emperor Ferdinand ordered every Jew coming to Vienna to report to the government office, wear a yellow cloth ring badge and stop only at two houses set apart for Jews; a mandate of Jan. 2, 1554 ordered the Jews to leave Lower Austria within six months.

Although there technically was a ban until 1624 on new settlement, this was repeatedly circumvented through the granting of exceptions, to the point that a new cemetery was established in the Seegasse in 1582.

comment: Privilege for the Jews of Villach (a Carinthian possession of the bishops of Bamberg): the Bamberg bishops Wulfing (1304-1319) and Heinrich II (1324-1328) granted and confirmed a set of rights, listed in regest Nr. 302 under the date range [1304-1328]. The text survives only as an insert in a charter issued at Wolfsberg on 24 August 1347 by Bishop Friedrich I of Bamberg, who confirmed Wulfing's privilege (the regest notes that Villach is named only in the closing formula of the 1347 confirmation). It follows Duke Frederick II's Austrian Jewish charter of 1244 but lets the Jews lend on all pledges except bloodied, wet and pierced ones "und auf kelych und mezzgewant" (chalices and mass vestments). Wiedl (p. 62 n.27) says it was issued for the Jews of Villach and probably extended to all Bamberg possessions in Carinthia, including Wolfsberg, "the second Bamberg possession that housed a considerably large Jewish community". comment: Event: Depping (p. 317) says that in 1421 public rumour accused the rabbis of Villach of profaning hosts; the authorities seized these leaders, tortured them and condemned them to death (footnote: Archiv für Geschichte, Vienna, April 1827). The Jews of Villach lived under the protection of the bishop of Bamberg. No online source found; source is the 1834 book (secondary, old). Caution: the Jewish Encyclopedia (Styria) records that on 11 May 1421 all the Jews of Styria were thrown into prison, some died at the stake and others were expelled (Duke Albert V's persecution of 1420-21), so Depping may be transferring that event to Villach in Carinthia. Event: expulsion of the Jews from Carinthia, decreed by Emperor Maximilian I in March 1496 (decree issued at Schwäbisch-Werd): the Jews had to leave Carinthia within six months. Carinthia offered 4,000 florins (Styria 38,000) to compensate the crown for the lost Jewish revenue; the decree accused the Jews of host desecration, ritual murder and fraud. Villach, the commercial centre of Carinthia in the territory of the bishop of Bamberg, had a considerable Jewish population with a synagogue and a cemetery near the village of Judendorf. Depping (p. 317) adds that the bishop no longer dared protect them, the Jews scattered to Gorizia, Udine and Venice, their synagogue was sold to a townsman, and Hebrew gravestones were found at Judendorf (footnotes: Archiv für Geschichte, Vienna 1826-27); the charges he lists are the murder of Christian children, coin forgery, forged seals and usury. Event: host-desecration accusation, 1370, with a Jewish presence at Enghien (Hainaut). Jewish Encyclopedia (Brussels): "A banker of Enghien, distinguished by his wealth as well as by his philanthropy, was assassinated in his own garden"; the assassins spread the report that the Jews had stolen consecrated wafers to pierce them, which led to the burning of hundreds of Jews at Brussels (22 May 1370) and a general banishment; the banker's wife and son took refuge in Brussels. Depping (p. 174) says the report was that "the Jews of the town of Enghien" had had sixteen consecrated hosts taken from the church in Brussels to pierce them in their synagogues; the elders of the Enghien synagogue were tortured and three of them were burned alive on 22 May 1370 near the Namur gate at Brussels (one, Jonathas, had grown rich by speculation); all other Jews of Brabant were banished and their goods seized; eighteen paintings for Sainte-Gudule and a fifty-year jubilee commemorated it (celebrated again in July 1820). Death-toll figures differ (Depping three burned; Wikipedia "six or about twenty" killed in Brussels; JE "hundreds"): see conflicts file; no number is used here. Population blank. Brussels already has 1370 rows on the map.

source: https://ubt.opus.hbz-nrw.de/files/817/FGJA10_Cluse.pdf | Cluse, 'The Structure of Medieval Jewish Settlement in the Southern Low Countries', Jewish Studies 40 (2000), p. 51*
comment: Possible Jewish moneylenders at Gembloux (uncertain): in 1329 Duke John III granted the abbot of Gembloux jurisdiction over the collection of debts owed to Lombards and Jews by inhabitants 'of the town of Gembloux and of the appendices belonging to the abbey'. A charter of 1307 (Mont-Saint-Guibert, Dion) only reserves the duke's rights over Lombards and Jews. Cluse says a Jewish presence in or near Gembloux is not proven but made more likely by the special clause; he maps it with a question mark and counts it as an uncertain settlement among 12 in Brabant-Limburg; a Lombard loan table is attested there. Online: dissertation pp. 47-48, 50. Confidence low. Source wording: "Ob Juden in oder um Gembloux wohnten, ist damit zwar nicht bewiesen". [Source detail: (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 47, PDF p. 55)]

source: https://ubt.opus.hbz-nrw.de/files/817/FGJA10_Cluse.pdf | Cluse, 'The Structure of Medieval Jewish Settlement in the Southern Low Countries', Jewish Studies 40 (2000), p. 48*
comment: Three Jews of Genappe (Jossialle, Helyas and Manassir, 'les juys de Genape') appear in the 1257 account of the bailli of Nivelles: one paid 20 shillings for the bailli's help in recovering a debt at La Hulpe, two paid an eight-pound fine for a scuffle. Genappe (a new town of about 1200 on a ducal domain) thus had Jews much earlier than the map's first Genappe row (1308, Depping); the 1309 episode on the map is the siege of Duke John II's castle there by crusaders. Online: dissertation p. 26. Confidence high. Source wording: "werden in der Rechnung des bailli von Nivelles aus dem Jahr 1257 aufgeführt". [Source detail: (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 26, PDF p. 34)]

No online source found; source is the 1834 book (secondary, old).

Hoeniger/Stern 1888, p. 101 no. 247). Evidence by name of origin only (Cluse marks such places '(H)' and warns that by-names can be inherited or taken from house names), so a Jewish settlement at Hasselt in 1303 is probable but not certain. comment: Event: Jews of this place were among the Jews of Hainaut arrested from the first days of August 1349 and burned, probably all of them, by the end of August (the Jews of Mons on 29 August), accused of poisoning wells in the Black Death persecution; Jews were still doing business normally in June and July. [Source detail: (Cluse, Aschkenas 35/2 (2025), pp. 351-371, section 1); (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 37, PDF p. 45)]

comment: Fourth Jewish settlement of the southern Low Countries before 1250. Thomas of Cantimpre's Life of Christina Mirabilis (written c. 1232) says the saint went among the local Jews to comfort the dying and calls their Jewry very large (Cluse's 'congregatio maxima'; the Latin reads 'congregatio in urbe maxima'). Sint-Truiden belonged half to the abbey and half to the prince-bishopric of Liege, with the duke of Brabant as advocate. The map's Liege row 1250 attributes this same 'congregatio maxima' to the city of Liege (see conflicts file). Online: dissertation p. 22 with n. 62 (Latin text). Confidence medium-high (hagiographic source, written within a decade of the saint's death). Source wording: "Christina even went into the local Jewry to give consolation to the dying". [Source detail: (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 22, PDF p. 30)]

comment: By the middle of the 13th century there must have been a Jewish cemetery in the episcopal half of Sint-Truiden. Cologne records of 1270-1291 name Jews 'of the city of Trude' (Gutheil, widow of Isaac de porta of Tienen; Joseph; Nathan ha-Levi) and a Sint-Truiden court under the 'great rabbi Isaac Qiton'. With Tienen the most important community of the region and the only certain settlement under the bishop's staff. Year 1250 = 'around the middle of the century' (approximate). Online: dissertation pp. 22, 24-25, 49-50. Confidence medium. Source wording: "there must have been a Jewish cemetery in the episcopal half of the town". Cluse counts Tienen with Leuven, Sint-Truiden and Jodoigne as the four Jewish settlements of the southern Low Countries before 1250 and notes that the tombstone implies a cemetery and 'a community of some importance'. comment: In 1266 Duchess Aleydis (Adelaide of Burgundy, widow of Duke Henry III) transferred to the Franciscans of Tienen a house with barn and orchard that had formerly belonged to a (late) Jew of Tienen. The Latin deed (van Ruysevelt 1970, quoted by Cluse) says 'vendidimus' (sold), the short paper says 'donated'; Cluse reads the owner's name as Judelin ('Yodolini quondam judei') and wonders whether it is linked to the demand to expel Jewish and Lombard moneylenders in Henry III's will of 1261 (the map has the will under Antwerpen), without proof that any expulsion was carried out. A sign of Jewish households at Tienen before 1266. Online: dissertation p. 30 with n. 110. Confidence medium (presence is inferred from 'formerly a Jew's house'). Source wording: "the Duchess of Brabant donated a house and garden at Tienen which had formerly belonged to a Jew". [Source detail: (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 30, PDF p. 38)]

Event: persecution of the Jews at Tienen at the time of the crusade of 1309. The Brabant continuation of Martin of Troppau and the third continuation of the Gesta abbatum Trudonensium say that a woman had been killed by Jews at Tienen (in Clement V's fourth year, i.e. 1308/09), that the Jews bought themselves free of punishment, and that crusaders then killed Jews 'everywhere in towers and villages' in that region; Cluse thinks the ritual-murder charge was raised afterwards by the persecutors to justify the killings. Not stated in the short paper (it only names Tienen among the oldest communities); taken from the dissertation. The map's Tienen rows have no persecution. Online: dissertation pp. 39, 199, 203-204; Radboud BA thesis names Tienen among the places hit in summer 1309. Confidence medium. Source wording: "apud Thenis in Monte in Brabantia quedam mulier a Iudeis fuit miserabiliter martyrizata". [Source detail: (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 203, PDF p. 211); (Driessen, BA thesis Radboud Univ. Nijmegen 2015, p. 3)]

pt.wikipedia (Erebango): around 1910, with the railway station and the Passo Fundo-Marcelino Ramos railway link, the ethnic diversification of the village began with the arrival of Jewish, German, caboclo, Italian, Polish and Ukrainian families ('por volta de 1910'; approximate year, Jewish families not counted).

pt.wikipedia (Erechim): the region was colonised mainly by Polish (1918), German (1912), Jewish (1911) and above all Italian immigrants; the article gives only the year for the Jewish settlement (it presumably relates to the ICA colonisation near Erechim; the Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the Quatro Irmaos colony to 1912, see the Quatro Irmaos rows).

Côte Saint-Luc has a very large Jewish community, with 69.1% of residents being Jewish. Several Jewish schools operate in the city, including JPPS-Bialik, Hebrew Academy, École Maïmonide, and Yeshiva Yavne.

The city is home to five major synagogues (Beth Zion, Beth Israel Beth Aaron, Tiffereth Beth David, Beth Rambam, and Or Hahayim) as well as Jewish educational institutions (Yeshiva Yavne, Hebrew Academy, Bialik High School, and École Maimonides) and healthcare/seniors residences with Jewish affiliations (Maimonides Hospital, Mount Sinai Hospital, B'Nai Brith House, King David Residence).
Noted as one of the three neighborhoods in the Montreal area that attracts the most Russian Jewish immigrants due to its high concentration of Jews
During the 1920s, German-Jewish immigrant families began moving to the town from Montreal

Assis (p. 233, citing Devic and Vaissette, Histoire generale de Languedoc II, Preuves cc. 211-212) reports a February 839 episode: three Jews "of Provence", named Gauzios, Jacob and Vivas, appeared at the palace of Louis the Pious in Frankfurt, asked for charters to replace lost ones, and the king granted the request and confirmed their ownership of their property. Identifying his three men with the EJ's Gaudiocus and his two sons (same year, same emperor, same landholding; Gauzios resembles Gaudiocus) is MY inference, not stated by either source; the row stands on the EJ alone for the presence at Carcassonne in 839. comment: The atlas has 'Dijon' labelled on the map 'Distribution of Jews, middle of the sixth century' (that map has no separate legend, so every labelled place is read as a place with Jewish evidence). No precise year is given, so 550 is the conventional midpoint of the period (middle of the 6th century). Presence only; no population stated. No online source found: the English Wikipedia article on Dijon was fetched and gives no statement of a Jewish presence for this period.
JE: About 1160 the scholars of Dijon took part in the synod of Troyes.

First explicit evidence of Jews: Duke Eudes III placed the Jews of Dijon under the jurisdiction of the commune and authorised it to admit more Jews (1196; Jewish Encyclopedia also records Jews of Fenay given to the town); ducal charters of 1197 and 1232 confirmed the commune's authority. Jewish Encyclopedia says Jews lived there 'from time immemorial'.

Jewish quarters: Rue de la Petite-Juiverie (today Rue Piron, with synagogue and Sabbath house), Rue de la Grande-Juiverie (Rue Charrue) and Rue des Juifs (Rue Buffon); cemetery on today's Rue Berlier.
Moneylending: Duke Eudes III ceded revenues to the Jewish creditor Valin (1204); loans to abbeys by Bandit ben Benion (1216) and Salamine (1223); Hugues IV annulled a debt to Dedone (1228).

JE: A Jew of Dijon, Bandit, the son of Benion, was the creditor of Philippe, Abbot St. Loup of Troyes, in 1216; another Jew, Salamine, made important loans to the abbeys of Sainte-Bénigne and Sainte-Seine in 1223, for which, however, Duchess Alix of Vergy, widow of Eudes III., made him sign a bill of release.
JE: Eudes III. annulled a debt due to the Jew Jessuel (1217), and Hugues IV. another, due to Dedone, "Judæus meus" (1228).
Scholars: a rabbi of Dijon (1250), R. Simhah Hazzan (1260), R. Jacob; about 50 13th-century Jewish tombstones were found in the cemetery between 1885 and 1900 (now in the Musee archeologique).

Event: expulsion of the Jews from France (1306); the Dijon Jewish cemetery was confiscated. Neighbouring Baigneux-les-Juifs shows the Burgundy communities were numerous and prosperous, but no Dijon count is given.
Return: some Jews came back to Dijon in 1315; a new expulsion under Philip V followed in 1321.

JE: In 1320 the cemetery was on the route to Beaune, in a place called "Les Baraques de Gevrey." Philip the Bold, in consideration of the sum of one franc in gold per capita, authorized the Jews of Dijon to own a cemetery close to the city (1373).
JE: In 1331 Duke Eudes IV. presented to the abbey of Bussière a part of this cemetery, valued at 400 livres, an enormous sum for that time.
After readmission of the Jews to the kingdom (1359) a more important community was re-established in Dijon.

Philip the Bold allowed the Jews of Dijon a cemetery near the city for one gold franc per person (1373; Les Baraques de Gevrey); in 1374 twelve Jewish families were allowed to settle in the duchy (regional figure, not Dijon).
JE: At the request of David Lévy and Joseph of St. Mihiel, Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, permitted twelve Jewish families to settle in his duchy in 1374.

Population: ten Jewish families settled at Dijon in 1379 (Jewish Encyclopedia); households x 5, source count 10 families. In 1382-84 fifty-two families were licensed for the whole of Burgundy and in 1387 only fifteen lived in Burgundy (regional, not used).

JE: The states of Burgundy demanded the expulsion of the Jews (1382-1384); but as the latter had lent to the duke 3,000 livres for the continuation of the war in Flanders, they were authorized to remain.

Gauthier (Léon), Les Juifs dans les deux Bourgognes, Revue des études juives 48 (1904), p. 227: 'En 1377, elle [la colonie juive de Dijon] était de 6 ménages; en 1378, de 10; en 1382, de 12, outre 3 ménages à Seurre'. Households x5. (The 1377 figure, 6 households, is within two years of the map's 1379 row and is in MWB_conflicts.csv.)

Gauthier, REJ 48 (1904), p. 228: 'En 1386-1387, la Bourgogne compte 13 ménages juifs : 9 à Dijon, 4 à Chalon' (duke's census of Jewish households paying 12 francs each; Year of Data 1386 = start of the fiscal year 1386-87). Households x5.
JE: In 1387 only fifteen families were living in Burgundy.
Gauthier, REJ 48 (1904), pp. 228-229: 'En 1388-1389, 9 [ménages]: 6 à Dijon, 3 à Chalon' (fiscal year 1388-89; the same count of 6 for Dijon in 1387-88, 1389-90 and 1390-91). Households x5.

Gauthier, REJ 48 (1904), p. 229: 'En 1392-1393, 15 ménages : 10 à Dijon, 4 à Chalon, 1 à Beaune'; the next year, 1393-94, 14 households (10 at Dijon, 3 at Chalon, 1 at Beaune), 'la dernière année où le cens ducal de 12 francs par ménage est soldé' before the expulsion of 1394. Households x5.

JE: Notwithstanding the exile of 1397, there were still some Jews at Dijon after that time: Solomon of Balme was living there as late as 1417.

IV) and the 1274 parliament act. Depping gives no footnote for the 1302 confirmation; the year was read from the scan. comment: Earliest Hebrew mention of Paris. In a responsum of Rashi to Yaqir ben Makhir of Orleans(?), dated only "fin XIe siecle" (Rashi died 1105), two Jews who have a dispute apply to the rabbinical court of Orleans; they meet in Paris, "ou n'apparait alors aucune autorite juive" (Nahon p. 258). So there were Jews in Paris at the end of the 11th century but no Jewish court there yet. Year of Data 1095 is a convention for "end of the 11th century". Online corroboration is only partial: the abstract of Pinchas Roth (Tsafon 90, 2025) says Rashi's responsum 241 concerns a dispute between two Jews in 11th-century Orleans and shows "important Jewish ties between medieval Orleans and Paris"; it does not mention the Paris meeting or date it. The map has Paris rows from 582 and from 1119 but none for the 11th century. No population. Confidence low-medium (date approximate). [Source detail: (partial online corroboration only: the abstract confirms Orleans-Paris ties; no online page found for the Paris detail; source is a scholarly volume)]

Jewish quarter (vicus Judaeorum) on the Ile de la Cite documented from 1119 at the latest; synagogue c. 8 x 31 m on today's Marche aux Fleurs site; Jews also on Rue de la Harpe and Rue de la Vieille Juiverie in the 10th-11th c.

Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 258
comment: The rabbinate of Paris is first formally attested c. 1125: the masters of Paris sent a consultation to the rabbis of Rome about an internal conflict, a newcomer to Paris who refused to submit to a Parisian taqqana of the herem ha-yishuv type restricting the settlement of strangers in the city; according to the Parisians it applied in Ile-de-France, Burgundy, Lorraine and Normandy. The Roman signatories (named by Nahon: Abraham-Ezra ben Mattathias and Menahem ben Judah) criticised the form and substance of the request (Nahon p. 258). Online: Encyclopaedia Judaica "Paris": "Rabbinical questions were addressed to the scholars of Paris from Rome around 1125"; Jewish Encyclopedia "Paris": a responsum of the sages of Rome to the sages of Paris, "dated at the beginning of the twelfth century". Nahon says "vers 1120"; the online c. 1125 is used (see conflicts file). The map has Paris 1119 (Jewish quarter) and c. 1145 (Troyes synod) rows but nothing on the rabbinate in between. No population stated. Confidence high for the fact, medium for the exact year.

Paris rabbis took part in the synod convened by Rashbam and Jacob Tam (c. 1145); a yeshivah headed by Mattathias Gaon and tosafists Yom Tov and Hayyim ha-Kohen are active in the 12th c.; Benjamin of Tudela calls Paris 'that great city'.

Benjamin of Tudela, Sefer ha-Massa'ot (Itinerary), c.1165: traveller names the place "Paris"; Adler translation, text marker [p.112]. Traveller's words: scholars 'unequalled in the whole world' and Jews hospitable to brethren; no number. Identification: Paris. No count given; Population left blank (presence only). Year 1165 = c.1165 (Benjamin travelled c.1165-1173).

Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), pp. 259, 263
comment: Event: after the Blois blood libel and burning of 1171 the leaders (qetzinim) of the Paris community went to the palace of Louis VII, who greeted them first and gave them sealed letters of protection against similar accusations. A letter of the Paris qetzinim describing the Blois tragedy, the audience and the royal guarantee survives (London, Jews' College MS Montefiore 28 = IHMM 4699, fol. 163; ed. Habermann 1946, p. 146) (Nahon pp. 259, 263). Online: Encyclopaedia Judaica "Paris": Louis VII, "in answer to the intervention of the leaders of the Paris community", promised that no similar accusation would arise and that no persecution would result. The Blois burning itself is already on the map (Blois 1171). No population. Confidence high.
JE: "In 1179 the Parisian Jews were accused of having murdered at Easter a Christian named "William." Banished by Philip Augustus."

Event: Philip Augustus imprisoned the Jews on a Sabbath and demanded 15,000 silver marks (c. 1180), then banished them in spring 1181 (Jewish Encyclopedia) or April 1182 (Rigord, Fordham; Encyclopaedia Judaica); the crown seized real estate and kept one-fifth of debts, four-fifths annulled.
JE: "In the spring of 1181 he banished them all, confiscated their lands and dwellings, and annulled four-fifths of their claims against the Christians, exacting the remainder for himself."

Event: the main synagogue (Rue de la Juiverie) was given to Archbishop Maurice and became Sainte-Madeleine-en-la-Cite; 24 houses went to the drapers and 18 to the furriers (Encyclopaedia Judaica), 24 houses leased to the cloth-makers' guild for 100 livres a year (Jewish Encyclopedia).
Event: Philip Augustus, short of money, readmitted the Jews; they repaired the Rue de la Tacherie synagogue and opened another in the Tour du Pot-au-Diable.

Nahon reads it as a synagogue inscription cut at the return of the Jews to Paris after the readmission of 1198, perhaps commissioned by Judah ben Isaac (Sire Leon) (Nahon p. 271, n. 64, Fig. 21). Year of Data 1199 (4960 AM runs from autumn 1199 to autumn 1200). The map has the 1198 readmission and synagogue repairs (Rue de la Tacherie, Tour du Pot-au-Diable) but no dated epigraphic evidence of that period. No population. Confidence medium.

comment: Judah ben Isaac "Sire Leon" re-established the rabbinical centre of Paris, which had disappeared in the expulsion of 1182-1198; with the lessons of Isaac ben Samuel of Dampierre he compiled the first collection of tosafot on the Babylonian Talmud, the basis of the Paris school, and Paris again attracted French and foreign pupils, among them Isaac ben Moses of Vienna (author of Or Zarua) (Nahon pp. 266-267). Online: Encyclopaedia Judaica "Paris": Judah b. Isaac "headed the yeshivah of Paris in the early years of the 13th century"; Jewish Encyclopedia "Paris": "About 1198 he was appointed head of the Talmudic school of Paris". Year of Data 1200 follows Nahon and EJ (JE says c. 1198; see conflicts file); it is a different fact from the existing 1198 readmission row. Named persons only in Notes; no population. Confidence high for the fact, medium for the exact year.

JE: "In 1212 the chevalier Etienne de Sancerre pawned all his property to the Jew Elijah de Braie of Paris and his son Merote as security for the sum of 80 livres which he had borrowed from them, and for which he was obliged to pay two deniers per livre each week as interest."
JE: "In 1217 Philip presented the grain-market in the Juiverie to his cupbearer Rinaldo."

JE: "In order that he might extort from them greater sums of money, the king permitted them to charge a high rate of interest, which, however, was subjected to certain restrictions by a decree issued in the year 1218."
JE: "(1223-26) the Jews were again molested."
Event: Talmud disputation (25 June 1240) between Nicholas Donin and four rabbis led by Jehiel b. Joseph; seized Hebrew books (24 cart-loads per Encyclopaedia Judaica) were burned afterwards.
In 1243, Louis ordered, at the urging of Pope Gregory IX, the burning in Paris of some 12,000 manuscript copies of the Talmud and other Jewish works.

It shows an organised system of schools and an active Jewish burial ground in Paris in 1247. Online context only (not this stone): Sonia Fellous (IRHT-CNRS) says Paris has the largest corpus of medieval French Hebrew epitaphs, 24 dated ones from 1139-1140 to 1364. The map has no Paris row for 1247. No population. Confidence medium.
JE: "But on his return from a crusade in 1254 he renewed his hostile attitude toward the Talmud and toward usury."
JE: "As an outcome many Jews received severe punishments, and in 1257 all the landed property they held, excepting cemeteries and synagogues, was confiscated by the king."
Event: Louis IX decree of 12 June 1269 requiring Jews to wear a badge; in 1257 he had confiscated Jewish landed property except cemeteries and synagogues.

comment: Event: the second Disputation of Paris, on the messiahship of Jesus, in which Paulus Christiani (Pablo Christiani) argued for the Christian side against Rabbi Abraham ben Samuel (Nahon: "of Radom"; the identification as "of Rouen" is contradicted by the royal officers' remark that most of the masters of the Law of France and Champagne had come at the king's order). The unfinished Hebrew report survives only in Moscow, MS Gunzburg 1390, published by J. Shatzmiller, La deuxieme controverse de Paris (1994); the debate was held in Latin and the rabbis knew Latin (Nahon p. 269). Nahon dates it c. 1272; the online page found (PredMed, Universitat Pompeu Fabra) dates it 1269 and the online year is used (see conflicts file). The existing map row for Paris 1269 is the badge decree of 12 June 1269, a different event. No population. Confidence low-medium (year disputed).
JE: "In 1271 the council of St.-Quentin reproached him for allowing Jews to sue Christians for debt in a court of justice."

Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 271 and Fig. 20
comment: Funerary stele of Rabbi Solomon son of Rabbi Juda, who died in 1281: the only stele from the medieval Jewish cemetery of the Paris Left Bank (excavated in 1849 under the Hachette bookshop, rue Pierre-Sarrazin) that survived completely intact; his title marks him as one of the spiritual leaders of the Paris Jewish community in the second half of the 13th century, and the cemetery was closed in 1306 after the expulsion (mahJ key work page). Nahon (p. 271) asks whether this otherwise unknown master succeeded Yehiel at the head of the school. The map has Paris rows for 1271 and 1283 but none for 1281. Named person only in Notes; no population. Confidence high.

comment: Under Philip III the Bold the Jews of Paris bought a garden from a canon, Maître Gilbert, to serve as a new cemetery, and the king approved the purchase; Depping cites a royal confirmation charter of 1283 (Trésor des Chartes, J 427 no. 13). Gallia Judaica (Gross) and the Jewish Encyclopedia (Paris) record the same cemetery purchase under Philip III but give no year, and Gross cites Depping for it; the year 1283 comes only from Depping's footnote, so the date is medium confidence. [Source detail: (Gallia Judaica, art. Paris: fact, no year); (fact, no year)]
JE: "In 1288 he subjected the Jews of Paris to a fine for chanting too loudly in their synagogues."
Event: the moneylender Jonathas was accused of host desecration and burned, his house razed; the Encyclopaedia Judaica calls this a main cause of the 1306 expulsion.
Population = households x 5: Paris tax rolls of 1292 and 1296 list at least 100 Jewish heads of families (Encyclopaedia Judaica); the count is a minimum.

Loeb, Le rôle des Juifs de Paris en 1296 et 1297, Revue des études juives 1 (1880), pp. 70-71: 'Le rôle de 1292 compte 121 personnes, celui de 1296 n'en compte que 85' (persons named in the tax rolls); Loeb, REJ 14 (1887), p. 170: 'la population juive, en 1296 et 1297, se composait, en tout, de 82 chefs de famille'. Households x5 (85 names in the 1296 roll). The 1292 figure (121 names, about 605) differs from the map's 500 and is in MWB_conflicts.csv.
JE: "About the year 1299 he imposed upon them a tax of 244 livres and 12 sous, Tours currency, called the "recepta" (revenue), and 50 livres for exemption from the wearing of the badge."

comment: Event: a Pentateuch copied by Abraham ben Jacob, with a colophon dated 7 March 1303 (Paris, BnF MS Hebreu 44, fol. 166v), is one of the three Hebrew manuscripts Nahon links to Paris; it shows Jewish scribal activity in Paris three years before the expulsion of 1306 (Nahon p. 270, Fig. 15). The BnF catalogue description found online (Torah, Haftarot, Megillot, with Latin glosses) does not give the date or the Paris attribution. The map has Paris rows for 1299 and 1306 but none for 1303. No population. Confidence medium.
Event: expulsion decree of 22 July 1306 by Philip the Fair; all Jewish property seized; Rue de la Tacherie synagogue given to the king's coachman in Dec. 1307.

Event: Louis X recalled the Jews and restored synagogues and cemeteries; numbers afterwards stayed close to the pre-1306 level (Encyclopaedia Judaica). In 1321 well-poisoning accusations led to burnings and expulsion; 5,300 of the 100,000 livres levied on French Jews in 1320 came from Paris.
JE: "In 1320 Philip V., the Tall (1316-1322), imposed a tax of 100,000 livres upon the Jews of his kingdom, and of this amount 5,300 livres were payable by the Jews of Paris."
JE: "In 1321 the accusation of poisoning the wells was made."
New Paris community formed in 1359 (Manessier de Vesoul, Jacob of Pont-Sainte-Maxence); Mattathias b. Joseph chief rabbi of France and head of the yeshivah 1360-1385.
JE: "In 1360 Manecier de Vesoul entered into negotiations for the return of the exiles to France."
JE: "The Jews were for a time harassed by the king's agent, who threatened to procure their expulsion from the city (1370); but Charles V. (1364-80) ordered that they should be left in peace."
Event: mob attacked and looted c. 40 Jewish houses in 1380 and children were baptized; renewed violence in the Maillotin uprising of 1381 (1382 in Encyclopaedia Judaica).
JE: "Shortly after, the insurrection of the Maillotins (1381) broke out, and the Jews again suffered severely."

comment: Event: Abraham of Bagnols, imprisoned in Paris c. 1390, copied the Sefer Mitzvot Qatan ('Amude Gola) of Isaac of Corbeil (New York, Jewish Theological Seminary MS Mich 8227 = IHMM 13.406, fol. 287a) (Nahon pp. 270-271, Fig. 17). Evidence of Jews, including one from the south of France, held in Paris in the last years before the final expulsion of 1394; "c. 1390" is Nahon's date. The map has Paris rows for 1381 and 1394 but none for 1390. Named person only in Notes; no population. Confidence low-medium.

Event: Denis Machault affair; seven notables condemned, commuted to a fine of 10,000 livres; Charles VI expelled the Jews from France and they left Paris on 3 Nov. 1394; Encyclopaedia Judaica finds no evidence of Jews in Paris in the 15th c.
Year rounded from a century-only statement. JE: "It was not until about 1500 that the presence of Jews in Paris is again noticed."
JE: "It was Francis I. also who founded a chair in Hebrew at the Collège de France (1538), and it was during his reign that Hebrew typography produced its most remarkable works."
A tiny enclave of about 500 Jewish émigrés emerged in Paris in the early 18th century
At the close of the Revolution, about 3,000 Jews lived in Paris
A letter from the minister of the interior to the emperor noted 2,543 Jews living in the capital, with more than 150 serving in the army
The Consistory of Paris was appointed and installed, consisting of 2,733 Jewish members

Event: Dreyfus affair: on 22 December 1894 seven judges of a Paris court-martial unanimously convicted Captain Alfred Dreyfus of treason and sentenced him to permanent exile in a fortification, cancellation of rank and military degradation; he was sent to Devil's Island. Retried at Rennes in 1899, exonerated in 1906.
Jews numbered about 375,000 (8 percent of the total Paris population) gathered throughout Paris and its environs
In July 1942, the French Police organized the 'Raffle du Vel d'Hiv' round-up, temporarily confining Paris Jews; more than 13,000 were arrested, including 4,000 children
An estimated 535,000 Jews lived in France, with about one half (267,500) thereof in Greater Paris

Jews already present in Périgueux in the 13th century: royal order of Philip IV (1301) to the seneschal of Périgord to expel the Jews (and other usurers) from the jurisdiction of the mayor and consuls of Périgueux, at the request of the consuls (BnF Fonds Périgord T. 72 f. 214, cited by F. Viey). No earlier dated document found; presence also shown by the rue Judaïque / ancienne juiverie behind the Musée du Périgord.

Event: expulsion of the Jews from Périgueux 1301 (JGuide Europe gives 1302; Viey cites the 1301 order). Five years before the general expulsion from the kingdom of France in 1306. No population figure in the sources.
'Jewish presence seems to date back at least to the 13th century, since Jews were expelled in 1302'; former Jewish quarter (juiverie, rue Judaique) behind the Musee du Perigord; no count
The current community formed in 1939-1940 from the large community of Strasbourg evacuated to the Dordogne in 1939 (no count)
In December 1940, Rabbin Elie Cyper was named deputy to the rabbi of Périgueux, Victor Marx, who was overwhelmed by the influx of 12,000 Jewish refugees relocated in Dordogne.

Event: the Jews of Pontoise accused of the ritual murder of the child Richard (Gross: 1179; EJ: close of the 12th c.); the body was taken to Paris and venerated.

Jews of Pontoise appear in the tax accounts of 1202; in 1204 an established community with a Christian provost of the Jews (praepositus Judaeorum Robert de Baan); in April 1296 Philip IV gave the Jew Joce of Pontoise and his children to Charles of Valois.

JE: "A document of 1294 relates that the abbé of Saint Denis bought a house at Pontoise belonging to a Christian heavily indebted to the Jews there, who were paid the purchase-money through the provost Robert de Baan."
JE: "In 1296 Philip the Fair made a gift to his brother Charles, Count of Valois, of Joce or Joucet, a Jew of Pontoise, and his children, David, Aroin, Haginot, Beleuce, Hanée, and Sarin."

JE: "In the same year Joucet of Pontoise was appointed financial agent between the crown and his coreligionists of Amiens, Senlis, and Champagne, and in 1297 Philip the Fair made him arbiter in a litigation which had arisen between himself and his brother Charles regarding forty-three Jews whom the latter claimed as natives either of his county of Alençon or of his lands in Bonmoulins and Chateauneuf-en-Thymerais."

comment: A Jewish street (vicus judeorum) is named at Provins in 1172 (Benner/Reverchon, Juden, p. 199 ff.). This is earlier than the "earliest evidence" of 1201 given by the Encyclopaedia Judaica and used by the existing map row (see conflicts). No population given. No online source found for 1172.

Early 13th century: the yeshivah of Provins was led by Jacob b. Meir, author of a lost biblical commentary (sometimes wrongly attributed to Jacob of Provence); Jewish Encyclopedia also names Meir ben Elijah and Isaac Cohen (in Paris 1217). Joseph the Zealot's polemic describes the importance of the Jewish market.

Earliest dated evidence of Jews in Provins is 1201 (Encyclopaedia Judaica entry by Blumenkranz, citing Gross Gallia Judaica, Bourquelot 1840, Veissiere 1961). Jews concentrated in Rue de la Vieille-Juiverie and Rue des Juifs and rapidly increased in number.

At least two synagogues and a cemetery are attributed to the community (Encyclopaedia Judaica); a special seal was used to ratify business documents involving Jews. A hall with ogive vaults in a modern house on Rue des Juifs is by local tradition the remains of a medieval synagogue (tradition only; undated).
