comment: The Jews of Provins have their own cemetery, first attested in 1264 (the Jews of the western Champagne had earlier been buried at Provins in the sphere of the archbishops of Sens, which suggests they originally belonged to the Sens kahal). Encyclopaedia Judaica mentions a cemetery and at least two synagogues without dates. No population given. No online source found for 1264.

JE: "In 1298 or 1299 Hagin, a Jewish resident of the town, was commissioned to deposit in the hands of the royal officials the proceeds of the taxes paid by his coreligionists of the bailiwick of Troyes."

Hagin, a Provins Jew, was commissioned in 1298 or 1299 to hand over to royal officials the tax paid by the Jews of the Troyes bailiwick (Jewish Encyclopedia); a Jewish tax-collection role under the Crown after Champagne passed to the king (1286).

1301: two sons of Simon the Jew sold half a plot in the Jewish quarter of Provins above the Porte Neuve for 21 livres Tours, next to an estate of the Jew Hagin Dalie; attests a distinct Jewish quarter.
Event: Provins declined after passing from Champagne to royal authority under Philip the Fair, and the Jewish community disappeared entirely after the expulsion of 1306 (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

1313: a clerk sold a house for 400 livres Tours formerly of the Jews Josson de Coulommiers and his son Croissant, adjoining the chateau enclosure and surrounding the Jewish school (Jewish Encyclopedia) - evidence of the former Jewish school after the expulsion.

Event: Some Jews were found in Champagne between 1315 and 1321 (readmission period) but do not appear to have returned after 1359 except converts (JVL Champagne article; regional statement, not specific to Provins).
Future rabbi Roger Kahn was born in Provins to a Jewish family of at least six (parents and four children), though the source notes there was no organized Jewish community at the time.

comment: Event: Jews of Reims, on their way to the Troyes fair, were plundered and taken prisoner (incident of 1015). The same incident gives the first hints of Jewish communities in the cathedral cities of Troyes, Sens, Auxerre and perhaps Châlons-en-Champagne. Burgard/Reverchon also mention an uncertain report that Abbot Fulrad of St. Vaast, expelled from his monastery in 1004, traded with Jews. The existing rows c. 1020 for Sens and Châlons (Toch, responsum of Joseph Tov Elem) may rest on the same early-11th-century Hebrew source (not stated by Burgard/Reverchon). The Encyclopaedia Judaica Rheims entry says Jews are first recorded at Reims only in 1077 (see conflicts). No online source found for 1015. No victim count.

No online source found; Encyclopaedia Judaica only says the cemetery lay at the junction of the roads to Châlons and Cernay.

comment: Resettlement after the expulsions of 1306/1322: from about 1356 Jews were admitted again in France. Reims became one of the few settlement centres (with Provins) of the temporary readmission 1356-1394 and the seat of a new regional organisation: its cemetery served the northern Champagne and parts of Picardy, taking over the functions of the old communities of Laon, Châlons etc. Some of the returning Jews had fled from the Romance parts of Lorraine; the readmission ended with the definitive expulsion of 1394. On Nov. 25, 1347 Charles IV for 60 marks in silver granted the Jews letters of protection and confirmed their former rights.
In November and December, neighboring towns reported confessions under torture accusing Jews, including Cantor Jacob of the Strasbourg synagogue, of poisoning wells.

Joseph the Younger, and Jacob b. Joseph; no dates given. Jewish Guide to Europe calls the medieval presence fleeting, often banned from settling.

A few Jews already before the end of the 13th c.; synagogue in the Grande-Rue; the banker Heliot (c. 1300) headed the Jews of the province; two commercial account books of the 14th c. were written at Vesoul (Gross). (century-only date, round year used.)

In 1315 Heliot, a banker of Vesoul, was one of the Jewish syndics who negotiated the return of the Jews expelled from France by Philip the Fair; in 1321 Philip V gave the estate of Heliot and his son Vivant to Queen Jeanne.
Names in documents indicate at least 15 families living there in 1332 (households x5, estimate based on families, a lower bound).
In 1342 Michelet, a Jew of Vesoul, furnished the King of France with a subsidy of 187 livres.

Event: at the Black Death the duke ordered the Jews arrested; 80 Jews (some from neighbouring places) imprisoned; condemned to banishment 27 Jan 1349; Manessier de Vesoul negotiated the return of the Jews to France in 1359.

Gauthier, REJ 49 (1904), p. 9: at Vesoul the arrests and seizures of 31 Oct 1348 were made 'chez Simon, Rubinine, Habrelin, Menessier, Mullequenet, Léaul (garde de la Synagogue), Éliet le Borgne, Éliot neveu de dame Lie, Mossel le Cellerier, Bienvenue, dame Lie, Banditet, Haronnin, Haquemant' = 14 named heads of household; the prison at Vesoul held 80 persons from 2 Nov 1348 (Jews from Apremont, Chariez, Fondremand, Gray, Jussey, Montbozon, Port-sur-Saône and Vesoul), so those 80 are not Vesoul's own. fr.wikipedia 'Histoire des Juifs à Vesoul' says the community 'comptait 86 personnes' in 1348, which looks like a confusion with the 86 families of the whole county in 1332-33 (REJ 7 p. 32); not used.

In 1360 Manecier (Menessier), a Jew of Vesoul, induced Charles V to permit the Jews to return to France; in 1384 Philip the Bold authorized fifty-two Jewish families to settle in Burgundy (duchy-wide, not Vesoul only); Hacquin of Vesoul was physician to Duke John the Fearless 1410-1419.

Richard, Deux lettres). Konrad II made Vic the cemetery of the bishopric at the very beginning of his settlement campaign. The Jews who came were often immigrants from France who had to flee in 1394. French Wikipedia confirms that Konrad II Bayer de Boppard favoured Jewish settlement at Vic-sur-Seille and Marsal and that his successor Georges de Bade confirmed it. No population given.

Jewish colony first mentioned in 1248 (Jewish Encyclopedia); Alemannia Judaica says Jews lived in the town at the latest in the 13th century under the protection of the Archbishop of Cologne (town rights 1248). Check coordinates: the point matches Ahrweiler old town; the existing kehilot.csv rows are filed under Bad Neuenahr-Ahrweiler.

Jews of Ahrweiler owned property in Cologne in the 1250s and 1260s (Jewish Encyclopedia); the Encyclopaedia Judaica speaks of a considerable community in the 13th century whose members owned houses in Cologne.
JE: In 1255 and 1262 a number of Jews of Ahrweiler acquired property at Cologne; some of them are referred to as living at Bacharach at the beginning of the fourteenth century.
A 'Judengasse' (today Niederhutstrasse) is first mentioned in a charter of 1290; Cologne records name Joseph von Ahrweiler the Younger (1291-1322) and Samuel von Ahrweiler (1318-1326).

Jews of Ahrweiler first named in the town itself; Archbishop Walram of Cologne granted them the right to trade in meat and livestock (salt and wine trade followed in the 14th century); Jews held settlement permission and protection against payment from the archbishop.

Population: households x 5. Local history (KuLaDig, LVR) states the number of Jewish families rose 'from 3 to 14' during the period of the archbishop's protection after 1335 (undated, before 1348); 14 families x 5 = 70. Date of the count is not given, 1335 is the start of the period.

JE: In the Palatinate records are to be found in addition: Simon, son of Vifanz (= Ḥayyim), 1346; Hanne (in Bacharach), 1367, widow of the preceding; to which may be added Baruch ben Simon, physician, poet, and glossarist (flourished in the fifteenth century). Ḥayyim Treves, son of Johanan Treves who wrote a commentary upon the Maḥzor and who succeeded Ruben Fulda in the rabbinate of Cologne, died at Ahrweiler in 1598.
Event: community destroyed in the Black Death persecutions of 1348/49 (Alemannia Judaica; Jewish Encyclopedia says it suffered greatly; no number of victims given).
Jews again documented as moneylenders in Ahrweiler in 1364; Alemannia Judaica reports Jews living in the town again 1367/70.

c. 1400: a courtyard 'in der Judengassen' is mentioned; a mikveh on the Ahr is evidenced (undated, rent paid to a Christian owner); the medieval synagogue cannot be proven, a prayer room existed at least temporarily; no expulsion is recorded.

Early 15th century (c. 1400-1425): Rabbi Isaak named as head of the Jewish court; Jewish Encyclopedia: Isaac of Ahrweiler wrote a Pentateuch commentary; community nearly destroyed again by soldiers from Brabant and Holland in the early 1400s (Jewish Encyclopedia, undated).
JE: Of its rabbis, a certain Isaac of Ahrweiler addressed ritual questions to Jacob Mölin of Worms (d. 1427), and wrote a commentary on the Pentateuch.

15th century: physician and Bible commentator Baruch ben Samson ('Meister Bendel') lived in Ahrweiler (Encyclopaedia Judaica); Frommet copied a legal work for her husband Samuel ben Moses in 1454 (Jewish Encyclopedia).

JE: In Ahrweiler was also Rabbi Issachar, whose daughter Frommet, that wife of Rabbi Samuel ben Moses, was so learned that she copied Samuel Schlettstadt's "ḳiẓẓur Mordecai," in 1454, for her husband.

A 'Juden Schul' first mentioned in 1427 (nothing more known; probably used as a residence after the 1391 expulsion). No Jewish settlement in the town afterwards; Pinkas says Jews were allowed back to the Alzey district in 1491 and the 1550 census lists none in Alzey.
Although there were Jews living in Alzey in the 16th century, an organized community was not established until about 1700. (century-only date, round year 1550 used)

Event: arrest and torture. In early 1556, shortly before Elector Frederick II of the Palatinate died at Alzey on 26 February 1556, the Heidelberg Jewish physician Lazarus appeared at his deathbed and proposed to the court preacher Ottmar Stab to pay off the heir Ottheinrich and hand the government to the elector's widow for two years instead. Back in Heidelberg he was arrested for this apparently treasonable plan and then tortured at Alzey ("wurde Lazarus wegen dieses hochverräterisch erscheinenden Plans verhaftet und anschließend in Alzey gefoltert") until he denounced some innocent Worms Jews as fellow conspirators ("einige unschuldige Wormser Juden als Mitverschwörer"). By his own account his motive was the fear that under Ottheinrich the Jewry would no longer be tolerated but expelled. One Jew arrested and tortured; the number of Worms Jews denounced and their fate are not stated (Mentgen, citing Weech 1873, pp. 236-279 (242f), and Hundsnurscher 1996, pp. 42f). No online source found (web searches for Lazarus, Ottmar Stab and Ottheinrich found nothing on it). The map has only a century-only (1550) Alzey row.

Late Roman Augusta Vindelicum (Raetia): fragment of an oil lamp with a seven-branched menorah, found in 1960 on the Gallusplatz near the Roman forum area; the Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte (HdBG) calls it the oldest depiction of a Jewish symbol in Bavaria ('Es trägt das Zeichen der siebenarmigen Menora') but adds that interpretation stays difficult because the lamp form is so widespread. DATING DIFFERS between the online pages: Ristow (APuZ 2021) 'late 3rd or early 4th century' (used here; 300 is the central value), jguideeurope.org '4th century', HdBG '5th century'. WEAK ITEM: one lamp can be a trade good and the menorah also occurs on Christian objects. Ristow also mentions a late antique building under the Gallus chapel with wall-painting fragments (probably Joseph before Potiphar) that cannot be classed as church or synagogue (not written as a row). JE: In 1349 the bishop again received Jews into the city, but six years later transferred to the city council both the duty of protecting them and the privilege of taxing them.

JE: In 1364 the council of Augsburg acquired possession of them.
JE: The emperor demanded 10,000 gulden (1 gulden = 41½ cents) from the Jews of Augsburg in 1373; and the council vainly sought to protect them from this amercement.

JE: In 1514 Erhard Oeglin printed the Decalogue and several parts of the New Testament in Boeschenstein's "Elementale Introductorium in Hebræas Literas," which is embellished with an elaborate border, falsely ascribed to Hans Holbein.

JE: Actual printing in Hebrew was practised by the traveling printer Ḥayyim Schwarz, who in 1533 completed the Megillot and Rashi's Commentary on the Pentateuch as the first printed production in Augsburg.

JE: On Jan. 19, 1534, the Passover Haggadah was completed; and in the same year there was published at Augsburg by an anonymous author a guide to correspondence which became very popular during the seventeenth century.

Estimate based on families. On 11 July 1586, a family Hertz paid 20 for a short stay in the city.

Jewish population rose to 653 in 1880.
Jewish population was 793 in 1900.
The synagogue on Turnerstrasse, which was established in 1905 and had 750 seats, was set alight (capacity used as presence metric).
On 20 September 1905, the synagogue was inaugurated for 800 Jews.
In 1925, in the Weimar period, the Jewish population reached a peak of 883.
Some 800 Jews lived in Bielefeld, Germany. [Also reported by: https://www.memorialmuseums.org/memorialmuseum/bielefeld-memorial?locale=en]
Jewish population was 860.
In October 1938, approximately ten Jews of eastern European origin were evicted from Bielefeld as part of the expulsion to Zbaszyn.
On November 12, the National Socialists deported 406 Jews - of whom 40 to 50 came from Bielefeld - from the Bielefeld main station to the Buchenwald concentration camp.
On 28-29 Oct. 1938, at least 11-13 Jews of East European origin were expelled.
The community started a Jewish school for 17 Jewish students in September 1939.
In the fall of 1941, some 500 Jews lived in Bielefeld, about 100 of them married to Christians.
The first deportation from Bielefeld took place on December 13, 1941: About 420 Jews from the area of Bielefeld were deported on that day.
On 13 December 1941, 88 Jews from Bielefeld disguised as 'deportation' were taken to Riga.
In fall 1941, 400 Jews were left in the city in addition to another 100 in mixed marriages.
By July 1942, 160 additional Jews had been deported from Bielefeld to ghettos and camps.
45 Jews were deported to the Warsaw ghetto or to the Lublin district (Poland) on 31 March 1942.
84 Jews were deported to Auschwitz on 2 March 1943 (including about 63 from the forced labor camp).
Subsequently another 20 were deported in small groups and on 19 September 1944, 30-40 Jews in mixed marriages were deported to Zeitz and Elben.
About 420 Jews were deported from Bielefeld overall. Only a few more than 60 survived.
At least 509 Jews perished in the Holocaust.
In the 1980s, about 30 Jews remained.

Traveller's words: listed among cities 'which have Hebrew congregations' (no number). Identification: Bingen am Rhein. No count given; Population left blank (presence only). Year 1165 = c.1165 (Benjamin travelled c.1165-1173).
Event: The Christian burghers attacked the small Jewish quarter on the Jewish New Year's Day of 1198 or 1199, and its inhabitants were then driven from the city.
Jews are again found in Bingen as moneylenders in the middle of the 13th century under the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Mainz. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)
JE: In May, 1254, Bingen joined the union of Rhenish cities which, for financial reasons, protected the Jews.
In 1343 French Jews settled in Bingen.
JE: But this favorable condition of things was soon changed, for at the time of the Black Death (1348-49) the Jews of Bingen, in common with the other Jews in Germany, suffered severe persecutions.

comment: Event: resettlement after the Black Death. Alemannia Judaica: the pogroms of 1348/49 destroyed the community and "Seit 1354 werden wieder jüdische Familien genannt" (since 1354 Jewish families are named again); in the following decades at least six to nine Jewish families lived in the town. Barzen's note 24 dates the resettlement of Bingen to 1357 ("Bingen, Sobernheim 1357"); the online page is earlier, so 1354 is used and the difference is listed in the conflicts file. Population blank (the 6-9 families are a range over decades). Confidence: medium.
In 1405, however, the archbishop declared a moratorium on one-fifth of the debts owed to Jews by Christians, and subsequently the archbishops repeatedly extorted large sums.
JE: In the first half of the fifteenth century a rabbinical synod assembled there. [Century-only date ('first half of the fifteenth century'): Year of Data set to a round year (1450).]
Event: The Jews were again expelled from Bingen in 1507, and did not return until the second half of the 16th century.

Event: in 1509 King Maximilian I authorised the confiscation of Hebrew books throughout Germany; the Jewish Encyclopedia lists Bingen among the places where confiscations were held (with Frankfurt, Worms, Lorch, Laufen, Mayence and Deutz). No count of books for Bingen. Book p. 270, ref 1509.2 names Frankfurt, Mainz, Bingen and other cities.

Burgaltendorf (south-eastern borough of Essen, on the Ruhr, east of the Rhine frontier): a fragment of a non-ferrous metal plate of c. 200 CE, found with other Roman-period objects of the 2nd-4th century, bears a graffito 'probably' read IVDAIIA (Ristow, APuZ 2021: 'Ein Graffito auf dem Tellerfragment ist wahrscheinlich als IVDAIIA zu lesen'). Ristow: a Jewish woman could have been the owner of the plate, or the word could point to origin from the province of Judaea (which also had non-Jewish inhabitants), so no closer conclusion is possible; the date c. 200 is the age of the object, the graffito may be later. VERY WEAK ITEM (uncertain reading, uncertain meaning). No population. comment: Estimate of the Jewish population of Cologne in the phase c. 1135-1170: about 290 persons (Cuno: 'ca. 290 Personen'). Method (Cuno, n. 11): 'Geschätzt nach den von Juden besessenen Häusern bei Ansetzung von pro Haus nur zwei Familien und einer Familiengröße von nur fünf Personen' (estimated from the houses owned by Jews, counting only two families per house and only five persons per family). The start year 1135 is the opening of the Cologne Schreinsbuch records of Jewish property (the Cologne archaeological-zone page says the Judenschreinsbuch was set up around 1135). The same lecture gives about 480 persons for 1170-1235, 500 for 1235-1300, 600 for 1300-1325 and 700 for 1325-1341 (the last phase is not written as a row because the map already has about 800 around 1340; see conflicts). Other online statements are higher or differ in kind and are not for the same years: the Cologne archaeological-zone page says the community 'comprised 800 -1000 members' in its heyday (no year), and the JVL text (Encyclopaedia Judaica) says the number killed in 1096 'indicates a community of approximately 1,000'. Cuno's house-count figures are conservative estimates. No online source found for Cuno's phase figures; the lecture is the only source. Confidence medium.

Event: Jews, who had lived in Dinkelsbühl only sporadically in the High Middle Ages (free imperial city since 1274), were driven out in the Franconian Rintfleisch persecution of 1298; Memorbuch entries suggest Dinkelsbühl Jews among the victims (indirect evidence).

Event: Jews expelled or killed in the Black Death persecution of 1348/49 (Pestzeitverfolgung); the Memorbuch indirectly points to Dinkelsbühl victims.
Emperor Charles IV granted the city on 2 March 1372 the right to hold, admit, protect and shield Jews; resettlement began in 1376 and is certain from 1384 (Alemannia Judaica).

Charles IV granted the Dinkelsbühl Jews four years of tax exemption in thanks for their financial support; the privilege was extended by ten years in 1376, with half of the protection money going to the imperial treasury.

Dinkelsbühl Jews are mentioned in the Archbishopric of Mainz in 1384 and in Zurich in 1385, later in Nuremberg (1398, 1407); the Jews lived chiefly from moneylending and the city and king disputed the Judensteuer until the early 15th century.

Event: in 1384/85 the city forcibly seized the Jews' bonds and pledges; many Jews fled and placed themselves under the protection of the Counts of Oettingen; by 1390 the community appears to have dissolved completely (Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte).

JE: Capital of the circle of the same name, in the district of Arnsberg and the Prussian province of Westphalia, situated on the Emster. That there were Jews in Dortmund in the middle of the twelfth century is shown by the fact that several Jews living at Cologne at that time were designated as natives of Dortmund (compare Höninger, "Das Judenschreinbuch der Laurenzpfarre zu Köln," p. 9). [Century-only date ('middle of the twelfth century'): Year of Data set to a round year (1150).]
The Jews paid a contribution of 15 marks to the imperial treasury from 1241 to 1250.
JE: A letter of protection was granted to the Jews of the city in 1250 by Archbishop Conrad of Cologne, Dortmund having been pledged to him in 1248 by King William of Holland.
JE: About 1250 the municipality issued regulations concerning the form and ceremonial to be observed in administering an oath to Jews ( see Oath).

By 1257 the community had a Magistratus Judaeorum, a rabbi (clericus or papen), a cantor, sho?et, and a Schulklopfer, and possessed a synagogue, a communal center, a cemetery, and a mikveh, for which ground rent had to be paid.
JE: The jurisdiction of the Archbishop of Cologne over the Dortmund Jews was confirmed by Albrecht I. in 1298.
JE: Like many other German communities, that of Dortmund was wiped out in 1349, at the time of the Black Death.
Event: In the Black Death period the Jews were expelled from Dortmund (1350); the Judenturm ("Jews' Tower") was built with the spoils seized from them.

Alemannia Judaica: "Während der Judenverfolgung in der Pestzeit 1348/49 wurden auch in Eichstätt Juden verfolgt"; on 12 November 1349 Bishop Albrecht pardoned the riot of the mob against the Jews of Eichstätt, "deren etliche erschlagen wurden" (some of whom were killed; some Christians were also hurt), which had happened against the will of the respectable burghers. JE: Town in the province of Hanover, Prussia. That Jews lived there at a very early date is shown by the fact that some Einbeck Jews were burned at the stake in 1298.
Judenstraße ('in der Joden straten') named in a deed of 6 June 1355; street named after a medieval synagogue (Judenschule) on the site; dating from property deeds
JE: An old and mutilated tombstone still exists to record the interment of a Jewess in the year 5160 (= 1400).

JE: It appears from an assignment of Duke Erich of Brunswick to his wife Ilse (Elizabeth), dated July 14, 1405, and from a letter of Duke Philipp to his brother Ernst, dated 1562, that the Jews of Einbeck paid a yearly tax which formed part of the revenues of the castle of Grubenhagen.
An "old" Jewish cemetery is referred to in 1454.
Judenschule (synagogue) in the Judenstraße referred to as 'yoddenschole' in a 1467 deed (earlier deeds 1355 and 1394 also refer to it)

JE: When the dukes Wolfgang and Philipp of Grubenhagen forbade all Jews not under their protection to pass through the principality, the envoys of the "Gemeine Jüdischheit" petitioned Emperor Maximilian (Feb. 25, 1570), who annulled their decree.

JE: A few years later, in 1579, when the fanatic Magister Johann Velius, pastor of the Jacobior Marktkirche at Einbeck, raised a storm of public feeling against the Jews of the town, the latter were expelled.

First known Jew by name, Jechiel ben Jakob, author of synagogal poetry (c. 1235); Alemannia Judaica English text gives 1241 as earliest evidence; community probably arose in the late 12th century, Jewish settlement in the Judengasse (today Karlstrasse) possibly under Landgrave Hermann I (1190-1217).
The Eisenach city law of 1283 contains provisions concerning Jewish residents. A scholar Samuel ben Jakob corresponded with Meir of Rothenburg (13th century).
Event: Part of the Judengasse burned down (1342 per German Wikipedia, 1343 per Alemannia Judaica). A medieval synagogue probably stood at Karlstrasse 23.

Event: Persecution of Jews during the plague (1348-49); Alemannia Judaica (English text) says all or most Jews were driven out. Jews resettled for some decades afterwards, probably around the Loebersgasse.

A Jew is documented in Eisenach again in 1378 after the 1349 pogrom (second half of the 14th century: resettlement for some decades; 10 Jewish taxpayers in 1418); the Wettin expulsions begun in 1430 (exact date for Eisenach unknown) ended this settlement. [Schulz paper p. 7; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 94]
Event: Jews expelled from Eisenach and other Thuringian towns in 1411 or later (German text of Alemannia Judaica); the English text gives 1458 as permanent expulsion. Sources conflict.

Taxpayers read as households x5 (weak): Schwierz, Zeugnisse jüdischer Vergangenheit in Thüringen (Landeszentrale für politische Bildung Thüringen, 2007), PDF page 94-95: 'Erst 1378 wird in Eisenach wieder ein Jude genannt. 1418 lebten ... zehn jüdische Steuerzahler in Eisenach' (the number is split by a page break; the Reichssteuer list of 1418). The community had been destroyed in the pogrom of 25 February 1349.
Jews permitted to trade in Eisenach for several years but not to settle.

The first 'Schutzjude' (protected Jew) of modern times is documented in 1752; in 1804 the first Jew received citizenship (the Alemannia page names the court factor Michael Rothschild, 1804). After 1850 many Jews moved to Eisenach from the villages (Geisa, Gehaus, Herleshausen, Stadtlengsfeld). [Schulz paper p. 7; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 95]

The Jewish community of Eisenach was founded in 1862 or 1864 (both years are given; 'at the beginning of the 1860s' per Alemannia Judaica); 72 persons belonged to it in 1864. Provisional prayer room (Jakobsplan 19) and first teacher in 1864, religious school 1865, cemetery plot granted in February 1867 (first burial June 1868; before that burials at Herleshausen). [Schulz paper p. 7; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 95]

The date carries a question mark in the source and no further detail is given there. Victims are not a population count. The LIST (p. 137, ref 1100.2) copies the same list item.
In 1209 the king also relinquished his right to collect taxes from the Jews, which in 1212 was explicitly granted to the archbishop.

Otto IV's letter assigns the Jewish protection money (Judenschutzgeld) of Erfurt to the Archbishop of Mainz; de.wikipedia calls this the first secure date for Jews in Erfurt, and Jewish Virtual Library notes the king gave up the Jewish tax right in 1209 and the archbishop was explicitly granted it in 1212.
Persecution of the Jews at Erfurt in 1215; persecutions continued with greater bitterness under Archbishop Rupert.

Event: pogrom of 26 June 1221 by Frisian crusader pilgrims; synagogue burned. Victim counts differ: 26 (Alemannia Judaica), 21 to 26 (de.wikipedia, he.wikipedia), about 26 or 86 in some sources with 21 named in the Mainz Memorbuch (Jewish Encyclopedia). Victim count only; the community survived and grew.

JE: When the Jews protested, the bishop decided (July 20, 1240) in favor of the prior; but the Jews, upheld doubtless by the municipal council, persisted in their refusal to pay, and the matter was finally submitted to arbitration.

Event: 13 January 1266 Archbishop Werner of Mainz granted the Jews a letter of protection for 100 silver marks a year plus 30 pfennigs per burial (Jewish Encyclopedia); Alemannia Judaica records the same year a plundering of Jewish houses and the synagogue.

New synagogue (the Old Synagogue's west facade with rose window dated to 1270, Alemannia Judaica); de.wikipedia and he.wikipedia say the building is first mentioned in 1287 and its oldest parts go back to the 11th century (c. 1094 in the UNESCO listing). Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel probably lived in Erfurt 1286-1293 (Jewish Virtual Library).

Victim counts differ: about 100 (Alemannia Judaica, de.wikipedia; 'over 100' in Jewish Virtual Library and encyclopedia.com), up to 900 (City of Erfurt Jewish heritage site; a 2011 article cited by Alemannia Judaica), about 3,000 in August 1348 (Jewish Encyclopedia, with 800 silver marks to the council). JE: As the old synagogue had passed into private ownership, the council granted (1357) a certain sum for the erection of a new one.
JE: In 1373 it issued a series of ordinances concerning the Jews, who were required to wear throughout the year long gowns, boots, and hats.

Cemetery land near St. Andreas rented for 5 shillings a year and cemetery expanded (Jewish Encyclopedia, Alemannia Judaica); tax agreement set the community's annual payment at 850 pounds of pfennigs (Jewish Encyclopedia). Ordinances of 1373 set up five parnasim and a rabbi (Jewish Encyclopedia).
JE: Thus, in 1377 they paid for this purpose 100 pounds of pfennigs.

households x 5: Jewish Encyclopedia reports that in 1380 the council required a list of 76 families paying their own dues and 26 whose dues were paid by others (102 families); also that year the council extracted 2,200 silver marks and barred Jews from employing Christian servants. The 5x multiplier is the brief's convention, not the source's.

Taxpayers read as households x5 (weak): Schwierz, Zeugnisse jüdischer Vergangenheit in Thüringen (Landeszentrale für politische Bildung Thüringen, 2007), PDF page 106: '1389 lebten 89 steuerzahlende erwachsene Juden und 25 nicht Steuerzahlende Arme in Erfurt'. 89 taxpaying adults x5 = 445 (the 25 poor non-taxpayers come on top); compare Alemannia Judaica 'about 350 members' for 1398 and the map's 76 families for 1380.

JE: The history of the Jews of Erfurt from the end of the fourteenth century to 1458, in which year they were banished from the city, records a long series of sufferings of various kinds. [Century-only date ('end of the fourteenth century'): Year of Data set to a round year (1390).]

Rabbinical synod held in Erfurt in 1391 (Alemannia Judaica; Jewish Encyclopedia says 1399, de.wikipedia says an assembly 1416-1421). Same year King Wenceslaus cancelled Christian debts owed to Jews and handed them to the town for 2,000 gulden (Jewish Virtual Library).
Alemannia Judaica: about 350 members of the community in 1398; the underlying document is not named on the page.
JE: In 1399 many rabbis gathered there for a synod and settled various ritual questions.

1414 council charter authorized a mikveh attendant (man and woman); 1436 the council confirmed the community's property rights to synagogue, mikveh, cemetery and the Tanzhaus; Jews withdrawn from protection 1453, none left by summer 1454
JE: Thus Sigismund in 1416 imposed upon the Jews of Erfurt the payment of 6,000 gulden, estimating this sum to be a third of the value of their possessions.
In 1418 they were compelled to declare the amount of their property on oath, in the synagogue, and the king collected new taxes from them on this basis.
JE: In 1438 Sigismund pledged the Erfurt Jews to the knight Matthes Schlick, Burgrave of Eger, for the sum of 1,000 Rhenish gulden.
JE: In 1442 they were again compelled to pay 6,000 gulden as a coronation gift to Friedrich III.

Jacob Weil (from Weil der Stadt) served as rabbi 1443-1453 (Alemannia Judaica; he.wikipedia says from c. 1443). Yom Tov Lipmann Muelhausen headed a yeshiva from c. 1413 (he.wikipedia). In 1436 the council confirmed the community's rights to synagogue, mikveh, cemetery and dance house (de.wikipedia).

JE: The latter complained to the emperor, who severely remonstrated with the council; but his remonstrances remained unheeded, and in 1450 the council succeeded in obtaining from Elector Dietrich of Mayence, in return for the payment of 450 silver marks and 4,000 gold gulden, permission to banish the Jews from the city.

Event: expulsion. The council withdrew protection in 1453 (Jewish Virtual Library, City of Erfurt site, Alemannia Judaica); no Jews remained in summer 1454, the synagogue became an armoury and the cemetery was razed; an agreement with the Archbishop of Mainz of 1457/58 sealed the exclusion (Alemannia Judaica, de.wikipedia, he.wikipedia). Jewish Encyclopedia gives 1450 or 1458, aish.com 1450.
JE: In 1454 John Capistrano visited Erfurt, and excited the mob to violence against the Jews.
JE: The history of the Jews of Erfurt from the end of the fourteenth century to 1458, in which year they were banished from the city, records a long series of sufferings of various kinds.

After the 1453/54 expulsion a single Jew obtained an exceptional permit to live in Erfurt in 1768 (an attempt of 1608 to resettle had failed); Alemannia Judaica: between 1768 and 1789 four Jews could stay for a longer time. [Schulz paper pp. 8-9; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 107]

David Salomon Unger became in 1810 the first Jewish citizen of Erfurt after the Middle Ages; he and his family founded the 'new' community (prayer room from 1806, cemetery at the Brühler Tor from 1811, over 300 Jews by 1823). [Schulz paper pp. 8-9; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 107]

Earliest documented Jew: on 10 Aug 1274 'Michahel Judeus de Fuhtewanch' lodged a complaint in the Achtbuch of the Rothenburg ob der Tauber Landgericht after being forcibly deprived of his property (Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte). Alemannia Judaica and German Wikipedia only say 'second half of the 13th century'; Alemannia's book reference dates the community from 1274.

Jews from Feuchtwangen are attested in the first half of the 14th century in business relations with Jews elsewhere; after 1340 the moneylenders Wolflin of Bamberg and Selmlin of Eggolsheim are recorded in the town (Alemannia Judaica, citing Germania Judaica II,1 p. 235 and III,1 p. 340). No synagogue, mikveh or cemetery is documented for the Middle Ages.

Event: Black Death persecution of 1348/49 ended Jewish life in Feuchtwangen; Jews of the town were murdered (Alemannia Judaica citing Germania Judaica; Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte: abrupt end). No victim count given. The sources do not tie Feuchtwangen to the 1298 Rintfleisch or 1336-38 Armleder persecutions.

Jews tolerated in Feuchtwangen again from 1414 (more than half a century after 1349) under the Nuremberg burgraves / Brandenburg-Ansbach margraves who held the town (pledged to them by Charles IV in 1376). Only the Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte gives the year 1414; not confirmed against a primary document.

A Feuchtwangen Jew was buried in Nördlingen in 1447, the only medieval burial mention (no Jewish cemetery in Feuchtwangen itself documented). The first expulsion edicts come only in the 16th century (1555), outside the range.

Event: in 1411 the territorial lord had the Jews of Freiberg arrested and expelled from the country because of usury; their property was divided between the lord and the town.
Shortly after the city's founding, Jews appeared in Freiburg as traders.
Jews were already living in Freiburg in the 13th century.
First mention of Jews in Freiburg or surrounding area.
First indication of Jews settled in Freiburg; there was a place of worship in Wasserstraße.
In 1300 the counts of Freiburg ratified the ancient rights of Freiburg Jewry.

From as early as 1310, the Counts of Freiburg had acquired the lucrative Schutzjude from the Emperor, but the taxes paid were not enough for them, meaning that Count Konrad II had amassed 400 silver marks in debts in 1326.
Synagogue documented at Weberstraße 6 in 1328; the late-medieval Jewish ghetto lay around Wasserstraße and Weberstraße; Counts acquired the Judenregal in 1310
Privilege of protection issued for 80 to 100 people granting tax exemption.
Mention of a synagogue on Weberstraße/Wasserstraße.
Eradication of the first Israelite community; members burned on Jan 30. Only the 12 richest Jews, pregnant women, and children were spared.
At the height of the plague epidemic, almost all the Jews of Freiburg were burned alive.
Emperor Charles iv permitted the counts to resettle Jews in Freiburg in 1359.
New settlement of Jews.
The city accepted the Jewish doctor Gutleben and his sons from Colmar with their families.

A synagogue was mentioned at Weberstraße/Raustraße; 60 Jewish inhabitants were counted, including a Jewish schoolmaster [Also reported by: https://historicgermany.travel/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Jewish-Themed-City-Map-Freiburg.pdf]
Duke Leopold of Austria forced all Jews to wear special clothes.
Jews arrested and subsequently expelled from Freiburg.
Right to reside and trade licence granted for individual Jews.
Expulsion of the Jews from Freiburg by King Sigismund.
Jews were finally expelled from the city.
The merchants in particular wanted to keep the banning of the Jews in Freiburg, which had existed since 1425 and confirmed in 1809, in fear of competition.
Settlement ban; Freiburg citizens forbidden to deal with Jews.
Between 1700 and 1732, army suppliers Oppenheimer and Sintzonheim opened branch offices in the city.
Tolerance edict granted free settlement in the cities.
First conferral of a doctorate for a Jew (Semion Hochheimer) at the University of Freiburg.
Jews were granted free access to Freiburg and temporary residence.
Opening of a Jewish guesthouse providing kosher food.
Composer Felix Mendelssohn lodged at the Hotel Zähringer Hof.
20 Jews now lived in Freiburg.
Cities given the right to issue naturalisation permits.
General law on equality of Jews in Baden.
Founding of the liberal Israelite religious community.
New Jewish community was officially founded.
Estimate based on families. 35 Jewish families reported to have a synagogue with organ accompaniment for Shabbat and holidays
By 1869/1870, the community built its own synagogue in Moorish-Byzantine style.
Inauguration of the synagogue on the ramparts; Jewish cemetery set up on Elsässer Straße.
A class room was provided for Israeli religious education at the primary school.
Private bank Elias Mayer established.
Contains selected records of the Jewish community of Freiburg im Breisgau from 1880 to 1942.
Israelite women's association was integrated in the municipal welfare work.
Breisgauer Loge B'nai B'rith order established (ran until 1937).
Setting up of an Israeli orphan fund and loan association.
Gustav and Dr. Robert Weil foundation for tuberculosis sufferers established (1885-1886); Dr. Adolf Lewin became rabbi (served until 1910).
Reading circle established under the chairmanship of D. J. Dukas.
Association for the promotion of crafts and workers health insurance association established.
Dr. Max Daniel Lasker founded Bad Rebhaus Sanatorium.
Mendelssohn Association established with chairman Samuel Nelson.
Dr. Max Eschelbacher became rabbi (served until 1912).
Max Mayer served on city council (until 1933); Lotte Bernstein and Ida Cohn were headmistresses of the Jewish girls school (until 1935).
Dr. Julius Zimels became rabbi (served until 1936).
Gift from Jewish property broker Jakob Nelson to the city.
Jewish population estimated at around 1000 to 1500.
36 Freiburg Jews fell in the First World War (1914-1918).
Founding of the Jewish agricultural association Pflug and the Reich Federation of Jewish Front Soldiers RjF.
About 1,400 Jews lived in Freiburg out of a total population of 90,000 (mid-1920s)
Highest number of Jewish inhabitants reached with 1,399 persons
Hannah Arendt lived in Freiburg as a student (1925-1926); Jewish football group established; synagogue expanded (1925-1926).
Three Jewish students (Werner Hamburger, Joseph Epstein, and Max Meyer) attended the Realgymnasium.
Start of National Socialist propaganda and boycott against Jewish businesses.
More than 1,100 Jews lived in Freiburg
1,138 Jewish persons lived in Freiburg; at the university there were 6 full and 7 associate Jewish professors, plus 8 Jewish private lecturers
Nuremberg Race Laws enacted.
Dr. Siegfried Scheuermann became rabbi (served until 1939).
Nov 9-10: Destruction of the synagogue; 52 Jewish men arrested and deported to Dachau. Julius Friedberger died in Dachau.
Nov 10: Synagogue set on fire by SA and SS; 140 Jewish men arrested and sent to Dachau.
On October 22, almost all of the 350 or so Jewish children, women and men still living in Freiburg were deported to Gurs
Oct 22-23: 450 Jews deported to Gurs; 71 people remained behind. Siblings Robert, Else, and Martha Liefmann and Friedrich Bloch deported.
At least 314 Freiburg Jews were murdered in the Holocaust (1942/1943)
Deportation to Theresienstadt began; Lotte Bernstein deported to Lublin.
10 Freiburg Jews who lived in 'Mischehen' (miscegenations) survived the persecution in their homeland
Return of 5 Jews to Freiburg. First Jewish worship service held. Israelite State Community South Baden founded.
10 Freiburg Jews in mixed marriages survived in the homeland; only 5 native Freiburg Jews returned after the war.
Community space set up at Hansjakobstraße 8.
Jewish lawyer Robert Grumbach became an honorary citizen.
Jewish community reached a settlement with the city regarding the synagogue land and cemetery.
Community moved to Holbeinstraße 25 and set up a prayer room.
Commemorative plaque put up at the site of the old synagogue.
A round bronze plaque was inaugurated on the site of the destroyed synagogue.
Laying of the foundations for the new synagogue.
A new synagogue was built near the Freiburg Minster.
Inauguration of the new synagogue.
First Jewish immigrants arrived from the USSR.
The square was renamed Platz der Alten Synagoge (Square of the Old Synagogue).
Founding of the liberal Jewish community Gescher.
Laying of stumbling blocks to remember the victims of the Nazi regime.
Lienhart bakery began supplying kosher bread.
Opening of the Jewish day care centre Shalom.
A water-filled basin memorial was opened on the square.
Since December 2020, a bronze model of the former synagogue complements the memorial.
Jewish religious community has over 730 members; liberal community Gescher has around 50 members.

The Flagellant movement caused Jewish persecutions in Görlitz, Glatz and Ober-Glogau in 1347; the Jews of Görlitz were later expelled by Duke John and their synagogue became the Chapel of the Holy Body.
Event: The persecutions in the wake of the Black Death brought the community to an end in 1349, but it was reestablished in 1364.
The Black Death reached Görlitz; the Jewish community was dissolved, Jews were scapegoated, and the synagogue, cemetery, and bath were seized.
Jews were expelled due to the plague.
Jews began returning to Görlitz around 1383, seeking refuge from persecution elsewhere.
Jewish scribe Shalom Sachs wrote a finely written Pentateuch with Rashi's commentary.
Following false accusations, the community was imprisoned, their homes seized, property confiscated, and they were expelled.
A final decree formally expelled all Jews from Görlitz; the synagogue was ordered to be converted into a chapel.
Emperor Sigismund permitted the resettlement of a few Jewish families, but the city declined to act on it.
Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel of Prague (the Maharal) visited Görlitz to discuss the Jewish calendar.
The Jewish community was founded.
A new foundation for the Jewish community was laid; the legal basis for synagogue communities was clarified.
The first burial took place following the reestablishment of the community.
The Jewish Cemetery in Görlitz was created by the Jewish community.
A provisional community board had been formed with Moritz Wieruszowski, Henschel, and Berliner.
The first burial took place at the Jewish cemetery.
The first official synagogue of the modern Görlitz community was inaugurated on 20 September 1853.
A statute formally defined the responsibilities of the synagogue community.
Rabbi Dr. Siegfried Freund became both the spiritual and organizational head of the revitalized community.
The Jewish cemetery was expanded.
Adolph Totschek founded the Totschek Department Store, a prominent Jewish business in Görlitz.
Görlitz abolished the discriminatory Judeneid (Jewish oath); a contract was negotiated for major renovations and expansion of the synagogue.
The newly refurbished synagogue was inaugurated on 23 January 1870; a construction fund for a new synagogue was established.

comment: Event: resettlement after the Black Death, date from Barzen only. His note 24 gives "Heidelberg, Mainz, Rüdesheim 1356". Barzen (p. 72) describes the post-plague Heidelberg community as the Jewish centre of the Palatinate with cemetery, synagogue and mikveh: "Der Kahal Heidelberg wurde zum Zentrum eines vom Landesherrn klar definierten jüdischen Steuerbezirks"; it ended with the expulsion of 1390. The map has Heidelberg 1357 (Encyclopaedia Judaica: a well-organized community functioning again at the latest in 1357), which is consistent. No online page found for 1356 (a search found only that Elector Rupert I settled Jews after 1348/49 and a 1360 protection agreement). Population blank. Confidence: medium.

Its development was halted abruptly, however, through the expulsion by elector Rupert ii in 1391 of all the Jews in his domain, including those of Heidelberg.

Jewish presence after the expulsion of 1390 (Mentgen, introduction): although Ruprecht II had expelled all Jews from his territory in 1390, Elector Frederick II of the Palatinate had time-limited protection letters (Schutzbriefe) issued in 1549 for a whole series of Jews, and the Jewish physician Lazarus (said to have served the King of France among others) was resident in the residence city of Heidelberg "spätestens seit 1553" (at the latest from 1553); for his arrest in 1556 see the Alzey row. Mentgen's sources: Weech 1873, pp. 242f, and Hundsnurscher 1996, Die Heidelberger Juden 1500 bis 1648, pp. 42f. Number not stated (one physician named). No online source found; the Jewish Encyclopedia (Heidelberg) says "Jews are not mentioned again at Heidelberg until the middle of the seventeenth century", which Mentgen's account contradicts (listed in the conflicts file). The archbishop of Mainz permitted four to five Jewish families to settle in the Eichsfeld in 1796, against the resistance of the magistrate of Heiligenstadt (a Jew who got a settlement permit in 1541 never used it). [Schulz paper pp. 10-11; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 147]

Six Jews lived in Heiligenstadt in January 1803 (of 2,796 inhabitants); 52 in 1818, 76 in 1850, 91 in 1871 and over 100 at the 1882 peak (already on the map). [Schulz paper pp. 10-11; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 147]

On 25 October 1817 the magistrate confirmed the site of the Jewish cemetery 'on the small old meadow below the Iberg' where a Jewish child was buried that year. [Schulz paper pp. 10-11; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 147]

First documentary mention of Jews in Hildburghausen: in 1331 Count Berthold of Henneberg gave the town the revenues from the Jews living there (the town received town rights in 1324). [Schulz paper pp. 11-12; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 156]

Event: Jews attacked on account of the Black Death, 1348-49 (date range; no exact year given for this town). The town is named in the Jewish Encyclopedia list of all towns where Jews were attacked on account of the Black Death, taken from the Nuremberg Memorbuch (same list in The LIST p.206-208, ref 1348.2); the list gives no death toll or other detail. Shows a Jewish community here in the mid-14th century. [Merge note: the source gives only the range 1348-49; dated 1349, the year of most Black Death attacks in the Empire.]

The Jew Gutkind lived in Hildburghausen between 1388 and 1412 in his own house, carried his own seal and granted large loans (financier of the counts of Henneberg); more Jews moved in 1423-1425 and lived partly in a 'Judenhaus'; in 1420 a weekly bathing day for Jews was set up in the municipal bath house. [Schulz paper pp. 11-12; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 156]
Estimate based on families. Four Jewish families likely moved from the Franconian region between 1423 and 1425.

Event: the Jews living in Hildburghausen were probably affected by the expulsions from the Wettin territories that began in 1430/36 (the German original says 'dürften betroffen worden sein'); the Judengraben at Wallrabs (1461) probably marks the oldest Jewish burial place. [Schulz paper pp. 11-12; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 157]

In 1714 the duke appointed a Jew court factor (Hoffaktor); 12 families of protected Jews lived in the town in 1726. Schulz says 1740; the German original gives 1714. Despite repeated expulsions (e.g. 1729 and 1743 from the residence town) an independent Jewish community developed. [Schulz paper pp. 11-12; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 157]

JE: the council admitted (Aug. 9, 1450) some Jewish families into the town for six years.
Event: all Jews were exiled from the diocese in 1457; the administrator Bernhard bound himself (March 29, 1457) not to tolerate Jews in the see of Hildesheim.
JE: at the time of the chapter feud in 1520 a Jew called 'der grosse Michel' was admitted to the city on account of his skill as a warrior.
Event: the other Jews were exiled once again in 1542 (Leifmann was allowed to remain).
JE: Elector Ernst II of Cologne, Bishop of Hildesheim, promised protection to the Jews on Nov. 29, 1585 (his Jewish physician Medicus Herz); the council also afforded protection (1587).
Event: the Jews were again driven out of the city in 1595 after Nathan Schay and Marcus married their deceased wives' sisters and the head pastor Hesshusius declared the marriages incestuous.

comment: In 1332 Count Walram of Sponheim, deeply indebted to Jews of the Trier archbishopric, pledged the small town of Kirchberg to Archbishop Balduin; "Daraufhin ließen sich in Kirchberg auch finanzkräftige trierische Juden nieder" (Haverkamp). Alemannia Judaica also says "Auch 1332 werden Juden in Kirchberg genannt". Burgard (2002) lists Kirchberg (1332) among the places acquired by purchase or pledge partly through debts to Trier Jews and says Balduin settled hereditary Jews (erbeigene Juden) there, shown by the feudal-court case against Count Walram (undated). His table (no. 24) gives 1287 (M) as the first evidence, which is already on the map.

Event: Jews killed at Kirchberg in the Armleder wave. Alemannia Judaica dates it 1337: Jews were killed, "Graf Walram von Sponheim hatte gemeinsame Sache mit den die Gegend heimsuchenden" the "Judenschläger" to be rid of his debts to Jewish creditors. Haverkamp dates the same crime 1338: Walram "ließ 1338 gezielt die Kirchberger Juden des Trierer Erzbischofs ermorden" while ordering that his own Jews be spared. Burgard's companion text (Balduin biography, p. 45) says only "in den dreißiger Jahren": the count had his own Jews led away and the Trier Jews killed and their goods confiscated. No victim count. Year 1337 follows Alemannia Judaica; sources differ by one year (1337/1338).

comment: Alemannia Judaica: the Wildgraf of Kyrburg took three Jews into his lands with the permission of King Albrecht in 1301, and "1330 bat Wildgraf Johann um eine Erhöhung der Zahl auf 15 Juden beziehungsweise jüdische Familien" (in 1330 he asked to raise the number to 15 Jews or Jewish families, which the Emperor allowed); six Jews had been killed at Kirn on 21 September 1287 (Nuremberg Memorbuch martyrology); the plague persecution of 1348/49 destroyed Jewish life. Barzen (p. 71, note 54) mentions a Jewish burial place at Kirn dated before 1350 and reads it as the burial of some persecution victims of the plague rather than a sign of a communal institution: "Eher ist bei diesen Orten an überlieferte Beispiele von Begräbnissen einiger Verfolgungsopfer aus der" Zeit der Pest zu denken. The map has only the Black Death row (1349) for Kirn. Population blank (15 is a permitted ceiling, not a count). Confidence: high.

comment: Jews with Romance (French-type) names are attested at Koblenz in 1330, the first of the dated cases in Barzen's note 42 (Koblenz is also first in the list of places in note 41). Barzen links Jews with Romance (French-type) names, which appear more often in the Middle Rhine towns from the 1330s, to immigrants after the expulsions from the kingdom of France of 1306 and 1322: "Seit den 1330er Jahren tauchten Juden mit franzöischen Namen oder" (sic, as printed). Note 42 gives the first dated cases: "1330 in Koblenz, 1333 in der Herrschaft Sayn, 1338 in Mainz, 1344 in Kaiserslautern, 1349 in Worms". No online page found (the Alemannia Judaica Koblenz page has nothing for 1330). The map has Koblenz rows for 1322, 1334, 1337 but none for 1330. Population blank. Confidence: medium (scholarly, single source).
JE: In 1334 the "Judenschläger" (Jew-beaters) attacked the Jews in Coblenz; in 1349 they suffered under the Flagellants, who killed almost all of them.
Event: The Jews were persecuted again in 1337, and most severely during the Black Death in 1348–49.

comment: Event: resettlement after the Black Death. Alemannia Judaica: the persecution of 1348/49 destroyed the community, then "1351 wurde wieder eine jüdische Familie in der Stadt aufgenommen" (in 1351 one Jewish family was taken in again); more families followed and a community smaller than before the persecutions formed, with 13 Jewish-inhabited houses in the Judengasse in 1351-1418. Barzen's note 24 lists the resettlement dates of the Middle Rhine places after the plague and begins with "Koblenz 1351". Population blank (one family at first). Confidence: high.
JE: The records show that from 1352 the houses of the Jews were frequently subject to confiscation and sale for the benefit of the reigning prince.
JE: The emperor Charles IV. ordered, in 1354, that a certain Jew named Samuel receive protection.
JE: In 1356 he granted Archbishop Boemund II. of Treves the right for Jews to settle in his district; and from 1366 Jews are found in Coblenz as house-owners.

JE: In 1418 Archbishop Otto drove them out of his domains, and in 1421 he gave in fief the Jewish cemetery of Coblenz to the daughters of Gottfried Sack of Dieblich, and presented the Jewish houses in the Burggasse to the religious order of St. Florin.
JE: Among the rabbis and scholars of Coblenz Moses Kohen ben Eliezer, the author of "Sefer Ḥasidim" (1473), should be mentioned.
No Jews were officially allowed to return to the city until the early 1500s.

JE: The Council first extended civil protection to them in 1518.
JE: In 1583 they were again ordered to leave, and until 1592 they were excluded from the electorate.

Event: during the Council of Constance the Jews of Konstanz went out in solemn procession to meet the newly elected Pope Martin V (Jewish Encyclopedia, with an illuminated chronicle picture of the scene); Encyclopaedia Judaica adds that a delegation of German Jewry met the pope, who in 1418 granted privileges confirmed by King Sigismund. Depping (pp. 280-281) says the Jews offered the pope the Pentateuch and the Decalogue in the public square and were rebuffed, that Martin V then included the Jews in the Maundy Thursday excommunication of heretics and infidels, and that the Council limited confiscation of converts' property to one half. Event: Armleder persecution and temporary expulsion, 1336-1338 (Year of Data = first year of the range). Alemannia Judaica: "1336-1338 kam es während der Armlederbewegung zur Verfolgung und zeitweisen Vertreibung der Juden"; the same page mentions a ritual bath (1334/36) and a dance house at the synagogue (1336) and a 1957 find of medieval gold coins hidden by a Jewish moneylender in his house at Bergstraße 1, which it links with this persecution. Mentgen, after Ziwes 1995 (Studien zur Geschichte der Juden im mittleren Rheingebiet, pp. 193f): the Jews of Limburg had to leave the town "auf Betreiben dortiger Kleriker" (at the instigation of local clerics), an expulsion as the alternative to murder that regularly accompanied the larger persecution waves. No count of victims or expelled. The map has Limburg rows from 1278 (first Jew named) and 1353 (Judengasse), nothing for 1336-1338; the map now also has a 1338 row (merged from the ATL3 batch, Beinart's Atlas) with Emperor Louis's order of 16 May 1338 that the burghers of Limburg take the expelled Jews back and return their property, which presupposes the expulsion documented here (different year and aspect, so not a duplicate).

Early in the 15th century a few Jewish families resettled in Lübben (year 1400 = round year of "Anfang des 15. Jahrhunderts"); Margrave Ludwig the Roman (1351-65) had expelled the Jews from almost all Lusatian towns.
The "Judengasse" of Lübben is first mentioned in the town book of 1525.
Event: after a great fire blamed on Jews, the Jewish families were expelled in 1541/42; after a quick resettlement the Landvogt expelled them again in 1573.
Event: in 1350 the city council wrote to Duke Otto of Brunswick-Luneburg requesting him to exterminate the Jews in his territory as responsible for the plague.
JE: the local chronographer Reimer Kock states expressly in 1499 that 'there are no Jews in Lubeck, as they are not needed here' (documented absence).

The first Jewish families settled in the manor village of Moisling in 1656 (Polish-Lithuanian refugees of the Cossack uprising, with permission of the Lübeck mayor Gotthard von Höveln, who held the manor); Jews were barred from Lübeck itself. First synagogue of Moisling 1727.
Lexikon page: the synagogue of Moisling was consecrated in 1827; it served 'der ca. 500köpfigen Gemeinde' (approximate).

Lexikon page: 'Als 1871/1872 nur noch knapp 30 Juden in Moisling lebten, wurde die Moislinger Synagoge geschlossen' and the Torah scrolls moved to Lübeck (just under 30; the cemetery of about 1670/1680 survives). Approximate figure.
On 7 May 1756 Michael Salomon and Joseph Joachim jointly received a privilege to settle and trade in Lübz (per the 1749-1760 Schutzjuden list of 1 Oct 1760).

Page (juden-in-mecklenburg.de): 'Lübzer Judenschaft... 1810 verfügte sie über nur 25 Mitglieder' (community members); Jewish cemetery only permitted in 1823 (before that the dead were buried in Parchim).
Page (juden-in-mecklenburg.de): numerical peak 'um 1866... nicht einmal 45 Personen' (just under 45, so approximate); fewer than ten Jewish persons by about 1900.

Community dissolved: resolution of 14 Jan 1916, dissolution contract 28 Mar 1916, members joined the Parchim community and the cemetery passed to the town; in 1919 three Jewish families are recorded; Lübz declared 'judenfrei' in Feb 1942.

First documented Jews: diploma of Otto I of 9 July 965 places the 'Jews and other traders' of Magdeburg under the jurisdiction of the archbishop; a charter of Otto II of 4 June 973 indicates a community of fair size and commercial importance.
Settlement: the Jews lived in a separate quarter outside the city, the Judendorf in the south, in the archbishop's domain, belonging politically to the archbishopric rather than the town.

Jewish Encyclopedia: a similar document of Otto II dated June 4, 973 (after Otto the Great's of 965) describes 'Jews and other traders'; the way Jews are described 'justifies the inference that even at that period they formed a community of fair size'.
Event: Jews took part in the funeral procession of Archbishop Walthard (1012), a sign of their standing in the town.
Event: the First Crusade is said to have caused the expulsion of Jews from the Judendorf (Jewish Encyclopedia, stated tentatively).
Event: troops of Otto IV destroyed the Judendorf; about four years later (1217) the Jews moved to nearby Sudenburg, where Jews already lived.

The cathedral chapter claimed jurisdiction over the Jews and the fines they paid in silver; fines in gold stayed with the archbishop (Encyclopaedia Judaica). The Jewish Encyclopedia reports for 1261 that Archbishop Robert seized Jewish valuables and ransomed the richest Jews.
Cemetery: dates from the 13th century; the oldest surviving gravestone is dated 1268. Enlarged in 1312 (purchase of four fields) and again in 1383/1385 (sources differ).

Earliest dated tombstone in the Jewish cemetery of Magdeburg: 1269 CE. Alemannia Judaica: of the medieval Magdeburg Jewish cemetery 'a tombstone of 1269 is still preserved'; German Wikipedia (Judenkever Buckau) mentions a stone of 1312 reused as spolia

Rabbis: R. Hayyim b. Paltiel was rabbi in 1291 and corresponded with Meir of Rothenburg (d. 1293); earlier R. Hezekiah b. Jacob corresponded with Isaac ben Moses (Or Zarua) of Vienna. A yeshiva and beth din are recorded.
Event: persecution; after a rumour about an effigy of Jesus the citizens plundered the Judendorf, killed some Jews and drove out others (Jewish Encyclopedia gives 1301, Encyclopaedia Judaica 1302).
Event: The Jews were persecuted in 1302 and again during the Black Death disturbances of 1349, despite the attempts of the archbishop and the city authorities to protect them.
JE: "A document of 1312 has been preserved, according to which the Jews bought four fields for the extension of their cemetery."

Event: Black Death persecution (1348/49): citizens and peasants looted the Judendorf and burned many Jews in their homes, despite protection by the archbishop and magistrates; Rabbi Shalom died as a martyr. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the persecution 1349.
JE: "A tombstone in the old Jewish cemetery also names a martyr, Samuel, of the year 1356."
Event: further attacks on the Jews during epidemics in 1357 and 1384 (a tombstone of the martyr Samuel is dated 1356).
Archbishop Dietrich employed a Jewish court banker (Schmoll/Shemuel) 1361-1367.
Archbishop Gunther issued a six-year letter of protection (Schutzbrief) in return for 40 silver marks from the community.
During the 15th century the community maintained a flourishing yeshivah. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)

Event: archbishop ordered the expulsion of all Jews from the city and archbishopric after a dispute with two monks; enforced 1493 (Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 1493, Jewish Encyclopedia 1492). The synagogue became the Marienkapelle and the cemetery was destroyed. The Jewish Encyclopedia says 'more than 1,400' emigrated (a count of emigrants, not a stated community size; Population left blank). Hebrew Wikipedia gives c. 1472 under Archbishop Adolf II, which conflicts with the other sources.

It was not until 1720 that a Jew, Gumpert by name, obtained permission to reside in the Altstadt of Magdeburg, and up to 1806 only one protected Jew at a time enjoyed this privilege."

First documented Jews: the scribe Isaak ben Samuel from Meiningen, expelled in 1242/43 and given refuge in Nuremberg (Alemannia Judaica); German Wikipedia says Jews are attested since 1243; Encyclopaedia Judaica lists a blood-libel persecution in 1243. Coordinates match Meiningen in Thuringia.
Event: community largely destroyed in the Rintfleisch persecution of 1298 (Alemannia Judaica; Encyclopaedia Judaica). No victim count given.

Event: plague-period persecution: on Good Friday 10 April 1349 a girl claimed to have heard Jews plotting an attack at the synagogue by the north gate; some Jews were imprisoned and, on the order of Bishop Albert of Wuerzburg, burned with wives and children on 17 July 1349 (Jewish Encyclopedia; Alemannia Judaica gives the same two dates). No victim count given; the community was destroyed.

Event: the emptied synagogue (called Judenkirche, standing at least in the first half of the 14th century) was converted into a chapel in 1384 (Alemannia Judaica; Encyclopaedia Judaica). The Jewish Encyclopedia instead says it stood closed 22 years after the expulsion before becoming the Chapel of St. Mary Magdalene; the sources differ.

Event: in 1422 it was ordered that no lodgings could be rented or sold to Jews in Meiningen (Jews are said to have lived in the town again in 1373). [Schulz paper pp. 13-14; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 175]
Resettlement: a Judengasse outside the city walls on the Werra is documented in 1432 (later renamed Hockergasse); Jews lived in the city again in the 15th century (Alemannia Judaica).
A property before the Niedertor is called Judengrab in 1486 and 1497, possibly the grave of murdered Jews or a mikveh called Judengrub (Alemannia Judaica).
Event: in 1525 the citizens of Meiningen demanded - unsuccessfully - the expulsion of all Jews. [Schulz paper pp. 13-14; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 175]

Event: all Jews expelled from the city by 1566 at the latest (Alemannia Judaica; German Wikipedia: all Jewish residents had to leave in 1566); outside the 1500 range, shown as the end of the late-medieval resettlement. No medieval population figure in any fetched source.

Estimate based on families. 28 families had moved to the town and founded the Israelitische Kultusgemeinde

The community bought its own cemetery in 1870 on the north side of the Christian cemetery (Berliner Straße); before that the Jews of Meiningen were buried in Dreißigacker or Walldorf. Meiningen became seat of the district rabbinate for Saxe-Meiningen in 1871. [Schulz paper pp. 13-14; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 176]

Event: the new synagogue at Pulverrasenweg/Mauergasse was inaugurated on 13/14 April 1883 (the road was renamed Synagogenstraße until 1933). [Schulz paper pp. 13-14; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 176]

Event: in the night of 9/10 November 1938 the synagogue was devastated and burned out; the ruins were cleared later. [Schulz paper pp. 13-14; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 177]

Event: from 1941 the remaining Jews were concentrated in a ghetto-like 'Judenhaus', the 'Brockenburg' (Sachsenstraße 5/6), where they lived in inhuman conditions until deportation in May and September 1942. [Schulz paper pp. 13-14; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 176, 177]

Jews reported in Meissen before the year 1000; margrave Gunzelin was deposed in 1009 by Henry II, among other things for selling Christian serfs to the Jews of the margraviate; the Jewish community of Meissen was entirely outside the city walls (Jüdenthor).
Earliest traces of Jewish life in Saxony are found in Meissen, with Jews mentioned in documents as early as the 11th century
An organized community in the city of Meissen dates only from the 12th century, when a synagogue and a cemetery were maintained. (century-only date, round year 1150 used)

Event: The Jews lived at first in a Judendorf outside the city walls near the "Jewish gate." In 1265 Duke Henry the Illustrious enacted a liberal decree securing the Jewish community undisturbed participation in the city's life for some 80 years.

Event: host-desecration accusation against the Jews of Meissen in 1297 (Jewish Encyclopedia chronological list of host-desecration cases; no outcome stated). WEAK: accusation only. Book p. 155, ref 1200.3.
In 1330 Emperor Louis iv transferred the protection of the Jews in Meissen to Frederick the Grave of Thuringia.
Event: The extermination of the Jews of Meissen began in 1349; in 1433 the Jews were expelled from Meissen and Thuringia by Frederick the Mild.

Event: partial expulsion of Jews from the margraviate of Meissen in 1411, rescinded in 1415 (JVL: "A partial expulsion took place in 1411, but the decree was rescinded in 1415"). The atlas (map 66) shows an expulsion arrow labelled 1411 at Meissen. Jews were not resettled in the town itself in the Middle Ages; Jewish moneylenders and traders stayed as taxpayers in the margraviate.

In 1425 Frederick the Warlike granted them protection for a yearly fee; however, during the course of the Hussite Wars (see Hussites), Frederick the Mild ordered the expulsion of all Jews from Meissen and Thuringia in 1430.

Jews are reported to have appeared in Saxony before the year 1000, in the train of the Lombards, settling principally in Merseburg, Naumburg, Torgau and Meissen (year approximate).

Earliest documentary evidence: Emperor Otto II granted Bishop Gisiler authority over the Jews, the merchants and the mint of the city (privilege renewed by Henry II in 1004). Community described as one of the oldest in Germany; German Wikipedia claims a community already in the 9th century but gives no document.
Event: Henry II renewed the 973 privilege placing the Jews, merchants and mint under the bishop.
Three Jews lent 80 silver marks to the burgrave of Merseburg (moneylending evidence; no population figure).

The convent of Pegau sold properties to repay debts owed to Merseburg Jews. Scholars R. Ezekiel and R. Samuel of Merseburg are active in this period (Ezekiel put halakhic queries to Meir b. Baruch of Rothenburg).
Event: A persecution of 1349-50 is sometimes asserted, but the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry says this rests on a confusion of similar place names; not reliably documented for Merseburg.

Jewish cemetery of the community existed at least from 1362. Rabbi Menahem of Merseburg (author of Nimmukim) is dated to the second half of the 14th century by the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry but to c. 1420-1450 by the Jewish Encyclopedia.
In a Hebrew source Menahem of Merseburg, author of Nimmukim, was a leading German rabbi in the second half of the 14th century. (century-only date, round year 1375 used)

Jews of the bishopric of Merseburg paid 100 gilders coronation tax to King Sigismund (1434); further taxes 1438 (3% income tax to Albert II) and 1440 (coronation tax). Tax amount, not a population figure.

Event: Jews left Merseburg at an unknown date after the 1440s amid economic decline and internal tension; in 1556 the historian Ernst Brotuff wrote that many Jews had formerly lived there and mentioned a synagogue near the cathedral chapter (c. 1450 used as approximate year; exact date unknown). Saxon rule from 1565 barred Jews.

In 1556 the Saxon historian Ernst Brotuff wrote, "Formerly many Jews lived in Merseburg who had their own synagogue with a courtyard in the small street west of the Cathedral chapter." In 1565 Merseburg came under the rule of Saxon, where no Jews were tolerated, and in 1815 under Prussia, which lifted the restrictions in the new territories only in 1847.

About four or five Jewish families lived in town in 1429 (range of families, so Population left blank). Paulus (p. 63) mentions the synagogue's roughly 300 years of other use before 1755. Jews first mentioned in Minden in 1270, under the protection of the bishop (Encyclopaedia Judaica, Brilling); a Westphalian survey (Westfaelische Zeitschrift 129) lists Minden among towns with Jews by 1270 and with synagogue and cemetery. Hebrew Wikipedia gives only 'from the 13th century'. Coordinates match Minden in Westphalia.
Population: households x 5. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Brilling): the small community numbered no more than 12 families in 1318, so 12 x 5 = 60 is an upper bound.

After 1336 the town agreed to recognize the bishop's rights over the Jews provided they paid municipal taxes as well as protection money to the bishop; moneylending was the only authorized Jewish occupation.
Population: households x 5. Encyclopaedia Judaica: ten families in 1340, so 10 x 5 = 50.

Medieval Jewish cemetery outside the Simeonstor, used late 13th to late 14th century; a gravestone fragment dated 1345/47 is in the Mindener Museum; the kahal provided its own burial ground in the first half of the 14th century (JewishGen Cemetery Project citing Brilling 1964, Brandhorst 1995).

Event: Jews of Minden killed on the eve of St Mary Magdalene, 21 July 1350, in the Black Death persecutions (Westfaelische Zeitschrift 129, 1979; chronicle phrase 'more pecorum mactaverunt'); Encyclopaedia Judaica says the Jews were expelled in 1350. No victim count given. Resettlement only in the 16th century (residence permits 1571).
Jews did not settle in Minden again until the 16th century. (century-only date, round year 1550 used)
In 1571 the council granted them residence permits of 12 years' duration and allowed them to engage in commerce and moneylending and to hold religious services.

comment: Event: massacre of 17 July 1287, part of the persecution wave that began at Oberwesel after the body of the boy Werner (the "good Werner") was found near Bacharach. About 90 Jews (men, women and children) were killed (Germania Judaica II/2, pp. 565 f., as quoted by Burgard; Alemannia Judaica: "etwa neunzig Männer, Frauen und Kinder"). The Nuremberg Memorbuch (martyrology) counts 22 families and, in addition, 8 unnamed "Bachurim" (visiting students, probably of the rabbi, who is not among the martyrs; Alemannia Judaica: "Unter den Ermordeten waren acht Talmud-Schüler"). The martyrology names the place only as "Münster" between Kobern and Trarbach; Burgard (and Mentgen 1995) identify it with Münstermaifeld. Burgard lists the toll of the other places of the wave for comparison (Cochem 17, Trarbach 36, Kobern 19, Braubach 2, Kirn 6, Oberlahnstein 6, Kirchberg 4, Koblenz 3, Bernkastel 14 in 1289): Münstermaifeld has the highest toll of the list. He treats the martyrologies as reliable (the name lists must rest on community tax lists) and concludes that a considerable community was wiped out ("ausgelöscht"), although no Christian source names a single member of it. Context given by Burgard: the town was an oppidum from 1259, with market, mint and the collegiate church of St. Martin and Severus, and ranked third among the Trier towns after Trier and Koblenz, good conditions for a growing Jewish settlement. No Jew is documented again until 1308. Victim count, not population: Population blank. Confidence: high.

comment: Presence: first Jew named in Münstermaifeld documents after the pogrom of 1287. In the will of the canon custodian (Stiftskustos) Johannes von Winnenburg (document of 12 April 1308) a creditor "Samuel Judeus" is left one mark of interest that the custodian had owed him since the previous Christmas (Landeshauptarchiv Koblenz, Best. 144 Nr. 104; Germania Judaica II/2, pp. 564 f., n. 11). Burgard thinks he is probably the Samuel of Münstermaifeld who is named as deceased on 3 Dec 1333 when his heirs owned a house in the Judengasse of Koblenz. Burgard: if Jews resettled after 1287, it can only have been a small number (Haverkamp 1985, p. 454). The online heritage page lists named Jews for 1308, 1333, 1339, 1352 and 1355 without details; the details are from the paper. Population blank. Confidence: high.

comment: Synagogue: first documentary proof of a synagogue of the Münstermaifeld Jews. On 9 March 1323 the couple Gobelinus (Gobel) Cryser and Irmgard sold the town hospital an annual rent of 2 marks for 26 marks, charged on their house in the town "prope synagogam Judeorum" (next to the synagogue of the Jews) and the house of Dittele Morshusen (Landeshauptarchiv Koblenz, Best. 660,1 Nr. 6; the charter is printed in the paper's source appendix, with the day given as 8 March in the text, corrected by Burgard to 9 March, fn. 38). The charter was known as a regest since Löhr 1902 but ignored by research; Burgard says it is the first proof of a synagogue in the first half of the 14th century, so that the large pre-1349 community had communal institutions, contra the view (Haverkamp 1985, p. 441) that the synagogue and cemetery known from the late 1360s and 1409 already existed before 1349. The synagogue is known only from a neighbour description; its location is unknown. The map already mentions the 1323 synagogue only in the Notes of its 1409 row. Population blank. Confidence: high.

Burgard wonders whether the first name is the "Noel" attested for a Jew in June 1369 (a Jew of Romance origin). The same year, on 3 Dec 1333, the heirs of the late Samuel of Münstermaifeld owned a house in the Judengasse of Koblenz (LHAKo 1 A Nr. 817), next to the house of Bendit the Jew of Montabaur. For comparison Burgard says that at Oberwesel in 1337 apparently all Jews were killed ("offenkundig alle Juden getötet"). Burgard (fn. 12) notes that a "Petir Jude von Muynster" named on 29 April 1337 was probably not a Jew. comment: Presence: on 21 July 1339 a sale deed for an hereditary rent (Erbzins) names the house of the Jew Baruch in Münstermaifeld as a landmark: the house sold lay by the bakehouse of Gerlach Becher called Caltbecher of Mertloch and his wife Diligen, near Baruch's house (Landeshauptarchiv Koblenz, Best. 144 Nr. 248). Together with the debt list of August 1339 (next row) Burgard counts seven Jews of Münstermaifeld known from the documents alone for the first half of the 14th century (Samuel, Nulle, Baruch, David, Salmann, the French Jew and Hermelinus) and concludes that a larger community must have lived there between 1307 and 1349 (its actual size cannot be established). Population blank (named persons are not a count). Confidence: high.

comment: Presence/credit: in the debt register of Count Rupert of Virneburg to Archbishop Balduin of Trier (5 Aug 1339) several Münstermaifeld Jews are named as creditors of the count, his vassals or protégés (debtors Grymmynk the younger of Mertloch for the first three, Johannes Grymmynk the elder for the last): David, Jew of Münstermaifeld, 33 marks Brabantine; Salmann of Münstermaifeld 19 marks (Holland marks); a certain French Jew of Münstermaifeld (his name unknown to the scribe) 10 marks Brabantine; Hermelinus of Münstermaifeld (spelled Hennelino in the Latin of fn. 14) 60 marks Brabantine (Landeshauptarchiv Koblenz, 1 A Nr. 5009; Lamprecht, Deutsches Wirtschaftsleben im Mittelalter, vol. 3, pp. 171 f. no. 143). Burgard: the French Jew, like other Romance-name Jews of the Trier towns, shows the immigration encouraged by Archbishop Balduin, partly from the French expulsions of the early 14th century. Amounts are debts, not population: Population blank. Confidence: high.

comment: Presence/end of a household: in May 1352 Archbishop Balduin granted the house in the Burngasse (vico dicto Burngasse, between the house of Gude de Kalte and the barn of Johannes called Hera) of the Jew David, which had fallen back to the archbishop on his death, to the archiepiscopal cellarer (Kellner) Thilman, son of the late Walter of Münstermaifeld (Landeshauptarchiv Koblenz, 1 A 2689; Alemannia Judaica: "verfügte Erzbischof Baldwin von Trier über das Haus des Juden David"). Burgard presumes this David is the creditor of 1339; the date of his death is not given. On 25 July 1359 a couple owed the hospital rent for a garden on the Santkule that had formerly been the property of David the Jew (LHAKo 660,1 Nr. 18). This shows a Jewish house-owner of the pre-1349 community, not a living community in 1352. Population blank. Confidence: high (fact), medium as evidence of presence in that year.

The map has Münstermaifeld rows for 1253 (range) and 1349 only. Population blank. Confidence: medium (scholarly, single source).

comment: Synagogue building still named: on 14 Nov 1357 (LHAKo 132 Nr. 132, so fn. 32 and p. 365; the text of p. 367 gives 25 July 1359 for the same lease, an internal inconsistency of the paper, July 1359 being the date of the hospital rent in fn. 15) the abbess and convent of Machern lease their house in Münstermaifeld that lay "hinter der Judenschule" (behind the Judenschule), opposite the house of Konrad Ennemenger, to the citizen Friedrich called Kelnere and his wife Aleyd. The Judenschule serves only as a topographical marker: Burgard cannot say whether the synagogue was used for worship again after the plague (the only Jew known in the town then is Lewen, documented 1355 to c. 1358). No online source found. Population blank. Confidence: medium.

Barzen (p. 73) cites the cemeteries of Münstermaifeld, Windecken and Neudenau as already reflecting the more rural settlement of early modern Judaism: "Die Einrichtung von Friedhöfen in Münstermaifeld, Windecken und Neudenau trug bereits den" ... The map has no Münstermaifeld row for the 15th century. Population blank. Confidence: high.
