comment: Presence: the Jew Koppelin "von Münstermaifeld" appears on 8 Dec 1410 in a loan deal with the nobleman (Junker) Friedrich Waldbott von Waltmannshausen (LHAKo 1 A 2672 f.; Germania Judaica III/2, pp. 913 f.); Alemannia Judaica: "Erst 1410 hört man wieder von Juden in Münstermaifeld", the nobleman owing 40 gulden then and 100 gulden four years later. Together with the Jew Menlin Koppelin had already done money business before April 1407 (LHAKo 144 Nr. 555 and 557), but Burgard is not sure he was settled in the town then. Burgard finds no clear evidence of other Jews in Münstermaifeld between Lewen (1355-1366) and Koppelin: a 1374 mention of the town priest in a Jewish debt, a forged debt letter of 1402 and an unexplained "Judengrube" (fovea iudeorum) of 1363 give no sign of Jews in town. Population blank. Confidence: high.

comment: Presence: on 9 May 1414 Koppelin applies before the Münstermaifeld Schultheiß (mayor) to be put in possession of the pledge of Junker Friedrich Waldbott and is explicitly styled "in Münstermaifeld wohnhafter Jude" (a Jew resident in Münstermaifeld; LHAKo 1 A 2672 f.; Germania Judaica III/2, pp. 913 f.). This is the first clear evidence of a Jew living in the town since Lewen (1355). Alemannia Judaica: four years after 1410 the nobleman again owed a Münstermaifeld Jew money (100 gulden), but it says no Jewish community was founded again in the 15th century. Population blank (one resident Jew). Confidence: high.

comment: Event: end of the Jewish presence (inferred). Burgard: the exodus of the few Jews still in the town was probably caused (the paper says "dürfte") by the expulsion edict of Archbishop Otto von Ziegenhain of 1418/19 for the Electorate of Trier, as in many other Electorate places. Evidence: the Kellnerei (archiepiscopal bailiff's) account of 1419/20 records income from a Judenhaus, i.e. a Jewish house had passed into Christian hands (LHAKo 1 C 6253, p. 3), and sale of Jewish pledges (Judenpfänder) to Peter Mercator, presumably confiscated in the archbishop's name at the expulsion (LHAKo 1 C 6253, p. 11); Germania Judaica III/2, p. 914 n. 9 interprets this differently. The once important community had never re-formed after the persecutions of 1287 to 1349. Date range 1418/19 written as 1418. The Electorate-wide expulsion itself is on the map for Koblenz, Montabaur, Bernkastel and others (Alemannia Judaica Koblenz: "1418 wurden infolge der Judenausweisung aus dem Erzstift Trier"), but no online page names Münstermaifeld in it (the Alemannia Judaica Münstermaifeld page is silent), so the local fact rests on Burgard alone. Population blank. Confidence: medium. [Source detail: (context: expulsion from the Electorate); no online source found for Münstermaifeld itself]

The rent is booked in the Kellnerei accounts of 1422/23 and 1425, so the former synagogue was in ordinary profane use. Alemannia Judaica dates the name to 1420 ("1420 judenschoille = Judenschule genannt"). Population blank. Confidence: high.

Haverkamp dates the coin to the 1170s; Alemannia Judaica says Kuno had the Jew David-ha-Kohn in service as mint master 'around the year 1180' (online year used; see conflicts file). The paper does not say where the coin was struck: it is evidence of a Jew in the service of the Muenzenberg lordship in the Wetterau, while Jews in the town itself are documented from 1188 (existing row). No population stated. Confidence medium-low for the town.

comment: David ben Kalonymos (son of Kalonymos ben Meir of Speyer, financier of Frederick I), a scholar named 'of Minzburg' in Hebrew sources, lived in Kuno's fortress or the settlement under its protection from at least the 1190s, after living at Speyer and Mainz; he was among the Mainz Jews who found refuge at Muenzenberg in 1188 (Haverkamp p. 199, citing Eleazar of Worms). Alemannia Judaica: in 1195 David ben Kalonymos settled in Muenzenberg (probably from Speyer) and called himself 'David of Muenzenberg', one of the most important Jewish scholars of his time, which made the town a regional intellectual centre of Judaism. Haverkamp leaves open whether he is the mint master David haCohen. No population stated.

Event: 26 June 1096 First Crusade; Jews of Cologne sheltered in Neuss by Archbishop Hermann III were attacked by crusaders and a mob and all massacred and their houses plundered; Samuel b. Asher and his sons tortured and killed on the Rhine bank. Jewish Encyclopedia cites Albert of Aachen that about 200 Jews lived there (many were Cologne refugees); Wikipedia says no organised community yet existed and about 200 were killed. Population 200 = Albert of Aachen's figure as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Jews resettled in Neuss after 1096 and within about a century formed a flourishing community with several eminent scholars (Jewish Encyclopedia); Wikipedia dates an organised community to the late 12th century (Staufer period) and the Old Synagogue article to a small community and synagogue in the 12th century. Year 1100 is approximate for the resettlement; sources differ.

Event: 27 January 1197 (Aronius Regesten give 17 February 1187) after a mentally disturbed Jew killed a Christian girl in front of witnesses he and six other Jews including the tosafist Samuel b. Natronai were broken on the wheel; his mother buried alive and his brother tortured to death; Jews paid a large sum to bury the victims and 150 silver pieces to Archbishop Adolf. Wikipedia names Ephraim of Bonn as source and says victims were buried in Xanten.

In 1283 the Jews of Neuss supported the pretender Frederick (der Juden-Koenig) with large sums against Rudolph I of Habsburg; he died 7 July 1284. In the 13th century many Jews emigrated from Neuss to Cologne (Jewish Encyclopedia).

By c. 1300 the Jews had moved from the harbour/market area to the Glockhammer quarter where synagogue and school stood; not a sealed ghetto. The Old Synagogue article also names the Judensteg near the later Hessentor. Year 1300 approximate (c. 1300).

No online source found (the Zion article is not online; hdbg.eu mentions only that from 1489 stays of foreign Jews were limited to three days).

Event: expulsion. Emperor Maximilian I approved the expulsion in 1498 (21 June per Jewish Encyclopedia); on 20 Feb 1499 houses, synagogue and cemetery were handed to the council and the families left in the following days (Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte; March 1499 per Encyclopaedia Judaica). Houses sold for 8,000 gulden; cemetery c. 7 ha with about 3,000 gravestones. Exiles went to Neustadt, Huettenbach, Ottensoos, Schnaittach, Frankfurt, Prague, Regensburg.
JE: "The day of the exodus was first set for Nov. 6, 1498, then for Candlemas, Feb. 2, 1499, and finally for Lætare Sunday, 1499."
JE: "The citizens of Nuremberg were not allowed to buy meat from the Jews of Fürth, and trade with Jews was finally forbidden altogether (1533)."
5638 Jewish citizens left Nuremberg between 1933 and 1939, including migrants to other German cities
1534 Jews were deported from Nuremberg to concentration camps, of which only 65 survived
More than 2300 native Nuremberg citizens and residents were murdered or forced to commit suicide during the Holocaust

1241/42: Jews first named in the Reichssteuerliste; the Oberwesel community paid 20 marks, 5 marks less than Boppard's (Alemannia Judaica; de.wikipedia). Alemannia Judaica also cites the Yad Vashem encyclopedia for a community in the mid-13th century.

Event: blood-libel accusation over the boy Werner (Womrath) on Maundy Thursday 1287; pogroms along the Middle Rhine lasting about two years. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Boppard entry) says 40 Jews were massacred in Boppard and Oberwesel combined (victim count, not community size; no separate Oberwesel number). The Cochem entry links 17 Jews killed there to the Oberwesel blood libel.
Event: King Rudolf of Habsburg fined the citizens of Oberwesel and Boppard and restored the expelled Jews' property, after which Jews lived in relative peace again.

Event: 1308/09 Henry VII pledged the Jewish tax of Oberwesel and Boppard to his brother Archbishop Balduin of Trier for 394 marks; the cities lost imperial immediacy (Alemannia Judaica says Balduin held Oberwesel in pledge from 1312).
Event: Armleder persecution (1336/37) in which Oberwesel Jews were attacked, some killed and houses plundered.

Households x 5: de.wikipedia (citing A. Schwarz, 'Eine Zeitreise durch Oberwesel') states 49 Jewish families are documented for 1338, so 49 x 5 = 245. On 18 March 1338 Archbishop Balduin forced the city to compensate for the plundering and set conditions for the Jews' residence.

Event: Black Death persecution destroyed the medieval community completely (Alemannia Judaica; no document named there). Before the violence 217 Christian citizens were indebted to 29 Jewish creditors of the town, about a third women (Schwarz; Kellenbenz, Monumenta Judaica 1963; creditor count, not population). Encyclopaedia Judaica entries for Boppard/Cochem mention 1349 Black Death killings regionally but do not name Oberwesel.

From 1372 individuals styled 'of Oberwesel' appear again, living in Cochem, Gelnhausen, Mayen, Strasbourg and Worms; a new local community probably did not yet exist. In 1379 Joseph son of Jakob of Montabaur, Jew in Oberwesel, is documented with a claim of 400 gold gulden.
Event: 1418/19 Archbishop Otto von Ziegenhain ordered the expulsion of Jews from the Archdiocese of Trier; unclear whether any Jews lived in Oberwesel then.
A Jewish school (Judenschule, also used for prayer) is documented in 1452; a medieval synagogue is not confirmed. Jews resettled in Oberwesel c. 1462 or shortly after (Alemannia Judaica).

Event: Armleder persecution; possibly all Jews of the town murdered or expelled; bishop Otto II von Wolfskeel then granted the empty synagogue complex in fief to Ochsenfurt burgher families.

c. 1300: Alemannia Judaica dates the Judenbad (mikveh) beneath Glaserstrasse 8 to c. 1300 ('presumably') and infers a larger community. Dating is disputed: the building-history study by Monika Porsche (2003) argues for the 16th-17th century because the stones were reused; Gutmann and Stude consider a medieval origin plausible. No written source names a medieval mikveh.

4 Dec 1338: Strasbourg protection letter lists Lenit of Offenburg and Gumpreht of Offenburg with their children among its Jewish protegees, the earliest evidence of Offenburg Jews (Stude; Gutmann). Gutmann: no reliable information on the size of the community. Encyclopaedia Judaica says Jews 'appear' to have lived there in the 13th century, without a document.

Gumprecht (resident in Strasbourg, ties to Offenburg, probably owned two or more houses there) appears in 1343 and 1346 in loans to the lords of Geroldseck; indicates a wealthy Offenburg-linked family (Gutmann).

Event: Jews arrested in the second half of December 1348 (before 24 Dec) on a well-poisoning accusation; Susskind and Schade tortured and burned, the rest of the community was offered safe departure or a fire (council letter to Strasbourg after 10 Feb 1349, UB Strassburg 5 no. 196). Encyclopaedia Judaica says three Jews confessed and the Jews were expelled; Alemannia Judaica says expelled, presumably dying in flames. M. Hildenbrand estimates 50 to 60 persons burned (cited in Stude; victim estimate, not a stated community size, so Population blank). Gutmann infers at least three further households remained. Also in the Martyrologium (Salfeld).

Event/status: Judenschul (synagogue) and Judengasse (later Baeckergasse, called Judengaesschen until 1824) mentioned 1393 in the property register of the Liebfrauenpfruende of the parish church. Stude: no evidence of Jews after 1349, so by 1393 the synagogue had passed to other hands; a new community is documented only from 1637 (Gutmann) and gates were not reopened to Jews until 1862 (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

comment: The atlas has 'Regensburg' labelled on the map 'Distribution of Jews, middle of the sixth century' (that map has no separate legend, so every labelled place is read as a place with Jewish evidence). No precise year is given, so 550 is the conventional midpoint of the period (middle of the 6th century). Presence only; no population stated. No online source found: the English Wikipedia article on Regensburg was fetched and gives no statement of a Jewish presence for this period.

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 36: Schmetzer (cited by Altmann) finds that the Jewish quarter of Regensburg, at the west gate of the old Roman castle, had by 919 lost its isolated position and become part of the centre of the town after Duke Arnold built the new fortifications. Presence of a Jewish quarter c. 919; the date rests on Schmetzer's reading (not on a document naming Jews).
Approximately 1,000 Jews live in Regensburg, the majority immigrants from the Former Soviet Union.

Jewish Encyclopedia: 'The Jewish quarter, Judaeorum habitacula, is mentioned as early as the beginning of the eleventh century (1006-28), and is the oldest German ghetto to which there is any reference in historical sources.' Year = start of the 1006-28 range (flagged).
Its Jewish quarter was the oldest in Germany (1020).
Wikipedia: 'Evidence exists of Jewish merchants from Regensburg trading in furs with Russia and Hungary as early as 1050.'

Event: First Crusade. Wikipedia's list of German massacres: 1096 pogroms attested in Regensburg ('forced baptism in Danube river with return to Judaism after one year'); Jewish Encyclopedia: 'During the first Crusade (1096) the community suffered like many others in Germany.'

source: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_(Prag) | Wiedl, "Sacred Objects in Jewish Hands. Two Case Studies", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 59 n. 9
comment: In 1107 Bishop Hermann of Prague pawned gold and pallia (liturgical stoles) to the Jews of Regensburg. German Wikipedia ("Hermann (Prag)"): "Bei den Regensburger Juden verpfändete Bischof Hermann 1107 Gold und Pallien"; it gives neither the number nor the purpose. Wiedl (p. 59 n.9, citing Müller 2012, pp. 193-94) adds that it was five pallia, given to add to the ransom of the Bohemian duke Svatopluk, who had been taken prisoner by King Henry V in 1107; she cites it as an example of the liberation of prisoners by ransom as a legitimate reason for pledging church objects. It shows Jewish moneylenders in Regensburg in 1107. The map has Regensburg rows for 1006, 1020, 1050, 1096 and 1150 but none for 1107. No population. Confidence medium (details from the book only).
In the 12th and early 13th centuries, Christians also lived in the Jewish quarter and owned homes there. (century-only date, round year 1150 used)

Benjamin of Tudela, Sefer ha-Massa'ot (Itinerary), c.1165: traveller names the place "Regensburg"; Adler translation, text marker [p.111]. Traveller's words: listed with 'many Israelites, wise men and rich' (no number). Identification: Regensburg. No count given; Population left blank (presence only). Year 1165 = c.1165 (Benjamin travelled c.1165-1173).

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 10: Rabbinic responsum of about 1175 by Isaak ben Mordekhai of Regensburg (on a Jew renting a building from a Christian), quoted by Altmann: a Jewish legal authority active in Regensburg around 1175.
JE: "The Jews were granted their first privileges there in a charter of 1182."
By the end of the 12th century Regensburg had become a religious and cultural center for German Jewry. (century-only date, round year 1190 used)

Earliest dated tombstone in the Jewish cemetery of Regensburg: 1200 CE. JE: "The first cemetery of the community of Ratisbon was situated on a hillock, still called the "Judenau." In 1210 the congregation bought from the monastery of St. Emmeram a plot of ground, outside the present Peterthor, for a new cemetery, which was destroyed in the course of excavations made in the city in 1877."

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 70: Frederick II called the Jews of Regensburg 'fideles nostri Ratisponenses Judaei' in a privilege of 3 January 1216 (the Jews as the king's own subjects).

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 28: Privilege of King Henry (VII) of 30 June 1230 settling the jurisdiction over the Jews of Regensburg: the judge had to be chosen from among the Jews themselves.

source: E. Haverkamp, "Jewish Images on Christian Coins: Economy and Symbolism in Medieval Germany", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 210, n. 84
comment: Event: Emperor Frederick II awarded Bishop Siegfried of Regensburg (1227-46) the imperial revenues from the Regensburg Jews and judicial rights over them, confirmed in 1233 (Haverkamp p. 210 and n. 84, citing Freimann in Germania Judaica I, pp. 285-305); Haverkamp suggests the Jewish hat on the contemporary Regensburg penny (c. 1210-25), a motif shared by ducal and episcopal coins, could also have symbolised this episcopal lordship over the community. The Jews already had imperial privileges of 1182 and a protection and trade guarantee from Frederick II in 1216 (both on the map). German Wikipedia 'Geschichte der Juden in Regensburg' mentions a different 1233 measure (a ban on contacts between Christians and Jews), not this grant. No population stated. No online source found; source is a scholarly volume. Confidence medium.

source: E. Haverkamp, "Jewish Images on Christian Coins: Economy and Symbolism in Medieval Germany", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 210-211, n. 85
comment: In 1243 the Jew Aaron of Regensburg and the Christian mint master Rudger ('Rudgerus monetarius', also attested in 1207) jointly provided the money for the purchase of a house (of Rappoto) by the Dominicans in Regensburg; Haverkamp suggests Aaron may have been the second mint master of the mint shared by duke and bishop in the first quarter of the 13th century (pp. 210-211 and n. 85, citing Emmerig 1990, pp. 32-33). Evidence of a Jewish financier active in Regensburg in 1243. No population stated. No online source found; source is a scholarly volume. Confidence medium.

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 35: The first record showing Christian citizens of Regensburg acting as judges of the Jews dates from 1287: Karl Prager and Rueger von Kapell, as judges of the Jews, sealed two documents of the Jew Gnenlin (building contract with the monastery of Rohr), a sign of the deterioration of the Jews' judicial position.

Event: The economic importance of the community enabled it to weather the Rindfleisch (1289), Deggendorf (1338), and Black Death persecutions (1348/49) and to reach new heights of prosperity by offering asylum to rich refugees.
In 1297, the Archbishop of Salzburg purchased the county of Gastein with money borrowed from Regensburg Jews.

An old chronicle is quoted as referring to the persecutions that took place in Franconia and Swabia in 1298: "The citizens of Ratisbon desired to honor their city by forbidding the persecution of the Jews or the slaying of them without legal sentence."  The community completed a new synagogue in the early 13th century The synagogue provided seating for over 300 people.

JE: "To these overlords the Jews of Ratisbon were pawned in 1322 for the yearly sum of 200 pounds of Ratisbon pfennigs; but they were also subject to taxation by the municipal council of the city, though they received some compensation in the fact that thereby they secured the protection of the city council against the excessive demands of the emperor and the dukes."

The wave of religious intolerance which swept over Germany in 1349 was checked again at Ratisbon, in a spirit similar to that of fifty years earlier, by the declaration of the magistrates and the citizens that they would protect and defend their Jews.

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 57: On 24 August 1355 Rabbi Suzzlein assessed the Jews of Regensburg for their contribution to the town taxes (Stern); within the next twenty years the town subjected the Jews to the town authorities in every respect.

Event: The municipal council again shielded them by punishing only the guilty when, in 1384, a riot occurred because some Jews had been convicted of giving false returns of their property to the tax-assessor.

JE: "The protestations of the magistrates, however, could not protect their wards against the exactions of the emperor Wenzel when (1385-90) he replenished his purse by contributions levied upon the German Jews."
This wealth is reflected in a cache of 624 14th-century gold coins, thought to be buried in 1388, found in the archaeological dig.

JE: "In the following years they were again heavily taxed by both emperor and dukes, and in 1410 the magistrates, tired of ineffectual protest, took part in the game of spoliation by making an agreement with the duke that the Jews should pay 200 florins a year to him and 60 pounds a year to the city, extraordinary taxes to be divided between the two. ."

The general decline and impoverishment of Regensburg, combined with growing social tension between the upper and lower classes of the citizenry, made the years 1475–1519 a period of increased bitterness against the Jews, a struggle that ended in their total expulsion.
The anti-Semitic preachings of Peter Nigri led to the confiscating of the Jews' property in 1476, and the community was then thrown into chaos by the Simon of Trent trial in Italy.

JE: "The Talmudic school of Ratisbon became famous in the fifteenth century; a chronicle of 1478 says, "This academy has furnished 'doctores et patres' for all parts of Germany." R. Israel Bruna (15th cent.) narrowly escaped falling a victim to an accusation of ritual murder."

JE: "In 1486 the duke placed their taxation entirely in the hands of the city council, "that the expulsion might be effected the sooner." The preacher of the cathedral, Dr. Balthazar Hubmaier, incited the people from the pulpit, and the more prudent counselors who still dared to take the part of the Jews were mockingly called "Jew kings." In 1498 the community was led by ten elders; its takkanot were enacted by majority vote in a council of 31.

c. 1329: first attested Jewish presence; a Reutlingen Jew became a citizen of Nuremberg (de.wikipedia 'Juden in Reutlingen'). Encyclopaedia Judaica and Alemannia Judaica give 1331 as the first mention instead. Yad Vashem encyclopedia (via Alemannia Judaica) says only 'a Jewish settlement existed in the 13th century' without a document.
Event: Emperor Ludwig the Bavarian gave the city the Jewish tax and the court (for four years) for 3,000 Pfund Heller.

Event: 10 Feb 1331, Ulrich III of Wurttemberg renounced his rights to pledges held; Jews named with court and taxes, earliest mention in Encyclopaedia Judaica (Germania Judaica 2, 1968, pp. 694-6). Jews were taxable as Kammerknechte of the king.
A Reutlingen Jew (Jakob Lange per de.wikipedia) receipted a debt payment to Abbot Ulrich of Zwiefalten; Encyclopaedia Judaica: a Jew made a loan to a monastery.
Event: during the Armleder uprisings the mayor Albrecht der Rote protected the Jews from the Judenschlaeger.

Jews from Hagenau and Hessenberg settled; David of Hagenau sold an Ewiggeld from his Reutlingen house (1339). Pawnbroking was the main livelihood; Jews owned houses and a synagogue was built of stone (Encyclopaedia Judaica).
Event: persecution of 8 December 1348 in the Black Death; the only surviving trace is the Deutz Memorbuch, which lists Reutlingen among eleven Wurttemberg towns with martyrs. No victim count given.

Event: 20 April 1349 Emperor Charles IV granted the city an amnesty for the persecution and gave the abandoned Jewish property to the Counts of Wurttemberg, who sold the Jewish houses to the city for 1,200 Gulden.

Jews recorded again (c. 1371): a 'Hans der Jude' appears in a document about a house in the Vochezengasse; Encyclopaedia Judaica says they rebuilt houses and institutions after permission to return. Reutlingen Jews appear in several Memorbuecher.
Charles IV transferred outstanding Judengelder (special Jewish taxes) to the city.

Judengasse first recorded, along today's Rebentalstrasse and part of Kanzleistrasse; residents lived mainly from moneylending. A medieval synagogue is placed by local tradition (Martin Crusius) at Kanzleistrasse 2, with no contemporary record; the jued-gemeinden.de page also mentions a ritual bath (not mentioned by de.wikipedia). No evidence of an own cemetery (possibly used Esslingen).
Jewish Encyclopedia (Wurttemberg article) states there were Jews in Gmuend and Reutlingen in 1433, i.e. a Jewish presence continued or returned after the 15th-century expulsion(s).
Event: after an expulsion decided between 1424 and 1476, Emperor Frederick III ordered the city to readmit Jews in 1476, which was carried out (de.wikipedia).
Event: Jews expelled with the approval of Emperor Maximilian I; the council's earlier expulsion orders had failed against Frederick III's protection. Local press (2003) speaks of pogroms 'um 1500'.
Event: Maximilian I allowed the city to bar Jews permanently, noting the 21-year absence had benefited it (c. 1515-16 per jued-gemeinden.de).

Event: after the Wettins bought the lordship of Römhild in 1555 they tolerated no Jews any more (individual Jews had lived there before: Jews 'of Römhild' are named in 1363, 1414 and 1459; in 1525 a Jew received escort from the rebellious peasants). [Schulz paper pp. 16-17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 208]

Jews moved to Römhild again in 1869, soon after freedom of movement, from neighbouring communities; never more than 20 to 30 persons in four to five families; they belonged to the community of Bibra and used a Rococo prayer room in the rear of Heurichstraße 8 (Adolf Kahn's house). [Schulz paper pp. 16-17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 209]

Event: the house of Adolf Kahn (Heurichstraße 8) was used by the Nazis as a 'Judenhaus' where all Jews of the town were forced to live until their deportation to the extermination camps in 1942 (Alemannia Judaica: from 1939). [Schulz paper pp. 16-17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 209]

Event: an SS 'work education camp' (Arbeitserziehungslager 'Großer Gleichberg'), set up at the wish of the mayor, used forced labour in the basalt quarry in 1943-1945; the memorial in the Römhild cemetery names 169 victims, among them the German Jew Israel Schönthal; in March 1945 the mayor, SS-Obersturmführer Alfred Schmitt, had 70 exhausted prisoners driven into a tunnel which was blown up (Jews certainly among them, per Schwierz). [Schulz paper pp. 16-17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 210]

Reichssteuerverzeichnis (imperial tax list) of 1241: the Rothenburg community as a whole paid only 10 silver marks per year, which the Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte takes to mean a small community; no head count given.

Rabbi Meir ben Baruch (Maharam, c. 1220-1293) active in Rothenburg as judge, prayer leader and head of a yeshiva from about 1245 (other sources 1246 or 1250) to 1286; the community grew in the second half of the 13th century; first Jewish quarter and synagogue at today's Kapellenplatz.

Population estimate: Alemannia Judaica states that 500 to 600 Jews lived in the city in the 13th century (lower bound entered; the page also gives about 500 Jews among about 5,000 inhabitants). Estimate on the page, no underlying count cited.
Event: in August 1251 King Conrad IV pawned the town together with its Jews (civitatem nostram Rotenburc et Judaeos ibidem commorantes) to Gottfried of Hohenlohe for 3,000 silver marks.

Oldest known Rothenburg Jewish gravestone dated 1266 (found 1989 in the castle wall); the medieval cemetery (Judenkirchhof, today Schrannenplatz) lay outside the first city wall and was used until the expulsion of 1520; 32 stones and a memorial stele for the 1298 victims were found there in 1914.
Event: Rabbi Meir ben Baruch arrested on the orders of Rudolf of Habsburg and held in Ensisheim (Alsace); he died there in 1293 refusing ransom.

Four years after the pogrom Jews were again living in Rothenburg: in 1302 houses that had belonged to victims were returned, and gravestones of 1305 show the cemetery in use again; the second community never regained its previous size.
Emperor Louis of Bavaria set the community's tax at 200 Haller pounds (Encyclopaedia Judaica via encyclopedia.com); in 1342 he levied one gulden per Jew.
The Jewish dance house (Tanzhaus, assembly hall) at Kapellenplatz is first documented in 1333; an old synagogue is mentioned in 1346, implying a newer one.
Event: series of attacks on the Jewish community in 1336, 1338 and 1342 (Armleder period).

Event: Black Death persecution; the town and its Jews were pledged to Bishop Albrecht II of Würzburg, whose contract clause allowing him to seize Jewish property on their 'Abgehen' probably led to the extermination of the community in autumn 1349 (some sources say 1350); the city kept 27 August as a day of 'salvation'.
Emperor Charles IV granted Rothenburg a general pardon for the murder of Jews within its walls; the town redeemed itself from the Würzburg pledge for 8,500 gulden.

Event: on 13 September 1353 Charles IV returned the synagogue and the Jewish cemetery to the care of the city as compensation; Jews resettled shortly afterwards (the Jewish Encyclopedia gives 30 September 1353 for the return of the Jews to the council's jurisdiction).

Judengasse is known from 1371 in the new quarter north of the first city wall on the filled moat, the second Jewish quarter; the Judentanzhaus with public mikveh and hostel near the Weisser Turm dates from about 1400, and the mikveh in the cellar of Judengasse 10 from about 1409/10.
Jews are listed again in the Bürgerbuch (citizens' book) in 1374, after resettlement following 1353.

Population: households x 5. The Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte reports 33 taxpaying heads of household (Hausväter) about ten years after the 1374 listing (c. 1383), whose taxes made up more than a third of the city's tax income. Source count: 33 households.
Between 1385 and 1414 the king, the city council and the Swabian League repeatedly extorted large sums from the Jews; debt annulments of 1385 and 1390 damaged the community.

JE: "Nevertheless they were required to pay certain taxes directly to the king; and Opferpfennig receipts for the years 1393, 1394, and 1395 have been preserved, given to Rothenburg Jews in the time of the emperor Wenzel by the latter's favorite Borziwoy of Swynar."

Event: partial and temporary banishment after inflammatory Good Friday sermons (Encyclopaedia Judaica, readmission about seven years later); the Jewish Encyclopedia citing Bensen and Merz says the council sold the synagogue and dance hall for 2,000 gulden and readmitted Jews in 1404. Sources conflict on details.

The old synagogue at Kapellenplatz, which the city had held since 1353, was sold to councillor Peter Kreglinger and converted into a Marian chapel; the city built a new synagogue at the Jewish cemetery (dated 1404/1407 in different sources).
Judengasse 10 built 1409 with a vaulted-cellar mikveh (only medieval mikveh in Germany preserved with its house); Judengasse houses from c. 1400
Event: imperial tax (via Erkinger of Sausheim) of 2,000 gulden; the council arrested all Jews in town until 21 community members agreed to pay; receipt signed by Sigismund 8 October 1414.

The city resisted the demand of Bishop John of Würzburg (2 May 1422) to imprison Jews and seize their property; the bishop's order imposed a badge and a usury ban and was later revoked.

Event: on 7 July 1517 Emperor Maximilian granted the Jews a privilege against extortion by the robber knight Klaus Wolgemuth; the council nevertheless acted after Maximilian's death in 1519.
Event: council decree of banishment on 7 November 1519; the preacher Johannes Teuschlein agitated against the Jews.

In Napoleonic times the landowner Erich Carl vom Hagen discovered the settlement of Jews as a source of income: five Jewish families lived in Rüdigershagen in 1808 (40 persons in 1823); synagogue on the estate's sheep farm mentioned 1847; cemetery outside the village (last burial 1908). [Schulz paper pp. 17-18; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 213]

The highpoint of the Jewish population was reached in 1840 with 75 persons (41 in 1852, 16 in 1871); Jews lived in the 'Judenhaus' near the synagogue until the 1920s. [Schulz paper pp. 17-18; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 213]

In 1434 Jews from Rudolstadt contributed, with other Jews of the territory of the Counts of Schwarzburg, to an imperial tax (first direct evidence; a Jew in Erfurt in 1357 named himself after Rudolstadt and may have lived there until the 1349 persecution). [Schulz paper p. 17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 211]
Event: in 1496 all Jews were expelled from the county of Schwarzburg; in 1554 a single Jewish woman still lived in Rudolstadt. [Schulz paper p. 17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 211]

A small Jewish community existed from 1784 to 1874: Prince Ludwig Günther II of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt permitted settlement and exercise of professions on 7 January and 3 March 1784. In 1796 the community was officially recognised and used a prayer room in the house of the merchant David Hirsch Schwabe (mikveh 1796-1816); cemetery from 1800. [Schulz paper p. 17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 212]

Event: the death of the last head of the community, Gustav Callmann, in 1874 ended the Jewish community of Rudolstadt (the last burial in the cemetery was in 1911; the cemetery was levelled in 1935 and became part of a porcelain factory). [Schulz paper p. 17; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 212, 213]

Event: Black Death persecution 1348-50; the Jews of Sinsheim were killed (with those of Bretten, Bruchsal, Waibstadt, Wiesloch, Eppingen); Alemannia Judaica adds that refugees from Worms and Speyer had been taken in and most were massacred. No victim number given.

Benedikt ben David of Sinsheim, one of the few who escaped, was taken under the protection of the Archbishop of Mainz in 1356; Engelhart von Hirschhorn (vassal of the Count Palatine) allowed Jews to find refuge again in Sinsheim against protection money shortly after the massacre.

Event: the Jews of Sondershausen (living there since the late 13th century, proved by a mikveh older than the town wall of about 1300) fell victim to the plague pogrom of 1349; no trace of Jewish settlement in the following centuries. [Schulz paper p. 20; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 234]

A Jewish school and prayer room in a private house are recorded in 1698, the purchase of land for a cemetery (at the Spatenberg) in 1699; in 1695 the Jews of the Schwarzburg residence got the status of 'Schutzbürger'. Event: a synagogue (modest building behind Bebrastraße 6) built 1825/26 was inaugurated on 1 September 1826; the community had at least 26 families; used until its desecration in 1938 (burned out in the 1945 bombing). [Schulz paper p. 20; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 234]

From 1842 Rabbi Philipp Heidenheim ran a private Jewish boarding school for boys; the Jewish school itself had been merged into the municipal schools in 1840. A law of 3 January 1860 created a synagogue community for the Principality of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen seated in Sondershausen (130 members in 1880, 75 in 1924/25). Although local traditions, largely legendary, speak of Jewish settlement in Speyer in Roman times, Jews probably first came to the city in the early 11th century. (century-only date, round year 1000 used)

Wikipedia: 'The first records of Jews in Speyer appear in the 1070s. They were members of the renowned Kalonymos family of Mainz'. Decade given, round year 1070 used (flagged); the formal settlement is 1084.

Bishop Rudiger Huzmann's charter of 15 Sept. 1084 (JE gives 13 Sept.) settled Jews, incl. refugees from Mainz, in a walled quarter in Altspeyer; annual payment 3.5 pounds Speyer money; cemetery land, trade, own chief rabbi.
Emperor Henry IV confirmed and extended the privileges on 19 Feb. 1090 (fines for forced baptism and for injuring a Jew).

Event: First Crusade attack on 3 May 1096 (8 Iyyar); 10-11 Jews killed (JE and Wikipedia say eleven; Encyclopedia.com ten); Bishop John sheltered survivors in his palace; a synagogue is documented in 1096.
Judenhof, central district of the medieval Jewish quarter with synagogue and mikveh, built c. 1100

Synagogue consecrated 21 Sept. 1104 in the Judenhof near the cathedral (second quarter, from c. 1100); mikveh dated 1128 (Wikipedia; Hebrew Wikipedia gives 1110-1120), oldest visible mikveh remains in central Europe.
Romanesque mikveh (Judenbad) in the Judenhof built c. 1110-1120 on architectural grounds (photo caption gives 1126); synagogue consecrated 1104
The mikveh, first mentioned in 1125, was in the vicinity.
Earliest dated tombstone in the Jewish cemetery of Speyer: 1144 CE. Epidat lists 50 inscriptions (1144/45-1408) of the medieval Speyer cemetery; earliest dated stone 1144/45 (CE as given by Epidat)
Only thirteen tombstones from the Jewish cemetery at Speyer have been preserved, the oldest dating from 1145.
Event: Second Crusade massacre; a woman, Minna, was martyred after refusing baptism (Jewish Encyclopedia).

Speyer, Worms and Mainz formed the SHUM federation (c. 1150 per Wikipedia) leading German Jewry until the mid-13th c.; rabbis include Kalonymus b. Moses, Isaac b. Asher ha-Levi, Eliezer b. Joel ha-Levi, Jacob and Solomon of Speyer.

comment: Kalonymos ben Meir, called 'the parnass' (leader) of the Speyer community, served Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa (reign 1152-1190) as financier and financial adviser; a passage of Or Zarua (Isaac of Vienna) tells that when the king demanded tax from the Jews of Speyer, Kalonymos helped them reach a compromise, obtained a reduction of his own share, and then paid with the community nevertheless (Haverkamp pp. 197-198 and n. 37). Online: Wikipedia 'History of the Jews in Speyer': 'Another Kalonymos from Speyer for some time was responsible for the finances of emperor Barbarossa'. No population stated.

Event: blood libel after a Christian was found murdered; R. Isaac b. Asher ha-Levi's daughter was disinterred and hanged, the rabbi and eight others were killed, those in the synagogue freed for a large ransom; Henry VI ordered compensation (1196 per Encyclopedia.com).
Event: In a series of synods beginning in 1196 they promulgated a series of communal decrees known as takkanot Shum, later to be of decisive influence on all Ashkenazi communities.

Altmann, B., 'Studies in Medieval German Jewish History', Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research 10 (1940), p. 71: On 15 March 1255 King William described the Jews of Speyer as 'camerae nostrae servi' (serfs of the royal chamber) (Hilgert, Urkunden zur Geschichte der Stadt Speyer, p. 64, as cited by Altmann).

Event: A flourishing community continued to exist in Speyer until the middle of the 14th century, although the Jews were drawn into a conflict between the bishop and the burghers in 1265, and in 1282 a blood libel brought suffering upon the community.

Event: In 1282 the Jews were accused by Herbord of murdering his grandson; Emperor Rudolph approved the decision in 1283 and ordered the Jews' property to revert to the royal treasury; some Jews emigrated to the Holy Land.

Event: accusation of murder in 1282-1283 (provincial synod Aschaffenburg, 8 Sept. 1282); in 1283 Emperor Rudolph ordered Jewish property confiscated to the royal treasury; June 1291 extra taxes to fund Fort Landau.
In 1286 many Jews of Speyer and the neighboring communities of Worms, Mainz, and Oppenheim were involved in the ill-fated attempt at immigration to Ere?
On June 24, 1291 Emperor Rudolph required the Jews of Speyer to maintain by extra taxes Fort Landau; on May 13, 1313 the Jews promised the emperor 1,500 pounds heller.
Jews owed the emperor 1,500 pounds heller (13 May 1313); in 1337 a diocesan tax fell with Speyer paying 600 pounds heller and the other towns 700.
In 1333 and 1344, the authority of the Jews council was expressly confirmed by the city council of Speyer.

Ludwig the Bavarian admitted six more Jews to the city on June 2, 1337 and imposed taxes on the Jews of Speyer and of Landau, Lauterburg, Deidesheim, Bruchsal, Waibstadt and Udenheim (Nov. 15, 1337); the city paid 600 pounds heller.
In December 1339 both the bishop and the municipality promised their protection to the Jewish community for a period of ten years.
Event: The community suffered somewhat during a blood libel in 1342; it was, however, to meet its destruction during the Black Death persecutions.
Event: after a Christian, Ludwig, was found dead many Jews were tortured and burned (1343); on 11 March 1344 the king approved the city's request to seize Jewish houses.
Event: During the great plague of 1348/49 pogroms swept through France and Germany, especially the Rhineland, and on 22 January 1349 the Jewish community of Speyer was totally wiped out.
Event: Black Death pogrom of 22 Jan. 1349, nearly all Jews including Rabbi Eliakim died, many by setting fire to their homes; on 29 March 1349 Charles IV declared Jewish property the city's.

Some of the Jews who had managed to escape returned to Speyer beginning in 1352, but were driven out anew the following year only to be allowed to return again in 1354, when they were assigned to quarters between Webergasse and the old school.
Jews expelled in 1353 (cemetery planted with corn) and readmitted on 24 Dec. 1354, regaining synagogue and school; the community never regained its former size or status (Wikipedia).
In 1364 Bishop Adolph borrowed 800 guilders from the Jews for a weekly interest of one Strassburg pfennig.

When Nicolaus became bishop (1390) he granted the Jews permission to settle in any city of the diocese for a yearly tribute of 15 gulden; from 1405 to 1421 the Jews were entirely excluded from the city.
In 1394 King Wenceslaus renewed the decree of 1349 by Emperor Charles IV, which declared the Jews to be the property of the city.
Event: Jews excluded from the city 1405-1421, a further expulsion in 1430 with return 1434.
Event: From 1405 to 1421 they were entirely banned from the city.
On Feb. 11, 1431 King Sigismund granted the Jews a privilege that complaints against them be heard only before the municipal court.
There is a document from 1434 in which the Speyer council renewed the right of the Jews to live in the city for another six years, for which 5 to 35 Gilders were to be paid per household.
Event: city council expelled the Jews on 5 May 1435 (8 May per Wikipedia), who had to leave by 11 Nov.; citizenship revoked.
In 1467 the city granted the Jews their protection for a period of ten years.

Population = households x 5: Schudt counted no more than ten Jewish families in Speyer c. 1468 (Jewish Encyclopedia). Bishop Mathias's decree of 21 Oct. 1468 imposed a yellow wheel badge; return allowed 1467-1472 under restrictions; 1469 one synagogue per town.
Event: many Jews died by suicide in 1472 to avoid forced baptism (Wikipedia); no Jews recorded in Speyer by 1500/1529.

120 Jews were martyred during the Rindfleisch disturbances; an established community existed by the end of the 13th century.

The community suffered again during the Armleder persecutions.

JE: In 1338 Archbishop Heinrich of Mayence released the knight Johann von Rieden and his family from all the claims of the Jews of Bischofsheim on account of the Jews that had been slain in that city.
JE: Another persecution took place in 1343; and on the appearance of the Black Death in 1348 many Jews were martyred.

comment: Jewish moneylender Salmann von Wittlich lived in Trier in 1325. Alemannia Judaica (Wittlich page, fetched) lists "Salman von Wittlich (1324-25 in Trier)". Anschuetz: on 18 Aug 1325 Salmann lent the knight Heinrich von der Leyen 4 pounds 10 shillings of Trier money (about 8.6 small florins) at a default rate of 3 pence per pound per week (65 percent a year); the two sureties, Heinrich's brother Nikolaus von der Leyen and the Trier citizen Heinrich Botton, had to keep Einlager (hostage lodging) in Trier, from which Anschuetz concludes that Salmann already lived in Trier (Urkundenbuch der Stadt Wittlich no. 122). The by-name von Wittlich points to Wittlich origin; the map already has a Wittlich 1324 row from the same Alemannia sentence. Salmann stayed the von der Leyen family's long-term creditor (at least 20 years, 1325-1343) and was dead by 12 March 1348 (LHAK Abt. 54 O no. 55). Confidence high for the presence in Trier (online), medium for the deed details (paper only).

Anschuetz thinks he is probably Isaak Sandermann, who became the main creditor of the lords of Neuerburg (the other candidate is Isaak, son of Videmann, brother-in-law of Salmann von Wittlich). The amount is not stated. No online source found. Confidence medium.

comment: On 4 May 1335 Friedrich the Younger von Neuerburg borrowed 2,450 pounds of small Turnosen (about 3,267 small florins) from the Trier Jew Isaak Sandermann and his consortium, secured by sureties including Walter von Clerveaux (Archives de Clerveaux no. 188); Anschuetz identifies the unnamed partners as Salmann von Wittlich and Meyer, Isaak's brother-in-law or son-in-law (gener). In the same year Salmann, called the Trier Jew, was promised 38 Malter of grain (15 wheat, the rest rye) by the steward of Heinrich von der Leyen on 2 July 1335 (Urkundenbuch der Stadt Wittlich no. 162), and the Trier Jew Muskinus received the pledge of half the Vogtei of Ockfen on 11 June 1335 (bought by Heinrich from the monastery of St. Martin for 200 pounds of Heller the same day) and a debt bond of 100 pounds of Trier pennies (about 133 small florins) on 13 June 1335; Anschuetz suspects Muskinus acted as the archbishop's straw man (Strohmann). Muskinus died in 1336. The Jewish Encyclopedia (fetched) dates Muskin's service to Baldwin: "Muskin (1323-36)" (already on the map's Trier 1323 row). Only the Muskin dates have an online page; the deeds are from the paper alone (no online source found for them). Amounts in small florins are Anschuetz's conversions. Confidence medium.

comment: Context of the Armleder persecution. On 6 Feb 1337 Salmann von Wittlich lent Heinrich von der Leyen 280 pounds of Trier pennies (about 373 small florins), a sum above 100 pounds being exceptional even for the leading Moselle lenders, with five sureties keeping Einlager and a clause letting Salmann's helpers or the archbishop's officials seize the pledges (Urkundenbuch der Stadt Wittlich no. 168); six days later (12 Feb) he lent a further 140 pounds of Heller with the same clause (no. 169). Anschuetz links the extra caution to the Armleder persecution, which had lasted from July 1336 into the autumn and was to break out again from summer 1337: although the uprising did not hit most places of the Archbishopric, "die Angst vor einem Übergreifen immens" (fear of spread was great, among the Jews and Archbishop Balduin himself); he finally concludes that the clause was probably only a standard formula for large loans. On 7 Aug 1337 Friedrich von Neuerburg sold estates around Waxweiler for 1,500 pounds of small black Turnosen (about 2,000 small florins) to the Trier Jews Isaak Sandermann, his brother-in-law Meyer and Salmann, with a right of repurchase (Balduineen no. 1251). Anschuetz does not say that Trier itself was attacked; the map's Trier 1336 row (Jewish Encyclopedia) has the Jews pillaged in the Armleder persecution (see conflicts file). No online source found for these deeds. Confidence medium.

Jakob Daniel, Balduin's finance administrator since 1336, had also collected the archbishop's claim on Friedrich (150 pounds of black Turnosen, deed of 10 May 1340, LHAK Abt. 54 N no. 175, Einlager in an open inn in Trier); Anschuetz infers that he was in the Neuerburg area and carried the money back to Trier. comment: On 14 Aug 1347 Friedrich von Neuerburg pledged the village of Oberweis (Eifelkreis Bitburg-Prüm; the paper's Weiß) for 1,000 pounds of Trier money (about 1,143 small florins) to the Jew Jakob Daniel and the heirs of little Isaak, probably the consortium of Salmann von Wittlich and Meyer, perhaps with Isaak Sandermann's son Samuel; they were to receive 100 pounds (about 114 small florins) and 100 Malter of grain each year for five years, with a right of redemption (LHAK Abt. 29 G no. 24). A supplementary declaration of the same day (no. 25) says the Jews could not be held liable for damage by robbery, fire or other causes in the village; Anschuetz asks whether this was mere precaution or a sign of "zunehmenden Judenfeindschaft" (growing hostility to Jews). Jakob Daniel is still active in 1347, whereas the Jewish Encyclopedia dates his service to Baldwin "until 1341" (see conflicts file); Alemannia Judaica (Bergzabern page, fetched) also has him after 1341: in 1344 Count Walram of Zweibrücken pledged Bergzabern to "den Juden Jakob Daniels von Trier und Vivelin dem Roten von Straßburg". Most Jews made their living through moneylending: in 1289 a Jewess, Guta of Ueberlingen, lent a considerable sum of money to Bishop Frederick of Montfort to permit him to participate in a Church Council in Wuerzburg.
The Jew Samuel lent money in 1290 to a minister of high position and to the bishop of Constance; even King Louis iv, the Bavarian, was a debtor of Ueberlingen Jews.

Event: Blood-libel accusation against the Jews of Überlingen in 1331. The Jewish Encyclopedia ('Blood Accusation') records it as "1331 Ueberlingen". The LIST (p. 506, appendix list of blood-libel accusations) lists it too. || Event: Host-desecration accusation against the Jews of Überlingen in 1331. The Jewish Encyclopedia ('Host, Desecration of') records it as "1331. Ueberlingen". The LIST (p. 519, appendix list of host-desecration accusations) lists it too. [Source detail: ; https://www.jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/7906-host-desecration-of]
During a particularly cruel suppression of Jews, some 300 to 400 Jews were burnt to death in their synagogue. Population left blank as this represents a massacre death toll.
A Hebrew inscription on a modern gravestone notes that the bones of unknown Jewish people were buried in the Jewish cemetery in 1349.
A Rabbi Menlin of Ueberlingen is mentioned by Jacob b. Moses Moellin (MaHaRil, 1365–1427).
Jewish settlement was renewed, however, in 1378.
Event: In 1429 a blood libel in Ravensburg brought about the arrest of all the Jews in Ueberlingen: 12 Jews were burned in 1430, and 11 saved themselves by accepting baptism.
David Meyer, a Jewish man from Oberhagenthal, escaped from the prison in Überlingen.
Überlingen is listed as a subcamp within the Dachau concentration camp system. Population left blank as this refers to a Nazi camp.

Prisoners were transferred to Überlingen am Bodensee to work underground on construction projects before being evacuated to Allach concentration camp in 1945. Population left blank as this reflects camp prisoners rather than a resident community.
Human bones from the 14th century were found during construction, identified as the remains of four Jewish people from the former Jewish cemetery.
A new gravestone with a Hebrew inscription was made for the 14th-century Jewish bones discovered in 2006, and they were buried in the Überlinger cemetery.

The first documentary evidence of a community in Ulm dates from 1241, when a sum of six silver marks in taxes was paid by Jews.

Earliest dated tombstone in the Jewish cemetery of Ulm: 1243 CE. German Wikipedia: the oldest Jewish tombstone from Ulm dates from 1243; the cemetery is first mentioned in 1281 (Alemannia Judaica also reports a reused stone of 1436)
As it grew during the 13th and early 14th centuries, its members were engaged primarily in moneylending. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)
A declaration of the city council of 1274 terms the Jewish community a privileged Darleihergenossenschaft (loan society).
Middle Ages Jewish cemetery first recorded in 1281
By the aid of a Jew the Bavarians reduced the city on April 20, 1316; on Nov. 10, 1324 Louis the Bavarian pledged the Jewish state taxes of Ulm to the counts of Oettingen.
Jews were allowed to own houses, and although a Judengasse is mentioned in 1331, Jews were not restricted to one quarter.

On Aug. 1, 1348 the Jews of Ulm were officially reprimanded for collecting part of their taxes from the Jews of Schelklingen and Ehingen; about this time (Black Death) the Jews of Ulm were accused of poisoning the wells and persecuted by mobs.

Event: Despite measures taken by the municipal council to protect the Jews, on Jan. 30, 1349, during the Black Death persecutions, the Jewish quarter was stormed by a mob and the community was all but destroyed.
Jewish community regained its synagogue in 1354 (and the cemetery 1356) after the 30 January 1349 pogrom burned the Jewish quarter
In 1366 a number of Jews were granted partial citizenship.

Aug. 11, 1392 edict of Wenceslaus on liquidating the Jewish debt (Eberhard III of Wuerttemberg); regulations of the Red Book dated Nov. 24, 1395 restricted the Jews (confined to the Jewish quarter from Palm Saturday to Easter Wednesday).
On Sept. 30, 1421 laws were promulgated forbidding Christians to be employed by Jews; on May 15, 1422 Jews were prohibited from lending on wool or cotton.
Event: In the middle of the fifteenth century the Jews of Ulm were accused of the ritual murder of the Swiss boy Ludwig of Bruck at Ravensburg in 1428.
Households x5: Lexikon table 'Juden in Ulm' gives um 1430 = '13 jüdische Familien' (approximate, c. 1430). Secondary compilation (Alicke Lexikon).

In the 15th century, Ulm grew in economic and political importance, while the Jewish community, oppressed by heavy taxation and regulations restricting their financial activities, declined. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)
Event: In 1457 Jewish noncitizens were expelled; in 1499 all Jews were given five months to leave the city.
Households x5: same Lexikon table gives 1495 = '11 jüdische Familien'.

Event: A Freiheitsbrief of Maximilian I published on Aug. 6, 1499 authorized the expulsion of the Jews; their real estate was sold to the city for 5,000 gulden; expulsion set five months later; no Jews were admitted in the district until 1526 (one at Albeck).
On July 18, 1541 Charles V issued a Freiheitsrecht forbidding the Jew in the Ulm district to borrow money; second Freiheitsbrief of Ferdinand I on March 28, 1561.

Walldorf, owned by three noble families who all took in protected Jews, grew from the 17th century into the largest Jewish community between Rennsteig and Rhön (the only one whose archive survives); a common cemetery has existed since 1737 (extended 1790); three communities, each with a prayer room and school, merged in 1789 and built a new synagogue and school. The Count of Henneberg demanded in vain the expulsion of these Jews in 1560. [Schulz paper p. 23; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 258]

Event: the three Jewish communities of Walldorf merged into one in 1789 and decided to build a new synagogue and school (synagogue extended 1845; school, bath-house and bakery burned in 1836). [Schulz paper p. 23; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 258]

After the 1349 persecution, Jews of Weimar are mentioned again in 1379 and 1390 (earlier Jews named after Weimar in 1323, 1327 and 1338); 8 adult taxpaying Jews in 1418; the physician Moses Staffelsteiner, in the service of the Elector of Saxony, lived here after 1529. Households x5: Alemannia Judaica: '1418 gab es in der Stadt acht erwachsene erwerbstätige Juden (sechs Männer, zwei Frauen in sechs Familien)'; six families x5. Money-lending community.

A new Jewish group (not an official community) arose after Duchess Anna Amalia appointed Jacob Elkan as court Jew on 7 April 1770; in 1789 three important families lived in Weimar (Elkan, Löser, Ulmann) as a 'private community'. [Schulz paper pp. 23-24; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 264]

Jacob Elkan laid out a Jewish cemetery in 1774 (first burial 1775, extended 1808, last burial 1898; part restored as a memorial on 20 November 1983); in 1805 he built a private prayer room (synagogue) and a mikveh in his house at Windischenstraße 25. [Schulz paper pp. 23-24; Schwierz 2007 (German original) p. 265]

The first Jews probably settled in Weißenburg at the end of the 13th century; in 1288 the town asked the Nuremberg council for its Jewish pledge law. A Jewish tombstone of a woman dated 19 Nov 1290 survives.
Event: Jews murdered in the Rintfleisch persecution of 1298; the names of some martyrs are preserved. In 1312 the Nuremberg Judenordnung was put in force or renewed.

Event: Jews murdered again in the plague-period persecution of 1348/49; a few Jews resettled some years later; a new pogrom with several dead followed in 1384 during a craftsmen's revolt against the patricians.

The Jewish Cemetery in Berlin's Weißensee district was established and inaugurated.
The Adass Jisroel Jewish cemetery in Weissensee began to be used.
Social politician Max Hirsch (1832-1905) was buried in the cemetery.
Publisher Rudolf Mosse (1843-1920) was buried in the cemetery.
Hebrew writer Micha Josef Bin Gorion (1865-1921) was buried in the cemetery.
A field of honour was established south of the main mourning hall for 395 Jewish soldiers who died during the First World War.
Painter Lesser Ury (1861-1931) was buried in the cemetery.
Sally (Salomon) Rehfisch passed away and was buried in the Weissensee Cemetery.
Publisher Samuel Fischer (1859-1934) was buried in the cemetery.
The cemetery contains a burial site for around 90 Torah scrolls desecrated during the pogrom night of 1938.
The Adass Jisroel Jewish cemetery in Weissensee, containing approximately 3,000 graves, ceased its primary period of use.
Rabbi Martin Riesenburger and his wife sought refuge within the cemetery walls from 1943 to 1944.
Rabbi Martin Riesenburger held his first post-war prayer service on May 11, 1945, and the first memorial plaque was installed in September.
From 1955 until unification, only the small Jewish community in East Berlin used the cemetery.
The main Jewish cemetery in Weissensee contained approximately 115,000 graves.
Large-scale restoration and preservation measures were taken at the Adass Jisroel cemetery in 1985/1986.
An exhibit about the Jewish cemetery at Weissensee was held from November 1988 to January 1989.
The Adass Jisroel cemetery in Weissensee was presumably used again for burials starting around 1990.
An urn containing the ashes of Auschwitz victims was placed in the cemetery in a solemn ceremony on January 27, 1992.
By 1998, more than 115,200 Jewish citizens of Berlin had been buried at the Weißensee Cemetery.
In October 1999, suspected Neo-Nazis vandalized about 100 graves at the Jewish Cemetery at Weissensee.

comment: Charter of 1212 concerning the Jews of Würzburg (Aronius, Regesten no. 386). Aronius's summary (OCR text): the Jews Jakob and Viskelin of Würzburg buy for themselves and their heirs the courtyard (Hof) of Albert Stukeler from his son Friedrich and from Heinrich; because Friedrich and Heinrich with their wives and sons returned the courtyard to the Neumünster chapter, the chapter conveys it to these Jews against a yearly delivery in autumn of one and a half urns ('Krügen') of wine (the OCR text is partly garbled here: it reads 'anderttialb Krllgen Wein' and, in the Latin quotation, 'dimidiam aannatini'), so that they and their heirs hold it in peace under the chapter's protection. The Jewish witnesses listed last include Nathan (called 'der Judenmeister' in Aronius's summary, i.e. the head of the Jews) and a man called Caleman, together with Jews named after Schweinfurt, Rothenburg and Augsburg (the map's Schweinfurt 1212 row comes from this same charter). Cuno (n. 54) cites the charter only as an early witness 'Caleman' at the end of a document concerning Würzburg Jews (Aronius no. 386, p. 172 in his edition); the year 1212 is Cuno's. In the archive.org OCR text the entry has no readable date line; its page shows the preceding Cologne entry cross-referring to no. 386 and dated 1212, and the book's index (OCR) lists Jews of Würzburg under 1212. Persons are named in the Notes only. The map has Würzburg rows for 1170, 1182, 1197 and 1250 but none for 1212. Confidence medium-high. [Source detail: (Julius Aronius, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden im fränkischen und deutschen Reiche bis zum Jahre 1273, Berlin 1902, no. 386; OCR full text)]

Mentgen quotes it as an example of expulsions in intra-urban conflicts that hit Christians and Jews alike (see Karlheinz Müller, Die Würzburger Judengemeinde im Mittelalter, 2004, pp. 79f). August 1265 ein Friedensvertrag geschlossen") but says nothing about Jews, so the Jewish clause rests on the paper alone (no online source found). Event: Rintfleisch persecution, 23 July 1298: Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte states that all 841 Jews of Würzburg were murdered plus a further 100 refugees from the countryside; names recorded in the Nuremberg Memorbuch. Population 841 taken from the source's wording 'all 841 Würzburg Jews'.
From the early 14th c. a new Jewish quarter formed on today's Marktplatz; the city council protected the Jews during the Armleder persecution of 1336.

Event: Black Death 'Weinreben-Pogrom' April 1349: Jews accused of well poisoning, many died in their burning houses and synagogue, the quarter was razed and a Marienkapelle built on the synagogue site; 1,455 gravestones from the cemetery found in the 19th-20th c. (JVL: 1,508 found in Pleich in 1987, dated 1138-1347); remains of a mikveh survive under the sacristy. Survivors fled to Erfurt, Frankfurt, Mainz.
Jews had returned by 1377 (JVL); from 1376/77 only individual families were tolerated when profitable to the bishop (hdbg).
Event: Bishop Johann II von Brunn ordered expropriation and expulsion of all Jews in 1422; the community avoided ruin only by paying a large sum.
A new synagogue was built in 1446 (JVL); the community remained small through the 15th c.

Population = households x 5, source count 20 households: hdbg says only about 20 Jewish households still lived in Würzburg c. 1450, when a badge was imposed, lending forbidden and expulsions occurred.

Event: expulsion order: Bishop Godfrey (Gottfried) of Würzburg, reigning duke of Franconia, issued under the influence of John of Capistrano an ordinance (1453) decreeing the banishment of the Jews of his duchy; towns and landowners were told to expel them and Jewish creditors lost part of their debts (JE 'Capistrano'). The LIST p.229 has Würzburg in its expulsion list under 1454 - year differs, see conflicts file. The ordinance covered the whole duchy; the city is the bishop's seat.
Event: Bishop Friedrich expelled the Jews of Würzburg in 1565 and Bishop Julius continued the work, banishing the community and confiscating the cemetery.
Event: In 1567 the Jews were expelled from the town and settled in nearby Heidingsfeld.

Event: Hep-Hep riots began here on 2 August 1819; after several days troops were called in and the Jewish population fled the city, spending several days in tents nearby. Wikipedia: many Jews injured and property destroyed, no deaths reported (the LIST says many Jews were killed).
By the end of the 19th century, the number of Jews in Würzburg was 2567, representing three percent of the city's population.
On the eve of the Nazis' rise to power in 1933, 2000 Jews lived in Würzburg, a rabbinic center and home to the Jewish Teachers Seminary.

In 1933 there were 2145 Jews living in Würzburg, two percent of the city's population. The community operated two synagogues, a community center, a ritual bath, and a cemetery. [Also reported by: https://germanhistorydocs.org/en/nazi-germany-1933-1945/jews-deported-from-wuerzburg-april-25-1942]
In 1936, the Jewish primary school had 180 students. The Bavarian Students' Association forbade renting rooms from Jews, and Jewish passports were confiscated.
On November 27, 1941, 202 Jews from the city were deported to a camp in Riga, Latvia; only fifteen survived the war.
A database record lists 276 persons deported from Würzburg.
On April 25, 1942, the third major forced removal occurred; 78 Jews from the city were among a transport of 852 Jews deported to Sobibor death camp.
An appendix in the Biographisches Handbuch Würzburger Juden 1900-1945 lists 276 Jews who were brought to Würzburg prior to their deportation.
The Würzburg Jewish Community Collection contains lists of Jewish survivors, including 34 returnees to Würzburg.

Roman Aquincum (Pannonia Inferior): funerary stele with a Greek memorial text, three menorahs (in the pediment, between the heads of the two adults and below the child's head) and the phrase 'one God' three times; catalogued as Pan 2 in Noy/Panayotov/Bloedhorn, Inscriptiones Judaicae Orientis I (2004) and dated 'late 4th century CE' in Hagith Sivan's review (BMCR 2005.09.58); the Biblical Archaeology Society image page says 4th century, 'a Jewish family from Panonia', and gives the Hungarian National Museum as holder. 375 is the central value of 'late 4th century'. The stone is a reuse: the original Latin funerary inscription on it commemorates Claudia Maximilla (aged 25) and Domitius Domnius (aged 37, died in Raetia). Sivan warns that associating an inscription with ethnicity or creed is difficult, but menorahs plus the 'one God' formula make a Jewish family very likely. This is a dated 4th-century fact that complements the existing undated Roman rows for Aquincum/Budapest (200 and 250, from Wikipedia/Patai). No population. Event: deportation. After the Ottoman victory at Mohacs, Sultan Suleiman decreed on 22 September 1526 that "all the Jews seized at Buda, Esztergom, and elsewhere, more than 2,000 in number" be distributed among Ottoman cities (Wikipedia). The atlas (map 108) gives 1526 as the year of an expulsion from Esztergom (Gran), "thought to be the result of an accusation of Jewish collusion with the invading Turks", and (box 5) a transfer of more than 2,000 Jews from Hungary by Suleiman. The atlas text (p. 108) also calls Esztergom the most important Jewish community of 11th-century Hungary.

Two Case Studies", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), pp. 72-75
comment: Charter of the Zalavár abbey of 1263 (22 May in the Hungarian edition; the Austrian regest discusses 8 February, 15 April, 22 May and 18 August as possible dates): Master Vid (Vitus) of the Gutkeled kindred gave the monastery of Csatár estates on the Mura and in Somogy county in compensation for its Bible, entrusted to him as patron, which he had pledged for 70 marks to "Farkas zsidónak, a vasvári" (iudeo Farcasio de Castroferreo, German Eisenburg) and which was lost. A note in the Bible itself (the Admont Giant Bible) records the deposit and the repayment terms (Wiedl: 24.5 marks, in instalments). The Jew Farkas is probably identical with Lublin (Wölfel), son of King Béla IV's court chamberlain Henel and a prominent financier of Hungary, Austria and Styria who appears from 1255 (Wiedl p. 73). The pledge was made some time before 1263. The map has Vasvár rows only for 1880-1941; this is the first medieval Jewish presence there on the map. No population. Confidence high. [Source detail: (Scheiber, ed., Magyar zsidó oklevéltár IX, Budapest 1966, section "Vasvár", pp. 8-9); (Brugger and Wiedl, Regesten zur Geschichte der Juden in Österreich im Mittelalter, Band 1: bis 1338, Innsbruck 2005, Nr. 40-41, pp. 55-56)]

Event: the Goa Inquisition was established (Wikipedia: 1560; infobox 1561). It originally targeted New Christians, i.e. Jews who had been force-converted and had migrated from Portugal to India; Goa was a sanctuary for such converts, who lived in what became known as the 'Jew street', and in 1557 a Goan New Christian woman named Caldeira and 19 others were arrested for Judaizing before the tribunal. Records show at least 57 people executed (the book gives the same figure, p. 295, ref 1560.2). The inquisition sat in Old Goa; the map's Goa marker is the state centroid. Disagreement: the book says it lasted 1560-1820, Wikipedia says it was finally abolished in 1812 (suspended 1774-1778). Listed in the conflicts file.

The Dutch defeated the Portuguese; the Jews rebuilt their synagogues and enjoyed civil and religious liberty.

Weak-to-moderate row - boundary evidence plus one named synagogue head. Achziv (Ecdippa; rabbinic Keziv/Chezib) is the northern limit of the territory re-settled by the returnees from Babylon: Mishnah Shevi'it 6:1 ('as far as Chezib'), Mishnah Challah 4:8 (Rabban Gamaliel, c. 80-118: three territories for hallah, 'from the Land of Israel to Chezib') - Sefaria texts of both consulted; Tosefta Demai 1:4 says 'Cheziv alone is exempt from demai' (the town itself was treated as non-Israelite for the purpose, because of its Tyrian population) and speaks of Jewish landowners in Syria. Wikipedia 'Achziv': Ecdippa was a Roman road station and Bordeaux Pilgrim station in 333 (an IIP milestone of 83 CE, achz0001, marks the Akko-Antioch road); Midrash Vayikra Rabba 37:4 and the Babylonian Talmud name it. Positive evidence of a Jewish community: Wikipedia 'Gamaliel II' reports that at Ecdippa 'the archisynagogue Scipio asked him a question which he answered by letter' (c. 80-118) - a synagogue head at Ecdippa - and a friendly conversation with a pagan on the road from Acre to Ecdippa. No Jewish archaeological remains from Achziv itself in 70-550 are reported in the sources I read (the IIP epigraphic corpus has no Jewish Achziv inscription); a pottery workshop belongs to the end of the Roman era. Year 200 is the conventional date of the Mishnah. Note: Hebrew Wikipedia's claim that Rabbi Akiva's students 'stayed with the Jewish community of Achziv' (b. Avodah Zarah 25b) is NOT supported by the text, which says they were travelling to Keziv and told bandits they were going to Akko.

Literary mention; identification DISPUTED, favoured: Khirbet 'En el-Kizbe (Boaz Zissu and Erasmus Gass 2011: it 'strongly support[s] identifying this site with ancient Achzib/Chezib/Chozeba'; the ancient name is preserved in the nearby spring 'Ain el-Kezbeh) (en.wikipedia Achziv of Judah). Year of Data -1200 = Joshua list convention. Josh 15:44: Achzib in Judah's lowland list with Keilah and Mareshah (checked on the fetched KJV chapter page); 1 Chr 4:22 'the men of Chozeba' (checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; Chozeba = Achzib per en.wikipedia). Rival proposals: Khirbet a-Sheikh Ghazi (some historical geographers); Tell el-Beida / Tel Lavnin (formerly tentative, rejected by Zissu because the site was clearly occupied in the Byzantine period, while Eusebius describes Chezib as a deserted place; BibleWalks still suggests Horvat Lavnin); ruins near Keilah and Khirbet Beit Nesib (Saarisalo, Elliger, Press); a place between Keilah and Mareshah (Cheyne 1898). Coordinates 31.6833 N, 35.0169 E are the Wikipedia infobox's general location for the site (about 0.2 km from the modern moshav Avi'ezer). Not the Achziv of Asher in the north, which already has a marker named 'Achzib'. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achziv_of_Judah; https://biblewalks.com/lavnin

Literary only: Mic 1:14: the houses of Achzib will prove deceptive (a wordplay on the name) to the kings of Israel; Mic 1:15 follows with Mareshah and Adullam (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; paraphrased). Year of Data -730 = late 8th century convention for Micah's oracle. Identification disputed as in the first Achzib row.

Only surveys; no strata, area or population estimate. Judahite.
Acre was a principal base of the Romans when they suppressed the Jewish revolt of 66-70 CE.
Jewish individuals originating from Hrubieszow recorded as living in Acre: Leah Bizan (Varman), Feyge Vidavski (Bernfait), Frida Pomp (Sol), and Yechezkel Shnaydman.

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Land of Israel: History': in the 66-70 war Greek cities massacred their Jews, 'such as in Caesarea, Beth-Shean, Acre, and Ashkelon'; these communities were later rebuilt and by the end of the first century 'there were flourishing Jewish communities in places like Caesarea' and the other coastal and Decapolis cities (Acre among those listed). Year 90 = conventional 'late first century'. Secondary; confidence medium.

Mishnah Avodah Zarah 3:4 (Sefaria): Proklos son of Philosophos 'once asked a question of Rabban Gamliel in the city of Akko when he was bathing in the bathhouse of Aphrodite' - so the patriarch Gamaliel II (nasi c. 80-118; Wikipedia 'Gamaliel II') was in Akko, using the town's bath, c. 100 (midpoint of his term). Wikipedia 'Gamaliel II' also records a friendly conversation with a non-Jew 'on the way from Acre to Ecdippa'. This shows a rabbinic (Jewish) presence/visits at Ptolemais-Acre, not a settled community by itself. Rabbinic-literary (tannaitic); the Mishnah text is high confidence.

Rabban Gamaliel II (nasi at Yavne, c. 80-c. 118; year 100 is the conventional midpoint) bathes in the bathhouse of Aphrodite at Akko and replies to the pagan Proclus son of Philosophos: Mishnah Avodah Zarah 3:4 (Encyclopaedia Judaica Acre: 'Rabbi Gamaliel II visited a bath dedicated to Aphrodite in Acre'; the Mishnah text was checked in Sefaria's API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Mishnah_Avodah_Zarah.3.4). Tannaitic literary source dating a sage's presence in Acre in the generation after 70; it does not say how many Jews lived there. Rabbinic law treated Acre as lying outside the halakhic Land of Israel (b. Gittin 2a) and the Jerusalem Talmud disputes whether the land-dependent commandments apply there, so Jewish settlement was partial or doubtful. Population blank.

Wikipedia 'Acre, Israel': Ptolemais 'grew to more than 20,000 inhabitants in the second century under emperor Hadrian' and 'greatly flourished for two more centuries'; 'most of the population was made of local Phoenicians and Jews' (undated statement). The 20,000 figure is for the whole city, not Jewish-only, so Population is left blank. Year 150 = conventional 2nd century.

Halakhic reference, not direct evidence of residents: Mishnah Gittin 1:2 records the tannaitic dispute over Acre's status - Rabbi Judah: 'from Akko northward is outside Eretz Yisrael, and Akko itself is like north of Eretz Yisrael'; Rabbi Meir: 'Akko is like Eretz Yisrael with regard to bills of divorce' (Sefaria API text consulted). R. Judah and R. Meir were active in the mid-2nd century (year 150 is a conventional placement). That Acre was legally a border town between the Land of Israel and Syria explains why the rabbis' own sources (Mishnah Shevi'it 6:1, Challah 4:8, Demai 1:3) place the northern limit of Jewish-settled territory at Acre-Chezib, and why the Jews of Acre (Encyclopaedia Judaica) buried their dead outside the city. Use as supporting context for the 100 and 250 rows, weak as proof of a resident Jewish population.

Later Roman/Talmudic Acre. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Avi-Yonah/Gibson): after the war the Jews re-established their community because Acre was 'the most convenient port for Galilee'; 'in later Roman times the Jewish and Samaritan quarters were also situated near the Old Port'; the dead were buried outside the city at the foot of Mt Carmel (to lie within the halakhic Land of Israel) and later at Kefar Yasif; Acre was the port of embarkation for the Patriarchs and other rabbis travelling to Rome and a home port for their commercial fleet; its fair was one of the three most famous in Eretz Israel (tj Av. Zar. 1:4, 39d). EJ gives no precise date ('later Roman times'), so year 250 is a conventional mid-3rd-century placement (Amoraic period) with low-moderate date confidence. In Byzantine times Acre was a bishopric under Tyre with 'a large Samaritan community' (EJ), i.e. a Jewish minority beside strong Samaritan and Christian populations. Not a population figure.

Gallus revolt: Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Land of Israel: History' - the revolt that began in June 351 at Sepphoris 'spread through Galilee and reached Lydda in the south'; 'the decisive battle took place near Acre'. Literary (Christian chroniclers) tradition as summarised by EJ; medium confidence.
