[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332). Replaces first-pass row for Persian, which said evidence at Dura itself was thin: Ofer's survey (1993 dissertation, as reported on Hamichlol and Hebrew Wikipedia; Kochavi 1967/8 survey site 154) records Persian-period pottery over about 12 dunams, similar to the late Iron Age remnant (Iron IID about 12 dunams) and much below Iron IIC (about 30 dunams). Hamichlol: resettled on a smaller scale after Sennacherib (701); whether it was destroyed by Babylon is unclear. People: Idumean/Edomite is likely (the Hamichlol Idumea article says some date Idumean settlement to the Persian period via Maresha ostraca, with no other historical evidence); no Jewish evidence. Identification Adoraim = Dura is the accepted one. Survey data are second-hand; the Ofer and Kochavi publications were not accessible. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167). Replaces first-pass row for Early Hellenistic: the first pass had no survey-based statement. Ofer's survey (via Hamichlol): Hellenistic is the strongest ceramic presence, about 29 dunams, near the 30-dunam maximum. Kochavi's 1967/8 survey (CMHL database) recorded handles of Rhodian amphorae (Kochavi and Ovadiah 1972) and Hellenistic pottery. Zeno visited it in 259 BCE and it was one of the 'chief cities of Idumea' (encyclopedia.com, Encyclopaedia Judaica text). Idumean population; no Jewish evidence. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63). Replaces first-pass row for Hasmonean on two points. (1) 1 Macc 13:20 only says Trypho 'circled around by the way to Adora' with Simon's army shadowing him; Adora is a route point, nothing in the verse says Simon 'stopped' Trypho there (usual date 142 BCE). (2) Josephus, Ant. 13.9.1 (penelope.uchicago.edu): Hyrcanus took 'Dora, and Marissa, cities of Idumea', subdued the Idumeans and let them stay if they accepted circumcision and Jewish law; ISBE cites the same passage. Date varies: c. 129 BCE (Josephus order) or 113-112 BCE (other sources). The Idumeans of Adora therefore became Jews by conversion; this is textual: no miqva'ot, ossuaries or Hasmonean coins from Dura itself were found in fetched pages. Ofer's survey: ceramic presence continues at Hellenistic scale (about 29 dunams; no finer subdivision). Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Replaces first-pass row for Early Roman on three points. (1) Correction: the first pass (and the Encyclopaedia Judaica text on encyclopedia.com, and a Schalit suggestion in Hamichlol) say Gabinius made Adora the seat of one of his councils. Josephus, Ant. 14.5.4 (penelope.uchicago.edu) lists the five councils as Jerusalem, Gadara, Amathus, Jericho and Sepphoris; and the 'Dora' Gabinius rebuilt in Ant. 14.5.3 (with Samaria, Ashdod, Scythopolis, Anthedon, Raphia, Marissa, Gaza) is not called Adora and is generally taken as coastal Dor. The Gabinius-council claim is not supported by the fetched Josephus text. (2) Ofer's survey (via Hamichlol): Roman 1 about 11 dunams (contraction from about 29); no Roman 2 sherds. (3) Jewish evidence in the area but not at Dura itself: Khirbet el-Muraq (Hilkiyah's palace), a Hasmonean-Herodian mansion c. 12-13 km west of Hebron, administratively part of the village of Dura/Adoraim, has stepped miqva'ot, chalk stone vessels and prutot of years 2-3 of the First Revolt (Damati excavated 1968-72; destruction 68 CE per Damati, 132-136 CE per Raviv and Langford); owners may be local Jews, Herodian settlers or converted Idumeans. It lay on the Judea-Idumea border and is a separate site, so it does not prove a Jewish population at Dura. Josephus War 4.9.7-9: Simon bar Giora and later Cerealis ravaged Idumea and took Hebron (Dura not named). Population blank.

Ancient Fiq/Aphek (kibbutz Afiq is next to the depopulated Syrian town of Fiq): a basalt column with a seven-branched menorah and the Aramaic inscription 'I (am) Yehudah the cantor (hazzan)' (IIP FIQG0001, Aramaic/Hebrew, dated 300-399 CE; year 350 = midpoint) presumably stood in a Byzantine synagogue; found in the 19th c., later recovered near Quneitra and now in the Golan Archaeological Museum. Jewish presence at Aphek is also attested in Mishnaic and Talmudic sources (en.wikipedia Fiq). The town was mixed in Late Antiquity: Greek inscriptions of the 5th c. mention a bishop Gerontius, a deaconess Nanna and Christian-style epitaphs. Bornblum 'Aphek (Fiq)': Jewish synagogue site, unexcavated; some decorated pillars from an Ark (?) are in Moshav Nov. An IAA trial excavation at Kibbutz Afiq (O. Zingboym, HA-ESI 121, 2009) records that surveys revealed 'numerous architectural elements from churches and a synagogue that indicated the area was inhabited during the Byzantine period' and found a basalt structure of the Byzantine period (4th-8th c.). Confidence medium.

Josephus (War 2.20.6) fortified 'the rock of the Achabari' (Acchabaron) in Upper Galilee in 66 CE; identified with caves in the 135-m cliff south of Akbara (Khirbet al-'Uqeiba is the Roman village Acchabare). Tradition holds the 129 interconnected caves sheltered Jews in the war with Rome. Dating basis: literary (Josephus). Confidence high for the fortification, medium for the identification.

Excavations in the Akbara caves found coins of Dor and Sepphoris dated to the reign of the emperor Trajan (98-117 CE), suggesting use of the cliff caves in the early 2nd century (conventional year 110). Dating basis: coins. Confidence low-medium (single secondary source).

Akbara (Akbari/Akbora) is mentioned in rabbinic literature from the second half of the 3rd century CE: R. Yannai, first-generation amora, established a bet midrash and agricultural community of his disciples there; the school of R. Jose bar Abin was also in Akbara; R. Elazar ben Simeon is said to have lived there and the tombs of several sages (R. Nehurai, R. Yannai, R. Dostai) are located there by later tradition. Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium.

Wikipedia 'Akbara': the village appears in rabbinic literature 'as early as second half of the third century CE' (midpoint 275 used) - Rabbi Yannai reportedly set up a bet midrash there, a school associated with Rabbi Jose bar Abin was there, and R. Yohanan debated the sages of Akbara; coins of Dor and Sepphoris from Trajan's time (98-117) were found in the cliff caves; Khirbet al-'Uqeiba is identified as Roman Achabare, with building foundations, wine presses, tombs and the walls of ancient synagogues ('early Galilean type' per Foerster, undated). Josephus fortified the rock of Acchabaron in 66-67. Rabbinic-literary and archaeological.

Jewish village (Akbaria), Leibner (2009), Table 11: size D (21-40 dunams) c. 50 BCE-350 CE, B (4-10 dunams) c. 350-550, then abandoned or in significant decline in the first half of the 6th c.; large amounts of Late Roman (3rd-4th c.) pottery versus limited Byzantine, so its monumental synagogue may belong to the first wave of the 3rd c. - insufficient data. Year 300 = conventional.

Synagogue: remains of a 20-m ashlar wall (up to three courses), part of a frieze and a decorated pilaster, possibly a Hebrew inscription (unpublished; Tfilinski 1965), documented by E. Damati (1988); G. Foerster identifies the ruins as an 'early Galilean type' synagogue. Late Roman and/or Byzantine (conventional year 400). Dating basis: architecture. Confidence low-medium.

Urman linked to lists of priestly courses (a competing reading). Evidence for a Jewish village and synagogue at the site Schumacher recorded as Shuwikha (possible biblical Sokho).

Remains of a Jewish village and synagogue of the Talmudic period (he.wikipedia; Bornblum: Jewish, Late Roman/Byzantine, unexcavated, in a military firing zone): lintel with an eagle, window lintel with two seven-branched menorahs, a stone with wreath and Heracles knot, Doric capitals; a gravestone read 'Shimon ben Yustinos' (Schumacher); Greek boundary stone naming two villages. Surveyed by Schumacher 1885/1913, Gutman 1968, Urman 1970, Ma'oz 1981. A Turkmen village later reused the stones; most of the documented pieces are now lost. en.wikipedia ('Al-Ahmadiyah') adds that the Gutman 1968 survey put the ancient settlement at 35 dunams, that two ancient synagogues are reported (Bornblum lists one), that it is 'possibly the site of the ancient Roman Jewish settlement of Ecbatana' (conjecture) and that a nine-branched menorah relief indicates Jewish settlement in the 4th c. Year 450 is a conventional date for undated Late Roman/Byzantine remains.

Ruins of Sokho/Ahmadiyya in the central Golan, 1.5 km SE of Ein Nashut: remains of a synagogue 'from the same period' as Ein Nashut (5th-7th c.) are reported (Wikipedia, Ein Nashut); Bornblum database: two stones with menorah reliefs, many architectural elements, fragments of a lintel with animals and Hebrew and Aramaic inscriptions (unexcavated). Conventional year 500 (5th-7th c.); low confidence.

Hasmonean (-167 to -63): fortress built by Alexander Jannaeus (104-77 BCE) (BibleWalks; Hebrew Wikipedia: named for Jannaeus, or possibly Salome Alexandra) as garrison, treasury and prison. 2025 excavation (Wikipedia; BibleWalks): Hasmonean building with white plaster walls, a miqveh (ritual bath) and columned structure, i.e. a Jewish royal garrison. Aristobulus II held it against Pompey (63 BCE); Gabinius demolished it in 57 BCE. Fortress not a town; no population estimate. Dates: construction placed in Jannaeus's reign (from 104 BCE), later than the period start.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Herod rebuilt it as a palace-fortress (peristyle with Doric columns, mosaics, painted plaster); imprisoned Mariamne and Alexandra and buried his sons Alexander and Aristobulus there (BibleWalks). Wikipedia, Israel365 and Times of Israel: destruction layer from Roman siege; ostraca with Jewish names (Pinhas, Levi, Eleazar bar Ger... from Beit Akiman) and Tiberius-era coins suggest rebel use during the Great Revolt (66-70 CE), not confirmed. Fortress razed in the Revolt and never resettled. Excavated 1980s (Tsafrir, Magen) and 2025-2026 (Raviv). Jewish garrison and royal use; no population estimate.

Remains of an ancient synagogue at Alma: a bilingual Hebrew-Aramaic lintel fragment with a blessing of peace on the place and on Israel and a dedication by the artisan Levi (dated with the Bar'am synagogues), a second two-line Aramaic inscription re-used in the modern synagogue; Byzantine ceramics; a Jewish town under Roman Judaea (Wikipedia: synagogue perhaps 3rd century, never excavated). Dating basis: epigraphy; conventional year 300 (3rd c. per Wikipedia; Bar'am parallel suggests later). Confidence low-medium. Tombs of tannaim (Eleazar ben Arach, 'Eliezer b. comment: Placed under the existing snapshot marker 'Anaharath' (snapshot pin c. 0.1 km from the summit of Tel Rekhesh, where the dig below took place; Anaharath is the biblical name proposed for Tel Rekhesh - that identification was not re-checked by me in a fetched source, but the pin location coincides with the tell). Early Roman assembly room, probably a synagogue, on a Jewish estate (farmstead) on top of Tel Rekhesh: a small room lined with limestone ashlar benches along the walls, excavated by M. Aviam, H. Kuwabara and Y. Paz, 'A First-Second Century CE Synagogue on a Jewish Estate on Top of Tel Rekhesh' (Tel Aviv 46, 2019; Ancient Synagogues Revealed 2023). en.wikipedia lists it among the Second Temple-period synagogues as 'destroyed in Bar Kochba revolt (?)'. Year 100 = conventional midpoint of the 1st-2nd c. CE span; the destruction hypothesis is flagged as uncertain. The 2009 season report (Tsukimoto, Kuwabara, Paz, HA-ESI 123, 2011) dates walls on the acropolis to the 1st c. CE, 'a period when a Jewish settlement flourished at Tel Rekhesh', with Roman remains of the 1st-2nd c. throughout the upper mound. The 2023 season (13th; S. Hasegawa, H. Kuwabara & Y. Paz, HA-ESI 137, 2025, https://www.hadashot-esi.org.il/report_detail_eng.aspx?id=27737) still describes 'the previously exposed synagogue of the Early Roman period (first-second centuries CE)' and 'additional remnants of the Jewish village of which the synagogue was part, located to its east'. The site lies in the Tabor valley (Lower Galilee), listed for this sub-area at the owner's request; may overlap with the Lower Galilee research.

comment: Tel Rekhesh (Tell el-Mukharkhash; the biblical Anaharath identification is conjectural): a Jewish farmstead established in the 1st c. CE before the First Revolt and deserted shortly after the Bar Kokhba revolt, with a small early synagogue (benches, not oriented to Jerusalem) dated by three coins to the 1st-early 2nd c. - a 'rare' rural pre-135 synagogue; a stepped installation may have been reused as a ritual bath (miqveh) in the Early Roman period (ESI 2018). Year = conventional 1st-early 2nd c. Dating basis: coins/pottery (Aviam 2016). Confidence high.

Anab / Ania, Wolf translation): 'another large village of the Jews called Ania in the Daroma nine miles south of Hebron'; a second Anaia, to the east of the first, was wholly Christian. Wikipedia 'Khirbet Ghuwein al-Fauqa': Eusebius describes Anim (Anaia) as two villages south of Hebron, one Jewish (Lower Horvat Anim, Khirbet Ghuwein al-Tahta) and one Christian (Upper Horvat Anim); Wikipedia 'Daroma' lists Lower Anim among the seven large Jewish villages of the Daroma. Yankelevich (entries 57 and 58, Anea (A) and (B)): Eusebius attests a very large village of Jews called Anea, 9 miles from Hebron in the Daroma, and a second Anea wholly Christian to its east. The marker is the map's Anim (Horvat Anim); the distance in Eusebius was not checked against the site. Year 320 = conventional date of Eusebius' Onomasticon (traditionally 'sometime before 324', Wikipedia 'Onomasticon (Eusebius)'; Wikipedia 'Daroma' says c. 300); the map's Juttah row uses 320 as well. Hasmonean (-167 to -63). Khirbet el-'Ormeh (Urma), 1.5 km NW of Aqraba, is a Hasmonean-Herodian fortress with Hellenistic-style towers and large cisterns; coins of Demetrius II, John Hyrcanus and Alexander Jannaeus found (Wikipedia; Bar-Ilan abstract on the Kh. el-'Urma 2009 documentation). Wikipedia suggests it protected the town of Aqraba during Hasmonean expansion. Hasmonean/Jewish control of the district, but the town itself is unexcavated; Population blank.

Jewish: Josephus names Acrabbene/Akrabatta as the northernmost Judean toparchy on the Samaria border; Simon bar Giora ravaged Acrabbene and gathered forces there (Josephus Wars 2.652, lexundria); Jewish Encyclopedia: many clashes between Judeans and Samaritans there before 70 CE; Mishnah (Ma'aser Sheni 5:2) names it (later than period); Hebrew Wikipedia: Second Temple remains found in the village; INN report of a Second Temple mikveh, stone tools and hiding chambers in the Akraba district (site within district, not necessarily Aqraba itself); Haifa abstract (Klein et al.) on a Jewish population in the toparchy and Bar Kokhba coins (later). Rock-cut kokhim tombs near the village (Wikipedia). No published population estimate; Population blank.

Literary only (conventional date -1200: the wilderness/conquest narratives). The Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, attacks Israel and the place is renamed Hormah (Num 21:1-3); the king of Arad is in the list of defeated kings (Josh 12:14); the Kenites settle in the wilderness of Judah in the Negeb near Arad (Judg 1:16). Identification: Tel Arad, proposed by Edward Robinson in 1841 on the name (English Wikipedia), confirmed by two ostraca bearing the name Arad (BibleWalks); Aharoni and all researchers accept it (Hebrew Wikipedia). Caveat: Tel Arad has no Middle or Late Bronze remains, which is hard to square with the Canaanite city of Numbers (English Wikipedia; BibleWalks); Tel Malhata has been proposed for Canaanite Arad. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%AA%D7%9C_%D7%A2%D7%A8%D7%93 ; https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Numbers.21?context=0&commentary=0&lang=en&version=english%7CThe%20Holy%20Scriptures%20by%20Jewish%20Publication%20Society%201917 ; https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Judges.1?context=0&commentary=0&lang=en&version=english%7CThe%20Holy%20Scriptures%20by%20Jewish%20Publication%20Society%201917

Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) invaded in Rehoboam's fifth year: 1 Kgs 14:25-26 and 2 Chr 12:2-4 ('he took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah'). The Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists conquered places (c. 925 BCE); the inscription gives no details of the expedition and Jerusalem is absent from the list (English Wikipedia 'Bubastite Portal', 'Shoshenq I'). Two Arads appear in the Negev section: no. 108 'Arad (Tel Arad)' and no. 110 'Arad (Tel Malhata?)', between them no. 109 'Great'; English Wikipedia 'Tel Arad' reads them as 'Arad the House of YRHM' (possibly Tel Arad, with Jerahmeelite families) and 'Great Arad' (possibly Tel Malhata). Epigraphic evidence; Year of Data -925 = conventional date of the campaign. No population figure.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722): Stratum XI, the first Judahite casemate fortress, built in the second half of the 9th c. BCE (English Wikipedia, following Herzog 2002). BibleWalks, following Aharoni's older chronology, has a 10th-c. fortress possibly built under Solomon and a 9th-c. fortress over it; the shrine (entrance hall, main hall, holy of holies, altar of about 5 cubits) is dated 9th-6th c. by BibleWalks; Aharoni's team dated its founding to the late 10th c., others to the late 8th/early 7th c. (Hebrew Wikipedia). About 200-235 ostraca were found (English/Hebrew Wikipedia). Fortresses about 50-55 m per side (Hebrew Wikipedia writes 'm2'). No population estimate for the garrison. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/telarad/

BCE); Stratum IX-VIII (second half of the 8th c.) ends with the destruction attributed to Sennacherib's campaign in 701 BCE (English Wikipedia, BibleWalks). The Hebrew ostraca are mostly military supply notes addressed to Eliashib (late 7th c., outside this window). Shishak's campaign of 1 Kgs 14:25 (5th year of Rehoboam, c. -925) is linked by BibleWalks to Arad's conquest in 924 BCE. No population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/telarad/

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63). Jewish. IDENTIFICATION: the coordinates are the moshav/Horvat Arbel (Khirbet Irbid); Hebrew Wikipedia notes that some scholars place ancient Arbel at Khirbet Wadi Hamam, c. 2 km west of the lake, and that the settlement began in the late Hellenistic period. New evidence: Leibner's final report (IES 2018) states Khirbet Wadi Hamam was established in the Hasmonean period, and coins of Alexander Jannaeus support a Hasmonean founding (English Wikipedia summarising the excavation); Shivtiel reports Early Roman pottery and some Hasmonean coins in cliff-base caves of the region (ANE Today 2020, sites not specified). Texts: Bacchides captured the 'mesaloth' at Arbela and killed the inhabitants (1 Macc 9:2; Jewish Virtual Library; Dead Sea Quake catalog); the Mishnah names Nittai of Arbela (Avot 1:6; Jewish Virtual Library says he may have come from here). No named-scholar population estimate; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Jewish. Khirbet Wadi Hamam: first village phase c. 100 BCE-135 CE (Leibner excavations 2007-2012: c. ten residential buildings, two olive presses, alleys, a two-story frescoed building built in Hauran dry-stone technique); a large stone krater in the destruction layer parallels late Second Temple vessels in Jerusalem; a coin hoard dates the destruction to Hadrian (c. 125-135 CE); pottery from the Jewish production centers Kfar Hananya and Shikhin (English Wikipedia summary; Leibner IES 2018 abstract); no miqveh is reported in fetched summaries of the village. Cliff caves: five miqva'ot hewn in caves, c. 35 plastered cisterns, over 500 refuge caves (Shivtiel, with Boslov; Reich documented the first three), Early Roman pottery, dated by context to the late Second Temple period and the Great Revolt (BAR Daily; ANE Today 2020). Texts: Zealots against Herod hid in the caves in 39/38 BCE (Ant 14.415-430; Jewish Virtual Library); Josephus fortified 'the cave of Arbela' in 66-67 CE (Life 188, lexundria.com). The visible synagogue (Roman-Byzantine) is later. Settlement size and any population: no named estimate in fetched sources (the c. 180-seat synagogue capacity is not a population estimate); Population blank.

Josephus fortified the cave-village of Arbela (the stepped cliff-caves of Mount Arbel) as a base at the start of the revolt (Life 188); EJ identifies the village at Khirbet Irbid (Horvat Arbel); some scholars (Shahar & Tepper 1991) would put ancient Arbel at Khirbet Wadi Hammam instead. Dating basis: Josephus. Confidence high for the revolt-period site, medium for the village location. Framing row.

Framing row: Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Arbel') - during the Jewish War (66-70) Josephus, then a local commander, had fortifications built in the area, probably at the cliff fortress above the valley or at Har Nittai (Life 188). Pre-70 context for the post-70 priestly settlement of the House of Jeshua.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Arbel'): after the Second Temple's destruction 'priests of the House of Jeshua' (Jeshua, the 9th priestly course, per Wikipedia 'Priestly courses') settled at Arbel; the Jerusalem Talmud (Pe'ah 7:4, 20a) praises the valley's fertility and Genesis Rabbah 19:1 says linen garments came from Arbel; Josephus fortified the area in 66-67 (Life 188). Priestly tradition; 70 used as the 'after the destruction' date. Medium confidence.

After the destruction of the Second Temple, priests of the House of Jeshua (one of the 24 courses) settled at Arbel; the valley was noted for fertility and linen (Jerusalem Talmud Pe'ah 7:4, Gen. R. 19:1). Conventional year (post-70). Dating basis: literary (Baraita of the 24 Mishmarot). Confidence medium.

Arbel synagogue (Galilean type; excavated by Kohl-Watzinger 1905 and B. Arubas 2012-18): the Wikipedia caption dates it to the 4th c. CE; INPA describes the remains of a splendid ancient Galilean synagogue in the Jewish settlement of Arbel. Dating basis: typology. Year 350 = 4th c.

ESI 2023 (amulet report): Horbat Arbel was a Jewish village in the time of the Mishnah and Talmud; the synagogue was suggested to have been built in the 4th c. CE and to have continued in use until the 8th c. (Ilan and Izdarechet 1989); a Byzantine-period amulet found near the synagogue and the village's synagogue in the 5th-6th c. suggest that Jews wore such amulets. Dating basis: typology/survey. Year 350 = 4th c.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Arbel'): the 'early Byzantine' synagogue's date is disputed - the earlier proposal of a 3rd-century date 'is no longer accepted by scholars'; excavated by Kohl & Watzinger in 1905 and Z. Ilan in 1987-89. Year 400 = conventional for 'early Byzantine' (324-c. 450). Archaeological, no precise date.

Leibner (2009), Table 11: Horvat Arbel was one of the two largest villages in the Eastern Galilee survey, 61-90 dunams (F) c. 1-250 CE and 41-60 dunams (E) continuously from 250 through 650 CE - one of the 15 survey sites still occupied in 350-400 CE, when occupied sites had fallen from 38 (200-250). Year 450 conventional.

ESI (2023): Horbat Arbel 'was a Jewish village during the time of the Mishna and the Talmud', with a flax industry and many visiting sages; the synagogue (built in the 4th c., used to the 8th c. per Ilan & Izdarechet 1989) existed in the 5th-6th c., when a Byzantine amulet with Greek inscriptions (5th-6th c.) was lost near it; Leibner's survey found pottery from the Hellenistic to the end of the Byzantine period. Conventional year (5th-6th c.). Dating basis: pottery/amulet typology. Confidence medium.

Synagogue rebuilt in the 6th c. with a Torah ark on the south wall facing Jerusalem; probably used continuously until the 8th c., when a conflagration (probably the 749 earthquake) destroyed it. Conventional year (6th c.). Dating basis: architectural phases. Confidence medium.

Leibner/Aviam: Arbel (Khirbet Irbid, survey site 39, map ref 1956/2467, 85 dunams) stayed settled through every Roman and Byzantine sub-period (estimated 61-85 dunams in the Early and Middle Roman periods, 41-60 dunams from the Late Roman to the Late Byzantine period; Late Roman Red Ware 28% of the finds). In the summer of 2000 M. Aviam excavated, at the northern edge, three Late Byzantine (550-650) dwellings, two of them with miqva'ot (ritual baths), and a floor with a 2nd-c. coin, pottery and stone vessels; the synagogue at the centre of the site was dated by Ilan to the 4th c. with repairs in the late 6th/early 7th c. and use until the 8th c. (not excavated). A ring with an eye and an animal found at the site is inscribed with the name Shmuel (IAA archive record, cited by Leibner). The miqva'ot indicate Jewish ritual practice in these dwellings. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 250-251, 262-265. Conventional year (Late Byzantine, midpoint 600). Dating basis: excavated dwellings + survey pottery. Confidence medium.

The Mishnaic Arav/Gabara of Hanina ben Dosa is the Galilean Arraba, not this one.

Arraba = the Jewish village Arav (Mishnah, Jerusalem Talmud) = Gabara of Josephus; Vespasian sacked it in the First Revolt, killing the Jews who had not fled. Identification by name/tradition. Dating basis: Josephus. Confidence medium. Framing row.

Wikipedia 'Arraba, Israel': the village is Arav in the Mishnah and Jerusalem Talmud (Gabara in Josephus); Hanina ben Dosa, who lived there 'in the first and second generations after 70 CE', has his grave there; Yohanan ben Zakkai is said to have lived there eighteen years (before 70); Vespasian sacked it during the revolt (66-73). Year 100 = conventional for the first/second post-70 generation. Rabbinic tradition; the grave is a later tradition; low-medium confidence. This is the Galilean Arraba, not Arraba near Jenin (the other marker named Arraba).

Arav is named as seat of the priestly course Pethahiah in the Caesarea Inscription (c. AD 300), implying Jewish resettlement in the 3rd-4th c.; a church with mosaic floor and inscription of the 5th-6th c. attests Christian residents, destroyed c. end of 6th/early 7th c. Dating basis: inscription. Confidence medium.

Priestly-courses inscription from Caesarea (IIP caes0684): 'The 19th course Pethahiah - Aklah Arab' (Akhla, Arav); date range 200-500 CE (midpoint 350). Wikipedia 'Arraba, Israel': because of the Caesarea inscription listing the course of Pethahiah as residing there, the town is 'presumed to have been resettled by Jews' in the 3rd-4th centuries; a church with a mosaic floor shows a Christian community in the 5th-6th century. Identification of Aklah-Arab with Galilean Arav/Arraba is the Wikipedia article's (and the Priestly courses table's), not certain.

Arraba in the Lower Galilee (not the Arraba near Jenin): identified with the Jewish village Arab of the Mishnah and Jerusalem Talmud and Josephus' Gabara; after the First Revolt it is presumed to have been resettled by Jews in the 3rd-4th c., since it is the residence of the priestly course Pethahiah in the Caesarea Inscription; Hanina ben Dosa's grave there; inhabited by Christians in the 5th or 6th c., as shown by a church. Identification and resettlement date are scholarly presumptions; confidence low-medium. Year 350 = 3rd-4th c.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Tyrian dependency (Pseudo-Scylax, 'Ashkelon of the Tyrians': Hebrew Wikipedia, Jewish Virtual Library, Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception). Resettled in the late 6th c. BCE after Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of 604 BCE; the Leon Levy Expedition (Stager, Master) found warehouses along the sea, villas nearer the centre and hundreds of individually buried dogs in open spaces; the Persian occupation ended in a destruction numismatically dated c. 290 BCE (EBR, Master), so on the source's dating this phase runs past -332. Boehm, Master and Le Blanc 2016: the Persian city was confined mostly to the older south tell area. Population: Phoenician/Tyrian and local; no Jewish evidence found. Identification: Tel Ashkelon (Yigael Yadin National Park, 60 ha site enclosed by the Middle Bronze ramparts per EBR); no dispute. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Ptolemaic free port and autonomous city (Jewish Virtual Library), later Antiochus III; Hellenized Greek/Phoenician city (Jewish Encyclopedia: Strabo calls it a small city; Theophrastus' Ashkelon onion in Hebrew Wikipedia). Jewish Virtual Library states that a Jewish community 'flourished' there under the Ptolemies but cites no inscription, find or text, and no excavation report fetched attests Jews in this period: treated as unsupported. Leon Levy excavations: the monumental Hellenistic complex in the forum area is dated Late Hellenistic (Boehm et al. 2016), not early; the Persian-period destruction c. 290 BCE (EBR) falls at the start of this period. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Gentile Hellenized city, not Jewish, outside the Hasmonean state. It received Jonathan Maccabee peacefully (1 Macc 10:86, 11:60; Jewish Encyclopedia; Josephus Ant. 13 on Wikisource) and later submitted to or resisted Alexander Jannaeus (Jewish Encyclopedia says submitted; Jewish Virtual Library and Hebrew Wikipedia say he and John Hyrcanus failed to take it and it stayed independent). Autonomous from 111/104 BCE with its own era and coinage (Jewish Virtual Library, Hebrew Wikipedia). Late Hellenistic monumental public or administrative building (phase 7, late 2nd to 1st c. BCE) in the forum area (Boehm, Master and Le Blanc, AJA 2016). No Jewish population evidence found; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Greek (Hellenized Phoenician) free and allied city outside Herod's kingdom; he nevertheless built colonnades, baths and fountains there (Josephus BJ 1.422, cited by Boehm et al.; Jewish Virtual Library), and his sister Salome received the royal palace at Ascalon (BJ 2.6.3, Wikisource). Archaeology: Boehm, Master and Le Blanc 2016 date the basilica/bouleuterion (phase 6) to the 1st c. BCE to 1st c. CE and show that Garstang's Herodian dating of the preserved architectural fragments is wrong (most are Severan). Hinterland farm and estate remains of Hellenistic to Early Roman date are published from the 'Third Mile Estate' (Levantine Ceramics database, citing Israel and Erickson-Gini, 'Atiqot 74, 2013). Jews: none evidenced in the city by excavation; synagogue remains and chancel screens are Byzantine (Jewish Virtual Library). In 66 CE Jews attacked and burned Ascalon and the Ascalonites killed 2,500 Jews and imprisoned others (BJ 2.18.1 and 2.18.5, Wikisource; Jewish Encyclopedia): a casualty figure, not a population. Hebrew Wikipedia: the Mishnah (Gittin 1:2) treats Ashkelon as southern/borderline territory. Population blank: no Jewish population estimate by a named scholar found.

comment: Event: Ashkelon shelters Jewish refugees and ransoms the captives of Jerusalem. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Ashkelon, fetched): "In the first period of Crusader rule over Palestine, a yet unconquered Ashkelon sheltered a large number of refugees, including many Jews." and "The Jewish community became a sanctuary for those escaping from Jerusalem, and dealt with such matters as ransoming captives and buying ritual objects from looted synagogues in Jerusalem." The book (ch. 5, images 063-064) says the Jewish captives of Jerusalem were ransomed by their brethren of Ashkelon, Egypt and Italy; those ransomed by Ashkelon were sent on to Egypt (some died on the way), some stayed in Ashkelon in worsening poverty, and a small minority whose ransom was high converted to avoid slavery. Population blank. Confidence high.

comment: Event: Ashkelon surrenders to the Crusaders in August 1153. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Ashkelon, fetched): "After the Crusader conquest in 1153, part of the Jewish population remained in Ashkelon." Wikipedia (Siege of Ascalon, fetched): "The citizens were allowed to leave in peace; most decided to leave for Egypt." The book (ch. 5, image 064) says the surrender did not prevent killing and looting, that Jewish settlement was not interrupted but some chose to emigrate to Egypt, and that Benjamin of Tudela (dated 1174 in the book; the map has the same counts at c.1165) found 200 Jews, 300 Samaritans and 40 Karaites among about 10,000 inhabitants, mostly Eastern Christians and Franks; the massacre claim is not supported by the online pages (disagreement in the conflicts file). Population blank. Confidence high.

Benjamin of Tudela, Sefer ha-Massa'ot (Itinerary), c.1165: traveller names the place "Ashkelon"; Adler translation, text marker [p.44]. Traveller's words: 'About 200 Rabbanite Jews dwell here ... also about forty Karaites' (and 300 Samaritans, not counted) = 240 Jews. Identification: Ashkelon (New Ascalon). Year 1165 = c.1165 (Benjamin travelled c.1165-1173).

comment: Event: Saladin destroyed Ashkelon's fortifications in 1191 and evacuated the town. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Ashkelon): "its Jewish population went to settle in Jerusalem." and Judah al-Harizi mentions "an excellent congregation from Ashkelon" among the Jews of Jerusalem; the Jerusalem entry adds that Jews from Ashkelon, destroyed on Saladin's orders, helped renew the Jewish community of Jerusalem. Shpak-Lissak (ch. 2, section D.5) dates the settling of Jews from Ashkelon, the Maghreb and France-England in Jerusalem to 1191-1211 and says three communities arose there. Population blank (no count). Confidence high.

Wikipedia: "In 1939-1948, tens of thousands of Jewish immigrants were interned here"; on 10 October 1945 the Palmach raided the camp and freed 208 detainees. Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550). Ceramic evidence for MB I and II; the city 'flourished' in the MB (BAS). Canaanite. Identification of Tel Azekah (Tell Zakariyeh) is standard; Wikipedia pages fetched did not contradict it. No population estimate found.

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Ceramic evidence for LB II and III; maintained autonomy from Egyptian overlords; major destruction near the end of the period (c. 12th c per he.wikipedia). Canaanite. No population estimate found.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Levantine Ceramics Project lists ceramic evidence for Iron Age IA only; other sources describe a gap after the LB destruction. Weak evidence; no population estimate found.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): BeinHarim tours states a Jewish village existed from the Second Temple Period through the Talmudic Period; Hebrew Wikipedia and Jewish Virtual Library date the visible remains to the 2nd-3rd century CE (synagogue 3rd c., or late 4th-early 5th c. per Hebrew Wikipedia) and the JVL page mentions no Second Temple evidence. Jewish population plausible but no ossuaries mikva'ot coins or inscriptions of the period found in fetched pages; the site is not named by Josephus or the Mishnah. Population blank.

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Land of Israel: History' counts Baram among the 'splendid synagogues' built chiefly in Galilee in the Severan period (193-235; midpoint 214); EJ 'Kefar Baram' dates the synagogue remains to 'the third century c.e.' (hill-top building about 18 x 13 m, porch with six columns, three doorways, lintel inscription naming the builder Eleazar b. Judan, Kohl & Watzinger 1916). Older dating; see the 400 row.

Kfar Bar'am: large Galilean-type synagogue, with a second smaller one (lintel with Hebrew 'Peace upon the place...' now in the Louvre). Wikipedia: completed in the 3rd c., 'likely by c. 220 CE'; Sukenik (1928) dated it to the 3rd c.; facade inscription 'Elazar bar Yodan built it'; Jewish village inhabited until the 13th c. Style-based date; see the 4th-5th c. row for the competing date.

Second, smaller synagogue at Kfar Bar'am (Bar'am North/Lower): little survives; its decorated and inscribed lintel (Hebrew 'Peace upon the place, and on all the places of Israel') is in the Louvre; excavated by C. Wilson (1866) and M. Aviam (1998), who also found an Aramaic amulet (Bornblum database). Period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'; conventional year 300 follows the style-based dating of the lintel to the same horizon as the main building; low confidence.

Hamichlol (Hebrew): Bar'am's synagogue dating has been revised to 'around the 4th-5th century CE' (earlier dated to the early 3rd century); the national-park article (Wikipedia 'Bar'am National Park') speaks of 'two ancient Jewish synagogues from the Talmudic period' and cites Aviam (2002) on their dating; the ancient village's original name is unknown. Midpoint of 4th-5th century (400) used. Archaeological; dating disputed (3rd vs 4th-5th century).

Israel Nature and Parks Authority (ceremony page) places the grand ashlar synagogue in the time of the Jewish community of the 4th and 5th centuries (Mishnah and Talmud periods), a Jewish settlement that thrived in the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods after Bar Kokhba; its facade has three doorways facing Jerusalem. Conflicts with the 3rd-c. style date. Conventional year 400.

Magness 2024 (Kfar Baram described among the three classic 'Galilean-type' synagogues with Capernaum and Chorazin): facade preserved to its original two-storey height, porch of columns, lintel of the central doorway carved with two winged Nikes holding a wreath (the figures were chipped away later, leaving the wreath); Aviam (2004, as reported by Magness) claims the large synagogue is built entirely of spolia, possibly a way to circumvent later Roman legislation against new synagogues. Magness dates Galilean-type synagogues generally to the 4th-6th c. against the traditional late 2nd-3rd c. style date (Kohl-Watzinger; Sukenik); the style date is given in the 220 row. Year 400 = centre of Magness's range.

Jewish village of the Talmudic period with a synagogue ~1.5 km NW of Ma'ale Gamla near the confluence of Nahal Daliyot and Nahal Batra, beside the historic road from the Galilee to the Gamla area (he.wikipedia: west wall and part of the north wall of the building survive, with capitals, mezuzah stones and vine-decorated lintels). Ma'oz (NEAEHL 1992) and D. Urman (BAR Int. S. 269, 1985, p. 199). Bornblum 'Batra': surveyed C. Epstein 1968, Z. Ma'oz 1978, Z. Ilan 1984. Year 450 conventional; the public building is dated only by the Byzantine pottery.

comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Jewish village with residential and public buildings, agricultural installations, pools and cisterns from the end of the Second Temple period (bibleplaces quoting IAA; INN 2008). Fragment of a limestone sarcophagus lid about 60 x 48 cm inscribed in Hebrew square script 'the son of the High Priest', dated by the excavators c. 30-70 CE, reused in an Early Islamic installation and probably from the nearby Jewish cemetery; a sarcophagus rather than an ossuary suggests a wealthy family; excavators propose a priestly estate (Beit Hanan family) whose name survives in Beit Hanina (en.wikipedia, interpretation not established). Revolt coin of year 2 (67/68 CE) in one structure; village abandoned in the First Jewish Revolt; cemetery used until the Bar Kokhba revolt (early 2nd-century glass and lamps). Robert Deutsch's alternative reading of the inscription is mentioned on bibleplaces. Population blank: no named estimate.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Capital of one of the toparchies of Judea (Idumea region) on the Beth Guvrin-Jerusalem road; Josephus records its capture and destruction by Vespasian and Titus in spring 68 CE (Wikipedia); Hebrew Wikipedia: excavations show a district city in the Second Temple period destroyed by Vespasian. Jewish cisterns and burial caves excavated; town predominantly Jewish until the Bar Kokhba revolt (Wikipedia). Baramki 1934 excavated two cisterns with pottery of the 1st-3rd centuries CE (Palestine Remembered/PalQuest). Seal reading Boule of Baitolethepha (Ecker and Zissu 2020, Roman period) shows toparchy council. Who lived there: Jewish. No published Jewish population estimate found, so Population blank. Year of Data set to period start -63; the destruction was 68 CE.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Jewish cemetery. Salvage excavation (Zissu and Moyal) found about 50 shaft graves on the southern terraces of the Rephaim Valley dated 1st century BCE to 1st century CE (so partly Hasmonean-late; source gives no finer dates); similar to Qumran graves; Zissu 1996 asks if they show an Essene community; used until the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135 CE) and at least two Second Temple tombs were reused later. Evidence is burial only; no source describes a settlement or gives a population; Population blank.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Two nearby sites. (1) Khirbet Siyar el-Ghanam (Latin Shepherds' Field): Corbo (1951-52) found caves with habitation in the Herodian and later Roman period and oil presses; the Franciscan Custody page says the hill was inhabited and farmed in the time of Jesus, probably a small farming village with mills, with Herodian pottery and coins of the first Roman procurators and the First Jewish War in the grottos; Murphy-O'Connor reads it as nomadic shepherds (via English Wikipedia). (2) Khirbet Beit Bassa: Encyclopedia.com lists terraces, cisterns and at least one rock-hewn stepped mikveh with double entrance dated to the Second Temple period; Hebrew Wikipedia mentions a burial cave with decorated ossuaries found there in 1994; but Abu Aemar and Carvajal (2014) date the 2009 pottery 1st-10th c. CE with occupation concentrated in the 3rd-4th and 6th-10th centuries, and say the site was most likely a small village in the Roman period. Jewish evidence is thus a mikveh and ossuaries at Beit Bassa only; no ethnic label for Siyar el-Ghanam. No population estimate in any fetched source; Population blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Shepherds%27_Field; https://www.travelpalestine.ps/en/Article/159/Shepherds'-Fields-The-Catholic-Shepherds'-Field; https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/bethbasi; https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/catalogue/adsdata/arch-5456-1/dissemination/2014/MedievalCeramics_2014-35_1-12.pdf; https://dspace.alquds.edu/items/33c8e1bb-4961-42dc-826e-a5378d0d1e36/full; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/בית_סאחור
Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550). Massive fortification system with city walls and gates. Canaanite. Identification with Tel Bet Shemesh (Ain Shams) is standard. No population estimate found.

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Prosperous city with Mycenaean imports (phases IVA/IVB per he.wikipedia); burnt in the 14th c BCE and rebuilt (BibleWalks). Tel about 32 dunams. Canaanite. No population estimate found.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Canaanite-tradition settlement, destroyed by fire c. 1100 BCE (he.wikipedia); town grew over the whole mound (BibleWalks). Iron I Levels 7-4 per Bunimovitz and Lederman (not directly fetched). No population estimate found.

First mentioned in the Book of Joshua (15) as a city in the territory of the tribe of Judah on the border of Dan, and later set aside as a Levite city. It is also mentioned in Samuel I as the first city to receive the Ark of the Covenant after its return by the Philistines.

Remains discovered from the Late Bronze Age (the period of the Judges—twelfth and eleventh centuries BCE), during which it was a border city of shevet Yehudah and a city of the Levi'im. It was also the site where the Ark of the Covenant was returned by the Philistines.

Remains discovered from the Iron Age (the period of the United Kingdom—tenth century BCE)
Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). Late Iron Age (8th-7th c) with 55 LMLK handles and a destruction layer tied to Sennacherib's 701 BCE invasion (BibleWalks). Judahite. No population estimate found.

Literary only: 2 Kgs 14:11-14 and 2 Chr 25:17-24: Jehoash of Israel and Amaziah of Judah meet at Beth-shemesh, Judah is routed, Amaziah is captured, about 400 cubits of Jerusalem's wall is broken down and treasures and hostages are carried to Samaria (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Possible archaeological echo: the Level 3 destruction in the first half of the 8th century (previous row), a link made in en.wikipedia.

Iron Age IIB, Level 2 (about -750 to -701 per the BAS Library NEAEHL page): a modest, probably unfortified town with olive-oil production, with pottery of the Lachish III horizon, destroyed by Sennacherib's army in 701 BCE; the page suggests Judah's border may have shifted west, leaving Beth-shemesh behind; Level 1 (about 650-635, Iron IIc) is a brief failed reoccupation of the water reservoir, after which the site never recovered. 2 Chr 28:18 (Philistines take Beth-shemesh in the reign of Ahaz, c. -735) is the corresponding literary mention. No population estimate in the fetched pages (BibleWalks gives only the modern city's figures).

Iron Age IIC / late monarchy (-722 to -586). Hebrew Wikipedia lists three Iron II phases spanning roughly 1000-586 BCE including IIC; page gives no detail. Weak evidence. No population estimate found.

Persian (-539 to -332): Tel Beth Shemesh (East): Iron Age agricultural installations kept in use; ceramics, coins, and four YHWD (Yehud) stamped handles of the 4th c. BCE; limited architecture. Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Agricultural installations continued to about 3rd c. BCE; a cave complex sealed about 2nd c. BCE; little settlement; no Jewish evidence stated; Population blank.

Abandoned after Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136 CE). No source gives a population figure; Population blank.

Josephus fortified Bersabe (Beersheba of the Galilee; 'Bersobe' in Life 188, 'Bersabee' in War 2.20.6) and describes the breadth of Upper Galilee as running from Bersabe to the village Baca (War 3.3.1). Identified with Khirbet es-Saba/Abu esh-Sheba' (472 m), less than 1 km from Kafr 'Inan (Kefar Hananya): a hilltop village of c. 70 dunams (17 acres) with a fieldstone wall 2.8 m thick on the north with three semicircular towers; a refuge of insurgents from across Galilee. Excavations/surveys: Aviam, Tal and others. Dating basis: literary (Josephus) plus survey; the 70 dunams is an area, not a population estimate. Confidence high for the fortification, medium for the site identification.

Post-70 continuation: pottery found at the site proves the continuation of the settlement deep into the 3rd century CE; coins span the 4th century BCE to the 2nd century CE; a Jewish tomb lies below the village ruins; Wikipedia calls it a Second Temple period Jewish village. Only one square near the wall was excavated, so later phases are poorly known. Dating basis: pottery/coins; conventional year 200. Confidence medium-low (single secondary source, Wikipedia summarising Aviam/Tal).

Beth Alpha synagogue (Byzantine basilica with apse, narthex and atrium): the Aramaic dedicatory inscription says it was built in the reign of Justin (probably Justin I, 518-527; the part of the date that specified the year is lost); a Greek inscription names the craftsmen Marianos and his son Hanina; excavated 1929 (Sukenik); hoard of 36 Byzantine coins in the apse floor. Midpoint of 518-527 is 522. Dating basis: dedicatory inscription naming the emperor.

Beth Alpha synagogue: Wikipedia 'Beth Alpha' - 'The synagogue was completed in the sixth century CE'; the partly damaged Aramaic inscription says the building dates to the reign of Justinus, 'probably Justin I (518-527 CE)' (midpoint 523); Greek inscription names the artisans Marianos and his son Hanina; mosaic panels of the Binding of Isaac, a zodiac wheel and a synagogue scene; excavations by E. Sukenik from 1929 and 1962. A hoard of 36 Byzantine coins was found in the apse. Epigraphic dating; high confidence.

comment: Event: Vespasian's campaign in Idumea during the First Jewish-Roman War (68 CE). Josephus: he seized two villages 'in the very midst of Idumea', Betaris and Caphartobas, slew above ten thousand of the people, carried over a thousand into captivity, drove away the rest and placed a large part of his forces there (War 4.8.1). English Wikipedia ('Bayt Jibrin') reads Betaris as Begabris, i.e. Beit Guvrin, and says Vespasian slaughtered or enslaved its inhabitants. The 10,000 killed and 1,000 captives are totals for the two villages together, not a population. The attached book (Shpak-Lissak, ch. 2, img022) attributes the 10,000 killed and 1,000 captured to Beit Guvrin alone, calls it a Jewish city founded by the returnees from the Babylonian exile, and says Septimius Severus made it the polis Eleutheropolis in 200 CE. [confidence: medium - the identification of Betaris with Beit Guvrin is a textual emendation] [Source detail: (Josephus, War 4.8.1, Whiston translation); (Wikipedia, 'Roman and Byzantine periods')]

Wikipedia 'Beit Jibrin': in 200 CE Septimius Severus gave the town municipal status under the new name Eleutheropolis, and 'the city was then inhabited by Jews, Christians and pagans'; it had 'continued to be a Jewish-inhabited city until the Bar Kokhba revolt'. Wikipedia 'Bar Kokhba revolt' lists Eleutheropolis among the places where Jewish communities persisted on the edge of Judea after the revolt. The book (late Roman period, 135-324) says the population was mixed, Jews and pagans, that Septimius Severus made Bet Guvrin a polis in 199-200 and renamed it Eleutheropolis, with a Roman garrison and Hellenistic buildings (amphitheatre, baths), and that the area north of Bet Guvrin was totally destroyed in the Bar Kokhba revolt. Presence only, no population stated: Population blank. The existing Bet Guvrin row (350) is an atlas marker for 2nd-6th-century synagogues. Book: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 037 (Screenshot_20221028-092833.jpg), img 034 (Screenshot_20221028-092631.jpg); page number not visible.

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Lower Beth-horon (Beit Ur al-Tahta) is the older of the two Beth-horons: pottery from the Late Bronze Age onward found at the lower town. Canaanite period. Identification note: Beth-horon is two towns (upper Beit Ur al-Fauqa and lower Beit Ur al-Tahta); coordinates given are the lower town. No population estimate found; Finkelstein and Lederman are cited for ~1.5 ha at upper Beit Ur only Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%91%D7%99%D7%AA_%D7%97%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%9F_(%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%A8_%D7%9E%D7%A7%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%99%D7%AA); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_Ur_al-Fauqa

Literary mention (Upper Beth-horon = Beit Ur al-Fauqa, 31.8858 N, 35.1142 E, 'identified with the ancient town of Upper Bethoron', en.wikipedia; the marker lies about 1.5 km from it by those coordinates): Year of Data -1200 = Joshua narrative convention. Josh 10:10-11: the coalition is chased past Beth-horon and struck by hailstones as it descends from Beth-horon; Josh 16:5: Ephraim's eastern border reaches upper Beth-horon; Josh 21:22: Beth-horon a Levitical city (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Archaeology: Iron Age potsherds in the village; Finkelstein and Lederman (1997) estimate the ancient site at about 1.5 ha (en.wikipedia). The existing Bet Horon rows also carry the Late Bronze lower-town evidence. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_Ur_al-Fauqa

Literary only: 1 Sam 13:17-18: three raiding parties leave the Philistine camp at Michmash, one toward Ophrah in the land of Shual, one toward Beth-horon and one toward the border above the Zeboim valley (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page); the text does not say whether upper or lower Beth-horon is meant. Year of Data -1020 = Saul's reign convention.

Iron Age II (source does not subdivide; entered at start of Iron Age IIA -1000). Hebrew Wikipedia: upper Beth-horon's earliest pottery is Iron Age II (46% of 322 sherds); en Wikipedia: Iron Age onward at upper town; the two towns are described as cities fortified under Solomon in the Bible. No fetched page gives Iron Age strata or dates for the lower town specifically. Israelite/Judahite. Population blank: no academic estimate found Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%91%D7%99%D7%AA_%D7%97%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%9F_(%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%A8_%D7%9E%D7%A7%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%99%D7%AA)

Literary only: 2 Chr 8:5: Solomon fortifies upper and nether Beth-horon with walls, gates and bars; 1 Kgs 9:17 names nether Beth-horon (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Year of Data -960 = Solomon convention. The existing Iron Age II row (Hebrew Wikipedia: earliest pottery at the upper town is Iron II) is the only archaeological tie; the Lower Beth-horon marker covers 1 Kgs 9:17.

Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) invaded in Rehoboam's fifth year: 1 Kgs 14:25-26 and 2 Chr 12:2-4 ('he took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah'). The Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists conquered places (c. 925 BCE); the inscription gives no details of the expedition and Jerusalem is absent from the list (English Wikipedia 'Bubastite Portal', 'Shoshenq I'). Beth-horon is no. 24 'Beth-Horon' of the list (the list does not say upper or lower). Epigraphic evidence; Year of Data -925 = conventional date. No population figure.

Literary only: 2 Chr 25:13: the soldiers Amaziah sent home raid the towns of Judah 'from Samaria even unto Beth-horon', killing 3,000 and taking much plunder (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; upper or lower town not specified). Year of Data -790 = Amaziah convention (c. -796 to -767).

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332). New row (first pass had none for Persian): Finkelstein and Magen, Archaeological Survey of the Hill Country of Benjamin (1993), as transcribed on the b-hebrew list (Mattfeld 2004): Beit 'Ur et-Tahta (site 22:15), c. 30 (?) dunams, Persian 3% of sherds; Beit 'Ur el-Fauqa 4%. Encyclopaedia Judaica (encyclopedia.com): Beth-horon was part of Judea in the Persian and Hellenistic periods. Judean settlement, thin sherd presence so small; no Jewish-specific finds. Population blank. Identification: two towns (upper el-Fauqa, lower et-Tahta); coordinates are the lower town. Sources disagree on the earliest phase: Encyclopaedia Judaica and Hebrew Wikipedia put Late Bronze pottery at the lower town, the survey list shows none (Mattfeld argues the LBA date is unsupported).

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167). Replaces first-pass row for Early Hellenistic by adding a second survey figure: Finkelstein and Magen (1993, via b-hebrew list) give Hellenistic 27% of sherds at Beit 'Ur et-Tahta and 12% at el-Fauqa; Hebrew Wikipedia gives 29% of 157 sherds from the northern mound of et-Tahta (the two figures differ slightly). The survey does not split early from late Hellenistic, so the evidence covers the whole Hellenistic phase. Hellenistic is the best-represented period at the lower town. Judean town; no estimate.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63). Replaces first-pass row for Hasmonean with sourcing: 1 Macc 3:13-24 (Judas defeats Seron on the Beth-horon ascent), 1 Macc 7:39 (Nicanor), 1 Macc 9:50 (Bacchides fortified both Upper and Lower Beth-horon; Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica via encyclopedia.com). No excavation has found the Bacchides fortification: no wall, gate or Hasmonean coin from either town appears in any fetched source. Hellenistic sherds are the main material evidence (see previous row). Jewish population presumed from the literary frame only; no estimate.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Replaces first-pass row for Early Roman: Hebrew Wikipedia (citing the survey) records a late Second Temple burial cave (1st c. BCE-1st c. CE) on the southern slope of the ridge of lower Beth-horon with arched entrance, rolling-stone frame and burial niches (the page does not call it Jewish explicitly; the type is typical of Jewish tombs); Roman sherds 17% of the 157-sherd sample at the et-Tahta tel and 6% at upper Beth-horon; Roman road with oil press at the upper town. Josephus BJ 2.19.8 (Jewish Encyclopedia): the Roman army under Cestius suffered heavy losses at Beth-horon in 66 CE; Encyclopaedia Judaica: Eusebius places it 12 Roman miles from Jerusalem. Hebrew Wikipedia: Josephus mentions friction between local Jews and Roman soldiers before the revolt. Jewish village likely; no ossuary, miqveh or estimate published. Population blank.

Beth-Lehem (Bethlehem of Galilee / Beth Lehem Zoriah of the Jerusalem Talmud) is the residence of the 5th priestly course Malkiah in DJE 23. Basis: the Hebrew stone pillar DJE 23 (Bayt Hadir, Yemen; dated 4th-5th c. CE) lists the Galilean residence of each priestly course - the settlement tradition of the Baraita of the Mishmarot - so it shows the place was remembered as a priestly (Jewish) village by the 4th-5th c., not that excavations confirm it. Year = midpoint of the 4th-5th c.; confidence low-medium; identification of the ancient name with the modern site follows the Wikipedia 'Priestly divisions' list.

Bethlehem of Galilee: until the late 19th c. (and Dalman's 1921 visit) the remains of a church and a synagogue could be seen; V. Guerin (1875) saw a destroyed building of good ashlar with a south-facing entrance that he took for a synagogue; A. Berman found an Early Roman chalk-vessel industry and a huge winepress; large Byzantine buildings with 4th-5th c. pottery. Not excavated as a synagogue; Christian settlement in the Byzantine period (the site is claimed as Jesus' Bethlehem by Oshri). Conventional year (Byzantine, 4th-5th c.). Confidence low.

Israelite per these sources but no population estimate. No academic population estimate found; Population left blank. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%AA%D7%9C_%D7%91%D7%99%D7%AA_%D7%A9%D7%90%D7%9F

Biblical mention and Israelite phase (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -960 = conventional date of Solomon's reign). 1 Kgs 4:12: Beth-shean ('which is by Zartanah beneath Jezreel') in Baana's district (Taanach, Megiddo, Beth-shean to the place beyond Jokneam); Wikipedia notes that the historical accuracy of this list is debated. Archaeomagnetic dates suggest that the first Israelite urban settlement was established in the Solomonic period or, at the latest, in the pre-Omride phase of the early kingdom of Israel, and that it was probably destroyed c. 935-900 BC (Wikipedia, Beit She'an). Level V (Iron IIA, Stratum S1) and Level IV (Iron IIB) follow, the latter a fortified city destroyed by Tiglath-Pileser III in 732 BCE. No population estimate.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). 8th c. BCE Four Room Building (Hebrew Wikipedia: with ancient Hebrew inscription); destroyed in Tiglath-Pileser III's Assyrian conquest 732 BCE; minimal settlement afterwards until the Hellenistic period. Israelite (northern kingdom). No academic population estimate found; Population left blank. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%AA%D7%9C_%D7%91%D7%99%D7%AA_%D7%A9%D7%90%D7%9F

Hellenistic Pottery and Material Culture 2) date a military stronghold and administrative centre on Tel Bet She'an to the mid-3rd c. BCE and the foundation of the polis (Nysa-Scythopolis) on Tel Iztabba to about 170 BCE; this differs from the first-pass framing (c.260 BCE Ptolemaic post; polis status under Antiochus IV per JVL/NEAEHL) mainly in putting the polis foundation on Tel Iztabba c.170. Population: Greek/Macedonian/Seleucid polis (NEAEHL: priests of Egyptian and Greek descent; cults of Zeus and Dionysus); no Jewish population attested; none of the fetched sources report miqva'ot or stone vessels. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for this period: excavation evidence added. Mazor and Atrash (2017), summarising the German-Israeli Tell Iztabba project, report the Seleucid-founded settlement was violently destroyed by the Hasmoneans in 108/107 BCE and not properly resettled (NEAEHL: city lay in ruins until Pompey 64/63). Hebrew Wikipedia: sons of John Hyrcanus destroyed it and Megillat Taanit records a holiday for the capture; EBSCO: inhabitants offered conversion to Judaism or exile, most left. No fetched source documents a Jewish settled population or Jewish finds (miqva'ot, stone vessels) here in this period. Population blank. Date differs by source: 107 BCE (JVL, Livius, EBSCO) or 108/107 (Mazor and Atrash).

comment: Event (Jewish community spared): Judas Maccabeus, returning to Jerusalem after punitive raids on the Gentile cities of Gilead, came to Scythopolis; the Jews who lived there testified to the goodwill and kind treatment they had received from the Scythopolitans, so Judas and his men thanked them and left the city unharmed (2 Maccabees 12:29-31). Evidence of a Jewish community in Scythopolis in the early 160s BCE and of a Hellenistic city that did not harm its Jews, unlike Joppa, Jamnia and the Gilead cities in the same chapter. The attached book (Shpak-Lissak, ch. 1, img013) gives the same episode and dates it 163 BCE; it adds that Scythopolis was conquered by Hyrcanus in 107 BCE (not used here). 2 Maccabees is a religious-historical source and the year is approximate (c. 164/163 BCE). [confidence: medium] [Source detail: (2 Maccabees 12:29-31, USCCB text)]

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds the primary text and states what is not documented. Josephus War 2.466-468: Jews of Scythopolis who fought alongside their Gentile neighbours against the rebels in 66 CE were led to a grove and slaughtered by the city's people; 'above thirteen thousand' slain (a casualty figure, not a population; JVL leaves the victim group unspecified). City refounded by Gabinius (57 BCE per EBSCO and Livius), chief city of the Decapolis, pagan/Greek majority with a Jewish minority (Hebrew Wikipedia; Jewish Encyclopedia). JVL gives no population figure for the Hellenistic, Hasmonean or early Roman periods; its only estimate is Byzantine (30000-40000, total, not Jewish); NEAEHL estimates c.20000 for the 2nd c. CE (total, not Jewish). No excavated Second Temple Jewish remains (synagogue, miqve, stone vessels) in the fetched sources. Population blank.

Great Revolt: when Jewish insurgents attacked Scythopolis the Jews of the city fought alongside their Gentile neighbours, who nevertheless lured them into a grove outside the city and on the third night cut their throats: Josephus (War 2.18.3) 'above thirteen thousand' slain (victim count, not a population), the city plundered; Simon son of Saul killed his own family and himself. Dating basis: Josephus. Confidence high. Framing row. (Wikipedia: the city is said to have sided with the Romans.)

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Land of Israel: History': Jews of Beth-Shean were massacred in the 66-70 war but the community was rebuilt; by the late first century 'flourishing Jewish communities' existed in cities including Beth-Shean (listed with Caesarea, Ashkelon, Acre). Wikipedia 'Beit She'an': Scythopolis 'is said to have sided with the Romans' in 66. Year 90 conventional.

Mosaic of Rehob (Baraita of the Boundaries; text with parallels in the Tosefta and Jerusalem Talmud, mosaic dated late 3rd-6th c.): Beit She'an, a frontier city not settled by the returning exiles although later Israelites joined the local inhabitants, had its home-grown produce exempted from tithing and seventh-year laws in the days of Judah ha-Nasi (c. 200); the inscription lists the gates and permitted limits of Scythopolis and the villages of Sussita's territory. Shows a Jewish minority in a gentile city, not a population figure. Dating basis: rabbinic text. Year 200 (Judah ha-Nasi's time).

Jewish Encyclopedia: the Talmud speaks of the fertile surroundings of Beth-shean and of the strictness with which the Jews living there fulfilled the Law (Neubauer, Geographie du Talmud 174 ff.); JE adds that in the war of independence Beth-shean was taken by the Jews but soon recaptured by the pagans, who took bloody vengeance on the Jews (see the 66 row). Conventional year (Talmudic period). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium.
Evidence of Jewish habitation during the Byzantine period (330-636 CE), including a Jewish synagogue featuring a mosaic with a menorah and the word shalom (House of Leontius).
The Late Antique city (330-638 CE) housed a religiously heterogeneous population, supported by evidence such as a synagogue and the proximity of Christian, Jewish, and pagan objects in local tombs.
"Rabbi Bagard, the grandson of Reb Velvl Yagodnik from Goworowo, served as the chief Rabbi in Beit She'an."
"Two Jewish cemeteries, 'Bet Shaan New' and 'Bet Shaan Old', are located in the municipality."

Epiphanius, Panarion 30.5-6 (Williams): Count Joseph, the converted Jewish 'apostle' of Tiberias, 'had moved from Tiberias, and owned a notable estate' at Scythopolis, where Epiphanius was entertained with Eusebius of Vercelli (exiled by Constantius); Joseph was the only orthodox Christian in the Arian city, 'but there was another, younger man in town too, an orthodox believer of Jewish parentage'. Wikipedia 'Joseph of Tiberias': the encounter was c. 355. Primary patristic source; evidence of Jewish converts in Scythopolis, not of a synagogue community.

Broshi (BASOR 236, 1979), Table 2: Late Roman-Byzantine Scythopolis (Beth-shan) covered 110 hectares (taken from Conder and Kitchener's PEF plan), the largest town of Western Palestine after Aelia Capitolina; a mixed city (Jews, Samaritans, Christians, pagans), so no Jewish population can be derived. Conventional year 400.

House of Leontis synagogue at Beth Shean: the excavator (Zori 1966) dated the mosaic floor to the mid-5th to 6th c.; Z. Safrai reads the building as a Judeo-Christian house of prayer and gives a 4th-5th c. date (as reported by Magness 2024, who notes the same pagan-style motifs occur at Huqoq). Dating basis: mosaic style. Midpoint of mid-5th-6th c. is about 500.

Identification conflict for the House of Leontis (Beth Shean, Byzantine, founded over a ruined Roman bath, exposed 1964): the IAA report (ESI 130, W. Atrash) calls it a Samaritan synagogue, while the Bornblum database lists it as a Jewish synagogue (menorah mosaic, Greek and Aramaic inscriptions) and Z. Safrai reads it as Judeo-Christian. Roman-period (2nd-4th c.) building and Kefar Hananya casseroles were found 100 m to the northwest. Year 500 (Byzantine, conventional).

Wikipedia 'Beth Alpha': the Greek inscription credits the artisans 'Marianos and his son Hanina', 'who also worked on the Beth Shean synagogue', and the Beth Alpha Aramaic inscription dates the building to the reign of Justinus, 'probably Justin I (518-527 CE)' (midpoint 523 used for the Beth Shean work). Implies a Jewish synagogue at Scythopolis/Beth Shean in the 520s. Epigraphic; indirect, medium confidence.

Byzantine (5th-6th c.) refuse site, presumably an abattoir, on the NW fringe of El-Muntar el-Abyad outside Scythopolis: bones of cattle and sheep/goat only (species 'pure in Jewish law'), no bones of the rear quarters of cattle, with butchering marks; the excavators reason that the dump 'was used by the Jewish and Samaritan population of Scythopolis' (ESI 2015). Conventional year (5th-6th c.). Dating basis: pottery (Byzantine cooking pots and frying pans). Confidence low (indirect, Jewish and Samaritan not distinguished).

Wikipedia 'Beit She'an': 'evidence of Jewish habitation and a Samaritan synagogue indicate established communities of these minorities' in the Byzantine period (324-636); a mosaic from a '5th-7th century synagogue in northern Beit Shean, possibly Samaritan'; the House of Leontius synagogue mosaic has 'a temple menorah and the phrase shalom'. Midpoint of 5th-7th century (550) used. Archaeological; Jewish vs Samaritan attribution partly uncertain. The city's maximum size of 40,000 in the 6th century is not a Jewish figure (Population blank).

Byzantine Scythopolis was primarily Christian, but evidence of Jewish habitation and a Samaritan synagogue indicate established minorities; the House of Leontius synagogue mosaic shows a temple menorah and the Hebrew word 'shalom'; a mosaic of a 5th-7th c. synagogue in the north of the city is possibly Samaritan; in the 6th c. the city reached its maximum of 40,000 inhabitants (all communities; no scholar named), so no Jewish population is entered. Year 550 = 6th c.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row: Erlich 2021 (HA 133): a long wall blocking the Hellenistic building and perpendicular walls built over silo mouths, dated to the 1st century BCE or start of the Early Roman period; a bath or small installation and in situ 1st-century CE pottery; the building may be a fort, possibly part of Queen Berenice's estate (Josephus). Erlich (via deadseaquake.info) suggests it may also be the camp of the Roman commander Aebutius. Josephus (Life 118-119) places Besara at the border of Ptolemais, 20 furlongs from Geba, with a great quantity of corn stored there; Hebrew Wikipedia (citing Life) says the grain belonged to Berenice, sister of Agrippa II: estate centre in 66 CE, a literary not archaeological mention. Avigad and Mazar phase I is Herodian to first half of 2nd c. CE with few wall remains. Jewish evidence: a stepped miqveh in Area Z is dated by plaster to the 1st or 2nd c. CE (not narrowed to before 70); no inscription or stone vessels dated before 70 in the sources fetched. Jewish Virtual Library gives 'founded end of 1st c. BCE under Herod', which conflicts with Erlich's 2nd c. BCE Hellenistic stratum; the excavation date is preferred. Population blank: no named-scholar estimate found.

Besara/Beth She'arim appears in Josephus (Life 118-119) as a centre of the estates of Berenice (sister of Agrippa II) in the Jezreel plain where royal grain was stored; Jewish village founded end of 1st c. BCE. Dating basis: literary. Confidence high. Framing row.

Tannaitic sages lived at Beth She'arim, e.g. R. Johanan ben Nuri (1st-2nd c.) and others cited in Tosefta Terumot 7:14 and Niddah 27a; its people were observant of ritual-purity laws (anecdote in Judah ha-Nasi's name). Conventional year (2nd c.). Dating basis: literary (rabbinic). Confidence medium.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Bet She'arim'): in the late 2nd century Judah ha-Nasi moved to Bet She'arim and made it the seat of the Sanhedrin (BT Rosh Hashanah 31a-b); Wikipedia 'Beit She'arim (Roman-era Jewish village)': the town flourished under his leadership and the Talmud lists it as one of the Sanhedrin's ten migratory stations; Wikipedia 'Judah ha-Nasi': after Usha and Shefar'am he headed the Sanhedrin at Beit She'arim, 'where he officiated for a long time' before moving to Sepphoris. 'Late 2nd century' (conventional year 180). Rabbinic-literary.

Late 2nd c.: peak of the site, when the Sanhedrin led by Judah ha-Nasi relocated to Beit She'arim and his family was interred there; the necropolis was used from the 1st to the 4th c. Beit She'arim is named with Yavne, Usha and Shefar'am among the Sanhedrin's moves (Wikipedia, necropolis article; literary/historical). Year 190 = conventional 'late 2nd c.'.

Necropolis: Wikipedia 'Beit She'arim (Roman-era Jewish village)' - 'The burial caves date from the beginning of the 3rd-century CE'; EJ: early 3rd century the necropolis became a central burial place for Jews of Palestine and the Diaspora (Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 3:5). Wikipedia 'Beit She'arim National Park': used from the 1st to 4th centuries, peak in the late 2nd century, 21 catacombs known ('more than 30 burial cave systems' in the lead), about 300 sepulchral inscriptions mostly in Greek, UNESCO World Heritage Site 2015. One catacomb held nearly 130 sarcophagi (Avigad); catacomb 14 bears the epitaph 'This is the burial place of Rabbi Gamaliel' and EJ identifies Hanina bar Hama as head of the yeshivah (Ketubot 103b). Conflict on peak: late 2nd century (National Park article) vs beginning of the 3rd (village article, EJ). Excavators' dating (Mazar/Avigad).

Judah ha-Nasi (d. c. 217 at Sepphoris) was laid to rest in the adjoining necropolis at Beit She'arim (Wikipedia 'Judah ha-Nasi': buried at Beit She'arim, 'about 15.2 km' from Sepphoris; Wikipedia 'Beit She'arim': 'After Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi's death around 220 CE, he was laid to rest in the adjoining necropolis'). Rabbinic-literary tradition; death year c. 217-220.

Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi dies c. 220 CE and is laid to rest in the adjoining necropolis at Beit She'arim (Wikipedia, village article); the village had flourished as a town under his leadership and was a centre of rabbinic scholarship. Dating basis: rabbinic tradition. Year 220.

Necropolis of Beth She'arim used for Diaspora burials: almost 300 epitaphs (mostly Greek - 218 per EJ - also Hebrew, Aramaic, Palmyrene) name deceased from Tadmor/Palmyra, Antioch, Byblos, Tyre, Sidon, Beirut, Mesene (Mesopotamia) and Himyar (Yemen); a Himyarite catacomb (Mazar 1937) dates to the 3rd c.; more than 30 burial cave systems (21 catacombs excavated), most remains 2nd-4th c. Conventional year (3rd c. peak). Dating basis: epigraphy, coins, lamps. Confidence high.

Village remains on the hill: a large synagogue (35 x 15 m) with a hall of two rows of eight pillars, a 40 x 15 m basilica, a late Roman stepped pool and three 3rd-4th c. ritual baths (mikvaot); Byzantine mosaics, gate and oil press. Excavated by Mazar 1936-40 and 1956, Avigad 1953-58 and Tepper 2006-07. Dating basis: stratigraphy. Year 260 = 3rd c. (conventional).

Synagogue: Wikipedia 'Beit She'arim': stone foundations of a large synagogue (about 35 x 15 m) in the north-eastern quarter. Encyclopaedia Judaica: the original excavators dated it to the 3rd century, but 'scholars now prefer the early 4th or 5th century' (conventional year 300 used at the boundary; range 3rd-5th century). Archaeological, dating disputed; low-medium confidence.

Necropolis (UNESCO 2015): 21 catacombs so far, most remains dated 2nd-4th c.; about 300 inscriptions (Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, Palmyrene) showing burials from Beit She'arim, elsewhere in Galilee and from Palmyra, Tyre, Antioch, Mesene (Babylonia), the Phoenician coast (Sidon, Beirut, Byblos) and Himyar; Himyarite tombs of the 3rd c. (Mazar 1937); Catacomb 14, probably the family of Judah ha-Nasi, has bilingual Hebrew-Greek tombs of 'R. Gamliel', 'R. Shimon' and 'Rabbi Anania'; Mazar's coins end with Constantine and Constantius II. Dating basis: coins, lamps, inscriptions. Year 300 = middle of the 3rd-4th c. diaspora burial phase.

Gallus revolt: B. Mazar argued the prosperous Jewish town was destroyed c. 351/2 (about 1,200 bronze coins of the first half of the 4th c. found in the destruction layer); more recent research (cited by EJ and Wikipedia) shows the impact was much smaller. Dating basis: coin hoard + literary. Confidence medium (destruction contested).

Gallus-revolt destruction: Wikipedia 'Beit She'arim' - Benjamin Mazar dated the village's destruction to the first half of the 4th century at the end of the revolt against Gallus ('ca. 351/2 CE'), though 'more recent research suggests the revolt had a much smaller impact'; EJ: about 1,200 bronze coins of the first half of the 4th century date the destruction of buildings; EJ 'Land of Israel': after the revolt Bet She'arim 'was left with only a meager population'. Wikipedia 'Jewish revolt against Constantius Gallus' does not mention Beth She'arim. Numismatic/stratigraphic; medium-low confidence.

Benjamin Mazar described Beth She'arim as a prosperous Jewish town destroyed in the first half of the 4th c. (c. 351/2 CE) at the end of the revolt against Gallus; 'more recent research shows that the Gallus revolt had a much lesser impact on the town'; the 363 earthquake damage is thought limited. Wikipedia also records a crisis in the 4th c. and a decline by the 5th c. from urban centre to rural village. Dating basis: coins/stratigraphy versus the historical hypothesis; contested. Year 352.

Encyclopaedia Judaica: a 363 earthquake damaged the town, which nevertheless recovered and 'flourishes into the Byzantine and early Arab periods' (paraphrase of the EJ entry; this conflicts with EJ 'Land of Israel', which says Bet She'arim was left with only a meagre population after 351/2). Geological/stratigraphic; medium-low confidence.

UNESCO World Heritage statement (2015): the catacombs developed from the 2nd c. as the primary Jewish burial place outside Jerusalem after the Bar Kokhba revolt (inscriptions in Greek, Aramaic, Hebrew, Palmyrene; flourishing 2nd-4th c. under Judah the Patriarch) but 'had ceased to be used for burial purposes by the 6th century' and were abandoned. Wikipedia adds that 6th-c. buildings and mosaics show a partial renewal of the settlement (not its former prosperity). Conventional year (6th c.). Dating basis: excavation synthesis. Confidence medium; continued Jewish character of the 6th-c. village is not documented in the sources read.

Buildings and mosaics of the 6th c. indicate some renewal of settlement, though not the former prosperity; the necropolis fell out of use in the late Byzantine period, with signs of human presence through the 6th c. and into the early Arab period. Year 560 = 6th c.
