Horvat Beth Netofa (Lower Galilee; Beth Netofa of the sources, identification reliable): size category D until c. 150 CE, E (41-60 dunams) c. 150-350 CE and then abandoned in the late 4th c.; Leibner takes its probable synagogue (ashlars, doorposts and roof tiles; Guerin saw a pillared building) to be of the simpler type, as at Khirbet Shema, and uses the abandonment as a terminus ante quem (late 4th c.) for its construction. Dating basis: survey pottery. Year 340 = end of the E-size phase.

Leibner (site 29, Khirbet Natif, map ref 1862/2488, 52 dunams): the late pottery matches the 363 destruction layer at Sepphoris with no later sherd, so the large village (estimated 41-52 dunams in the Middle and Late Roman periods) was finally abandoned in the second half of the 4th c.; ashlars, roof tiles, column drums and a pillared building reported by Guerin and Ilan (remains near the spring have since been destroyed by a pump installation) point to a monumental public building, apparently a synagogue, without decorated stones (like the Khirbet Shema' synagogue) and built before the mid-4th c. Leibner notes that rabbinic sources name only the Beth Netofa valley (Mishnah Shevi'it 9:5, R. Shim'on, mid-2nd c.), never the settlement itself, and that the valley name could outlive the village; the Jewish character is therefore inferred from the rabbinic and archaeological context, not from an inscription. Compare the 400 row (Bornblum: Late Roman/Byzantine, 4th c.): Leibner gives a firmer terminus ante quem. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 195-200, 400-401 (note 7). Conventional year (second half of 4th c.). Dating basis: survey pottery + destruction-layer parallel. Confidence medium.

Beth Netofa (Khirbet Natif), NE edge of the Beit Netofa valley, a Jewish settlement of the Mishnaic period that gave the valley its name (Mishnah Shevi'it 9:5): Guerin reported a pillared building and Z. Ilan (1985) column drums, ashlars and roof tiles of a probable synagogue of the Late Roman/Byzantine period; the remains have since been destroyed. Wikipedia: settled from the Iron Age to medieval times. Conventional year (4th c.). Dating basis: Mishnaic mention + architectural fragments. Confidence low-medium. Coordinates from the Bornblum DB map link.

Literary only (conventional date -1200: Joshua's allotment). Beth-anoth is in Judah's eighth hill-country group: Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, Maarath, Beth-anoth, Eltekon, 'six cities with their villages' (Josh 15:58-59). Identification disputed, favoured: Khirbet Ras et-Tawil (Hebrew Wikipedia, citing Ofer 1993), against Khirbet Beit 'Ainun near the village Beit 'Ainun (35.126 E, 31.562 N), which Robinson proposed and which was held 'almost without dispute'; the two lie about 1.5 km apart. Coordinates entered are Ras et-Tawil (Israel grid 1636.1083, 1,013 m). Weak identification: no population figure derived. Further sources: https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Joshua.15?context=0&commentary=0&lang=en&version=english%7CThe%20Holy%20Scriptures%20by%20Jewish%20Publication%20Society%201917

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000): about 23 dunams at Khirbet Ras et-Tawil (Hebrew Wikipedia, area per Ofer's survey; Iron 2a about 28 dunams, 2b about 33; no calendar dates, no excavation). Identification disputed (see the literary row), so no population is derived. Period labels (Iron 2a/2b/2c/2d) follow Avi Ofer's 1993 Tel Aviv University survey of the Judean hills as reproduced on Hebrew Wikipedia, which gives no calendar dates here; they are mapped to the project's Iron IIA/IIB/IIC convention, so the date is approximate.

Iron Age IIC (-722 to -586): about 44 dunams in Iron 2c, 45 dunams in Iron 2d (the site's peak, persisting 'even after Sennacherib's campaign') at Khirbet Ras et-Tawil (Hebrew Wikipedia citing Ofer 1993). The size is large for a minor town, which is part of why the identification is disputed; no population is derived. Period labels (Iron 2a/2b/2c/2d) follow Avi Ofer's 1993 Tel Aviv University survey of the Judean hills as reproduced on Hebrew Wikipedia, which gives no calendar dates here; they are mapped to the project's Iron IIA/IIB/IIC convention, so the date is approximate.

Literary only (conventional date -1200: Joshua's allotment). Beth-arabah lies on Judah's northern border, 'north of Beth-arabah' (Josh 15:6), is the first town of the wilderness group (Josh 15:61) and is in Benjamin's list (Josh 18:22) (verses as cited by Hebrew Wikipedia). Identification disputed, favoured: Ain el-Gharabeh south of Wadi Qelt, where the ancient name is 'commonly assumed' to survive; Khirbet el-Gharabeh in the Jericho plain (mostly Byzantine finds) is rejected, and a candidate site of about 30 dunams on the south bank of Wadi Qelt has sherds of the later Iron Age phases (Hebrew Wikipedia; further pottery dating pending). Coordinates are Ain el-Gharabeh (OpenBible geocoding). The site may belong to a Jordan Valley/Jericho sub-area as well. Population none. Further sources: https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Joshua.15?context=0&commentary=0&lang=en&version=english%7CThe%20Holy%20Scriptures%20by%20Jewish%20Publication%20Society%201917

Iron Age IIC / late monarchy (-722 to -586). Identification with Ramat Rahel is a scholarly proposal (Lipschits and Na'aman; en.wikipedia says 'some scholars'; he.wikipedia 'possibly'). Judahite royal palace/citadel (Aharoni Stratum Va; he.wikipedia dates it 8th-7th c. BCE); Lipschits introduction: Judah an Assyrian/Egyptian/Babylonian vassal 732-586; palatial compound built Iron IIC. Judahite settlement. No academic population estimate or built-up area found in fetched pages.

Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332). Renewed excavations (Tel Aviv-Heidelberg 2005-2010) show the palatial complex was not destroyed in 586 BCE and continued at least to the end of the Persian period; zenith in the Persian period as imperial administrative centre and probable governor's residence of province Yehud (Lipschits). Lion- and yhwd-stamped jar handles. Inhabitants: Judeans/Yehud administration. No population estimate found.

city_other: תל ג'נין / تل جنين (Tell Jenin; also Tell el-Nawar)
comment: Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Identification: Tell Jenin is the leading candidate (openbible.info ~80% confidence; alternatives incl. Khirbet Beit Jann etc. under 10%) and Beth-haggan is sometimes treated as the same place as En-gannim/Anem; sources disagree. Canaanite Gina of Amarna letter 250 (14th c BCE) is identified with Jenin (en.wikipedia Gina; Jenin). Canaanite vassal of Egypt. No population estimate found. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jenin; https://www.openbible.info/geo/ancient/aaa2f54/beth-haggan

city_other: תל ג'נין / تل جنين (Tell Jenin; also Tell el-Nawar)
comment: Iron Age (-1200 to -586; en.wikipedia says only 'Iron Age' occupation phase, not subdivided, so entered at Iron Age I start). Biblical Ein-Ganim (Issachar Levite city) and Beth-haggan of 2 Kings 9:27 (Ahaziah's flight from Jehu, 9th c BCE) are linked to Tell Jenin. Israelite site per biblical tradition. No excavation report or population estimate found; tell lies under Jenin's business district. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/ג'נין

Literary only (no Iron Age remains reported in the fetched pages); dated by convention to the tribal-allotment narrative c. -1200. Josh 15:6 (the border of Judah goes up to Beth-hogla and passes on the north side of Beth-arabah), Josh 18:19 (Benjamin's southern border runs to the north side of Beth-hoglah), Josh 18:21 (Jericho, Beth-hoglah and the valley of Keziz in Benjamin's city list). Identification: the name is preserved in the monastery Deir Hajla and the spring 'Ein Hajla east of Jericho (Joseph Schwarz; the accepted view per Hebrew Wikipedia 'Beth-hoglah'), and the city may have lain on one of the ruins nearby; Josephus' Bethalaga and Jerome's Bethagla are probably the same (English Wikipedia 'Deir Hajla'). Eusebius' Onomasticon puts Bethagla three Roman miles from Jericho and two from the Jordan. Coordinates entered are Deir Hajla (31.8203 N, 35.5019 E); the exact tell is not located. No population figure.

Iron Age II (source does not split IIA/IIB/IIC; start taken as -1000; continues to -586). Hebrew Wikipedia: survey site 1/45/309; among the twenty largest settlements in the Judean hills in Iron Age II; ancient core ~20 dunams under the modern village. Judahite town (Josh 15:53; list possibly reflects Josiah's reign). Identification with Taffuh not certain (English Wikipedia: some experts do not accept). No published population estimate found; left blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row: Joan E. Taylor (BAR Winter 2025; summarised by BAS) says the Lower Aqueduct from Solomon's Pools to Jerusalem, passing through the centre of Bethlehem, was likely built in the Hasmonean period, and argues the water system implies a sizeable town; the only fetched evidence for this period. English Wikipedia calls Bethlehem a Jewish settlement for about 1,100-1,300 years but cites no Hasmonean finds. Most remains lie under the modern city and are unexcavated. Population presumably Jewish; no named estimate; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row and records a disagreement. Taylor (BAR 2025) argues Josephus calls Bethlehem a polis and that it was a flourishing Judean town until Bar Kokhba, citing the aqueducts (Upper Aqueduct probably Herodian). Against this, Haaretz (via Hayadan; Ran Shapira) reports IAA archaeologist Aviram Oshri saying excavations in Bethlehem near Jerusalem since the British Mandate found no signs of Jewish settlement in the Herodian period and no pottery or buildings of the time of Jesus's birth in the Church of the Nativity (Byzantine and medieval buildings only); Oshri 2005 proposed Bethlehem of Galilee, where stone vessels, a stone-vessel workshop and a synagogue-shaped mausoleum indicate Jews in Herod's time. English Wikipedia records Murphy-O'Connor (2011) defending the Judean site. Hamilton 1934 (QDAP 3) atrium excavation was seen as a bibliographic entry only. Absence of evidence partly reflects the town being built over, so Jewish presence is neither proven nor disproven by excavation. Population blank.

During the wars between Arabs and Jews, the town of Bethlehem remained unoccupied.

comment: Iron Age I/IIA (c. -1050; foundation). Et-Tell is the capital of the Aramean kingdom of Geshur according to the archaeologists who 'tend to agree' (English Wikipedia; sometimes identified with New Testament Bethsaida; Arav 2018 links the Iron Age city to biblical Zer, Josh 19:35). English Wikipedia: settlement founded in the 11th century BCE, the Stratum VI city gate (northwest chamber wall) dated 11th-10th c. BCE; Golan Research Institute dig 1987-89, Rami Arav 2008-10 and 2014. Geshur was a neighbour, not an Israelite town: Israel did not drive out the Geshurites (Josh 13:13); David married Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (2 Sam 3:3); Absalom fled to Geshur for three years (2 Sam 13:37-38). Population blank.

comment: Iron Age IIA (-950 to -850; Stratum VI per the New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations entry on Bethsaida/et-Tell). Foundation of a thriving city: terraces over basalt boulders supporting two parallel walls (inner wall up to 8 m wide), a monumental east gate (outer gate room 7.5 x 5.9 m), a bit hilani palace 28 x 15 m, granaries; the stratum ends in the 9th c. BCE in a great conflagration (about 1 m of debris). The entry says the wealth of the Iron Age remains suggests the capital of Geshur in the 10th-9th c.; mound size '20 acres' (about 8 ha). Aramean (Geshurite) rather than Israelite. No population estimate for this phase; Population blank.

comment: Iron Age IIB (-850 to -732; Stratum V). City rebuilt on the old walls: outer wall rebuilt, four-chamber gate 35 x 17 m, northeast tower 21 x 8 m; the gate area of Strata VI-V has five high places and eight stelae including a bull's-head moon-god stela; the gate is destroyed by fire (dozens of iron arrowheads, pottery and 14C evidence) in the 732 BCE campaign of Tiglath-pileser III, which ended the kingdom of Geshur (New Encyclopedia entry; English Wikipedia, which adds that in Iron II it was 'easily the largest and strongest city' east of the Jordan Valley). Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Josephus (Ant. 18.28) says the tetrarch Philip raised the village of Bethsaida to a city (polis) by adding inhabitants and fortifications and renamed it Julias; Philip died there (Ant. 18.108) (as quoted by Aviam and Notley); Hebrew Wikipedia notes Josephus gives two namesakes (Livia in War, Julia daughter of Augustus in Antiquities) and one coin of Philip at et-Tell. NEAEHL: a Roman temple in Area A (20 x 5 m) over the Iron Age gate, a private Roman residence in Area B. EL-ARAJ (Aviam and Notley, Kinneret College): Roman pottery from the late 1st c. BCE to 3rd c. CE, a bathhouse, a denarius of Nero 65-66 CE and about 20 fishing weights (from later levels), and Urman's survey coins of Philip and Agrippa II; the team calls it a Jewish fishing village that became a polis; Arav says the bathhouse is an Agrippa II mercenary camp and found only beach deposits in 1987. The identification and which site is Julias remain disputed, so the coordinates given (et-Tell) may not be the first-century village. Rabbinic sources name it Tzaidan (Aviam and Notley, citing Freund). No named Jewish population estimate (neither the el-Araj team nor Arav gives one): Population blank.

Literary only; Year of Data -1200 = conventional date of the settlement narrative. Identification: Khirbet Ibziq (disputed alternative Salhab); the Iron Age pottery is on the upper ruin only. Muster point of Saul's army. 1 Sam 11:8: 'when he numbered them in Bezek, the children of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand' (a census-style figure for the army, not a town population, and not used as one); from Bezek Saul's three companies relieved Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite (1 Sam 11:1-11). Identification: Khirbet Ibziq, about 20 km north-east of Nablus; most scholars hold it to be the Bezek of 1 Sam 11, although an alternative site at Salhab has been proposed on archaeological grounds (English Wikipedia 'Ibziq'). The upper ruin has pottery from the Iron Age to the medieval period without a published sub-period. Literary only; Year of Data -1020 = conventional date of Saul's reign. No population figure. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibziq

Year 200: the baraita is late 2nd-3rd century (the Rehob mosaic copy is dated late 3rd-6th/7th c.). Evidence is textual only; no excavated Jewish remains reported in the sources read. Later Christian use of the same place: IIP has a church mosaic of 567/8 at 'Bezeth' (beze0001), so the Jewish phase did not continue into the Byzantine period at least in the epigraphic record.

Cabul is Kabul, 14-16 km east of Acre (32.8697 N 35.2022 E, Wikipedia; Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities, no '?'): Josh 19:27 (Asher's border 'goeth out to Cabul on the left hand', after Beth-dagon, Beth-emek and Neiel). The excavated Iron Age site is Khirbet Rosh Zayit, 2 km NE of Kabul, where Wikipedia (Cabul) reports an Israelite settlement of the 12th century BCE; the village of Kabul itself yielded only Persian and later pottery (Wikipedia, Kabul). Exact site disputed (BibleWalks lists Tel Kison as another possible Cabul); favoured: Kabul with Rosh Zayit. No population estimate. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabul%2C_Israel ; https://www.biblewalks.com/west_galilee_gallery/Kisson ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+19&version=KJV ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua

Biblical mention and Phoenician fortress (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -960 = conventional date of Solomon's reign). 1 Kgs 9:11-13: Solomon gave Hiram of Tyre twenty cities in the land of Galilee; Hiram, displeased, 'called them the land of Cabul unto this day'. Archaeology (Wikipedia, Cabul): at Khirbet Rosh Zayit, 2 km NE of Kabul, a Phoenician fortification of the 10th century BCE was built on the Israelite settlement; the excavator suggests it shows Solomon's transfer of the area to Tyrian control. Identification as in the previous row (Kabul/Rosh Zayit, disputed on the exact site). No population estimate. Further source: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Kings+9&version=KJV

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row: the first pass implied plausible Jewish settlement from the conquest; the archaeology complicates this. Hamichlol (citing Stieglitz 1993, Raban, Will 1987): the latest Hellenistic finds are early Eastern Sigillata A of the 2nd half of the 2nd c. BCE, with no clear 1st c. BCE material, so the town appears to have lapsed about the start of the 1st c. BCE and continuous Jewish settlement after Jannaeus is hard to confirm; Hebrew Wikipedia (Megillat Taanit, 14 Sivan) says Jewish settlement began with the conquest. Conquest dates conflict: 103 BCE (Livius), c. 100 BCE (Dead Sea Quake catalogue), 90 BCE (Hebrew Wikipedia and Hamichlol). Mixed or unclear population; no excavated Jewish finds; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row with stronger evidence. Herod founded the city 22-10/9 BCE with the Roma and Augustus temple on a platform, circus and harbour (NEAEHL); area about 45 ha (Livius). Jews: NEAEHL reports one loculi cave with a bone-collection pit in the Roman cemetery that 'apparently served the Jewish community' (menorah lamps from a SE cave are Samaritan, not Jewish); Josephus War 2.285-292: a Jewish synagogue beside a plot owned by a Greek, and the Greeks held the government of the city by Nero's decision; War 2.457: above twenty thousand Jews killed in one hour and the city emptied of Jews in 66 CE (casualty figure, not a population); Lee Levine (as quoted on a UMD course page) says Herod's city 'housed a large and powerful Jewish community'. Total-city estimate, NOT Jewish: Robert Bull 125,000-250,000 at the Roman peak (Christian Science Monitor 1980). No named estimate of the Jewish population, so Population blank. Mixed city: Greek/Syrian pagans, Samaritans, Jews, Roman soldiers.

source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_War_of_the_Jews/Book_II | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Antonius_Felix | Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), ch. 2, img024 Screenshot_20221028-091944.jpg (supporting detail only)
comment: Event: Dispute between the Jews and the Syrians (Greeks) of Caesarea over the city's character and the Jews' rights: the Jews claimed the city because Herod, a Jew, had built it; the Syrians answered that it was a Greek city. When the Jews had beaten the Syrians, the procurator Felix ordered them off the market-place and, as they would not obey, sent soldiers who killed a great many Jews and plundered their property (Josephus, War 2.13.7). Josephus gives no year; Felix was procurator in 52-60 CE (Wikipedia), so 60 is an approximation for the end of his term. The attached book (Shpak-Lissak, ch. 2, img024) tells the same incident (the Jews won the struggle but Felix, enraged, sent an army that plundered and killed many). This is the earlier incident, not the 66 CE massacre of about 20,000 Jews that the map already has. [confidence: medium - year approximate] [Source detail: (Josephus, War 2.13.7, Whiston translation); (Wikipedia, procurator 52-60 CE)]

Framing row: Jewish Encyclopedia ('Caesarea') - after an insult to the Jewish synagogue in 66 the Jews fought the Greeks, lost and fled to Narbata; when the wider war broke out the pagans massacred the Jews (reportedly about 20,000 'in one hour'); the synagogue where the fighting began is linked to the rabbinic 'riotous synagogue of Caesarea'; Vespasian then made Caesarea a Roman colony-province. (Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima' gives the same Josephus trigger: Greeks sacrificing birds in front of a local synagogue.) Year 66 = pre-period framing.

Outbreak of the Great Revolt at Caesarea. Josephus (War 2.14.4-5, Whiston translation): after a Caesarean Greek sacrificed birds at the entrance of the Jewish synagogue the quarrel turned to blows, and (War 2.18.1) on the day the Roman garrison at Jerusalem was killed the people of Caesarea slew the Jews of the city: 'in one hour's time above twenty thousand Jews were killed, and all Caesarea was emptied of its Jewish inhabitants' (Florus sent survivors to the galleys). The 20,000 is Josephus' victim count, almost certainly exaggerated, and is not a population estimate (population left blank). Framing row (pre-70). Encyclopaedia Judaica (Caesarea) adds that the city's population was about half gentile and half Jewish and that the clashes between the two communities sparked the revolt.

After the fall of Betar (Bar Kokhba war, 132-135) 'several prominent Jewish leaders, including R. Akiva, were martyred' at Caesarea, headquarters of the Roman commander Julius Severus (Encyclopaedia Judaica, Caesarea). Literary tradition, not independently confirmed archaeologically. Shows the city as seat of Roman authority after 70, rather than a documented community; included as a dated event. After 135 the province was renamed Syria Palaestina with Caesarea as capital.

Mosaic of Rehob (Baraita of the Boundaries): Caesarea was an enclave on the coast not settled by the returning exiles; in the 1st c. it was principally gentile, and later Jews joined the inhabitants; Judah ha-Nasi (2nd-3rd c.) released the city and its bounds (Zuwarnah, Inn of Tabitha, 'Amuda, Dor, Kefar Saba) from tithing and seventh-year restrictions, with only the demai tithe retained on some products. Shows a Jewish community inside a mixed city; no population figure. Dating basis: rabbinic text. Year 200.

Jewish Encyclopedia ('Academies in Palestine'): the Caesarea school gained prominence 'owing solely to the influence of Hoshaiah, who lived there in the first half of the third century'; JE 'Caesarea': 'In Talmudic times there was here a large Jewish population with many synagogues'; the Jews 'were completely Hellenized, and in the third century the Shema' was said in Greek'. Year 225 = middle of the first half of the 3rd century. Rabbinic-literary.

Rabbinic academy: the amora Hoshaiah (Hoshaya Rabbah) 'lived in Caesarea in the first half of the third century' and taught there at the same time as the church father Origen, with whom he had personal intercourse; Caesarea 'came into prominence, owing solely to the influence of Hoshaya' (Jewish Encyclopedia, Academies in Palestine). Wikipedia (Hoshaiah Rabbah) adds, citing Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 11, 30b, that the aged master moved his school to Caesarea. Year 225 is the conventional midpoint of 'first half of the 3rd century'; literary dating, good confidence that a school existed, exact dates vague.

Synagogue, stratum IV (third century). Epidentity (Univ. of Warsaw) database summary of Avi-Yonah's 1956/1962 excavations (Field O, the 'Synagogue site'): a synagogue about 18 x 9 m, facing south and entered from the short east side, was established in the third century on a fill of debris; its mosaic included a dedicatory text naming Iulis and fragments of a Hebrew inscription listing the 24 priestly courses. Stratum II below may preserve a first, Herodian-period synagogue, but the summary calls this uncertain. Dating by stratigraphy and mosaic; no final excavation report has been published (Avi-Yonah 1993 summary; Joint Expedition Field O volume 2009). Jodi Magness's review of that volume (American Journal of Archaeology 114.1, 2010) stresses the problems: five strata per Avi-Yonah (possible Early Roman house-synagogue in stratum II, synagogue buildings in strata IV and V), but the priestly-courses plaque and the chancel-screen fragments were found 'in other areas more than 70 m away' from Avi-Yonah's area A, much of the original data is lost, and 'none of the inscriptions (all of which are in Greek) is unambiguously Jewish'; she nevertheless concludes that from Avi-Yonah's descriptions 'there seems little doubt' that one or more superimposed synagogue buildings were found (menorah capitals, lulav and ethrog screen, dedications). Encyclopaedia Judaica adds that Jewish life 'flourished from the third century onward' and that the Talmud mentions 'the synagogue of Caesarea' near the harbour where prayers were said in Greek (tj Sot. 7:1, 21b). Conventional year 250 for 'third century'. The Jewish Encyclopedia (Caesarea, Gottheil/Krauss) adds that the Caesarean Jews 'were completely Hellenized', that in Talmudic times 'there was here a large Jewish population with many synagogues', and that the riot synagogue of 66 is probably the 'riotous synagogue of Caesarea' still named in third-century rabbinic sources (Y. Sanh. 18a; Y. Naz. 56a; Lam. R. 1:3), although the Byzantine writer Malalas says Vespasian turned it into an odeon.

Jewish quarter in an ethnically divided city: a 1980 Christian Science Monitor report on the Joint Expedition to Caesarea Maritima quotes Professor Robert J. Bull (excavation director) that in its heyday 'the city consisted of four ethno-religious quarters: pagan, Samaritan, Jewish, and (by the 3rd century) Christian' (his demographic deduction for the whole city in Roman times is 125,000-250,000 - a total, not a Jewish figure, so Population is left blank). Reported at second hand in a newspaper, not from Bull's excavation volumes, and the location of the Jewish quarter is not given in the article (the synagogue site at Field O is on the shore north of the Crusader city). Year 260 is a conventional placement for 'Roman times, Christians by the 3rd century'. Low-moderate confidence; no archaeological delimitation of a 'Jewish quarter' is cited.

source: Yankelevich, R., Cathedra 61, pp. 172-173 (entry 62; n. 156-157: Y. Demai 2:1, 22c, and Tosefta Ohalot 18:13)
comment: Ethnic composition of Caesarea, end of the 3rd century. Yankelevich (entry 62, Caesarea): the Great Revolt began in Caesarea and the city was emptied of its Jews (Josephus); afterwards a Jewish community was organised there and it remained a minority; the city was regarded as a city of idolatry (Tosefta Hullin 2:13). Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, who acted to ease the position of Jews living among gentiles, also exempted Caesarea from the Sabbatical-year commandments. At the end of the 3rd century (Jerusalem Talmud Demai 2:1, 22c) the population consisted of three ethnic groups, gentiles, Samaritans and Jews, and none of them formed a majority. This is the only direct ratio statement for Caesarea in the paper (the map already has the Mosaic-of-Rehob exemption at 200 and Bull's four ethno-religious quarters at 260; the Christians of Bull's list fall under 'gentiles' here). Year 290 = the paper's 'end of the 3rd century' (conventional). No figure: Population blank. I checked Sefaria's Jerusalem Talmud Demai 2:1 (Guggenheimer) for the passage but did not locate it there. No online source found; source is a scholarly article (Hebrew). [confidence: medium]

Abbahu: Wikipedia 'Abbahu' - Talmudist at Caesarea 'from about 279 to 320 CE' (born c. 279, died 320; midpoint 300 used), rector of the Caesarean academy, preached against Christian dogma; JE 'Academies in Palestine': 'the sages of Caesarea' were respected in Tiberias throughout the 4th century. Jewish Encyclopedia ('Caesarea'): he served as a judge and was the antagonist of Christianity and of the Cuthaeans (Samaritans). Rabbinic-literary.

Rabbi Abbahu (third-generation amora, in Caesarea c. 279-320; year 300 is the midpoint) was rector of the rabbinic academy of Caesarea and the Jewish community's representative before the Roman governor (b. Ket. 17a per Encyclopaedia Judaica; Wikipedia 'Abbahu': Talmudist in Caesarea Maritima 'from about 279 to 320 CE'). Encyclopaedia Judaica names further Caesarean sages: R. Abba, R. Adda, R. Hanina, R. Assi, R. Hoshaiah, R. Hezekiah, R. Ahava b. Zeira. Jewish Encyclopedia: 'throughout the whole of the fourth century the opinions of the sages of Caesarea were taken into respectful account, even in Tiberias'. The Jerusalem Talmud also says Caesarea held many Samaritans recruited for the city guard (tj Av. Zar. 1:2, 39c) - the mixed Jewish/Samaritan/pagan setting behind the tensions of 556. The Jewish Encyclopedia (Caesarea) adds the Samaritan friction: 'The Cuthaeans of Caesarea disputed with R. Abbahu' (Y. Av. Zar. 44d) and mocked the Jews at his death; R. Jose of Caesarea speaks of the 'Christianized Jews' of the city (Eccl. R. 7:26), and Abbahu was an antagonist of Christianity. Literary dating.

Marble fragment of a list of the 24 priestly courses from a synagogue at Caesarea (found 1962), dated c. AD 300 (late 3rd-early 4th c., palaeography), assigns courses to Galilean villages including Nazareth. Dating basis: palaeography (not stratigraphic). Year 300.

Priestly-courses inscription found at Caesarea (1962; three fragments; Avi-Yonah, IEJ 12): Hebrew list of the localities of the 24 priestly courses; Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine gives 200-500 CE (midpoint 350), Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima' 3rd-4th century and links it to Jewish resettlement in the Galilee after 70; it names Nazareth, Migdal Nunaiya and Aklah-Arab (see those towns). The find shows a Jewish (synagogue-related) community at Caesarea that valued the Galilean priestly tradition. Epigraphic.

Destruction of the third-century synagogue (stratum IV) c. mid-fourth century: a hoard of about 3,700 bronze coins, almost all of Constantius II (r. 337-361), was found near a synagogue wall; 'Avi-Yonah assumed that the hoard was buried and the synagogue destroyed ca. 355 C.E.' (J. Magness, American Journal of Archaeology 114.1, 2010, reviewing the Field O volume; the Epidentity summary likewise says 'likely concealed shortly before the building's destruction around the mid-fourth century'). Magness also reports that Avi-Yonah dated the construction of the stratum V synagogue to the mid-fourth century. The source gives no cause; a link to the Gallus revolt of 351 is a plausible conjecture but is not stated by the source and is not used as evidence. Dating by coin hoard (terminus post quem 337-361); good confidence for 'mid-4th century'.

Hebrew priestly-courses (mishmarot) inscription found in the sand at Caesarea in 1962 by Israeli-American excavators: three fragments of a list of the 24 priestly courses with the Galilean villages where the priests settled after the Second Temple's destruction (readable lines include 'The 17th course Hezir - Mamliah; the 18th Hapizzez - Nazareth; the 19th Pethahiah - Aklah/Arab; the 20th Ezekiel - Migdal Nunaiya'; Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine caes0684). Dates differ: Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima' gives third-fourth centuries, IIP gives 3rd-5th century (200-500; midpoint 350 used here), J. Price (CIIP no. 1145, cited on the Bornblum synagogue database) 4th-5th century. Evidence that Caesarean Jews (or priestly families linked to the Caesarea synagogue) kept the priestly-course tradition in late antiquity; also a source for named Jewish villages in Galilee (Nazareth, Migdal, Arab).

Greek prayer plaque 'God is one! May he help Iouda the elder. In the year 471' (Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine caes0137), dated 409-411 CE by the editors with a question mark (the conversion of the era year is theirs and uncertain). Classified Jewish by IIP; the 'God is one' formula is also found among Samaritans and Christians, so the attribution is a judgement. Weak-to-moderate row: one short inscription indicating Greek-speaking Jews in the early 5th century.

Synagogue, stratum V (DATE CONFLICT: mid-fifth century per the Epidentity summary, but Magness 2010 reports that Avi-Yonah himself dated its construction to the mid-fourth century; the IIP editors date the Beryllos pavement 400-650 and the mosaic inscription to 'fourth to mid-seventh centuries'; year 450 follows Epidentity): a new, long and narrow hall (c. 11 x 2.6 m) rose on the ruins of its predecessor; its Greek mosaic inscription reads 'Beryllos, son of Iouda, head of the synagogue and curator, donated the tessellated pavement of the triclinium at his own cost' (IIP caes0079; IIP editors date it 400-650 CE, the Epidentity summary of Avi-Yonah's excavation dates the stratum to the mid-5th century). Other finds: two columns with seven-branched menorahs (one with the monogram of Patricius), a column inscription of Theodorus for his daughter Matrona, an inscription 'May the Lord be our helper. An offering of the congregation under Marouthas' (caes0080). The building was used into the 6th and possibly 7th century. J. Magness's 2010 review in the American Journal of Archaeology cautions that none of the Greek inscriptions is unambiguously Jewish except by association with the building (the Beryllos title is partly damaged - only 'archi' is clearly legible - and the 'Lord is our helper' formula was used by Christians and Jews alike); the Bornblum database lists the site as an excavated Jewish synagogue (Late Roman/Byzantine).

Synagogue at Caesarea with a mosaic floor bearing Hebrew and Greek inscriptions (excavated by J. Ory 1947 and M. Avi-Yonah 1956, 1962; Bornblum database period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'). Conventional year 450, low confidence on the date. A mixed city: the Mosaic of Rehob refers to the non-Jewish population of Caesarea.

Jewish funerary epigraphy: the Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine corpus classifies 51 Caesarea inscriptions as Jewish, of which about 35 are marble funerary plaques or epitaphs (IIP caes0165-0196, 0518-0523, 0532, 0673, 0675), mostly dated only '4th to mid-7th century' (range 300-650, midpoint c. 475) and many undated. The earliest dated Jewish funerary texts are 3rd-century (caes0532, 'Tomb of Jacob, son of Julianos, fellow craftsman', 200-299; caes0189, 'third to sixth century'). Identification as Jewish is by the editors (names, formulae, menorah) and some are uncertain (e.g. caes0675). Indicator of a sizeable Jewish burial population in late antique Caesarea, not a population figure (blank).

Framing row just after the period: Jewish Encyclopedia ('Caesarea') - under Justinian 'Jews allied with Samaritans and harassed Christian residents', killing the governor Stephan in July 556; Samaritans had instigated bitter riots against Christians in 484 and 548. Shows a large, assertive Jewish community at Caesarea in the mid-6th century. Literary (Procopius/Malalas tradition).

Joint Jewish-Samaritan revolt at Caesarea (July 556): Wikipedia 'Samaritan revolts' says 'the Jews and the Samaritans seem to have made common cause, beginning their rebellion in Caesarea early in July', killing Christians, plundering churches and killing the governor Stephanus; reprisals appear limited to the Caesarea district. The earlier Samaritan revolt of 484 (king Justa/Justasas) also reached Caesarea and destroyed the church of St Procopius, but the sources do not name Jews there. Late framing row (556 is after the 550 limit) recording Jewish-Samaritan relations on the coast. Literary dating (Byzantine sources); casualty figures in the article are not used.

Benjamin of Tudela, Sefer ha-Massa'ot (Itinerary), c.1165: traveller names the place "Caesarea"; Adler translation, text marker [p.32]. Traveller's words: 'about 200 Jews and 200 Cuthim (Samaritans)'. Identification: Caesarea. Year 1165 = c.1165 (Benjamin travelled c.1165-1173).

Isaac ben Joseph ibn Chelo, The Roads from Jerusalem, 1334: traveller names the place "Kaisarieh"; Adler, Jewish Travellers (1930), p.142-143 (OCR page markers). Traveller's words: As in the days of R. Benjamin there are few Jews at Kaisarieh (no number). Identification: Caesarea. No count given; Population left blank (presence only). Year 1334 as given for the journey.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): NEAEHL (Ma'oz): Herod built the Augusteum in 19 BCE (phase Va) and Philip founded the city Paneas/Caesarea Philippi in 2/1 BCE; the town-centre palace may be Agrippa II's residence. Contradiction in the sources: the BAR article on the renewed excavations says there was never a temple in front of the cave and dates the courtyard, by radiometric dating of aqueduct plaster, to the last third of the 1st c. CE under Agrippa II. Josephus (Antiquities 15.363) places a white-stone temple near Panium (the page does not name the builder). The city was Greek/pagan; Jewish Virtual Library (Enc. Judaica) names Jews only for 70 CE, when Titus held games there and executed Jewish captives, and for the medieval community; Hebrew Wikipedia notes Mishnah Parah 8:11 mentions the cave of Pamias as a water source. This is not evidence of a resident Jewish population, so the first-pass phrase 'with Jewish residents' is unsupported; Population blank. Built-up area c. 730 dunams is given for the late 1st to 5th c. CE (Hebrew Wikipedia), not a Jewish figure.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): supporting - Jewish Virtual Library (Enc. Judaica, Banias): Titus held games at Caesarea Philippi in 70 CE with many Jewish captives executed; Jews called the place Dan or Mivzar Dan; Talmud 'Keissariyyon', Mishnah 'cave of Pamias'; no population figures. Population blank.

Jewish community at Paneas/Banias: Z. U. Ma'oz (NEAEHL 1993, quoted at deadseaquake.info) writes that 'the Jewish community in the town is alluded to, in the early second century, by the sukkah of Rabbi Yohanan son of Rabbi Ila'i (B.T. Suk. 27b)'. In ancient Jewish sources the town is Keisarion/Kisrin and the cave Pamias/Panias. Earlier, Josephus (Life 51-61, 74) records that the town's Jewish community was imprisoned in the First Revolt and massacred on the order of Varus (66-67, before the period). Banias was 'predominantly pagan' of Iturean and Phoenician makeup and fully Hellenized in names, so the Jews were a minority. Year 110 = early 2nd c.; confidence medium (a Talmudic allusion, not archaeology).

Banias 'was considered outside the halakhic boundaries of Palestine, and a list of "forbidden" edible species was compiled for use by its Jewish inhabitants (Tosefta Shev. 4:11; J.T. Shev. 36c)' (Ma'oz, NEAEHL 1993, at deadseaquake.info). Tosefta c. 200 CE; shows a Jewish population served by a halakhic dispensation. Year 200 conventional; confidence medium.

'Jewish legends connect the emperor Diocletian to Banias' (Ma'oz, NEAEHL 1993): one places his residence here, to which Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi II was summoned on the eve of the Sabbath (Bereshit Rabbah 63:8; JT Terumot 8:10); another recounts that the people of Banias, under heavy taxation, petitioned the emperor and threatened to flee ('we are going', JT Shevi'it 9:2). Modern scholars link the Shevi'it passage with tax pressure after Diocletian's reforms and an exceptional concentration of Diocletianic boundary stones in Paneas' hinterland (22 of ~40 known; en.wikipedia 'Banias'). The passage does not state that the petitioners were Jews. Christianity was also established (bishop Philocalus at Nicaea 325). Year 300 = reign of Diocletian (284-305); confidence low-medium for the Jewish identity of the inhabitants.

city_other: כפר נחום (tel: תל חום) / Tell Hum
comment: [Second-pass revision] adds excavation attribution. Hasmonean (-167 to -63): the Franciscan excavations (Corbo and Loffreda, 1968-1986) indicate that the fishing village was founded at the start of Hasmonean rule, with the earliest coins from the 2nd c. BCE (Israel Tour Guide summary; Hebrew Wikipedia: Hasmonean coins); Jewish Virtual Library gives 'Hellenistic period, 2nd century BCE', and the lowest level of the House of Peter is a 1st c. BCE dwelling. The ethnic character of this earliest phase is not stated in any fetched source and no stone vessels or miqva'ot are reported for it; Population blank. The Madain Project says only that Capernaum 'likely existed' under the Hasmoneans and may be earlier.

city_other: כפר נחום (tel: תל חום) / Tell Hum
comment: [Second-pass revision] adds named-scholar attributions. Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): large, predominantly Jewish fishing village (Jewish Virtual Library: 'a large Jewish village' at the start of the 1st c. CE) with some non-Jews (Chancey 2002, 101-5, cited by Capes and by Cirafesi 2019; Mattila 2015 in Fiensy and Strange, Galilee in the Late Second Temple and Mishnaic Periods vol. 2, pp. 217-257, also cited for a predominantly Jewish village). Chancey (bibleinterp) lists stone vessel fragments among the finds, an indicator of Jews. Housing: black basalt blocks with courtyards; the white limestone synagogue visible today is late 4th-5th c. CE (not Second Temple; an earlier basalt synagogue is suggested but disputed). Population: Horsley 1996 (Archaeology, History and Society in Galilee, p. 115, as quoted by Capes) conservative estimate 1200-1700 inhabitants, midpoint 1450 (village mostly Jewish; the small non-Jewish part not separated). Conflicting figure: about 1500 in the 1st c. CE (English Wikipedia and Madain Project, citing Reed 2002 without a page) not entered separately because it could not be verified. Reed's 1992 paper 'The Population of Capernaum' exists but its text was not reachable. No Capernaum miqva'ot reported (lake bathing is the usual explanation).

Dating basis: literary, conventional year 110. Confidence low-medium. (Reed's estimate of c. 1,500 inhabitants in the 1st century is quoted by Wikipedia; not used here as it predates 70.)

comment: Epiphanius (Panarion 30.11) reports that until the 4th century Capernaum was inhabited only by Jews, who would not tolerate gentiles, Samaritans or Christians in their midst, though the Jewish population included minim; the village's period of maximal expansion began in the 4th century (c. 10-12 acres, c. 300 m along the lake shore). Also states that in the 4th c. a house room (venerated as Peter's) became a small public structure and in the mid-5th c. an octagonal church was built. Conventional year 350 (3rd/4th-c. dispute).

Epiphanius met Joseph c. 355; Panarion written 374-377. Primary patristic source; hearsay account, medium confidence. (Joseph's attempt to build in Capernaum is not said to have succeeded; EJ 'Land of Israel': he 'succeeded only in building a small church at Tiberias'.)

comment: Literary: Epiphanius, Panarion 30 (composed 374-377 CE) says Capernaum, like Tiberias, Diocaesarea/Sepphoris and Nazareth, had no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians among its population, which is why Joseph the Comes could not found churches there; quoted by Magness 2024, who finds no evidence that the churches were actually built at the minor sites. Year 375 = midpoint of the composition date.

comment: Egeria's pilgrimage (via Peter the Deacon, De locis sanctis 194; Hebrew University Corpus of Christian pilgrims page for Capernaum): 'There also is the synagogue where the Lord cured a man possessed by the devil.' Egeria's visit is dated 381-384 (383 used; the same page also gives 361-364 for her visit, a conflict). The page notes Peter the Deacon (12th century) excerpted Egeria, so the wording is second-hand. Literary pilgrim source; confidence medium.

comment: White limestone synagogue: Wikipedia 'Capernaum' - 'built around the 4th or 5th century', on top of a basalt foundation that Loffreda thinks is a 1st-century synagogue; in the 4th century the village houses were rebuilt with good-quality mortar and fine ceramics; an octagonal church was built over Peter's house in the mid-5th century. Conflicting dates: Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Capernaum') 'between the 2nd and the 5th centuries a.d.'; EJ 'Land of Israel' Severan period (193-235); Hamichlol: built in the 4th century. Midpoint of 4th-5th century (400) used; excavators' dating (Franciscans Corbo/Loffreda coins vs IAA/others).

city_other: כפר נחום (tel: תל חום) / Tell Hum
comment: White limestone synagogue (the 'classic' Galilean-type building). Date disputed. Kohl-Watzinger (1905-07) dated the Galilean type by style to the late 2nd-early 3rd c.; Arubas and Talgam (2014) put it in the 3rd c. and rebuilt after the 363 earthquake; Franciscan excavations (Corbo, Loffreda, from 1968) found over 25,000 small bronze coins and pottery of the 4th-5th c. sealed under the paving, the latest c. 500 CE or later, so Magness argues construction no earlier than the first half of the 6th c. Dating basis: coins and pottery under the floor versus architectural style. Conventional year 400 (centre of the contested range). A basalt foundation beneath is read by Loffreda as a 1st-c. synagogue (contested).

city_other: כפר נחום (tel: תל חום) / Tell Hum
comment: Jewish Virtual Library (Archaeology in Israel: Capernaum): in the Late Roman and Byzantine periods (3rd-7th c.) a prosperous town spread over some 13 acres (c. 5 ha, c. 53 dunams) along the lake shore, with houses in blocks and streets; Byzantine Christian sources describe a village inhabited by Jews and Christians; the Franciscan excavators, from pottery and coins under the floor, date the limestone synagogue 'not earlier than the 4th, or the beginning of the 5th century' while most researchers date the Galilean synagogue type to the Roman period (2nd-3rd c.); all agree it is not the 1st-c. synagogue of Jesus' time. No population figure given. Year 410 = c. 4th/5th c. boundary.

comment: Monumental white-limestone synagogue (prayer hall 24.4 x 18.65 m; Greek and Aramaic donor inscriptions; five- and six-pointed stars and palm trees) built on an artificial platform over the earlier basalt village. Excavator S. Loffreda dated construction from numismatic evidence to the last decade of the 4th to the middle of the 5th century (midpoint 421); Magness (2001) proposed a terminus post quem in the 3rd quarter of the 5th c. and a 6th-century construction; Loffreda also suggests a basalt foundation beneath it belongs to a 1st-century synagogue. Dating basis: coins under floors. Confidence medium; date contested.

Theodosius mentions Capernaum in AD 530 (Wikipedia). Dating basis: epigraphic (6th c., conventional 550). Confidence medium.

Biblical Carmel of Judah (Josh 15:55; Saul 1 Sam 15:12; Nabal the Carmelite, David) described as an Israelite/Judahite town; no fetched source reports Iron Age archaeological remains, so the date is the period of the biblical narrative. Hebrew Wikipedia describes it as a very large village with water from Ein el-Karmil. No population estimate found. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%9B%D7%A8%D7%9E%D7%9C_(%D7%90%D7%AA%D7%A8_%D7%9E%D7%A7%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%99)

comment: Jewish village in the southern Hebron hills in Eusebius' time. Eusebius, Onomasticon (s.v. Zeib/Zif, Wolf translation): Karmelos 'is the name given today to a village of Jews'. Wikipedia 'Al-Karmil' (citing Mader): to Eusebius it is a 'Jewish village', with a Roman garrison there at the start of the 4th century; three later Byzantine churches show it became preeminently Christian afterwards; A. Negev proposed that most of old Carmel's Jews had moved c. 150-300 to Khirbet Susiya, which kept the name Carmel. Wikipedia 'Daroma' (after Avni) lists Carmel among the seven large Jewish villages of the Daroma described by Eusebius. Yankelevich (entry 45, Carmel): 'in the time of Eusebius a village of Jews in the south of Mount Hebron'. Year 320 = conventional date of Eusebius' Onomasticon (traditionally 'sometime before 324', Wikipedia 'Onomasticon (Eusebius)'; Wikipedia 'Daroma' says c. 300); the map's Juttah row uses 320 as well. No figure: Population blank. [confidence: medium] [Source detail: (Eusebius, Onomasticon, Wolf translation)]

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). English Wikipedia lists Iron I occupation at Khirbet Kefireh (Vriezen surveys 1970 and 1973-74); hill about 4-5 acres. Identification as Chephirah is the one most Bible dictionaries give; no excavation possible. Israelite/Gibeonite-region town. No population estimate found.

Iron Age II (starting -1000; the source does not split IIA/IIB/IIC). Wikipedia: Iron II occupation with significant architectural changes; city walls with nine towers and three gates; LMLK-stamped jar handle found (late 8th c. Judah). Judahite/Benjaminite. No population estimate found.

Iron Age (starts -1200; sub-period not given by source). Biblehub states surveys at Tel Iksal reveal Iron Age and later occupation layers (pottery cisterns rock-cut tombs). Identification doubtful: Hebrew Wikipedia says the name is preserved in Iksal but Albrecht Alt placed ancient Iksal about 2 km north at Khirbat Tira (now Nof HaGalil); only Roman-period remains mentioned for the village itself. Biblical Kisloth-Tabor in Zebulun's border. No population estimate found; no settlement-size data. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%90%D7%9B%D7%A1%D7%90%D7%9C

Iksal (Josephus' Xaloth; Eusebius: Chasalous in the plain below Mt Tabor, 8 miles from Diocaesarea): U. Leibner says Iksal is one of several Galilean villages with a Jewish population in the Roman period, joined later by Christians; rock-cut tombs, glass and jewellery of the Roman-Byzantine periods; a bishop Parthenius of Exalus attended the 536 council. Conventional year (Roman period). Dating basis: survey/excavation + secondary statement. Confidence low-medium.

Rock-hewn burial caves at Iksal containing sarcophagi and ossuaries with funerary assemblages of pottery, glass vessels and jewellery from the Roman and Byzantine periods (IAA salvage excavations reported 2008 and 2011); ossuaries point to the Jewish burial custom of the Roman period, though the ESI reports do not state the religion of the buried. Conventional year (Roman-Byzantine, 3rd-4th c.). Dating basis: grave goods. Confidence low-medium.

Middle Bronze IIb (source: 1750-1550 BCE; brief range -2000 to -1550). Resettlement after an EB-MB gap per he-wiki. Canaanite. Site c.40 dunams (he-wiki). Identification Tel Kinrot = Kinneret/Chinnereth is standard; Tel Kinrot also called Tell el-Oreimeh. No academic population estimate found in fetched sources; Population left blank.

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Important city in Canaanite-Egyptian relations (he-wiki); Kennartou in Thutmose III list (en-wiki and kinneret-excavations.org). No academic population estimate found in fetched sources; Population left blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinneret_(archaeological_site)

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Early Iron Age Strata VI-IV on SE slope (kinneret-excavations.org); en-wiki: Iron IB cities of this area probably reflect the Kingdom of Geshur. he-wiki dates the new fortified city to the 10th c BCE. Not clearly Israelite. No academic population estimate found in fetched sources; Population left blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinneret_(archaeological_site)

Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900). New fortified city c.25 dunams founded 10th c BCE with Phoenician influence (he-wiki); en-wiki links Iron IIA-B cities to expansion of Aram-Damascus. No academic population estimate found in fetched sources; Population left blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinneret_(archaeological_site)

Search-result snippet (not a fetched page) called it an Israelite fortress; the fetched pages do not state this. No academic population estimate found in fetched sources; Population left blank. Further sources: https://kinneret-excavations.org/tel-kinrot

[Second-pass revision] the first pass accepted Hebrew Wikipedia's early-1st-c. start with doubt; the primary and scholarly sources fetched now agree that a 1st c. settlement is NOT demonstrated by excavation. Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): NEAEHL (Yeivin, in Stern 1993, via the Dead Sea quake catalogue) says only that the town began in the 1st or 2nd c. CE in the northern higher part of the hill and was fully built in the late 3rd-early 4th c.; the Creighton Virtual Reality page states that identifiable remains from the earlier level of settlement have yet to be found; the JVL entry (Encyclopaedia Judaica) says it was apparently first occupied in the 1st or 2nd c. CE with most ruins of the 3rd-4th c.; the 2022 IAA Hadashot Arkheologiyot report of the synagogue reports only Late Roman pottery and no Early Roman or Hellenistic finds. The only Second Temple-period hint is Z. Ilan's suggestion (EJ) that a columned building cleared by Ory in 1926 may be an earlier, Early Roman synagogue, and a BAS popular article that suggests a late Second Temple synagogue beneath the later one, both unexcavated hypotheses. Jewish evidence (basalt synagogue, miqveh beside it, Judah son of Ishmael inscription, oil press) is Late Roman and later; the Gospels (Matt 11:21) and Talmud (wheat of Chorazin) are textual. Who lived there in this period: unknown, presumably Jewish if settled. Population blank: no estimate in any fetched page (JVL and BAS give only a site area of about 25 acres). Hebrew Wikipedia gives the existence of the town as early 1st c. CE to the 8th c. without excavated support.

Founding of the Roman-period Jewish village: Z. Yeivin (NEAEHL): Chorazin began in the 1st or 2nd century CE in the northern, higher part of the hill and later spread south and west; EPI database: occupation began in the late 1st or early 2nd century. Dating basis: pottery/coins (surveys 1962-64, excavations 1980-84). Confidence medium. Conventional year 100.

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Land of Israel: History' groups Korazim (Chorazin) with Kefar Nahum and Baram among the 'splendid synagogues' of the Severan period (193-235; midpoint 214). Older dating; see the 400 row for the later datings. Medium-low confidence.

Wikipedia 'Chorazin': the synagogue 'was built in the late 3rd century, destroyed in the 4th century, and rebuilt in the 6th century' (Negev & Gibson 2005); the main settlement dates to the 3rd and 4th centuries (ruins about 25 acres, synagogue at the centre); the town was partially destroyed in the 4th century, possibly by earthquake. Excavations 1905-09, 1962-64, 1980-87. Archaeological; the datings of Galilean synagogues are disputed.

In the late 3rd or early 4th century the town covered most of the hill, flourished, and its civic center and basalt synagogue (12-column hall, ritual bath nearby, 25 acres in five quarters) were built (Yeivin, NEAEHL); Wikipedia: synagogue built in the late 3rd c., destroyed in the 4th, rebuilt in the 6th; the Hebrew encyclopedia dates it to the early 5th c. (Byzantine). Houses and synagogue were partly destroyed in the early 4th century (possibly an earthquake). Dating basis: pottery/coins; conventional year 300. Confidence medium; synagogue date contested. No population figure.

Israel Nature and Parks Authority (Korazim National Park): remains of a Jewish village of the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods; five quarters, the wealthy main quarter partly excavated (insulas delimited by four streets), a Galilean-type basalt synagogue (nave 16.7 x 22.8 m, twelve columns for a second storey, Moses seat with a dedicatory inscription), a ritual bath (mikveh) complex among the public buildings, rooms next to the synagogue that apparently served as an inn and study halls, and Mamluk arched houses built on 4th-c. foundations. Year 300 = conventional Mishnaic/Talmudic floruit.

ESI 2019 (A. Kohn-Tavor, D. Ben-Yosef; educational excavations 2014-17): the wealthy dwelling 'Building A' (renamed Building D) of the main quarter was founded, according to Yeivin, in the late 3rd or early 4th c. CE, three strata (III-I) with Stratum III dated late 3rd/early 4th c.; the structure ceased to be used in the 9th-10th c. Dating basis: Yeivin's excavation and the new stratigraphy. Year 305 = c. 300.

Jewish Virtual Library (Archaeology in Israel: Chorazin): the town was apparently first occupied in the 1st or 2nd c. CE, with remains from the Roman period to the 7th c.; the site spans 25 acres (c. 10 ha, c. 100 dunams) with 'irregular, unplanned growth as the population increased'; the synagogue was apparently built initially in the late 3rd or early 4th c. CE; the town and synagogue were apparently destroyed in the late 4th c. and rebuilt in the 5th (differs from Wikipedia's 6th-c. rebuild). No population figure given. Year 310 = late 3rd/early 4th c.

Eusebius, Onomasticon (Wolf translation): 'Chorazein. Village of Galilee over which the Christ suffered ... Now deserted two miles from Capharnaoum.' Composition of the Onomasticon is dated before 324 (traditional) or 313-mid-325 (Taylor) (Wikipedia 'Onomasticon (Eusebius)'; 320 used). Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Chorazin') cites the same passage ('reported to be in ruins in the fourth century') and adds that Petrus Diaconus reports 'repeated attempts by Jews to rebuild it'. Conflict: the Galilean synagogue at Chorazin is dated by archaeologists to the 3rd-5th century; Eusebius' 'deserted' may mean the village was temporarily abandoned or destroyed in the early 4th century. Literary; high confidence in the text, low in what it means.

Eusebius (Onomasticon 174:23) states that Chorazin was in ruins in his day and 2 Roman miles from Capernaum (Yeivin, NEAEHL); Jerome places Chorazin on the shore of the lake (Wikipedia, quoting Jerome). The archaeology shows the town actually flourishing in the 4th century, so the patristic 'desolation' is not matched by excavation (the Gospel curse tradition). Dating basis: literary, conventional year 330 (Eusebius d. c. 339). Confidence medium-low.

Synagogue chronology per the excavator Yeivin (2000 report), as summarised by Leibner 2009: construction began at the beginning of the 4th c., stopped for a long period and was completed only in the late 4th c., not to the original plan. Leibner treats Chorazin, with Hammath Tiberias and Meroth, as an exception to the 'late 3rd c.' first wave of monumental synagogues. Dating basis: excavation stratigraphy. Midpoint of c. 300-390 is about 345; conventional year 350.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Chorazin'): the conventional date of Galilean-type synagogues is the 2nd-3rd century CE, but 'recent research' supports 'a fourth or fifth century c.e. date' for the Chorazin basalt synagogue (midpoint 400 used); a stone 'seat of Moses' carries an inscription naming Judah son of Ishmael as benefactor; Talmud (Menahot 85a) says wheat was produced at Chorazin. Hamichlol also dates the synagogue's foundation to the early 5th century and use to the 7th. Archaeological; dating disputed.

'Seat of Moses' (cathedra) from the synagogue with an Aramaic inscription: 'Remembered for good Judan son of Ishmael who made the columns and the steps from his own means; may his portion be with the righteous' (CIJ 981; Naveh 17); Aviam holds that it served as a seat for a community notable. The settlement is also named in the Babylonian Talmud (Menahot 85a) for the Omer offering. Dating basis: inscription undated; conventional year 400 (Late Roman/Byzantine). Confidence medium.

Rebuilding and continuity: the town was rebuilt on the same plan within the same boundaries in the mid-4th and early 5th centuries and continued, with repairs and additions, until the Early Arab period (8th century), then declined (Yeivin, NEAEHL; excavations 1962-64, 1980-84). Dating basis: stratigraphy. Confidence medium. Conventional year 450.

Synagogue rebuilt in the 6th c. after a 4th-c. destruction (Wikipedia, Chorazin); the settlement itself is dated mainly to the 3rd-4th c. and was partly destroyed in the 4th c., possibly by an earthquake. Conventional year 550 (6th c.). Confidence medium: the 6th-c. rebuild is a one-line statement in the article.

Dabaritta/Daberath (Daburiyya): in 66 young men of Dabaritta ambushed Ptolemy, Agrippa II's financial overseer, and his sister Berenice and brought the loot to Josephus at Tarichaeae (Josephus Life). Dating basis: Josephus. Confidence high. Framing row.

Eusebius, Onomasticon (Wolf translation), s.v. Dabeira: 'There is another Jewish village on Mt. Thabor in the region of Diocaesarea.' Onomasticon composed 313-mid-325 or before 324 (Wikipedia 'Onomasticon (Eusebius)'; 319 used). Wikipedia 'Daburiyya': Eusebius calls the place Dabeira/Dabrath 'a village of Jews'; Josephus' Dabaritta (a group of young men from Dabaritta ambushed Ptolemy in 66 CE); 'sparse building remains from the Late Roman or Byzantine period'. Identification of Eusebius' Dabeira with Daburiyya (Daberath of Josh 21:28; Josephus' Dabaritta) is the standard one but conjectural. Literary primary source; the clearest Eusebian statement of a Jewish village in the north.

Eusebius' Onomasticon (early 4th c.), entry Dabeira: 'There is another Jewish village on Mt. Thabor in the region of Diocaesarea' (Wolf trans.); Wikipedia: Eusebius refers to Dabeira/Dabrath as 'a village of Jews' and identifies it with Daburiyya at the foot of Mt Tabor. Identification with Daburiyya conventional but not certain. Year = conventional date of the Onomasticon (c. 330). Dating basis: patristic. Confidence medium.

Wikipedia (Galilee): settlements such as Rama, Magdala, Kafr Kanna and Daburiyya, 'materially Jewish during the Roman period', were predominantly inhabited by Christians or had a significant Christian population in the Byzantine period; Safrai and Leibner see the Jewish population decline and Christian expansion as separate events. Daburiyya itself: Late Roman or Byzantine building remains and Roman-Byzantine pottery from small digs (Wikipedia, Daburiyya). Year 400 = conventional centre of the process; low confidence.

Synagogue (12.5 x 15 m, south facade of ashlar, prayer hall with eight columns) dated to the 5th c. and used until the 6th c. (he.wikipedia; rescue excavation Z. Ma'oz 1982, published in 'Atiqot 20, 1991 with pottery by A. Killebrew and coins by D. Ariel). Village settled from the Hellenistic period; 4th-c. structures and coins from the 4th to the mid-5th c. were found. Decorated stones include a seven-branched menorah, wreaths and Ark fragments; a Greek inscription 'Jesus son of Seilos, aged sixty' (IIP lists only a Greek epitaph here). Dating basis: coins/pottery; confidence medium-high.

Debia/Dabiyye ruins in the central Golan, c. 3 km east of Ein Nashut: remains of a synagogue 'from the same period' as Ein Nashut (5th-7th c.) are reported (Wikipedia, Ein Nashut); Bornblum database: excavated by Z. Ma'oz in 1982 (part of the original southern facade, a stone with a menorah). Conventional year 500; low confidence.

Lintel from a mosque at Dabbura (Dabura), central Golan, with two birds of prey and the inscription 'This is the beth midrash of Rabbi Eliezer ha-Kappar'; the only archaeological find from the Tannaitic era mentioning a beit midrash (exhibited in the Golan Archaeological Museum, Katzrin); Bornblum database: unexcavated synagogue site with inscriptions from a Jewish public building. The lintel's real date is not given by the sources; Wikipedia links it to the Tannaitic era. Conventional year 200 (age of R. Eleazar ha-Kappar), low confidence.

Further Jewish lintels from Dabbura: 'They made the house of ... May he be blessed' (DABB0004, 200-299 CE, text and decoration suggest a synagogue or school; wreath relief) and, in the same IIP series, 'made the gate' (DABB0005) and ' ... [H]inenna ... blessed' (DABB0003), all Late Roman (200-337); another lintel shows an eagle with a wreath and two fish (he.wikipedia). Year 250 = midpoint of the 3rd-c. date of DABB0004. Corroborates a 3rd-c. synagogue/study-house complex at Dabbura, earlier than most Golan synagogues.

Three-fragment architrave with Aramaic/Hebrew and Greek lines: 'El'azar son of Rabba made the columns above the arches and beams ... Rusticus built (it)' (IIP DABB0001), the Greek line apparently naming the craftsman as at Beth Alpha; dated 200-337 CE (Late Roman; year 268 = midpoint; no dating basis stated). Indicates a monumental Jewish public building (synagogue) at Dabbura in the 3rd-early 4th c.

Biblical mention and identification (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -1100 = conventional date of the Judges period). Identification: Tel Dan (Tell el-Qadi, 'mound of the judge'), 33.249 N 35.652 E; first identified by W. F. Lynch in 1849 and by E. Robinson in 1852, 'now securely accepted' (Wikipedia). Mound about 200 dunams (BibleWalks; Hebrew Wikipedia). Judg 18:7 (the five Danite spies find Laish quiet and secure like the Zidonians, far from Zidon); Judg 18:27-29 (the Danites burn Laish and build a city called Dan after their father); Josh 19:47 (the same story, with the name Leshem). The 600 Danites of Judg 18 are a biblical figure, not a town population. Archaeology (Wikipedia): in Iron Age I Laish was independent and allied with Sidon until the 10th c. BCE, when it was annexed by the northern kingdom of Israel or an Aramean kingdom. Existing rows of this marker give the Iron Age periods and Dever's 3,000; no further estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/telldan ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges+18&version=KJV ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+19&version=KJV

Royal sanctuary of Jeroboam I (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -930 = conventional date of Jeroboam I). 1 Kgs 12:28-30: Jeroboam made two golden calves and put one in Bethel and the other in Dan, 'and this thing became a sin: for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan'. Archaeology (Wikipedia; BibleWalks): a cultic compound with a large four-horned altar and rich cult paraphernalia; the ashlar podium ('high place', bamah, about 18 x 18.7 m inside a precinct of 45 x 60 m) was first used c. 930 BC per BibleWalks, enlarged in the 9th c. and again in the 8th c. under Jeroboam II, and destroyed by Tiglath-Pileser III in 733/732 BCE; the 9th-c. outer gate and the Tel Dan stela (Aramaic, 'House of David' and 'King of Israel', attributed by the excavators to Hazael c. 840 BCE) come from the same city. No population estimate beyond the rows already on the map. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/danhighplace ; https://www.biblewalks.com/danisraelitecity

Wikipedia 'Deir Aziz synagogue' (southern Golan): the synagogue is 'dating from the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods'; coins under the hall floor date to the time of Justinian I ('second quarter of the 6th century', midpoint 537 used) and the stones 'may originate from the synagogue destroyed in the 749 CE earthquake'; excavated 1998-2004 (Ben David, Maoz, Zingboim for Bar-Ilan University and Kinneret College); a menorah and a crown/atarah are engraved on a stone and a Greek inscription reads AZIZO. The coin evidence dates the floor, not necessarily the first building. Archaeological.

Jewish village (pottery under the synagogue foundations shows settlement already in the 1st-2nd c. CE; flourishing from the Late Roman period to the 8th c.) whose only excavated building is a basilica-type synagogue (11 x 18 m; apse with Ark podium in the south wall; benches; atrium; narthex; women's gallery staircase). IAA report (O. Zingboym, HA-ESI 123, 2011): six construction phases of the synagogue 'dating from the sixth century CE until the modern era' (Ma'oz & Ben-David, Qadmoniot 131, 2006); pottery in the adjoining spring structure runs to the mid-6th c., its early floor is dated to the second quarter and its late floor to the third quarter of the 6th c. and may correspond to synagogue Phases 1 and 2; the structure probably collapsed in the earthquake of 551 CE. Stern et al. 2008 (NEAEHL suppl., quoted at deadseaquake.info): phase 1, mid-6th c., prayer hall built under Justinian (527-565) with 'hundreds of worn-out bronze coins ... and two gold coins' in the foundation. Creighton University's Deir 'Aziz project: 'built in the mid-sixth century'. Excavators Z. Ma'oz and Ch. Ben-David 1998-2004; O. Zingboim 2010, 2014-16. A window bears the Greek inscription AZIZO, possibly the Talmudic village name (en.wikipedia). Destroyed by the 749 earthquake, rebuilt, used until the 9th c. Confidence high.

Phase 2 of the synagogue (renovation): 'late 6th' per Stern et al. 2008 (quoted at deadseaquake.info) - renovation in semi-fine masonry, construction of the Ark of the Law, partial replacement of the southern benches by perhaps a bema, burial of architectural elements incl. a Greek inscription, an antechamber on the east (or phase 4); a hoard of 14 gold coins of Justinian's reign comes from this phase (a terminus post quem; the renovation may fall after his death in 565). The IAA report (Zingboym 2011) puts the corresponding late floor of the spring structure in the third quarter of the 6th c. Slightly after the 70-550 window; shows the community still investing before the general late-6th/early-7th-c. Golan abandonment. Year 570 = third quarter of the 6th c.; confidence medium.

ESI 2016 trial excavation in the village of 'Illut (Lower Galilee): finds of the Roman period, including fragments of Kefar Hananya bowls, 'substantiate the evidence for the existence of the settlement 'Ayyatalu, which is mentioned in the Talmud' (the identification Illut = Ayyatalu is the excavators'; the Bornblum database lists an unexcavated synagogue site 'Eilut' with a menorah capital). Dating basis: Kefar Hananya ware (Roman). Year 300, conventional; weak row.

Eilut, Lower Galilee: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Capital with menorah and other monumental architectural stone remains. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Ilut (Eilut) near Nazareth: a capital carved with a menorah and other monumental architectural stones (surveys by A. Berman 1987 and Z. Ilan) suggest a Jewish public building/synagogue of the Late Roman and/or Byzantine period; unexcavated. Conventional year (Late Roman-Byzantine, 3rd-7th c.). Dating basis: architectural fragment typology. Confidence low.

city_other: עינות צוקים (עין פשחה) / عين فشخة (Ain Feshkha)
comment: Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Period I at Ein Feshkha, known only from some pottery and a few coins that Schiffman (1994, citing the excavators) correlates with Qumran period Ib (Hasmonean); the site was not in use in Qumran period Ia. De Vaux dated the complex 100-31 BCE (Bible Interpretation summary) whereas Hirschfeld (2001 excavation; IEJ 54 2004) concluded construction began only after 37 BCE under Herod (deadseaquake.info summary), so the Hasmonean phase is disputed. Excavators judged it related to Qumran with similar inhabitants (Jewish sectarian or estate workers; not stated). Jewish evidence: Hebrew/Aramaic-script inscribed vase and a mikveh (see next row). No population estimate found; Population blank. Also an Iron Age (7th-6th c. BCE) guard tower; no Persian or Early Hellenistic evidence in fetched pages.

city_other: עינות צוקים (עין פשחה) / عين فشخة (Ain Feshkha)
comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Period II, a walled agricultural farm and industrial complex (main building 24 x 18 m with courtyard; plastered basins; possibly balsam/opobalsam, date wine or tanning, function unresolved) matching Qumran period II and ending in fire (Schiffman 1994; Bible Interpretation summary of Hirschfeld 2001; Hebrew Wikipedia). Hirschfeld dated construction to after 37 BCE and use until about 130 CE; de Vaux placed the start at 100-31 BCE. Hebrew Wikipedia: farm began in the 1st c. BCE, was destroyed in the Great Revolt and resettled until the Bar Kokhba revolt (Schiffman describes period III between the two revolts). Jewish evidence: ritual bath for workers, inscribed vase in Jewish script, stone weight dated to year 5 of Agrippa (probably Agrippa I). Residents Jewish, presumably linked to the Qumran estate; no population figure from any source; Population blank.

Persian / Yehud (-539 to -332): Textual only. Nehemiah 3:14 names Beth-haccerem as a district centre in the Persian period whose returnees helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls; Ein Karem is one of several proposed identifications (others: Ramat Rachel, where Persian yehud seal impressions were found; the Herodium mount; Bethacharma), so the identification is disputed although Hebrew Wikipedia says most researchers favour Ein Kerem. No Persian-period remains at Ein Karem itself in fetched sources; Middle Bronze Age pottery near the spring is the earliest find reported. Jewish (Yehud) population presumed from the biblical text only; no estimate; Population blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ein_Karem; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/עין_כרם

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Jewish settlement. (a) 2015 IAA find of a plastered rock-hewn miqwe (3.5 x 2.4 x 1.8 m, staircase) under a house, with first-century CE pottery, stone vessel fragments and traces of fire possibly from the 66-70 destruction; Jerusalem District archaeologist Amit Re'em said it reinforces the hypothesis of a Jewish settlement in Ein Karem in the Second Temple period and that remains of that period there are few and fragmented. (b) A mikveh beneath the Church of St John in the Mountains (Franciscans, 1940s; recognised as a mikveh in 2004 by Tamar Hirdani per Hebrew Wikipedia); the Franciscan 1941-42 excavation found a rock-cut chamber with pottery from about the 1st c. BCE to 70 CE (English Wikipedia); other finds: a few graves, wall fragments, an olive press; a reservoir mentioned in the Copper Scroll. (c) Mishnah Middot 3:4: stones for the Temple altar and its ramp came from the valley of Beth Kerem (identification with Ein Karem not certain). A marble Aphrodite/Venus statue, probably Roman, was found at the Church of St John. No population estimate in any fetched source; Population blank. Further sources: https://www.srugim.co.il/119379-מדהים-מקווה-בן-2000-שנה-מתחת-לסלון; https://themedialine.org/life-lines/lifestyle/living-room-renovations-reveal-2000-year-old-ritual-bath/print/; https://www.israel-tourguide.info/blog/ein-karem-barluzzi-visitation-church; https://www.mishnah.org/?p=2668; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Saint_John_the_Baptist,_Ein_Karem; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ein_Karem; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/עין_כרם

Possible rabbinic mention: some scholars identify the Jewish village 'Einosh' ('Ayyanosh), named in the Tosefta, the Jerusalem Talmud and the Mosaic of Rehob among the towns of Susita's territory, with Ein Nashut; others reject this as too far from Susita and prefer 'Ein 'Awanish, a ruin below Mitzpe Ofir north of Susita (he.wikipedia 'Einosh'). Contested identification; low confidence. Year 250 = conventional date of the Rehob baraita (late 2nd-3rd c.).

Cemetery across the Nahal Meshushim (rock-cut tombs found while building a military installation): an Aramaic sarcophagus lid 'Shimon, son of Abun, [aged] twenty-six' (IIP EINN0003, dated 200-640 CE = Late Roman or Byzantine; year 420 is the midpoint of that wide range) and a Greek burial cover 'Yosa Zanno, aged seventy' (he.wikipedia). Names repeat those of the synagogue donor (Abun, Yose) - suggestive of the same community but not proven. Confidence medium-low for date.

Wikipedia 'Ein Nashut': a synagogue 'built in the 5th century CE' (coin evidence) in a 'Jewish settlement from the Talmudic period', in use until the 7th century and abandoned afterwards; one of the two oil presses was in use in the 4th-6th century; Schumacher first explored it in the 1880s; excavations in the late 1970s. Archaeological; high confidence for date range.

ESI 2020 (O. Zingboym, R. Assis; educational excavation 2017): the synagogue, excavated 1978-79 (Ma'oz 1993), was built in the 5th c. CE on a terrace at the NW end of the settlement; remains beneath it are dated to the 3rd-4th c. CE; the massive structure and rich finds attest to the strength of the Jewish settlement that thrived here until the beginning of the 7th c. CE. Dating basis: excavation finds. Year 350 = pre-synagogue 3rd-4th c. phase.

Jewish settlement and synagogue in the central Golan (Khirbat Deir er-Rahib), excavated in the late 1970s; the synagogue was built in the 5th c. on the evidence of coins - 51 small copper coins of 425-450 CE found in a chamber below the floor (Jerusalem Post, quoted on Wikipedia) - repaired several times and abandoned in the 7th c. Dating basis: coins. Year 450 (mid-5th c.).
