Literary only: 1 Sam 5:10: the Ark is sent on from Gath to Ekron, where the people panic; 1 Sam 6:16-17: the lords of the Philistines return to Ekron the day the Ark reaches Beth-shemesh, and the gold tumors are counted one for each Philistine city including Ekron; 1 Sam 7:14: Israel recovers the cities from Ekron to Gath (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -1050 = convention for the Ark narrative (BibleWalks dates the Aphek battle c. 1050). Identification: Tel Miqne (Khirbet el-Muqanna), proposed by Naveh and Kallai in 1957-58 and excavated by Trude Dothan and Seymour Gitin 1981-1996 (en.wikipedia Tel Miqne); coordinates 31.7789 N, 34.8499 E. Philistine city, not Israelite. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Miqne; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekron

Literary only: 1 Sam 17:52: after David's victory the men of Israel and Judah pursue the Philistines and the wounded fall along the road to Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -1020 = Saul's reign convention. Josh 15:11, 45-46 (border to Ekron and Judah's list) and Josh 19:43 (Ekron in Dan's allotment) are the earlier list mentions; Judg 1:18 says Judah took Ekron (checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages).
Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900); NEAEHL: Stratum III, 2nd quarter of 10th-9th c. BCE. Philistine. No population figure found.
Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722); NEAEHL: Strata IIB and IIA = 1st and 2nd half of 8th c. BCE; Philistine; Assyrian conquest 721 BCE (he.wikipedia). No population figure found.

Literary only: 2 Kgs 1:2-3: Ahaziah, king of Israel, injured in a fall at Samaria, sends messengers to ask Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether he will recover; Elijah intercepts them (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -850 = Ahaziah of Israel convention (reign c. -853 to -852). Ekron was then a Philistine city with a famous oracle; the 7th-century Ekron inscription naming Ikausu (Achish), son of Padi, is cited by en.wikipedia Ekron.

Literary only: Amos 1:8: the LORD will turn his hand against Ekron and the remnant of the Philistines will perish (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; same verse names Ashdod and Ashkelon). Year of Data -760 = mid-8th century convention for the oracle (the prophet's date is not argued here).

Iron Age IIC / late monarchy (-722 to -586); NEAEHL: Strata IC-IB 7th c. and IA 7th/6th c.; site expanded to about 85 acres as an Assyrian vassal city-state with 100+ olive oil presses; destroyed 604/603 BCE by Babylon (en/he.wikipedia). Philistine. No published population estimate found in readable sources (Gitin and Broshi-Finkelstein not readable). [Broshi and Finkelstein 1992, BASOR 287: 47-60 give a built-up area of 25 hectares in the 7th century (much smaller in the 8th); at the paper's 250 inhabitants per hectare that would imply about 6,250 for the 7th century, but the paper gives no population for this site, so none is entered]

Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332); he.wikipedia: after the Babylonian destruction the upper city was not resettled; a small settlement briefly occupied the lower city in the 6th century BCE before abandonment. No population figure found.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Replaces first-pass omission of Persian and Early Hellenistic rows (first pass saw only a gap after the Babylonian destruction). Gitin (Tel Miqne-Ekron final-report introduction) identifies a 'Persian-Hellenistic' cultural horizon on the mound, represented by partially excavated Building 850 in Field IV that re-used walls of the Iron IIC Temple Complex 650; the report does not split this horizon into Persian and Hellenistic and gives no absolute dates. He.wikipedia (not primary) says only a small lower-city settlement of the 6th c. BCE existed after 604/603 BCE and was then abandoned, so the extent of Persian occupation is unclear. Identification: Tel Miqne = Ekron is secure (Ekron dedicatory inscription). No Jewish evidence of any kind; Philistine/local remnant at most; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Same Persian-Hellenistic horizon (Building 850) as the Persian row; Gitin does not separate the two periods, so this row only records that the horizon extends into the Hellenistic period without finer date. No Jewish evidence; Population blank. Caveat: he.wikipedia places the Hellenistic settlement called Accaron at the Arab village of Aqir (Albright preferred Qatra), not on the Tel Miqne mound.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for this period (which located Hellenistic Ekron at Aqir on he.wikipedia's say-so): Accaron/Ekron and its district were given to Jonathan by Alexander Balas in 147 BCE (1 Macc 10:89; Josephus Ant. 13:102; Encyclopaedia Judaica). That is a textual statement of Hasmonean control, not evidence of a Jewish population. The IAA salvage excavation at 'Aqir (2013; Hadashot Arkheologiyot 128, 2016) found nothing earlier than Roman (Stratum III, c. 2nd to early 4th c. CE), so no excavated Hellenistic or Hasmonean settlement is documented at Aqir either. Where Hasmonean-period Accaron lay is unresolved; coordinates kept at Tel Miqne as instructed. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row: Gitin lists a 'Roman-Byzantine' horizon on the mound, a large villa/farmhouse (Building 950, two phases) built over Temple Complex 650; the introduction does not date it within the Roman-Byzantine range, so it is not secured to -63..70. Eusebius (Onomasticon, early 4th c. CE, outside this period) calls Akkaron 'a very large Jewish village' (Encyclopaedia Judaica; also cited in the 'Aqir report): a later Jewish presence at Aqir, not evidence for 63 BCE-70 CE. Population blank.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000), biblical mention and tentative identification (new marker; no marker within 3 km). Josh 19:21: En-haddah, with Remeth, En-gannim and Beth-pazzez, in Issachar's list. Identification: Tel Ein Haddah beside the former village of el-Hadatheh / Hadatha, 12.5 km SW of Tiberias east of Mount Tabor (32.683 N 35.489 E, Wikipedia Hadatha); proposed in 1927 by Aapeli Saarisalo (BibleWalks) and repeated in the 20th century (Hebrew Wikipedia: Iron Age sherds were found around the village); the Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities names no site, so this is a single proposal rather than a consensus ('disputed, favoured: Tel Ein Haddah'). WEAK identification. Archaeology (BibleWalks): Saarisalo reported a high concentration of Iron Age I pottery; the Iron Age city is described as about 20 dunams (upper city 150 x 75 m), while Saarisalo's settlement mound is given as about 100 dunams, so no population is derived. Wikipedia (Hadatha) itself reports only late Roman and Byzantine ceramics. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadatha ; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%9F_%D7%97%D7%93%D7%94_%28%D7%90%D7%AA%D7%A8_%D7%9E%D7%A7%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%99%29 ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+19&version=KJV

Subterranean hiding complex on the east slope of the Nazareth Hills beneath a residential building inhabited in the Roman and Byzantine periods 'at the heart of the Jewish settlement in the Galilee'; apparently quarried in connection with the Jewish revolts of the 1st and 2nd centuries and designed from the outset as a hiding complex (U. Leibner, N. Distelfeld, Y. Shivtiel; ESI 128). Dating basis: pottery of the end of the 1st century BCE to the First Revolt period. Year 130 = Bar Kokhba horizon, conventional; the Galilean involvement in 132-136 remains debated.

er-Rafid (also e-Rafid), Golan: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Monumental architectural stones. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Site of a Late Roman/Byzantine synagogue hypothesis: G. Schumacher surveyed it in 1889/90; C. Watzinger proposed an ancient (Mishnaic-Talmudic) synagogue on the basis of a pair of fish carved on a stone (a motif also at Baram); E. Sukenik (1933) did not find the building but recorded decorated stones (egg-and-dart, shell, a human figure with animals); Z. Ilan saw Byzantine and early Islamic remains; Y. Gal (1968) thought the basalt columns were a basilica (he.wikipedia 'Horvat a-Rafid'); Bornblum 'er-Rafid': Jewish, Late Roman/Byzantine, unexcavated, monumental architectural stones now largely in the Golan Archaeological Museum; Encyclopaedia Judaica lists al-Rafid among sites where Schumacher noted Jewish symbols. The site on the Jordan (inside Jordan Park, ~52 m asl) is also studied as a mixed Late Roman/Byzantine village ('Rafid on the Golan', not read). Year 450 conventional. Weak-moderate evidence: no inscription, no excavation.

Small agricultural village founded perhaps in 23 BCE in Herod's settlement scheme for the Golan, then 'a predominantly Jewish area bounded by Paneas and Hippos'; possibly one of the villages of the district of Josephus' fortified Sogane. D&G (Cathedra 73, 1994): the presence of Jews is attested by menorahs engraved on four lintels found re-used at the foot of the hill (undated); archaeological evidence suggests the settlement prospered without interruption to the 2nd c. CE; economic decline in the 3rd c. (nomad incursions, heavy Roman taxation, shift from grain to herding; a watch-tower of Philip the Arab, 244-249). The village is Greek 'Ramathana' on a Diocletianic boundary stone (c. 300; en.wikipedia). From the 4th c. it was Christian (martyrium of John the Baptist consecrated 377; Ghassanid pilgrimage centre; no remains of other religious groups in the Byzantine period, en.wikipedia). Weak row: Jewish presence rests on undated menorah lintels. Year 150 = end of the documented 'prosperous' Early/Middle Roman phase.

Josephus Antiquities 13.394 (lexundria translation) lists the fortress of Gamala among places taken by king Alexander (Jannaeus); English Wikipedia dates the Hasmonean takeover to 81 BCE and the civilian settlement to the last quarter of the 2nd c. BCE; Danny Syon (as cited there) argues for a Jewish presence before Jannaeus and a Jewish-majority population under John Hyrcanus; Jewish Magazine (Schaalje 2001) says new settlers came c. 150 BCE; the Jewish Virtual Library says Jannaeus founded it. NEAEHL (renewed excavations) finds Hasmonean-period remains in Area B abandoned at the very end of the 1st c. BCE. Evidence of Jews: thousands of Hasmonean coins and ritual baths (English Wikipedia); Mishnah and Tosefta list Gamla among walled towns of Joshua's time (Hebrew Wikipedia). Walls enclose about 180 dunams, of which about 7.5 dunams (5 percent) excavated (English Wikipedia). Population blank: no named estimate specific to this period.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row (which left Population blank). English Wikipedia attributes an estimate of 3000 to 4000 pre-revolt inhabitants to 'Weiss (in Schwartz, ed.)'; midpoint 3500 entered; I could not see the underlying study so the author's full name and basis are unverified. The town is treated by all sources as Jewish (four miqva'ot, stone vessels, synagogue; Jewish Magazine 2001; CBN/Turnage article). Josephus War 4.1 (penelope.uchicago.edu): about 4000 slain on the citadel and about 5000 threw themselves into the valley, the town being filled with refugees: casualties, NOT a population (Atkinson calls the 9000 clearly exaggerated per English Wikipedia). Josephus War 1.166 lists Gamala among cities restored by Gabinius c. 57 BCE. Synagogue dating corrected: NEAEHL (Syon and Yavor) says the earlier attribution to Alexander Jannaeus seems most unlikely and the hall is not earlier than the end of Herod's reign and probably later; Steven Fine dates it after 40 BCE and Ma'oz (2012) c. 50 CE with the mikveh added only in 67 CE (English Wikipedia Gamla Synagogue), so the late 1st c. BCE date in the first pass is the earliest option only. Also found: Gamala coins, one in building 2100 (NEAEHL) and revolt coins reading for the redemption of Jerusalem the holy. Destroyed by Vespasian in autumn 67 CE and never resettled.

Framing row: Gamla, a Jewish town of the Golan, fell to Vespasian's army in autumn 67 CE after a siege and its inhabitants were massacred; walls enclosed about 180 dunams and the town was a refuge for fugitives (hearths and storage jars indicate a large population); abandoned in 67 CE. The synagogue near the wall is dated to the late 1st c. BCE.

Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550). Hebrew Wikipedia (Tel Tzafit) says the settlement was reduced in the Middle Bronze Age after a large Early Bronze city. Identification of Gath with Tell es-Safi is the accepted view but Hebrew Wikipedia says it is not certain (Beit Guvrin Tel Erani Tel Nagila were proposed). No population estimate.
Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Hebrew Wikipedia says the settlement expanded again in the Late Bronze Age ('Canaanite Gath'). No population estimate.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Philistines took Gath in the 12th century and it became their most significant city, Philistine decorated pottery found (BibleWalks; excavations of Aren Maeir). No population estimate in fetched pages. Population would be the whole Philistine city not Israelites.

Literary only: 1 Sam 17:4: Goliath is 'of Gath'; 1 Sam 21:10-15: David flees to Achish king of Gath and feigns madness at the gate; 1 Sam 27:2-4: David and his 600 men settle with Achish, king of Gath (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Year of Data -1020 = Saul's reign convention. Identification: Tell es-Safi (31.7042 N, 34.8469 E), 'widely accepted by scholars' (BibleWalks); Albright had proposed Tel 'Erani, but the Tell es-Safi/Gath excavations (Aren Maeir) supported Tell es-Safi. Philistine city at this time; Iron IIA area 45-50 ha per BibleWalks (see the existing Gath rows). Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/gath/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gath_(city)

Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900; BibleWalks gives 1000-925). Peak: city of 450-500 dunams (45-50 hectares) probably the largest city in the land; Hebrew Wikipedia says about 500 dunams in the 10th century vs about 120 for Jerusalem. No academic population estimate found in fetched pages (Maeir's own papers were blocked), so left blank. Whole Philistine city not Israelites.

Fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chr 11:8, 'And Gath'), a Philistine city on one of the largest Bronze and Iron Age sites of the country; English Wikipedia 'Tell es-Safi' reports evidence of destruction by Hazael of Aram-Damascus around 830 BCE. Identification: Tell es-Safi, widely identified with Gath although Albright objected because it lies only 8 km from Ekron (Tel Miqne); Aren Maeir has directed the Tell es-Safi/Gath Project since 1996. Literary only for the Rehoboam fortification; Year of Data -925 = conventional date. No population figure. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell_es-Safi

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). Massive destruction c. 830 BCE by Hazael of Aram (BibleWalks; BAR article by Chadwick: Philistine Gath over 125 acres), abandoned for decades, earthquake c. 759 BCE, then rebuilt as a Judahite city in the mid to late 8th century of about 60 acres. Source dates differ slightly from the brief's ranges. No population estimate. Philistine then Judahite city.

Iron Age IIA/B transition: 2 Kgs 12:17: Hazael king of Syria fights against Gath and takes it, then turns to Jerusalem, where Joash buys him off with temple and palace gold (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Archaeology: a thick destruction layer and a siege trench about 2 km long, 3-5 m deep and 8-10 m wide attributed to Hazael (BibleWalks: c. 830 BCE; Hebrew Wikipedia 836; BYU article 'around 840'); Maeir gives the destruction as late 9th century (bibleinterp). Source dates differ by up to a decade; Year of Data -830 follows BibleWalks.

Literary only: 2 Chr 26:6: King Uzziah goes to war against the Philistines and breaks down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod, building towns in Ashdod and elsewhere in Philistia (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -760 = Uzziah convention (Azariah, reign c. -785 to -733). The BAR article cited on the existing rows describes Gath rebuilt as a Judahite city of about 60 acres in the mid-to-late 8th century.

Literary only: Mic 1:10: keep the news out of Gath, let no one weep there (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; paraphrased); BibleWalks reads it as evidence that Gath had already fallen. Year of Data -730 = late 8th century convention for Micah's oracle.
Iron Age IIC (-722 to -586). Judahite Gath of about 60 acres lasted until c. 701 BCE (BAR article by Chadwick; BibleWalks). No population estimate. Judahite not Philistine in this phase.
Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332). Settlement resumed at reduced levels with limited activity on the site (BibleWalks). No population estimate.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Replaces first-pass row, which rested on a blog and BibleWalks: Maeir (Encyclopedia of the Bible and its Reception 9, 2014) writes that evidence is minimal for the Babylonian period and the early Persian period (late 6th and 5th c. BCE), with some activity only in the second half of the Persian period, including a cultic repository found by Bliss and Macalister. The deadseaquake.info summary of the 1996 survey calls Persian settlement 'intense' (disagrees with Maeir; survey-based). biblical-archaeology.org says the site was resettled from the mid-6th c. Identification: Tell es-Safi = Gath, used without reservation by Maeir (project director). No Jewish evidence; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Replaces first-pass row: Maeir (EBR 2014) says that after the Persian period archaeological evidence at the site wanes through the Classical periods (4th c. BCE to 7th c. CE) into the Early Muslim period; biblical-archaeology.org says activity dwindled dramatically from the Hellenistic period onward. No dated Hellenistic structures are reported in the fetched sources. No Jewish evidence; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): No change in substance to the first-pass row, now backed by a scholarly source: Maeir (EBR 2014) gives only sparse evidence across the Classical periods; no Hasmonean or Herodian-period evidence, Jewish or otherwise, is reported in Maeir's summary, biblical-archaeology.org or the bibleinterp project summary. Population blank. Hasmonean period (-167 to -63) omitted: not separately attested.

city_other: תל גת חפר / Khirbet ez-Zurra / Tell el-Zur'a (near Meshhed)
comment: Iron Age (sub-period not specified by sources; Israelite period). Pottery of the Israelite period found at Tell el-Zur'a (he.wikipedia); Iron Age pottery on the tell surface (encyclopedia.com). Identification: Tell el-Zur'a / Khirbet ez-Zurra near Meshhed is the usual one; Jerome placed it near Sepphoris (he.wikipedia). Search snippet (not fetched) gives area about 30 dunams. Israelite (Zebulun) border town in the 8th c BCE per 2 Kings 14:25. No academic population estimate found; left blank. Further sources: https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/gath-hepher; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gath-hepher

city_other: תל גת חפר / Khirbet ez-Zurra / Tell el-Zur'a (near Meshhed)
comment: Biblical mention and identification (literary only; Year of Data -780 = conventional date of Jeroboam II). 2 Kgs 14:25: Jeroboam II restored the coast of Israel according to the word spoken by Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet 'which was of Gath-hepher'; Josh 19:13 (Gittah-hepher, KJV 'Gittahhepher', on Zebulun's eastern border; Wikipedia: a copying error in the form of the name). Identification: ruins on a hilltop near Mashhad, 5 km N of Nazareth (32.7417 N 35.325 E, Wikipedia; traditional tomb of Jonah), the tell known as Khirbet ez-Zurra'/Tel Gat Hefer (Wikidata 32.738 N 35.320 E); the Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities lists Khirbet Umm Jebel as another candidate for Gittah-hepher ('?'), so 'disputed, favoured: Mashhad/Khirbet ez-Zurra''. Border town of the northern kingdom around the 8th c. (Wikipedia). The existing row already gives the pottery evidence. No population estimate. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashhad%2C_Israel ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+19&version=KJV ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Egyptian administrative and military centre of Canaan for about 300-350 years (Thutmose III onward); Gaza itself not excavated in modern excavations. City is Canaanite (later Philistine) not Israelite. Identification: Tell Harube (most scholars) but largely unexcavated beneath modern Gaza; Tell el-Ajjul is a separate nearby candidate for the Bronze Age city. No population estimate found.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000; sources say conquered by Philistines in the 12th century BCE; one source c.1175). Southernmost city of the Philistine pentapolis; the inhabitants are Philistines (not Israelites). Temple of Dagon; Philistine pottery. No academic population estimate found.

Literary only: Samson at Gaza. Judg 16:1-3: Samson spends a night in Gaza, the men of the city lie in wait at the gate, and he leaves at midnight carrying off the gate doors and posts to a hill near Hebron; Judg 16:21-30: the Philistines blind him, bring him to Gaza, bind him in fetters, and he pulls down the temple of Dagon (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; BibleWalks places the Samson stories here). Year of Data -1100 = Judges period convention. Philistine city.

Iron Age II (source: c.1175-600 BCE spans Iron Age I-II; start of IIA used). Philistine city; burnished ware; Tiglath-pileser III captured it in 734 BCE but it stayed Philistine; limited excavations (1922 walls and glacis; 1995-2005 rampart under Achaemenid houses). No academic population estimate found. [Broshi and Finkelstein 1992, BASOR 287: 47-60 give a built-up area of 6 hectares (Oren's estimate, which the authors think may be too small); at the paper's 250 inhabitants per hectare that would imply about 1,500, but the paper gives no population for this site, so none is entered]

Literary only: Amos 1:6-7: for Gaza's repeated wrongdoing (seizing whole communities and selling them to Edom) the LORD will send fire on Gaza's wall to consume its fortresses (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -760 = mid-8th century convention. BibleWalks places the Assyrian period of Gaza at 732-630 BCE.

comment: Event: Sargon II's campaign against the southern coast, c. 720 BCE. The king of Gaza (Hanunu) rebelled and an Egyptian army marched out to help him; Sargon defeated them at Raphia (Rafah) and had the king taken away to Assyria, and says he destroyed and burned Raphia (the paper does not name the king in this passage). Online: Wikipedia 'Sargon II' says "Hanunu of Gaza in the south also rebelled against Assyria" and that the Assyrians "defeated Hanunu, whose army had been bolstered by allies from Egypt, at Rafah"; Wikipedia 'Hanunu' says "Hanunu was put in bondage and brought to Assur". Gaza itself stayed a semi-autonomous vassal state and was not annexed (Wikipedia 'Sargon II'). Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) tells the same story and dates the campaign 720. The year is 720 in Na'aman, in 'Sargon II' and in the Hebrew page; Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Rafa') says 721 and Wikipedia 'Hanunu' says 711 (see conflicts). Population blank. Confidence high for the event, medium for the exact year.

Literary only: 2 Kgs 18:8: Hezekiah strikes the Philistines as far as Gaza and its borders, from watchtower to fortified town (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -705 = Hezekiah convention for the Philistine campaign (the verse is undated; Sennacherib's 701 campaign follows). BibleWalks adds that Sennacherib later rewarded Sillibaal, king of Gaza. No Iron Age population estimate in the fetched pages (the PEF survey figure of about 18,000 in 1875 is modern).

Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332). Relative independence and prosperity under the Persian Empire; Persian-period occupation noted. Philistine/Gazan population. No academic population estimate found.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Royal fortress after Cambyses' siege in 529 BCE (Jewish Virtual Library); Herodotus' Kadytis; terminus of the Arab incense trade; many Persian-period coins (Hebrew Wikipedia/Hamichlol). Population mixed Philistine/Phoenician/Arab merchants; no Jewish evidence. Identification: the Gaza city mound (about 100 ha, 10 m high) under the old city, never excavated by modern methods apart from Phythian-Adams' soundings of the 1920s (Clarke, Steel and Sadeq, Levant 36, 2004; BAS page names the site Tell 'Azza); the physical evidence for this period is nearly absent. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Only city of the region to resist Alexander, taken after a siege of about nine weeks in 332 BCE (Hebrew Wikipedia/Hamichlol; Jewish Virtual Library: people sold into slavery), then a Ptolemaic outpost until Antiochus III took it in 198 BCE (Jewish Virtual Library, BAS). Greek polis with Marnas as chief god; no Jews evidenced. BAS: 'No significant Hellenistic remains were found on the mound'; Hellenistic settlement is linked to the coast and to Anthedon at Blakhiyah, a Greek city with agora and temples (English Wikipedia, citing Josephus). Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Gentile (Greek, Philistine and Nabatean-linked) city that Jews attacked. Jonathan besieged it c. 145 BCE (Jewish Virtual Library says he did not take it; Josephus Ant. 13 says Gaza made a league and gave hostages). Alexander Jannaeus took and destroyed it after about a year's siege: dated 96 BCE by Jewish Encyclopedia and Jewish Virtual Library but 101 BCE by Hebrew Wikipedia/Hamichlol. Josephus Ant. 13.13.3: Apollodotus was killed by his brother Lysimachus who surrendered the city, and five hundred senators were slain in the temple of Apollo. Hebrew Wikipedia says a Jewish community is first mentioned in the Hasmonean period but gives no source; Jewish Virtual Library says no Jewish community is known before 70 CE. No archaeological Jewish evidence; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Pompey restored it, Gabinius rebuilt it in 57 BCE (Jewish Virtual Library, Jewish Encyclopedia; Clarke et al. give 58 BCE for Roman rule and the growth of the port Maiumas), Augustus gave it to Herod in 30 BCE (Jewish Encyclopedia; Anthedon article citing Ant. 15.7.3) and after Herod's death it was detached and added to Syria (BJ 2.6.3, Wikisource). In 66 CE Jewish rebels demolished Gaza and Anthedon (BJ 2.18.1, Wikisource; Jewish Encyclopedia: 'completely destroyed'). Pagan city (Marnas cult, school of rhetoric); Jewish Virtual Library and Jewish Encyclopedia: no Jewish community known before 70 CE; the synagogue mosaic found in 1965 is dated 508 CE. No Jewish population estimate exists; Population blank.

comment: Event: Battle of Dathin near Gaza, 4 February 634, the first Arab victory over the Byzantines in Palestine. Wikipedia quotes the Anonymous Syriac chronicle: "Some 4000 poor villagers of Palestine were killed there, Christians, Jews and Samaritans." (The older edition reads 40,000; Wikipedia gives 4,000 civilian dead.) Shpak-Lissak (ch. 1, section B) says the Arabs killed about 4,000 Jews, Christians and Samaritans in the Gaza area and destroyed their villages; she gives no year there, the 634 date is from Wikipedia. The dead were villagers of the district, so this is a regional victim count with an unknown Jewish share, not a Gaza Jewish population; Population blank. Confidence high for the event, medium for the Jewish share.

Meshullam of Volterra, 1481: traveller names the place "Gaza"; Adler, Jewish Travellers (1930), p.179-181 (OCR page markers). Traveller's words: about fifty (sixty) Jewish householders, artisans. Identification: Gaza. Estimate based on families: ~250 = 50 households/families x 5 (low confidence). Text gives 50 with a variant 60; 50 x 5 used (60 x 5 would be 300).

comment: Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Jaba survey sherds: Iron I 2% of assemblage (Wikipedia en); JHS article cites the Feldstein et al. 1993 survey of 284 sherds at Jaba but gives no periods. Tell el-Ful (Gibeah) by contrast has abundant Iron I. Some scholars (Miller 1975; Arnold 1990) argue Geba and Gibeah were the same place - disputed. Identification of Jaba with Geba is secure per Wikipedia en. Israelite (Benjamin; Philistine garrison in 1 Sam 13). No population estimate found. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%92'%D7%91%D7%A2_(%D7%A0%D7%A4%D7%AA_%D7%90%D7%9C-%D7%A7%D7%95%D7%93%D7%A1); https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%92%D7%91%D7%A2_(%D7%99%D7%99%D7%A9%D7%95%D7%91_%D7%9E%D7%A7%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%99)

city_other: ג'בע (Geva Binyamin is the nearby settlement) / جبع (Jaba')
comment: Literary mention; Saul and Jonathan, dated by convention c. -1020. 1 Sam 13:3 (Jonathan smites the Philistine garrison in Geba, which triggers the war), 1 Sam 14:5 (the southern crag stands 'over against Gibeah' - Geba in the Hebrew - across the Michmash pass), Josh 18:24 (Benjamin's city list; KJV spells Geba 'Gaba') and Josh 21:17 (Levitical city). Identification: Jaba', 9.1 km north-west of Jerusalem, is 'securely identified with the ancient Geba of the tribe of Benjamin' (Wikipedia; first suggested by Guerin, Clermont-Ganneau and Conder and Kitchener), on the biblical description of Geba as just across the wadi from Michmash and on the heavy Iron Age II occupation. Robinson's older idea that Jaba' was Gibeah rather than Geba is not followed (most identify Gibeah with Tell el-Ful; see the Gibeah rows). Asa's fortification of Geba (1 Kgs 15:22) and Isa 10:29 are in the existing rows.

Gebul (also Jabbul), Lower Galilee: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Architectural fragments, menorah, lulav and other ritual objects, mosaic stones. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Gebul (Jabbul), Beth Shean valley edge near Kokhav HaYarden: architectural fragments, a menorah, lulav and other ritual objects and mosaic stones (Z. Ilan, c. 1980) from an unexcavated Late Roman/Byzantine synagogue; nothing visible today. Conventional year (3rd-7th c.). Dating basis: sculpture typology. Confidence low. Coordinates from the Bornblum DB map link; the Jordan Valley sub-area may also list it.

Byzantine-period remains ~3 km S of Kokhav HaYarden, including two stone slabs engraved with a seven-branched menorah beside an incense shovel, shofar and Four Species, and the remains of a large public building with ashlars, a marble slab, a mezuzah stone and mosaic tesserae, typical of ancient synagogues of the region (he.wikipedia; Bornblum 'Gebul': Jewish, unexcavated). The place 'Gebul' is mentioned by Ashtori ha-Parhi in the early 14th c.; it is suggested as the origin of the amora Jacob Gabolai (Jerusalem Talmud, Hallah 59a) - conjecture. Year 450 conventional.

city_other: גינוסר (בקעת גינוסר) / Tell el-Oreimeh (Tel Kinrot); Khirbet Abu Shusha proposed for Gennesar
comment: [Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63). IDENTIFICATION DOUBTFUL and unchanged: Gennesar(et) is a plain and a town name; Leibner proposes Khirbet Abu-Shusheh c. 3 km NW of Kibbutz Ginosar, which is not on the shore as the Gospels seem to imply, so the location of the town remains uncertain (Danny the Digger summary; Leibner 2009 survey full text not readable). The coordinates are the kibbutz. Tel Kinrot (Tell el-'Oreimeh) at the north end of the plain is the Bronze/Iron Age Kinneret; its final report (Kinneret II/1, 2024) has a 'Post-Iron Age' section not available in the fetched pages. Plain-wide evidence of Jewish settlement in this period comes from Magdala, the main town and port of the plain: Stratum IV Hellenistic (late 2nd-mid 1st c. BCE) per the Atiqot 90 abstract (Zapata-Meza et al. 2018), and a Hasmonean-era (1st c. BCE) harbor dated by pottery and coins (Turnage, CBN). Ken Dark reports a very large Late Hellenistic and Roman settlement between Magdala and Ginosar (lecture summary, unpublished). The Ginosar boat is dated 100 BCE-70 CE by C-14 and pottery. No synagogue, miqveh or stone-vessel evidence for a town called Gennesar itself; Population blank.

city_other: גינוסר (בקעת גינוסר) / Tell el-Oreimeh (Tel Kinrot); Khirbet Abu Shusha proposed for Gennesar
comment: [Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Jewish plain, town uncertain. Josephus (War 3.516-521) describes the Gennesar plain as 30 furlongs long and 20 wide, with walnuts, palms, figs, olives and grapes and a fertile spring, naming no town on it apart from the fountain 'Capharnaum' (lexundria.com, Whiston translation). Magdala on the plain: Stratum III Early Roman (mid-1st c. BCE-67 CE; Atiqot 90 abstract), a synagogue of the early-mid 1st c. CE with a menorah stone, several private groundwater-fed miqva'ot, urban street grid, stone houses with mosaics (CBN/Turnage; ASOR 2017: four groundwater miqvaot) - this is evidence for Jewish life on the plain, not for the town Gennesaret. Tel Kinrot: first-century evidence is scarce (Danny the Digger). Population: no named estimate for Gennesaret; Population blank.

city_other: גינוסר (בקעת גינוסר) / Tell el-Oreimeh (Tel Kinrot); Khirbet Abu Shusha proposed for Gennesar
comment: Gennesar as a settlement (not only the name of the valley) first appears in tannaitic traditions reflecting the 2nd c.: Yonatan ben Harsha 'a man of Gennesar' asks the sages of Yavneh about date-palm cultivation (Tosefta Kelim 5:6; Jerusalem Talmud Ma'aserot 1:2, 48d), and R. Yehuda bar Ila'i (first half of the 2nd c.) uses Gennesar as his example for turning a public into a private domain on the Sabbath (eruv). Leibner identifies it with Khirbet Abu Shusheh/Giv'at Ayala (site 26, map ref 1978/2512, 52 dunams) because only this site in the valley has Hellenistic and Roman settlement pottery; the Middle Roman period was its peak (estimated 41-50 dunams). Identification is argued from pottery against other proposed sites (Tell Oreimeh, Khirbet Minya, Tel Hunud, Migdal), not proven by an inscription; the Jerusalem Talmud list equating biblical Kinneret with Gennesar (Megillah 1:1, 70a) shows the sages knew the site but, as Leibner notes, not necessarily that it was settled in their day. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 180-185. Survey periods: Early Roman = mid-1st c. BCE-135 CE, Middle Roman 135-250, Late Roman 250-350, Early Byzantine 350-450, Middle Byzantine 450-550, Late Byzantine 550-650. Conventional year (2nd c.). Dating basis: tannaitic traditions + survey pottery. Confidence medium.

city_other: גינוסר (בקעת גינוסר) / Tell el-Oreimeh (Tel Kinrot); Khirbet Abu Shusha proposed for Gennesar
comment: Khirbet Abu Shusheh = Gennesar of Josephus and rabbinic literature (reliable identification per Leibner Table 15; Ottoman Mazra'at Janusar): survey size category D (21-40 dunams) from the Hellenistic period to c. 150 CE, E (41-60 dunams) c. 150-250, D c. 250-350, then abandoned in the 4th-c. settlement crisis (Leibner 2009, Table 11). Dating basis: survey pottery. Year 300 = late phase; Jewish identity inferred from the sources and regional pattern, no synagogue attested.

city_other: גינוסר (בקעת גינוסר) / Tell el-Oreimeh (Tel Kinrot); Khirbet Abu Shusha proposed for Gennesar
comment: Abu Shusheh (= Gennesar per Leibner): late Roman pottery (27.8% of finds) is largely the intermediate type KH1e, three imported vessels of the types found in the 363 destruction layer at Sepphoris show occupation to at least the mid-4th c., then decline (estimated 21-40 dunams Late Roman, 11-20 dunams Early Byzantine) to the end of settlement around the second half of the 4th c.; no remains of a monumental public building (an alleged synagogue buried at the Ginosar kibbutz dock could not be verified). Part of the 4th-c. settlement crisis in the eastern Galilee: Leibner's regional estimate for the whole survey area (all inhabitants, not Jewish only; method: settled dunams x 16-35 persons per dunam, expressed as ranges) is c. 23,062 (range 10,496-39,165) at the peak in the first half of the 3rd c. and c. 8,606 (range 3,824-14,805) in the second half of the 4th c., a decline of over 60%, and he lists Abu Shusheh (Category E, 41-60 dunams) among the larger settlements abandoned in that period, with Migdal and the two sites with monumental synagogue remains, Netofa and Hamam. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 180-185, 349, 358. Population left blank (regional estimate, not a town figure). Conventional year (second half of 4th c.). Dating basis: survey pottery. Confidence medium.

Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900); en.wikipedia: peak urban development in the 10th century BCE (Stratum 8 six-chambered gate; radiocarbon c. 983-913 BCE for Strata 8-7 per PMC10651010). Population 2500 = William G. Dever estimate for the 10th century BCE as reported on en.wikipedia (original Dever publication and basis not stated there and not fetched). Dating of Stratum VIII is disputed (Finkelstein: 9th century).

Literary mention with archaeology: 1 Kgs 9:15-17: Solomon's levy builds Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer; Pharaoh king of Egypt had captured Gezer, burned it, killed its Canaanite inhabitants and given it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife; Solomon rebuilt Gezer and lower Beth-horon (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -960 = Solomon convention. Archaeology: Stratum 8 (Iron IIA) with the six-chambered 'Solomonic' gate, destroyed in the third quarter of the 10th century, probably in Shoshenq I's campaign; radiocarbon dates the Stratum 8 destruction to c. 969-940 BCE (68.3%), so Stratum 7's fit with Shishak 'does not fit well' (Webster et al. 2023, via en.wikipedia); the unnamed pharaoh is Siamun for Kitchen, Shoshenq I for Lipinski; Stratum VIII dating is disputed (Finkelstein: 9th century). Site 130 dunams (en.wikipedia); Dever's 2,500 and 3,000 are already on the existing Gezer rows.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722); Population 3000 = Dever estimate for the 9th-8th centuries BCE as reported on en.wikipedia (basis not stated there; original not fetched). he.wikipedia gives Iron Age II (Hebrew monarchy) c. 950-732 BCE with Solomonic gates and fortifications.
Iron Age IIC / late monarchy (-722 to -586); he.wikipedia lists Assyrian/Persian periods (7th-4th centuries BCE) at the site; en.wikipedia: Iron Age II to 586 BCE. No population figure found.

Event: foreign exiles settled at Gezer, 651-649 BCE. Two cuneiform land-contract tablets found at Gezer are dated by Assyrian eponyms to 651 and 649 BCE and contain 21 complete personal names. Na'aman: only one name (Netanyahu) is Israelite; of the other 20, twelve are Akkadian, five West Semitic and one Egyptian, so most of the people are Babylonian by name and apparently exiles brought to Gezer (whether by Sargon II or by a later king cannot be told). He adds, following Zadok, that exiles and Assyrian officials were also brought to nearby Beth-horon, and concludes that the northern Shephelah (Gezer and its surroundings), like the Bethel district, belonged to the parts of the Assyrian province of Samaria that received foreign population. Online: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Jewish Virtual Library, 'Gezer') says "In the Assyrian period Gezer's population was augmented by foreign settlers" and that contracts "of two of these, written in cuneiform from the years 651 and 649 B.C.E.", survive; Wikipedia 'Gezer' adds that Tiglath-Pileser III besieged Gezer in 734-732 BCE. Population blank. Confidence high.

Persian (-539 to -332): Site resettled after Assyrian abandonment, part of province Yehud; wealthy graves, house walls, cisterns. Population not Jewish-attested by fetched sources (Jewish Virtual Library only says settlement remains of the period exist); Population blank. No published population estimate found.

Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Hellenistic settlement in 3rd-2nd c. BCE; royal/Seleucid fortress and military centre; population Greek/Seleucid garrison and local inhabitants, no Jewish evidence in fetched sources; Population blank.

Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Simon conquered Gezer c. 142 BCE (JVL: 142; BibleWalks: 139 BCE for boundary-stone article), expelled gentile/Greek inhabitants and resettled with Jews; John Hyrcanus made it military/administrative base. Jewish evidence: bilingual 'boundary of Gezer' inscriptions (Hebrew plus Greek 'of Alkios'; dated end 2nd-1st c. BCE or Herodian by some), added cisterns/ritual immersion pools per Hebrew Wikipedia, possible miqveh in a Jewish house (BibleWalks/search summary). Mixed Greek and Jewish at the start; Population blank: no source states a Jewish population figure.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Declining importance under Herod; graves, bathhouse, small structures and a large boundary wall; some scholars date the boundary inscriptions to Herod's time. Jewish evidence only indirect (inscriptions if Herodian); Population blank. Eusebius later calls it a village.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row: adds the secondary reading of the excavation results. Two coins of Alexander Jannaeus (104-76 BCE, Jerusalem mint) and one coin dated 103-76 BCE come from the 1977-78 synagogue-area deposits (ancientsynagoguecoins; found in late contexts, so they show circulation, not a Hasmonean stratum). Horsley (1995, citing Meyers et al. 1979): Hasmonean coins and ceramics, and a likely Hasmonean-Herodian fortress (an inference from Josephus and m. Arakhin 9:6). No miqveh, stone vessels or ossuaries are reported in any fetched source for this period, so a Jewish population is plausible but not demonstrated. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): New row. Josephus (War 2.575-2.592, 2.625): John son of Levi repaired the walls of his native Gischala with Josephus's permission. War 4.84-4.120: 'the small city of Gischala', most inhabitants farmers; Titus came with 1,000 horsemen, John fled to Jerusalem by night and the townspeople opened the gates (67 CE); Josephus gives 6,000 women and children killed and almost 3,000 captured of those who had left with John (casualty figures, not a population; Notes only). Hebrew Wikipedia: the main Jewish centre of the Upper Galilee in Second Temple times; Hamichlol: Jewish settlement from the Second Temple period. A Claudius coin (51-52 CE, Scythopolis mint) was found in the 1977-78 deposits. No miqva'ot, stone vessels or Herodian-period excavated remains are reported in the fetched sources; the excavated synagogue is Late Roman (c.250 CE). Jewish community known from literary evidence. No population estimate by a named scholar in any fetched source (Hebrew Wikipedia, Hamichlol, karamel, en.wikipedia, JVL checked). Population blank.

Josephus (War 2.20.6 and Life 189) says Gischala had a wall built by John son of Levi 'with the consent of Josephus' when Josephus fortified the Galilean towns in winter 66/67; E. Meyers (NEAEHL) dates the rebuilding of its walls to 66 CE. Dating basis: literary (Josephus). Confidence high. Pre-70 framing row for the Jewish-war context.

Titus takes Gischala, the last Galilean stronghold: Josephus (War 4.2.1) calls it a small city whose multitude were desirous of peace, being generally husbandmen, but a band of robbers around John son of Levi had corrupted part of it; NEAEHL (Meyers): the city surrendered to Titus without a fight in 67 CE, John fled to Jerusalem. Dating basis: literary (Josephus). Confidence high. No population figure given.

Josephus (via Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Giscala' and Wikipedia 'Gush Halav'): John (Johanan) b. Levi of Giscala, a Zealot leader, fortified the city; Gush Halav was the last Galilean stronghold to fall to the Romans (66-73). EJ: Jews lived there in the tannaitic and amoraic periods; the community persisted until at least the 13th century. Framing row for the pre-70 context; year 70 conventional.

Talmudic tradition: Eleazar b. Simeon (son of Shimon bar Yochai, a very large, very strong man) was a resident of Gush Halav and, in one version, first buried there before reburial at Meron next to his father. Dating basis: literary (Talmud), conventional year 175 for a late-2nd-century sage; the Wikipedia article cites no passage. Confidence low-medium. (Another tradition places him at Akbara.)

Wikipedia 'Gush Halav': the Talmud describes Eleazar b. Simeon (son of Simeon bar Yochai), 'a very large, strong man', as a resident; one version says he was first buried in Gush Halav and later reinterred in Meron (Eccl. R. 11:3: quarrel between Meron and Giscala over his remains, Jewish Encyclopedia 'Meron'). Year 180 conventional (late 2nd century). Rabbinic-literary.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Giscala'): the city's livelihood came mainly from olive oil and its inhabitants also produced silk (Tosefta Shevi'it 7:15; Eccl. Rabbah 2:8); the Jerusalem Talmud uses Giscala with Meron as a boundary marker for Sabbatical-year olives (JT Sheviit 9:2, Jewish Encyclopedia 'Meron'). Coins show strong commercial ties with Tyre. Year 200 conventional (tannaitic compilation). Rabbinic-literary.

Mishnah Arakhin 9:6 lists 'the fortress (ḥakra) of Gush Ḥalav' among cities walled since the days of Joshua son of Nun (Mishnah redacted c. 200 CE; year 200 conventional). Gush Halav is also known in Tosefta Menahot 9:5 and Bavli Menahot 85b for fine olive oil, and the Talmud mentions silk production there. Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium: shows a Jewish town in the Mishnaic period but nothing site-specific archaeologically.

ESI preliminary report (M. Hartal, G. Jaffe, excavation 2009 in Gush Halav): a stepped ritual bath (miqwe) of the Early Roman period yielded cooking vessels and jars dating to 90-320 CE and glass of the late 1st-early 2nd c.; the excavators conclude that the inhabitants of the Jewish settlement continued to practise purification rituals after the destruction of the Second Temple; a Byzantine-period wall adds to the scanty remains of that period; Iron Age walls found for the first time within the village. Dating basis: pottery and glass in the miqwe. Year 205 = midpoint of 90-320.

Two synagogues in use in the Roman-Byzantine periods (3rd-6th c.). Lower synagogue (by the spring, Nahal Gush Halav) excavated 1977-78 (E. Meyers, C. Meyers, J. Strange): basilica with eight columns, lintel with eagle, coin hoard, Aramaic inscription on a column 'Yose son of Tanhum'. Meyers et al. (1979) date its construction (Stratum VI) to c. 250 CE on pottery plus 6 coins, with destruction ~306 (VIa), continuation to the 362/363 earthquake (VIb), Byzantine Stratum VII, final destruction by the 551 earthquake; the Hebrew encyclopedia gives four phases 250-550. J. Magness (2001) argues the first synagogue was built no earlier than the second half of the 5th c. and perhaps in the first half of the 6th; Spigel (2016) supports the excavators. Upper synagogue (under the Maronite church) unexcavated: lintel and heart-shaped pillar. Dating basis: pottery/coins. Confidence medium; date contested.

Gush Halav lower synagogue (Galilean type), excavated 1977-78 by E. Meyers, C. Meyers and J. Strange. Dating dispute: Leibner and the older typology place the earliest Galilean synagogues incl. Gush Halav in the 2nd-3rd c.; Magness proposes the 5th c. (second half) on archaeological evidence, to which E. Meyers objected. Conventional year 250 (traditional 3rd-c. date); Magness date would be about 450.

Mausoleum on the western slope with stone sarcophagi like those at Beit She'arim and ten hewn loculi (kokhim); skeletons, oil lamps and a glass bottle of the 4th c. found inside. Wikipedia (Jish): Jewish structures and burial sites dated 3rd-6th c.; two ancient synagogues; a column inscribed in Aramaic 'Yose son of Tanhum'. Year 350 = 4th c. (conventional).

IAA trial excavation (2010, Gush Halav A): stratified fill at the foot of the tell with potsherds overwhelmingly of the 3rd-4th centuries CE, read as a landslide, 'probably in the wake of an earthquake in the fourth century CE, most likely 363 CE', which destroyed most Roman-period remains (earlier excavations found the same landslide). Dating basis: pottery/stratigraphy. Confidence medium.

Jerome (De viris illustribus 5, written 392/393) states that Paul 'was of the tribe of Benjamin and the town of Giscalis in Judea' and that when it was taken by the Romans his parents moved to Tarsus: patristic testimony that Gischala was known as a Jewish town captured in 67 CE. Dating basis: literary (patristic), year = Jerome's text; the Pauline tradition itself is uncertain. Confidence low-medium as evidence for Jewish presence after 70.

Synagogues: Wikipedia 'Gush Halav' - two synagogues were in use in the Roman and Byzantine periods (3rd to 6th centuries), 'Jewish structures and burial sites dated to the 3rd through 6th centuries', and Jewish and Christian amulets nearby; Meyers dated one destruction of the lower synagogue to 'the earthquake of 551'. EJ 'Giscala': the second synagogue (excavated 1977-78 by E. Meyers, J.F. Strange and C. Meyers) is dated 250-551 CE (midpoint 400); the first (Kohl & Watzinger 1916) has an Aramaic column inscription naming Yose son of Tanhum. Archaeological; coin and stratigraphic dating.

Burial and Byzantine remains: IAA excavations (Gush Halav B, 2009) record a meagre amount of Byzantine remains, including a pool and burial caves (Makhouly 1938), and remains of a mausoleum from the earlier Roman period; Wikipedia describes a mausoleum on the western slope with stone sarcophagi like Beth She'arim, ten kokhim, skeletons, oil lamps and a glass bottle dated to the 4th c. (flagged 'citation needed'). Dating basis: archaeological, imprecise (conventional year 400). Confidence low.

Upper (hilltop) synagogue of Gush Halav, below the Maronite church (found by Kitchener of the PEF; Bornblum database 'Gush Halav Upper', unexcavated): decorative architectural stones including a lintel and a heart-shaped pillar; period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Conventional year 400; low confidence on the date.

One destruction of the lower synagogue (which had several construction and reconstruction phases) is dated by excavator E. Meyers to the earthquake of 551. Dating basis: excavation stratigraphy attributed to a historical earthquake.

comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Cohen 2018 (Hadashot Arkheologiyot 130): four hewn quarries on the Nahal Revida slope; pottery includes an Early Roman hemispherical bowl, cooking pots of the late 1st c. BCE to 1st c. CE and 1st-century CE jars, a flask and a jug; a rock-cut burial cave (L105) opens in the wall of Quarry 2 and was not excavated; its sunken-frame entrance made for a square sealing stone is called characteristic of the Second Temple period. The report does not itself call the site Jewish; a Jewish attribution rests only on the Second Temple burial-cave type common around Jerusalem. No miqveh, ossuary, coin or inscription evidence and no settlement found; the area was quarries on the edge of the Jerusalem necropolis. Gibson's 1997 excavation at Giv'at Shaul (licence A-2611/1997) is listed in the IAA Favissa archive but the record gives no finds. Population blank (no source gives a figure). Further sources: https://publications.iaa.org.il/favissa/244/

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): New row (first pass had only Early Roman). Hebrew Wikipedia: Josephus mentions Gophna in the battles of Judas Maccabeus; en.wikipedia places a Josephus episode of Judah's escape from Antiochus V c.164 BCE (no precise citation there). Burial cave found at Jifna in 1995 with pottery of Hasmonean, Herodian and early Roman periods (Zelinger 2001, Hebrew, Ariel 10, as cited by en.wikipedia; not seen directly). Ossuary inscription 'Bilga' (priestly course name; dated 63 BCE-70 CE in the Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine database; Sukenik 1933, a cave on the Jerusalem-Shechem road) indicates Jewish burial. Jewish population (priestly families per Talmud); no population estimate in any fetched source; no settlement excavation reported. Population blank. Identification Gophna = Jifna is standard; the link with Ophni of Josh 18:24 is only a proposal.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds burial and epigraphic evidence of a Jewish population and the primary Josephus text. Josephus War 3.55 lists Gophna as the second of the Judean cities, next to Acrabatta; Encyclopedia.com: Gofnah replaced Timnah as toparchy centre under Herod, Cassius sold its inhabitants into slavery in the mid-1st c. BCE (en.wikipedia places the Cassius episode c.50 CE: sources disagree), Vespasian garrisoned it in 68 CE and gathered surrendered priests there. Jewish tombs with inscribed ossuaries at Jifna: Hebrew ossuary 'Yo'ezer son of Yehohanan the scribe' (dated 70-132 CE in the database, after this period; van der Brink and Yannai 2002), an Aramaic ossuary of Judah son of Eleazar and a Greek inscription of Salome daughter of Iakeimos (Encyclopedia.com). Population: Jewish (priests and farmers; wine and oil for the Temple per Hebrew Wikipedia). No named-scholar population estimate in the fetched pages. Population blank.

Event: end of the Jewish presence. Wikipedia 'Jifna': Gophna remained predominantly Jewish under Roman rule, had a sizeable priestly Jewish population around the Bar Kokhba revolt of the 130s, and its Jewish presence 'is thought to have ended in the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba revolt' (the synagogue congregation may have moved to Sepphoris by the 3rd century). The book says the whole Gophna district was inhabited by Jews who took part in the revolt, which ended its Jewish character; from the mid-2nd century a pagan Hellenistic population settled (E. Klein, from 2nd-4th-century sarcophagus-lid art and inscriptions), with coins of Licinius (308-324) and a late Roman villa. Year 135 = end of the revolt. Population blank. Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200): per en.wikipedia a 12th c. BCE cistern with remains of at least 20 individuals and Canaanite pottery; NOBTS lists Late Bronze (1550-1200 BC) habitation. Canaanite population. No estimate. Identification of Tel Hadid with biblical Hadid is standard; Hadid is first named in Ezra 2:33. Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900): cultic refuse pit with figurines and chalices; only slight remains. Probably Israelite but source does not say. No estimate.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722): minimal settlement traces per en.wikipedia; Hebrew Wikipedia (citing Tel Aviv University 1995-97 salvage excavations) says the settlement peaked in the 8th c. BCE under the Kingdom of Israel. Israelite. No published population estimate found; built-up area not found. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%AA%D7%9C_%D7%97%D7%93%D7%99%D7%93

Iron Age IIC (-722 to -586): major domestic occupation with 28 olive presses plus winepresses; two cuneiform tablets (698 and 664 BCE) with Mesopotamian Aramean and local Hebrew names show an Assyrian-settled exile community replacing the earlier Israelite one (2 Kings 17). Population mixed; not a Judahite settlement; no estimate found. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%AA%D7%9C_%D7%97%D7%93%D7%99%D7%93; https://www.nobts.edu/news/articles/2019/TelHadid2019.html

Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332): Hadid appears in Ezra 2:33 and Neh 7:37 among towns of returning exiles; 2008 excavation found scant remains and a building from the Iron Age and early Persian period. No estimate. Further sources: https://www.nobts.edu/news/articles/2019/TelHadid2019.html

Wikipedia 'Haifa': the name Efa 'first appears during Roman rule, some time after the end of the 1st century, when a Roman fortress and small Jewish settlement were established not far from Tell es-Samak' (year 110 conventional). Secondary; medium confidence.

Wikipedia 'Haifa': 'In about the 3rd century CE, Haifa was first mentioned in Talmudic literature' as a Jewish fishing village, home of Rabbi Avdimi, and a dye-making centre; 'Haifa' appears more than 100 times in the Talmud. Eusebius' Onomasticon mentions 'Hefa or Hepha', said to be another name for Sycaminum (the Wolf translation reads 'the maritime village ... on the way from Caesarea to Ptolemais near Mt. Carmel is said to be Epha'); Moshe Sharon argues the twin settlements became the 'twin city' Sycaminon. Year 250 = conventional 3rd century. Rabbinic-literary; Jewish presence stated, population not.

Haifa appears in Talmudic literature 'about the 3rd century CE' as a Jewish fishing village and home of Rabbi Avdimi (Abdimi, Dimi) of Haifa and other scholars (Tosefta Yevamot 6:8; Encyclopaedia Judaica Haifa; Wikipedia Haifa). Jewish Encyclopedia: Haifa 'had a Jewish community during the Talmudic period'; sages named Abba of Haifa, Ami, Isaac Nappaha and Abdima, with a yearly Jewish pilgrimage to Abdima's tomb in the Jewish cemetery (a later tradition). Its inhabitants could not distinguish the gutturals het and ayin (tj Ber. 2:4); the murex was caught 'from Haifa to the Ladder of Tyre' (b. Shabbat 26a). Roman-period tombs including Jewish burial caves were found in the vicinity, and the Jews of Haifa were on hostile terms with the Samaritans of neighbouring Castra (EJ). Identification note: the ancient settlement is generally sought at Tell Abu Hawam/Tell es-Samak or at Haifa el-Atika/Bat Galim; the University of Haifa's Zinman Institute says Tell es-Samak was 'wrongly identified with the Jewish Shikmona' and is the Christian town of Porphyreon. The National Maritime Museum exhibition text 'Shikmona and its Treasures' (older view) still reads the Talmudic and pilgrim mentions of Shikmona as showing 'the city's large Jewish population' at Tel Shikmona itself, which the University of Haifa now rejects. Year 250 is conventional ('about the 3rd century'); the existing marker row dates the first Talmudic mention at 350.

Rabbi Abbahu (late 3rd-early 4th c., see Caesarea) in Lamentations Rabbah describes 'Castra to Haifa' (Midrash Eikhah Rabbah: 'as the Lord commanded Jacob that his neighbours be his foes - Helmish to Nawe, Sussita to Tiberias, Castra to Hufa, Jericho to Noaran, Lod to Ono') as a hostile non-Jewish city near Haifa (Hebrew Wikipedia, Horvat Castra: 'a hostile gentile city next to Haifa'). Evidence of a Jewish settlement at Haifa that felt itself neighboured by a hostile (Samaritan/pagan/Christian) town, consistent with Encyclopaedia Judaica's remark on hostility with the Samaritans of Castra. Year 300 = Abbahu's activity (c. 279-320). Literary evidence, confidence moderate; the quoted Midrash text as given in Hebrew Wikipedia (I did not read Eikhah Rabbah itself).
Haifa is first mentioned in the Talmud, indicating early Jewish presence.

Greek visitor graffiti in the Cave of Elijah on Mount Carmel (Haifa) classified as Jewish by the Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine editors and dated 'sixth century CE' (500-599) or the whole Roman-Byzantine range 54-601: haif0008 'Yohanan and Honi and [...] remembered Nomas of Emmaus ...', haif0005 '... Psalmus ... Samuel', haif0003 'Remembered Polemus who (is also) Sabinus'. The cave was a pilgrimage place shared by Jews, Christians and others, so these show Jewish visitors, not necessarily a resident community; attribution of individual graffiti to Jews is the editors' inference from names and context (weak-to-moderate row). The same cave also has graffiti dated 54-70 CE (pre-70). Year 550 is the midpoint of the 6th-century range.

Framing source just after the period: the Piacenza Pilgrim (c. 570; Jacobs translation, section 3): 'From Ptolemais across the sea to the Jewish city of Sycamina is about half a mile as the crow flies.' Sycamina (Sycaminum) is the Byzantine name of the Haifa/Shiqmona settlement (identification generally accepted; Wikipedia 'Haifa' associates Hepha with Sycaminum). Shows a mainly Jewish settlement at Haifa in the 6th century; the Haifa Wikipedia article also notes a kinah mourning the destruction of Haifa's Jewish community on the Byzantine reconquest of 628. Literary pilgrim source.

Event: Crusader siege of Haifa (25 July to 20 August 1100): the Jewish community helped the Fatimid garrison defend the city; after it fell on 20 August the crusaders (under Tancred) and the Venetians massacred the civilians including the Jewish community, which Wikipedia says 'effectively destroyed' the community. No victim count is given. The LIST (p. 138, ref 1100.3) tells the same story from Albert of Aachen.

Isaac ben Joseph ibn Chelo, The Roads from Jerusalem, 1334: traveller names the place "Haifa"; Adler, Jewish Travellers (1930), p.142-143 (OCR page markers). Traveller's words: In this city there is a Jewish congregation renowned for its piety (no number). Identification: Haifa. No count given; Population left blank (presence only). Year 1334 as given for the journey.

Wikipedia 'Hammat Gader': bath complex begun in the 2nd century by the Tenth Roman Legion; rabbinic sources record sages visiting from the mid-2nd century, 'starting with Rabbi Meir', and discussing the Sabbath-boundary status of the site relative to Gadara. Rabbinic-literary; the 2nd-century date is from the article, not from the Talmudic text.

Hot-springs site visited by Talmudic sages from Rabbi Meir (mid-2nd c.), who discussed its Sabbath-boundary status relative to Gadara; Roman bath complex begun in the 2nd c. by the 10th Roman Legion (garrisoned at Gadara). Jewish presence at the site itself is attested by the later synagogue (5th c.); for the 2nd c. the evidence is literary only. Year 150 (mid-2nd c.).

Hammat Gader ('Hammath-by-Gadara') was 'a Jewish town in the Roman and Byzantine periods', heavily populated in Talmudic times, and visited for the hot springs by sages from the south, the Golan and Galilee, including Judah ha-Nasi with his pupils (c. 200) (EJ) and, per Wikipedia, R. Meir (mid-2nd c., who discussed its Sabbath-boundary status relative to Gadara); the Roman baths were built by Legio X from the 2nd c. (Wikipedia). Year = c. 175 (between R. Meir and Judah ha-Nasi). Dating basis: literary (Talmud). Confidence medium. Site lies on the Israeli-controlled side of the Yarmuk valley; Gadara (Umm Qais) is across the border in Jordan.

Epiphanius, Panarion 30.7.5-8 (Williams): the young patriarch (Judas, son of 'Ellel') and his guardians Joseph and another elder 'went to Gadara for the hot baths. There is a gathering there every year. Persons who wish to bathe for a certain number of days arrive from every quarter ... the bathing there is mixed.' The 'hot baths of Gadara' are the Hammat Gader springs (an inference of mine from the name; Wikipedia 'Hammat Gader' speaks of baths 'relative to Gadara'). Year 350 = conventional (events during Joseph's years in Tiberias, before 355). Primary patristic source; confidence medium.

Earlier phases of the Hamat Gader synagogue found beneath the mosaic by G. Foerster (1982-83): a white mosaic floor, then a second phase with an opus sectile pavement 'dated to the latter half of the fourth century' (Epidentity); the 2024 ESI report adds that a bema was attached to the south wall, facing Jerusalem, in the intermediate phase. Dating basis: stratigraphy/floor typology. Confidence medium.

Wikipedia 'Hammat Gader': 'A large synagogue was built in the 5th century CE', with four Aramaic mosaic inscriptions recording donations from various localities; Sukenik's 1932 excavation. EJ 'Land of Israel' lists Hammath-Gader among the Byzantine synagogues built or renovated in the north. Archaeological (inscriptions/mosaics), 5th century = conventional 450.

Large synagogue (main hall about 13 x 13 m with two rows of columns, apse, bema; enclosing wall 32.5 m) built in the 5th c.; four well-preserved Aramaic mosaic inscriptions plus donor inscriptions naming donors from various places; excavated by Sukenik 1932, Foerster 1982 re-examined earlier phases. Conventional year 450 (5th c.).

ESI final report on the Hammat Gader synagogue (J. Foerster, P. Porat, trial excavations beneath the mosaic in 1982-83): the original excavator dated the synagogue to the 5th c. CE on coins and inscriptions; Foerster and Porat date it to the Byzantine period (4th-6th c.) on ceramics; the synagogue was part of a nearby Jewish settlement and existed throughout the Byzantine period; a bone box and Byzantine lamps found. Dating basis: coins and inscriptions versus ceramics. Midpoint of the 4th-6th c. range is 450.

Final basilical synagogue at Hamat Gader (about 13 x 14 m, apse and bema, mosaic with four Aramaic donor inscriptions, one with two lions; marble chancel screen with menorah in a wreath and Greek inscriptions): E.L. Sukenik (1932) dated it to the 5th c. from coins and inscriptions, M. Avi-Yonah to the 6th c.; Foerster and Porat date the synagogue to the Byzantine period (4th-6th c.); CIIP inscriptions AD 500-599. Conventional year (5th-6th c.). Coins: 22 Byzantine and 28 Roman/'Arabic' (probably Early Islamic). Dating basis: coins/epigraphy. Confidence medium.

Mosaic donor inscriptions of the synagogue (Aramaic, panels edited in CIIP V/2 and Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine HGAD0001-2, dated 6th c., 500-599 CE): a Greek-named family incl. 'Comes Pheroros' donating five gold coins; 'Rav Tanhum the Levite son of Halfa', a man 'of Sepphoris', 'Lord Patricus of Kefar Aqabyah' and 'Yoseh son of Dositheus of Kefar Nahum' (Capernaum), 'Yudan the architect (?) of Emmaus' and 'the people of Arbela' - evidence of donors from Galilean and Judean Jewish communities travelling to the spa. Year 550 = end of the IIP range; the date differs from Sukenik's earlier (mid-5th c.) terminus.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Hammath'): 'After the Second Temple's destruction, priests of the Maziah course settled there' (Baraita of the Twenty-Four Mishmarot) and Hammath was 'joined to Tiberias for halakhic purposes' (Meg. 2b; Tosefta Eruvin 7:2; JT Eruvin 6); R. Meir was one of several talmudic scholars who lived there; a Jewish community is attested until the Cairo Genizah. Year 100 = conventional (post-70). Rabbinic-literary; the residence list is a later baraita.

Earliest substantial stratum at the later synagogue site (Level III, 1st-2nd c.): a public building around a courtyard with rooms on at least three sides and two entrances to the south; it may already have functioned as a synagogue, but this is uncertain. Year = conventional middle of the 1st-2nd c. range. Dating basis: stratigraphy (Dothan 1961-63). Confidence low-medium.

R. Meir, a leading Tanna, was one of the many sages who lived at Hammath; the hot baths were famous in Talmudic times (Meg. 2b; Tosefta Eruvin 7:2). Conventional year (mid-2nd c.). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium. A Jewish community is attested there up to the Cairo Genizah period (EJ).

Synagogue strata (Dothan 1961-63; Slouschz 1920): Wikipedia 'Hammat Tiberias' - Synagogue B's first synagogue 'built around 230 CE'; Synagogue A 'first built in c. 250 CE'; EJ: Dothan's second synagogue has a 3rd-century phase. Midpoint of 230-250 used. Archaeological (stratigraphy, pottery).

Zodiac synagogue (Level II): nave mosaic with Torah shrine, zodiac around Helios, donors' inscriptions in Greek ('Severus, pupil of the most illustrious Patriarchs'). Dating conflict: inscriptions dated AD 270-325 (CIIP/Epidentity); EJ 'beginning of the 4th century'; Dothan/Wikipedia 'second half of the 4th century'; JVL '341'. Year 325 is a compromise (range 270-400). Destroyed by an early-5th-c. earthquake. Dating basis: epigraphy/stratigraphy. Confidence medium (date contested).

Synagogue B, 4th-century stage: mosaic with zodiac, Helios, four seasons and the dedicatory inscription 'Severus, the pupil of the most illustrious Patriarchs, has made this blessing. Amen.' Wikipedia 'Hammat Tiberias' dates the mosaic to the second half of the 4th century ('the earliest mosaic pavement found in a synagogue'; midpoint 375 used) and says this building was destroyed by an early-5th-century earthquake; EJ 'Hammath' dates the basilica to the beginning of the 4th century (conflict). Archaeological/epigraphic.

Larger synagogue of the 5th-6th centuries: Wikipedia 'Hammat Tiberias' - a larger synagogue of the 5th-6th centuries, 'eventually destroyed in the 8th century'; EJ 'Hammath': sixth-century basilica with an apse and geometric mosaics (about 62 x 49 ft). Hamichlol dates Hammat Tiberias synagogues 3rd-6th century. 5th-6th century midpoint 500 used. Archaeological.

Synagogue B ('Synagogue of Severus', excavated by M. Dothan 1961-63) stages: a 1st-c. public building; a first synagogue c. 230 CE (small mosaic section survives), apparently destroyed in the same century; a 4th-c. synagogue with the Helios-zodiac mosaic, destroyed by an early-5th-c. earthquake; a much larger 5th-6th c. synagogue destroyed in the 8th c. Context: Tiberias was seat of the Sanhedrin from 193 CE to the late 4th c. per this article.

Synagogue A (north) on the lakeshore: square basilical hall with courtyard, first built c. 250 CE, main use 4th-5th c., later phases to the 10th-11th c.; found 1921 (Slouschz). Hammat Tiberias was a village distinct from Tiberias according to the Jerusalem Talmud; finds range from the 1st to 8th c. Year 250.

Synagogue B 4th-c. phase: Helios and zodiac mosaic with Greek donor inscriptions naming 'Severus, pupil of the most illustrious Patriarchs'. Dothan dates the building/mosaic to the early (first half of the) 4th c. and Avi-Yonah no later than mid-4th c., while Magness (2005) dates it to the late 4th c. Dating basis: archaeological context versus reassessment. Year 350 = middle of the contested 4th-c. range.

Biblical mention and identification (literary only; Year of Data -1200 = conventional date of the Joshua conquest/allotment narrative (the allotment lists themselves are of disputed date); new marker, nearest marker Poriyya-Newe Oved 2.9 km, unrelated). Josh 19:35 (Hammath among the fenced cities of Naphtali, with Ziddim, Zer, Rakkath, Chinnereth); Josh 21:32 (Hammoth-dor, Levitical city of the Gershonites in Naphtali) and 1 Chr 6:76 (Hammon) are probably the same place (Wikipedia, List of minor biblical places). Identification: Hammat Tiberias, the hot springs at the southern end of Tiberias, 32.7686 N 35.5485 E (Wikipedia: 'archaeologists have concluded it was built on the ruins of the biblical city of Hammath'; Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities, which also lists Tel Raqqat/Khirbet el-Qanitriyeh as an alternative for Hammath and Hammoth-dor). BibleWalks adds that Hammath may be in the 13th-c. Anastasi Papyrus. No Iron Age finds: the excavated remains of Hammat Tiberias date to the 1st-8th centuries CE (Wikipedia), so this is a literary-only row; disputed, favoured: Hammat Tiberias. No population estimate. Excavation inside the modern settlement of Haspin (IAA final report, O. Zingboym & A. Kleiner, HA-ESI 136, 2024, 'Synagogues in the Golan: Education and Community' project; 40 sq m, 2014-2019): remains of 'what appears to have been a public building', founded in the Middle-Late Roman period ('second-early third centuries CE'); the excavators take a lion sculpture from the site (now in the Golan Antiquities Museum), Kefar Hananya and Hawarit wares (typical of Jewish villages of the Golan) and the neighbouring Jewish villages as signs of a Jewish public building. A 2018 survey found two earlier coins, one of Hadrian (Tiberias mint) and one of Marcus Aurelius (Sussita mint). The authors suggest the site may be the 'Hasppiya' of the Baraita of the Boundaries (prohibited towns of Susita's territory; see the 250 row), and suggest the name may have passed to the Byzantine site 2.5 km east of Haspin (north of Ramat Magshimim) after the Roman settlement was abandoned. Jewish identity is inferred (lion statue, ware types, neighbouring Jewish villages Majduliyya and Nov), not proved by an inscription; no synagogue was identified. Year 200 = midpoint of 'second-early third century' for the foundation; confidence medium.

ESI final report (O. Zingboym, A. Kleiner; 2014-19 excavation within the project 'Synagogues in the Golan'): remains of a public building dated between the second-early third centuries CE and the middle of the 4th c.; it may belong to the Jewish settlement of Hasppiya, listed among the 'prohibited towns' in the territory of Sussita in the Baraita of the Boundaries; Kefar Hananya ware, lion sculptures and Hawarit ware point to a Jewish village; coins end in 346 and none are known from 346 to the 363 earthquake, so the settlement may have been deliberately abandoned before 363. Identification with Hasppiya is conjectural. Midpoint of 2nd/3rd c.-mid-4th c. is about 250.

End of the Roman-period settlement (same IAA report, HA-ESI 136, 2024): ten coins of the 3rd-4th c. show occupation after 306 CE; the absence of any coin of 346-363 CE, a span in which coins are normally common, 'raises the possibility that the settlement was abandoned, perhaps in a planned deliberate manner' before the 363 earthquake; the building 'was probably abandoned by the mid-fourth century CE or even at the end of the first third of that century'; pottery mostly 2nd-6th c., reducible to the beginning of the 4th c. by the coins. The authors cite the Golan survey (M. Hartal 2012): settlements of the Nahal Samakh basin were abandoned in the early or mid-4th c., 'followed by a period during which Jewish settlements flourished in the central Golan' (cause unclear; the earthquakes of 306 and 363 are floated), and suggest the Haspin community may have relocated to the central Golan. A rare dated 'move to the central Golan' datum. Year 340 = between the end of the first third and mid-4th c.; confidence medium-high for abandonment, low for the cause.

Literary only (conventional date -925: Rehoboam, c. 931-913 BCE). Rehoboam fortified Hebron as the last of 15 towns of Judah and Benjamin (2 Chr 11:5-10; Hebron in v. 10, fortifications and garrisons v. 11-12). Dating caveat: no fetched source shows a 10th-century fortress at Tel Rumeida; the Hebrew Wikipedia article ties the later Iron Age city to the 'lamelekh-Hebron' jar-handle seals of the kingdom of Judah (no date given there), and English Wikipedia describes 8th-century four-room houses and a possible Hezekiah-era strengthening of older fortifications. No population estimate found. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Rumeida ; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%97%D7%91%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%9F

Late 8th c. administrative centre of Hezekiah's Judah. Jar handles stamped 'lmlk' (belonging to the king) name four places - Ziph, Hebron, Socoh and 'mmst' (unidentified) - read as four administrative regions of the kingdom; the seals were first issued under Hezekiah around 700 BCE and complete jars lay under the Sennacherib destruction layer at Lachish (English Wikipedia 'LMLK seal'). 'lmlk Hebron' jar handles have been found, for example at Lachish (English Wikipedia 'Hebron'). Year of Data -701 = Sennacherib's campaign. Archaeological/epigraphic evidence; no population figure. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron
