Persian (-539 to -332): English Wikipedia (Tel Rumeida): the town's population became predominantly Edomite (Idumean) through the Babylonian and Persian periods; not Jewish; no estimate.

Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Idumean settlement attested in Hellenistic times (English Wikipedia Tel Rumeida); Emek Shaveh guide dates occupation from the Hellenistic period; no Jewish evidence in this period; no estimate.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for Hasmonean: the fetched excavation sources date the Second Temple phases of Tel Hebron from the late Hasmonean period c. 100 to 37 BCE (not from 167 BCE) through to the Bar-Kokhba revolt (Ben-Shlomo and Eisenberg 2014 excavation as summarised in BAS). Farhi and Ben-Shlomo 2016 (Tel Aviv 43) present the first numismatic study: coins show a Second Temple period settlement on the mound with a domestic and industrial quarter in use from the Hasmonean period. TheTorah.com (Ben-Shlomo) lists two houses on either side of a street, a pottery workshop and agricultural installations plus chalk stone vessels (read as a Jewish purity marker) and two stepped plastered pools read as miqva'ot (supported by Reich's identification of such pools); Ben-Shlomo concludes the town was Jewish in the Hasmonean and Roman periods whether by Judean settlement or Idumean conversion. Before this the area was Idumean (1 Macc 5:65 Judah attacked Hebron; Josephus Ant. 13 Hyrcanus converted the Idumeans). Emek Shaveh cautions only the mound margins were excavated. Population blank: no named-scholar estimate for Hebron in any fetched source.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): additional source for the row above. Ben-Shlomo (BAR Sept/Oct 2017) concludes the Second Temple population was still Jewish; Eisenberg and Ben-Shlomo (eds.) 2017 final report The Tel Hevron 2014 Excavations (Ariel University Press) includes Rachel Bar-Nathan on pottery and Yoav Farhi on coins; the ritual-bath chapter is by Ben-Shlomo pp. 251-261. Hebrew Wikipedia (Tel Hevron) also says the 2014 excavation found a fortified well-planned town with drainage and an industrial quarter and that the miqva'ot indicate Jewish population. No population figure.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row: adds that the western miqveh is a rock-cut pool about 7.3 x 4.4 m with 14 plastered steps and over 3 m deep and the eastern one has about 13 steps with double separation walls forming three lanes (TheTorah.com, Ben-Shlomo); the western one was converted to a roofed reservoir in the Late Roman period. Herod built the monumental ashlar enclosure over the Cave of the Patriarchs (style-based attribution); Ben-Shlomo suggests Herod saw Hebron as a Jewish city, others say it was for his Idumean kin. Josephus (War IV.529, 554): Simon bar Giora took Hebron and Vespasian's army burned it; per the article the city was resettled and remained inhabited until the Bar-Kokhba revolt (132-135 CE). Emek Shaveh: a large early Roman (1st c. BCE) compound found in Lot 53. Jewish population (Idumean converts and/or Judeans); no estimate by any named scholar, Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): additional support. BAS summary of the 2014 excavation (Ben-Shlomo and Eisenberg): four occupational phases from late Hasmonean (c. 100-37 BCE) to the Bar-Kokhba revolt; houses, pottery workshops, wine and oil presses, two large miqva'ot; Josephus on Vespasian burning Hebron. Emek Shaveh 2014 report dates the compound in Lot 53 to the early Roman period. Identification note: the Second Temple town lay on Tel Rumeida (Tel Hebron) per Ben-Shlomo; English Wikipedia (Tel Rumeida, citing Auerbach 2009) says the Idumean population moved to the Machpelah area after 167 BCE, a view not confirmed by the excavation reports fetched.

The book describes a different fact: Hebron was rebuilt after the Great Revolt with few inhabitants, and after Betar fell its inhabitants fled and the city was destroyed; it adds (Amit and Eshel) that the Jews of the southern Hebron hills took an active part in the revolt and the Roman army destroyed the whole area, about 20 settlements. [Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Hebrew Wikipedia dates Alexander Jannaeus's conquest to 83-80 BCE (a 101 BCE date is marked unsourced) and says Josephus reports forced conversion of the inhabitants; the Josephus passage was not fetched, so that part is second-hand. A lead sling bullet inscribed with the Greek word for 'Learn' (Armstrong Institute report on a Hippos project find) may belong to Greek defenders against Jannaeus c. 101 BCE, but the researchers say it could date from any Hellenistic battle; the page says Jannaeus took Hippos in 83 BCE. No ritual baths, chalk vessels or Hasmonean coins from Hippos appear in any fetched page, so Jewish presence is textual only; Population blank. An Acta Archaeologica Lodziensia article (a search snippet describes a Greek city with a small Jewish admixture from 83-80 BCE) could not be read and is not used as evidence.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Josephus, Jewish War 2.478 (Whiston, lexundria.com): the people of Hippos and Gadara put to death the boldest of the Jews among them and held the rest in custody; War 2.459 has Jews attacking Gadara and Hippos in 66 CE. This confirms a Jewish minority inside the city in 66 CE (no number). The Hippos project says Pompey freed it in 63 BCE (Decapolis), briefly Herod's territory, then Syria; the Jerusalem Talmud and halakhic literature regard Hippos as mostly non-Jewish and it was an enemy of Jewish Tiberias. The first-pass claim that Jews from Hippos joined the revolt at Tarichaea is not in any fetched page (Hebrew Wikipedia says they attacked Magdala). Greek city; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): supporting - Hippos Excavations Project: Pompey's order freed Decapolis cities; Hippos a Decapolis city, briefly given to Herod; Talmudic sources treat it as mostly non-Jewish; no population estimate. Population blank.

At the outbreak of the war Jews led by Justus of Tiberias devastated Hippos and the inhabitants massacred Jews in revenge (Josephus B.J. ii.18.1, 5, as cited by the Jewish Encyclopedia; War 2.478). The Talmud calls the city Susita and treats it as Gentile-inhabited (Yer. Rosh Hashanah ii.1).

Jewish villages in Hippos' territory (NEAEHL entry 'Hippos', 1993, quoted at deadseaquake.info): 'Jewish villages east of the lake were included in the territory of Hippos and were exempt from tithes in the time of the patriarch Judah I, being considered beyond the frontiers of the land of Israel proper (Tosefta, Shevi'it 4:10; Tosefta, Ohal. 18:4)'; Hippos was 'the sworn enemy of Jewish Tiberias' (Lam. Rab.) despite trade (JT Shevi'it 8, 38a); 'Remains of ancient synagogues have been found at Fiq (Aphek) and at Umm el-Qanatir, both of which lay within the territory of Hippos.' The city itself was pagan then Christian (bishop by 359; none of the c. 16 IIP inscriptions from Hippos is Hebrew or Aramaic), so this row records rabbinic-territorial evidence for the Jewish villages around Hippos, not a Jewish community in the city. The Mosaic of Rehob lists nine villages 'in the region of Susitha' (see Kefar Haruv, Nov, Haspin rows). Year 200 = Judah I (c. 200). Josephus (War 3.542) also has Jews from Hippos among the defenders of Tarichaeae in 67 (framing). Borderline row; confidence medium.

Regional row for the territory of Hippos/Sussita (Hippos itself was a Greek-pagan then Christian city, not a Jewish community): ESI 2018 southern Golan survey (S. Fridman, Bar-Ilan University, 2005-07 and 2014-16; 98 sites incl. 62 settlements) - settlements peaked in the Early (50 BCE-150 CE) and Middle Roman (150-250) periods; by the beginning of the Byzantine period (c. 350) only slightly more than half of the Roman-period settlements remained inhabited, the rest abandoned or sharply reduced, and hardly any new ones founded; chalk vessels at 13 settlement sites indicate a Jewish population (with some pagan evidence); (the Baraita of the Boundaries, see the Rehov and Haspin rows, lists 'prohibited' towns in Sussita's territory). No Jewish population figure is given. Dating basis: pottery survey. Year 350.

Event: Tiglath-pileser III's Galilee campaign (734-732 BCE). Na'aman reads Marum (Merom) as one of the places listed among the towns of the Lower Galilee and the western Jezreel valley that the Assyrian annals record as captured, and puts it at Tel Qarney Hittin (the Horns of Hattin hill); the number of captives from Marum is lost. The same annals fragment says that sixteen districts of Bit-Humria (the land of Omri, i.e. Israel) were turned into ruins, and a second fragment records 13,520 people taken captive, which Na'aman thinks is probably the total deported from this area (his inference; the link is not preserved in the text). Online: Wikipedia 'Horns of Hattin' says the hilltop fortress Tel Qarney Hittin was "identified by Zvi Gal with Meron/Merom of the Hebrew Bible" and that Merom is attested for "Tiglath Pileser III in 733/32 BCE". The existing marker 'Hittin (Kefar Hittaya)' (a Roman-period village, 0.8 km from the tel) is used for the tel. Population blank (no town figure). Confidence medium: the identification Marum = Tel Qarney Hittin is a scholarly proposal (Gal, Na'aman). Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) repeats the place list with Marum at Tel Qarney Hittin and the 13,520 captives.

R. Jacob of Kefar Hittaya, a Palestinian scholar of the 2nd c., contemporary of Judah I, who visited his teacher every day (Hagigah 5b). Conventional year (late 2nd c.). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium. Identification of Kefar Hittaya with Hittin is the standard one (Klein, Dalman).

Kefar Hittaya ('Grain village'), a Galilean village identified with Hittin: seat of R. Jacob (Hagigah 5b) and R. Azariah (PdRK 54); it had a synagogue (Genesis Rabbah 65:16) and gave refuge to R. Simeon b. Lakish when he fled the wrath of the patriarch Judah II (JT Sanhedrin 2:1); building remains and ancient tombs found. Wikipedia calls it a Jewish rabbinical town in the 4th c. Conventional year (3rd c., Resh Lakish and Judah II). Dating basis: literary (rabbinic). Confidence medium-low; no excavated Jewish remains reported.

IAA (ESI 2010): the Arab village of Hittin 'was situated on the remains of the Jewish village Hittiya, which is mentioned in the literary sources from the time of the Mishnah and Talmud'; no Jewish remains of the period are described from the excavation itself. Conventional year (Mishnaic-Talmudic period). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium-low.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): quarries and a workshop for chalk-stone vessels at Hizma excavated by Magen (The Stone Vessel Industry in the Second Temple Period: Excavations at Hizma and the Jerusalem Temple Mount, Israel Exploration Society 2002; Hebrew 1988). Chalk vessels are typical of Jewish sites from the second half of the 1st century BCE to 132 CE (English Wikipedia). Other Jewish evidence: a burial cave found in 1931 with six ossuaries, two inscribed in Hebrew or Aramaic script (Hoshea, Mariam), and an ossuary said to come from Hizma naming a granddaughter of the high priest Theophilus (Barag and Flusser, IEJ 1986; antiquities-market find, findspot not excavated). Hebrew Wikipedia also cites Second Temple ossuaries with Hebrew inscriptions. A Jewish village is indicated, but no source gives a population estimate, so Population is blank. The fetched pages do not give a precise start date of the quarry within the Early Roman period.

Jewish village of the Late Roman/Byzantine period 8 km east of Acre (Horbat 'Uza, Arabic Khirbet el-'Ayadiyya; main salvage excavation 1991, a 1963 dig by Y. Ben-Yosef, and a further salvage dig in late 2011 for the Akko-Karmiel railway; on the Acre-Safed road west of the Kafr Yasif junction). Stratum 8, dated c. 340-410 CE (midpoint 375 used), has 'elements of Jewish material culture': a group of ceramic stands that supported oil lamps ('Sabbath lampstands', one engraved with the Hebrew word shabbat; a device for keeping the lamp burning through the Sabbath, cf. Mishnah Shabbat 2:4), storage jars decorated with polychrome menorah patterns, and a cave with Jewish burials. The settlement existed until c. 630 and had a church (Christians), and pottery manufacture began in the 4th century. Caveat: the lampstand type shows 'Jews or Samaritans' (Wikipedia) and the burial cave is not described in detail in the source I read. Wikipedia 'Horbat 'Uza' (English) and the Hebrew article (layers 6-9, pottery industry from the early 4th century) were read; not the IAA final report. Population: none given.

Menorah bread stamp (6th century CE) from Horbat 'Uza, excavated by the Israel Antiquities Authority (directors Gilad Jaffe and Danny Syon) before building the Akko-Karmiel railway: a fired-clay stamp with a seven-branched menorah and, in Greek on the handle, the baker's name, probably Launtius (L. Di Segni). The directors say it 'proves that a Jewish community existed in the settlement of Uza in the Christian-Byzantine period', 'in a region that was definitely Christian at this time', and speculate that the village supplied kosher bread to the Jews of Acre. First menorah bread stamp from a controlled excavation (JVL/IAA press release, January 2012; Wikipedia 'Horbat 'Uza'). Dated by stratigraphy/pottery (6th c.); the year 550 is the conventional mid-6th-century figure. Confidence good for a Jewish presence in the 6th c.; interpretation as 'kosher bakery' is a conjecture.

Weak row - Roman-period Jewish finds under a mainly Christian Byzantine city. Hebrew Wikipedia (Horvat Castra, on a spur of Mount Carmel at Kfar Samir, south Haifa; salvage excavations 1993-97 for the Carmel Tunnels, Z. Yivin and G. Finkelstein): from the Roman period graves, a ritual bath (mikveh) and a clay bread stamp bearing the word 'Shevi'it' were found, 'evidence of a Jewish population in the settlement in this period'. In the 4th-6th centuries the site was a city of more than 250 dunams with two churches (Christian city, 14 wine presses, 13 olive presses). The Roman phase is not dated more closely in the source (year 200 is a conventional placement). Identification doubt: the site is conventionally identified with 'Castra of the Samaritans' of the Piacenza Pilgrim, but the excavators' finds do not confirm that identification (Samaritan evidence absent); the talmudic Castra of R. Abbahu is an enemy gentile city near Haifa (see Haifa 300). The 'Atiqot 75 (2013) article on two subsurface features at Horbat Qastra was not read.

comment: Jewish village of the Second Temple period in the Judean Shephelah (Zissu and Ganor excavations 1999-2001). Wikipedia and the NEAEHL entry: the village reached its greatest extent in the decades before the First Jewish Revolt, a built-up area of about 10 dunams (c. 2.5 acres); its Jewish residents are attested by ritual baths, stone vessels and ossuaries; it was partly destroyed in the First Jewish Revolt (66-70) and abandoned for a short period, then resettled at about half its size and destroyed again in the Bar Kokhba revolt. Population left blank: the attached book (Shpak-Lissak, ch. 2, img019) gives a peak area of about 20 dunams and computes about 700 inhabitants (35 per dunam), which does not match the online area of about 10 dunams (see conflicts file). No existing map marker for this site. [confidence: medium] [Source detail: (Wikipedia, 'Horvat Ethri'); (NEAEHL, "'Ethri, Horvat", Zissu and Ganor)]

After the Great Revolt the village was rebuilt, never regaining its former size, and its inhabitants were Jews; about 60 years later, in preparation for the Bar Kokhba revolt, hiding complexes were cut under the village; the site also has a large building with a ritual bath and a public building that was probably a synagogue (Hamichlol, 'Horvat Atari', the same site as the map's Horvat 'Ethri). Year 129 = 69 + 60. Presence evidence only: Population blank.

source: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 037 (Screenshot_20221028-092833.jpg; page number not visible)
comment: Event: the book (in its section based on E. Klein's survey) says the village was destroyed during the Bar Kokhba revolt and resettled in the late Roman period (135-234), this time by non-Jews, who built a villa on the site; Klein also adduces Jewish sources saying that gentiles of eastern origin entered Judea after the revolt. no online source found; Hamichlol does not mention the Bar Kokhba destruction or the later non-Jewish resettlement; source is the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew). Population blank.

Ruin on the east slope of Ramat Sirin ~1.5 km NW of Kibbutz Gesher by the 'Ein Adama spring: mainly Late Roman and Byzantine remains, several large public buildings with many ashlars and a basalt lintel engraved with a bird of prey, like lintels of ancient synagogues of Lower Galilee and the Golan. Some propose it preserves the name of the Talmudic town Idma, home of the amora Rabbi Kyros of Idma (Jerusalem Talmud) - conjectural identification. Survey only (A. Schiller, Ariel 52, 1987). Year 450 conventional; weak-moderate evidence of a Jewish village.

Wikipedia 'Hurvat Amudim' (south-east of the Beit Netofa Valley): Dalman linked the site to Kefar Uzziel, tied to priestly families who settled in the Galilee 'from the 2nd century CE onward' (Wikipedia 'Priestly courses' lists Kfar Uziel for the 8th course, Abijah; identification conjectural); the synagogue 'was built at the end of the 3rd century or the beginning of the 4th century' (Y. Levin's 1979 excavation; also Kohl & Watzinger 1905); an Aramaic mosaic inscription names 'bar Tanhum' as the maker of the pavement; Zingboim/Dalali-Amos (2011) and Tsinmon/Porat (2012) excavations found quarries, a burial cave and tombs with pottery from the 1st century BCE to the 10th century CE. Archaeological; end of 3rd/beginning of 4th century = 300.

Wikipedia 'Hurvat Amudim': 'The town was abandoned in the late 4th century' (385 used for 'late 4th century'); no cause stated (cf. 363 and 419 earthquakes, Khirbet Wadi Hamam abandoned c. 400, Shikhin 4th century). Archaeological.

Town abandoned in the late 4th c. according to Wikipedia. Leibner (2009) dates the synagogue to the late 3rd/early 4th c. and thinks it was apparently abandoned not long after its foundation, yet his own survey tables show reduced occupation continuing (size category E, 41-60 dunams, c. 50 BCE-350 CE, then C, 11-20 dunams, to c. 550, B to 650) - conflicting evidence, low confidence.

'Kefar Uzziel' is the residence of the 8th priestly course Abijah in DJE 23; G. Dalman identified Kefar Uzziel with the Jewish village of Hurvat Amudim because of the nearby Arab village Uzeir - speculative (the Amudim synagogue was abandoned c. 400). Basis: the Hebrew stone pillar DJE 23 (Bayt Hadir, Yemen; dated 4th-5th c. CE) lists the Galilean residence of each priestly course - the settlement tradition of the Baraita of the Mishmarot - so it shows the place was remembered as a priestly (Jewish) village by the 4th-5th c., not that excavations confirm it. Year = midpoint of the 4th-5th c.; confidence low-medium; identification of the ancient name with the modern site follows the Wikipedia 'Priestly divisions' list.

Weak row. Hebrew Wikipedia: Horvat Belia (Kh. el-Mibeliyya, western Galilee between Tuval and Palekh, 490 m) has remains of an oil press, agricultural installations and large cisterns 'mainly from the Roman and Byzantine periods', and next to the site is a burial cave in which an engraving of a seven-branched menorah was found - an indicator of a Jewish settlement, but the page gives no dating basis or excavation report (listed in the Hebrew Wikipedia category of Jewish settlements of the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods). Year 300 is a conventional placement for 'Roman-Byzantine'. Druze lived there until the late Ottoman period. Confidence low.

Weak row - possibly Jewish Carmel village. Hebrew Wikipedia (Horvat Karakh, Kh. el-Karak, on the Carmel ridge near Keren HaCarmel, listed in its category of Jewish settlements of the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods): remains of a settlement 'perhaps Jewish' of the 2nd to 6th centuries (Late Roman and Byzantine) with an olive press, a winepress, rock-cut burial caves, plastered cisterns and terraces; no synagogue was found, 'but it is possible that the inhabitants were Jews because similar settlements in the area, where a synagogue was found, ...' (the article's own wording, marked citation needed). Never excavated. Year 350 = midpoint of 2nd-6th century. Low confidence; the same article also repeats the unsourced idea that Jews expelled from Judea after the Great Revolt settled here.

Rural Galilean settlement with a monumental building excavated by the Kinneret Regional Project (J. Zangenberg; Bern, Helsinki, Leiden, Mainz): about 500 bronze coins in and below the courtyard suggest the building with its monumental wall, benches and pilasters was in use c. 400 CE; the Bornblum database classes it as a synagogue (columns, bema, benches; small remains of a mosaic with menorah and inscription) of 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' date. Dating basis: coins from the courtyard (2008/2010 seasons). Conventional year 400.

Synagogue of the rural Roman-Byzantine site of Horvat Kur (Kinneret Regional Project, since 2008): a basilical broadhouse built in the first half of the 5th c. (coins c. 400 and pottery) over an earlier Jewish prayer building (a JPA inscription belongs to the earlier phase); mosaic fragment with menorah. Dating basis: coins/stratigraphy. Confidence medium-high. Coordinates from Epidentity site list (32.885 N, 35.537 E).

Jewish village (c. 30 dunams, tens of buildings, mikveh, oil press, rock-cut loculi tombs, mosaic-floored building) on a hill beside Tel Kinrot (Kinneret) on the NW shore of the Sea of Galilee. Excavated 2008-2013+ by the Kinneret Regional Project (Univ. of Bern, Helsinki, Leiden, Mainz: J. Zangenberg, S. Muenger, R. Hakola, B. McCane). IAA preliminary report (HA-ESI 125, 2013): a synagogue (N-S axis c. 11 m) with a western portico; the fill dumped outside it (about 1,000 coins in the 'coin layer') holds pottery and readable coins 'predominately of the early Byzantine period (c. 380-425 CE)', the early coin cluster 'gives the terminus post quem for the construction of the first phase of the synagogue, i.e. not longer after c. 425 CE'. he.wikipedia: built 'apparently a little after 425', with a bema, a stone seat (first in the north) and an ornamented basalt table. Bornblum: Aramaic inscription with a menorah in a mosaic (CIIP V/1 no. 421). Year 440 = 'shortly after 425'. Identification with the Late Second Temple village 'Koreai' (B. Rosenfeld) is a hypothesis. Confidence high for a 5th-c. synagogue.

Phase II of the synagogue: the original mosaic floor was removed and replaced by a plastered floor in a major rebuilding (HA-ESI 125, 2013), dated 'to the second half of the sixth century CE at the earliest' by the second, small coin cluster (four coins of Marcian 450-457 and two of Justinian 527-565 among the fill; two possible Umayyad sherds). he.wikipedia adds gold coins of Justin II (565-578) and Tiberius II (578-582) and Umayyad-period pottery, and says the settlement ended with the earthquake of 19 January 749. The coin sequence documents a Jewish village still active in the later 6th c. on the Kinneret - in contrast to the late-6th/early-7th-c. abandonment of most upland Golan sites. Year 575 = second half of the 6th c.; slightly after the window; confidence high.

After earthquake damage the synagogue was rebuilt in the late 6th c. (portico, benches, large bema), refitted c. 600, abandoned in the second half of the 7th c.; ESI preliminary reports date the building's final use to the mid-8th c. Framing row (just after the period). Dating basis: stratigraphy/coins. Confidence medium.

Mashkanah (survey site 44, Kh. Meskeneh, map ref 1886/2433, 35 dunams) is named twice in the Jerusalem Talmud as a place on the road between Tiberias (7 miles) and Sepphoris (9 miles): R. Shim'on ben Lakish (c. 250-280) uses two men from Tiberias and Sepphoris meeting there as an illustration (Berakhot 9:5, 14d) and R. La (c. 280-310) uses litigants located there (Sanhedrin 3:1, 21a), apparently showing the place was inhabited in his day. Survey: a large village settled continuously from the Early Roman period (11-20 dunams) at least to the Early Islamic period, estimated 21-35 dunams from the Middle Roman period on and with abundant Byzantine pottery (65 Late Roman Red Ware vessels, 27% of the finds); cist tombs, columbaria, an oil press, a wall of dressed ashlars with a carved column base or capital, doorpost and architrave pieces - a monumental building, 'apparently a synagogue' (Leibner's inference; no synagogue remains were reported by earlier scholars). Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 280-284. Conventional year (c. 250-310). Dating basis: Jerusalem Talmud traditions + survey pottery. Confidence medium.

Khirbet Mashkana/Horvat Mishkena (Tur'an valley; Mashkanah of rabbinic literature, mentioned twice in the Jerusalem Talmud in the 3rd-4th c. per ESI 125): size category C (11-20 dunams) c. 50 BCE-150 CE and D (21-40 dunams) c. 150-650, occupied continuously through the Byzantine period (Leibner 2009); ashlars, a carved column base and doorpost fragments of a possible synagogue (Bornblum database); a hiding complex was documented in 2017 (ESI 134). Dating basis: survey pottery. Conventional year 400.

Khirbet Mashkana/Horvat Mishkena (near Golani Junction, Tur'an valley; rabbinic Mashkanah): ashlars including one carved column base or capital in relief, parts of a doorpost and of an architrave, surveyed by U. Leibner, suggest a Late Roman/Byzantine synagogue (unexcavated). Conventional year (3rd-7th c.). Dating basis: architectural fragments. Confidence low. Coordinates from the Bornblum DB page.

Horvat Mimla (Kh. Mamelia, survey site 24, 60 dunams; Arabic name preserves the ancient Mimla; Ottoman census Mamliya) is the rabbinic Mimla: Genesis Rabbah 59:1 (edited in the 5th c.) has R. Meir (active in Tiberias in the mid-2nd c.) visit Mimla and ask its people whether they descend from the priestly house of Eli; Klein used this as evidence that priests lived there. It appears in the list of priestly courses (17th course Hezir) in a fragment from Caesarea and in piyyutim of the courses. Survey: settled from the Hellenistic period without a break (Early Roman 7% of the pottery finds, Middle Roman 15.7%, Late Roman 22.6%). Coordinates computed from Leibner's grid reference 1917/2514 relative to Arbel (grid reference 1956/2467 and Wikipedia coordinates), accurate to about 0.5 km; no Wikipedia or Wikidata entry exists for the site. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 169-177. Conventional year (mid-2nd c. tradition set in the time of R. Meir; the source is much later). Dating basis: rabbinic tradition + survey pottery. Confidence medium-low.

A sage called R. Yosi of Mimla is attested: Lamentations Rabbah 1:37 has R. Yohanan and Resh Lakish attend his funeral (second generation of amoraim, c. 250-280), but a tradition with R. Yehoshua of Sakhnin (fourth generation) points to a later date, so Klein proposed two sages of this name, one in the 3rd and one in the 4th c.; Leibner does not decide. Survey: 'a monumental public building at the site' shown by architectural elements, a column-lined building and ashlars; Ilan thought it a synagogue on the southern slope. Mimla is therefore a Jewish village of the 3rd c. with a sage and probably a synagogue, but the synagogue date is unknown. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 172-177. Conventional year (c. 250-280). Dating basis: rabbinic traditions. Confidence medium-low.

Khirbet Mimla (Lower Galilee; = rabbinic Mimla/Mamli', identification reliable per Leibner Table 15): size category D (21-40 dunams) to 150 CE, E (41-60 dunams) c. 150-350, D c. 350-550, C c. 550-650 - occupied without a break through the Byzantine period; architectural elements of a monumental building (synagogue suspected by Ilan) and a rock-hewn burial cave with vaulted niches in the survey. Dating basis: survey pottery. Conventional year 400.

Leibner: Mimla is one of the survey sites occupied without interruption from the Hellenistic period to the Early Islamic period; the Byzantine sub-periods are 'richly represented' (Late Roman Red Ware 17% of the finds, 19 imported vessels in the Middle Byzantine period), although the settlement shrank to the western hilltop after the Late Roman period and in the fourth century; burial caves with niches and arcosolia, olive and wine presses. Piyyutim of the priestly courses by Haduta (late 6th/early 7th c.) and ha-Qallir place the course Hezir at Mimla, which Leibner takes as showing that the paytanim knew a still-settled village; the nature of the sources does not permit more than that. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 169-178, 411. Survey periods: Early Roman = mid-1st c. BCE-135 CE, Middle Roman 135-250, Late Roman 250-350, Early Byzantine 350-450, Middle Byzantine 450-550, Late Byzantine 550-650. Conventional year (Byzantine continuity). Dating basis: survey pottery. Confidence medium.

ATTRIBUTION UNCERTAIN (Jewish or Samaritan) - Carmel estate with a synagogue. Ḥorvat Raqit lies on a spur of Mount Carmel 5 km from 'Usfiyya (Isfiya); excavated 1996-2002 by Shimon Dar (Bar-Ilan Univ./Mount Carmel National Park): a large Roman-Byzantine estate (the 'estate of Marinus', after a Greek tomb inscription) with a synagogue 10.3 x 7.0 m 'incorporated into an earlier building complex in the second half of the third or beginning of the fourth century CE' (year 300 used), a polychrome mosaic with a medallion reading in Greek 'God, help. One is the only God' (a formula 'common among Jews and Samaritans'), benches seating about 80 people (a capacity, not a population), and a lintel with menorahs and conch niches. In the mid-5th century the hall was paved over and the estate was destroyed/abandoned, 'perhaps a result of persecution and discriminatory legislation against the Jewish and Samaritan communities'; settlement renewed in the first quarter of the 6th century, abandoned in the first half of the 7th. The Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine corpus labels the inscription Jewish (4th-5th c.) but its commentary says 'Building may be a Samaritan synagogue'; the Bornblum synagogue database lists it as Samaritan. Included because the attribution is genuinely disputed; the reviewer may drop it if only securely Jewish sites are wanted.

Wikipedia 'Horvat Rimon': a Jewish village 'occupied from the late Second Temple period into the early Islamic era' about 500 m south of Kibbutz Lahav, with a large synagogue complex built in three phases from the 3rd to the 7th century (first phase late 3rd c.), identified with En-Rimmon, 'a sizeable Jewish village' mentioned by Eusebius. The book lists Rimmon among the seven Jewish villages of the southern Hebron hills in Eusebius' day and mentions a large Jewish settlement of the 4th-6th centuries near Kibbutz Lahav. Coordinates from Hebrew Wikipedia (31.3736 N, 34.8663 E); the English infobox (31.4886 N) contradicts the article's own text. Year 300 = late 3rd c. Population blank. Book: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 039 (Screenshot_20221028-092952.jpg), img 049 (Screenshot_20221028-093637.jpg); page number not visible.

H. Simwai, Upper Galilee: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Architectural stones and ashler wall. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Founding phase: Wikipedia 'Horvat Sumaqa' (summarizing S. Dar's excavations 1983-1993/5) says the Jewish town was founded 'toward the end of the Early Roman period, as suggested by remains beneath the synagogue that predate its construction, including fragments of a Herodian lamp and terra sigillata'. Year 70 is the conventional end of the Early Roman period (an approximation). Site on Mount Carmel, about 350 m above sea level, no perennial spring (cisterns).

Wikipedia 'Horvat Sumaqa' (Mount Carmel): 'Sumaqa contains the remains of a Jewish town from the Roman and Byzantine periods'; founded toward the end of the Early Roman period, with main growth in the 3rd-4th centuries; the Phase I synagogue is dated to the 3rd century (the building's identification as a synagogue is disputed - east-west orientation, no bema or Torah niche - per A. L. Porter); excavated by Kohl & Watzinger (1905) and Shimon Dar (1983-1995). Year 250 = conventional 3rd century. Archaeological; synagogue identification contested.

Village at its height (3rd-4th/5th century): Wikipedia reports 'main phase of growth and prosperity in the 3rd-4th centuries CE'; a residential insula of about 25 x 35 m with most finds of the 3rd-5th centuries, a terracotta lamp with a seven-branched menorah, a rock-cut cellar possibly a mikveh, wine presses (four known; one with a 10,000-litre vat), an oil press (24 4th-century coins in its fill), workshops with grooved pillars, rock-cut tombs with seven-branched menorahs carved on their facades ('Cave of the Menorahs') and the 'Bull and Lion' tomb. Hebrew Wikipedia (Z. Amar) suggests tanning and dyeing workshops using sumac (the name Sumaqa may derive from it). Pig bones in the later phase may indicate a change of population in the Byzantine period. Year 350 is the midpoint of 3rd-5th century finds; the village's size (about 35 dunams) is the only demographic indicator given.

Wikipedia 'Horvat Sumaqa': the Phase I synagogue was 'apparently destroyed deliberately in the 4th or early 5th century'; coin finds show a break in occupation from the early 5th to the mid-6th century (possibly connected with Byzantine persecution of Jews or the Samaritan revolts, which also destroyed Husifah); the settlement was resettled in a smaller late-Byzantine phase and abandoned c. 650. Year 415 = conventional 'early 5th century'. Archaeological; cause uncertain.

Decline and occupation gap: 'the settlement declined sharply and appears to have been briefly abandoned' in the 5th century, 'possibly in connection with Byzantine persecution of Jews, or with the Byzantine suppression of the Samaritan revolts' which also destroyed the nearby Jewish settlement of Husifa (Isfiya); 'coin finds indicate a break in occupation from the early 5th to the mid-6th century' (Wikipedia 'Horvat Sumaqa'; the causes are the editors' suggestion, not established). Year 450 is a conventional midpoint of the 5th century. The Wikipedia 'Mount Carmel' article makes the same suggestion for the Carmel Jewish villages generally.

Decline and partial abandonment in the 5th c., possibly connected to Byzantine persecution or the Samaritan revolts (which also destroyed the nearby Jewish settlement of Husifa/Isfiya); coin finds show a break in occupation from the early 5th to the mid-6th c.; Phase II (5th-7th c.) a smaller rebuilt synagogue (about 10 x 15 m) with a menorah scratched on the facade; a hoard of six Byzantine coins, the latest of 618/619; abandoned again around the mid-7th c. Year 480 = midpoint of the early 5th-mid 6th c. gap.

Phase II (late Byzantine reuse, 5th-7th centuries per the source): the synagogue hall was narrowed, reused grooved pillars from the workshops repaired it, a small menorah was scratched on the facade (suggesting continued Jewish worship), and a hoard of six coins had a latest date of 618/619 CE (Heraclius). Occupation resumed after the coin gap (mid-6th century) and ended around the mid-7th century; a small Christian population may have lived there at one stage. Year 575 is an approximation for 'resettlement mid-6th century to 7th century'; row falls after the 550 cut-off and is included as the end of the sequence. Some tombs lack inscriptions and were looted.

Ruin (Arabic Khirbet Umm Tsboni, 300 x 300 m) below the Kokhav HaYarden plateau near Kibbutz Neve Or: in 1982 a Jewish tombstone with Hebrew text (read '... Yeshua ... son of Av ... rest in peace', restored 'Yeshua son of Abraham, rest in peace' on the pattern of other regional tombstones) was found beside the ruin, together with ashlars, a mezuzah stone and mosaic remains which may come from a synagogue of the Talmudic period (he.wikipedia, citing Schiller, Ariel 52). Undated beyond Roman-Byzantine/Talmudic; year 450 conventional; weak evidence.

Dating basis: survey pottery (Leibner 2009 Table 11), synagogue date unknown ('Late Roman and/or Byzantine'). Conventional year 400.

Rock-cut hiding-complex system (largest known in the Galilee) used in the first and second centuries, with pottery of the Kefar Hananya tradition; finds suggest preparation for unrest in the first half of the 2nd c. (Bar Kokhba period), though Galilean participation in the revolt is uncertain. The Roman-period village was large and Jewish (synagogue, absence of pig bones); Talmudic sources show it survived the revolt. Year 130 (revolt of 132-136).

Hiding complexes (largest in the Galilee, at least three rock-cut systems, two under the later synagogue) used intensively in the 1st-2nd c.: most finds attest use in the First Revolt (66-70), a few artifacts and the pottery (Kefar Hananya ware) show preparation for the Bar Kokhba revolt (c. 132-136); abandoned after its suppression. Dating basis: pottery, coin hoard (22 coins). Confidence medium-high. Whether Galileans actually fought in 132-136 is uncertain.

Huqoq is attested in Late Roman/Byzantine-period rabbinic sources (Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmud), which together with the archaeology show that the Jewish village survived the Bar Kokhba revolt; no pig bones; large prosperous village on a constant spring. Conventional year (Mishnaic/early Talmudic period). Dating basis: literary + archaeology. Confidence medium.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Hukok'): the Jerusalem Talmud (Sheviit 9:1, 38c) mentions a settlement 'Hikok' near Tiberias 'in the time of Resh Lakish' (Resh Lakish c. 200-c. 275, Wikipedia 'Resh Lakish'; 250 used), with the remains of an ancient synagogue; four rock-cut burial caves and two small tombs excavated in 1956 (Ravani) date from the second half of the 1st century and were reused in the 2nd-4th centuries. Wikipedia 'Huqoq': hiding complexes date to the First Jewish-Roman War and the Bar Kokhba revolt and the village is cited in both Talmuds. Identification of Yerushalmi Hikok with Huqoq is the EJ's ('may be identical'). Rabbinic-literary.

Leibner's survey (2009), Table 11: Huqoq settlement size category C (11-20 dunams) from c. 150 to 450 CE, B (4-10 dunams) 450-550 and A (0.5-3 dunams) 550-650. Regional context (50-site Eastern Galilee survey area, not Huqoq alone): estimated settled area 656-1,119 dunams in the Middle Roman period (10,496-39,165 people at 16-35 per dunam, average 23,062) falling to 239-423 dunams (3,824-14,805; average 8,606) in the second half of the 4th c. Occupied survey sites: 38 (200-250), 32 (250-300), 27 (300-350), 15 (350-400).

Monumental late Roman synagogue with biblical-scene mosaics, excavated 2011-23 (J. Magness). Radiocarbon dating (Mizzi, Schindler, Boaretto, Chazan, Magness; PLOS ONE) concludes it was built around the beginning of the 5th c. CE; bedding fill under the mosaic contains 2nd-3rd c. material, so the 14C samples give a terminus post quem and corroborate the ceramic dating. Year 400 = approximately 'beginning of the 5th c.'.

Monumental synagogue (c. 20 x 15-16 m) with elaborate mosaics (Samson, Noah's Ark, the Twelve Spies, Red Sea, Jonah, Tower of Babel, an Alexander-the-Great meeting scene with war elephants, Hebrew inscriptions). Year 425 = first half of the 5th c. Dating basis: pottery/coins. Confidence medium-high.

Archaeological (excavators' dating).

I'billin was an ancient Jewish settlement: ritual baths (mikva'ot) and hiding complexes used in the First Jewish-Roman War have been found; identified with the Jewish town Evlayim/Abelim of Talmudic sources. Conventional year (First Revolt, c. 66-70). Dating basis: archaeology. Confidence medium.

Rabbinic Jewish town Avlayim/Oblin (Abelim), whose name the Arab village Ibillin is thought to preserve (Hebrew Wikipedia, with the usual 'according to the suggestion' caveat; an alternative derivation is from a Crusader 'Bayt Ibelin'): the Tosefta names the fifth-generation tanna Rabbi Eleazar b. Judah 'of Avlin' (fifth generation tannaim, active c. 170-200, so 185 used), and records Rabbi Eliezer's visit 'to Oblin' to his pupil R. Yose b. Perida regarding eruvin law. Identification is by name similarity (conjectural). Cairo Genizah documents mention the Jewish community of Ibillin in the late 1st millennium. Literary evidence plus the stones below.
Evlayim/Abelim (I'billin) attested in Talmudic sources from the 3rd c. CE. Conventional year (3rd c.). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium.

Epigraphic/archaeological evidence for a synagogue or public building at Ibillin: Hebrew Wikipedia says stones with an engraved menorah and a stone with an ancient Aramaic inscription were found in the village; the Bornblum synagogue database lists Ibliin (Abelim) as an unexcavated Late Roman/Byzantine synagogue site, surveyed by Joseph Braslavy in 1934, main find an Aramaic dedicatory inscription from a public building (Naveh 1978: 42-44; CIIP V/1: 678-679), region Lower Galilee. The inscription is not precisely dated (year 400 is a conventional placement for 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'). Moderate confidence for a Jewish public building; no excavation.

Synagogue lintel with a Jewish Palestinian Aramaic dedication ('Remembered for good Baruch ... who supported and made this gate. Amen. Peace'), reused as a step on the street to the village church; dated 4th-6th c. (CIIP/Epidentity AD 301-600; year = midpoint); the synagogue itself is unexcavated. Dating basis: palaeography. Confidence medium.

Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550): walled town in the Early Bronze and Middle Bronze Ages (BiblePlaces.com summary of excavations at Khirbet Bal'ama; site ruins about 9 hectares - built-up area not stated). Canaanite. Population blank; no estimate found.
Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200): city appears in the list of Thutmose III (1490-1426 BCE) per Hebrew Wikipedia; Canaanite. Population blank; no estimate found.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000): walled town at end of Late Bronze / early Iron I (BiblePlaces.com); Joshua 17:11-12 says Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants and imposed tribute (Hebrew Wikipedia), so population mainly Canaanite; blank. Later 'possibly Iron II' per BiblePlaces; Hebrew Wikipedia says Israelite-period finds and a Levitical city in the monarchy and the Jehu episode (2 Kings 9:27), but no stratum dates given, so no Iron II row. No estimate found. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/יבלעם

Biblical mention (literary only; Year of Data -841 = conventional date of Jehu's coup). 2 Kgs 9:27: when Jehu's men shot Ahaziah of Judah in his chariot 'at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam', he fled to Megiddo and died there. Identification as in the previous row (Khirbet Belameh, disputed with Yubla). Existing rows of this marker already hold the Iron I archaeology; no population estimate. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua

Contested between Aram-Damascus and Israel; Population blank (no academic estimate; Israelite status unclear). Only limited excavation (1927 1933 1954 1957) and no settlement size given. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%93%D7%99%D7%91%D7%99%D7%9F_(%D7%9E%D7%A8%D7%92'_%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%95%D7%9F)

Iron Age IIB end / Assyrian conquest. Tiglath-Pileser III conquered Ijon about 733 BCE with deportations (English Wikipedia Tell Dibbine). Evidence is historical not stratigraphic. No population estimate found.

Iksal (Josephus' Xaloth): Roman and Byzantine remains incl. rock-cut tombs, glass vessels, a lion ring and a plastered winepress; Uzi Leibner is quoted by Wikipedia as saying Iksal is one of several villages in Galilee that had a Jewish population in the Roman period, joined later by Christians (the Galilee article lists it among villages predominantly Christian in the Byzantine period). Dating basis: survey/excavation finds; no synagogue attested. Year 300, conventional; low confidence.

Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Greek inscription, Ionic and Corinthian capital, decorated lintel, pedestals, monolithic pillar, marble chancle screen, large ashlar block. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Not firmly Jewish. Conventional year (3rd-7th c.). Dating basis: architectural fragments. Confidence low.

Weak-to-moderate row - rabbinic Jewish village. Hebrew Wikipedia (Iqrit, a Christian Arab village in the Western Galilee depopulated in 1948): 'in the Mishnaic and Talmudic period the Jewish settlement Yokrat was at this place, in which lived and worked the amora Rabbi Yose of Yokrat (Yose de-min Yokrat)'. No Jewish archaeological remains are reported in the sources read (the Hebrew Wikipedia article on the Western Galilee also states that Iqrit and Bar'am preserve the names of Mishnaic-period Yokrat and Bar'am). Low-moderate confidence.

Weak row - Roman-period burials at Isfiya (Husifa) on Mount Carmel. Epidentity (Univ. of Warsaw): 'ancient burials within the village and numismatic evidence attest to an early Jewish presence on Mount Carmel', including a hoard of 4,560 silver coins, the latest of 52-53 CE (pre-70; Temple-tax coinage, mostly Tyrian shekels and half-shekels per Hebrew Wikipedia; English Wikipedia's '4,500 gold coins' conflicts with this silver count). Wikipedia 'Isfiya' adds a Roman building of the 2nd-4th centuries (ceramics and coins) and a rock-cut burial cave on HaHoresh Street with pottery coffins, eight ossuaries and a Greek ossuary inscription naming Maia, daughter or wife of Saul - ossuary burial and the name Saul are consistent with Jewish burial but the sources do not state the ethnicity of the dead. Year 150 is a conventional placement for 'Roman period' (no excavation report consulted). Confidence low.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Usifiyya'): the village is linked to Husifah, mentioned in an ancient kinah (dirge) lamenting the destruction of its Jewish community; S. Klein dates that destruction to the 4th century CE, while Y. Press suggests it may relate to Heraclius' reconquest in the early 7th century (conflict). Year 350 follows Klein. Literary (liturgical poem) + identification; low-medium confidence.

Remains of the 5th-century Jewish town of Husifa/Huseifa (Mount Carmel) unearthed in 1930: a synagogue with a mosaic floor bearing Jewish symbols and the inscription 'Peace upon Israel' (Makhouly and Avi-Yonah per Bornblum database, with a zodiac fragment - Hachlili 1977 dates it to the 5th c.; Avi-Yonah classed it as 'Transitional type', 4th-5th c.). A rock-cut burial cave on HaHoresh Street with pottery coffins and eight ossuaries (one inscribed in Greek for 'Maia, daughter or wife of Saul') was also found (date not given in the article). Year 450 = 5th c.

Synagogue of the Jewish village of Husifa (Isfiya), Mount Carmel, excavated 1933 by Naim Makhouly and Michael Avi-Yonah (published 1934 as 'A sixth-century synagogue at 'Isfiya'). Basilical hall with a tripartite mosaic: a zodiac in the largest eastern field, a vine trellis with two birds in the middle, an Aramaic dedicatory inscription in the west panel ('...blessed be Halifo, the wife of Rabbi ...; let every one who promised and gave his donation be of good memory ... Josiah who gave ...') and a wreath enclosing a Hebrew inscription between two menorahs reading 'Peace upon Israel' (Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine isfi0001, isfi0002). Dating: IIP gives mid-5th to early 6th century (425-550, midpoint 488 used here) for the dedicatory mosaic and 5th-6th c. for the 'Peace upon Israel' panel; Avi-Yonah and Makhouly argued for the 6th century; Wikipedia calls Husifa a '5th-century Jewish town'. Epidentity: the synagogue appears to have been destroyed during Justinian's measures against the Jews (an alternative suggestion links the 5th-century Carmel disruptions to the Samaritan revolts); the village is remembered in a Hebrew elegy (piyyut) from the Cairo Genizah on destroyed Jewish villages, Hebrew Wikipedia places the destruction 'probably at the end of the Byzantine period'. Dating basis: mosaic style, inscriptions, no coin or stratigraphic date reported in the sources read.

Mount Carmel synagogue: Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Usifiyya') - remains of a '5th- or 6th-century synagogue' with a mosaic floor showing a seven-branched menorah, etrogim, lulav, shofar, vine and birds and the inscription 'Shalom al Yisrael'; Wikipedia 'Isfiya': in 1930 remains of a '5th-century Jewish town, Husifah', were unearthed (its bibliography cites 'A sixth-century synagogue at Isfiya'); a 2nd-4th-century building was also excavated. Midpoint 500 used. Archaeological; excavators' dating.

[Second-pass revision] adds excavations. Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): called Iamnia, first part of Idumea then of the Paralia (NEAEHL); the name may be Ptolemaic; a 2nd c. [Second-pass revision] dates and archaeology. Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Seleucid-held base repeatedly attacked: Gorgias 165 BCE (1 Macc 4:15), battle of 163 BCE with 2,000 Jewish casualties, Apollonius 147 BCE, Cendebaeus 139-137 BCE (Varga and Betzer 2025); Judas burned the harbour (2 Macc 12:8-9; NEAEHL; Jewish Encyclopedia). Capture dated differently: Simon in 137 BCE or Hyrcanus 135-104 BCE (NEAEHL), Hyrcanus in 122 BCE (Varga and Betzer), Simon (Josephus Ant. 13 on Wikisource); Jewish possession became firm only under Alexander Jannaeus (Jewish Encyclopedia, NEAEHL, Hebrew Wikipedia). Josephus Ant. 13.15.4 lists 'Jamhis' among Jannaeus' coastal cities (probably Jamnia; Wikisource). A pit in Area H held Hellenistic pottery and a lead sling bullet reading 'victory of Heracles and Hauronas', the pagan patron gods (Varga and Betzer; HA-ESI Area H). No miqveh, chalk vessel or Hasmonean coin attested in Hasmonean layers in the fetched reports; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] adds archaeology and sources. Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Pompey freed it, Gabinius rebuilt it c. 57 BCE, Augustus gave it to Herod, who left it to Salome (BJ 2.6.3, Wikisource; Jewish Encyclopedia), then Livia and Tiberius (NEAEHL). Jewish majority: Philo, Legatio 30, says the inhabitants were mostly Jews (Jewish Encyclopedia); NEAEHL cites the altar Herennius Capito set up to provoke the Jewish majority; Hebrew Wikipedia: mixed city, mostly Jewish. Excavation: HA-ESI Area H shows an Early Roman wall, floor and refuse pits, one with a chalk-stone measuring-cup handle, and no miqveh; the large building there is Middle Roman (1st-3rd c.). IAA Yavne-East press release: industrial building (1st-3rd c.) with chalk-stone measuring cups and a cemetery of spaced tombs (late 1st-2nd c.), the excavators saying it is too early to tell whether the dead were Jewish or pagan. The Early Roman harbour site Yavneh-Yam (separate site) was probably predominantly Jewish (Liber Annuus 70, 2020 abstract). Strabo: the city with its villages could field 40,000 men (Jewish Encyclopedia): a military figure, not a population. Population blank: no named-scholar Jewish population estimate found.

Jamnith/Iamnia of Upper Galilee (to be distinguished from Jamnia/Yavne in Judaea), a fortified hilltop town on Har Yavnit, 3.4 km NE of Safed (Kh. Banit; now under a military installation). Josephus lists it among the Upper Galilean places he fortified (War 2.20.6 'Jamnith'; Life 37/188 'Jamnia, Meroth and Achabare') and says he helped build its wall; cisterns on the site; the fate of its defenders is unknown (presumably surrendered after Tarichaeae fell). Identification with Kh. Banit is the leading but not certain proposal. Dating basis: literary (Josephus). Confidence medium. NB Wikipedia's coordinates for Jamnith practically coincide with those for Nabratein (a different site in the same Biriya forest area, c. 100 m on the map).

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63). Netzer (NEAEHL, Jericho) dates the pillared hall to the end of Alexander Jannaeus's reign, probably phase 2 under Salome Alexandra (76-67 BCE): hall about 16.5 x 11.5 m, 12 pillars, benches for about 140 (deadseaquake.info says about 150), with a mikveh (immersion pool plus otzar) fed from the Na'aran conduit, and more mikva'ot in the workshop area. Palaces and pools begin with Hyrcanus I or Jannaeus. Complex destroyed probably in the 31 BCE earthquake or shortly after. The synagogue identification is disputed (Stacey: estate administrative hall of c. 75 BCE serving a very limited part of the community). Residents were estate officials and staff; the site is part of a Jewish-occupied Jericho throughout the Second Temple period. Hebrew Wikipedia adds a western-hills cemetery of c. 100 BCE-68 CE with Jewish ossuaries bearing Hebrew inscriptions (Hachlili and Killebrew, IAA Reports 7, 1999). Arensburg and Smith (PEQ 115, 1983, appendix 'The Jewish Population of Jericho 100 BC-70 AD') is a named population study but its figure could not be read in any fetched page, so Population is blank. Seats are capacity, not population.

Palace burned by Simon after Herod's death (Wars 2.4) and rebuilt by Archelaus; Cypros destroyed by rebels 66-67; Vespasian found Jericho desolate in 68 (Wars 4.8; biblewalks.com). comment: Event: Persecution of Judaism under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Wikipedia also quotes 2 Maccabees 5:11-14 for the earlier sack (traditional claim: 80,000 lost, 40,000 killed and as many sold into slavery) - casualty claims, not a population. The attached book (Shpak-Lissak, ch. 1, img012) adds that the decrees were imposed on the Jews in all parts of the Land of Israel, with executions (the story of Hannah and her seven sons) and sale into slavery, and that Jerusalem had been turned into a Hellenistic polis, Antiochia, in 175 BCE. Year of Data 167 = the year of the decrees. [confidence: high] [Source detail: (Wikipedia, section 'Persecution of the Jews and the Maccabean revolt')]

Framing row (pre-70): Josephus (War 2.18.9, Whiston 'Zabulon', Loeb 'Chabulon' 2.503): Cestius Gallus marched to the strong city of Chabulon in Galilee, 'which divides the country of Ptolemais from our nation', found it deserted by its men, who had fled to the mountains, and let the soldiers plunder and burn it, 'although it was of admirable beauty, and had its houses built like those in Tyre, and Sidon, and Berytus'. Josephus used the village as headquarters in 67 (Vita 43 - 'Chabolo ... in the confines of Ptolemais'). Shows a Jewish Galilean town on the Ptolemais border; the site is the modern Arab town Kabul, 14 km east of Acre.

Framing row: Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Cabul') - Cabul ('Chabolo') was attacked by Cestius Gallus in 66 (Josephus, War 2:503) and served as Josephus' headquarters in Galilee in 67 (Life 213, 227, 234); in the Second Temple period it was a border city between Galilee and Ptolemais-Acre. Pre-70 context for the post-70 priestly settlement.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Cabul'): after Jerusalem fell in 70 'priests of the Shecaniah family settled in Cabul'; Cabul was also Josephus' Galilee headquarters in 67 (Life 213, 227, 234) and attacked by Cestius Gallus in 66 (War 2:503). Wikipedia 'Kabul, Israel': 'excavated burial chambers, used from the 1st to the 4th centuries'; Hellenistic-Early Roman, Roman and Byzantine pottery found in the village; a family of kohanim (Shecaniah) lived there. Gamaliel III (patriarch 220-230), visited Kabul and were received with great honour and a visit to the local bath; Kabul was the seat of R. Zakkai (JT Megillah 4, 78b), noted for wine and oil, and had a synagogue and public baths (Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Cabul'). Year 240 = conventional (sons of a patriarch of 220-230). Rabbinic evidence of a Jewish village: the youths Judah (II Nesiah) and his brother Hillel, sons of Gamaliel III, 'were received as guests in Cabul with great honor and paid a visit to a local bath' (Tosefta Shabbat 7:17 and Tosefta Mo'ed Katan 2:15, as cited by Wikipedia 'Cabul'); Wikipedia 'Judah II' adds that, as youths, Judah and Hillel visited Cabul and Biri 'each time behaving in ways which offended the local population'. A rabbi named Zakkai of Cabul appears in Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4, 78b. Judah II lived in Tiberias in the middle of the 3rd century (year 250). Identification: the Cabul of the rabbis is identified with modern Kabul; Josephus' Chabolo. Literary dating, moderate confidence for the date (the visit anecdote is told of youths, in the mid-3rd century).

comment: Population: Z. Weiss, as quoted by Shpak-Lissak, estimates the Galilean village of Kafr Kanna at about 500 inhabitants in the first century CE; the book lists it among the excavated sites for the eve of the Great Revolt, so Year of Data 66 is the book's frame, not a dated census. Presence: English Wikipedia says Kafr Kanna was a Jewish village during the first century CE, mentioned by Josephus in his Life; Hebrew Wikipedia adds that Josephus lived there and fortified it as governor of the Galilee in the Great Revolt. No online source found for the figure 500; the figure comes from the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew), which names Weiss but not the publication. The map's rows for Kafr Kanna start in 150 CE. [confidence: medium for presence, low for the figure] [Source detail: (Wikipedia: Jewish village in the first century CE; presence only); (Hebrew Wikipedia; presence only)]

Wikipedia 'Kafr Kanna': the village was Jewish in the 1st century and Josephus mentions it; a burial cave with ossuaries was used 'in the years following the Bar Kokhba revolt' (conventional year 150); a 2nd-century discus lamp bears the potter Iason's signature. Wikipedia 'Priestly courses' lists Kafr Kana as residence of the 11th course, Eliashib (baraita; 'some identifications are uncertain'). Archaeological; Kafr Kanna's identification with Cana of Galilee is traditional (Garis is an alternative).

Tradition places the tomb of Rabbi Simeon ben Gamaliel II (nasi/head of the Sanhedrin in the Galilee in the 2nd c.) in one of the Roman rock-cut burial caves on the outskirts of Kafr Kanna; the caves show the area was a Roman-period burial ground. Wikipedia dates this Simeon ben Gamaliel to 50 CE (conflict). Conventional year (mid-2nd c.). Dating basis: pilgrimage tradition + Roman caves. Confidence low (tradition only; the Jewish village of Karm er-Ras has Roman-period pottery including Kefar Hananya and Shikhin wares).

Karm er-Ras (Kafr Kanna), IAA excavation (Y. Alexandre, ESI 120): a Roman house with several rooms and a large stepped ritual bath (miqwe) in a Jewish village; the miqwe went out of use at some stage in the Middle Roman period (135-250) and was deliberately filled with stones from its collapsed ceiling. Kafr Kanna Roman-period burial caves with Jewish characteristics (ossuaries, Herodian lamps) are also recorded (ESI 127). Dating basis: pottery and stratigraphy. Year 190 = midpoint of the Middle Roman period.

Burial cave with carved limestone ossuaries found in May 2023 on a private lot near Kafr Kanna (Mashhad), reported by the IAA Theft Prevention Unit: Eitan Klein says the carved ossuaries indicate Jewish settlement in the area in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, when Jews moved to the Galilee after the Bar Kokhba revolt and brought the ossuary custom; lids with Greek-influenced wreaths, glass vessels and beads. Dating basis: typology of the ossuaries (not a stratigraphic excavation), press headline 'about 1,800 years old'. Year 200 = 2nd/3rd c. Note: Kafr Kanna is one candidate for NT Cana (Khirbet Qana is the other).

Excavation beneath the Franciscan church (Loffreda 1969, Alliata 1997 per the Bornblum database, which lists a synagogue here) uncovered mosaic floor panels with Aramaic donor inscriptions in the square Jewish script ('Yose son of Tanhum son of Botah' and his sons; another may mention Yeshu'a). The tomb of Rabbi Simeon ben Gamliel on the outskirts is a Jewish pilgrimage site. Date of the mosaic not given by Wikipedia; Bornblum period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Conventional year 400, low confidence.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Kefar Kanna'): the village church 'stands on the ruins of a Byzantine synagogue' whose mosaic pavement bears an inscription naming 'Yose, the son of Tanhum, and his sons'; Wikipedia 'Kafr Kanna' confirms mosaic panels naming Yose son of Tanhum son of Botah (undated) and a 5th-century Latin burial inscription (Legio X Fretensis) and a 5th-7th-century Aramaic amulet. Year 450 = conventional 'Byzantine period' (no date in the EJ entry). Archaeological/epigraphic; dating approximate.

A Byzantine-period synagogue stood in the old village nucleus under the present Franciscan Wedding Church: the mosaic floor bears Aramaic donor inscriptions, one commemorating Yose son of Tanhum son of Buta who with his sons made the pavement (EJ; JPA inscription dated AD 301-700, a second fragment AD 401-600 per CIIP/Epidentity; year = midpoint). Identification: Kafr Kanna is the traditional (not the archaeological) Cana of the Gospels. Dating basis: epigraphy. Confidence medium-high for a Byzantine synagogue, wide date range.

Jewish magic amulet from Kafr Kanna: a metal charm with 41 lines of Aramaic in Jewish script against fevers (Abraxas, Sabaoth), dated 5th-7th c.; a Latin burial inscription of the 5th c. mentioning Legio X Fretensis from Karm er-Ras shows Roman soldiers at the village edge. Midpoint of the 5th-7th c. range is the 6th c., year 550.

A Spanish Franciscan monk who visited in 1553-1555 found families of Spanish exiles settled there. The Jewish village emptied in the 17th century because of murder and robbery by Bedouin tribes and the Ottoman taxation of non-Muslims (Hebrew Wikipedia: the Jewish community ended in the 17th century). Population = 77 x 5. Confidence: high for 77 households.

Kafr Manda is identified with Kefar Mandi/Mandi, a Jewish village of Talmudic and Midrashic literature (Tosefta Yevamot 13); an amora, Issachar of Kefar Mandi, studied Torah at Sepphoris; Roman and Byzantine remains (architectural fragments, columns) were reported, and a 2014/2016 ESI excavation found a plastered rock-cut basin possibly a ritual bath (miqwe) plus Roman pottery; medieval tradition places graves of three Mishnaic sages here. Conventional year (3rd c., amoraic period). Dating basis: literary + pottery. Confidence low-medium.

Kafr Manda is identified with Kfar Mandi, a Jewish village in Talmudic and midrashic literature (the amora Issachar of Kfar Mandi studied Torah in Sepphoris); Roman and Byzantine remains incl. architectural fragments, columns and capitals (Wikipedia). ESI 2016 trial excavation found a rock-hewn cave with Roman pottery, a burial-cave door fragment and a possible open miqwe, but the finds are mostly Mamluk (undated installations). Literary identification; weak row. Year 300 = conventional.

source: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך היגרו הערבים והמוסלמים לארץ ישראל מהכיבוש הערבי עד מלחמת העולם הראשונה (640-1914) (Yedioth Ahronoth / Sifrei Hemed), ch. 1, section D.2 (Jews), 'Jewish population centres - the Galilee', img 082 (Screenshot_20221028-100147.jpg); e-reader page number not visible in the screenshots
comment: Geniza-period Jewish village (10th-11th centuries; Year of Data 900 = start of the range, the convention of the map's existing Geniza-village rows). Shpak-Lissak lists Kafr Manda (Kefar Mandi) among the Galilean villages mentioned in the Cairo Geniza in the 10th-11th centuries as places where Jews lived (after Moshe Gil's study of the Geniza); she adds that most of these were Jewish villages and some had a mixed population, and that the list is not complete because it was gathered from letters. She adds that Geniza letters name refugees in Egypt who came from Kafr Mandi, Ibelin, Amuqa and other places, in the context of the insecurity and decline of the 11th century. No online page found that states this for Kafr Manda (Kefar Mandi) (English and Hebrew Wikipedia and the Encyclopaedia Judaica pages were checked). Population blank (the book gives no count). Confidence medium (scholarly book, no contradicting map row).

Wikipedia 'Kafr Misr' (about 3 km SE of Mount Tabor): a synagogue 'thought to have been built' in the 3rd century (Stemberger 2000; Alexandre 2008), 'evidence for the existence of a Jewish community inhabiting Kafr Misr then'; a Hebrew mosaic inscription around the bema names Abraham and Isaac. 3rd century = conventional 250. Archaeological; the article cites 1948-1987 excavations.

Synagogue at Kafr Misr (Mt Tabor, excavated J. Buchman/J. Porat 1984, A. Onn 1985): Phase I, 3rd c. to the end of the 4th c., a 13.5 x 17.5 m rectangular hall with eight square column bases, benches on all four walls and a flagstone/plaster floor (sherds from as early as the 1st c.); ESI (2008, 2017) dates the synagogue 3rd-early 7th c. and speaks of a Jewish community with a synagogue at Kafr Misr in the Roman and Byzantine periods. Year = conventional 3rd-4th c. Dating basis: stratigraphy/pottery. Confidence medium.

Wikipedia 'Kafr Misr': in the 4th century, after earthquake damage, the synagogue was renovated; a Torah niche was added and later replaced by an apse, 'which suggests the building was converted into a church'. Conventional 4th-century year 350; interpretation of the apse is the article's. Archaeological.

Phase II (4th-early 5th c.) of the Kafr Misr synagogue: a permanent Torah-ark installation, possibly screened by a curtain, and a mosaic floor replacing the plaster one (Wikipedia: the renovation followed earthquake damage in the 4th c.). Dating basis: stratigraphy. Confidence medium.

Phase III (5th to the early 7th c.) of the Kafr Misr synagogue: limestone apse (2.8 m), new western door, new mosaic in the central hall and a panel of floral ornament, Jewish symbols (menorahs) and an inscription fragment near the bema (Aramaic per Epidentity; CIIP/Bornblum list it as Hebrew). Conflicting reading: Wikipedia, following the excavator's earlier reports, says the Torah niche was later replaced by an apse suggesting conversion into a church; Epidentity (CIIP) keeps the building Jewish to the early 7th c. Year = midpoint of the 5th to early 7th c. Dating basis: stratigraphy/epigraphy. Confidence medium.

Synagogue with impressive mosaic floors at the ancient centre of Kafr Misr (Lower Galilee, near Mount Tabor): ESI 2017 reports remains of a synagogue 'dating to the third-early seventh centuries CE' revealed in the 1980s and a Byzantine-period synagogue located north of the trial area; ESI 2006 calls it 'an ancient synagogue from the time of the Mishnah and Talmud'. Bornblum database: excavated 1984-85 (J. Buchman, J. Porat, A. Onn); columns, benches, mosaic with menorahs, ritual objects and inscriptions. Dating basis: stratigraphy and ceramics over a long period; centre of 3rd-7th c. is about 450 (conventional).

Jewish burial cave of the Mishnaic-Talmudic period at Kefar Yasif: Hebrew Wikipedia (Kefar Yasif, ancient settlement) says that in 1902 a Jewish burial cave was found in the village; the stone door of the cave (78 x 62 cm, now in the Louvre) is 'dated to the second and third centuries' and is decorated with a seven-branched menorah and the opening of a Torah ark (year 200 = the 2nd-3rd century range). Conflict: the Louvre/Warburg Institute Eranos Archive catalogue dates the same door 300-500 (see the 400 row). The article calls the place a Jewish settlement in the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods (Roman, Byzantine and Crusader remains, mostly destroyed or buried) and adds a Greek votive inscription to the pagan gods Hadad and Atargatis and a 5th-century Greek mosaic inscription near the village (so the village was mixed/pagan-Christian too). Dating of the door is by style/iconography only (a chance find, no excavation); Jewish identification by the menorah and Torah-shrine. Moderate confidence; source cites U. Kohane's 1986 study on the Jewish settlement and cemetery of Kefar Yasif.

Jewish antiquities at Kafr Yasif (Western Galilee, 10 km NE of Acre): (1) a limestone lintel from a synagogue, now a UN gift (UNNY223G), with a high-relief menorah, a lulav within a circle and a shofar, dated 'Late Roman-early Byzantine, about 4th to 5th century CE' (United Nations Gifts page UNNY223G, an Israeli government gift of 1999, which gives no excavation context; the Jewish Virtual Library/Encyclopaedia Judaica describes a stone tablet with a candelabrum, shofar and lulav affixed over the door of a village house, evidently the same or a similar piece, so the lintel is a re-used stray find and the synagogue is inferred, not excavated); (2) a stone door of a burial cave with relief of a candelabrum and an ark, in the Louvre, which the Jewish Virtual Library (Encyclopaedia Judaica) cites as proof of 'the Jewish antiquity of the locality' and the Warburg Institute's Eranos Archive catalogues as 'Jewish, 300-500'. Year 400 = midpoint of 300-500/4th-5th c. Dating basis: iconography and style (no excavation context). Also: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Acre) says Acre's Jews were buried at the foot of Mt Carmel in antiquity and later (18th-20th c.) at Kefar Yasif; Hebrew Wikipedia says Roman-Byzantine-Crusader Jewish settlement remains are mostly destroyed or buried (unsourced); a village tradition (F. M. Abel) that Josephus fortified Kafr Yasif and named it after himself is legend.

Horvat Kanaf (ancient Jewish village at the foot of the modern moshav; unrelated to Deir Aziz 2 km SE). Dating conflict, first reading: the 2018 excavations by O. Zingboym are published under the title 'Horbat Kanaf - New Excavations of the Synagogue Dating to the Third-Fourth Centuries CE' (New Studies in the Archaeology of Northern Israel, IAA 2021; title only seen, via the Bornblum bibliography); BibleWalks likewise calls it a '3rd century' Late Roman synagogue. Second reading (6th c.) in the next row. Year 330 = midpoint of 3rd-4th c.; confidence low-medium (full text not read).

Golan synagogue site at Kanaf: Bornblum database records an excavated synagogue (Z. Ma'oz 1978-81 and 1985; O. Zingboym 2018) with columns, ornamental architecture incl. portal fragments, and inscriptions; period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Wikipedia's article on Kanaf describes a Byzantine-era synagogue near the Kanaf River (eight pillars, basalt floor, hundreds of Byzantine coins under the floor) but its text duplicates the Deir Aziz synagogue description, so it is not used for dating. Conventional year 500 (Golan synagogues are mostly 5th-6th c. per Ma'oz, as quoted by Magness), low confidence.

Synagogue of Horvat Kanaf dated to the early 6th c. on the evidence of finds, per he.wikipedia (13 x 16 m, basalt ashlar, faces west) and Dan the Digger (about 1,000 coins under the floor; Z. Ma'oz excavated 1978-81 and 1985, final report 2015). Aramaic dedication on the doorframe lintel: 'remembered for good Yose son of Halfu son of Honyo, who made this lintel' (IIP HKAN0001, dated 324-638); first recorded by L. Oliphant, published by E. Sukenik in the early 1930s. Two copper healing amulets found nearby name 'the daughter of Marin' and 'Elazar son of Esther' (Dan the Digger). Dating conflict with the 3rd-4th c. reading above unresolved. Confidence medium.

Biblical mention and identification (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -1200 = conventional date of the Joshua conquest/allotment narrative (the allotment lists themselves are of disputed date)). Identification: Tel Kedesh (Tell Qades / Qadas), 3 km NE of Kibbutz Malkiya, 33.1116 N 35.5295 E, disputed, favoured: Tel Kedesh in Upper Galilee (Wikipedia: 'many hold'); Aharoni placed Kedesh-Naphtali at Khirbet Qadish in Lower Galilee and the Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities marks the choice with '?' (Tell Qadas, Khirbet el-Kidish; some passages may refer to Tell Abu Qudeis). Josh 12:22 (king of Kedesh among the defeated); Josh 19:37 (Kedesh a fortified city of Naphtali); Josh 20:7 (Kedesh in Galilee, in mount Naphtali, set apart as a city of refuge); Josh 21:32 and 1 Chr 6:76 (Levitical city of the Gershonites). Archaeology: BibleWalks mentions a glacis wall protecting the 'Canaanite/Israelite city' on a mound of 20-25 acres; the 1997-2012 excavations found mainly Persian and Hellenistic buildings, and an 'important Israelite centre in Iron Age II' is only cited in a footnote of Wikipedia. No population estimate; the existing rows of this marker do not cover the Iron Age. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/upper_galilee_gallery/kedeshbiblicalCity ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+20&version=KJV

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63). Latest dated Rhodian wine jars are 144 or 143 BCE; the building was abandoned in haste with many objects left behind (Archaeology 2012). Herbert and Berlin tie this to the Hasmonean victory of Jonathan over Demetrius II in the Hazor plain and the pursuit to Kedesh (1 Macc 11:63-74; Aviam 2013, citing Herbert and Berlin BASOR 329, 2003); this is an interpretation, the excavators' earlier report could not link the vessels to a specific event. NEAEHL: building later burned and the area reoccupied in the last third of the 2nd c. BCE with imported tableware, residential use ending early in the 1st c. BCE. No evidence that the occupants were Jews (no miqveh, stone vessels or Hasmonean coins reported from the tell in fetched pages). Nearby, the Hellenistic fortress at Qeren Naftali 2 km east had a miqveh inserted and Hasmonean coins, which Aviam reads as evidence for the later Hasmonean conquest of the area (not Kedesh itself). Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). NEAEHL states there is no evidence of Roman-period occupation in the excavated area of the southern mound, even though the Roman temple (built c. 117 CE; flourishing 2nd-3rd c. CE per Dead Sea Quake catalog) stood nearby; Josephus names the village Kedesh/Cydessa 'of the Tyrians' in the revolt of 66 CE (deadseaquake.info; BibleWalks), a Tyrian and pagan neighbour hostile to Galilean Jews. So the first-pass wording that the settlement simply moved to the eastern mound is not confirmed by an excavation report; the first-century village is textual. Tyrian population, no Jewish evidence. Population blank.

comment: Geniza-period Jewish village (10th-11th centuries; Year of Data 900 = start of the range, the convention of the map's existing Geniza-village rows). Shpak-Lissak lists Kedesh Naftali among the Galilean villages mentioned in the Cairo Geniza in the 10th-11th centuries as places where Jews lived (after Moshe Gil's study of the Geniza); she adds that most of these were Jewish villages and some had a mixed population, and that the list is not complete because it was gathered from letters. She also cites the 10th-century geographer al-Muqaddasi that Gush Halav and Kedesh Naftali each had a large Jewish settlement. Later (c.1170) Benjamin of Tudela says no Jews lived at Kedesh (Adler translation), so the 10th-11th century presence did not last. No online page found that states this for Kedesh Naftali (English and Hebrew Wikipedia and the Encyclopaedia Judaica pages were checked). Population blank (the book gives no count). Confidence medium (scholarly book, no contradicting map row).
