Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). Ancient Kefar Hananya = Khirbet Kafr 'Inan; NEAEHL (Adan-Bayewitz 1986-89 excavations): settlement founded in the Early Roman period; a Tyrian coin of 41-42 CE under a clay-tank floor. Kfar Hananya ware (Levantine Ceramics Project) produced from the mid-1st c. BCE (so the pottery start may fall at the end of Hasmonean or start of this period) to mid-5th c. CE; supplied most Galilean kitchen pottery. Mishnah (Shevi'it 9:2) uses Kfar Hananya as the Upper/Lower Galilee boundary (Mishnah is later than this period). Jewish village per BibleWalks and Wikipedia; nearby Bersabe (Khirbet Abu esh-Sheba <1 km) fortified by Josephus in 66-67 CE and BibleWalks/Eshchar say the population moved down to Kfar Hananya after 67 CE. Rock-cut synagogue with ritual bath is Byzantine (5th c.) not of this period. No published Jewish population estimate found; Population left blank.

Bersabe (Beersheba of Galilee, Khirbet es-Saba/Abu esh-Shebaa), a Jewish village less than 1 km from Kefar Hananya on the Upper/Lower Galilee boundary, fortified by Josephus in the First Revolt as one of the most defensible places and a refuge for insurgents from across the Galilee; survey: c. 70 dunams, wall 2.8 m thick with three semi-circular towers. Dating basis: Josephus + survey. Confidence medium-high. Framing row.

Boundary village between Upper and Lower Galilee (Mishnah Shevi'it 9:2) and a famous pottery-production centre; R. Halafta of Kefar Hananya (2nd century CE) is quoted several times in tannaitic texts; Tosefta Bava Metzia 6:3 mentions 'those who make black clay, such as Kefar Hananya and its neighbours'. Rabbinic sources of the 1st/2nd-4th centuries call it a well-known pottery centre. Identified with Kafr 'Inan (Kh. Kafr 'Anan) on geographic, archaeometric and phonetic grounds. Dating basis: literary plus pottery studies (Adan-Bayewitz). Confidence high. Conventional year 150.

Mishnah Sheviit 9:2: 'From Kefar Hananiah upwards, the region where sycamores do not grow, is Upper Galilee. From Kefar Hananiah downwards, where the sycamores do grow, is Lower Galilee' (Sefaria text). The Mishnah was redacted by Judah ha-Nasi c. 200-220 (Wikipedia 'Mishnah': late 2nd-early 3rd century; 200 used). Identification: Talmudic Kefar Hananiah = Kafr 'Inan (Encyclopaedia Judaica), about 6 miles SW of Safed. Rabbinic-literary, early (tannaitic) evidence of a Jewish village; high confidence for existence, location approximate.

Ancient Kfar Hananya was a Jewish village in the Roman and Byzantine periods, on the border between Lower and Upper Galilee (Mishnah Shevi'it 9:2) and the leading pottery centre of Roman Galilee: Kfar Hananya ware was produced from the mid-1st c. BCE to the mid-5th c. CE and supplied most Galilean cooking ware; excavations revealed column shafts and bases, caves, a pool and a burial ground; ruins lie about 1 km north of the modern village. Year 200 = conventional centre of the period.

EJ: R. Abba Halafta (Tanna, 2nd-3rd c.) lived at Kefar Hananyah (Bava Metzia 94a); its potters' vessels are mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud (Pe'ah 7:4) and Lam. Zuta; hawkers lived there; remains of an ancient synagogue and tomb caves of Talmudic times have been found. Conventional year (c. 3rd c.). Dating basis: literary + archaeology. Confidence medium-high.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Kefar Hananyah'): 'a village of potters' using black soil (Tosefta BM 6:3) or white soil (BM 74a); special vessel forms from its workshops are mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud (Pe'ah 7:4) and Lamentations Zuta 1:5; hawkers living there visited four or five villages (JT Ma'as. 2:3); R. Abba Halafta lived there (BT BM 94a); remains of an ancient synagogue and talmudic-era tomb caves have been found (no dates). Year 250 = conventional 'talmudic period'. Rabbinic-literary and archaeological, dating approximate.

Pottery industry: most cooking ware in the Galilee between the 1st century BCE and the beginning of the 5th century CE was produced here; Late Roman kiln with a stone-paved approach excavated in 1992-93 by D. Adan-Bayewitz; olive-oil installations (Frankel). Founded in the Early Roman period and inhabited into the Byzantine period. Dating basis: pottery, archaeometry. Confidence high. No population figure. Conventional year 300 (Late Roman peak).

Leibner (2009), Table 11: Kefar Hananya settlement size D (21-40 dunams) 50 BCE-150 CE, E (41-60 dunams) c. 150-450, C (11-20) 450-550, B (4-10) 550-650; occupied continuously. Bornblum database (unexcavated synagogue site): walls of a public building and architectural elements; a bronze lamp with an inscription may come from the synagogue (Ilan 1991). Year 300 = conventional centre of the E-size phase.

Wikipedia 'Shikhin': in the mid-fourth century wares from Shikhin and Kefar Hananya (the two Galilean pottery centres) 'suffer a pronounced decline', suggesting an economic break around 350; Wikipedia 'Shikhin' also says Shikhin was abandoned in the 4th century. Archaeological (pottery distribution); interpretation only.

Wikipedia 'Kfar Hananya': the village was a Jewish village 'under Roman and Byzantine rule' and a centre of pottery production in Galilee; 'Kfar Hananya ware' was made from the mid-1st century BCE to the mid-5th century CE (end year 450 used) - the Babylonian Talmud has Rabbi Jose ben Halafta praising its vessels as 'not likely to burst'; a tomb is attributed to Rabbi Hananya ben Akashya (a traditional attribution). Biblewalks adds that the Jewish village existed 1st-7th century. Archaeological (pottery distribution); end date of the industry, not of the village.

Rock-cut synagogue east of the village (carved out of the rock, probably in the 5th century CE per Wikipedia; identified by Braslavsky 1933, surveyed by Ilan 1989; the 12th-c. traveller Jacob b. Nathanael saw a synagogue 'quarried from the hill with only one built wall'); a bronze polycandelon with an Aramaic dedication 'to the holy place of Kefar Hananya' (5th or 6th c., found at el-Makr near Acre). Dating basis: architecture/epigraphy; conventional year 450. Confidence low-medium.

Bronze polycandelon (now in the Mariemont museum, Belgium) with a Jewish Palestinian Aramaic dedication 'to the holy place of Kefar Hananyah. May they be remembered for good. Amen, selah, shalom', decorated with two menorahs, lulavim and shofar: the only synagogue dedicatory inscription in Aramaic/Hebrew naming a place. Found in Kefar Misr but attributed to Kefar Hananya. Dated AD 400-600 (CIIP/Epidentity; Wikipedia 5th or 6th c.); year = midpoint. Dating basis: epigraphy. Confidence medium-high.

Ancient Jewish village Kefar Yahrib (Kefar Harub), identified with Arabic Kafr Harib, now Kibbutz Kefar Haruv (he.wikipedia 'Ketovet Rehov': preserved names in Susita's territory include Kefar Yahrib = Kafr Harib, Nov = Khirbet Nab, Hispiyya = Khisfin, Semah = Samakh, 'Einosh = 'Ein 'Awanish, 'Ayun = Khirbet 'Ayun). The Mosaic of Rehob (halakhic baraita laid in a synagogue floor near Beit She'an; late 3rd-6th c. CE, text close to late-2nd-c. rabbinic literature - Tosefta Shevi'it 4:8-11, Jerusalem Talmud Demai 2:1, Shevi'it 6:1; V. Vitto dates the final mosaic to the 6th-7th c., others place the baraita's composition in the late 3rd c. at the earliest) lists, under the heading 'the towns that are prohibited in the region of Susitha (Hippos)', nine places in Hippos' territory: 'Ayyanosh, 'Ain-Hura, Dambar, 'Ayun, Ya'arut, Kefar Yahrib, Nob, Hisfiyya, Kefar Semah (Judah ha-Nasi permitted Kefar Semah). he.wikipedia explains such towns as 'cities of gentiles' in which Jewish farmers lived and were from time to time granted dispensations from Sabbatical-year and tithing law. Year 250 is a conventional date between the baraita's late-2nd-c. content and the 6th-c. mosaic. The identification with Kafr Harib rests on name preservation. Confidence medium.

The village is recorded as Kapar Haribos (Kapar Hariboy) on a Diocletianic boundary stone of c. 300 CE (en.wikipedia 'Kfar Haruv', citing the Diocletianic boundary-stone corpus), and is mentioned in the Tosefta and Jerusalem Talmud as Kefar Harub in the territory of Hippos. The boundary stone is Greek and does not itself prove Jewish residents; Jewishness rests on the rabbinic mentions. Confidence medium.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Kefar Hattin, Hittaya'): Kefar Hittaya was the seat of R. Jacob (Hag. 5b) and of R. Azariah (Pesikta de-R. Kahana 54), had a synagogue (Genesis Rabbah 65:16), and served as a refuge for R. Simeon b. Lakish, who 'escaped from the wrath of the patriarch Judah II' (JT Sanhedrin 2:1, 19d); the Jerusalem Talmud identifies it with the Ziddim-Zer of Joshua 19:35. Wikipedia 'Judah II' / 'Nasi': Judah II Nesiah was patriarch 230-270, so 250 used. Rabbinic-literary; identification with Hittin (moshav Kefar Hittim) is traditional.

Hittin (rabbinic Kefar Hittaya - reliable identification per Leibner Table 15): a medium village (category C, 11-20 dunams) occupied through the Roman and Byzantine periods with reduced size (B, 4-10 dunams) c. 250-450 and again C from 450 to 650 (Leibner 2009, Table 11). Dating basis: survey pottery. Year 300 conventional; no synagogue is attested.

Year 200 = Judah ha-Nasi (c. 200). Confidence medium for the rabbinic mention, low for the location.

comment: Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Canaanite city-state: Amarna letters (14th c. BCE) mention Qeilah and king Suwardata; pottery of the period. Canaanite so Population blank. No estimate found. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keilah

city_other: תל קילא / חורבת קילא / قعيلة (Qeila) / Khirbet Qila
comment: Iron Age (sub-period not specified by the fetched sources; start of Iron Age I used as Year of Data; sources say settlement in the Israelite period, so range -1200 to -586 assumed from the general statement). Judahite city in Joshua 15:44; early 20th c. probes reportedly found Iron Age strata (search summary only). No published population estimate found; built-up area not given for the Iron Age specifically. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keilah

city_other: תל קילא / חורבת קילא / قعيلة (Qeila) / Khirbet Qila
comment: Literary only: 1 Sam 23:1-13: the Philistines attack Keilah and rob its threshing floors; David asks the LORD, defeats them and saves the town; when Saul plans to besiege Keilah David asks whether its people will hand him over, is told they will, and leaves with his 600 men (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -1020 = Saul's reign convention for David's outlaw period. Josh 15:44: Keilah in Judah's lowland list (checked). Identification: Khirbet Qeila (Qeyla), identified by Conder and Kitchener and by Guerin and adopted by the IAA (en.wikipedia Keilah; coordinates 31.6161 N, 35.0031 E); Benjamin of Tudela earlier took Qaqun for Keilah. The page describes walls, a gate approach and burial caves with almost continuous pottery from the Bronze Age to the Mamluk period but does not date features to the Iron Age. Keilah was a Canaanite city-state in the 14th-century Amarna letters (king Suwardata). Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keilah

Literary mention (conquest narrative, dated by convention c. -1200); the biblical town of Ai ('the Ai', 'the ruin'). Josh 7:2-5 (Joshua's spies; defeat at Ai, 36 men killed), Josh 8:1-29 (the ambush, the burning of Ai 'an heap for ever', the king hanged), Josh 12:9 (list of defeated kings: the king of Ai, which is beside Beth-el). Identification is disputed and unsettled (weak row). English Wikipedia: most scholars identify Ai with et-Tell (3 km east of Beitin, next to Deir Dibwan; Robinson 1838 and C. Wilson 1866, Albright 1924), where Marquet-Krause (1933-35) and Callaway (1964-70) found a large Early Bronze city destroyed c. 2400 BCE, then no occupation until an unfortified Iron I village founded c. 1200 BCE and abandoned c. 1050 BCE; Hebrew Wikipedia gives the Iron I village as 12 dunams. Bryant Wood and others instead propose Khirbet el-Maqatir (1 km west), which was a Late Bronze I fortress destroyed in the late 15th c. BCE (English Wikipedia). Hebrew Wikipedia ('Ai') differs: it calls Khirbet Haiyan / Tell Khayin, next to et-Tell under the old core of Deir Dibwan, the most common modern identification, and says the et-Tell = Ai equation is now widely held to be wrong (et-Tell would be the Canaanite Beth-aven and Ai a small settlement beside it); it also lists proposals at Khirbet Nisya (D. Livingston's group), Jabr et-Tinteni and Kh. Marjameh. So: disputed, no clear favourite across references; English Wikipedia favours et-Tell (used here as the working site). The coordinates entered are those of the existing Khirbet el-Maqatir marker, 1 km from et-Tell (31.9169 N, 35.2611 E). Literary mention for this row; Iron I village figures are in the other rows.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Population estimate: English Wikipedia 'Khirbet el-Maqatir' (summarising the Associates for Biblical Research excavations 1998-2016 directed by Bryant G. Wood, and B. Seevers) describes the Iron Age I (Stratum 6, c. 1187-701 BCE) settlement as 'a small, poor, and largely self-sufficient agricultural village of roughly 35 to 40 inhabitants'; midpoint 38 entered. The page does not name the author of the estimate or give the method (house count and area); treat as the excavators' estimate. About 93 percent of more than 1,100 Iron Age sherds date to Iron I, pointing to a major abandonment at the Iron I/II transition with only limited activity until Iron IIC. Houses were built into the ruined Bronze Age fortification wall. See the Ai row for the identification issue.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000), et-Tell (identified with Ai by the majority according to English Wikipedia; Hebrew Wikipedia disputes that and treats et-Tell as Beth-aven), 1 km east of this marker. For comparison the excavators of nearby Khirbet el-Maqatir give 35-40 inhabitants for a much smaller Iron I village. Destroyed ca. 69 CE, attributed to Vespasian's campaign (arrowheads, ballista balls, hobnails); later reuse of hiding complex in Bar Kokhba revolt (coin of year 3). Nator (also Khirbet Natur), Upper Galilee: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Remains of basalt walls and limestone ashler stones. Architectural elements. Thousands of coins were removed in an illegal excavation. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

If Samuel Klein's identification is right, Khirbet Qana is Garis/Kefar 'Aris (Tosefta Kelim Bava Metzia 11:2), a Jewish village c. 4 km east of Sepphoris where Josephus' camp stood in 67 and from which his men dispersed when Vespasian approached (War 3.6.1). Other proposals: Tell Bedeiwiyeh/Hannaton, or Karm er-Ras at Kafr Kanna. Dating basis: Josephus + conjectural identification. Confidence low. Framing row.

Wikipedia 'Khirbet Qana': a pottery ostracon with three letters in Jewish script, 'dating back to the late first or early second century AD', is called by its publisher the first abecedarium found in a Jewish village in the Galilee; the site was used from the Hellenistic to the Early Arab period; the article mentions a Jewish synagogue and tombs (no dates given). Identification: Khirbet Qana is a candidate for the Cana of the Gospels and (per the article's citations of Josephus, War 3.127/5.473 and Vita 71) for Garis; Kafr Kanna is the traditional rival. Archaeological (palaeography/pottery); medium confidence.

Wikipedia 'Khirbet Qana': 'A lack of coinage from the late 4th to early 5th centuries may indicate a decline in Khirbet Qana' (400 used); contrast the same article's statement that the town shows expansion in the Late Byzantine period (late 5th-7th centuries), the latest coin dating to 613, and abandonment likely in the first half of the 7th century. Archaeological (coin series); an argument from silence, low-medium confidence.

Synagogue at Khirbet Qana (Qana) excavated by Douglas Edwards and Tom McCollough (1998): bema on the southern side, pillar and bench remains; Bornblum database period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Conventional year 450 (centre of the period), low confidence.

Wikipedia 'Khirbet Qana': 'The town shows expansion during the Late Byzantine period' (late 5th to 7th centuries; start of the range, 480, used); the cave complex later became a Christian pilgrimage site (Crusader-era carbon dates 1024-1217). The article does not date the synagogue or tombs; the Jewish character of the late-5th/6th-century expansion is therefore inferred, not stated. Low-medium confidence.

Literary mention; identification DISPUTED, favoured: Sha'arayim ('Two Gates'), proposed by the excavators Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor on the strength of the two gates (en.wikipedia; BibleWalks calls it 'almost certain' per the excavators but notes Na'aman disputes parts of their reading). Year of Data -1020 = Saul's reign convention (c. -1020) for the David-and-Goliath narrative. 1 Sam 17:52: wounded Philistines fall 'by the way to Shaaraim' as they flee toward Gath and Ekron after the battle in the Elah valley (1 Sam 17:1: camp between Socoh and Azekah); Josh 15:36: Sharaim in the Judean lowland list beside Adithaim and Gederah; 1 Chr 4:31: Shaaraim a Simeonite town 'unto the reign of David' (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Rival identifications (en.wikipedia): Neta'im (Galil 2010), Adithaim (Dagan), Gob (Na'aman, who also links it to Philistine Gath), Azekah (the excavators' own first proposal, 2007), Ma'gal of 1 Sam 17:20 (Levin; rejected by the excavators). The site sits on a hill at 328 m (BibleWalks). Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khirbet_Qeiyafa; https://www.biblewalks.com/shaaraim/; Josh 15 and 1 Chr 4 chapter pages at biblegateway.

Wikipedia 'Khirbet Shema': occupied from c. 180 CE (infobox 'built 180') to 417, on coin evidence; excavated by Eric Meyers 1970-72 (ASOR; report 1976), over six acres and more than 4,000 artifacts; broadhouse-plan synagogue with walls nearly two feet thick; tombs that tradition links with Shammai found no archaeological support. Archaeological (coins/stratigraphy).

Broadhouse-plan synagogue (not basilical), with thick foundations, wide entrance staircase and underground chambers. Excavators (Meyers, Kraabel, Strange 1976): two buildings, Synagogue I destroyed ~306 and Synagogue II destroyed 419 CE; Wikipedia infobox 'built 180'. Per the Meiron Project the synagogues were built in the 2nd-3rd centuries (year 200 = conventional midpoint). J. Magness (1997): no solid evidence for a Synagogue I; Synagogue II built late 4th-early 5th century (coin of Constans 337-341 sealed in the bema; coin of Gratian 367-383 in a fill, terminus post quem 337-383). Russell (1980) re-dated the quakes to 363 and 419. Spigel (2016) argues for the excavators' chronology. Dating basis: coins/stratigraphy. Confidence low-medium; date contested.

Wikipedia 'Khirbet Shema': the village was destroyed by an earthquake and abandoned in 417 CE (infobox 'abandoned 417'). The article does not mention the 363 earthquake; EJ attributes abandonment of nearby Meron to 363 and Wikipedia to 409 - the regional earthquake chronology (363/409/419) is unsettled. Archaeological (Meyers); medium confidence.

End of the village: excavators attribute the destruction of Synagogue II to the 419 CE (Monaxius and Plinta) earthquake; Wikipedia gives c. 417 CE for the earthquake that destroyed the village. Magness (1997) instead suggests the site was abandoned when an earthquake brought down Synagogue II sometime before the 8th century. Dating basis: stratigraphy/coins. Confidence low-medium.

Framing row. Large Jewish village (founded c. 100 BCE) destroyed c. 125-135 CE, dated by a coin hoard to the reign of Hadrian: possibly linked to the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136) or to suppression of unrest on the arrival of Legio VI Ferrata (c. 123-127). Excavated 2007-12 by U. Leibner (Hebrew University). Cooking pots made at Kfar Hananya, jars at Shikhin. Identification with Arbel of the sources (Shahar and Tepper) is conjectural.

Large Jewish village (founded c. 100 BCE) of eastern Galilee destroyed in a violent conflagration dated by a coin hoard to the reign of Hadrian (c. 125-135 CE): either the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136) or suppression of unrest on the arrival of Legio VI Ferrata (c. 123-127). Cooking pots came from Kefar Hananya, jars from Shikhin. Excavated by U. Leibner 2007-2012. Dating basis: coin hoard/pottery. Confidence high. Ancient name unknown (some identify it with Arbel).

Village re-established c. 200 CE; monumental Galilean-type synagogue (basalt, 12.8 x 15.4 m, c. 180 seats) built c. 200 CE according to Leibner, damaged in the late 3rd c., rebuilt c. 300 with a figured mosaic, mosaic partly replaced and a stone bema added in the late 4th c.; collapse late 4th/early 5th c. Magness (2024) re-analyses the pottery and dates the synagogue(s) to the second half of the 4th through the 5th c. Dating basis: pottery (Kefar Hananya ware), coins; disputed. Year 200 = Leibner's date.

Mosaic floor of the synagogue dated by the excavator to the late 3rd/early 4th c. (earliest figured synagogue mosaic known; only about 6% preserved: Samson, Red Sea, Tower of Babel, zodiac traces; Aramaic dedications 'The sons of Simon made this panel', 'Samuel the scribe'); 4th-c. inscribed metal amulet found. Year 300.

Settlement gradually abandoned in the late 4th or early 5th c. CE (agricultural zone abandoned by the mid-4th c.); the synagogue collapsed, probably in an earthquake, in the late 4th/early 5th c. (possibly 419); latest floor finds are dated 378-383 CE (chronology disputed by Magness).

Talmudic Tiv'in (Tivon, Tiv'on; the Kiryat Tivon area, SE of Haifa, next to Beit She'arim) - earliest tannaitic reference after 70: R. Eleazar b. Zadok (II, active c. 90-130) says 'my father carried two things from Tiv'in to Yavne' (cited in Hebrew Wikipedia, Kiryat Tivon, which also names the tanna Abba Yose Halikufri of Tivon in the Mishnah and the homilist R. Hanina of Tivon in the Sifrei on Deuteronomy). Hebrew Wikipedia: 'during the Second Temple, Mishnaic and Talmudic periods Tiv'in was a central Jewish town in the south-western Galilee, together with Simonia, Bethlehem of Galilee, Beit She'arim and Usha'. Year 90 is a conventional placement for the first post-Temple generation (the father's transport to Yavne, when the Sanhedrin sat there). Identification: the source says the ancient town lay next to, not under, the modern settlement; the usual identification is with the Arab village Tab'un/ruin near the Haifa-Nazareth road. Literary evidence only.

Synagogue at Tiv'in in the mid-2nd century: Hebrew Wikipedia (Kiryat Tivon) cites the tradition 'it happened that Rabbi Meir read the Megillah in the synagogue at Tiv'in while seated, and the congregation sat' (Tosefta/Talmudic Megillah tradition) - evidence of a synagogue and an organised Jewish congregation; and that R. Meir, sitting in the neighbouring Ardiskin (Kh. Kuskus, north of Tivon), ruled on the Sabbath-limit of the Tiv'in people. R. Meir was a fourth-generation tanna active c. 140-165, so year 150. The same page names Abba Yose Halikufri of Tiv'in (Mishnah) and R. Hanina of Tiv'in (Sifrei Deut.). Literary evidence only (no synagogue excavated at Tivon itself; the nearby Beit She'arim lies in the same hill belt).

Tiv'in (Tivonin), together with Haifa and Beth She'an, was a place whose Jews could not pronounce the gutturals correctly, 'the people of Beth She'an, the people of Haifa and the people of Tivonin are not sent down before the ark [as prayer leaders] because they pronounce alef as ayin and ayin as alef' (Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 and Babylonian Talmud, quoted in Hebrew Wikipedia, Kiryat Tivon; Encyclopaedia Judaica Haifa gives the same Palestinian Talmud reference for Haifa). Amoraic period, year 250 a conventional placement (the sayings are usually attributed to the 3rd-4th generations of amoraim); shows a Jewish community at Tiv'in still functioning in the Talmudic period, with synagogue worship.

'Qeshet' site in the Kiryat Tiv'on area (near Beth She'arim): marble menorah and other architectural stones (G. Foerster 1974; Z. Ilan 1986) from a Late Roman/Byzantine synagogue; nothing visible at the site. Conventional year (3rd-7th c.). Dating basis: sculpture typology. Confidence low.

Jewish settlement on Kursi Beach (c. 1 km NW of the Byzantine monastery of Kursi National Park): the Avery-Tsui excavations of Univ. of Haifa (H. Cohen, M. Artzy, 2015-18) uncovered the SW part of a public building, possibly a synagogue, with a bema in an E-W wall and, in an opus sectile floor, a broken imported-marble plaque (1.25 x 0.7 m) with eight lines of Hebrew and Aramaic beginning 'To be remembered in good memory' and ending 'amen' (first of its kind in Israel). Pottery from the squares is Byzantine, Umayyad and Early Abbasid, with three 7th-8th-c. coins and a Byzantine coin; the excavators write that the inscription 'reinforces the assumption that the building was part of a Jewish settlement during the Byzantine, Umayyad and the beginning of the Abbasid periods' (Cohen & Artzy, HA-ESI 129, 2017, preliminary report on the first season, Nov-Dec 2015; also reproduced at deadseaquake.info). Date conflict: epigrapher H. Misgav dated the script 'likely ... around the 4th or 5th centuries CE' (Times of Israel, 21 Dec 2015; excavator Cohen called the settlement '1,600-year-old'; en.wikipedia c. 500 CE and donors from Tiberias). Year 425 = midpoint of Misgav's 4th-5th c. (the building's use continued later). The Christian monastery (baptistery 585) is a separate, neighbouring community. Confidence medium; function (synagogue) is 'possible' per the excavators.

Kursi Beach (east shore of the Sea of Galilee, Golan): ESI 2017 (H. Cohen, M. Artzy, 2015 season) exposed the SW part of a public building, possibly a synagogue (threshold, bema, opus sectile floor) with a marble plaque bearing eight lines of Hebrew and Aramaic ('To be remembered in good memory ... amen'), which supports a Jewish settlement during the Byzantine, Umayyad and early Abbasid periods; pottery Byzantine-Early Abbasid, coins 7th-8th c. Identification with the Kursi/Gerasa of the sources is traditional. Conventional year 550 (Byzantine period); low-medium confidence on the earliest date.

Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550). Source: MB I resettlement from 2000 BCE; MB IIB-IIC (1630-1550 BCE) a major fortified city with glacis. Canaanite. No academic population estimate found in fetched pages.

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Level VII (Fosse Temple II) and Level VI 'prosperous, densely populated and unfortified Canaanite city'; destroyed c. 1150 BCE (Wikipedia; other sources say c. 1130). Canaanite. No academic population estimate found.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Canaanite rebuilding after the LB destruction then a second destruction c. 1130 BCE; extended sparse occupation (Level V per Wikipedia; BibleWalks and JVL place Level V in the 10th c). Source periodisation is loose. No academic population estimate found.

Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900). Level V (small houses; possibly Rehoboam's fort c. 925 BCE) and start of Level IV royal Judean fortified city (late 10th c). Dates per source. No academic population estimate found.

Literary mention with an archaeological hook: 2 Chr 11:5-12: Rehoboam fortifies Lachish among his defensive cities in Judah, stocking them with food, oil and wine (verse range checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -925 = Rehoboam convention. BibleWalks: Level V (Iron IIa, 10th century) small houses, and a wide wall unearthed in 2019 that may be Rehoboam's; Level IV (Judean kingdom) dated 10th century to 750 BCE. Dating caveat: en.wikipedia lists Level V as Iron Age I and others place it in the 10th century; the existing Lachish rows (Iron I-IIB) already carry the period summaries. Mound top 72 dunams (about 7 ha) per BibleWalks.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). Level IV (to c. 760 BCE per JVL) then Level III 'densely populated city' (destroyed by Sennacherib 701 BCE, which falls in IIB per BibleWalks; the brief's range ends -722). Mound top 72 dunams. Judahite. No verified academic population estimate: a search snippet mentioned about 3500 (40-50 persons per dunam) but no fetched page confirmed it so it is not used.

Literary only: 2 Kgs 14:19 and 2 Chr 25:27: conspirators in Jerusalem plot against Amaziah; he flees to Lachish and is pursued and killed there (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Year of Data -770 = convention for Amaziah's death (reign c. -796 to -767). Archaeology: Level IV city of the Judean kingdom was in use (10th century to c. 750, BibleWalks), so a fortified Lachish is consistent with the story, but no stratum is tied to the event.

Literary only: Mic 1:13: Lachish is told to harness its swift horses to the chariot and is called the source of sin for the people of Zion, because Israel's rebellions were found there (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page; paraphrased). Year of Data -730 = late 8th century convention for Micah's oracle against the Shephelah towns (Mic 1:10-15). Level IV/III city; BibleWalks and en.wikipedia give no population estimate.

Iron Age IIC / late monarchy (-722 to -586). Level II (Iron IIc) built perhaps under Josiah; 'sparsely populated settlement' per BAS Library; destroyed 588/586 BCE by Babylon; Lachish Letters. Judahite. No academic population estimate found.

Iron Age IIB, 701 BCE: Sennacherib besieges Lachish. Biblical text: 2 Kgs 18:13-17 (Hezekiah sends to the Assyrian king at Lachish, pays 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold; the Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh are sent from Lachish with a large army against Jerusalem), 2 Kgs 19:8 and Isa 36:1-2, 37:8 (the Assyrian king leaves Lachish and is found warring against Libnah) (checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Archaeology: Level III, destroyed in 701 BCE, with the Assyrian siege ramp and Judean counter-ramp; a gate shrine destroyed in the assault (BibleWalks; en.wikipedia quoting Ussishkin 'Level III had been destroyed in 701 BCE'). Size: mound top 72 dunams = about 7 ha (BibleWalks); en.wikipedia says the city 'occupied an area of 8 hectares (20 acres)' (citing Rocca 2012). No population estimate in either page (the 1,500 skulls in a nearby cave are a burial count of uncertain date, not a population).
Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332). Level I: Babylonian Persian and Hellenistic periods; Persian-period resettlement with fortifications and Solar Shrine. No academic population estimate found.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Replaces first-pass row, giving the excavators' own account. Hasel et al. (AJA 125, 2021, Fourth Expedition): Level II destroyed 586 BCE; Level I rebuilt in the Persian period (5th c.) with a 2.5 m stone city wall, fortified in all three phases of Level I in Area CC; a 'residency' palace over the Judahite palace and the nearby Solar Shrine. Kang and Garfinkel (2021): the earlier two Level I phases are Persian, the later Hellenistic; there was an occupational gap after the Babylonian destruction; Tufnell dated Level I to 450-150 BCE while Fantalkin and Tal (2004, 2006) argued Level I was fortified only in its second sub-phase. Ussishkin (per BAR review) thought the Solar Shrine Persian rather than Hellenistic. Jewish evidence is textual only: Nehemiah 11:30 lists Lachish among the places where Judeans settled, and Encyclopaedia Judaica reads this as returnees settling under Nehemiah; no ritual baths, chalk vessels or other Jewish markers are reported in the fetched excavation reports. Provincial administrative centre; population mixed or unknown. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Replaces first-pass row on abandonment. Hasel et al. (AJA 2021) are internally inconsistent: one passage says Level I existed until its abandonment in the second century, the summary says that in the third century Mareshah became the dominant city and Lachish was abandoned and never resettled as a city. Kang and Garfinkel assign the latest Level I phase to the Hellenistic era; Encyclopaedia Judaica (via cojs.org) dates the Solar Shrine to c. 200 BCE; Tufnell's date ran to 150 BCE. Hasmonean and later rows omitted (no settlement evidence on the tell). Not to be confused with the Hellenistic fortress in the Lachish Forest (a separate site, destroyed c. 112 BCE by John Hyrcanus, part of Maresha's defences; IAA 2021 via BAR). No Jewish-specific archaeological evidence; Population blank.

'The inn of Levi/Lavi' (pundaqa de-Levi) appears in two Jerusalem Talmud traditions of the 4th c.: a wheel of cheese found there was permitted because most travellers on these roads were Jews (Shekalim 7:3, 50c, a case involving R. Elazar son of R. Yosi, fifth generation of amoraim), and R. Yirmiya (fourth generation, Tiberias) said grace for the donkey drivers there (Berakhot 7:4, 11c). Leibner places it at el-Khirbeh (survey site 49, map ref 1898/2421, about 2 km south-west of the modern kibbutz marker; 30 dunams, 21-30 dunams from the Early to the Late Roman period, 11-20 in the Early Byzantine, 4-10 in the Middle Byzantine, none in the Late Byzantine, i.e. decline in the first half of the 6th c.), next to the Arab village of Lubieh; ashlars and architectural elements of a monumental structure are scattered in Lubieh (column drums, capitals and lintels reused in village houses led Ilan to infer a monumental synagogue there; Leibner thinks the stones came from the hill of el-Khirbeh). The identification is uncertain: the best manuscripts read Levi, some read Lubai; Sokoloff reads it as a functional name 'inn of the caravans', Sussmann as a personal name, Demsky places it in Samaria; Leibner finds it reasonable that the name Lubieh preserves an ancient name and so supports Klein's identification, but calls the question undecidable on the texts alone. The row therefore shows Jewish traffic on the Tiberias-Sepphoris road in the 4th c., with a possible small village attached. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 300-304, 402. Conventional year (4th c.). Dating basis: Jerusalem Talmud traditions + survey pottery. Confidence low-medium.

A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Survey-level synagogue site (Jewish; Late Roman/Byzantine; unexcavated): architectural elements including a lion, noted by L. Oliphant 1885, surveyed by D. Urman 1968 and Z. Ma'oz 1980 (Bornblum); Encyclopaedia Judaica lists 'Lawiyya' among the sites where Schumacher noted Jewish symbols. Year 450 conventional. Weak evidence.

Wikipedia 'Gamaliel II': the patriarch Gamaliel II 'seemed to have settled initially in Kefar 'Othnai in Lower Galilee' before the war and moved to Yavne (nasi c. 80-118; 100 used). Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Kefar Otnay'): Talmudic sources (Gittin 7:7) treat it as the southernmost boundary of Galilee towards Judah; it was the home of R. Shemaiah, pupil of Yohanan ben Zakkai; the patriarch Gamaliel occasionally visited it; in Hadrian's time (117-138) it was chosen as the camp of the Sixth Legion and renamed Legio (Greek Caparcotnei). Identification: Kefar Otnai = the Roman Legio / Caparcotna south of Tel Megiddo (earlier suggestions Kafr Dan / Kafr Qud rejected); coordinates are those of Wikipedia 'Legio'. Rabbinic-literary and Roman-military.

Kefar 'Othnay (Caparcotna), a Jewish village on the imperial road from Caesarea Maritima to Scythopolis, next to the camp of Legio VI Ferrata. Yotam Tepper, Matthew Adams and Jonathan David (Popular Archaeology 2015, summarising Tepper's survey and the Jezreel Valley Regional Project): the Sixth Ferrata Legion was deployed 'near the beginning of the Second Century'; sources place its base 'in the vicinity of the Jewish village of Caparcotani/Kaperkotnei (Kefar 'Othnay)', and three settlements existed at Legio: the Jewish village of Kefar 'Othnay, the Roman legionary base, and the Byzantine polis of Maximianopolis (4th-7th c.). Finds in the Megiddo Prison area south of the base (including a 3rd-century Christian prayer hall dedicated by the centurion Gaianus) suggest it was 'the Jewish-Samaritan (and apparently Christian) village'. Year 200 is the midpoint of the '2nd-3rd century CE' military presence; evidence for Jewish population at the village is literary (Gamaliel II's early residence there, Talmudic mentions) plus this identification, no excavated Jewish remains reported in the source.

The Iron IIB level was apparently destroyed, probably during Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign; an LMLK seal of Hezekiah's time indicates Judahite fortification (BibleWalks). No population estimate found in either page.

Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550; source: 18th-16th c. BCE). Unfortified settlement, domestic pottery and two burials outside settled area (Lydda 2024 article). Canaanite. No population estimate.

Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200; source: 15th-13th c. BCE). Settlement likely shifted south; very limited inhabited area in the northern tell. Lod appears in Thutmose III list c.1465 BCE (he.wikipedia). Canaanite. No population estimate. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%9C%D7%95%D7%93

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000; source: 11th c. BCE). Continuous occupation without clear structures; Philistine-style and Egyptian-influenced pottery, ties to coastal Sea Peoples settlements. Not Israelite per source. No population estimate.

Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900; source: 10th-9th c. BCE). Ceramics show ties inland to Shephelah (Gezer, Batash). Bible (1 Chr 8:12) lists Lod as a Benjamin town built by Shemed (he.wikipedia). Population blank: no academic estimate found; no built-up area given. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%9C%D7%95%D7%93

Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332). Renewed settlement attested by scattered sherds in pits; Ezra 2:33 and Neh 7:37 list returning Lod residents. Population blank: no estimate found. Note: no pottery from 8th c. BCE onward until this period (possible Assyrian exile, per source), so Iron Age IIB and IIC have no row.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Lod is listed among towns resettled after the return (Ezra 2:33, Neh 7:37) and among Benjamite settlements (Neh 11:35), per Jewish Virtual Library. Jewish settlement from textual evidence only; no excavation evidence for this period was found. Sources disagree on status: Hebrew Wikipedia says Lod belonged to the district of Samaria (flagged there as needing clarification) while an Israeli Archaeology Association page calls it an important Jewish centre. No Jewish population estimate by a named scholar. First pass had no Second Temple rows for Lod (only modern 1948+ rows), so this row is new. Identification Lod/Lydda is secure.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): after Alexander's conquest (333 BCE) Lod stayed in the district of Samaria and outside Judea until Demetrius II ceded it to Jonathan in 145 BCE (Jewish Virtual Library; Hebrew Wikipedia). The Israeli Archaeology Association page says Demetrius I (161-150 BCE) proposed moving it to Judea because of its Jewish majority, i.e. a Jewish majority is claimed for the end of this period; no excavation evidence quoted. Population blank: no named-scholar estimate.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): annexed to Judea 145 BCE (1 Macc 11:34) and became a toparchy (Ant. 13:127; Wars 3:55); a purely Jewish town in Maccabean times (Jewish Virtual Library). Rosenfeld (Lydda vol. 2, 2024) has Lod as seat of the toparchy of the Plain of Lod from c. 150 BCE to 70 CE (citing Avi-Yonah, Stern, Schwartz). Rural Jewish settlement around Lod (Hasmonean villages and farmsteads with mikva'ot, stone vessels, Hasmonean coins, synagogues in larger settlements; Zelinger 2010 Bar-Ilan thesis under Kloner) is from search-result snippets only, the pages were not fetched. The Israeli Archaeology Association page states 'a population of about 2,500' without naming a scholar or basis, so it stays in Notes and Population is blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): toparchy seat; Julius Caesar restored the privileges of its Jews (Ant. 14:208); Cassius enslaved its inhabitants 43 BCE, freed by Antony (Ant. 14:275); Josephus calls it a village 'not smaller than a city' (Ant. 20:130); Cestius Gallus burned it in 66 CE finding it nearly empty at Sukkot because residents had gone to Jerusalem; Vespasian took it 68 CE. Jewish city before 70 CE (Rosenfeld). Early Roman material of the 1st c. BCE-1st c. CE is from tombs and excavations in the northern industrial area (Haddad 2008; Haddad and Amitai-Preiss 2004; Yannai and Marder 2000, as cited by Rosenfeld); the main remains (mosaic house, cemetery) are post-70. Rosenfeld's estimate of about 4,100 up to about 6,000 residents is for 70-132 CE, built from area times density, so it is not entered for this period; Population blank. About 2,000 Jews killed by Gallus (Hebrew Wikipedia) is casualties, not population.

Wikipedia 'Lod': the city 'reached its height as a Jewish center ... again in the days of Judah ha-Nasi' (c. 200) with schools, study houses and synagogues, and in 200 CE Septimius Severus raised it to a city, Colonia Lucia Septimia Severa Diospolis; Wikipedia 'Bar Kokhba revolt' lists Lod among the Jewish communities that persisted on the edge of Judea after 135. The book says that in the late Roman period (135-324) Lod was inhabited by Jews, Samaritans and pagans, that a large Jewish centre remained in a pagan city while nearby Ono stayed Jewish, and cites the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin) for 24 towns in the Lod area in the days of Judah ha-Nasi. Difference: Wikipedia adds that at that point 'most of its inhabitants were Christian' (see conflicts file). No population stated: Population blank. Book: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 037 (Screenshot_20221028-092833.jpg), img 036 (Screenshot_20221028-092754.jpg), img 038 (Screenshot_20221028-092908.jpg); page number not visible.

Iron Age (Israelite/Judahite period; the fetched page gives no finer dating than 'Iron Age'; year -1200 is the start of Iron Age I used as a convention, not a source date). Wikipedia: potsherds from Early Bronze Age and Iron Age including LMLK jar handles; Hellenistic onward remains. Identification: Khirbet Ma'in / Horvat Ma'on is the standard identification of biblical Maon (Josh 15:55; David in the wilderness of Maon). No stratigraphy or population or area figure found. Judahite town.

[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): New period row (first pass had no Persian row). Greenberg and Keinan (2009) gazetteer entry no. 943 for Kh. Ma'in (H. Ma'on; Tell Ma'in), the 1987-88 excavation of Zvi Ilan and David Amit (licences L-427/1987, L-444/1988), lists the Persian period among 'other periods' (major periods: Iron IIb, Iron IIc, Byzantine). The gazetteer gives no finds, structures or population for this phase. Inhabitants not stated; no Jewish-specific evidence for this phase; Population blank. CAUTION: the HA-ESI Horbat Ma'on reports (Nahshoni and Seriy 2004; Nikolsky 2010), which the English Wikipedia article cites and which I fetched, concern Ma'on-Nirim in the western Negev, a different site; their Persian-period pit does NOT belong to this site.

[Second-pass revision] the first pass rested on a Wikipedia sherds statement. The same gazetteer (Greenberg and Keinan 2009, entry 943) lists the Hellenistic period among the periods represented in the 1987-88 Ilan-Amit excavation and states that it merges 'Hasmonean' into 'Hellenistic', so the early phase (-332 to -167) and the Hasmonean phase (-167 to -63) cannot be separated; treat as one Hellenistic presence of unspecified density. Jewish settlement not demonstrated for this phase in any fetched source; Population blank.

Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Hebrew Wikipedia states Maon was a Jewish settlement throughout the Second Temple period (general statement only; no Hasmonean-specific finds, coins or baths in fetched pages). Weak evidence for this sub-period. No population estimate found.

[Second-pass revision] the first pass said only 'Roman-period sherds' from Wikipedia. Greenberg and Keinan (2009, entry 943) record Early Roman (Rom1) and Late Roman (Rom2) as separate periods at Kh. Ma'in in the 1987-88 Ilan-Amit excavation, so Early Roman occupation is attested by excavation records (the gazetteer uses 'Early Roman' for Herodian). Jewish character: Hebrew Wikipedia (and Hamichlol, which copies it) states that Maon of Judah remained a Jewish settlement through the Second Temple period and was damaged in suppressing the Great Revolt, citing a midrash (Mekhilta) about Yohanan ben Zakkai; Eusebius' 'very large Jewish village' is 4th c. These are literary and late; no ritual bath, chalk vessel or coin from this site is reported in the fetched pages. The synagogue and marble menorah are 4th-7th c. (Amit and Ilan 1990; Amit 1997, 2003), not Second Temple. Amit (1994, JSRS 3) published Second Temple miqva'ot of the Hebron hills but no fetched page ties one to Ma'on. Population blank: no named-author estimate found.

Wikipedia 'Maoz Haim Synagogue': 'Constructed in the third century as a simple Byzantine-era type basilica building' (3rd century = conventional 250); discovered in February 1974 by Avshalom Ya'aqobi and excavated February-March 1974 under Vassilios Tzaferis ('The Synagogue at Ma'oz-Hayim', Qadmoniot 1974). Archaeological (stratigraphy/coins). The article's 'Byzantine-era type' for a 3rd-century building is its own wording; confidence medium.

Wikipedia 'Maoz Haim Synagogue': in the 4th century renovations added an apse in the southern wall and the building was reoriented toward Jerusalem; fifty Byzantine coins were found hidden outside the southern wall, apparently emergency funds. Archaeological; 4th century = conventional 350.

Wikipedia 'Maoz Haim Synagogue': the chancel screen 'was further modified in the 6th century to include a raised platform' (conventional 550); the screen bore a menorah and Hebrew letters, 'Shalom' being the only Hebrew word in the building while the other inscriptions are in Greek; mosaic motifs include birds, a menorah, an etrog, a shofar and grapes; the synagogue was destroyed by fire in the early 7th century and its symbols and birds were covered up in the 7th century. Archaeological; the 6th-century phase is stated without a year.

End of the Ma'oz Hayyim synagogue: destroyed by fire in the early 7th c.; before that, in the 7th c., the symbols and birds were covered over by a new geometric floor, making the synagogue aniconic. Framing row just after the period. Dating basis: coins/stratigraphy. Confidence medium.

[Second-pass revision] adds coin and excavation evidence. Hasmonean (-167 to -63): sources differ on the start of settlement. Callegher 2023 (reviewed in BMCR) catalogues the Magdala coins: the coin record begins in the 3rd c. BCE and most coins are Hasmonean (140-37 BCE) or Roman, with a statistical analysis of Alexander Jannaeus issues. Abu-'Uqsa 2005 (HA-ESI 117, Recital Beach, Stratum IV) reports Hellenistic Galilee Coarse Ware under the Early Roman layer but no Hasmonean-specific stratum. The Franciscan excavations (Corbo and Loffreda 1971-1977, per the World History Encyclopedia summary) place the founding in the late Hellenistic period; an IAA 2006 summary (Wikipedia) gives the 2nd-1st c. BCE. Hasmonean coins are the main evidence for this phase and are consistent with a Jewish population; no miqveh or synagogue is dated to it, so Population blank. No evidence of another ethnic group in the period.

comment: [Second-pass revision] adds primary excavation sources. Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Jewish town and port (Tarichaeae in Josephus). Synagogue found by Avshalom-Gorni and Najar (IAA, 2009), dated to the 1st c. CE by coins and pottery, with the Magdala Stone carved with a seven-branched menorah (earliest outside Jerusalem); a second Second Temple synagogue announced in Dec 2021 near a residential street (University of Haifa); Reich and Zapata Meza (IEJ 64, 2014): groundwater-fed stepped miqva'ot (three installations in their report; four in the 2017 BAR article by Zapata-Meza and Sanz-Rincon) in a late Second Temple village; Abu-'Uqsa 2005 found a Herodian coin minted in Jerusalem in the Early Roman stratum; harbor and fish-trade quarter flourish until 67 CE, when the town fell in the Revolt (Josephus BJ 3.462ff: natural inhabitants versus many foreigners and refugees, great slaughter). Josephus BJ 2.608: the people of Taricheae 'about forty thousand in number'; Zapata-Meza and Sanz-Rincon 2017 read Josephus as implying about 30,000 for the city. These are Josephus's war-time figures that include refugees and are not a Jewish population estimate by a named scholar, so they stay in Notes and Population is blank. The identification of Magdala with Tarichaeae is the standard one but not unanimous (Pliny places Tarichaeae south of Tiberias).

Event: Cassius Longinus, governor of Syria after Carrhae, took the stronghold of Tarichaea (= Magdala) and carried about 30,000 Jews into slavery (Josephus, War 1.8.9, Whiston: 'upon his taking Taricheae, he carried thirty thousand Jews into slavery'; Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Cassius Longinus': he 'carried away captive 30,000 Jews'). Captive count, not a population: Population blank. Year uncertain: Cassius governed Syria 53-51 BCE (the usual date is 52 BCE); the book puts it in 54-53 BCE (30,000 captives taken to Rome after the Galilee revolt was crushed) and lists 30,000 killed or captured in 51 BCE (Cassius against Pitholaus) as another item, apparently the same episode counted twice. Book: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 034 (Screenshot_20221028-092631.jpg); page number not visible.

Framing row: two Second Temple-period synagogues (first excavated 2009, second 2021) and a lead weight dated 71/2 or 82/3 CE; a collapse layer supports Josephus' account of the Roman destruction in 67; excavations show that after the destruction, in the Byzantine and Early Islamic periods, the settlement moved slightly to the north.

Archaeology of Magdala: a collapse layer of the Second Temple period supports Josephus' account of the Roman destruction; the 2009 synagogue (dated 50 BCE-100 CE; 'Magdala stone' with a menorah) and a second synagogue found in 2021 belong to the town destroyed in 67; excavations show that afterwards, in the Byzantine and early Islamic periods, the city moved slightly to the north; the 2006 IAA dig found the settlement ending in the late Roman period (3rd c.). Conventional year (post-70). Dating basis: stratigraphy/coins. Confidence medium; the post-70 population is not shown to be Jewish.

Wikipedia 'Magdala': the Babylonian Talmud (Pesahim 46a) and Jerusalem Talmud (Ta'anit 4:8) mention Magdala Nunayya and Magdala Tza'baya (the article notes it is unclear whether these are the same place); a Second Temple synagogue (50 BCE-100 CE) was found in 2009. Conflict: IAA excavations (2006) found the late Roman (3rd century) settlement ended and the town moved slightly north in the Byzantine/early Islamic period; a 4th-century church of Mary Magdalene's house is attributed to Helena; a Byzantine monastery was excavated in 1971-76. Year 250 = conventional (Talmudic period; 3rd-century end of the Roman settlement). Rabbinic-literary; low-medium confidence for continuous Jewish presence after 70.

Leibner (site 34, Migdal, 90 dunams): two rabbinic traditions mention a synagogue at Migdal. The first (R. Shim'on bar Yohai, mid-2nd c., in the story of the purification of Tiberias) is aggadic, so Leibner draws no firm conclusion from it. The second (Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 3:1, 73d) is a concrete halakhic question: the people of Migdal asked R. Shim'on ben Lakish (second generation of amoraim, c. 250-280) whether stones of a synagogue of their town could be used to build a synagogue in another town - from which Leibner infers a destroyed or dilapidated synagogue in the second half of the 3rd c. No monumental synagogue was found by the surveys; the Franciscan 'mini-synagogue' is a spring-house (Netzer 1987), so these 3rd-c. synagogues were probably not monumental. The Franciscan excavations found no destruction level or occupation gap in the second half of the 1st c. (Loffreda 1976), which conflicts with the 'collapse layer' attributed to 67 in the 'Archaeology of Magdala' row. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 229-230, 215, 224 note 94, 400 note 9. Conventional year (c. 250-280). Dating basis: rabbinic traditions. Confidence medium.

Leibner (2009, site 34 Migdal): the largest settlement of the Eastern Galilee survey (61-90 dunams, category F) c. 50 BCE-250 CE; category E in 250-300; B in 300-400 with decline; probably abandoned c. 400-550 and resettled c. 550-650 (monastery). Rabbinic traditions about sages of the second half of the 3rd c. mention a synagogue at Migdal, but no monumental synagogue was found (Corbo's 'mini-synagogue' is a nymphaeum per Netzer). Year 270 = decline phase c. 250-300.

ESI preliminary report (D. Avshalom-Gorni and A. Najar, 2009-13 salvage excavation on the Kinneret shore): four strata - Hellenistic, Early Roman, Late Roman (Stratum 2) and Byzantine (Stratum 1); Migdal (Migdal Nunia/Taricheae) was the only urban centre on the western shore until Tiberias was founded in 19 CE; it reached its zenith in the Early Roman period and continued 'on a smaller scale' in different periods until the Middle Ages. Dating basis: stratigraphy, pottery, coins. Year 300 = Late Roman stratum (conventional).

Leibner: the pottery shows a sharp decline of this largest settlement of the survey area from the late 3rd/early 4th c. (Late Roman finds 30%, few fourth-century types; the 4th-c. coins all belong to the first half of the century, Constantine I, 308-324). The Franciscan excavators concluded that the buildings of the town were abandoned early in the 4th c. (except a pool in Area E), and a fortified Byzantine monastery was later built over the ruins. Leibner's regional chapter nevertheless lists Migdal among the larger settlements abandoned in the second half of the 4th c. (a mild internal tension between c. 300-325 and the later date). He infers that by the time of the 6th-7th c. piyyutim of the priestly courses no Jewish community remained at Migdal. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 232-235, 358. Conventional year (decline c. 300, abandonment early to later 4th c.). Dating basis: survey pottery, coins and the Franciscan excavation. Confidence medium.

Priestly-courses inscription from Caesarea (IIP caes0684): 'The 20th course Ezekiel - Migdal Nunaiya', i.e. Magdala (Migdal Nunayya); date range 200-500 CE (midpoint 350). Wikipedia 'Priestly courses' lists Magdala as the residence of the 20th course (Jehezkel) in the baraita. Epigraphic; identification of Migdal Nunaiya with Magdala/Tarichaea is the standard one (and EJ/Talmud use the same name).

Roman-period Jewish village of Khirbet Majduliyya, ~2 km NE of Natur on the border between the districts of Gaulanitis and Hippos (32.8634N 35.7674E, Bornblum pin; HA-ESI map ref 27200/75220). Excavations (M. Osband, B. Arubas, Zinman Institute, Univ. of Haifa; co-directed with M. Eisenberg; since 2014): 'most of the finds belong to the late first-third centuries CE'. IAA preliminary report (HA-ESI 134, 2022): the chronology 'is consistent with the settlement history of the Golan, as discussed by Ben-David (2005), suggesting that Jewish settlement in this region continued after the First Jewish Revolt'. IEJ 70:2 (2020) abstract: settlement 'from the first century BCE through the late third century CE'; BAS dig page: 'a Jewish village dating to the Roman period (first-early fourth centuries CE)'. Year 100 conventional (1st-2nd c. phase, i.e. across the 70 and 135 breaks); confidence high.

Golan village and synagogue excavated by M. Osband and B. Arubas (University of Haifa; 2014-19 seasons; ESI 134): the synagogue is tentatively ascribed to the Early Roman period, possibly the early 1st c. CE, and continued in use until the late 3rd c. CE (with additions: tiled roof, mosaic floor, piers, annexed rooms), when the site was abandoned; its closest parallels are the Early Roman buildings of Gamla and Magdala, both destroyed in 67; the excavators call it the first synagogue operating in the Late Roman period found in the Golan. Dating basis: stratigraphy and pottery. Year 200 = 2nd-3rd c. of use (70-290).

Roman-period synagogue (IAA preliminary report, HA-ESI 134, 2022): a rectangular building 13 x 23 m, N-S, with a two-room annex on the north; sunken central hall, raised aisles, peripheral and interior stepped benches, Doric capitals, at least three building phases; mosaic floors (rich figurative animal composition in the central hall, geometric pattern in the aisles). Construction 'tentatively ascribed to the Early Roman period, possibly the early first century CE', continuing in use 'through the third century CE' with additions (tiled roof, mosaic floor, piers, annex rooms = phases 2-3; dating still under study); closest parallels are the Early Roman synagogues of Gamla and Migdal/Magdala (both ended 67 CE). The authors stress this 'is a significant find, as no other synagogue operating in the Late Roman period has been discovered in the Golan'. Dating conflict: Mosaic Magazine's summary of Times of Israel (2019) speaks of 'a synagogue from the 3rd century CE' and a 'transition from study hall to prayer hall'. Identification cautious (Osband to Haaretz 2014: 'we don't know of any other purpose for such a building'). Year 250 = use and mosaic phase (3rd c.); confidence high for use to the 3rd c., medium for the 1st-c. foundation.

Abandonment: 'Majduliyya was abandoned in the late third century CE' (HA-ESI 134, 2022): coins and pottery from the dwelling complex in Area M assign its last phase to the 3rd c.; a screw-press structure yielded a coin of the mid-3rd c.; the pottery kiln and the screw press (one of the earliest of its type in the region) belong to the Late Roman phase. BibleWalks: last coin of 270 CE; BAS 2014: abandoned at the end of the 3rd or beginning of the 4th c. for an unknown reason; IEJ 70: did not continue into the Byzantine period (brief Early Islamic and Mamluk reuse). M. Eisenberg & M. Osband (ARAM 2022/24, as cited at deadseaquake.info) place the broader settlement decline in the Hippos region in the late 3rd-mid 4th c. Gives a firm negative datum: this Jewish village ended c. 270-300, before the 5th-6th c. flowering of other Golan villages. Year 270 = last coin / late 3rd c.; confidence high.

Iron Age (span given by source 1000-580 BCE; used from Iron Age IIA start): part of an enclosure and a gate structure found by Mader (1920s) and re-examined by Magen (1980s); generally associated with the Judean kings but debated. [Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Replaces first-pass row: Kloner and Zissu (Hypogea 2015 preview) say the city flourished in the Hellenistic period, with Upper City (tell), Lower City and Subterranean City; the Lower City was mainly built up in the Hellenistic period; necropolis with 40+ rock-cut tombs used throughout the 3rd and 2nd c. BCE. Tomb inscriptions show Idumeans, Phoenicians (Sidonians), Greeks, some Egyptians and 'possibly a few Judeans' (Kloner and Zissu). Ian Stern (BAR 2013, BAS summary) describes a community of Idumeans, Judeans, Phoenicians and Arabs with nearly two dozen bath-chambers that may be ritual baths, hundreds of perforated vessels and aniconic Qos depictions: suggestive of Judean-like purity practice but not proof of a Jewish city. Zissu and Kloner 2019 (Cornucopia, Arthur Segal volume) discuss population estimation for residences in Areas 53, 61, 930 but the abstract gives no figure. Population blank.

That is a whole-city figure for a mostly Idumean, Phoenician and Greek city, not a Jewish population, so Population blank. Hebrew Wikipedia: Hellenistic polis and capital of Idumaea; Heliodorus inscription of Seleucus IV (178 BCE).

Judas Maccabeus burned the city c. 163/2 BCE (Wikipedia). Wikipedia notes Hyrcanus-era reoccupation is very meager and that circumcised phalli found predate the conquest, challenging Josephus's forced-conversion story (Stern 2012, Strata 30, as cited). Kloner and Zissu: city destroyed by the Hasmoneans c. 111 BCE; ynet: city declined after conquest. People: Idumean, Phoenician and Greek city; Jewish only through conversion of Idumeans (Josephus) or a few Judeans; no named-scholar Jewish population estimate, Population blank.

Hebrew Wikipedia says a sparse settlement continued into the 2nd c. CE and underground complexes served as Bar-Kokhba-revolt hideouts; BAS (Stern) found Roman-period lamps and a casserole in a subterranean complex. Thin settlement; Population blank, no estimate.

Josephus lists Meroth among the Upper Galilean places he fortified in 66 CE (War 2.20.6; Life 188) and as the northern end of Upper Galilee's length ('from Meloth to Thella', War 3.3.1). Z. Ilan and E. Damati identify Meroth with Khirbet Marus (Horvat Marish), 7 km NE of Safed; the older identifications were Maroun al-Ras and Meiron (Meyers originally proposed Meiron, later accepted Ilan's view per BAR 1989). First occupied in the 2nd c. BCE; defensive wall, hewn moat and refuge tunnels possibly Second Temple. Dating basis: literary (Josephus) plus survey. Confidence medium (identification disputed; marker is the Khirbet Marus site).

Wikipedia 'Meroth': an ancient synagogue 'built in the late 4th or early 5th century' (midpoint 400), a related bet midrash dated to the 7th century, a cache of coins from the 5th to 9th centuries; village 7 km NE of Safed; Josephus (first century) called it a border town and fortified it, and Zvi Ilan proposed identifying Marus with Meroth. Hamichlol: the synagogue was founded in the late 4th century and used from c. 450. Archaeological (coins/stratigraphy). Identification Marus = Meroth is proposed, not certain. Marker named 'Marot' (the Hamichlol/Hebrew name) on purpose: the map already has a different 'Meroth' marker about 10 km to the west (35.4086, 32.9919), apparently Josephus' Meroth near Meron, which is not merged with this site (35.528, 33.029).

Population estimate: Ilan's survey/excavation summary (as given in the EPI-IDENTITY database): at its peak the settlement covered roughly 10-12 acres and likely accommodated approximately 1,000-1,200 inhabitants (Population column = midpoint 1,100 of that stated range). The source does not date the 'peak'; year 450 is a conventional placement in the Byzantine period (synagogue 4th/5th-12th c.). Economy: olive oil, wine, cereals, cattle. Confidence low-medium.

Third (flagstone) floor of the Marus synagogue dated 'quite accurately' to about 475 CE by the latest of hundreds of coins placed beneath and between the flagstones; it replaced a mosaic floor (second floor) laid about 25 years after the original plaster floor. Dating basis: coins. Confidence high (Ilan & Damati).

Synagogue at Khirbet Marus (Marot) in Upper Galilee, excavated by Z. Ilan and E. Damati 1983-89: the excavators dated the first phase of the building to the end of the 4th/beginning of the 5th c.; finds include benches and columns, an amulet, a coin hoard and mosaic fragments; zodiac slabs reported from Meroth. Identification caveat: Josephus' fortified Meroth is placed by some at Marus and by others at Marun er-Ras (Lebanon) or Meiron - conjectural. Dating basis: excavators' stratigraphy (as quoted by Leibner 2009). Year 400.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for this period: stronger statement of the evidence. Josephus (War 7.8.3) says Jonathan the High-priest first built a fortress on the summit and called it Masada; excavators have not found Hasmonean buildings. NEAEHL (Netzer and Stiebel 1995-2000 summit excavations) says whether parts of Masada were built in the Hasmonean period 'remains an open question': cisterns 2006 and 2007 'may date to the Hasmonean period' (plaster analysis by Porath) but soundings in the Western Palace and small palaces in 1989 and 1995-2000 yielded no supporting pottery; the AJA 124.3 (2020) review of Magness calls the Hasmonean foundation debatable. No population stated; no evidence of a resident community, so Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds named excavation reports and the Josephus text. Herod built the fortress as a refuge (Jewish Virtual Library gives 37-31 BCE); NEAEHL reports three Herodian building phases in the northern complex from floors and assemblages found by Netzer and Stiebel (1995-2000) and an amphora fragment naming 'Herod king of Judea'. Residents: Herod's court and a Roman garrison, then Jewish rebels (Sicarii under Menahem, with refugees) from 66 CE until the fall in 73/74 CE. Jewish evidence: Zealots' ritual bath (miqveh 1301) and a structure used as the Zealots' synagogue (NEAEHL); two miqva'ot and a synagogue in Yadin's 1963-65 excavation (Jewish Virtual Library); Hebrew and Aramaic ostraca incl. the 'Room of the Lots' (NEAEHL). Josephus (War 7.9.1): the last besieged group was 'nine hundred and sixty in number: the women, and children being withal included' - a count of the besieged at the end, treated as a garrison/casualty figure under the brief, so Population left blank. Excavations found only about 25-28 skeletons (Jewish Virtual Library; Hebrew Wikipedia). Stiebel's 2017 Tel Aviv University season found remains of a First Revolt refugee camp (Area A).

Event: the Sicarii stronghold of Masada, held by rebels and resident Jewish families, fell to the Roman siege (breach on 16 April 73 by the traditional dating; a later date, late 73 to early 74, has been proposed). Wikipedia gives the strength inside as 967 including non-combatants; per Josephus 960 died in a mass suicide and 7 (2 women, 5 children) were captured. The suicide account rests on Josephus alone. The 967/960 figures are a besieged-group and casualty count, so Population is left blank (same treatment as the existing Masada -63 to 70 row, which this row complements). The LIST p. 23, ref 73.1 gives the same 960.

Solomon/Omride dating of the Iron IIA buildings (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -960 = conventional date of Solomon's reign). 1 Kgs 9:15 (Solomon's levy built the house of the Lord, his palace, Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer); 1 Kgs 4:12 (Megiddo in Baana's district together with Taanach and Beth-shean, 'to the place beyond Jokneam'). Archaeology (Wikipedia, Tel Megiddo): the six-chambered gate 2156 (Stratum VA-IVB) was long attributed to Solomon (Yadin); Finkelstein and the Tel Aviv expedition date it to the Omrides, c. 886-835 BCE (late Iron IIA), and the stables of Stratum IVA to Ahab's time (two complexes, 450-480 horses); Bruins (2023, IntCal20 recalibration) puts the founding of Stratum VB in the 10th century (medians 961 and 928 cal BCE) and Stratum VA-IVB in the Omride period (865-857 cal BCE). The destruction of Stratum V is ascribed to Shoshenq I c. 926 BCE (Yadin, Mazar) or to Hazael c. 835 BCE (Finkelstein). Who built what is therefore chronology-dependent (high versus low chronology). No population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Kings+9&version=KJV ; https://www.biblewalks.com/megiddo

Event: exiles brought to Megiddo after the Assyrian conquest of 732 BCE (undated). After Tiglath-pileser III took Megiddo it became the capital of an Assyrian province and was rebuilt with a governor's palace and well-planned residential quarters; Na'aman says there is no doubt that exiles were brought to this provincial capital, at an unknown time, and that the Assyrians probably did the same at other places (he cites the Assyrian administrative building found at Ayyelet ha-Shahar near Tel Hazor). In his summary he adds that the excavations of Megiddo, Samaria and Ashdod give only scant archaeological evidence for exiles brought from afar, so the written sources count for more than the finds. Online: Wikipedia 'Tel Megiddo' says "Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Megiddo in 732 BCE, turning it to the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire's province of Magiddu" but does not mention exiles; Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) says Megiddo, the provincial capital, was rebuilt with a governor's palace and planned residential quarters and that exiles were brought to it, and that an Assyrian administrative building was found at Ayyelet ha-Shahar near Tel Hazor. The existing Megiddo rows (-745 to -610, -722 to -587) already record the conquest and the administrative centre; this row only adds the exiles. Year -732 is the conquest, the arrival of exiles is undated. Population blank. Confidence low-medium.

Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Meyers' excavation found Hellenistic remains at the foundation of ancient Meiron (7 layers Hellenistic to Mamluk per Hebrew Wikipedia); the sources say only 'Hellenistic' without a sub-period so this row is a coarse placement. Inhabitants culturally tied to Tyre and southern Syria (en.wikipedia Meiron); ethnicity not established. IDENTIFICATION DOUBTFUL: the Meiron site (Khirbet Meiron) vs Khirbet Marus / Horvat Marish near Hazor (Ilan and Damati) as Josephus' Meroth; Hebrew Wikipedia says Meyers proposed Maroth=Meiron. Coordinates are Meiron as given. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): the first-pass placement in Early Hellenistic is not supported by the sources fetched. Meyers (in Stern et al., NEAEHL 1993, as tabulated on deadseaquake.info) dates Meiron Stratum I to 200-50 BCE: 'scattered artifactual remains; traces of structures'. Encyclopedia.com (Meron, Encyclopaedia Judaica) says only a small settlement in the late Hellenistic period (ca. 200-63 BCE). The source range 200-50 BCE overlaps the end of the Early Hellenistic period and the Hasmonean period, so it is placed here by the larger part of its range. Inhabitants not specified; no evidence of Jews in this phase; Population blank. IDENTIFICATION NOTE: Encyclopedia.com states no fortification of Josephus's Meroth was found at Meiron and the excavators abandoned the identification; Meroth is placed at Marus (Ilan and Damati excavation, 1980s). A BAS Library article footnote (Meroth synagogue) says Meyers changed his mind and accepts that view. Hebrew Wikipedia likewise prefers Khirbet Marus. The coordinates given are of Meiron as instructed.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for Early Roman: Meyers dates Stratum II to 50 BCE-135 CE with 'limited architecture', a small, growing village; his population 'grew steadily from late Hellenistic times' (NEAEHL 1993 via deadseaquake.info). Encyclopedia.com: the Early Roman period left even fewer remains than the late Hellenistic. Jewish character: the fetched sources give no miqveh, stone vessel or inscription specifically dated before 70 CE; the ritual baths (Hebrew Wikipedia) and synagogue belong to Strata III-IV (135-365 CE); the priestly family Jehoiarib tradition (Mishnah Ta'anit 4:2) is rabbinic and not proof for this period. Josephus (War 2.573) lists Meroth among the Upper Galilee places fortified; see identification note in the first row (Meroth probably Marus, not Meiron). Population blank: no named-scholar estimate for the Jewish population of Meiron before 70 CE found.

Wikipedia 'Simeon bar Yochai': a 2nd-century tanna (born c. 90, died 160) who 'settled afterward at Meron' after thirteen years in a cave; his and his son Eleazar's burial at Meron is Tosefta Demai 4:13 tradition per Encyclopaedia Judaica but, per Wikipedia 'Meron, Israel', the tomb's existence there is attested only from the 12th century. Jewish Encyclopedia ('Meron'): Meron was a city of priests (JT Ta'anit 4:5; Jehoiarib course), Meron and Giscala fought over the remains of R. Eliezer b. Simeon (Eccl. R. 11:3), and the Talmud uses Meron with Giscala as a boundary marker (JT Sheviit 9:2). Year 150 conventional (2nd century). Rabbinic-literary; tomb tradition is late.

Rabbinic tradition: the ministry of R. Shimon bar Yohai is placed at Meiron (Tosefta Dem. 4:13), and Meiron is named as the seat of the priestly course Jehoiarib (Mishnah Ta'anit 4:2; Tosefta Dem. 4:13). Dating basis: literary only; conventional year 150 = mid-2nd century floruit of bar Yohai. The tombs of bar Yohai/his son Eleazar, Hillel and Shammai at Meiron are first reported by Benjamin of Tudela (12th c.) and Samuel ben Samson (1210), so this is NOT archaeological confirmation. Confidence medium-low.

Ancient Meiron (Khirbet Meiron; this marker already holds Meiron's earlier rows), Stratum III, 135-250 CE (conventional year = midpoint 193): 'first major insula; village expansion' after the Bar Kokhba war. E. Meyers (NEAEHL): population grew steadily from Late Hellenistic times, especially after the wars with Rome; priestly families may have settled here after the destruction of the Temple. Excavations 1971-72, 1974-75, 1977 (Meyers, Strange, Meyers). Dating basis: stratigraphy, pottery, coins. Confidence medium. NB Josephus' fortified 'Meroth' (66 CE) is identified by Ilan with Khirbet Marus (separate marker 'Marus'); Meyers first proposed Meiron.

Large basilica-type 'Galilean' synagogue (eight columns per side, three-door southern facade, earliest of the Galilean type per Wikipedia). Excavators (Meyers, Strange, Meyers): built in Stratum IV (250-365 CE); Wikipedia: erected in the last decade of the 3rd century; year 270 = conventional midpoint of 250-290. Wikipedia: survived an earthquake in 306, severely damaged/destroyed by one in 409. J. Magness argues instead for construction in the late 4th, 5th and even 6th century; C. Spigel (BASOR 376, 2016) re-examined unpublished Khirbet Shema/Gush Halav data and supports the excavators' chronology. Dating basis: pottery, coins (Probus 276-282). Confidence medium; dating contested.

Peak of prosperity in Stratum IV: coin of Emperor Probus (276-282 CE) and African ceramics of the later 3rd century; coins mostly from Tyre (many also from Hippos) show a northern, Tyre-oriented economy (Meyers); olive oil famed in the Talmudic period (J.T. Shevi'it 38d), sheep-raising also mentioned in the Talmud; a 2nd-century tower still stands 5.5 m high. Dating basis: coins/ceramics. Confidence medium-high. No population figure given by the sources for the Roman period.

Synagogue: Wikipedia 'Meron, Israel' - 'In the last decade of the 3rd century CE, a synagogue was erected in the village' (one of the largest basilica-style Palestinian synagogues); a coin of Probus (276-282) and African ceramics of the latter half of the 3rd century suggest commercial prosperity; the synagogue 'survived an earthquake in 306 CE'. Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Meron'): dated to the 3rd century from rubble-foundation material, final use c. 363; Meyers' American team 1971-77 (publ. 1981), N. Feig's salvage excavation (publ. 2002); heyday ca. 135-363. Archaeological (coins/ceramics).

Meiron synagogue (Galilean-type basilica, eight columns each side), erected in the last decade of the 3rd c. according to Wikipedia: a coin of Probus (276-282) and African ceramics of the later 3rd c. were found; it survived an earthquake of 306 but was severely damaged or destroyed by one in 409; the same article says Meiron was abandoned in the 4th c. (internal tension). Excavated 1971-77 by E. and C. Meyers. Year 295 = late 3rd c.

Jewish village of the Mishnaic and Talmudic periods excavated in the 1970s; Pringle (cited by Wikipedia) describes it as a former Jewish village with a synagogue and tombs dated to the 3rd-4th c. The tradition that Hillel, Yohanan ha-Sandlar and Shimon bar Yochai are buried at Meron is attested only from the 12th c. Talmud mentions sheep rearing and olive oil. Year 300 = conventional 3rd/4th-c. boundary.

ESI preliminary report (Y. Tepper, 2014 salvage excavation in the Rabbi Shim'on Bar Yochai compound): the 1970s excavations (Meyers, Strange, Meyers 1981) determined that the Roman settlement was established in the 2nd c. CE and reached its zenith in the 3rd-4th c., the time in which the synagogue was constructed; Year 300 = zenith (conventional).

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Meron'): the great earthquake of 363 'contributed to the abandonment of the site' and the lower town was abandoned in the second half of the 4th century; the synagogue's final use was c. 363. Wikipedia '363 Galilee earthquake' lists Nabratein and Sepphoris, not Meron. Conflict: Wikipedia 'Meron, Israel' dates the severe damage/destruction to an earthquake of 409 and says the village was abandoned 'some time in the 4th century ... for reasons as yet unknown'. Archaeological; date conflict 363 vs 409.

End of Stratum IV and systematic abandonment: Meyers: conditions from the period of Gallus Caesar (351-352 CE) to the great earthquake of 363 CE led to abandonment; Stratum V (365-750 CE) = village largely abandoned (small finds of nomads/wayfarers). A thick destruction layer in the lower city and northern suburb (Russell 1980 would assign it to the 363 quake); Wikipedia: abandoned in the 4th century, a 409 quake damaged the synagogue. Dating basis: stratigraphy, coins. Confidence medium; excavators first said 'abandoned not destroyed'.

Wikipedia 'Meron, Israel': excavations indicate the synagogue/village was 'severely damaged or destroyed by another earthquake in 409 CE'; 'some time in the 4th century CE, Meron was abandoned for reasons as yet unknown'. Alternative to EJ's 363 abandonment date (see the 363 row). Archaeological; medium-low confidence.

comment: Samuel ben Samson, pilgrimage of 1210 (Adler, Jewish Travellers 1930): at Meron the party found the school and tomb of Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai and "In the city we found a tomb with a crown upon it as well as a very fine synagogue"; Wikipedia (Meron) notes the 1210 visit and that from the 13th century Meron became the most frequented Jewish pilgrimage site in Palestine. The book (ch. 2) says he found 20 Jews in Meron (and in Kisma and Gush Halav); Adler's text gives no count for Meron (listed in the conflicts file). Meron is on the book's 13th-century list of Galilean Jewish villages. Population blank. Confidence medium.

source: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader image 108 (Screenshot_20221028-101659.jpg), ch. 3 (Mamluk period), sec. ה.3 'The Jews' (villages from travellers) (e-reader page number not visible in the stitched screenshot, cited by image file)
comment: Presence (weak, century-only date): the book says another Jewish traveller toured the Galilee in the 14th century and reported a series of settlements 'mostly inhabited by Jews': Bar'am, Alma, Dalata (Dalton), Akbara, Sakhnin, Safed, Meron, Gush Halav, Julis and Beit She'an (the traveller is not named in the book and is not identified here; Year of Data 1300 is the start of the century, range 1300-1399). No online source found; source is the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew). Population blank.
