comment: Z. Vilnay wrote that in the 18th century a few Jews lived in the Arab village of Meiron (Muslims and Christians); his source is R. Yosef Sofer's visit in 1762 (book). no online source found; source is the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew). Confidence: medium.

comment: Five families of survivors of the Safed earthquake founded the village of Jarmaq on Mount Meron on the initiative of Israel Bak (book); Encyclopaedia Judaica: Bak's Hebrew press was moved after the earthquake to Kefar Jarmaq (Mount Meron). Confidence: high.

source: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader p. ~369-376 (image 132 (Screenshot_20221028-102958.jpg))
comment: Jarmaq (Mount Meron): Judith and Moses Montefiore visited on 23 May 1839 and recorded ten families; the book also says that in 1839 the village had 15 families from Russia (the two counts are not reconciled, so Population is left blank). no online source found; source is the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew). Confidence: low-medium.

source: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/מירון_(מושב) | Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader p. ~369-376 (image 132 (Screenshot_20221028-102958.jpg))
comment: Jewish farmers from Kurdistan settled in Meron from 1870 on land bought by Safed Jews led by the Abu family (Hebrew Wikipedia, Meron moshav). The book speaks of several dozen Kurdish Jewish families on about 7,000 dunams bought by Rabbi Shmuel Abu to return Jews to farming (its text mixes this with the 1762 visit). Confidence: medium-high.

source: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/מירון_(מושב) | Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader p. ~369-376 (image 132 (Screenshot_20221028-102958.jpg))
comment: Laurence Oliphant (1883): much of the village belonged to R. Yaakov Abu, who settled six Jewish families from Morocco there; 12 Muslim families also lived in Meron and relations between Jews and Arabs were friendly. Michael Goldschmidt reported in HaMagid (1883) Jewish families supported by a rabbi encouraging settlement; the book adds that in HaHavatzelet Rabbi Shmuel Abu appealed to Jews to return to farming in the Land of Israel, citing the land he bought at Meron and its spring (Hebrew Wikipedia mentions the 1883 Oliphant and Goldschmidt reports). Population = 6 x 5. Confidence: high.

comment: A pioneer reported in 1892 that Maghrebi (North African) Jews lived in Meron and that half the village belonged to Sephardim (book). no online source found; source is the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew). Confidence: medium.

city_other: תל מרים (Tel Maryam) / מעלה מכמש (settlement) / مخماس (Mukhmas)
comment: Literary mention; Saul and Jonathan, dated by convention c. -1020. 1 Sam 13:2 (Saul with 2,000 in Michmash and mount Beth-el), 1 Sam 13:5 (the Philistines pitch in Michmash, eastward from Beth-aven), 1 Sam 14:5 (the crag Bozez and Seneh over against Michmash/Gibeah), 1 Sam 14:31 (the rout from Michmash to Aijalon), Isa 10:28 (the approach of an Assyrian army: Aiath, Migron, 'at Michmash he layeth up his carriages'). Identification: Mukhmas in the West Bank, which preserves the ancient name (English Wikipedia 'Michmas'); it lies on the north side of the Wadi es-Suweinit, across from Jaba' (Geba). The Israeli settlement Ma'ale Mikhmas is named after it. Not disputed.

comment: Babylonian / Persian (-586 to -332). Textual not archaeological: sources say after the exile the men of Michmash returned (Ezra/Neh tradition; en.wikipedia Michmash and he.wikipedia). No archaeological evidence for this period found in fetched pages. No population estimate. Judean returnees. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/מכמש

city_other: תל מרים (Tel Maryam) / מעלה מכמש (settlement) / مخماس (Mukhmas)
comment: [Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): Textual only. Ezra 2:27 and Neh 7:31 list returnees, men of Michmas (Wikipedia Michmas; Carta). No excavation report or survey data found for this period. Jewish (Benjaminite) returnees by the lists. Population blank.

city_other: תל מרים (Tel Maryam) / מעלה מכמש (settlement) / مخماس (Mukhmas)
comment: [Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass absence. 1 Maccabees 9:73 (c. 160 BCE): after the peace with Bacchides, Jonathan dwelt at Michmas and began to govern the people (Times of Israel; Hebrew Wikipedia; Carta). Archaeology: the 1980s Benjamin Region Survey recorded four clusters of tombs, about 70 burial caves, at Mukhmas; one has a seven-branched menorah graffito, published by Dvir Raviv, Strata 36 (2018) 87-99; the press dates such menorahs about 150 BCE to 136 CE, and Raviv cautions that the dating is hard and a priestly group may have arrived only between the revolts. Mishnah Menahot 8:1 names Michmas as a source of fine flour for the Temple. Jewish settlement likely (Raviv suggests a priestly agricultural settlement). No population estimate; Population blank. Identification: Hebrew Wikipedia puts the biblical city at Tel Miryam / Khirbet el-Hara el-Fauqa on the northern edge of the village.

city_other: תל מרים (Tel Maryam) / מעלה מכמש (settlement) / مخماس (Mukhmas)
comment: [Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass absence. The same tomb clusters (about 70 burial caves) and menorah graffito are dated by Raviv (Strata 2018) to between the Hasmonean era and the Bar Kokhba revolt; his abstract suggests the village of Mukhmas was a priestly settlement during the Second Temple period (a suggestion, not settled). Mishnah Menahot 8:1; Wikipedia reports the village inhabited until Bar Kokhba and an ossuary inscribed Shimeon L[evi] bought from the village in the 1990s (not independently verified). Eusebius (Onomasticon) calls it a large village. Population blank: no scholar's estimate.

Literary only (conventional date -1200: Joshua's allotment). Middin is in the wilderness group of Judah: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah (Josh 15:61, 'six cities with their villages'). Identification disputed, favoured: Khirbet Abu Tabaq in the north of the Hyrcania/Buqe'ah valley, proposed by 'some scholars' (Hebrew Wikipedia); the page notes that no extra-biblical source or archaeological find confirms the city's existence. Coordinates are Khirbet Abu Tabaq. No population figure. Further sources: https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Joshua.15?context=0&commentary=0&lang=en&version=english%7CThe%20Holy%20Scriptures%20by%20Jewish%20Publication%20Society%201917

comment: Literary only (Benjamin's city list, dated by convention to the Joshua / tribal-allotment narrative c. -1200). Josh 18:26 (Mizpeh, Chephirah and Mozah). Identification: Tel Moza (Khirbet Beit Mizza), on the outskirts of Jerusalem next to Motza, is the customary identification of biblical Mozah (English Wikipedia 'Tel Motza'; Hebrew Wikipedia 'Motza': 'the place is customarily identified with Mozah of Joshua 18:21-28'). Oded Lipschits (2019) has proposed that Kiriath-jearim was actually at Motza - a minority view. The Iron Age archaeology is in the next row. The existing Motza rows cover only the Persian and Early Roman periods.

city_other: מוצא; תל מוצא; חירבת מזיזה / قالونيا (Qalunya); خربة ميزة (Khirbet Mizza)
comment: Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900 by the conventional chronology; the Hebrew source dates the settlement to about the 9th century BCE). Tel Moza: three excavation seasons in 1993-2003 uncovered an Iron Age IIA settlement (public building, storehouses and silos); salvage excavations in 2012 (IAA: Shua Kisilevitz, Zvi Greenhut, Anna Eirikh-Rose) exposed a temple with an east-facing entrance and a cache of cult vessels and figurines, dated to the 9th c. BCE, i.e. a Judahite cult site alongside the Jerusalem Temple (Hebrew Wikipedia 'Moza temple'; English Wikipedia 'Tel Motza': Iron Age Israelite settlement c. 1000 to 500 BCE). Jar-handle stamps reading 'Moza' in Aramaic script are customarily dated to the early Babylonian period after 586 BCE (Hebrew Wikipedia 'Motza'). Judahite. No population estimate found.

city_other: מוצא; תל מוצא; חירבת מזיזה / قالونيا (Qalunya); خربة ميزة (Khirbet Mizza)
comment: Persian (-539 to -332). Biblical Mozah of Benjamin (Josh 18:26). EVIDENCE CONFLICTS: Hadran says seals from early Second Temple times at Jericho and Gibeon bear the name Motza, implying a community; BAR (endnote) says two structures excavated 2012-2013 'may have continued into the Babylonian and perhaps early Persian periods (586-332 BCE)', tentative; en.wikipedia and hamichlol give 'Persian/Hellenistic' sherds (about 8-16% of the 1973/2001-3 sherd count) without separating them; but the NEAEHL Moza entry lists no Persian stratum (Iron IIC goes straight to Hellenistic). Population blank: Jewish presence plausible (Yehud) but no estimate. Identification note: Tel Moza (Khirbet Mizza) vs Qalunya/Colonia area; the coordinates are for Motza.

city_other: מוצא; תל מוצא; חירבת מזיזה / قالونيا (Qalunya); خربة ميزة (Khirbet Mizza)
comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70). NEAEHL: Early Roman settlement remains found by E. Eisenberg in 1973 near the highway; Mishnah Sukkah 4:5 and Talmud name Motza/Kolonia as a Temple-time willow source; seetheholyland (Bivin) says excavations revealed an upper-class first-century Jewish village (not corroborated by any other fetched page). Jewish population likely, but no stated estimate. After the revolt Vespasian settled 800 veterans at Ammaus/Emmaus 30 stadia (some texts 60) from Jerusalem (Josephus BJ 7.217), usually identified with Colonia Moza, settlement c. 70-130 CE (Ad, Bar-Nathan, Taxel 2022; earliest phase 'shortly after AD 70', so no pre-70 phase of that settlement); noted for context only, post-70. Emmaus identification disputed (Thiede for Moza; Emmaus-Nicopolis, Abu Ghosh). Population blank.

The Haganah had offered protection to the village beforehand.

Biblical mention and cult site (literary only; Year of Data -860 = conventional date of Elijah under Ahab, who reigned c. 874-853; new marker, nearest marker Yagur 2.7 km, unrelated). 1 Kgs 18:19-20 (Ahab gathers Israel and the prophets of Baal to Mount Carmel); 1 Kgs 18:30-40 (Elijah repairs the broken altar of the Lord, fire consumes the sacrifice, the prophets of Baal are slain at the brook Kishon); 2 Kgs 4:25 (the Shunammite goes to the man of God at Mount Carmel). Identification: the Carmel range, 32.733 N 35.05 E (Wikipedia), certain; the exact place of Elijah's altar is not archaeologically fixed: tradition and BibleWalks favour Keren-Carmel (Muhraqa) or Khirbet Dubbah on the next hill, L. Oliphant (1883) proposed Khirbet Din; BibleWalks reports no Iron Age altar or finds there and a nearly empty Carmel in biblical times. Wikipedia: Carmel was a sanctuary of Hadad/Baal-shamin (some scholars, e.g. Avi-Yonah, think the Baal of the story was Hadad rather than Melqart) and may have been sacred since the 15th c. BCE (Maspero). So this is a literary-only row for a cult site (disputed, favoured: Muhraqa for the altar). No population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/carmel_gallery/KerenCarmel ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Kings+18&version=KJV ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2+Kings+4&version=KJV

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Ritual enclosure 'el-Burnat' on the north-eastern spur of Mount Ebal at 785 m (summit about 940 m), found on 6 April 1980 in Adam Zertal's Manasseh Hill Country Survey and excavated from autumn 1982 to 1989: an 8-shaped enclosure about 230 m long and 25-100 m wide (about 14 dunams per BibleWalks), with a smaller inner area of about 4 dunams, and inside it a stone-built structure 9 x 7 m (about 4 m high, filled with ash and stones, with a ramp and two paved courtyards); two Iron I strata separated by a time gap. Zertal dated the site to the last quarter of the 13th c. BCE and identified the structure as Joshua's altar (Deut 27:4-8, Josh 8:30-35; the blessings and curses of Deut 11:29). Disputed: the great majority of archaeologists reject the altar identification (Zertal's view is almost his alone) while most accept an Iron I cultic site; whether its users were proto-Israelites or Canaanites is debated, and no final excavation report was published. The site is certain, the biblical identification of the structure is not. A cult place, not a town: no population figure. The coordinates (Hebrew Wikipedia) are 2.8 km from the existing Shechem marker.

Literary only (no Iron Age remains are reported in the fetched pages); narrative dated by convention to the entry into Canaan c. -1200 and to the Judges period. Deut 11:29 (the blessing put upon Mount Gerizim, the curse upon Ebal), Deut 27:12 (six tribes stand on Gerizim to bless), Josh 8:33 (half of Israel over against Mount Gerizim), Judg 9:7 (Jotham stands on the top of Mount Gerizim and tells the fable of the trees to the men of Shechem). English Wikipedia ('Mount Gerizim'): Jotham's fable is 'the first parable in the Bible'. The cult site is later (Persian-Hellenistic Samaritan temple; existing rows). Gerizim is a mountain, not a settlement: no population figure.

Persian (-539 to -332): Samaritan sacred precinct (temple) built mid-5th c. BCE (NEAEHL and Wikipedia: c. 450 BCE; Hebrew sources: late 5th c.); precinct c. 96x96 m (98x96 m) with a gate of six chambers. Used by Samaritans; no Jewish population. A city around the temple began only at the end of the 4th c. BCE; no estimate for the Persian phase.

Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Samaritan city grows around the temple from the end of the 4th c. BCE; temple rebuilt on a larger scale c. 200 BCE (212x136 m precinct). Population blank (not Jewish; Samaritan). Published estimates for the Samaritan city, in Notes only: BibleWalks says the city covered 400 dunams (40 ha) with a population of 10,000, mostly priests; Hebrew Wikipedia/Hamichlol says 400 dunams of urban structures indicating about 10,000 inhabitants (Magen excavations 1982-2003); English Wikipedia gives c. 500x800 m. No evidence of Jews.

Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Samaritan city flourished in the 2nd c. BCE (peak) until John Hyrcanus I destroyed temple and city; coin evidence dates the destruction c. 110 BCE (NEAEHL, Wikipedia) rather than c. 128 BCE (Josephus-based dating given by Bible Odyssey and Samaritans.net). Samaritan, not Jewish; population blank. Early Roman period: precinct abandoned until the 5th c. CE (a Zeus temple only from c. 160 CE), so no Early Roman row.

Literary mention; Solomon's high places, dated by convention c. -960. 1 Kgs 11:7 (Solomon builds a high place for Chemosh and for Molech 'in the hill that is before Jerusalem'), 2 Kgs 23:13 (Josiah defiles the high places 'that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption', built by Solomon for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom). Hebrew Wikipedia ('Mount of Olives') takes 'the mount of corruption' (Har ha-Mashhit) as probably a corruption of 'Mount of Anointing' (Har ha-Mishha), another name of the Mount of Olives, and the Kings passages as referring to it (the identification of the hill 'before Jerusalem' with the Mount of Olives is an inference, not stated in the verses). Literary only.

Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Jewish rock-cut tombs on the slopes. Hebrew Wikipedia dates the Bnei Hezir tomb (priestly family inscription) to the Hasmonean period; Dominus Flevit excavation (Bagatti 1953-55) found a necropolis used from 136 BC (Terra Sancta/BibleWalks give 2nd century BC to 1st century AD). Burial ground only: Jewish (priestly families named in inscriptions). No settlement or population estimate in any fetched source.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Dominus Flevit necropolis (Bagatti) with kokh tombs and dozens of ossuaries mostly Jewish with inscriptions in Hebrew Greek and Aramaic plus a hoard of silver shekels of the Great Revolt (66-70 CE). Mishnah Parah: red heifer burned on the mount facing the Temple reached by a bridge over the Kidron; Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:5 mentions shops selling sacrificial doves on the mount; the new-month announcement held there. Josephus (War 5.2.3 = 5.70) Titus ordered the Tenth Legion to camp on the mount 6 furlongs east of the city; Josephus also reports the 'Egyptian' prophet's followers gathering there under Felix (War 2.261-263). Burial and ritual site not a town: no resident population; Jewish. Population blank; no source estimate (Wikipedia gives about 150000 graves today only).

city_other: הר קרנטל (Har Qarantal) / جبل القرنطل / جبل الأربعين (Jabal al-Arba'in); Dayr al-Qarantal; Latin Mons Quarantana
comment: Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Dok (Dagon in Josephus) fortress on Jebel Qarantal existed by 135 BCE when Simon the Hasmonean and two sons were murdered there by Ptolemy son of Abubus/Habubu (1 Macc 16:11-16); Wikipedia says Bacchides fortified it earlier; Hasmonean-period remains found; water system of aqueduct two pools and nine pits (Meshel and Amit survey 1972). Jewish (Hasmonean) military fortress; no population estimate. Identification Dok = Jebel Qarantal is standard; Encyclopedia.com places it about 5 km north of Jericho and ties the name to nearby 'Ayn Duq.

city_other: הר הצופים (Har HaTsofim) / Jabal al-Mushrif / Ras al-Mushrif / Jabal Scopus
comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Jewish burial necropolis north-east of Jerusalem. Abu-Raya and Zissu ('Atiqot 40 2001) describe three burial caves used by Jewish family groups for about 150 years in the late Second Temple period and apparently ceasing in 70 CE. Nicanor Cave (found 1902 now the Botanical Garden; courtyard and five room complexes; ossuary inscribed Nicanor linked to Nicanor of Alexandria donor of a Temple gate; Hebrew University). Nazirite tomb (1967 Avigad) with ossuaries of Hanania son of Jonathan the Nazirite. Kloner and Whetstone 2016 publish a Second Temple burial complex with ossuaries. IAA found a Second Temple stone-vessel (chalk) workshop in a cave on the eastern slope with miqveh water reservoirs and quarry. Josephus (War 2.19.4 or 2.528) records Cestius Gallus camped on Scopus 7 furlongs from the city in 66 CE; War 5.2.3 (5.67-70) records Titus camping two legions there in 70 CE. This was a necropolis and military camp site not a town: no resident population; Jewish identity shown by ossuary inscriptions and Jewish stone vessels. Population blank: no source estimate.

Biblical mention and identification (literary only; Year of Data -1100 = conventional date of the Judges period; new marker, 1.7 km from the Daberath marker and 2.7 km from Kefar Tavor, different places). Josh 19:22 (Issachar's border reaches Tabor, Shahazimah and Beth-shemesh); Judg 4:6, 4:12, 4:14 (Barak gathers 10,000 men of Naphtali and Zebulun on Mount Tabor, Sisera is told he has gone up, Barak goes down from it to defeat him); Judg 8:18 (Zebah and Zalmunna asked about the men they slew at Tabor); 1 Sam 10:3 (the plain of Tabor); 1 Chr 6:77 (Tabor, a Levitical city of the Merarites in Zebulun, possibly a town near the mountain); Hos 5:1 ('a net spread upon Tabor'). Identification: Mount Tabor, 613 m, 32.6872 N 35.3903 E, certain (Wikipedia; BibleWalks); it marked the border of Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali. No Iron Age finds or fortification are reported for the summit (Wikipedia; BibleWalks name only Hellenistic/Roman and later remains), so this is a literary-only row for a landmark and battle site, not a settlement; no population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/tabor/ ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges+4&version=KJV ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges+8&version=KJV ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hosea+5&version=KJV

Itabyrion/Mount Tabor, one of the sites fortified by Josephus in 66 (Life 188; Wars 2:573, 4:54-61), where Galilean Jews held out against a Roman force of 600 horsemen under Placidus sent by Vespasian in 67. Dating basis: Josephus. Confidence high. Framing row.

After the destruction of the Second Temple 'Jewish settlement on Mount Tabor was renewed' (Wikipedia, unreferenced sentence); a Byzantine church of the 5th/6th c. later stood on the peak (Origen 3rd c. first identified the Transfiguration with Tabor), EJ notes remains of an earlier (Jewish?) wall. Conventional year (post-70). Dating basis: literary/uncertain. Confidence low.

No online source found; source is the attached book (scholarly, Hebrew). (Adler's abbreviated English translation of Meshullam has no Nablus passage.) The book adds that the 1525/6 census does not cover the Nablus area and that Jews were not mentioned in the next census (1533/9), giving about 420 Jews in the Nablus sanjak at the end of Mamluk rule; Beider reports 71 Jewish households in Nablus in 1538/39 (see conflicts file).

Midpoint of the century (1550) used as a conventional year. No online source found (the Wikipedia article on Nablus has nothing on 16th-century Jews); weak item.

Wikipedia 'Nabratein synagogue': Meyers' excavators dated the first synagogue to the Middle Roman period (135-250; midpoint 192 used), rebuilt in the Late Roman period (250-350/363). Doubts: Jodi Magness argues for a single synagogue not built before the second half of the 4th century. Nabratein = Talmudic Kefar Neburaya (Wikipedia; EJ identifies Khirbat al-Nabratayn, ~4 km N of Safed); Eleazar of Modi'im and Jacob of Kfar Neburaya are said to be buried there. Archaeological (stratigraphy); date disputed.

Synagogue 1 (Period II, Middle Roman, ca. 135-250 CE; conventional year = midpoint 192): four-column broadhouse with the Ark on the western bema (Meyers & Meyers 2009; excavations 1980-81). Phasing is debated: J. Magness (BASOR 358, 2010) holds that only one synagogue existed, built no earlier than the second half of the 4th century; Meyers & Meyers (BASOR 359) reply. Dating basis: stratigraphy/pottery/coins. Confidence low-medium.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Kefar Neburaya'): Jacob of Kefar Neburaya was a 'popular preacher of the third century c.e.' who often clashed with the rabbinic authorities and was suspected of heresy (JT Yevamot 2:5); the village is identified with Khirbat al-Nabratayn, about 4 km north of Safed; synagogue about 17 x 12 m, facade facing Jerusalem, lintel with a menorah in a wreath. Rabbinic-literary.

Synagogue rebuilt/enlarged in the Late Roman period: 'Synagogue 2a' 250-306 and 'Synagogue 2b' 306-350/363 according to the 1980-81 excavators (Meyers). Year 300 = approximate boundary of the two phases.

Synagogue 2 (Period III, Late Roman, ca. 250-363 CE; 2a ca. 250-306, 2b ca. 306-363; conventional year = midpoint 306): six-column basilica, enlarged and embellished in the later 3rd century, with a Torah Shrine at the south end (reconstructed on the western bema or against the south wall) (Meyers & Meyers 2009). The village was Jewish (Y. Conventional year (time of Jesus, c. 30). Dating basis: archaeological estimate (settlement area/density). Confidence low-medium; upper bound. Whole village = Jewish.

Strange (Meyers & Strange 1981) of 'roughly 1,600 to 2,000 people' for Nazareth at the time of Jesus (value entered = midpoint 1,800 of that range); later revised downwards by Strange himself to a maximum of about 480 (see other row). Conventional year (c. 30). Dating basis: archaeological estimate. Confidence low (superseded).

A marble fragment of a list of the 24 priestly courses from a synagogue at Caesarea (found 1962), dated c. AD 300 (late 3rd-early 4th c.), assigns the course Hapizzez to Nazareth - the first non-Christian reference to Nazareth - showing a Jewish (priestly) Nazareth. Dating basis: palaeography. Year 300.

Priestly-courses inscription from Caesarea (Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine, caes0684; Avi-Yonah, IEJ 12, 1962): 'The 18th course Hapizzez - Nazareth'; Hebrew list of the localities where priestly courses settled after the destruction of the Temple. IIP gives the date range 200-500 CE (midpoint 350 used; 'terminus post quem 200, ante quem 500', no justification given on the page); Wikipedia 'Nazareth' dates the inscription 'late 3rd or early 4th century / c. AD 300' and calls it the first non-Christian reference to Nazareth. Epigraphic; the inscription records an older tradition of priestly settlement, so it proves Jewish (priestly) residence at Nazareth in late antiquity.

Epiphanius, Panarion 30.11.9-10 (Williams): Nazareth is one of the Jewish towns where 'there are no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians' and 'the rule of having no gentiles among them is observed especially at Tiberias, Diocaesarea, Sepphoris, Nazareth and Capernaum'; Count Joseph obtained an imperial rescript to build churches there (a 'church of Nazareth' is inferred from this passage, Wikipedia 'Nazareth': small church that may have enclosed a cave complex, early 4th century). Epiphanius met Joseph c. 355 (Wikipedia 'Joseph of Tiberias'); Panarion 374-377 (Wikipedia 'Nazareth' gives c. AD 375). Primary patristic source; medium confidence for the Jewish-only claim (Epiphanius' report).

Epiphanius, Panarion (c. 375): Nazareth counted among the towns devoid of a non-Jewish population (with Tiberias, Diocaesarea, Sepphoris, Capernaum); Wikipedia concludes the town stayed Jewish until the 7th c. Early-Roman Nazareth: Strange's earlier estimate of 1,600-2,000 inhabitants was revised to a maximum of about 480 (Meyers and Strange 1981; Anchor Bible Dictionary 1992) - a pre-70 figure, therefore not entered as a population.

Wikipedia 'Nazareth': the Byzantine church at the site of Mary's house was built in the mid-5th century and replaced an earlier Judeo-Christian 'synagogue-church'; Jerome (early 5th century) calls Nazareth a mere village (viculus). Archaeological/inferred; Jewish character of the earlier building is the excavators' interpretation (Bagatti).

Framing source just after the period: the Piacenza Pilgrim (c. 570; Jacobs translation) describes a synagogue in Nazareth containing the book in which Jesus learned his letters and a bench that Christians can move but Jews 'are entirely unable to move' (section 5), and notes 'In that city the Jewish women are of such beauty' and that 'there is little love between Christians and Jews'. Shows an active Jewish community in Nazareth in the 6th century (Wikipedia 'Nazareth': Heraclius expelled the Jews c. 630). Literary/pilgrim source; the miraculous detail is legend.

The Anonymous of Piacenza (c. 570) went from Sepphoris to Nazareth and saw in the Jewish synagogue the books from which Jesus learnt his letters and a bench he sat on; the Jews were expelled c. 630 under Heraclius. Jerome (early 5th c.) calls Nazareth a mere village (viculus). Literary evidence. Year 570.

comment: Iron Age (source gives no sub-period; start -1200 used as placeholder for Iron Age I). Hebrew Wikipedia: Khirbet Beit Nasib has an eastern ruin with Iron Age and earlier finds and a western ruin of Roman-Byzantine date; identified by Schwarz and PEF. Identification with Nezib (Josh 15:43) is the conventional one; excavation data are lacking. No population estimate found; left blank.

Literary only (conventional date -1200: Joshua's allotment). Nibshan, the City of Salt and En-gedi are 'six cities with their villages' of the wilderness group (Josh 15:62). Identification disputed, favoured: Khirbet el-Maqari in the south of the Hyrcania valley, proposed by Jozef Milik (Hebrew Wikipedia, which cites Encyclopaedia Miqra'it vol. 5). The page reports Israelite-period finds, a Hebrew ostracon, large pools (Ma'ar a-Tabaqa), dams and ancient agricultural installations, without dates or excavators. Dating caveat: the Buqe'ah group is dated 7th-early 6th c. by Gibson, Lewis and Taylor 2023 (see Secacah). Population none. Ancient Jewish village Nob (Nov), identified with Khirbet Nab (Mazra'at Nab) where the Israeli moshav Nov stands. IAA excavator Z. Daniel (HA-ESI 120, 2008): Nov 'is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud (Shebiit 4:10) among the list of forbidden towns in the vicinity of Sussita' (a trial dig at the edge of Tel Nov found an undated pool, outside the settlement boundary). Listed in the Mosaic of Rehob among the Hippos-territory villages (he.wikipedia 'Ketovet Rehov': Nov = Khirbet Nab). The Mosaic of Rehob baraita (late 3rd-6th c. CE; content close to late-2nd-c. rabbinic literature; full description in the Kefar Haruv row) lists it among nine places 'in the region of Susitha (Hippos)'. Year 250 conventional. Some decorated Ark pillars from Fiq are kept in Moshav Nov (Bornblum). Identification by name preservation. Confidence medium.

comment: Bronze Age (sub-period not specified by source; placed at Middle Bronze start): Hebrew and English Wikipedia state 2009 excavations (N. Golding-Meir for Hebrew Union College; J. Marcus for IAA) found Bronze Age occupation. Identification doubtful: most scholars say Kafr Ana (now Or Yehuda) but some say nearby Khirbat Kafr Juna, with Kafr Ana a Byzantine-period expansion. The NGSBA preliminary report of one 2009 excavation found only a Byzantine/Early Islamic cemetery. Canaanite. No population estimate found. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ono,_Benjamin; https://ngsba.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/Contract_archeology_or_yehuda_OrYehudaEng.pdf

source: Yankelevich, R., Cathedra 61, pp. 159 (n. 25), 164, 170 (entries 9 and 46) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kafr_%27Ana
comment: Jewish town in the Lod plain in the Talmudic period, with a Jewish majority. Yankelevich (entry 9, Ono, and entry 46, Lod; note 25): in the 4th century Ono was still regarded as a Jewish city in contrast to its gentile neighbour Lod (sources cited in n. 58: Leviticus Rabbah 23:5, Lamentations Rabbah 1:17, Babylonian Talmud Ketubot 111b 'from Lod to Ono', and the Jerusalem Talmud, Gittin 4:6, which names Oni as a Jewish place); in the time of R. Abbahu (c. 300) the gentile settlement of Lod harassed the Jewish settlement of Ono (the saying 'Lod to Ono' in Lam. Rabbah, on 'his neighbours shall be his foes'); and at the end of the 3rd century Ono was made a polis although most of its population was Jewish (one of the few poleis with a Jewish majority, like Sepphoris and Tiberias). Year 300 = midpoint of the paper's 'end of the 3rd century' and '4th century' statements (conventional). Presence/majority only, no figure: Population blank. Wikipedia 'Kafr 'Ana' identifies Ono with the site under Kafr 'Ana / Or Yehuda and says the Jewish classical writings mention it as formerly walled; it gives nothing on the 3rd-4th century Jewish character. The map's existing Ono rows are biblical (-2000 to -586). No online source found; source is a scholarly article (Hebrew). [confidence: medium] [Source detail: (identification of the site only)]

city_other: עפרה (ישוב מודרני בסמוך); האתר: טייבה / al-Taybeh (الطيبة)
comment: Literary only; Saul's wars with the Philistines, dated by convention c. -1020. Josh 18:23 (Ophrah in Benjamin's city list, with Parah and Avim), 1 Sam 13:17 (a Philistine raiding company turns 'unto the way that leadeth to Ophrah, unto the land of Shual'). Identification: Taybeh (Ramallah) - the 1882 Survey of Western Palestine suggested it as Ophrah of Benjamin and 'prominent scholars have backed this identification since then' (English Wikipedia 'Taybeh, Ramallah'); Wikipedia 'Ophrah' (from Easton) calls it 'probably identical with Ephron (2 Chr 13:19) and Ephraim (John 11:54)'; Epiphanius places it 5 miles east of Bethel. Not to be confused with Ophrah of the Abiezrites (Gideon, Judg 6:11), a city of Manasseh near Shechem identified with Fara'ata. The fetched Wikipedia pages report no Iron Age finds at Taybeh, so the Iron Age presence is literary only.

Jewish village in Leibner's Eastern Galilee survey (Parod = rabbinic Farod; the name is preserved - reliable identification): Table 11 size category C (11-20 dunams) from c. 50 BCE to 350 CE, then abandoned in the 4th c. (doubtful minor use c. 500-600). ESI 125 (Parod survey) states that Parod and Kefar Hananya continued and developed into Jewish settlements of the Mishnaic and Talmudic eras. A columbarium at Parod was converted to a burial cave in the Early Roman period. Dating basis: pottery survey. Year 250 = middle of the occupation range.

Leibner: the absence of Late Roman Red Ware of the second half of the 4th c. and the paucity of local Byzantine pottery show a sharp decline or abandonment of Parod not later than about the mid-4th c.; the larger part of the dated finds (50%) is KH1e, so the decline cannot be dated more precisely. A small settlement was probably renewed in the first half of the 6th c. (four clearly Byzantine vessels date from the beginning of the 6th c. or later), with no sign of a monumental public building. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 119-121. Conventional year (mid-4th c.). Dating basis: survey pottery. Confidence medium.

Josephus (War 3.3.1) names the village Baca as the border that separates Upper Galilee from the land of the Tyrians ('the breadth of Upper Galilee ... as far as the village Baca'); Wikipedia: 'thought to be Peki'in' (identification of Talmudic Peki'in with this village dates only from Ottoman times; other candidates exist). Dating basis: literary (Josephus, c. 67 CE framing); identification uncertain. Confidence low. The marker 'Peqi'in Hadasha' is the modern moshav next to the old village; this new marker is the old village (Buqei'a).

Ancient synagogue evidence at modern Peki'in (Buqei'a): carved stones reused in the 1873 synagogue show a menorah with lulav, etrog, shofar and incense shovel, a Torah shrine and a grapevine, dated late 2nd-early 3rd c. (Sukenik 1931; Huttenmeister 1977); a capital with two Hebrew dedicatory inscriptions ('about 1,800 years old', Roman period) was found in 2017. Identification caveat: scholars disagree whether the rabbinic Peki'in (R. Joshua b. Hananiah; Shimon bar Yochai) is this village. Style-based date, medium-low confidence. Year 200 = late 2nd/early 3rd c.

Stones with a menorah, incense shovel, shofar and lulav, and a stone with a conjectured depiction of a Torah ark, now displayed in the Peki'in synagogue (built 1873): evidence of an ancient (Late Roman and/or Byzantine) synagogue; unexcavated (surveyed by Ben-Zvi c. 1930). The documented Jewish community of Peki'in is attested only from the 16th century (Wikipedia), and the village named 'Peki'in' in the Tosefta (Sotah 7:9) may be a different place near Lod/Yavne (Hebrew encyclopedia), so continuity from antiquity is NOT established. Dating basis: iconography, imprecise (conventional year 400). Confidence low.

comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Josephus: Herod founded Phasaelis c. 8 BCE north of Jericho and named it for his brother Phasael (d. 40 BCE) in an arid valley made fertile; famous for palms and dates (Jewish Encyclopedia; Encyclopedia.com). Bequeathed to Salome then Livia; per Gofna later with Agrippa I and II until 70 CE. Israeli excavations 2011-2012 (Hebrew Wikipedia citing the Civil Administration archaeology unit) found a luxurious residence and a bathhouse; stone vessels and oil lamps indicate Jewish presence continuing to 70 CE. BibleWalks: aqueduct c. 6 km and 40x40x8 m reservoir. Population Jewish per stone-vessel evidence; no source gives a population estimate. Identification: Khirbet Fasayil is the accepted site; Hasmonean or earlier phases not attested in fetched pages.

Period approximate: Hebrew Wikipedia (surveys) says ancient building remains and cisterns with pottery from the 'Israelite period' through Ottoman times; no stratum or date given so Iron Age I start used as the start of the Israelite era (-1200 to -1000). Identification with Farata is common but disputed (Farata lies north of Wadi Qana; en Wikipedia/Wikipedia he note tribal-border doubts; alternative sites proposed). Home of Abdon son of Hillel (Judg 12:13) and Benaiah (David's warriors). No excavation or published population estimate found; population left blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirathon

Literary mention (period of the Judges, dated by convention c. -1100). Judg 12:13-15 (Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judges Israel eight years and is buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim 'in the mount of the Amalekites'), 2 Sam 23:30 (Benaiah the Pirathonite, one of David's thirty) and 1 Chr 27:14 (Benaiah, captain for the 11th month). Identification: Far'ata (Fara'ata), 10 km south-west of Shechem, identified with Pirathon already in the 14th c. by Ishtori Haparhi; a survey found building remains and pottery of the Israelite period, which supports the identification (Hebrew Wikipedia 'Pirathon'). Zeev Safrai disputes it because Far'ata lies north of Wadi Qana, i.e. in Manasseh, and proposes Farkha; Yehuda Elitzur answers that Ephraimite cities lay inside Manasseh (Josh 17) - disputed, favoured: Far'ata. No population figure.

Qasabiyye, Golan: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Many stones of a public building. Menorah, stone fragments with eagle (2 different stones), and head of a bull. Possibly the remains of a building (Urman and Flescher 1995: 484-485). The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Jewish settlement of the Talmudic period with an unlocated synagogue: column fragments, capitals, an eagle lintel with outspread wings and a stone with a carved menorah (he.wikipedia; Bornblum 'Qasabiyye': also a bull's head; surveyed 1971 and 1974/1986). Unexcavated; year 450 is a conventional date for undated Late Roman/Byzantine remains. Weak-moderate evidence.

Village continuity before the first synagogue: Stratum VI (Late Roman) has building remains with ceramic and numismatic finds, dated 3rd-4th c. by Z. Ma'oz (NEAEHL 1993) and 2nd-3rd c. by M. Eisenberg & M. Osband (ARAM 2022/2024, p. 169), who see continuity at Qasrin 'from the Middle and possibly Early Roman periods through the Byzantine period'; the earlier strata (Hellenistic, Iron Age, Middle Bronze) are represented by sherds only. The Roman-period occupants are not shown to be Jewish by these finds alone; the Jewish identity rests on the synagogue and inscriptions of Strata V-IV. Year 250 = midpoint of the 2nd-3rd/3rd-4th c. readings; confidence medium-low.

Stone vessels, Jewish purity laws: O. Zingboym's 2015 excavation near the Qazrin Park entrance (IAA final report, HA-ESI 129, 2017) found two fragments of stone vessels of the 2nd-3rd c. CE, 'the first stone vessels found in Qazrin', which 'may indicate that a Jewish population, which still maintained the ritual laws of purity and impurity, resided there during the second-third centuries CE'; the pottery from the dig ranges from the Roman period (3rd-4th c.) to the Mamluk period. The excavator words it as a possibility (two fragments only). Year 250 = midpoint of 2nd-3rd c.; confidence medium-low. Complements the Late Roman strata row (250) which could not show Jewish identity.

Ancient Jewish village of Khirbet Qazrin (archaeological park ~1.5 km E of the modern town, 32.9891N 35.7042E). One of four Aramaic inscriptions found in the village (only one complete) reads 'Rabbi Avun, his resting place in honour'; Dan Urman believes it is the tombstone of the amora Rabbi Avin, who lived at the end of the 3rd and in the first half of the 4th c. CE. Year 325 = conventional midpoint of that range; the identification of the deceased is Urman's inference (inscription + prosopography; confidence medium-low). he.wikipedia calls the site a Jewish settlement of the Mishnaic-Talmudic periods, c. 2nd-7th c.; en.wikipedia gives 4th-8th c.

Late Roman-early Byzantine buildings outside the park core: O. Zingboym's trial excavation near the Qazrin Park entrance (IAA, HA-ESI 121, 2009) found two buildings with a plaster floor over pottery of Kefar Hananya ware (3rd-4th c.), glass of the 3rd-4th c. and six coins of the 3rd-4th c., the latest minted in 383 CE (IAA 111587); he concludes the buildings were founded in the Late Roman period (latter part of the 3rd c.) and used until the end of the 4th-beginning of the 5th c., and that the settlement already extended over a wide area in the 4th c., 'not just in the fifth-sixth centuries CE, as the excavators of the site had previously thought'. The report summarises the earlier excavations as 10 habitation levels, mostly Byzantine (5th-8th c.) and Mamluk, plus a Byzantine-period synagogue. The Jewish character of these particular buildings is inferred from the village context. Year 340 = midpoint of late 3rd-end 4th c.; confidence medium-high for the dates.

Fourth-century coin hoards in the residential quarter (House C): numerous 4th-c. hoards, one with 8,550 coins; a 20% sample (1,608 coins) is all Hasmonean/4th-c. coins dated 310-367 CE, and five coins postdate the 363 earthquake, so the hoard was deposited after 367 CE (Eisenberg & Osband 2022:169 summarising J. Betlyon & A. Killebrew 2016, 'A Fourth-Century CE Coin Hoard from the Qasrin Village'). Qasrin thus shows post-363 settlement continuity and that the first synagogue stratum (Stratum V, late 4th c.) rests on a prosperous 4th-c. village; a small 2005 dig (Zingboym) found 4th-c. occupation with six coins, the latest of 383 CE. Year 370 = deposit date; confidence high for the coin data.

Wikipedia 'Katzrin Ancient Village': a Talmudic-period Jewish village of the 4th-8th century (mainly Byzantine); beneath the later synagogue lie the remains of 'a more modest, probably late-4th-century synagogue' (375 used for 'late 4th century'); excavated 1971-84 (synagogue found 1967). Archaeological; the village's Jewish character is inferred from the synagogue and finds.

Ancient Jewish farming village (Talmudic period, 4th-8th c.) at Katzrin; the earlier, more modest synagogue is 'probably late-4th-century'. Synagogue found 1967 and excavated 1971-84; other parts of the village from 1983. Year 390 = late 4th c. Medium-low confidence (dating of the earlier building is a probability statement).

First synagogue at the ancient village: per researchers cited by he.wikipedia (Z. Ilan, Ancient Synagogues in Israel, 1991) a square building with plaster floor of the late 4th-early 5th c.; en.wikipedia: 'a more modest, probably late-4th-century synagogue' lay beneath the 6th-c. building (other popular summaries say 3rd-4th or 4th-5th c.). Discovered by S. Gutman 1967/68; excavated by D. Urman 1971-72, M. Ben-Ari 1976-77, Z. Ma'oz with A. Killebrew (and R. Hachlili) 1982-84. Dating basis: stratigraphy (Stratum V, 'late 4th-5th centuries': erection of Synagogue A - Ma'oz in NEAEHL 1993; Ma'oz & Killebrew 1988 estimate it 'first constructed in late 4th century', as quoted at deadseaquake.info) and ~180 coins found under the upper bench (he.wikipedia); Eisenberg & Osband (2022) also put the first synagogue in the 4th c. Year 400 is a conventional midpoint; confidence medium-high.

Jewish Virtual Library (Archaeology in Israel: Katzrin): the village, founded on minor Iron Age remains in the Hellenistic period, was most prosperous in the Roman-Byzantine era (4th-7th c.); the synagogue (trapezoidal, c. 17.6 x 15.3 m, oriented north-south toward Jerusalem) was first built in the 4th-5th c. and rebuilt on a larger scale in the 6th c.; a hoard of 9,000 coins of the 4th c. was found; the village was abandoned in the Mamluk period. Dating basis: coins and pottery per the excavators. Year 450 = 4th-5th c. boundary.

Regional context for the central Golan (Wikipedia, Golan Heights - not specific to Qazrin): Jews again sought refuge in the Golan after 135, increasing its Jewish population; in the late 3rd/early 4th c. (Diocletian-Constantine) Jewish life revived and 25 locations with ancient synagogues or remains have been found, all in the central Golan, including Umm el-Qanatir, Qatzrin and Deir Aziz; several Golan sites show destruction from the 351 Gallus revolt; by the 6th c. the Golan's population peaked (Jews, pagans, Ghassanid Christians); most sites were abandoned between the late 6th and early 7th c. Survey-based picture, not a population count. Year 500 = conventional.

Population estimate by Zvi Ma'oz (the site's last excavator): the ancient village had 75 families, about 300 persons (stated in he.wikipedia, citing Z. Ilan's synagogue survey). The source does not date the estimate or give the method; year 500 is a conventional date within the village's Byzantine peak (4th-7th/8th c.). Treat as an order-of-magnitude figure for the Jewish farming village, not a census.

Synagogue extended north to its present plan (15.4 x 18 m, two storeys, two rows of columns with Greek capitals, bimah on the south wall facing Jerusalem, small side room possibly a genizah, mosaic floor) in the early 6th c. per he.wikipedia; en.wikipedia states the synagogue 'was built in the 6th century CE atop a more modest, probably late-4th-century synagogue' (Ma'oz & Killebrew 1988). An Aramaic donor inscription records 'Uzi servant of Dan' giving two minas for a banquet/assembly hall. A new plaster floor followed in the early 7th c. Dating basis: coins (~180 under the upper bench) and architecture; confidence medium-high.

Wikipedia 'Katzrin Ancient Village': the 6th-century synagogue (infobox 'c. 6th-century CE'; conventional 550) was built atop the earlier one; town and synagogue were destroyed in the 749 Golan earthquake and Katzrin abandoned in the 8th century. Archaeological.

Main synagogue built in the 6th c. in an architectural style characteristic of southern Syria, two rows of four columns, bimah and geniza under it; town and synagogue destroyed by the 749 earthquake and abandoned. Conventional year 550 (6th c.).

Framing row after the period: the village and synagogue were destroyed by the 749 'Sabbatical-year' earthquake and the village was abandoned (he.wikipedia; en.wikipedia 749; en.wikipedia 'Golan Heights' says 746). A mosque was later built in the northern half of the ruin in the Mamluk period (13th-15th c.). Outside 70-550; included only to bound the sequence.

Greek lintel inscription 'for the salvation of our lords the Emperors Septimius Severus, Caracalla and Geta, and Julia Domna, in accord with the vow of the Jews' found at Qision (Qazion) beside a monumental public building. Dated 195/6 CE in Wikipedia; the Heurist 'Judaism and Rome' database dates it 198-211 CE from the imperial titles (midpoint 204). The building (Hachlili & Killebrew surveys 1992, 1997) is debated: synagogue, building for the imperial cult built by Jews, a Syro-Phoenician temple, or a priestly cult/communal complex; Killebrew dates the complex late 2nd-early 3rd c. Dating basis: inscription (imperial titles). Confidence high for Jewish dedicants and date; building function uncertain.

Rabbinic: R. Yohanan de-Qasyon (of Kasion/Qarsion), a 3rd-century sage, in the Jerusalem Talmud, and y. Betzah 5:5 indicate Jewish presence in the northern area of Qazion; Wikipedia: these passages and the surveys point to a Jewish community here in the 2nd-3rd centuries; later (16th-c. Safed) tradition places the tombs of R. Yohanan and Resh Lakish here. Dating basis: literary plus survey (primary occupation 2nd-3rd c.). Confidence medium. One of the northernmost Jewish settlements in Galilee.

Khirbet Qazion/Qaisun (Upper Galilee): Greek dedicatory inscription of Jewish origin with prayers for the peace and prosperity of the emperor Septimius Severus and his family (192-211), long cited by Avi-Yonah and Foerster as the only dated evidence for 'Galilean-type' synagogues; Hachlili and Killebrew (excavations 1992, 1997) conclude the public building is not a synagogue (a building dedicated to the emperor by Jews, or a temple built by Jewish priests). Dating basis: inscription naming the Severan dynasty. Year 201 = midpoint of 192-211.

Hebrew Wikipedia gives construction c. 150-130 BCE. Function disputed: sectarian (de Vaux, Broshi, Magness), Hasmonean fortress or forward post (Hirschfeld; Magen and Peleg; Humbert as villa), villa rustica (Donceels), pottery workshop (Magen and Peleg). Jewish evidence: miqva'ot (Broshi: 10 of 16 water installations; Magen and Peleg dispute) and a cemetery of about 1,100-1,200 graves. Population 175 = midpoint of Broshi's 150-200 for the community, as cited by Hachlili (cojs.org; basis not stated there; stated for the community in general, Periods Ib and II, not per sub-period). Identification Khirbet Qumran is secure; some link it to Sakkah (Josh 15:61).

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63), conflicting estimate: Patrich 50-70 inhabitants, midpoint 60, quoted by Hachlili (cojs.org); Patrich's basis is available living quarters, with no tent remains or adapted caves (Orion post by Gmirkin, 2000, which also reports Humbert at 10-15 and Gmirkin himself at 10-40; Notes only). Stated for the community in general (Periods Ib and II), not per sub-period.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): site abandoned c. 31 BCE (about 30 years, de Vaux) then reoccupied in Period II c. 4 BCE-68 CE under Archelaus (cojs.org; Hachlili); buildings renovated, water system partly repaired, scriptorium and mill added; destroyed by the Romans in the Great Revolt 68 CE, then Period III Roman garrison c. 68-73 (cojs.org). Magness dates the sectarian settlement c. 100-50 BCE; Magen and Peleg see a pottery workshop to 68 CE (BAS). Jewish evidence as above (miqva'ot, cemetery). Population estimates exist only for the community in general (see Hasmonean rows), so this row is blank.

comment: Event: Sargon II destroys and burns Raphia (Assyrian Rapihu) in 720 BCE after defeating Gaza's king and the Egyptian relief army, and carries off 9,033 people with their large property. Na'aman points out that so large a figure cannot be the population of one town: it must come from a district (perhaps a wide one) whose people were gathered and deported. Online: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Jewish Virtual Library, 'Rafa') says "the Assyrians burned the city and deported 9,033 inhabitants", but dates the battle to 721 (Na'aman, Wikipedia 'Sargon II' and the Hebrew Wikipedia page 'ההגליות האשוריות', which repeats the 9,033, give 720; see conflicts). Raphia is not yet on the map; coordinates are those of modern Rafah (Gaza Strip, filed under Israel as the map files Gaza). Population blank (9,033 is a deportee count). Confidence high for the deportation, medium for the year.

Biblical mention and identification (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -1200 = conventional date of the Joshua conquest/allotment narrative (the allotment lists themselves are of disputed date); new marker, nearest markers Tiberias 2.1 km and Magdala 2.6 km, different places). Josh 19:35 (Rakkath among the fenced cities of Naphtali, between Hammath and Chinnereth). Identification: Tel Rakkath (Tel Raqqat, Khirbet el-Quneitriyeh), on the lake shore between Tiberias and Magdala, 32.806 N 35.526 E (Wikidata Q49004203), the site favoured by BibleWalks; one Talmud passage identifies Rakkath with Sepphoris and another (Megillah 2,2) places it near Tiberias, and the Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities gives no site for Rakkath but lists Tel Raqqat as an alternative for Hammath, so 'disputed, favoured: Tel Raqqat'. Archaeology (BibleWalks): unexcavated apart from a Highway 90 section; inhabited from the Early Bronze Age through the Israelite period, 'declined during the Iron Age and was abandoned', probably destroyed in the Assyrian conquest of 732 BCE (2 Kgs 15:29). No Iron Age sub-period, size or population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+19&version=KJV ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua

Remains south and south-east of the village (lintel with an Aramaic inscription 'Remembered for good ...' flanked by two cherub-like/Nike figures and a wreath) indicate a 3rd-4th-century synagogue; also Roman baths (2nd-4th c.), a large basilica-type building with mosaics, and Late Roman pottery of the 4th-5th c. Dating basis: epigraphy/architecture; year 325 = midpoint of 3rd-4th c. Confidence low-medium. Not to be confused with the biblical Ramah of Asher/Naphtali.

Rameh (Upper Galilee): building foundations with an Aramaic lintel inscription in Jewish script ('Remembered for the good be Rabbi Elazar son of Perahiah(?) and his sons ... the gate'), with reliefs of two cherub-like figures flanking a wreath, indicate a 3rd-4th c. synagogue; Roman baths and oil presses of the 2nd-4th c.; a large basilica (excavated 1972) with polychrome mosaics; Late Roman (4th-5th c.) pottery. Galilee article: Rama later predominantly Christian. Dating basis: typology/palaeography of the lintel (not stratigraphic). Year 350 = 3rd-4th c.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000) and identification note. Tel Rehov (Tell es-Sarem), 32.457 N 35.498 E, about 4-5 km south of Beth-shean in the Beth-shean valley, was occupied in Iron Age I-II from the 12th century BCE; Wikipedia counts it among the largest cities of the region in the Late Bronze and Iron I-IIA; Amihai Mazar excavated it for 11 seasons 1997-2012 (Strata VII-II are Iron Age). Area: 11 ha including slopes, 7 ha mound tops (Wikipedia); about 100 dunams on the mound (BibleWalks; Hebrew Wikipedia). Biblical name: none accepted. Wikipedia states that Tel Rehov does NOT correspond to the biblical Rehob places (Rehob of Asher, Josh 19:28 and 19:30, Judg 1:31); the name survives in the tomb of esh-Sheikh er-Rihab and the Byzantine Jewish town of Rohob. BibleWalks suggests Zarthan (1 Kgs 4:12; 7:46) as the ancient name, which is not an established identification. Rehov appears in Shoshenq I's list (c. 925 BCE). Included because it is a major Israelite city of the Beth-shean valley with a published population estimate (next rows); since no verse names this tell, this is not a literary-only row. No Iron I population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/rechov ; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%AA%D7%9C_%D7%A8%D7%97%D7%95%D7%91

Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) invaded in Rehoboam's fifth year: 1 Kgs 14:25-26 and 2 Chr 12:2-4 ('he took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah'). The Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists conquered places (c. 925 BCE); the inscription gives no details of the expedition and Jerusalem is absent from the list (English Wikipedia 'Bubastite Portal', 'Shoshenq I'). Tel Rehov is read as no. 17 'Rehob' of the Karnak list (BibleWalks 'Tel Rechov': #17 r-h-b), for which BibleWalks suggests a destruction in Stratum V. Literary and epigraphic evidence; Year of Data -925 = conventional date of the campaign. No population figure. Further source: https://www.biblewalks.com/rechov/

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722): population ESTIMATE of 2,000 by William G. Dever for the 9th and 8th centuries BCE, as quoted on Wikipedia ('an estimated population of 2,000 during the 9th and 8th centuries BCE, according to archaeologist William G. Dever'; the Rehov article gives no page, other Wikipedia site articles cite Dever 2017, Beyond the Texts, pp. 392-393 for the same series of estimates, which I could not check). Stratum III lasted until the Assyrian conquest of 734-732 BCE (the defence wall collapsed during the assault; two skulls, one decapitated, in the top layer, BibleWalks); Stratum II after 732. A sherd of the second half of the 9th c. may carry the name Elisha (2013 Elisha ostracon, disputed reading; Abel-meholah of Elisha, 1 Kgs 19:16, lies in this region). Iron II city of the northern kingdom of Israel (Wikipedia). The same figure of 2,000 is attributed to Amihai Mazar for the Iron IIA hive period in the previous row. Further source: https://www.biblewalks.com/rechov

Tel Rehov and its surroundings yielded inscriptions naming the family of Nimshi, and a 9th c. ostracon reconstructed as 'Elisha' (the reconstruction is disputed) (English Wikipedia 'Tel Rehov'). In the Bible Jehu, who seized the throne of Israel c. 841 BCE, is 'the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi' (2 Kgs 9:2; 2 Kgs 9:20 'Jehu the son of Nimshi'). Year of Data -840 = conventional date of Jehu's revolt. Epigraphic hint only; no population figure. Further source: https://www.biblestudytools.com/kjv/2-kings/9.html

Wikipedia 'Mosaic of Rehob': per archaeologist Fanny Vitto the synagogue near Tel Rehov (Ein HaNetziv) 'was first built as a basilical hall in the 4th century CE', was destroyed by fire and rebuilt in the following century (new bemah and mosaic floor), and in its last phase (6th or 7th century) received a narthex whose mosaic carries the long halakhic 'Baraita of the Boundaries' inscription (29 lines, c. 364 words); other scholars date the creation of the inscription's text to the late 3rd century at the earliest. Excavated in 1973 (Vitto); on display at the Israel Museum since 1978. Archaeological/epigraphic; the inscription names Beth Shean (Scythopolis), Susita, Naveh, Tyre, Achziv, Akko, Caesarea, Paneas and Sebaste as reference points.

'Rehob synagogue' and the Baraita of the Boundaries mosaic, in a Late Roman-Byzantine Jewish village about 1 km NW of Tel Rehov (the site, Horbat Parva, has no known ancient name). Excavated by F. Vitto in 1973-80: per Vitto the synagogue was first built as a basilical hall in the 4th c., destroyed by fire and rebuilt in the following century with a bema, new mosaic floor and inscribed plaster, and in a last phase (6th or 7th c.) a narthex was added whose floor carries the long halakhic inscription (the Mosaic of Rehob, listing the permitted and prohibited areas around Beth Shean, Hippos, Tyre, Caesarea and Sebaste); others date the text late 3rd c. at the earliest. Abandoned after an earthquake. Conventional year 400 (4th-c. first phase).

Phase II (late 4th-5th c.) renovation of the Rehob synagogue: a raised platform (bema) on the south side, walls and columns plastered and painted with red/green vegetal motifs and inscriptions, including a list of annual fast days, halakhic inscriptions, a large donor list of about thirty names, and a roster of the priestly courses (mishmarot) - evidence for an organised Jewish community of the Beth Shean valley. Year = conventional end of the 4th-5th c. Dating basis: stratigraphy/palaeography. Confidence medium.

ESI final report (A. Kohn-Tavor, 2015-18 excavations at Horbat Parva): the basilical synagogue paved with mosaics has three construction phases from the 5th c. CE until its violent end in the 7th c. (possibly an earthquake); it yielded the 'Baraita of the Borders' inscription (Israel Museum) with information on the Jewish settlement of the valley; a marble chancel screen with a menorah and a hoard of gold coins were found at the site; a 3rd-4th c. pottery workshop and Kefar Hananya cooking pots show earlier occupation. Conflicts with Vitto's 4th-c. start. Conventional year 450.

Wikipedia 'Tel Rehov': 'Remains of a mainly Byzantine-period synagogue built in three successive phases between the fourth and the seventh century CE' at Khirbet Farwana / Horvat Parva; the Byzantine Jewish town of Rehob stood 1 km north-west of Tel Rehov. Midpoint of the 4th-7th century (c. 500) used. Archaeological.

Phase III (late 5th c. or later) of the Rehob synagogue: a narthex whose mosaic carries the 'Baraita of the Boundaries' (Mosaic of Rehob, 29 lines, 364 words, the longest Hebrew mosaic inscription in Israel and the oldest known Talmudic text), listing the produce of Scythopolis, Susita, Naveh, Tyre, Paneas, Caesarea and Sebaste villages exempt from tithes and the boundaries of the Land of Israel; the building was destroyed in the 7th c., perhaps by an earthquake. Dating conflict: F. Vitto 6th-7th c.; others late 3rd c. at the earliest; CIIP inscriptions AD 475-600 (year = midpoint). Dating basis: palaeography/stratigraphy. Confidence medium.

Wikipedia 'Tel Rehov': the Rehob mosaic inscription is 'a very long sixth-century inscription in Aramaic' in the narthex of the synagogue floor (a halakhic text on the status of Beth Shean valley localities and Sabbatical-year law); 6th century = conventional 550. Epigraphic; the content preserves older (Tannaitic/Amoraic) lists.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). English Wikipedia ('Rammun'): sherds of Iron Age I, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Crusader/Ayyubid and Mamluk periods have been found at Rammun, 12 km east of Ramallah and 3 km south of Taybeh, with ancient cisterns and mosaics. Identification: Rammun was taken by van de Velde (1854) to be the biblical Rimmon / Sela Rimmon, and it also fits the Onomasticon's Remmon, 15 miles north of Jerusalem between Bethel and Jericho (Madaba Map). Judges-period Benjaminite refuge (see the next row). No population estimate found.

Literary mention (Judges 19-21 episode, dated by convention c. -1100). Judg 20:45-47 (after the defeat at Gibeah 600 Benjamites flee to the wilderness unto the rock Rimmon and stay there four months), Judg 21:13 (the congregation sends to the Benjamites in the rock Rimmon and proclaims peace). Identification as in the previous row (Rammun, van de Velde 1854; Iron I sherds support a Judges-period site). Literary mention only for this row.

Iron Age I (end of the 13th to beginning of the 12th c. BCE, c. 100 years), Stratum III: an oval enclosure protected by a casemate-type wall around a large central courtyard for livestock; site size 2.2 dunams. Population estimate: 40-50 people (midpoint 45), by Israel Finkelstein, the excavator, as tabulated by BibleWalks 'Eben Ezer (Izbet Zarta)' with the source note 'Israel Finkelstein, Debate on EbenEzer and Aphek, pp 33-35' (the original publication was not fetched; BibleWalks dates the stratum to the end of the 13th / early 12th c., Year of Data -1200 = start of Iron Age I). Site: Izbet Sartah (Hebrew Izbet Zartta), a small hill about 3 km east of Tel Aphek, excavated in 1976-1978 by Moshe Kochavi and Israel Finkelstein; the marker is the modern town of Rosh HaAyin, about 2 km away, whose existing row already mentions the Izbet Sartah excavations. Identification with biblical Eben-ezer is proposed, not settled: English Wikipedia 'Eben-Ezer' says many Israeli archaeologists place the Eben-ezer of 1 Sam 4 near Kafr Qasim with Izbet Sartah as the proposed location, while its location 'has not been identified with much certainty' (Beit Iksa and Dayr Aban are other proposals). Disputed, favoured: Izbet Sartah. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eben-Ezer

Excavations at Izbet Sartah in the Rosh HaAyin forest revealed an ancient Israelite agricultural settlement from the middle of the 12th century BCE (First Bronze Age), yielding an ostracon with one of the earliest known Hebrew texts.

The IGRA database contains 34,615 records from various registers documenting the temporary settlement of Jewish immigrants from Yemen in Rosh HaAyin (this figure represents a database record count, not a verified resident population total).

Literary setting of the battle of Eben-ezer. 1 Sam 4:1: Israel 'pitched beside Eben-ezer: and the Philistines pitched in Aphek'; the Ark is lost (1 Sam 4:11) and taken 'from Eben-ezer unto Ashdod' (1 Sam 5:1); Samuel later sets up a stone and names it Eben-ezer (1 Sam 7:12). Framing row: Wikipedia 'Sakhnin' - the town is mentioned as 'Sogane, a town fortified in 66, by Josephus' (Josephus, Vita 188 and War 2:573 per Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Sikhnin'); Hanina ben Teradion's later residence there (c. 135) and the 4th-century amora Joshua of Sakhnin are given in the other rows. First literary attestation of the Jewish town.

Haninah ben Teradion, arrested by the Romans (Hadrianic persecution), is said to have run a Torah academy at Sikhnin; the village Kfar Sikhnin appears in rabbinic accounts of the trial of R. Eliezer ben Hyrcanus for minut. Identification of rabbinic Kefar Sikhnin with modern Sakhnin is uncertain (alternative: Shikhin near Sepphoris). Conventional year (early/mid-2nd c.). Dating basis: literary. Confidence low-medium.

Wikipedia 'Hanina ben Teradion': 'His residence was at Sikhnin' where he directed religious affairs and a school; executed 'following the Bar Kokhba revolt' in the Hadrianic persecutions (BT Sanhedrin 32b: 'Follow Rabbi Haninah ben Teradion in Sikhnin'; Avodah Zarah 17b-18a for the martyrdom); no year is given, 135 used as the end of the war. Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Sikhnin') also names R. Judah and R. Joshua, and a synagogue (JT Megillah 4:5, 75b). Rabbinic-literary; Sikhnin = Sakhnin (identification generally accepted).

Sakhnin = Josephus' fortified Sogane (66) and the Kfar Sikhnin of rabbinic accounts; Haninah ben Teradion, arrested by the Romans for heresy (minut), is said to have run a Torah academy there; a cistern near the mosque contained pottery of the 1st-5th c. CE. Literary identification; year 135 = Hadrianic persecution after Bar Kokhba, conventional; low confidence.

Wikipedia 'Sakhnin': Rabbi Joshua of Sakhnin, an amora, 'lived in the village in the 4th century CE'; a cistern near the mosque yielded pottery 'dating from the 1st to the 5th century CE'; columns, cisterns and a Roman-period sarcophagus shrine on the ancient site; Hanina ben Teradion is said to have run a Torah academy there. Josephus fortified Sogane in 66 (outside the period). Amoraic-literary and archaeological; medium confidence.

Salabe, Golan: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Walls built of basalt ashlar stones with entrance on the southern side. Column remains. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Selamin/Selame (Khirbet Selameh = Tzalmon, next to Sallama), a Jewish village of vineyards (Mishnah) fortified by Josephus (Life 188, 'Selamin') and taken by the Romans after the fall of Tarichaea; the Tosefta (Parah 9:2) records that its spring ceased to flow during the Roman siege; Klein thinks the priest Joseph b. Dalaiah who died in the Temple's destruction came from here; the course of Dalaiah is later linked with the village (Kalir, c. 570-640). Unexcavated; Aviam's survey found a moat, wall segment, pottery and coins in situ. Dating basis: Josephus + survey. Confidence medium. Framing row; the nearby Tzalmon synagogue fragments (Ilan) are in the 450 row.

The priestly course Delaiah (23rd) is traditionally located at Tzalmon (Sallama); Wikipedia's list of the courses' 'Mishnaic residences' (from the Baraita on the priestly courses and Kalir's elegy) places it here. Undated settlement tradition; conventional year 300 (Caesarea inscription c. AD 300; the Baraita is Talmudic-period). Identification uncertain; the Bornblum DB lists architectural fragments of a possible synagogue at Tzalmon. Confidence low.

Tzalmon/Sallama (north edge of the Beit Netofa valley): decorated lintel, columns, mosaic stones and fragments of a marble chancel (Z. Ilan 1981-88) interpreted as a Late Roman/Byzantine synagogue; unexcavated. Conventional year (3rd-7th c.). Dating basis: architectural fragments. Confidence low.

Event: Arab tribes settled in Samaria. Sargon II defeated the distant desert tribes Tamud, Ibadidi, Marsimani and Haiapa and, in the words of his Khorsabad annals as quoted by Na'aman, deported their remnant and settled it in the city of Samaria. Na'aman links the episode to the tribute brought by Pharaoh, Samsi queen of the Arabs and Itamra of Saba and dates it to 715 BCE, five years after Samaria's annexation, making these Arabs the first group of exiles brought into Samaria. Online: Wikipedia 'Annals of Sargon II' says Sargon attacked Arab tribes, "deporting the survivors of his campaign to Samaria", and files it under 714; Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) dates the inscription 715. Because the online sources disagree and the paper agrees with the Hebrew page, 715 is used (see conflicts). No number of settlers is given. Population blank. Confidence high for the event, medium for the year.

Event: Babylonian exiles settled in the cities of Samaria. Na'aman dates the main deportation into the province of Samaria to after Sargon's Babylonian campaigns of 710-709 BCE (against Marduk-apla-iddina): the sacred Babylonian cities Babylon and Cuthah (Kutha) and the peripheral places Ava, Hamath (near Ava, not the Syrian Hamath) and Sepharvaim named in 2 Kings 17:24 match the two groups Sargon deported from Babylonia in those years (his inscriptions give 90,580 deportees from Bit-Yakin and neighbouring tribes), so the people brought to Samaria came from Babylonia. The number of settlers is not stated. Online: 2 Kings 17:24 (KJV) says the king of Assyria "brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria"; Wikipedia 'Sargon II' says "In 710, Sargon decided to reconquer Babylonia". The 710-709 date of this particular deportation is Na'aman's inference, repeated in Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent). Population blank. Confidence medium.

Event: Esarhaddon's deportations to the Samaria region. Ezra 4:2 has the people of the land say they have sacrificed to Israel's God "since the days of Esar-haddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither"; Na'aman reads this as evidence of a further deportation into the land in Esarhaddon's reign (681-669 BCE; Year of Data = start of the reign, the exact year is unknown). Nothing is known about the background or the number of settlers; Assyrian inscriptions of the period rarely mention deportations to the land. Esarhaddon also renewed the Assyrian advance to the south (campaigns against Egypt, 671 BCE). Online: Ezra 4:2 (KJV) as quoted; Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) says the origin of these exiles is unknown. Population blank. Confidence low-medium.

Event: Ashurbanipal's deportations to Samaria. Ezra 4:9-10 lists Babylonians, Archevites (people of Erech/Uruk), Susanchites (Susa) and Elamites among the nations that "the great and noble Asnapper" (Ashurbanipal) set "in the cities of Samaria". Na'aman dates the Babylonian group after Ashurbanipal's conquest of Babylon in 648 BCE (end of the revolt of Shamash-shum-ukin) and the Elamite group after 646 BCE, when he destroyed Susa; since Assyrian records of these years say little about deportations, the biblical text is the main evidence. No numbers. Online: Ezra 4:9-10 (KJV); Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) repeats the 648 and 646 dates. The map's Susa row dates the destruction of Susa 647; Na'aman's text says 646. Population blank. Confidence medium.

Date of capture: 107 BCE (Hebrew Wikipedia), 108 BCE (Livius, Encyclopaedia Judaica via earlier pass), c. 110 BCE (JVL). Afterwards: Encyclopaedia Judaica says resettled under Jannaeus; Josephus War 1.166 (lexundria) lists Samaria among cities Gabinius restored (57 BCE per Livius). Greek and mixed city; no evidence of a Jewish population; Population blank.

Josephus War 2.460: in 66 CE Jewish rebels attacked Sebaste and burned it, so the town was not Jewish; Livius also says Jewish rebels razed it. No miqva'ot, stone vessels or ossuaries reported in fetched pages; no named estimate; Population blank.

Literary only (conventional date -1200: Joshua's allotment). Secacah is the third town of the wilderness group: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah (Josh 15:61). Identification disputed, favoured: Khirbet es-Samrah in the Buqe'ah (Hyrcania valley), placed there by Frank M. Cross and Jozef Milik ('Explorations in the Judaean Buqe'ah', BASOR 142, 1956) because it is an Iron Age settlement in the same wilderness; John Allegro (1960) identified it with Khirbet Qumran from the Copper Scroll (3Q15), and an LMLK seal was found at both (English Wikipedia). Hebrew Wikipedia: es-Samra has Israelite-period structures, walls, dams, pools and LMLK impressions. Coordinates are Khirbet es-Samrah. No population figure. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%A1%D7%9B%D7%9B%D7%94 ; https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Joshua.15?context=0&commentary=0&lang=en&version=english%7CThe%20Holy%20Scriptures%20by%20Jewish%20Publication%20Society%201917

Iron Age IIC/III (7th to early 6th c.; row placed at -700): the Buqe'ah plateau settlements are dated to the 7th and early 6th centuries BCE by Gibson, Lewis and Taylor (2023, Springer chapter, abstract); earlier work read them as permanent paramilitary farming establishments with run-off farming, the 2023 authors as pastoralist rangeland posts. The abstract does not name individual sites; Cross and Milik's 1956 Buqe'ah survey covered Khirbet Abu Tabaq, Khirbet es-Samrah and Khirbet el-Maqari (BAS endnote). Dating caveat: later than the 12th-8th c. window; no 8th-c. date was found in the fetched sources. Population blank.
