[Second-pass revision] Persian (-539 to -332): NEW period row. Meyers et al. (1992 excavation report, as summarised on the Dead Sea Quake catalog page) report Iron Age II sherds (7th-6th c. BCE) and Persian finds (black Attic ware, an animal-shaped rhyton, a drinking goblet) and infer a small settlement by the mid-5th c. BCE, possibly a garrison; the BAS sidebar likewise says a Persian garrison in the 5th-4th c. is possible; C.L. Meyers, 'The Persian Period at Sepphoris', Eretz-Israel 29 (2009) 136*-143* is the dedicated study (record seen, no abstract). The same summary says the Jewish population goes back at least to Hellenistic times and perhaps to the Persian period (Meyers et al.). No numbers; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Replaces first-pass row, which found no Jewish evidence for this period. Fetched sources: Seleucid fort built by Antiochus III or Antiochus IV (c. 200 BCE; BAS sidebar); Meyers et al. (1992) date the residential area on the western acropolis from Hellenistic times (about 100 BCE) onward and say the Jewish population goes back at least to Hellenistic times. Weiss and Netzer 1996 ('Hellenistic and Roman Sepphoris: the archaeological evidence', Sepphoris in Galilee, pp. 29-37) is the main synthesis (record seen, no abstract). Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row (which said miqvaot were undated by phase): Jewish Virtual Library says the earliest occupation of the acropolis dates to the Hasmonean and Herodian periods (late 2nd c. BCE to 1st c. CE) with one- and two-storey houses on a paved street and many plastered rock-cut miqvaot in the domestic houses. Meyers et al. cite Hasmonean coins including Alexander Jannaeus; Josephus (Ant. 13.12.5) has Ptolemy Lathyrus attack the city c. 100 BCE; Gabinius made it a council seat in 57 BCE (Ant. 14.5.4); Stern et al. 1993: probable Hasmonean administrative centre of Galilee. Jewish city. Debate: Eshel argues some Sepphoris stepped pools are not miqvaot, Meyers and Reich say they are (BAR 2000, 2002). Population blank: no fetched named estimate for this period.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row: adds excavation evidence. Reich (BAR 28:2, 2002) counts 22 stepped plastered installations, three of Jerusalem type 'almost surely' Second Temple; an ASOR photo record dates a miqveh in Area 84.2 (Western Summit) to Early Roman 37 BCE-132/5 CE (final publication Meyers et al., PSUP/Eisenbrauns 2018); Weiss (Hebrew Univ.) says the city had a rural look in the 1st c. BCE-CE without Roman public buildings and was urbanized only after 70; stone vessels and a low proportion of pig bones indicate a Jewish population (BibleInterp essay; Chancey and Meyers BAR 26:4). Herod took it 37 BCE; burned by Varus after Judas's revolt 4 BCE; rebuilt by Antipas (Josephus per Jewish Encyclopedia). Population blank: an unattributed 8,000-12,000 inhabitants (BibleInterp essay; total, basis not given), a 15,000-20,000 peak after the Great Revolt (Weiss team page), and Schumer's 2,000-4,300 for early Roman Sepphoris (J. Ancient Judaism 8, 2017, pp. 90-111; seen only in search results, publisher page 403, not fetched) are not Jewish-only figures from a fetched source. Mixed Jewish and some pagan population per Meyers.

Great Revolt: Sepphoris, a Jewish city, did not join the revolt of 66 CE; Josephus twice failed to take it; coins struck c. 68 CE under Vespasian read 'Eirenopolis-Neronias-Sepphoris' (city of peace). Dating basis: numismatic + Josephus (literary). Confidence high. Framing row for the period.

Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Sepphoris'): 'Over 20 ritual baths [mikva'ot] on the western summit date to the Roman period'; the theatre is 'probably dated to the period after 70 CE'; the water system (aqueducts) dates 'to the end of the first century' and was operational until the Byzantine era; the lower city's crossing main streets date from the early Roman period and stayed in use into the Byzantine era (excavations from 1931, Waterman; later Meyers, Netzer, Weiss). Archaeological evidence of Jewish habitation of the post-70 city; the EJ summary gives no more precise year (100 = conventional end of the 1st / start of the 2nd century). Medium confidence.

Renaming: Wikipedia 'Sepphoris' - 'the city's name was changed to Diocaesarea in 129/30, just prior to the Bar Kokhba revolt' (Schafer; G. F. Hill, from coins); other scholars (Celdran) date it to Antoninus Pius (138-161) and Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Sepphoris') to the start of Antoninus' reign (138) with the Sixth Legion stationed at nearby Legio; EJ 'Galilee' says Hadrian made it a Roman city called Diocaesarea 'though its population remained largely Jewish'. Numismatic/literary; the year is disputed (129/30 vs 138).

After the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135) rabbinic families from Judea relocated to Sepphoris, which became a centre of Jewish religious and spiritual life (Wikipedia, citing S. Miller 1984); academies (yeshivot) were based there before the move of the Patriarchate/Sanhedrin to Tiberias. Dating basis: literary (rabbinic) + historical inference. Confidence medium-high.

City renamed Diocaesarea (Greek, 'city of Zeus and Caesar'; Jewish sources keep calling it Zippori). Dating conflict: 129/30 CE under Hadrian (G.F. Hill, P. Schaefer 1990) vs the reign of Antoninus Pius 138-161 (P. Celdran 1995); year given is the midpoint of 129-161. Basis: coin legends 'DIOKAISAREIA HIERA ASYLOS KAI AUTONOMOS'. The Roman name does not show the Jewish share of the population (Jewish majority attested by later sources). Confidence high that the city was renamed; medium on the exact year.

Yose ben Halafta (Wikipedia): born in Sepphoris, a 4th-generation tanna of the 2nd century, he settled at Usha (then the Sanhedrin seat) 'before the Romans forced him back to Sepphoris', where he established a flourishing school ('follow Jose to Sepphoris'); 'it seems that he died there'. No exact dates in the article; 160 is a conventional mid-2nd-century year. Rabbinic-literary.

Jewish Encyclopedia ('Johanan b. Nappaha'): Johanan was born in Sepphoris 'in the last quarter of the second century' and first taught there, then moved to Tiberias and founded a school after disagreeing with his teacher Hanina (bar Hama); his teacher Hoshaiah moved to Caesarea. Year 190 = conventional (last quarter of the 2nd century). Wikipedia 'Resh Lakish' places Resh Lakish at Sepphoris for most of his life. Rabbinic-literary.

After the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135) many Jewish refugees from Judea settled at Sepphoris/Diocaesarea, making it a centre of Jewish religious life; Judah ha-Nasi moved there with the Sanhedrin, and some yeshivot were based there before the move to Tiberias by 220; Galilee was predominantly Jewish from the end of the 2nd to the 4th c. (Wikipedia, historical summary based on rabbinic tradition). Year 200 = conventional, before 220.

Archaeology of the Roman city (excavator Z. Weiss, NEAEHL): the city expanded eastward in the early 2nd c. with a colonnaded street grid; houses of the Roman period on the hill contain 'a large number of ritual baths (mikvehs)', which together with the Aramaic mosaics of the later synagogue mark a Jewish population; the large House of Dionysos was built c. 200 CE; the theatre early in the 2nd c.; the reservoir (2nd c.) was in use to the 7th c. Dating basis: stratigraphy and mosaics. Year 205 = c. 200.

Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, compiler of the Mishnah, lived at Sepphoris (last ~17 years of life) and the Sanhedrin sat there; EJ (E. Meyers): the city reached its zenith as a Jewish seat of learning under Caracalla (198-217) and the Mishnah was edited and published there; 20+ ritual baths (mikva'ot) in the western-summit houses date to the Roman period; water system dated to the end of the 1st c. Year = midpoint of 198-217. Wikipedia: academies moved to Tiberias by c. 220. Dating basis: literary (Talmud) + archaeology. Confidence high for presence, medium for exact years.

Judah ha-Nasi and the Sanhedrin at Sepphoris: Encyclopaedia Judaica - 'Sepphoris reached its zenith as a Jewish seat of learning and cultural center during the reign of Caracalla (198-217)'; the Sanhedrin moved there, Judah ha-Nasi lived in the city and the Mishnah was edited and published there (midpoint of 198-217 used). Wikipedia 'Judah ha-Nasi': he moved the court to Sepphoris and spent at least 17 years there. Wikipedia 'Mishnah': compiled 'either in Beit Shearim or in Sepphoris' in the late 2nd / early 3rd century, so the place of redaction is uncertain. Rabbinic-literary.

Death of Judah ha-Nasi 'c. 217 CE' (precisely 15 Kislev 3978 AM, about 1 Dec 217) in Sepphoris; he was buried in the Beit She'arim necropolis about 15 km away, the funeral procession making eighteen stops (Wikipedia 'Judah ha-Nasi'). The article gives his tenure as nasi c. 165-220. Rabbinic-literary tradition.

Hanina bar Hama (d. c. 250), third-generation amora and leading halakhic authority, 'continued his residence at Sepphoris', headed the academy there after Epes the Southerner and died in Sepphoris (Wikipedia 'Hanina bar Hama'). Wikipedia 'Resh Lakish' (c. 200-c. 275): he 'lived most of his life in Sepphoris' before going to Tiberias with Johanan. Rabbinic-literary. (Wikipedia 'Jerusalem Talmud' calls the Yerushalmi 'a compilation of teachings of the schools of Tiberias, Caesarea, and Sepphoris'.)

Wikipedia 'Sepphoris': in the 3rd-4th century the city is believed to have been settled by the priestly course of Jedaiah (the Wikipedia 'Priestly courses' table lists the second course, Jedaiah, at Tzippori; the residence list derives from a baraita, 'some identifications are uncertain'). Year 300 = conventional mid-point of the 3rd-4th century; low confidence for the date. The same article says 'Galilee was predominantly populated by Jews' from the late 2nd to the 4th century.

Population: Z. Weiss (Sepphoris excavation website, Hebrew University) writes that, thanks to its wealth and economy, the city's population reached a peak of 15 to 20 thousand inhabitants (no date given; growth after the Great Revolt). Lower bound of Weiss's range. This is the whole city's population (Jews, pagans, Christians) but Sepphoris was predominantly Jewish (Epiphanius c. 375: no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians among the population); treat as an upper bound for the Jewish population. Year 300 = conventional (Late Roman peak); low confidence on date. The Wikipedia article's 'some 30,000' (no scholar named) is not used.

Population: Z. Weiss (Hebrew University) - upper bound of the 15-20 thousand peak population of Sepphoris (see companion row). Whole-city figure; the city was predominantly Jewish in the 3rd-4th c.; conventional year 300; low confidence on date.

Jewish Encyclopedia ('Academies in Palestine'): Jose ben Halafta taught at Sepphoris and Judah I completed the Mishnah there (c. 219), and 'Sepphoris regained importance in the 4th century' after Tiberias' primacy in the 3rd; the Jerusalem Talmud was completed at Tiberias about a century and a half after Johanan's death (d. 279), linked by the article to the end of the patriarchate c. 425. Year 350 = conventional mid-4th century. Rabbinic-literary summary; medium-low confidence on the 4th-century revival.

Gallus revolt: Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Land of Israel' - 'In June 351 a revolt of the Jews broke out at Sepphoris against Gallus, the Roman ruler in the east'; COJS: 'The rebellion started at Sepphoris where the Jews managed to gain possession' and 'In Sepphoris itself the uprising was put down but the city was not destroyed'; the Roman general Ursicinus put it down and a permanent garrison occupied Galilee afterwards. Literary (Socrates, Sozomen, Jerome, Aurelius Victor); the tradition that the rebels were led from Diocaesarea is Christian.

Jewish revolt against Constantius Gallus, 351-352: Diocaesarea (Sepphoris) was the epicentre and was razed. Philostorgius: 'The Jews of Diocaesarea also took up arms and invaded Palestine and the neighbouring territories, with the design of shaking off the Roman yoke...' (quoted by Wikipedia). The city was further affected by the earthquake of 363 but rebuilt and retained its importance in the Jewish community of Galilee. Literary source; archaeological confirmation of the destruction is uncertain. Year 351.

Wikipedia 'Jewish revolt against Constantius Gallus': Diocaesarea (Sepphoris), the revolt's epicentre, was 'razed to the ground' by Ursicinus (351 or 352) and later rebuilt; Sozomen says Gallus 'defeated them, and destroyed Diocaesarea'. Wikipedia 'Sepphoris': Diocaesarea 'was razed' in 351-352. Conflict: COJS says the city was not destroyed; EJ 'Sepphoris' attributes serious damage to the 363 earthquake and says it was rebuilt soon after. Destruction layer attribution (Gallus vs 363) remains debated; medium-low confidence.

Epiphanius, Panarion 30.11-12: Sepphoris/Diocaesarea is named among the Jewish towns where 'there are no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians' and the 'rule of having no gentiles' is observed 'especially at Tiberias, Diocaesarea, Sepphoris, Nazareth and Capernaum'; Count Joseph 'completed buildings in Diocaesarea and certain other towns' (30.12.9). Epiphanius met Joseph c. 355; Panarion 374-377. (Epiphanius lists Diocaesarea and Sepphoris as if two towns; they are one.) Wikipedia 'Sepphoris' adds that in the late 4th century Epiphanius 'described Sepphoris as predominantly Jewish'. Primary patristic source; medium confidence.

Galilee earthquake: Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Sepphoris' - 'Though it suffered greatly from the earthquake of 363 c.e., it was rebuilt soon after'; Wikipedia '363 Galilee earthquake': 'Sepphoris, north-northwest of Nazareth, was severely damaged'. Geological/literary event, affects the Jewish city.

Excavator's summary (Z. Weiss, NEAEHL): mid-4th c. damage 'most probably caused by the earthquake of 363 CE'; the Orpheus house (built in the second half of the 3rd c.) was probably destroyed by a mid-4th-c. earthquake and immediately renovated (finally destroyed at the beginning of the 5th c.); the forum-like building was in use until the mid-4th c.; a 3rd-c. farmhouse was destroyed in the 4th c. Dating basis: stratigraphy. Year 363.

Epiphanius, Panarion 30 (composed 374-377) names Diocaesarea/Sepphoris among the Jewish towns (with Tiberias, Nazareth, Capernaum) with no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians among the population; quoted in Magness 2024. Year 375 = midpoint of the composition date.

Broshi (BASOR 236, 1979), Table 2 'Area of Late Roman-Byzantine towns': Diocaesarea (Sepphoris) 60 hectares (estimate credited to A. Siegelmann). Broshi's maximum density for walled/dense towns is 400 persons per hectare minus a quarter for open space and he printed no per-town population, so none is entered (his coefficient would give a ceiling of c. 18,000 for all inhabitants, not only Jews - my arithmetic, not Broshi's). Dating basis: plan-based area estimate for the Late Roman-Byzantine city. Conventional year 400.

Second synagogue site in the west of Sepphoris: a mosaic with an inscription excavated by P. Viaud in 1909 (Bornblum database 'Sepphoris (west)'), period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Conventional year 400, low confidence.

Synagogue dated by the excavator Z. Weiss to the early 5th c. CE, in the northern part of the city, built over ruined Roman-period structures and used until the early 7th c.; elongated hall c. 20.8 x 7.7 m, entrance on the south side, not facing Jerusalem, narthex, seven bands (14 panels) of mosaic with Abraham scenes, zodiac and Aramaic dedicatory inscriptions. INPA and Magness 2024 also call it fifth-century. Dating basis: excavator's stratigraphy (details not given in the NEAEHL entry). Year 410 = early 5th c.

Synagogues: Wikipedia 'Sepphoris' - 'Remains of a synagogue dated to the first half of the fifth century were discovered on the northern side of town' (midpoint 425 used); the lower-city synagogue with the zodiac mosaic and the Nile-festival building mosaic are dated to the 5th century; more than sixty mosaics date from c. 3rd-6th century. Excavators' dating (mosaic style/stratigraphy); EJ lists a 'synagogue with a zodiac mosaic' among the Byzantine buildings. Sepphoris' total population is given as 'some 30,000' for the whole Roman-Byzantine period (not a Jewish-only figure, so Population left blank).

Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine SEPP0003 - black-and-white floor-mosaic dedication in a square panel of the northern aisle of the Sepphoris synagogue: 'Remembered be for good Yudan son of Isaac the Priest and Parigri his daughter. Amen. Amen.' Date range 400-500 CE (midpoint 450; the database gives terminus post quem 400, ante quem 500, with no further justification on the page); bibliography Z. Weiss, The Sepphoris Synagogue (2005). A priest (kohen) donor in the 5th-century synagogue; consistent with the Wikipedia 'Sepphoris' dating of the synagogue to the 5th century and with the priestly-course tradition for Sepphoris (Jedaiah). Epigraphic; high confidence for the text, medium for the exact date.

Sha'ab (cf. Josephus' Saab, per Guerin): Midrash (Leviticus Rabbah 20:9) mentions R. Mani of Sha'ab together with R. Joshua of Sakhnin and R. Johanan bar Nappaha, i.e. a rabbi from the village in the 3rd c. Wikipedia lists Sha'ab among ancient Jewish settlements of Galilee but no excavated Jewish remains are described. Conventional year (3rd c., R. Johanan's generation). Dating basis: literary. Confidence low.

Jewish town Sha'av/Sha'ab on the road between the large Jewish centres of Sakhnin (east) and Kabul (west), in the Western/Lower Galilee: Hebrew Wikipedia says it is mentioned in the Talmud as home of the third- and fourth-generation amoraim Rabbi Zakkai of Shav'ab and Rabbi Mana of Shav (year 300 used for the 3rd-4th generations, c. 290-340), that it survived the destruction after the Great Revolt and appears in M. Avi-Yonah's survey of Jewish settlements in Galilee after the revolt, and that the Jewish community continued until the Crusader period (an 11th-century document records a Jew who died there). Josephus' Eleazar b. Sameas, defender of Jotapata, came from Saab (pre-70). Literary evidence; no excavation in the sources read. Note: a 'Rabbi Zakkai' is also attributed to Cabul in Wikipedia 'Cabul' - the two attributions may be the same man.

Literary mention; identification: Salbit (31.8694 N, 34.9864 E per en.wikipedia, about 0.5 km from the marker, the modern moshav Sha'alvim), proposed by the PEF Survey of Western Palestine (Conder and Kitchener, 1883) as Shaalabbin/Shaalbim, 5 km northwest of Aijalon (Yalo); G. A. Cooke 1918 and the Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible are also cited (en.wikipedia Salbit). Treated as 'accepted but unexcavated': the Salbit page mentions no Iron Age remains, only a late 4th/early 5th-century Samaritan synagogue excavated in 1949. Year of Data -1200 = Judges/Joshua narrative convention. Judg 1:34-36: the Amorites hold Mount Heres, Aijalon and Shaalbim until the house of Joseph subdues them to tribute; Josh 19:42: Shaalabbin in Dan's allotment (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter pages). Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salbit

Literary only (no Iron Age finds in the fetched pages); Danite territory, dated by convention c. -1100. Judg 1:35 (the Amorites would dwell in Mount Heres, in Aijalon and in Shaalbim, until the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed and they became tributaries), Josh 19:42 (a city of Dan, with Aijalon). Biblical town SHAALBIM (entered on the existing marker of the kibbutz Sha'alvim, 0.3 km from the site, named after it). Identification: Salbit, a village depopulated in 1948, about 7.5 miles (12 km) south-east of al-Ramla, identified with Shaalabbin by the PEF Survey of Western Palestine in 1883 and located 5 km north-west of biblical Aijalon (English Wikipedia 'Salbit'); the kibbutz Sha'alvim (1951) is named after it. No population figure.

No archaeological or textual evidence found in available sources. Identification with Salbit is from the PEF Survey of Western Palestine 1883 and is regarded as uncertain; fetched pages mention only Samaritan synagogue (4th-5th c CE) and later remains Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%A1%D7%9C%D7%91%D7%99%D7%AA

Literary only: 1 Kgs 4:9: Shaalbim is in the second district of Solomon's twelve officers (the son of Dekar, with Makaz, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan) (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -960 = Solomon convention. No excavated Iron Age evidence at Salbit in the fetched pages; identification as in the first Sha'alvim row (Salbit, PEF 1883). The existing Sha'alvim row records that the identification rests on the PEF survey.

Shefar'am as seat of the Sanhedrin: Wikipedia 'Sanhedrin' - 'The Great Sanhedrin moved in 140 to Shefaram under the presidency of Shimon ben Gamliel II'. Babylonian Talmud Rosh Hashanah 31b lists 'from Usha to Shefaram' among the Sanhedrin's moves (Sefaria text); Jewish Encyclopedia 'Shefar'am': 'In the second century it served as a refuge for the Sanhedrin'; EJ: 'a seat of the newly reconstituted Sanhedrin' after the Bar Kokhba war and Hadrian's persecutions (RH 31a-b, Sanh. 13b-14a, Av. Zar. 8b). Conflict: Wikipedia 'Shefa-Amr' places the Sanhedrin here 'during the reign of Marcus Aurelius' (161-180). Identification: Shefar'am = modern Shefa-Amr (JE: 'the modern Shef'a 'Amr, about twelve miles east of Haifa'). Rabbinic-literary.

Wikipedia 'Shefa-Amr': the town is 'one of the cities the Talmud mentions as holding the seat of the Sanhedrin during the reign of Marcus Aurelius' (161-180; midpoint 170 used); the name first appears in the Tosefta (Mikvaot 6:1) and the Talmud mentions it in Avodah Zarah 8b and Rosh Hashanah 31b; the article also records the tomb of the 2nd-century rabbi Judah ben Baba (tradition) and Byzantine-period (5th-6th century) decorated burial caves identified as Christian. Secondary-source dating; conflicts with the 140 date above.

source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimron | https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%94%D7%94%D7%92%D7%9C%D7%99%D7%95%D7%AA_%D7%94%D7%90%D7%A9%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%95%D7%AA | Na'aman, Cathedra 54 (1989), pp. 47, 49 and n. 23 (PDF pp. 5, 7)
comment: Event: Tiglath-pileser III's Galilee campaign (734-732 BCE). In a broken fragment of his annals that lists Galilee and Jezreel-valley towns with their captives, Na'aman reads one entry as Shimon (Shimron, Khirbet Samuniya) with 650 captives; the restoration of the name is not certain. Two other entries give 625 and 650 captives for towns whose names are broken (one perhaps Kesalot). Na'aman's note 23 treats Shimon as the one city whose captive count survives under a recognisable name, and adds that surveys put its Iron Age II-III settled area at about 30 dunams, which would give an average of about 22 persons per dunam; he points out that the three surviving numbers (625, 650, 650) are strikingly alike and that the captives may include villagers who had taken refuge in the town, and therefore advises against computing populations from the inscription. Online: Wikipedia 'Shimron' says a broken annals fragment "has been restored as Samhuna, which Nadav Na'aman and others have associated with Shimron" and that Tiglath Pileser III "performed massive deportations in the Jezreel and Lower Galilee". Tomb of Benei Hezir and other Kidron monumental tombs belonged to Jewish priestly and elite families; Shanks BAR 1994 reports no Second Temple village at Silwan itself and Roman Aelia Capitolina later quarried the necropolis. Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Jewish burial ground. The East Talpiot rock-cut tomb (found 1980; Kloner Atiqot 29 1996) held ten limestone ossuaries; excavators dated it to the Second Temple period; wealthy Jewish families used such ossuaries from the 1st century BCE to 70 CE. About 900 similar family tombs ring Jerusalem (Kloner and Zissu 2007). A nearby tomb (Tabor and Arav) lies close to a mikveh, cisterns and an olive press suggesting an agricultural estate. No Jewish population estimate found; Population left blank. No period earlier than Early Roman is attested in fetched pages (First Temple royal estate at Armon HaNatziv is out of scope).

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000): Stratum VII (dated Iron I, 1200-900 in the excavation summary) is known from limited exposure: stone-lined grain-storage pits and Philistine-style pottery (bibleinterp); en.wikipedia describes the Iron I town as small and inhabited by Israelites. Excavated by the Lahav Research Project (bibleinterp).

Iron Age IIB estimate (9th-8th centuries BCE; -900 = start of Iron IIB): William G. Dever estimates about 300 people (en.wikipedia Tel Halif). No method stated on the page; original publication not fetched.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722): Stratum VIC (9th century) precedes Stratum VIB (800-700), the best-exposed phase: a Judahite town with casemate wall and pillar-courtyard houses (9th-8th centuries), a textile workshop (many loom weights), contents left in situ, destroyed by fire from a military assault, probably by Sennacherib in 701 BCE (bibleinterp; en.wikipedia).

Iron Age IIC (-722 to -586; Stratum VIA is dated 700-650 BCE in the excavation summary): possibly settled by refugees from VIB and then abandoned in haste, attributed to continued Assyrian hostilities (bibleinterp); en.wikipedia: briefly reoccupied in the early 7th century, later abandoned under Persian rule.

Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900): Stratum V, late 10th c. BCE (Hebrew Wikipedia: Iron strata V-III, Stratum IV 8th c., Stratum III 7th c.; the page's heading '586-950' is inconsistent with its own sub-dates). Whole site about 15 dunams; excavated 1967 and 1971 (Kochavi), 1990-96 (Beit-Arieh and B. Carson), 2025 (IAA). Identification disputed with no favourite: Moladah (Robinson, Guerin; but English Wikipedia 'Moladah' calls Khirbet el-Waten more likely), Hormah (Garstang, B. Mazar), 'Arad of Beth-Yeroham' in Shishak's list (Aharoni), Baalath-beer (Kochavi), Telem (Na'aman); Roman Mouliatha. Included as a site because the assignment lists it; no accepted biblical name. Population blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moladah

Iron Age IIB (c. -800): Stratum IV, 8th c. BCE (Hebrew Wikipedia). No area or fortress description for this stratum on the page; Stratum III (7th c.) is outside the window. Same identification caveat as the -925 row. Population blank.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000): Stratum III, the first Iron Age village. Stratum IIIB (first half of the 12th c.) has ash pits, ovens and silos; Stratum IIIA (mid-12th c.) the first permanent buildings, four-room houses (Tebes 2003, Aula Orientalis 21: 64). Stern et al. 1993 / Kempinski 1978 date Stratum III from the end of the 13th to the mid-12th c. (deadseaquake.info). Khirbet el-Meshash, excavated 1972-75 (Aharoni, Fritz, Kempinski) and 1979 (Kempinski); Iron I settlement about 200 x 150 m, about 15 acres (6 ha). No accepted biblical name: Yohanan Aharoni proposed Hormah (followed by Fritz and Kempinski); Kochavi, Na'aman and Finkelstein object (Kochavi: 'the town of Amalek', 1 Sam 15:5; Finkelstein: not an Israelite site): disputed, no clear favourite; included because the assignment lists the site. Population blank for this stratum. Further sources: https://deadseaquake.info/EarthquakeCatalogOfTheDeadSea/Sites/Archaeo/TellMasos.html ; https://moses.creighton.edu/vr/Masos/txt/intro.html

Event: Sennacherib's campaign in Judah, 701 BCE. Na'aman lists Tel Beit Mirsim with Beth-shemesh and Tel 'Eton (Eglon) among the central Shephelah sites that were destroyed in the campaign and never settled again, while Lachish survived in weakened form (poorer fortifications and building) and Ekron on the Philistine coast flourished in the 7th century. BibleWalks (read through WebFetch) says "Beit Mirsim was destroyed again at the end of the 8th Century, probably during the Assyrian conquest" and "The Israelite city was never built again after 701 BC". Wikipedia 'Tell Beit Mirsim' still gives Albright's strata down to around 589 BCE (see conflicts) and notes that Albright's identification of the site with Debir is no longer accepted (the map's 'Debir' is Khirbet Rabud, 15 km away). Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) repeats that Beth-shemesh, Tel 'Eton and Tel Beit Mirsim were not resettled. Population blank. Confidence medium.

Event: exiles settled in the Besor region, 716 BCE. A fragment of Sargon's inscriptions (quoted by Na'aman) records that he settled deportees, whose land of origin is lost, in a city on the border of the Wadi of Egypt (the Besor) and placed them under the sheikh of the city of Laban; Na'aman suggests that this settlement included Tell Jemmeh (Tel Gamma), perhaps the Arza of the Assyrian inscriptions, where two ostraca of the late 8th or early 7th century BCE (published by Naveh) list mostly non-Semitic personal names next to a few West Semitic ones (Shalom, Ba'alshama and similar). Naveh took the unusual names for local Philistine names or for foreign mercenaries; Na'aman argues instead that they belong to the deportees, or their sons, brought by the Assyrians in 716, whose origin he places on the Iranian plateau (Media). Online: Wikipedia 'Tell Jemmeh' mentions "an Assyrian structure, probably a palace, from the Assyrian occupation" and that "Four seventh century BC ostraca were found" (the paper discusses two); it says nothing about deportees, so the deportee reading rests on the paper alone. Population blank. Confidence low-medium. The map's nearest marker is the kibbutz Re'im (1.4 km), a different, modern place.

source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell_Ruqeish | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargon_II | https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%94%D7%94%D7%92%D7%9C%D7%99%D7%95%D7%AA_%D7%94%D7%90%D7%A9%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%95%D7%AA | Na'aman, Cathedra 54 (1989), pp. 53, 55, 57 and n. 50 (PDF pp. 11, 13, 15)
comment: Event: Assyrian settlement at the Egyptian border, 716 BCE. Na'aman ties the founding of the fortified, planned settlement at Ruqeish (Rukeis) near Deir el-Balah, between the Besor (the Wadi of Egypt) and Rafah, to Sargon II's policy of developing and holding the border with Egypt: the site covers 80-100 dunams and was founded in the second half of the 8th century BCE, and its founding required population groups to be brought in. He thinks a part of the exiles brought from the Iranian plateau in 716 and settled in the Wadi-of-Egypt area were settled at Ruqeish, which would date the founding to that year (his inference); the town later became an important trading centre on the southern Philistine coast and lasted to the end of the Persian period. Note: Na'aman (n. 50) withdraws the earlier proposal (Oren and colleagues) to identify Ruqeish with the 'sealed karu of Egypt', because he reads the word in Sargon's Nimrud-prism sentence as kisurru 'border', not karu 'trading quarter'. Online: Wikipedia 'Tell Ruqeish' still reports that Oren "suggested that Tell Ruqish may be the site referred to as "sealed Karum of Egypt" in a late 8th-century BC inscription from Nimrud", and Wikipedia 'Sargon II' says Sargon "established a new trading post near the border of Egypt in 716, staffed it with people deported from various conquered lands" (see conflicts). Hebrew Wikipedia 'ההגליות האשוריות' (a close paraphrase of the paper, so not independent) also links the founding of the settlement at Ruqeish, between the Besor and Rafah, with Assyrian strengthening of the Egyptian border and says it grew into an important trading centre on the southern Philistine coast. Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200). Identification doubtful: Thebez is generally identified with Tubas (name similarity) but Malamat proposes Tirzah (Tell el-Far'ah North) or reads Thebez as a corruption of Tirzah (he.wikipedia; biblexika). biblexika lists Late Bronze Age occupation (1550-1150 BCE per that source) at Tubas; no excavations since the modern town overlies the remains. Canaanite period. No population estimate found. Further sources: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/תבץ

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). biblexika: Iron Age I-III (1150-333 BCE per that source) attested by surface survey pottery only; no large-scale excavation. Judges 9 has Abimelech killed at Thebez in this period (biblical tradition). Population: none published found; blank. Further sources: https://www.hamichlol.org.il/טובאס

Iron Age IIA to Babylonian/Persian (-1000 to -332), combined in one row because the source does not subdivide: biblexika lists Iron Age I-III surface pottery; hamichlol (Hebrew wiki mirror) says remains from the Israelite period exist in the village and surroundings. Israelite site per biblical tradition (Manasseh/Ephraim area). No population estimate found. Further sources: https://www.hamichlol.org.il/טובאס

[Second-pass revision] adds excavation and Josephus evidence. Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): city founded by Herod Antipas c. 18-20 CE as his capital (dates vary by source: 18 CE in NEAEHL and Friends of IAA, c. 20 CE in Hebrew Wikipedia). Josephus Ant. 18.36-38 (Whiston, lexundria.com): Antipas built it on Lake Gennesareth, settled outsiders and many Galileans, people he forced to move from his own territory, the poor and freed slaves, and cleared graves although Jewish law makes such residents unclean for seven days; so Jews lived there by compulsion or inducement, not as a self-selected Jewish town. Chancey (bibleinterp, 'The Myth of a Gentile Galilee') reads Josephus (Life 64-67 Greeks massacred as a minority; a Sabbath-observing assembly in the proseuche) and Antipas's aniconic coins as a predominantly Jewish city, with limited archaeology because the city lies under the modern town. NEAEHL entry (Hirschfeld and Gutfeld): Early Roman sherds from the founding at the sewage plant (Edelstein and Vitto 1972); Early Roman stadium base at the Galei Kinneret Hotel (Hartal 2002) that the excavators link to the stadium of Josephus; stone vessels ('measuring cups') cited as evidence of a Jewish community in the 1st-2nd c. CE; no Hellenistic remains reported, so no pre-Roman period row is justified (Rakkat of Joshua 19:35 is placed at Tel Raqat north of the city). A Jewish rock-cut burial cave with ossuaries and Greek inscriptions in the northern necropolis dates to the late 1st and mainly the 2nd c. CE (IEJ 2022 abstract), i.e. mostly after this period. No miqveh of the period is reported in the NEAEHL entry. No named scholar gives a Jewish population figure for the 1st c.; Population blank (the English Wikipedia total of 4500-15000 is unnamed and not Jewish-only). Mixed city: Jews plus Greeks and other settlers.

First Revolt: Tiberias was split between Zealots and the well-to-do, and surrendered to Vespasian in 67 - spared destruction; at the outbreak Jewish fishermen formed the majority of a mixed population (EJ). The city 'became a mixed city after the fall of Jerusalem in 70' as Judean Jews moved north. Population: J. Reed (2002) estimates 4,500-15,000 for the 1st c. CE (whole city, mixed - not Jewish-only, so left blank here). Dating basis: Josephus. Confidence high. Framing row.

Tiberias 'became a mixed city after the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE' and the surviving southern Jewish population moved to Galilee (Wikipedia 'Tiberias'). Secondary source; the article gives 70 explicitly. The city's founding is dated around 20 CE (outside the period). The same article notes there is no direct indication that Tiberias took part in the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136), so it survived the Hadrianic devastation of Judea.

Municipal coinage: the Tiberias mint produced city coins from 99 (Trajan) until the reign of Elagabalus (218-222), per Encyclopaedia Judaica. Numismatic evidence for a functioning autonomous city whose character EJ says 'changed completely in the first half of the second century' when R. Simeon b. Yohai purified it. The coins themselves do not state the religion of the citizens; confidence medium.

After the expulsion of Jews from Judea following the Bar Kokhba defeat (135), 'Tiberias and Sepphoris became the major Jewish cultural centres' (Wikipedia 'Tiberias'). Secondary source; date is the end of the Bar Kokhba war used as a conventional year.

Per the Talmud, Simeon bar Yochai 'cleansed the city of ritual impurity' (the cemetery problem), making Tiberias fit for Jewish habitation; Wikipedia gives 145 CE but tags the claim 'citation needed'. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Tiberias) says only 'first half of the second century', after which the patriarch and Sanhedrin chose it as their residence. Rabbinic literary tradition; date approximate.

Burial cave of a local family at the Arbel Vista neighbourhood (c. 2 km N of the Roman-Byzantine city, near Tel Raqqat) used for generations from the 1st c. to the 3rd c. CE: two ossuaries (limestone and a ceramic 'bathtub' type), one with the red-painted Greek name 'of Tyrannis' (palaeography 1st-2nd c.), Kefar Hananya and Shihin pottery of the 2nd-3rd c. and two 1st-c. types; the authors argue the ossuary custom reached the Galilee before 70 and that the cave was used by a Jewish population (Hebrew/Aramaic name rendered in Greek). Conventional year (1st-3rd c., mid). Dating basis: pottery/inscription palaeography. Confidence medium-high (burial custom, not an explicit Jewish text).

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906): the sources mention no definite Jewish settlement at Tiberias until the second half of the 2nd c., although Jewish scholars (e.g. Ben Azzai, early 2nd c.) knew its streets; Simeon ben Yohai, who recovered in the springs, declared it clean; Judah ha-Nasi also resided there; named synagogues include the Kifra and the Old Synagogue of Serongin; the baths were famous by the 3rd c.; from the settlement of Johanan b. Nappaha the city became the centre of scholarship, and it was the last city where a Sanhedrin sat. Conflicts with EJ ('first half of the second century'). Conventional year (late 2nd c.). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium.

Burial cave with ossuaries found in 2018 in the Arbel Vista neighbourhood (north Tiberias; IAA, Y. Amitzur, ESI 134): probably hewn in the 1st c. CE and used throughout the 2nd-3rd c.; the Aramaic-speaking rural population nearby means it belonged to a family from Tiberias; the authors argue it challenges the idea that ossuary burial reached the Galilee only after 70 or after Bar Kokhba, through refugees. Dating basis: pottery, ossuary burials, entrance decoration. Year 200 = 2nd-3rd c.

Seat of the Sanhedrin: Wikipedia 'Sanhedrin' says the Great Sanhedrin 'finally moved to Tiberias in 220' under Gamaliel III (after Shefar'am, Beit She'arim and Sepphoris); Wikipedia 'Tiberias' says 'about 220 CE'. Babylonian Talmud Rosh Hashanah 31a-b lists Tiberias as the last of the Sanhedrin's migrations (Sefaria text). Conflicts: Wikipedia 'Hammat Tiberias' says Tiberias was the seat 'from 193 CE to the late 4th century'; Conder & Kitchener (1881, quoted in the Tiberias article) say about the middle of the 2nd century. Rabbinic-literary date; medium confidence.

The Sanhedrin, after several moves, settled in Tiberias in about 220 CE; Tiberias became the focus of Jewish scholarship in the land and its 13 synagogues served a growing Jewish population in the Late Roman period (Wikipedia; historical summary from rabbinic tradition, dates conventional). Population: the city is estimated to have had 4,500-15,000 inhabitants in the first century CE (Reed 2002, p. 82, cited by Wikipedia) - a pre-70 estimate for a mixed pagan/Jewish city, therefore not entered as Jewish population. An epitaph at Taenarum (Greece) names a Justus son of Andromache of Tiberias, probably a refugee after 70.

Academy of Yohanan bar Nappaha: Wikipedia 'Tiberias' says the Jerusalem Talmud 'was compiled by his school in Tiberias between 230-270 CE' (midpoint 250 used); Johanan died 279. Wikipedia 'Resh Lakish' says Resh Lakish (c. 200-c. 275) accompanied Johanan to Tiberias 'when Johanan founded an academy there'. Caveat: Wikipedia 'Jerusalem Talmud' dates the final redaction to the second half of the 4th / first half of the 5th century and says it 'probably originated in Tiberias in the School of Johanan bar Nappaha'; so 230-270 is the formative school period, not final redaction. Rabbinic-literary.

Archaeology: Wikipedia 'Tiberias' reports excavators uncovered a structure dating to the 3rd century CE 'that may have been the seat of the Sanhedrin' (3rd century = conventional mid-century year 250; low-medium confidence because of 'may have been'). The article also lists earthquakes known at the city in 306, 363, 419 and 447.

Patriarch Judah II Nesi'ah (Nasi 230-270; 'a sage from the middle of the third century CE') 'lived in Tiberias' and supported Johanan's Academy of Tiberias; Resh Lakish left and was invited back; Graetz/Wikipedia: the 'patriarch Joullos' with whom Origen conversed at Caesarea on biblical subjects was probably Judah II (Origen misreading). Mid-3rd-century patriarchal residence at Tiberias. Rabbinic/patristic; 250 = midpoint of 230-270.

Beth Ma'on (Bethmaus; Leibner's survey site 46, Nasr ed-Din, map ref 1995/2428, 45 dunams, just west of Tiberias on the Sepphoris road; Tel Ma'on, site 45, is only a 2-3 dunam sherd scatter and is rejected) in the 3rd c.: R. Shim'on ben Lakish (third quarter of the 3rd c.) says he can treat Beth Ma'on as continuous with Tiberias for the Sabbath limit (Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 5:1, 22b); Yosi of Ma'on preached in 'the synagogue of Ma'on' against the house of the patriarch (Genesis Rabbah 80:1; the parallel in Sanhedrin 2:5 puts the scene in a Tiberias synagogue); the synagogue of Ma'on is the example of a building 'visible' from Tiberias (Megillah 1:11, 72d; also Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 139a, Zevahim 118b, Hullin 97a). The villagers were day labourers in Tiberias (Bava Metzia 7:1). The priestly course Huppah is placed here in a Yemeni inscription (5th-6th c.) and in piyyutim. Excavation (H. Ben Nahum, 1999) found dwellings dated to the 2nd-3rd c.; the village was abandoned around the second half of the 3rd c. and re-settled only in a very limited way in the second half of the 5th/6th c.; no monumental synagogue remains were found, so the synagogue was probably not monumental. Source: U. Leibner, Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine Galilee (Mohr Siebeck 2009), pp. 286-295, 400. Conventional year (c. 250-280). Dating basis: rabbinic traditions + excavation and survey. Confidence medium. Supplements the 300 row for Beth Ma'on, whose tentative identification with Tel Ma'on/Nasr ad-Din Leibner resolves in favour of Nasr ed-Din.

Jewish Encyclopedia ('Johanan b. Nappaha'): Johanan, who moved from Sepphoris and founded a school at Tiberias, 'died at Tiberias 279'; later Talmudists credited him with compiling the Palestinian Talmud and modern scholars think he 'projected the compilation, which ... was not completed till over a century after him'; he aided the patriarch Judah II (Wikipedia 'Judah II': Nasi 230-270, who 'lived in Tiberias') in repealing the ban on oil of pagans, and received a pension from the patriarch. Rabbinic-literary; high confidence on the death place/year.

Jewish Encyclopedia ('Ammi'): R. Ammi (third-generation Palestinian amora, third century) studied under Johanan at Tiberias, became 'the center of a large circle of learned friends' and 'eventually succeeded to the rectorate of the college at Tiberias' (Hullin 134b), ordained at the same time as R. Assi; as a youth he had attended the college at Caesarea under R. Hoshaiah I; the article's one dated event is his visit to Queen Zenobia (267-273). Year 280 = conventional date for the succession after Johanan's death (279); the entry gives no date for it. Rabbinic-literary; medium confidence.

Beth Ma'on (Bethmaus; Josephus' village four stadia from Tiberias where he met the leaders of Tiberias) was a Jewish village of the Late Second Temple and Mishnaic periods on the hill NW of Tiberias (Midrash Genesis Rabbah 85:7: 'they ascend to it from Tiberias'); in DJE 23 (4th-5th c.) it is the residence of the 13th priestly course Huppah. Tentatively identified with Nasr ad-Din/Tell Ma'un, now within Upper Tiberias. Conventional year (Mishnaic-Talmudic period). Dating basis: literary + inscription. Confidence low-medium.

Comes Joseph (Joseph of Tiberias, Jewish convert to Christianity) tried under Constantine to build a church in Tiberias, 'in vain' (EJ; the story is known from Epiphanius, Panarion 30, as summarised in Wikipedia's 'Joseph of Tiberias'); Wikipedia notes scholarly doubts on the historicity of Epiphanius' account but Tiberias is described as predominantly Jewish. Year = conventional, Constantine's last years (d. 337). Dating basis: patristic source. Confidence medium.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Tiberias): a rectangular building with a mikveh, dated 'early 3rd century to mid-Byzantine period' (midpoint c. 340 used), was identified by the excavator Y. Hirschfeld as the bet midrash 'founded by Rabbi Johanan' where the Jerusalem Talmud was redacted. Hirschfeld's identification is an interpretation of stratigraphy/typology; medium-low confidence. EJ also says R. Johanan, R. Simeon b. Lakish, R. Ammi and R. Assi presided over the academy and that 'thirteen synagogues' are mentioned in the sources (including those of the Babylonians and Tarsians).
Josefa Malowany, originally from Ostrolenka, was noted as living in Israel as the wife of the Deputy Mayor of Tiberias.
A Talmudic teaching mentions that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi had thirteen batei kenesiot (synagogues) in Tiberias.

Gallus revolt: 'The city revolted against Gallus Caesar. Roman commander Ursicinus occupied it but it suffered no damage' (Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Tiberias'). Conflicting accounts: Wikipedia 'Jewish revolt against Constantius Gallus' lists Tiberias and Diospolis (Lydda) as 'two of the cities conquered by the rebels' that were 'almost destroyed'; COJS says the revolt 'spread to Tiberias and Lydda'; EJ 'Land of Israel' says Tiberias, Sepphoris and Lydda 'were rebuilt shortly after the revolt'. Literary (Jerome, Sozomen, Socrates) tradition; damage uncertain.

Under the persecutions of Constantius and Gallus the Tiberian scholars decided to intercalate a month for the year 353, but for fear of the Romans the letter announcing it to Raba at Mahoza wrote 'Rakkath' instead of 'Tiberias' (Sanhedrin 12a); their sessions were held in a grotto near Tiberias (Genesis Rabbah 31). Evidence that the rabbinic centre still determined the calendar in 353, two years after the Gallus revolt. Dating basis: literary (Talmud). Confidence medium-high.

Epiphanius, Panarion 30.4-12 (Williams translation): Count Joseph of Tiberias, a Jewish 'apostle' (assistant to the patriarch) who converted to Christianity, received an imperial rescript 'to build Christ's churches in the Jewish towns and villages where no one had ever been able to found churches, since there are no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians among the population'; 'This rule of having no gentiles among them is observed especially at Tiberias, Diocaesarea, Sepphoris, Nazareth and Capernaum' (30.11.9-10). In Tiberias he began a church in an unfinished temple 'they may have called the Adrianeum', met Jewish sorcery and violence, and 'finished a small church' (30.12). Epiphanius met Joseph (then about 70) at his estate in Scythopolis (30.5); the Hebrew Gospels of John, Acts and Matthew were kept in the Jewish 'treasuries at Tiberias' (30.3.8); the bishop 'who then lived near Tiberias' baptised the dying patriarch Ellel (30.4). Year 355 = Epiphanius' encounter with Joseph (Wikipedia 'Joseph of Tiberias'); Panarion written 374-377; the rescript itself belongs to Constantine's reign (d. 337). Primary patristic source (translation PDF); Joseph's story is hearsay, so medium confidence.

Calendar: Wikipedia 'Sanhedrin' - 'The last universally binding decision of the Great Sanhedrin appeared in 358 when the Hebrew calendar was established' (the same article seats the Sanhedrin in Tiberias from 220; its Patriarchate section gives 359). Wikipedia 'Hillel II': Hai Gaon dates the calendar event 670 Seleucid = 358/9 CE; Hillel II was Nasi 320-365. The attribution to Hillel II is a later tradition (EJ 'Land of Israel': 'per a later tradition ... in 359'); the articles do not name Tiberias in the calendar sentence, the link is through the Sanhedrin's seat.

Wikipedia 'Tiberias' lists earthquakes known at the city in 30, 33, 115, 306, 363, 419, 447 and 631-32, so the 363 Galilee earthquake is among them. No site-specific Jewish damage is described; low-confidence event row.

Epiphanius, Panarion 30 (composed 374-377 CE): Tiberias is the first of the towns (Tiberias, Diocaesarea, Sepphoris, Nazareth, Capernaum) with no Greeks, Samaritans or Christians; Joseph the Comes began a small church in Tiberias on the unfinished Hadrianeum. Magness notes the large three-aisled basilica excavated in Tiberias (30 x 30 m) dates to the 4th-5th c. (IAA) or 5th c. (Cytryn-Silverman 2015) and cannot be Joseph's small church. Year 375.

Jewish Encyclopedia ('Jerome'): Jerome (settled at Bethlehem c. 385) studied Hebrew with a Tiberian Jew, 'Baranina, i.e. Bar Hanina, of Tiberias', who came at night only and sometimes sent a certain Nicodemus (Epistolae 84.3) and 'acquainted Jerome with a mass of Hebrew traditions, some of which referred especially to his native place, Tiberias'. Year 385 = start of Jerome's Bethlehem residence (undated in the entry). Patristic source showing a Jewish scholarly community at Tiberias in the late 4th century; medium confidence on the year.

Broshi (BASOR 236, 1979), Table 2: Late Roman-Byzantine Tiberias covered 40 hectares (estimate credited to G. Foerster). Broshi gave no per-town population (ceiling by his own coefficient, 400/ha less 25%, would be about 12,000 for all inhabitants - my arithmetic, not Broshi's). Conventional year 400.

Synagogue at Tiberias excavated by Ariel Berman (1978-79) and Alexander Onn (1989): column bases and part of a mosaic with a Greek inscription and lulav and etrog decoration; Bornblum database period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Conventional year 400; low confidence on the date.

End of the Patriarchate: Tiberias was the Sanhedrin's 'final meeting place before its disbanding in 425 CE' (Wikipedia 'Tiberias'); Gamaliel VI, last nasi, died 425 (Wikipedia 'Sanhedrin'/'Nasi'). Related imperial acts, not Tiberias-specific in the sources: edict of 20 Oct 415 stripping Gamaliel VI of his honorary prefecture and banning new synagogues (Wikipedia 'Gamaliel VI'; Jewish Encyclopedia gives 17 Oct 415); a 426 decree diverted the patriarchal tax; a 429 law (EJ 'Land of Israel') mentions the death of the nasi. EJ 'Tiberias': a Christian community with a bishop was established in the 5th century. Dates for the formal abolition differ (425/426/429).

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Tiberias): in 520 Mar Zutra, son of the exilarch of Babylonia, settled in Tiberias and became head of the academy; Wikipedia 'Sanhedrin' says the Sanhedrin 'continued to function in some capacity in the 6th century' at Tiberias under the rashei ha-perek. Literary (geonic) tradition.

6th c.: the Letter of Simeon of Beth Arsham urged the Christians of Palaestina to seize the leaders of Judaism in Tiberias and compel them to restrain the Jewish king Dhu Nuwas (persecution of Christians in Najran) - evidence that Tiberias was recognised as the headquarters of Judaism. Conventional year for 'the 6th century' (letter usually dated c. 524). Dating basis: literary. Confidence medium.

Procopius (cited in Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Tiberias'): the city wall of Tiberias was built in the reign of Justinian (527-565; midpoint 546 used). Roman literary source showing the city's continuing importance; not itself evidence of Jewish residents.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Tiberias): a synagogue with mosaic floors excavated in 1978-79 (6th century; conventional year 550) is identified by EJ with one of the thirteen synagogues mentioned in the Talmud; Wikipedia 'Tiberias': 'In the 6th century Tiberias was still the seat of Jewish religious learning.' Archaeological with an inferred identification; medium-low confidence.

Event: Benjamin of Tiberias, a man of immense wealth, 'enlisted and armed Jewish soldiers from Tiberias, Nazareth and the mountain cities of Galilee' who joined the Persian army and marched on Jerusalem, which fell in 614 (Wikipedia 'Benjamin of Tiberias'). The book: about 20,000 Jewish volunteers from the Galilee helped the Persians. Rebel numbers, not a population: Population blank. Book: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 047 (Screenshot_20221028-093521.jpg); page number not visible.

Event: when Heraclius re-entered the country after defeating the Persians, 'the Jews of Tiberias and Nazareth, under the leadership of Benjamin of Tiberias, surrendered and asked for his protection'; Benjamin was persuaded to convert and the emperor promised not to punish the Jews (Wikipedia 'Benjamin of Tiberias'; 'Jewish revolt against Heraclius'). After the emperor reached Jerusalem he broke the promise under pressure from the Church and a general massacre followed that 'devastated the Jewish communities of the Galilee and Jerusalem' (same article). The book gives 629 for Heraclius' stay at Benjamin's house in Tiberias; Wikipedia dates his entry into Jerusalem to 21 March 630 (some sources 629). Population blank. Book: Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך חוסל הרוב היהודי בארץ ישראל (Carmel), e-reader screenshot img 047 (Screenshot_20221028-093521.jpg); page number not visible.

comment: Synagogues and a Jewish community at Tiberias in the early Muslim period. Wikipedia (Tiberias, fetched): "Willibald visited in 724 and noted several churches and synagogues. In 808, Tiberias had five churches and one convent." The book (ch. 4, images 053-054) says that under Arab rule the Jews were the largest community of Tiberias, in two congregations (of Jerusalem and Babylonian origin) with several synagogues, the Christians second (five churches) and the Muslims smallest (one mosque), and that the city flourished in the 8th and 9th centuries and kept its standing as the main Jewish settlement of the Galilee until the end of the 10th or the 11th century; the five churches agree with Wikipedia, while the one-mosque count is not on the Wikipedia page (its first known mosque mention is al-Muqaddasi in 985). Year 724 is the dated online fact. Population blank. Confidence high for the synagogues, medium for the rest.

source: https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%98%D7%91%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%94 | Shpak-Lissak, R., מתי ואיך היגרו הערבים והמוסלמים לארץ ישראל מהכיבוש הערבי עד מלחמת העולם הראשונה (640-1914) (Yedioth Ahronoth / Sifrei Hemed), ch. 1, section A.3 (cities), Tiberias, img 078 (Screenshot_20221028-095940.jpg); e-reader page number not visible in the screenshots
comment: Synagogues: Hebrew Wikipedia (Tiberias): the great Sabbatical-year earthquake (dated 745-749) hit the city and, according to the contemporary historian Michael the Syrian, thirty synagogues in Tiberias collapsed, which the article reads as a sign of a strong Jewish community in a mixed Muslim, Christian and Jewish city. Shpak-Lissak (ch. 1, section A.3, Tiberias) says only that the synagogue of Proclus was damaged in the 749 earthquake and repaired, and records a dispute over the largest community: Jewish sources make the Jews the largest community under Arab rule, while the archaeologist Avni infers from five churches against one mosque that the Christians were the largest community and the Muslims the smallest. The two sources give different details of the same earthquake. No count; Population blank. Confidence medium.

comment: Event: dispute over the jizya of the Jews of Tiberias. Princeton Geniza Project, document ENA NS 18.26 (fetched): a reply to a complaint that a local official was "overcharging jizya payments" from the Jews of Tiberias (some paid 5 dirhams, some 10, some were exempt as Khaybari Jews; the Jews held receipts going back years). Dating: "ca. 1030 CE (Gil), or at least ca. 1020–50". The book (ch. 4, image 055) says the Cairo Geniza has evidence of disputes in 1030 between the authorities and the Jews of Tiberias over the size of the community's total tax. Population blank. Confidence high.

Benjamin of Tudela, Sefer ha-Massa'ot (Itinerary), c.1165: traveller names the place "Tiberias"; Adler translation, text marker [p.45]. Traveller's words: 'about fifty Jews'. Identification: Tiberias. Year 1165 = c.1165 (Benjamin travelled c.1165-1173).

Petahiah of Regensburg, Sibbub ha-Olam, c.1180: traveller names the place "Tiberias"; Adler, Jewish Travellers (1930), p.85 (OCR page markers). comment: Event: Mamluk conquest of the Lower Galilee and destruction of Tiberias. The book (ch. 6, image 065) says Baybars conquered the Lower Galilee in 1263 and the city of Tiberias was razed to its foundations (the Upper Galilee fell in 1266, the Western Galilee in 1271); in the Mamluk period the city stayed in ruins and the Jewish community, which had been the leading one of the Galilee, lost its place to Safed. No online page states the 1263 destruction, but Wikipedia (Tiberias, fetched) agrees on the result: "In 1325, Ibn Batuta described Tiberias as a ruin." Basola found it in 1522 "ruined and desolate", and "Ottoman tax registers between 1528 and 1596 do not list a Jewish community in Tiberias." Year 1263 comes from the book only. Population blank. Confidence medium.

Event: Doña Gracia Mendes Nasi obtained tax-collecting rights in Tiberias and its villages from Sultan Suleiman (Wikipedia gives 1558; Beinart map 79/text p. 90 gives 1560, confirmed for her nephew in 1561); in 1561 Joseph Nasi, Lord of Tiberias, encouraged Jews to settle and rebuilt the city walls (completed 1565 per Beinart) and planted mulberry trees for silk. Wikipedia adds that Ottoman tax registers between 1528 and 1596 do not list a Jewish community in Tiberias, so the real size of the resettlement is doubtful. Year 1561 = Nasi resettlement call.

No population figure found.
Late Bronze (-1550 to -1200); he.wikipedia: circa 1600-1200 BCE (near-continuous settlement from Chalcolithic to Persian period; 12 strata per en.wikipedia). Canaanite. No population figure found.
Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000); en/he.wikipedia: Philistine settlement, fortified city with dense mud-brick construction (11th-12th centuries per he.wikipedia). No population figure found.

Literary only: Judg 14:1-5: Samson goes down to Timnath and wants a Philistine woman from there as his wife (en.wikipedia also notes the vineyards of Judg 14:5); Judg 14:19: he then kills thirty men at Ashkelon to pay the riddle wager (verses checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -1100 = Judges period convention. Josh 15:10: the Judah border passes Beth-shemesh and Timnah (checked). Identification: Tel Batash (Tell Butashi) in the Sorek valley about 7 km NW of Beth-shemesh, excavated by Amihai Mazar and George Kelm 1977-1989; the name migrated to Khirbet Tibna (en.wikipedia Tel Batash, 'Timnah'). Archaeology: Iron I Philistine fortified city with dense mud-brick construction (existing Timnah rows). Gen 38:13 (Judah and Tamar at Timnah) is a patriarchal mention (also en.wikipedia). Site 10 acres = 4 ha. Further source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Batash
Iron Age IIA (-1000 to -900); he.wikipedia lists Iron Age II beginning in the 10th century BCE. No population figure found.

Literary only: 2 Chr 28:18: the Philistines take Timnah (with Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Shocho and Gimzo) in the reign of Ahaz and settle there (verse checked on the fetched KJV chapter page). Year of Data -735 = Ahaz convention. Archaeology: Judahite Iron II fortifications and buildings of the 8th-7th centuries with an LMLK seal impression (en.wikipedia); Dever's estimate of about 500 inhabitants in the 9th-8th centuries is already on the existing Timnah Iron IIB row.

Iron Age IIC / late monarchy (-722 to -586); en.wikipedia (Timnah): fortifications and buildings of the Kingdom of Judah from the 7th-8th centuries BCE incl. LMLK seal impression. No population figure found for this period.

city_other: חירבת תיבנה / תל תבנה / Khirbet Tibnah (Khirbet Tibna)
comment: Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000) with literary mention. BibleWalks ('Tibneh - ancient Timna'): Khirbet Tibneh in the hill country of Ephraim is identified as Timnath-serah / Timnath-heres, Joshua's inheritance and burial place; the survey sherds date from the Middle Bronze II on and the peak of the city was in Iron Age I; in Iron II it was an 'administrative city'; the ruins cover about 50 dunams (5 ha) in the BibleWalks text and in Hebrew Wikipedia, 35 dunams in a BibleWalks photo caption; Hebrew Wikipedia: surface sherds from the Early Bronze to the Ottoman period, most numerous in Iron II, Early Roman and Byzantine, and a first excavation season in July 2022 (Dvir Raviv, Bar-Ilan University) exposed Iron Age, Hellenistic and Early Roman remains on the summit. Josh 19:50 (Joshua is given Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim, builds the city and dwells in it), Josh 24:30 (buried 'on the north side of the hill of Gaash'), Judg 2:9 (the same burial, spelled Timnath-heres). Identification with Timnath-serah goes back at least to Schurer in the 1880s and is the usual one (English and Hebrew Wikipedia 'Khirbet Tibnah'), but it is not proven; Kifl Haris, another place with a Tomb of Joshua, is the rival. No population figure.

Identification doubtful: Wikipedia and he.wikipedia also propose Kifl Hares; Khirbet Tibnah used as given. Site about 50 dunams (en.wikipedia) incl. slopes; no academic population estimate found. Population left blank.

city_other: תל אל-פארעה (צפון) / تل الفارعة (Tell el-Far'ah north)
comment: Literary mention; Tirzah as capital of the northern kingdom, dated by convention c. -930 to -880. Josh 12:24 (the king of Tirzah in the list of defeated kings), 1 Kgs 14:17 (Jeroboam's wife returns to Tirzah and the child dies), 1 Kgs 15:21 and 1 Kgs 15:33 (Baasha reigns in Tirzah), 1 Kgs 16:8-10 (Elah reigns two years in Tirzah and is killed there by Zimri), 1 Kgs 16:17-18 (Zimri burns the king's house over him), 1 Kgs 16:23 (Omri reigns twelve years, six of them in Tirzah; he then buys the hill of Samaria, v.24), 2 Kgs 15:14 (Menahem from Tirzah, c. -745). Identification: Tell el-Far'ah (North), 180 dunams in total, in the Wadi Far'ah north-east of Nablus (English Wikipedia 'Tirzah (Tell el-Far'ah North)'; standard identification). Stratum VIIb (radiocarbon, first half of the 10th c. BCE) shows residential quarters, streets and a shrine, 'apparently a seat of the early kings of Israel'. The existing rows give the Iron periods; this row adds the verse references. No population figure.

Coordinates are those of the modern village (the exact site is not given in the sources). Late Roman and/or Byzantine, conventional year 400. Dating basis: architecture. Confidence low.

Tur'an (Tir'an) 'was a Jewish village' in the Roman and Byzantine (Mishnaic and Talmudic) periods according to Wikipedia; Iron Age wall and Early Islamic/Mamluk finds are described but no Roman-Byzantine Jewish remains. Leibner (2009, site 47) is more cautious: Tur'an occurs only once in rabbinic literature, in Song of Songs Rabbah 6:9 (edited in the 6th-7th c.), probably a corrupt reading, and a 2003 salvage dig found only Kefar Hananya-type pottery (3rd c.) and Byzantine body sherds. Conventional year (Mishnaic-Talmudic period). Dating basis: single secondary statement. Confidence low (possibly not a Jewish village of the period).

Settlement date from the ceramic survey: Ch. Ben-David (2005, Golan Studies 1, p. 172) posits that the Umm el-Qanatir settlement was founded in the 2nd or early 3rd c. CE and continued through the Byzantine period (quoted at deadseaquake.info from Dray et al. 2017). Conflicts with the older view of a 5th-c. foundation; the Jewish character of the earliest phase is not demonstrated (the synagogue itself is later). en.wikipedia: a Roman-period pagan town venerating the spring, with Jewish settlement later; Jews began to settle in the vicinity in 23 BCE (claim without a named source) and processed flax sold to Susita and Bethsaida. BibleWalks (Em HaKshatot page) states that 'several structural remains of a Roman period synagogue were found under the floor of the Byzantine period synagogue' and that the Byzantine one was built in the 5th c. 'as established by the excavations' (not confirmed in a primary report I could read); it also notes the conjecture that the place is the Talmudic Kamattirya (a man Simon of Kamattirya appears in JT Berakhot 9:2). Year 225 = midpoint of 'second or early third century'; confidence low-medium.

Spring compound of the village (IAA preliminary report, O. Zingboym, HA-ESI 136, 2024, on the 2016 and 2018 seasons; earlier seasons 2000-2003): a built spring compound with two arched troughs, a plastered pool and a southern complex of two troughs. The site (c. 100 x 300 m) is described as 'remains of a Roman-period settlement' with 'buildings, a synagogue (Area B; Ben-David, Gonen and Drei 2006) and an olive press, as well as a cemetery'. Ceramics date the compound's construction 'between the second half of the third century CE and the first half of the fourth century CE'; a channel with mostly 1st-2nd c. sherds is 'the first evidence of construction in the spring compound as early as the first and second centuries CE'; the pottery beneath the paving is mid-3rd to mid-4th c.; apart from one trough no finds postdate the mid-4th c., so 'the entire complex was probably used until no later than the earthquake of 363 CE', and one trough was used 'for a brief period not exceeding the end of the fourth century CE'. This dates a Roman-period (not 5th-c.) phase of the settlement, in line with the Roman-period synagogue remains reported beneath the Byzantine building (225 row); the Jewish character of the spring users is inferred from the site context, not stated by the report. Year 300 = midpoint of second half of 3rd-first half of 4th c.; confidence medium-high for the dates.

Wikipedia 'Umm el-Qanatir': the synagogue was built in the 5th century CE and decorated in the 6th (about 18 x 13 m); main phase 'mid-5th-8th centuries'; the 749 Golan earthquake destroyed it and the Jewish inhabitants left; first documented by Oliphant and Schumacher in 1884; reconstruction from 2003. Archaeological; high confidence for the 5th-6th century occupation.

Jewish village with a very large basalt synagogue (about 18.8 x 13.8 m per Kohl & Watzinger's plan; en.wikipedia 18 x 13 m and ~12 m high - one of the largest of at least 25 Golan synagogues). DATING IS CONTESTED (history of opinions quoted from Dray et al. 2017 at deadseaquake.info): Kohl & Watzinger (1905) 5th c., on a basket capital; M. Avi-Yonah and Huettenmeister & Reeg (1977) 3rd c. because no apse was found; G. Foerster 'Byzantine'; Z. Ma'oz (1995), on artistic style, 'the second half of the fifth century CE'; en.wikipedia 'apparently in the fifth century', embellished in the 6th. Year 475 follows Ma'oz. Ben-David's ceramic survey (2005) is the basis of the settlement-date row below. Ancient name unknown: proposals are Kantur (Menahem di Luzzano, 16th/17th c.), Qamtra/Kamtria of the Talmud, or one of nine unidentified towns of Susita's territory, possibly 'Ein ha-Sha'ar' (Z. Ilan, per he.wikipedia) - all conjectural. Documented 1884 (Oliphant, Schumacher); Kohl-Watzinger 1905 (four-day dig); reconstruction by Y. Dray, Ch. Ben-David and I. Gonen from 2003. Confidence medium.

Synagogue embellished in the 6th c.: en.wikipedia says the Jewish residents built it in the 5th c. and 'embellished' it 'during the sixth century'; a carved vulture (a motif common in Golan and Galilee Jewish art) appears on a double column and the front gable and may come from the same workshop as the decorated Torah-shrine base from 'En Samsam. he.wikipedia adds that the almost intact Torah shrine (heikhal, ~5.25 m high) with a bima, a vine growing from an amphora, column tops with seven-branched menorahs, censer, shofar and Four Species were found - the only early synagogue with a heikhal. The building fell in the 749 earthquake (en.wikipedia) and its stones stayed in place. Year 550 = conventional mid-6th c.; the 6th-c. phase is stated without a published dating basis; confidence medium.

Synod and Sanhedrin of Usha: Encyclopaedia Judaica - 'In about 140 c.e., at the end of the period of persecution following the suppression of Bar Kokhba's revolt, the surviving scholars gathered there, reestablished the Sanhedrin and instituted the regulations known as the Enactments of Usha' (Song of Songs Rabbah 2:5, no. 3). Jewish Encyclopedia ('Synod of Usha'): held 'in the middle of the second century' under Antoninus Pius, after the repeal of Hadrian's decrees, with R. Judah (b. Ilai), R. Nehemiah, R. Meir, R. Jose, R. Simeon b. Yohai and others; the patriarch Simeon b. Gamaliel II was in Usha. Wikipedia 'Sanhedrin' places the seat at Usha in 80 and 116 under Gamaliel II (doubtful) and the move to Shefar'am in 140. Rabbinic-literary; year 140 is the EJ date.

Wikipedia 'Usha (ancient)': Rabbi Akiva's pupils who lived there included Shimon bar Yochai, Judah bar Ilai (whose original home was Usha) and Jose ben Halafta; a Talmudic passage places the death of Judah ben Bava on the boundary between Usha and Shefa-Amr after he ordained seven elders. Encyclopaedia Judaica (encyclopedia.com 'Usha', fetched separately): R. Judah ha-Nasi studied at Usha under R. Judah b. Ilai, 'an inhabitant of the town' (Tosefta Megillah 2:8), and R. Isaac Nappaha owned five courtyards there (Tosefta Eruvin 7:7). Year 150 = conventional mid-2nd-century; rabbinic-literary.

Archaeology (Hurvat Usha, excavated 2008-2012, 2014; declared a national park 2009): two mikvehs carved into bedrock in the 2nd century and used until the 6th century, beside wine and olive-oil installations (Wikipedia 'Usha (ancient)'); a Bar Kokhba-era hiding complex was found cutting through an earlier mikveh (2012). The article identifies the ruin under the Arab village Hawsha (identified by Guerin in the late 19th century). Excavators' dating.

ESI Horbat Usha (2008-09 educational excavations by A. Oshri; 2015 report on a burial cave and winepresses): Roman/Byzantine remains incl. a ritual bath (miqveh), an oil press, a double winepress, hiding refuges, and a burial cave whose staircase fill contained fragments of ceramic ossuaries with pottery of the Late Roman-Early Byzantine period (3rd-5th c.). ESI 2012 notes that according to historical sources a Jewish settlement was at Usha, where the Sanhedrin relocated after the Bar Kokhba Revolt, and reports the first excavation at the site (Byzantine winepress; Roman-period rock cuttings). Identification of Horbat Usha with Usha is traditional. Dating basis: pottery. Year 300 = middle of the 3rd-5th c. range (conventional).

Wikipedia 'Usha (ancient)': 'In the 6th century the Jewish inhabitants left and the mikvehs were filled in' (conventional year 550 for the 6th century); Byzantine-period metalworking (iron slag, hammer-head, c. 1,400 years old) was found in 2019 and the site was abandoned in the 8th century. Excavators' dating; end-of-Jewish-presence date is approximate.

comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): caves in Nahal Darga used as a refuge. Anchor Bible Dictionary entry (Murphy-O'Connor and O'Brien 1992 via cojs.org): coins dated 42/43 58/59 and 69/70 CE and pottery paralleling Qumran II show Jewish refugees in the First Revolt (66-70 CE); an IOU dated 55/56 CE (Mur 18) is linked to this phase. Later and more important Bar Kokhba phase (132-135 CE) is outside the range. Not a settlement: temporary cave refuge; Population blank. No Hasmonean evidence reported. Earlier use Chalcolithic and sparse MB/Iron II. Hebrew refuge-cave page (hamichlol) places the main use in the Bar Kokhba revolt.

Beginnings of the Jewish settlement: on pottery evidence it is 'assumed' to start in the 2nd c. CE, after the destruction of Gamla (1.5 km NW of the Gamla falls); ceramics range from Middle Roman through Late Roman to Byzantine (he.wikipedia, citing Ma'oz's 1981 survey, R. Lavi documentation). Inference, not a dated stratum; confidence low. Year 150 conventional.

Wakhshara (also Beit Lavi), Golan: synagogue site known only from surface remains (unexcavated). Finds recorded in the Bornblum Eretz Israel Synagogues database: Southern wall with preserved entrance made of basalt ashlar. Architectural elements. Stone with lion and inscription. The database dates it only 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine' (c. 3rd-7th c.); the year 400 is a conventional centre of that range and the date is low-confidence. A synagogue implies a Jewish village; no separate settlement chronology is available. Coordinates from the database.

Talmudic-period synagogue at the west end of the ruin: ashlar building facing south, mezuzah stones, carved capitals, a lintel with a lion in relief beside a tabula ansata bearing an unread Aramaic inscription (he.wikipedia; Bornblum 'Wakhshara': also 'Beit Lavi'; unexcavated, in a military firing zone; the lion stone is now at Midreshet HaGolan, Hispin). A temporary Bedouin village later occupied the site. Year 450 conventional.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row: Josephus (Life 188) lists Japha among the Lower Galilee places he fortified ('Jotapata, Capharecho, and Sigo, and Japha, and Mount Tabor'); BibleWalks and Hebrew Wikipedia cite him calling it the largest village of Galilee (Life 45; the lexundria Life 45 page fetched did not contain this line, so unverified here). Vespasian sent Trajan against Japha, near Jotapata, with 1000 horse and 2000 foot (War 3.289); after its fall no males remained besides infants, who with the women were enslaved (War 3.304). The figures of about 15000 slain and 2130 captives (BibleWalks) are casualty numbers, not a population (Notes only); the 17000 'population' on BibleWalks and encyclopedia.com is unsourced and not used. Hebrew Wikipedia: a Roman burial cave (1992, Hadashot Arkheologiyot) with Herodian-type lamps, dated 1st-2nd c. CE, is the only archaeological item of the period found. No miqveh or stone vessels reported. The synagogue (Sukenik 1950) is 3rd-4th c. CE and the lintels (Vincent 1921) are Late Antique. Jewish population is supported by Josephus (it joined the revolt) and the burial cave only; Population blank. IDENTIFICATION: Yafia matches Josephus's Japha by name and proximity to Jotapata; not disputed in pages fetched. The Hadashot Arkheologiyot 128 (2016) trial-excavation report could not be retrieved.

Framing row: Josephus (via Wikipedia 'Yafa an-Naseriyye') fortified Japha in 66 CE, calling it 'the largest village in Galilee'; Roman forces under M. Ulpius Traianus and Titus captured it in spring 67. Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Japhia'): the town 'remained a Jewish town' afterwards. First documented Jewish presence for the period.

Wikipedia 'Yafa an-Naseriyye': part of a mosaic-paved synagogue excavated by Sukenik in 1950 yielded a mosaic fragment with three Hebrew letters and an animal's head, dated to 'the 3rd to 4th centuries AD' (midpoint 300); a Roman-period quarry was in use from the late 1st century to the mid-4th century. EJ 'Japhia' describes a basilical hall about 14 x 15 m with a pavement showing an eagle, tigers, dolphins and 12 figures (Sukenik read '[Eph]raim', Goodenough a zodiac). Archaeological; Hamichlol also gives 3rd-4th century.

Synagogue at Yafia (Sukenik 1950; lintel found 1921): partial plan of a basilical hall c. 19 x 15 m oriented east-west, polychrome mosaic of animals and vegetal motifs, a 3.8 m circle with twelve roundels (zodiac or the Twelve Tribes, with the letters of 'Ephraim' per Sukenik), eagle on volutes. Dated on stylistic grounds to the late 3rd-4th c.; Aramaic fragment 3rd-4th c. Year = midpoint of late 3rd/4th c. Dating basis: art-historical. Confidence medium.

ESI (2012, 2015) on Yafi'a: a synagogue excavated by Sukenik in 1950 on the east slope of the hill dated to the Late Roman or Byzantine periods; a stepped miqwe and several Roman-period burial caves with loculi east of the hill; a 4th-c. (Late Roman, Stratum I) quarry close to the synagogue 'suggests it served the builders', i.e. a 4th-c. construction date for the synagogue is plausible but not established. Year 350 = 4th c.

Synagogue excavated by Sukenik in 1950 (mosaic fragments with a large circle and 12 dots, zodiac or Twelve Tribes). Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000) and identification. Tel Yin'am (Tell en-Naam), the mound above Yavne'el (85 m across, 12 m high), is identified by 'scholars' (none named by BibleWalks) with Jabneel, a southern border town of Naphtali: Josh 19:33 (Naphtali's border: Heleph, Allon to Zaanannim, Adami, Nekeb, Jabneel, unto Lakum, outgoings at the Jordan). The PEF surveyors preferred Yemma (Kefar Yamma) on the Talmudic identification, and the Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities gives no site; disputed, favoured: Tel Yin'am. Archaeology (BibleWalks): after a Late Bronze II Canaanite town destroyed by fire (c. 1300-1200 BCE, with an iron-smelting furnace and a bronze plough), Iron Age I (1200-1000 BCE) Israelite settlers rebuilt on the Canaanite ruins using the same plan. No population estimate. Further sources: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+19&version=KJV ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua

Framing row (pre-70): Yehudiyya (Arabic Yahudiyye, 'Jewish') is one of several proposed sites of Sogane/Soganaea, the Gaulanitis village which Josephus walled for the revolt (Life 37, Whiston translation: he built a wall about Seleucia and Soganni, villages naturally of great strength). he.wikipedia says the cliff-top, walled settlement fits the description and the ruin's wall survives, but no find confirms the identification (another proposal: Kefar Yehuda of Tosefta Kilayim 2:12, based on the name only). Identification conjectural.

Roman-Byzantine village on a cliff above Nahal Yehudiya, surrounded by a wall (5-6 courses survive, tower foundations): reused stones include a five-branched menorah on an ashlar and an oil jug on a lintel probably from a synagogue (he.wikipedia); Bornblum: Jewish, Late Roman/Byzantine. Jewish presence reported after the Arab conquest and into the Crusader period; the Arab settlers knew its Jewish past (hence the name). Year 450 conventional for undated remains.

Wikipedia 'Yehudiya' (central Golan, abandoned village; the name means 'Jewish'): the article links Roman-Byzantine artifacts to a settlement, mentions Jewish presence there after the Arab conquest 'according to multiple testimonies', suggests it as one possible identification of Josephus' Soganaea (fortified before 66), and reports that archaeologists of the University of Haifa and Kinneret College 'unearthed a 1,500-year-old synagogue near the village' in October 2025 (c. 500 used as '1,500 years old'). Preliminary report; low-medium confidence; the Soganaea identification is only one possibility.

Yehudiyye (Golan, near Qatzrin): synagogue site with menorah reliefs, pillars and capitals and remains of a building, excavated by Mechael Osband (2025) per the Bornblum database; period 'Late Roman and/or Byzantine'. Conventional year 400, low confidence on the date.
