Framing row: siege and fall of Yodfat/Jotapata on 20 July 67 (Josephus); mass grave and weapon finds in M. Aviam's 1992-2000 excavations. Josephus' victim count (40,000 killed, 1,200 women and children enslaved) is a literary figure, not a population estimate; the village covered about 50 dunams in the 1st c. CE (Wikipedia).

Wikipedia 'Yodfat': after the Romans destroyed Jotapata on 20 July 67 ('razed and burnt on the first of Tammuz'; three legions, 47-day siege, 40,000 Jewish deaths per Josephus), 'Yodfat was re-established at a nearby site by refugees from Jerusalem', including the priestly family of Miyamin, the sixth priestly course; the Talmud mentions it as the home of Rabbi Menachem. Framing/first post-war row; year 70 conventional for the post-destruction refounding. Priestly-course tradition; low-medium confidence for details.

After 67 the town was re-established at a nearby site by refugees from Jerusalem, among them the priestly family of Miyamin (inscriptions give Yodfat as the sixth priestly course); the Talmud mentions Rabbi Menachem the Yodpaite. Dating basis: literary/epigraphic; low confidence. Year 80 = re-establishment after 67.

Wikipedia says the re-established Jewish town 'flourished for another 300 years before being destroyed' (no more exact date; 67 + 300 = about 367). Low confidence: derived from an unreferenced round figure.

Wikipedia 'Yodfat': the re-founded Jewish town 'flourished for another 300 years before being destroyed' (the article gives no year; its category 'Roman Empire 4th-century disestablishments' implies the 4th century - 67 + 300 = 367, rounded to 370). Inference from a single undated sentence; low confidence.

Ancient Farj (Arabic Farj, Israeli grid 2627/2284; Moshav Yonatan was founded on the ruin in autumn 1975). Claudine Dauphin & Shimon Gibson (Cathedra 73, Sept. 1994, Hebrew version of their 1992-93 survey report on Kafr Naffakh, Na'aran, Farj and Er-Ramthaniyye) describe Farj as a small, unfortified 'town' fitting the halakhic definition of an 'ir (semi-circular plan of at least ten courtyard houses); menorahs, lulavs, ethrogs and shofars engraved on many lintels and Hebrew and Aramaic inscriptions show 'at least part of the population of this small town was Jewish'; the northern of the two large villas was apparently Jewish-owned for a time; stones with Jewish symbols and Hebrew/Aramaic texts are concentrated in a central courtyard, where a monumental building (synagogue or beit midrash?) may have stood. The main building phase (phase B) is dated to the Byzantine period (c. 4th-7th c.) by wall-construction typology compared with Butler's dated Hauran buildings (no dated inscription is cited for Farj). Authors also see Jewish-Christian (Ebionite/Nazarene) symbols and a later Ghassanid Christian component. DISPUTE: Z. Ma'oz presented an alternative interpretation of the remains at Farj and Na'aran (PEQ 117, 1985); IIP lists only Greek epitaphs from Farj. Year 450 conventional; confidence medium-low.

Biblical mention and identification (literary plus archaeology; Year of Data -1200 = conventional date of the Joshua conquest/allotment narrative (the allotment lists themselves are of disputed date)). Identification: Tel Yokneam (Tell Qamun), north part of Yokneam Illit, 32.664 N 35.102 E, secure (Wikipedia; Wikipedia table of Joshua's cities). Marker 'Yoqne'am Illit' reused (0.2 km from the tell). Josh 12:22 (king of Jokneam of Carmel among the 31 kings defeated); Josh 19:11 (Zebulun's border reaches the river before Jokneam); Josh 21:34 (Levitical city of the Merarites, with Kartah); 1 Kgs 4:12 (Baana's district extends to the place beyond Jokneam). Archaeology (Wikipedia, Ben-Tor's Yoqne'am Regional Project 1977-1988 per BibleWalks): city rebuilt c. 12th/early 11th c. after the Late Bronze destruction (probably by Canaanites with Phoenician and Philistine help); its destruction is linked to David; rebuilt in the 10th c. with a 5 m wide casemate wall; razed and resettled in the 9th c. (probably after Hazael's invasion) with a double (corridor) wall; ended by Tiglath-Pileser III in 732 BCE, when it was 'one of the largest cities in the Jezreel Valley' (Broshi and Finkelstein 1990, p. 7, as quoted by Wikipedia). Mound c. 40 dunams, c. 80 dunams with slopes. Further sources: https://www.biblewalks.com/yokneam ; https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Joshua+12&version=KJV ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_the_Book_of_Joshua

comment: Event: Pope Gregory I's letter to the defensor Fantinus (Register 8.23, c. 598): the abbess of the monastery of St Stephen near Agrigento reported that "many of the Jews, divine grace inspiring them, wish to be converted to the Christian faith"; Gregory sent Fantinus to encourage them, ordered baptismal garments for the poor at the church's expense and left the choice between baptism after forty days of penance and waiting for Easter. The atlas (map 12 p. 22, callout 5, attached by its leader line to Agrigento; no year given) says Gregory opposed forced conversion but ordered that a group of Jews who wished to convert be given financial aid and baptized at once, before they changed their minds. The year is the letter's date on the romanletters edition.
The community continued to exist throughout the period of Muslim domination and Girgenti is mentioned in a letter from the Cairo Genizah c. 1060.
The Jewish community is recorded in 1254 when the revenues from the Jews were taxed in favor of the church.
In 1397 the Jews of Agrigento had to equip a force of 200 foot soldiers for one of King Martin i of Aragon's military expeditions.
In 1426 the citizens of Agrigento petitioned unsuccessfully for royal permission to enforce anti-Jewish measures.
Jews are attested in the town in the 15th century

In 1476 King John ii ordered that the money bequeathed by Solomon Anello to promote Hebrew learning in Agrigento be given instead to Guglielmo Raimondo Moncada (alias Flavius Mithridates), a Sicilian Jewish convert to Christianity.
In 1477 a compromise was reached and the Jews of Agrigento were ordered to provide Moncada a house in Palermo instead of the school building in their city.
JE: With the year 1492, in which all Jews were banished from the island, the history of this congregation came to an end.

Cristina Mirabello): the racial laws of 1938 hit the Jewish community, long settled in La Spezia, which counts about seventy persons (merchants, professionals, teachers, soldiers), which had to set up an elementary school for its children (late 1930s; 1938 = year of the laws, count is 'circa una settantina').

Istituto Storico della Resistenza spezzino, 'Deportati Ebrei, Largo': after the RSI order of November 1943 the arrests led to the deportation of 13 persons from La Spezia, all of whom died at Auschwitz or Flossenburg (deportee count - NOT a population); many Jewish families had left the city for nearby villages such as Monterosso al Mare, Vernazza and Vezzano Ligure at the outbreak of the war.

Year 63 is only a conventional central value inferred from Josephus's age (born c. 37, so c. 62-64); neither source gives a year. Jansen (SHAJ XIV 2022): Alexander Jannaeus besieged Gadara at the beginning of the 1st c. BCE and took it after ten months (Josephus Ant. 13.356, confirmed in the fetched Whiston text: 'He also took Gadara, after a siege of ten months'); after the defeat by the Nabatean Obodas I the Hasmoneans gave up their Transjordanian conquests; an inscription records that Philotas and the polis of the Seleuceans repaired the fortress in 85/84 BCE (Worrle 2000), probably under Antiochos XII, which Jansen reads with Gadara coins (Noeske 2013) as a Seleucid base against Hasmoneans and Nabateans; in 83 BCE Jannaeus succeeded in a second attempt; Hasmonean rule ended with Pompey (Jansen: 64 BC), who according to Josephus (Ant. 14.75; War 1.7.7) rebuilt the city 'destroyed by the Jews'. Peleg (NEAEHL 2008, via deadseaquake.info) adds the city wall was destroyed in the Maccabean invasion and then repaired. Hebrew Wikipedia says self-government was taken away after the siege. Greek (Seleucid) city under Hasmonean control; Hasmonean garrison or officials at most; no archaeological evidence of a Jewish population (no mikva'ot, vessels or tombs reported in the fetched reports); Population blank. [Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds sources and a conflict. Josephus (War 1.104; Ant. 13.393, cited by Applebaum and Segal) has Zeno and Theodorus, tyrants of Philadelphia, deposit part of their treasure at Gerasa under Jannaeus; Jannaeus captured the city in the last years of his reign and died besieging Ragaba (Ant. 13.398); the city 'remained under Hasmonean rule until Pompey' (Applebaum and Segal). The Princeton Encyclopedia says Janneus annexed it early in the 1st c. BCE; Encyclopaedia Judaica says Yannai took it from Zeno and Theodorus; Hebrew Wikipedia instead says Queen Shlomtzion (Salome Alexandra) took the city when she continued the siege after her husband's death, so the sources differ on the conqueror. Archaeology: Becht (SHAJ XIV 2022, after Seigne 1997) dates a second altar phase and enlargement of the Zeus terrace to about 100 BC and the first temple (Hellenistic Naos) to about 60 BC. Mixed Greek/Syrian city under Hasmonean rule; a Jewish community is asserted by Encyclopaedia Judaica ('A Jewish community continued to live there') but no fetched excavation report documents Jewish remains of this period; Population blank. Further sources fetched: https://publication.doa.gov.jo/uploads/publications/224/Binder1-en-145-166.pdf ; https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0006:entry%3Dgerasa ; https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/gerasa ; https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%92%27%D7%A8%D7%A9

Alexander Jannaeus conquered Gerasa in the early 80s BCE and brought it into the Kingdom of Judea; Roman conquest ended the 'short-lived Jewish rule' in 63 BCE (English Wikipedia 'Jerash'; 'History of the Jews in Jordan'). Conventional year -83 for 'early 80s'. Jewish rule, not a Jewish population.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds primary text and excavation evidence. Pompey took the city in 63 BCE and it was listed in the Decapolis (Applebaum and Segal; Princeton Encyclopedia). Josephus War 2.18.1 (Whiston text, sections 458 and 480): Jewish raiders 'laid waste' the villages of the Syrians and cities including Gerasa, but 'as for the Gerasens, they did no harm to those that abode with them; and for those who had a mind to go away, they conducted them as far as their borders reached'; Encyclopaedia Judaica reads this as Gerasa protecting its Jews. Applebaum and Segal: the city was never in rebel hands, and the Gerasa taken by Rome in War 4.487-488 is probably a different town. Synagogue architectural fragments were found in the fill of Hadrian's arch; they show either destruction of the community in the revolt or destruction under Trajan (inscriptions dated 115 CE). Becht (SHAJ XIV 2022): the Hellenistic Naos of Zeus, probably destroyed in the First Jewish War, was replaced in 69/70 CE by the Naos of Theon; terrace works 9/10 CE and about 30 CE (architect Diodoros of Gerasa). Mixed Greek/Syrian city with a Jewish minority; the Princeton Encyclopedia gives 10,000-15,000 inhabitants in the early 2nd c. CE for the whole city (not Jewish, outside the period); no Jewish population estimate found; Population blank. Further sources fetched: https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0006:entry%3Dgerasa ; https://publication.doa.gov.jo/uploads/publications/224/Binder1-en-145-166.pdf ; https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/gerasa ; https://www.lexundria.com/j_bj/2.457-2.480/wst

Josephus described Gerasa as mainly Syrian, with 'a small Jewish community'; at the outbreak of the war the people of Gerasa did not kill or imprison the Jews and escorted those who wished to leave to the border (War 2.480; English Wikipedia 'Jerash'); the Encyclopaedia Judaica text says a Jewish community continued to live in the city after Pompey and the inhabitants 'sent the Jewish population away unharmed'. 'Small' is Wikipedia's wording; no figure.

Synagogue at Gerasa dated 'approximately the third or fourth century CE' (English Wikipedia 'Synagogue-Church at Gerasa'; conventional year 300 for the earlier building found beneath the church). Other databases date the Hebrew-Aramaic inscription differently (see 530).

Dedicatory Hebrew-Aramaic mosaic inscription ('Peace be upon all Israel, Amen, Amen Selah', naming Pinhas son of Baruch, Jose son of Samuel, Yudan son of Hezekiah) dated 530-531 CE by the Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine database; the building was converted into a church c. 530 or 531 under Justinian's anti-Jewish measures (English Wikipedia); the Encyclopaedia Judaica text says the synagogue mosaic (donor inscription, Noah's Ark, candelabrum) lay under the foundations of a church built 530-33 and that one of 11 churches built 464-611 stood on a synagogue ruin. Terminus post quem 530, ante quem 531.

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Identification: Tell Hesban (Tall Hisban, Arabic حسبان, Hebrew חשבון) is the standard identification of biblical Heshbon, but archaeology fits poorly (disputed, favoured: Tell Hesban): English Wikipedia says the Bronze Age Heshbon of Sihon 'has not been identified'; Dever finds only scattered 12th-11th c. BCE sherds without architecture and no 13th c. occupation (town 'founded only in the Iron II period'); LaBianca and Walker note Late Bronze/Early Iron remains mostly in secondary deposits. Madaba Plains Project period table lists a 'Canaanite (Israelite)' phase, Strata 21-17 (intermittent): reservoir, wall segments, possible podium, a female plaque. Bible: Sihon's capital (Num 21:25-30), rebuilt by Reuben (Num 32:37), in Reuben's list (Josh 13:17), on Gad's border (Josh 13:26), Levitical city (Josh 21:39), Israel dwelt in Heshbon and its towns (Judg 11:26). No population estimate found; Population blank.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). Madaba Plains Project period table: Moabite phase (Stratum 17: replastered reservoir, Moabite ceramic forms), Aram-Damascus (Stratum 17, no finds listed), Neo-Assyrian (Strata 16-17, Assyrian-influenced building plans), Ammonite (Stratum 16: ostraca, graffito, horse-and-rider figurines). Bible shows Heshbon in Moabite hands (Isa 15:4, 'Heshbon shall cry'; Jer 48:2) and Wikipedia reads Jer 49:3 as a later Ammonite occupation, so the town is not Israelite-held in this period; the Israelite (Reubenite/Gadite) layer is the Iron I row. Dating of strata given only as Iron IIB-C ranges by the table; -900 is the period start. No population estimate found; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds archaeological evidence. Madaba Plains Project period table (129-63 BCE) lists Hasmonean coins as the only local evidence (no architecture or pottery tagged Hasmonean) and cites Josephus Ant. 13.9.1 and 13.15.5. Jewish Encyclopedia: Heshbon became a Jewish possession under Alexander Jannaeus (Ant. 13.15.4). English Wikipedia reports five Hasmonean coins from the late Hellenistic fortress, one of Antigonus II Mattathias (40-37 BCE), which D. Raviv reads as possible pro-Antigonus activity in Transjordan (Wikipedia is the only fetched page for this; Raviv's own paper not reached). Mitchel: Stratum 15 (c. 198-63 BCE) fort with small dependent community; the Stratum 16 reservoir largely filled in, suggesting few inhabitants. Jewish presence is by political control and coins only; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds end-date dispute and literary events. Mitchel Stratum 14 (63 BCE-130 CE): settlement grew somewhat, fort kept in use, many bedrock-cut underground installations, ending in an earthquake. Mitchel dated it to c. 130 CE from an Aretas IV coin (9 BCE-40 CE) in silo fill D.3:57; the Dead Sea earthquake catalogue page (citing Russell 1985 and Ambraseys 2009) says this date is uncertain and the quake could be the 31 BCE Josephus quake or early 2nd c., so the end of Stratum 14 is disputed. Madaba Plains Project table adds a Rolling Stone Tomb, abundant terra sigillata and Roman coins for 63 BCE-330 CE. Literary (as summarised on the catalogue page): Herod the Great fortified Esebon and settled veterans there; Jews sacked Heshbon at the start of the First Revolt 66 CE. No ritual baths or Jewish stone vessels are reported in fetched pages; Population blank (Mitchel gives only qualitative growth).
During the Macabean Period (164-63 B.C.), Hisban was a Jewish settlement and part of a separate political area.

city_other: עיראק אל-אמיר / عراق الأمير (Iraq al-Amir / Araq el-Emir); قصر العبد (Qasr al-Abd)
comment: Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): Tobiad estate Tyros. Zenon papyrus of 259 BCE: Tobias sent horses camels dogs from his estate west of Amman; Hyrcanus son of Joseph built Qasr al-Abd in the first quarter of the 2nd century BCE (c. 200-175 BCE; Netzer dates a first villa to the 3rd century) and left it unfinished; Josephus Ant. 12.4.11 says he built a fortress named Tyros and killed himself in 175 BCE (Encyclopedia.com argues he lived to c. 169-168). Rock-cut caves with Aramaic Tobiah inscriptions; stabling for about 120 horses; village stratum IV (c. 200-175 BCE) with Rhodian stamped handles. Evidence of a Jewish (Tobiad) elite estate; no population estimate; site c. 600 dunams (Hebrew Wikipedia).

city_other: עיראק אל-אמיר / عراق الأمير (Iraq al-Amir / Araq el-Emir); قصر العبد (Qasr al-Abd)
comment: Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): second source: Madain Project: palace built first quarter of 2nd c. BCE; Hyrcanus head of the Tobiad family and governor of Ammon; cave facade with 5 Aramaic letters for Tobiad; building unfinished at his death and seized by Antiochus Epiphanes. No population estimate.

city_other: עיראק אל-אמיר / عراق الأمير (Iraq al-Amir / Araq el-Emir); قصر العبد (Qasr al-Abd)
comment: Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Encyclopedia.com: estate overrun in 163 BCE by the Seleucid general Timotheus who killed about a thousand Jews (2 Macc.); Judah Maccabee crossed the Jordan to avenge them and the Tubian Jews sided with the Hasmoneans. Madain Project: nearby caves settled in the second half of the 2nd century BCE. Village strata IIIa-IIIb (c. 100 BCE-50 CE) per the Dead Sea quake catalog (Lapp). Jewish population plausible (Tobiad Jews) but no stated figure; Population blank.

Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550). English Wikipedia: potsherds of Middle Bronze Age I-IIA found (surface). Identification debated: most scholars identify Jabesh-gilead with Tell el-Maqlub but Tell Abu al-Kharaz (Glueck) is the main alternative; Hebrew Wikipedia says Finkelstein proposed Maqlub and critics note it is far from Khirbat Ibziq (Bezek). Wadi Yabis may preserve the name. Canaanite-era; Population blank; no excavation, only survey. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabesh-Gilead; https://www.hamichlol.org.il/%D7%99%D7%91%D7%A9_%D7%92%D7%9C%D7%A2%D7%93

Iron Age I (-1200 to -1000). Survey found Iron Age I and II pottery (Hamichlol Hebrew; English Wikipedia: Iron Age I-II). Israelite town per the Bible (Transjordan Manasseh; Judges 21; 1 Sam 11) but no study gives population; blank. Further sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell_el-Maqlub

Iron Age II (sub-period not given; entered at -1000). English Wikipedia describes the Iron Age town as large and fortified with a massive defensive wall partly still visible; BiblePlaces: surface survey found Iron Age pottery. Population blank: no academic estimate found. Further sources: https://www.bibleplaces.com/gileadupper/

Literary only (conventional date -1200 = start of Iron Age I, used for the Transjordan settlement/conquest tradition; the Bible gives no absolute date). Jahaz / Jahzah / Jahazah (Hebrew יהץ, יהצה): Sihon gathers his people and fights Israel at Jahaz (Num 21:23), Israel strikes him; in Reuben's list (Josh 13:18) and a Levitical city of the Merarites (Josh 21:36, 'Jahazah'). Identification disputed, favoured: Khirbet Mudayna on the Wadi ath-Thamad (Arabic خربة المدينة, 31.5887 N 35.9078 E; proposed by Aharoni, Dearman, Finkelstein and Lipschits; Lemaire only places it along Moab's northeast border) (English Wikipedia, Jahaz and Khirbet Mudayna). Population blank.

Iron Age IIB (c. -880, Omride period; the stele says the king of Israel built Jahaz). Mesha Stele (Livius section 8): the king of Israel built Jahaz and stayed there while fighting Mesha; Chemosh drove him out, Mesha took 200 men there and annexed it to Dibon; Wikipedia notes Jahaz was taken 'without destruction', unlike Ataroth. Archaeology of the favoured site (English Wikipedia, Khirbet Mudayna on the Wadi ath-Thamad, Daviau 1995-2012): fortified Iron Age II town built in the 9th c. BCE, casemate wall 5 m thick, six-chamber gate 15.8 x 16.4 m (gate beams radiocarbon dated about 810-755 BCE), Late Iron II sanctuary; Finkelstein and Lipschits read it as an Omride state fortress later taken by Moab, with no 9th c. destruction; destroyed in the 7th or 6th c. BCE. Isa 15:4 and Jer 48:21 show Moabite Jahaz later. Population blank; no estimate given.
The Hasmonean Kingdom under Alexander Jannaeus conquered Jerash and established a Jewish colony, controlling the city until 63 BCE.

city_other: ח'רבת ג'ביהא (not confirmed) / Khirbet Jubeiha / Rujm el-Jebeha
comment: Literary only (convention: Gideon c. -1150). The Gadites built Jogbehah (Num 32:35); Gideon goes up 'by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah' to attack the Midianite camp (Judg 8:11). Identification: English Wikipedia says Jogbehah was 'probably an Ammonite fortress, now Rujm al-Jubayha' (proposed, not firm; Khirbet Jubeiha about 11 km NW of Amman per the existing row; disputed, favoured: Khirbet/Rujm Jubeiha). Archaeology is on the existing row. Population blank.

city_other: ח'רבת ג'ביהא (not confirmed) / Khirbet Jubeiha / Rujm el-Jebeha
comment: Evidence limited: Hebrew Wikipedia reports an Ammonite watchtower plus finds from the Israelite period at Khirbet Jubeiha (11 km NW of Amman); English Wikipedia says Rujm el-Jebeha has an Ammonite fortified tower and was proposed as Jogbehah. No stratum dates or excavation report found so year -1000 is a placeholder for Iron Age and the identification is only proposed. Population blank (Gadite/Ammonite; no estimate).

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). Identification with Kerak (al-Karak) is the standard one (Kir of Moab; en.wikipedia). Source says only that Kerak was inhabited since at least the Iron Age and was an important Moabite city; the El-Kerak Inscription dates to the late 9th c. BCE; row placed in Iron IIB from that 9th c. date (brief ranges used; source gives no strata). 2 Kings 3: Mesha besieged at Kir-hareseth. Moabite city. No population estimate or built-up area found in fetched pages.

Event (town: Karak, marker named Kir-hareseth): in 1896 the Ottoman governor of the Karak region, Hilmi Pasha, invited Shabtai Hizkiya, one of the first settlers of Hartuv, and offered him land to buy for a Jewish colony near the city (English Wikipedia, History of the Jews in Jordan, late Ottoman period).

Town: Karak (marker named Kir-hareseth). Abraham Moses Luncz's Eretz Yisrael calendar of 1900 reported 12 Jewish 'artists' (artisans) living in the city without their families (English Wikipedia, History of the Jews in Jordan); 12 men, not a family community.

Town: Karak (marker named Kir-hareseth). Yitzhak Ben-Zvi wrote that in the 1920s one Jewish family lived in Karak and that by the 1930s there were no Jews in the city (English Wikipedia, History of the Jews in Jordan); one household x5, 1925 is a conventional mid-1920s year.

[Second-pass revision] Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds source for Jannaeus and the identification problem. Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent): Alexander Jannaeus took Betharamphtha from the king of the Arabs c. 80 BCE, citing Ant. 14.1.4 (I could not verify that section in the primary text). No excavation exists: English Wikipedia Tell er-Rameh says a Muslim cemetery on the acropolis prevents digging and lists Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad cultures only, so no Hasmonean material is attested at the coordinate site. Identification doubtful: Glueck argued Tell er-Rameh pottery does not fit biblical Beth-haram; Graves and Stripling (2011) put the administrative centre at Tall el-Hammam and the residential and commercial centre at Tell er-Rameh. Presence is textual only; Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Replaces first-pass row for this period: adds citations. Josephus via ISBE and Jewish Encyclopedia: Herod the Great had a palace at Betharamphtha, destroyed after his death (Ant. 17.10.6; War 2.4.2); Antipas fortified it and named it Julias (Ant. 18.2.1; War 2.9.1; the Whiston text at lexundria says Herod built a wall round the already existing city and called it Julias); Nero gave the city and its 14 villages to Agrippa II (Ant. 20.8.4) and Placidus took it in 68 CE (War 4.7.6) (both via Wikipedia Livias). Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 9:2 gives Beit Ramata (via Wikipedia). Perea had a Jewish population and Josephus calls Julias a polis, but no ritual baths, stone vessels or coins are reported for the site. Population blank; no estimate exists.

source: Beinart, Atlas of Medieval Jewish History (Carta, Jerusalem 1992), map 7 p. 18
comment: The atlas has 'Ma'an' marked 'city or town with Jewish community' on the map 'The Jews in the Arabian Peninsula, beginning of the seventh century'. No precise year is given, so 600 is the conventional midpoint of the period (beginning of the 7th century). Presence only; no population stated. No online source found: the English Wikipedia article on Ma'an was fetched and gives no statement of a Jewish presence for this period.

city_other: מכוור / Mukawir; Qal'at al-Mishnaqa / قلعة المشناقة
comment: Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Fortress built by Alexander Jannaeus c. 90 BCE; destroyed by Gabinius in 57 BCE. Military fortress, Jewish (Hasmonean) garrison; no resident population estimate.

city_other: מכוור / Mukawir; Qal'at al-Mishnaqa / قلعة المشناقة
comment: Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Rebuilt by Herod c. 30 BCE as palace-fortress with monumental miqveh (12 steps; largest found in Jordan); John the Baptist imprisoned c. 32 CE; destroyed by Nabatean Aretas IV in 36 CE per excavators; held by Jewish rebels 66-71/72 CE until Roman siege (Bassus). Josephus's 1700 men killed in the lower city are casualties, not a population. Identification Mukawir is secure. No population estimate; Population blank.

city_other: מכוור / Mukawir; Qal'at al-Mishnaqa / قلعة المشناقة
comment: Event: early in the revolt the Jews took the fortress of Machaerus after the Roman garrison withdrew (Josephus War 2.485-486; English Wikipedia 'History of the Jews in Jordan'). A rebel garrison, not a civilian community.

city_other: מכוור / Mukawir; Qal'at al-Mishnaqa / قلعة المشناقة
comment: Event: Lucilius Bassus besieged Machaerus in 71 CE; the rebels surrendered after Eleazar was captured; about 3,000 rebels led by Judah ben Ari were reportedly killed in the forest of Jardes (English Wikipedia 'History of the Jews in Jordan', citing Millar and Davies). Casualty figure, not a population.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Late Bronze to Iron Age I (source dates 1300-970 BCE; overlaps Late Bronze -1550 to -1200 and Iron I). Western hill: scattered finds and early fortification walls but little architecture (he.wikipedia; en.wikipedia). Identification: Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi = Mahanaim is the post-1970 mainstream view, but other sources say the identification is uncertain, and Griffin (drbill.net) argues against a twin-site reading; fortifications undated without excavation. Population unknown ethnicity; no estimate found. Population blank.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Literary only (convention: Ish-bosheth's reign right after Saul's death, Saul c. -1020, so c. -1010). Mahanaim (Hebrew מחניים) was Ish-bosheth's capital: Abner brought him to Mahanaim and made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin and all Israel (2 Sam 2:8-9). Name origin Gen 32:2; on the Gad/Manasseh border (Josh 13:26, 13:30) and a Levitical city (Josh 21:38). Identification: Tulul adh-Dhahab, western hill (Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi), the mainstream view after 1970 per English Wikipedia; Finkelstein: western hill = Mahanaim, eastern = Penuel; radiocarbon dates the earliest settlement 1300-970 BCE (disputed, favoured: western hill). Population blank.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Iron Age II (-1000 on; source gives no subdivision). Evidence of habitation and cult in Iron Age II on the western hill (amudanan page, citing Dortmund/Basel excavations since 2005; en.wikipedia: two main occupation periods Iron II and Hellenistic). Pola et al. 2024 title asks 'An Israelite Residency at Mahanaim?' (page not readable, so Israelite status not confirmed). Biblical Mahanaim is Israelite (David, Ish-bosheth). Population blank: no academic estimate found.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Literary only (convention: Absalom's revolt in David's later reign, David c. -1000 to -960, so c. -975). David flees to Mahanaim; Absalom crosses the Jordan and camps in Gilead (2 Sam 17:24-26); at Mahanaim Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbah, Machir son of Ammiel of Lo-debar and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim bring supplies (2 Sam 17:27-29). 1 Kgs 2:8 recalls Shimei cursing David on his way to Mahanaim. English Wikipedia (Tulul adh-Dhahab): David fled to Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt. Archaeology is on the existing rows (Iron II habitation and probable cult on the western hill). Population blank.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Literary only (convention: Solomon -960). Solomon's district list: 'Ahinadab the son of Iddo had Mahanaim' (1 Kgs 4:14), so Mahanaim is an Israelite administrative seat under Solomon; the district officer for Gilead is Geber son of Uri (1 Kgs 4:19) and the son of Geber at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 4:13). English Wikipedia (Tulul adh-Dhahab): carved limestone ashlars with cultic iconography reused later may date from 1300-970 or 900-700 BCE; a possible sanctuary on the western hill in Iron II. Population blank.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) invaded in Rehoboam's fifth year: 1 Kgs 14:25-26 and 2 Chr 12:2-4 ('he took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah'). The Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists conquered places (c. 925 BCE); the inscription gives no details of the expedition and Jerusalem is absent from the list (English Wikipedia 'Bubastite Portal', 'Shoshenq I'). Mahanaim is no. 22 'Mahanaim' of the list; Maspero, Champollion, Rosellini and Budge read Ma'hanema as Mahanaim (English Wikipedia 'Mahanaim'). Epigraphic evidence; Year of Data -925 = conventional date. No population figure.

city_other: תל אל-דהב אל-גרבי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab)
comment: Persian-Hellenistic (source gives 375-175 BCE; only the start falls before -332): foundations of structures on the western hill (he.wikipedia). Population blank; no estimate found.

Middle Bronze (-2000 to -1550): English Wikipedia says Madaba dates from the Middle Bronze Age; ACOR Jordan says Bronze and Iron Age occupation at Tall Madaba. Population unknown; no academic estimate found. Identification with Madaba is not disputed in the fetched pages.

Iron Age I/IIA (-1200 to -900; the Madaba Museum summary gives 12th-10th centuries BCE). Tall Madaba Archaeological Project (University of Toronto, Harrison and Foran): a large residential building with many storage vessels in Iron Age I/IIA; the Iron IIB four-room house and cult objects (9th-7th c.) are on the existing -900 row. Medeba (Madaba, Arabic مادبا, Hebrew מידבא): Num 21:30 (laid waste 'unto Medeba'), Josh 13:9 and 13:16 (plain of Medeba, in Reuben's territory). Whether the Iron I inhabitants were Israelite/Reubenite is not stated in the sources. No population estimate found; Population blank.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722): Moabite border city; control alternated between Israel and Moab (Mesha Stele; Num 21:30; Josh 13:9). University of Toronto excavations found a 7.5 m wide fortification wall built in the 9th century BCE (dated by source as 9th c.; mapped here to the start of Iron IIB) and Moabite pottery. Inhabitants Moabite (at times Israelite-ruled) so Population left blank; no published estimate found.

Iron Age IIA/IIB (c. -880; Omri reigned 884-873 per Livius). Mesha Stele (Livius section 4): Omri king of Israel took the whole land of Medeba and Israel held it in his days and half the days of his son, about forty years; Mesha says Chemosh restored it in his own days. English Wikipedia (Medeba): control of the city alternated between Israel and Moab, and the Toronto excavations found a 7.5 m wide fortification wall built about the 9th century BCE. Israelite-held c. 880-840 BCE per the stele; population blank, no estimate found.

[Second-pass revision] Early Hellenistic (-332 to -167): New period row. The Madaba Museum site summary of the Tall Madaba Archaeological Project (TMAP, Harrison and Foran, Univ. of Toronto, 1996-2012) lists a Hellenistic phase (dated 3rd-1st c. BCE, not subdivided) with fortified tower-like structures and re-use of the pre-classical fortification wall; the first pass skipped this period. The source's range overlaps the Hasmonean row, so early and late Hellenistic are not separated. Inhabitants not stated (a Nabataean tribal presence is mentioned for c. 160 BCE by ACOR); no Jewish evidence; Population blank. The identification of Medeba with Tall Madaba is not disputed.

[Second-pass revision] strengthens the textual evidence with fetched primary text. Josephus Ant. 13.9.1 (Whiston translation, Perseus): Hyrcanus took Medaba only in the sixth month of the siege; Ant. 13.15.4: among cities the Jews held in Moab are 'Heshbon, and Medaba, Lemba, Oronas, Gelithon, Zara' (listed as held, not as a conquest by Jannaeus); Ant. 14.1.4: Hyrcanus II promises Aretas to restore Medaba. 1 Macc 9:35-42 (c. 160 BCE, sons of Jambri, described by ACOR as apparently a Nabataean tribe of Madaba). This shows Hasmonean control, not a Jewish population: no ritual bath, chalk vessel, ossuary or inscription from Madaba is reported in any fetched page. Ferguson's 2017 chapter and dissertation 'Madaba Between Judaea and Nabataea' (late Hellenistic and early Roman phases) were only seen in search-result summaries, not fetched, so not relied on. Population blank.

[Second-pass revision] the first pass relied on a search summary of TMAP ('page not fetched'). The Madaba Museum TMAP summary (now fetched) reports for the Early Roman phase (1st c. BCE/1st c. CE) an elite Nabataean residence with a substantial amount of ceramics imported from Petra; Josephus Ant. 14.1.4 has Medaba ceded to Aretas III; Madaba entered the province of Arabia in 106 CE (JVL, citing Encyclopaedia Judaica). Population Nabataean. Jews are attested in Madaba only in Mishnaic times (Mik. 7:1; JVL), probably as a minority, which is after 70 CE. No Jewish evidence for 63 BCE-70 CE; Population blank.

Encyclopaedia Judaica: Jews lived at Madaba (Medeba) in Mishnaic times (Mishnah Mikvaot 7:1), 'but they were probably a minority'. Undated within the Mishnaic period (Mishnah c. 200 CE, not stated on the page; conventional year 200). The sixth-century Madaba Map shows Jewish lore but is not evidence of a community.

Literary only (conventional date -1200 = start of Iron Age I, used for the Transjordan settlement/conquest tradition; the Bible gives no absolute date). Mephaath (Hebrew מיפעת) is associated with Umm ar-Rasas (Arabic أم الرصاص, 31.5008 N 35.9203 E): Eusebius's Onomasticon places Mephaat at a Roman army camp near the desert and a Byzantine church inscription names the area 'Castron Mephaa' (English Wikipedia; disputed, favoured: Umm ar-Rasas; no Iron Age occupation is claimed by the Wikipedia article, whose documented history begins with Roman military use, so this is a name-based identification only). Bible: in Reuben's list (Josh 13:18), a Levitical city of the Merarites (Josh 21:37), a Moabite plateau town in Jer 48:21. Population blank.

city_other: הר נבו (Har Nevo) / جبل نيبو (Jabal Nebo / Jabal Siyagha)
comment: Literary only (conventional date -1200 = start of Iron Age I, used for the Transjordan settlement/conquest tradition; the Bible gives no absolute date). The biblical town Nebo (Hebrew נבו) is identified with Khirbet al-Mukhayyat (Arabic خربة المخيط, 31.7678 N 35.7253 E, about 3.5 km from the mountain peaks; the marker sits on the same spot). English Wikipedia: the Mesha inscription seems to describe a settlement and no significant Iron Age remains were found on the mountain, so the village is the more likely site. Bible: Gad and Reuben ask for Nebo (Num 32:3), Reuben builds it, 'their names being changed' (Num 32:38), Bela dwelt in Aroer 'even unto Nebo and Baal-meon' (1 Chr 5:8). Population blank.

city_other: הר נבו (Har Nevo) / جبل نيبو (Jabal Nebo / Jabal Siyagha)
comment: Iron Age IIA/IIB (c. -840). Mesha Stele (Livius section 7): Chemosh tells Mesha 'take Nebo from Israel'; Mesha attacks at night, takes it by noon, kills about 7,000 and brings the vessels of YHWH before Chemosh, so Nebo was an Israelite (Reubenite/Gadite) town before c. 840 and Moabite after. Archaeology (English Wikipedia, Khirbet al-Mukhayyat): the Town of Nebo project (Debra Foran, since 2014) found an Iron Age tower, probably part of wider defenses, later altered in the Hellenistic period, and more than 75 upright buried cooking pots; no sub-phase date given. Later prophecies on Moabite Nebo: Isa 15:2, Jer 48:1. No population estimate; Population blank.

city_other: הר נבו (Har Nevo) / جبل نيبو (Jabal Nebo / Jabal Siyagha)
comment: Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Madain Project chronology says the Asmonaeans (Hasmoneans) settled in Khirbet al-Mukhayyat the area around Mount Nebo about 200 BCE (a general timeline; the page itself gives c. 200 BCE which is earlier than -167); the Madaba Museum page lists a ritual bath (miqveh) in the Hellenistic phase which points to Jewish use (Foran and Dolan 2016 interpret it in Hasmonean terms but that article was seen only in a search snippet and not fetched). 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 places Jeremiah's hiding of the tent ark and incense altar in a cave on the mountain (a legend with no archaeological confirmation per Custodia). Jewish (Hasmonean) agricultural settlement likely; no population estimate in sources so Population blank.

Russian Jewish engineer Pinhas Rutenberg began constructing a hydroelectric power plant, providing employment for 3,000 workers; a model community, Tel Or, was built for the Jewish workers who supervised the plant.

Pella was destroyed around 82 B.C. by the Hasmonean Jewish king Alexander Jannaeus, who then ruled the area. [Review fix: population 1 (legacy placeholder) cleared to blank = presence documented, no count; year_end 2024 cut to the start year: the row records an event, the old end year was not a real end]

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Pompey detached Pella from Jewish rule in 63 BCE and it joined the Decapolis; town council and own coinage (Wikipedia); Odeon and baths (bibarch). Dead Sea Quake: Early Roman material found only in small quantities and disturbed deposits, architecture mostly the Civic Complex in Wadi Jirm al-Moz and tombs. Greek / Roman city population. Flight to Pella tradition (Eusebius 4th c.; Jewish Virtual Library) says Jewish Christians fled there in 66-70 CE: late tradition, not archaeological evidence for a Jewish population. No Jewish population estimate (the 25,000 figure in bibarch is for 6th c. CE Byzantine Pella, not used).

city_other: תל אל-דהב א-שרקי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab), eastern hill: Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh
comment: Late Bronze / Iron Age I (about 1300 BCE evidence, no architecture; amudanan page, which discusses the twin hills and mainly the western one). Eastern tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh = Penuel is Finkelstein's proposal; before 1970 the whole site was identified with Penuel and the identification is doubtful (no Iron Age temple found; en.wikipedia/Penuel). Population blank; no estimate found.

city_other: תל אל-דהב א-שרקי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab), eastern hill: Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh
comment: Literary only (convention: Gideon c. -1150; the Judges chronology is conventional). The men of Penuel refuse Gideon's 300 pursuers bread (Judg 8:8-9); on his return he beats down the tower of Penuel and kills the men of the city (Judg 8:17). Name origin Gen 32:30 (Jacob saw God face to face; English Wikipedia, Penuel). Jeroboam I's fortification of Penuel (1 Kgs 12:25) is already on the existing -1000 row. Identification (disputed): eastern hill Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh per Finkelstein (before 1970 the whole twin-peaked Tulul adh-Dhahab; some scholars prefer Tall al-Hammah near the Jabbok ford); no temple found. Population blank.

city_other: תל אל-דהב א-שרקי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab), eastern hill: Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh
comment: Iron Age II (-1000 on). Eastern hill has remains of defensive walls (amudanan), but Gordon and Villiers (1980/82 survey, via drbill.net) say fortifications cannot be dated without excavation. Biblical Penuel was fortified by Jeroboam I (1 Kgs 12:25), Israelite; this is textual only (en.wikipedia/Penuel). Population blank: no academic estimate found.

city_other: תל אל-דהב א-שרקי (תולול אל-ד'הב) / تلول الذهب (Tulul al-Dhahab), eastern hill: Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh
comment: Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) invaded in Rehoboam's fifth year: 1 Kgs 14:25-26 and 2 Chr 12:2-4 ('he took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah'). The Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists conquered places (c. 925 BCE); the inscription gives no details of the expedition and Jerusalem is absent from the list (English Wikipedia 'Bubastite Portal', 'Shoshenq I'). Penuel is no. 53 'Penuel' of the list. Epigraphic evidence; Year of Data -925 = conventional date. No population figure.

city_other: פטרה / البتراء (Rekem in Josephus Ant. 4.7.1 per Jewish Encyclopedia)
comment: Hasmonean (-167 to -63): Nabataean capital; Judas and Jonathan Maccabee dealt with Nabataeans and Alexander Jannaeus took trans-Jordanic cities from Obodas I (Jewish Encyclopedia). In 65 BCE Antipater brought the deposed Hasmonean Hyrcanus II to Petra to the palace of Aretas III who then marched on Jerusalem (Josephus Antiquities 14.14-21 in Attalus translation): this shows a Jewish visitor only, not a Jewish community. 62 BCE: Aretas paid tribute to Pompey (Ancient Rome Live). Archaeology (deadseaquake.info): late 13th-early 12th c. [Second-pass revision] adds archaeological and Jewish-context evidence. Wikipedia (Ghor es-Safi) reports excavations showing 'a population with a Nabataean character' on the south-east Dead Sea shore from the 1st to 6th c. Politis (BAS) places the large Nabataean cemetery at Khirbet Qazone (c. 15 miles north, 1st c. BCE-4th c. CE), a different site, and says Jewish families moved into the area 'around the Nabatean period' and bought date orchards, without giving a date. The Jewish community is documented only afterwards: the Babatha archive (c. 94-132 CE) places Maoza in the district of Zoara (Saldarini 1998; Cotton and Greenfield 1995 discuss Maoza and Zoar as her patria, abstract not read), and the Jewish Aramaic tombstones are dated by the era of the Destruction (4th-6th c.; BAS). Zoara was an important Jewish centre in the 4th-5th centuries: about 300 funerary steles were found in 1995 at Khirbet Sheikh 'Isa, most in Greek (Christian) and several in Aramaic (Jewish), with Christians and Jews buried in the same cemetery (English Wikipedia 'Zoara'); Rendsburg's slides speak of thousands of Jewish and Christian burials, 3rd-6th centuries. Event: July 1507 decree of King Sigismund, citing the impoverished condition of the Troki Jews, confirms their ancient privileges: own elder appointed by the waywode, suits against Christians before the waywode, taxes once a year on equal terms with other citizens, exemption from customs, free travel.

source: Burgard and Reverchon, Juedische Siedlungsgeschichte der Maas-Mosel-Lande (Haverkamp (ed.), Geschichte der Juden im Mittelalter, FZGJ A 14/1, Hannover 2002), p. 89
comment: Earliest certain evidence of Jews in the city of Luxembourg after the Black Death: in 1372 the Jew Salomon of Luxembourg lends money to a knight (Yante, Les Juifs, Anhang III no. 59). Earlier steps: in 1350 Charles IV, probably acting as count of Luxembourg, asked the inhabitants to admit Jews into their city again (he had tried unsuccessfully to protect them in the plague pogrom), and in 1356, when Luxembourg became a duchy, he transferred the rights over the Jews to his half-brother Wenceslas. Gela of Bastogne, wife of Samuel of Ehrenbreitstein (named in the Trier region from 1353), had left Luxembourg long before the plague. The existing map rows for 1350 and 1367 differ (see conflicts). No population given. No online source found.

Event: after a temporary return following the plague expulsions of 1349, the Jews were expelled from Luxembourg again in 1391, 'allerdings nur kurzzeitig' (only briefly) (de.wikipedia); en.wikipedia: 'Deprived of Imperial protection, in 1391, Luxembourg's Jewish population was expelled'. No count.

comment: Immigration from German-speaking regions into the city of Luxembourg: Lazarus of Frankfurt is documented there in 1397 (Yante, Anhang III no. 30); later Salomon of Düren and Salomon of Neumagen (from 1445), Jakob of Bonn (1446), Jakob of Wiesbaden at Diedenhofen (1450). Immigration from the duchy of Lorraine after its expulsion of 1477 is also certain; Abraham of Nancy, living at Diedenhofen and then in the city of Luxembourg (from 1469), had kin ties with the Luxembourg Jews already before 1477. Luxembourg's Jewish settlement of c. 1400-1517 concentrated on the German-speaking south of the territory. No population given. No online source found.

Event: some Jewish families were allowed to settle again in 1405 ('1405 durften sich einige jüdische Familien wieder niederlassen', de.wikipedia); en.wikipedia: after the expulsion of 1391 'the ban was not thoroughly enforced, and a few Jewish families began to return to Luxembourg from 1405 onwards'. comment: Event: end of the Jewish settlement of the duchy of Luxembourg. German Wikipedia: in 1515 only eight Jewish households were left in the city of Luxembourg and 11 in the whole duchy; "in the following two years almost all Jews left the duchy of Luxembourg", the reason is not exactly known, the ducal archives document neither a pogrom nor a state decree. English and French Wikipedia date an expulsion to 1530 and the Jewish Encyclopedia has no Jews after 1527 (see conflicts). Number of Jews who left not given.

Lb.wikipedia (Synagog Munneref): '1867 huet sech déi éischt jiddesch Famill zu Munneref niddergelooss' - the first Jewish family settled in Mondorf in 1867; the Jewish community there then grew.

In 1900 Jacques Zacharias Cerf, Marx Marx and Wolff Marx and the mayor Cerf Block bought a plot in the Millewee for a synagogue; building began 1907 and the synagogue was consecrated on 26 September 1908 (with municipal funding) in the presence of Chief Rabbi Samuel Fuchs. Until 1940 Jewish families from the whole region came to Bad Mondorf, which had Jewish hotels (Bristol, Hemmendinger, Auberge Gittler), to celebrate festivals there.

The synagogue was damaged by arson in WWII (damage estimated at 59,000 francs) but not demolished; re-consecrated on 25 July 1953 after renovation. Use declined because of the war losses; closed in 1974 (furniture moved to the Hotel Bristol), municipal property from 1995, listed national monument in 2018.

A plan only, never implemented.

Six burial sites with carved menorahs in the Rabat catacombs (each about a dozen tombs) show Jews living alongside Christians and pagans in Malta in the 4th-5th centuries; the community, led by a gerousia, could have counted up to 300 people (a capacity estimate, not a census; conventional year 450).

comment: A gate of the Jews (porta Iudeorum, later Jodenpoort, renamed Onze Lieve Vrouwepoort; the present Vughterstraat was once the Jodenstraat) is first mentioned in a charter of 10 September 1309 (Oorkondenboek van Noord-Brabant I, ed. Camps 1979, no. 786): the earliest reliable sign of Jews in the town. The short paper calls it a 'Jewish row', the dissertation 'porta Iudeorum'; the dissertation's reading is used. The 16th-century tradition that Jews settled soon after the town was founded (1185) and were burned at Vught has no confirmation; Cluse thinks it echoes 1309. This is stronger evidence than the map's existing c. 1300 row (a 1558 document). Online: dissertation p. 21 n. 58-59. Confidence high. Source wording: "Im Jahr 1309 ist erstmals von einer porta Iudeorum die Rede". Event: persecution at 's-Hertogenbosch in 1309. The Radboud thesis lists 's-Hertogenbosch among the places of the summer-1309 incidents. Late and partly legendary source. Online: dissertation pp. 21, 202; Radboud thesis. Confidence low-medium. Source wording: "diese ihnen die Juden auslieferten, welche dann schwer mißhandelt wurden". comment: Event: about 110 Jews from Sittard and Susteren who had taken refuge in the castle of Born were killed (burned alive according to nl.wikipedia) when crusaders of the 'Armenkruistocht' stormed it in July 1309; the castle burned down and the lord who had protected them was killed too (the thesis calls him Jan van Valkenburg, nl.wikipedia Reinoud van Valkenburg). Called the first Jewish pogrom on the territory of the present Netherlands; a memorial plaque was placed at Kasteelhof 3 in 2013. Annales Tielenses: 'castrum de Born subvertebat, in qua interfecti sunt 110 Iudei'. The map has this fact only inside its Roermond 1309 row, at the wrong place (see conflicts). Born is named in the Hebrew martyrology and dated to 1309 by Stengers, Beem and Cluse. Online: nl.wikipedia Born; dissertation p. 200; Radboud thesis. Confidence high. Source wording: "castrum de Born subvertebat, in qua interfecti sunt 110 Iudei". [Source detail: (Cluse, Studien zur Geschichte der Juden in den mittelalterlichen Niederlanden, FGJ A 10, Hannover 2000, p. 200, PDF p. 208); (Driessen, BA thesis Radboud Univ. Nijmegen 2015, p. 3)]

Fate of the Jewish community sealed during the bubonic plague epidemic; Conradus de Judia and his fellow townsmen were murdered.
Jewish citizens Johannes dicto Joede and Henricus dictus Jode recorded as living in Deventer.
Jewish citizens again noted in Deventer.
One Jew with a courtyard next to the city barn had settled in Deventer.
One more Jew settled in Deventer.
One more Jew settled in Deventer.
A Jew had rented a piece of land with a courtyard next to the city barn.
Johan de Joode visited Deventer as a representative of the Count of Gelderland.
Several Jews asked the municipality for permission to live and exercise their trades in Deventer, but the request was not granted.
A number of Jews dispelled from Gelre applied for settlement in Deventer, but the request was rejected.
The municipality was requested to restrict Jews from trading along streets, except for lime and lemons.
Jews were not allowed to live in Deventer, but could run businesses there.
The municipality asked that all Jews be restricted from trading in the commercial part of the town.
Jews were permitted to sell oranges and lemons for the benefit and service of everybody.
Attempted to permit Jews to partake in the licensing of a loan-bank, but it was rented by a Christian applicant instead.
Jacob Mozes and his three sons requested and were granted the right to live in Deventer and receive citizenship.
The oldest minutes book of the young Jewish community dates from this year.
Parnassim bought a yard and house near the Brink to transform into a synagogue; Mr. Ansj Katz appointed shamash; tried to attract Rabbi Mozes from Poland.
Steps taken to obtain a bigger and permanent synagogue; Jewish society Gemielos Chasodiem existed.
Artifacts used during ceremonial services were recorded; Joel son of Mozes, Jacob son of Joel Segal, and Menachem son of Jona each donated a Tora scroll.
The Jewish community bought a garden and small house outside the Brinkpoort for a cemetery.
The community possessed a synagogue, bathhouse (mikve), house, and a courtyard with a small gardenhouse used as a cemetery.
Population consisted of about 20 families with numerous children; King Louis Napoleon visited Deventer and received Jewish delegates.
The Jewish community notified the mayor that their synagogue could hold 200 persons but was not yet completed.
23 certificates of names adoption were recorded in the register of names of parents and children of the Jewish community.
Isak Mozes Heilbron and Isak Hartog van Aalbergen received assistance to establish a bakery.
First registration of a funeral recorded in the archives of the Jewish community.
Vexation over valid votes and careless administration became public domain within the Jewish community.
Quarrels characterized the atmosphere; about 30 members separated to establish the New Israelite Community.
The municipality offered property next to the General Cemetery for a new Jewish cemetery.
The new Jewish cemetery was put into use, and the old cemetery was closed.
The Jewish community board formally notified the Mayor that the old cemetery would be declared closed as from September 1870.
Birth of Israel Noach in Deventer.
Chief Rabbi Tal made efforts to bring the two separated communities together.
David Cohen, a future professor and Jewish leader, was born in Deventer.

c. 1250: Jewish community begins in Maastricht (dutchjewry.org, which calls it the oldest Jewish community in the Netherlands); Hebrew Wikipedia dates the finds (synagogue, mikveh, Vicus Judeorum) to the late 13th century.

Event: the Jodenstraat (platea Judeorum) is first named in an aldermen's deed of 1295, earliest written evidence of the community; the street is named after a synagogue, so a synagogue existed before 1300. English Wikipedia also says a synagogue with mikveh existed before 1295 (uncited there).

Event: Black Death reaches the region 1348; Jews accused of well-poisoning and persecuted. dutchjewry.org says the community was destroyed in 1350 through pogroms and loss of its commercial role (moneylending and old-clothes trade); jck.nl dates the destruction to the first half of the 14th century. No victim count given.

Event: dutchjewry.org states Jews were expelled in 1370 (to Gelderland, the Gulik region, German lands, Eastern Europe), while the same page dates the community's end to 1350, so the dates are inconsistent and 1370 is not corroborated elsewhere. Four medieval Hebrew leaves reused as bindings of Maastricht record books (one from 1366-1374) are possibly from this community.

The synagogue was no longer in use by 1377, when the former synagogue serves as a location marker (dutchjewry.org). English Wikipedia (uncited): hardly any Jews lived in Limburg 1350-1650; stated for Limburg, not Maastricht alone.

Jews of Nijmegen pay taxes to the Duke of Guelders: the duke received 132 pond yearly (Jewish Encyclopedia); a tax sum, not a population. jck.nl: in the first half of the 14th century the most important Jewish community of the present Netherlands, mainly moneylenders, with a cemetery southeast of town.
Event: community destroyed in 1349 during the plague-year persecutions (jck.nl). A Dutch essay (Maatstaf) says all Jews of the city probably fell victim in 1349. No victim count given.
Revived community: cemetery outside the Wijmelpoort first mentioned 1382; by 1386 several resettled Jews held town citizenship (jck.nl); Jewish Encyclopedia confirms a cemetery by 1382.
Jews have been settled in Nijmegen, the oldest settlement, in Doesburg, Zutphen and in Arnhem since 1404.

Early 15th century: community bought four houses in an alley later called Jodengasch, one became the synagogue (schola judeorum); Jewish Encyclopedia has a synagogue by 1426. In 1430 permission was granted to build a ritual bath (jck.nl). Nijmegen became an important financial centre drawing many Jewish families (JVL).

Event: Cologne church synod of 1452 required Jews to wear a distinguishing badge, also applied in Nijmegen; the Jewish population then declined and the community ceased to exist by the end of the 15th century (jck.nl). A new attempt to settle failed in 1544.

Earliest evidence: 1275-1288 the Judenschreinsbuch of the Cologne parish of St. Laurence records Jacobus de Ruremunde son of Alexander as house owner, and 1275-1279 the brothers Nathan and Vivus de Ruremunde (Lifman and Gottschalk): Jews with a Roermond origin name living in Cologne; Roermond-resident evidence comes later. jck.nl dates Jewish presence in Roermond 1275-1443.

Event: c. 1309 'Armenkruistocht' band: 110 Jews who had fled to the castle of Born near Sittard are said to have been killed there (Annales Tielenses). The location is disputed and Born is not Roermond; no Jews are found in the Overkwartier in the following years, so a regional effect is suspected. Not a Roermond count.

Duke Reinald II of Guelders receives the Jewry regalia from the Emperor (1339); in 1343-45 Reinald III issues a statute with legal rules for Jews in the duchy, and in 1345 admits Vivus of Wessem with family for six years for 4 gold shields a year (van der Bruggen).

Account of the Overkwartier receiver 1346-47 names ten Jews resident in Roermond (Ysaak von Luxemburg, Vivus von Wessem, Baroec and daughter, Simon, Menken and mother Alede, Johannes, Vallen); count of named persons, a minimum. A 'Jodenbisschop' (leader or cantor) lived in Erkelenz.
Same 1346-47 account: van der Bruggen says the ten named persons were 'possibly seven families'; Population = households x 5 (7 families, the source's own tentative count).

Event: Black Death period 1346-53 / persecutions of 1349 in Guelders: nothing more is heard of the ten Jews of Roermond and for over twenty years there are no Jews in Roermond (killed or driven out, fate unknown). A 1350 ducal account of seized Jewish goods suggests the Guelders duke took part; in Geldern Jews died in a camp 1349-50.
1369: Godert Jude lives in Roermond and pays a tax (not a Jewish tax, so doubtful whether he was Jewish); the same year the duke had 109 silver Jew hats made, which may mean Jews were admitted again.
Johel of Worms is granted a permit by Duke William of Jülich to settle with his family in Roermond for ten years for 12 gold gulden a year (dated 1385; Venner dates it between 1376 and 1392).

1386: the ducal receiver accounts 30 guilders received from Jews in Roermond, which appears to cover two families (van der Bruggen). In 1390 the duke grants Jews at Nijmegen the same rights as his Jews at Nijmegen and Roermond.
1391: Saulus and Manus 'Joede tot Ruermunde' each paid 15 guilders; van der Bruggen concludes two Jewish families lived there. Population = households x 5 (2 families).

1396: Gadert (Godert?) de Jude lives on the Markt and Gaeden de Joede in the Brugstraat; 1406 and 1413 further Jews (Bonnen der Joed) are recorded. Around 1400 a Jewish cemetery (Jodenkerkhof) outside the walls, possibly near today's Buitenop, must have existed, and a Roermond law of 1400 (alt-heerkommen) allows pledges to be lent against Jews.
1423/24 and 1424/25: Aleyt de Joedynne of Roermond pays 5 marks tax each year (Cluse).

Event: 1443 Jews of Roermond pay 30 guilders (toll account of Lobith) for permission to keep living in Guelders, at least two households; last recorded medieval Jewish residence (jck.nl: continuous presence 1275-1443). In 1476 the Jodenkerkhof between the Maas and the Arloe is mentioned and in 1494 Duke Charles gave the Jewish cemetery to the burgher Johan Moeyss in settlement of a 61 guilder debt.
After the middle of the sixteenth century, the city did not have any Jewish inhabitants for centuries

According to Pyzewska the Białystok ghetto saw no mass liquidation actions until Feb 1943, when the Germans carried out a partial liquidation; on the night of 15/16 Aug 1943, when the Germans entered to liquidate it, the Jewish self-defence (mostly very young people) began the armed fight prepared for months; it was crushed within days and the rest of the population was deported to Treblinka and Auschwitz, a few hundred people being kept to clear the ghetto area. Białystok was, with Warsaw, the second city where Jews fought the ghetto liquidation with arms. Online: en.wikipedia (Bialystok Ghetto, fetched) dates the German raid and the start of the uprising to 16 Aug 1943 and the first deportation of about 10,000 Białystok Jews to Treblinka to 5-12 Feb 1943. The map has no Białystok row after 1941. Confidence high.

comment: Event: tension and attacks after liberation. In the city itself there was no pogrom like those in the region, but a rumour of a planned pogrom circulated (testimony of Michal Majek, a survivor of the Sokoły shooting), there were attacks on Jewish houses and institutions with windows smashed, and survivors said they sat "as on hot coals". Renia Kantorowicz-Plonski, who lived with other returnees in a ruined house at ul. Polna 24, recalled being attacked every night: "We had legally one rifle and illegally other weapons ... we were still forced to defend ourselves". Dates are not given beyond "after the war" (1945-46; the Majek account is from early 1945). No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish). Confidence medium.

comment: Jewish life in 1946: the Voivodeship Jewish Committee (branch of the Central Committee of Polish Jews) was chaired first by Szymon Datner, then by Pesach Bursztejn; in Jan-June 1946 the Committee registered 1,567 Jews (827 men, 740 women) by place of last stay before liberation: 920 had survived in the USSR, 146 in bunkers, 125 in camps in Poland, 96 hidden among Poles (13 men, 83 women), 74 as partisans, 41 in camps in the Reich, 37 in forests, 128 other. That count is of registrations, not of city residents (the pre-war residence of those registered is unknown), so Population is blank. In the first half of 1946 only 51 children up to age 6 (49 of them survivors from the USSR) and 95 aged 7-14 were registered; in Sept 1946 the Committee's social department looked after 51 boys and 61 girls in homes and care. Online: en.wikipedia (Szymon Datner, fetched): after the war Datner "served for two years as head of the Białystok branch of the Central Committee of Jews in Poland" and deposited his testimony at the Jewish Historical Commission in Białystok on 28 Sept 1946. comment: Event: homage oath of 1831. After the Sejm's resolution of 8 Feb 1831 (which followed the dethronement of Nicholas I as king of Poland on 25 Jan), all inhabitants of the Kingdom of Poland aged 18 or more had to swear allegiance to the national cause. At Chęciny (Kraków voivodeship) 162 Christians and 289 Jews signed the text of the oath at the Municipal Office; the Jews added fitting phrases from the Torah to the formula. Saletra stresses that the homage books do not show what share of the Jewish population took the oath, so 289 is a count of signers, not the town's Jewish population (Population left blank; the map has 1,740 Jews for 1827). Evidence of a large Jewish community in Chęciny in 1831. No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish). Confidence medium.

comment: Event: tax complaint during the uprising. The Jews of Chęciny (the paper names Markus Spira, Nefbek Gizenberg and Berek Morgenstern) complained to the Kraków Voivodeship Commission about being overburdened in the tax assessments; the Commission told the town authorities that all property owners, merchants and other traders, not only Jews, had to contribute to the levy for the cavalry then being formed. Saletra adds that the plan to requisition church silver was extended to the houses of worship of other faiths, including synagogues, and that the Jewish communities were also loaded with deliveries for the uprising (see the PRZ3_totals file for the sheepskin-coat levy). Undated in the paper; placed in 1831 (the cavalry was being formed in the first months of 1831). Archive reference in the paper: State Archive Kielce, Radom Governorate Government, file 2206, f. 88. comment: Mid-18th-century status, from the Danzig Wette (commercial court) records 1741-1765: Jews had no right to settle in Danzig, only a licensed temporary stay for trade on safe-conducts (Judengeleit; nominally a few weeks, in practice some lived in the city for years, e.g. Jochem Benjamin of Ciechanow for 15 years). Kizik estimates the unstable community, with families and travellers, at 150-200 persons (a range, so Population is blank). Licensed residents were 2 rabbis, 4 cooks (soon 8) and butchers, who paid quarterly and lodged in inns on Dlugie Ogrody and Matenbuden; other Jews could enter during the Dominican Fair on simple fair passes and at other times only on special safe-conducts (Judengeleit), often issued at the request of a Danzig merchant partner. Just over 1,000 Jews lived in the suburbs outside the council's control in 1764-65 (see conflicts file). The Wette punished offences such as unlawful long stays, brokerage and currency speculation with fines, flogging, prison or expulsion - e.g. Moses of Kazimierz (expelled in 1757, readmitted in 1758, later flogged and banished for life), Joel Meyer (1760: lifelong ban), Chaim Schmul (1763: ordered out within 8 days, commuted to a fine at the petition of Danzig merchants), Janckel Raphael (1777: ordered to leave). Kizik finds the court impartial: these were penalties for trade offences, not communal persecution. Year 1741 is the start of the range 1741-1765. No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish).

Pinkas Hakehillot: "In June 1940, the governor of Jędrzejów district published a decree regarding the establishment of a ghetto open to the Jews of the city"; it was closed and fenced with barbed wire in March 1942. The USHMM Encyclopedia of Camps and Ghettos (Holocaust Historical Society page) says it was "established as one of the first in the Generalgouvernement in the spring of 1940", possibly as early as February, in the eastern part of the town (Kilinski, Pinczow, 3 Maja, Duch-Imbora and Lysakowska streets), and gives nearly 4,200 inmates in 1940. About 4,000 Jews lived in the town in 1939. Population blank (ghetto counts include outsiders). Confidence high for the ghetto, medium for the exact month.

comment: Event: liquidation of the Jędrzejów ghetto and deportation to Treblinka. Pinkas Hakehillot: the ghetto was surrounded on 15 Sept 1942, the Jews had to assemble in the market square on 16 Sept, about 250 people with needed trades were kept back and "The remainder, numbering 4,556, were marched to the train station"; "On September 17th, 1942, the trains arrived at Treblinka." The USHMM Encyclopedia of Camps and Ghettos (Holocaust Historical Society page): "The Germans liquidated the ghetto on 16 September 1942." On 28 Aug 1942 Jews of nearby localities (Sobków 800, Małogoszcz 830, Nagłowice 152, Nawarzyce 193 and smaller groups) had been brought in, swelling the ghetto to some 6,000 by 4 Sept. A group of about 230 workers stayed in a small ghetto, liquidated on 2 Sept 1943 (Pinkas) or in Feb 1943 (USHMM, Encyclopaedia Judaica); of about 4,500 Jews of the town only 80 survived (Pinkas). Piasecka's version differs: 4,000 Jews of Jędrzejów were expelled in one day, 2 Oct 1942, in an unknown direction (her words), the young and able probably to the weapons factory at Skarżysko and the rest to camps, and in the whole county 11,069 of 11,108 Jews were expelled between Aug 1942 and Sept 1943, 39 being left to serve the gendarmerie and other German units. Online date used; see the conflicts file. Population blank. Confidence high for the deportation, medium for the exact date.

Party data counted about 80 persons of Jewish origin in the whole Kielce voivodeship (voivodeship total, not the town's), and the voivodeship militia commander's report of 10 April 1968 counted about 80 Jews, of whom 15 had voiced criticism of the authorities; for 7 Jews in leading posts a request for removal was sent to the party (one was dismissed, party measures were taken against another). The voivodeship party first secretary reportedly told the culture-house head (his recollection) that Kielce, remembering its bad name from 1946, would have no anti-Semitic fuss; Wrobel found this untrue. comment: The German census of June 1940 counted 185 Jews in gmina Markowa (more than 100 in the village itself), who were quickly deprived of all rights and forced to work for the occupier (billeting, surrender of furs, blankets and valuables, snow clearing 10 km away in Łańcut; an early victim was a mentally ill Jew shot by a German policeman). Population left blank because 185 is the gmina total and the village figure is only "over 100". The German register of March 1943 gives 3,875 inhabitants for the village against about 4,500 in June 1940, a drop Szpytma cannot explain (the missing Jewish community was at most 120 persons).No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish).

Event: late July / early August 1942 (Operation Reinhard in Jarosław county): Jews were ordered to report for "resettlement" to the transit camp at Pełkinie; only a few reported (probably 6-8 per Wikipedia; "a few, mostly elderly, and one rich family" per Szpytma p. 215), the rest, several dozen, went into hiding in fields, ravines and farm buildings and were hunted by German gendarmes and the Polish "blue" police. Szpytma's footnote 49 quotes E. Podhorizer-Sondel (1959): about 10,000 Jews concentrated at Pełkinie and deported to Bełżec in early August. Szpytma p. 215 (PDF p. 212) also says the mass extermination of most Markowa Jews was carried out on the spot.

Event: 14 December 1942: after a manhunt ordered on 13 December by the village head at the Germans' request (fire brigade and village watch), a dozen to 25 captured Jews were held overnight in the village jail and shot next day by German gendarmes from Łańcut at an old trench used as an animal burial site (Wikipedia, Ulma family). Szpytma (pp. 216-217, PDF pp. 213-214) puts the mass shootings in summer and autumn 1942 (chronology uncertain; some villagers say mostly August): the Jews caught were held in a house at the main crossroads and shot in groups next morning at a former animal burial ground at the edge of the village, at least 50 victims, possibly up to 120 including Jews from neighbouring villages; the Rejestr (1984) lists 28 Sep 1942 (10 persons), 7 Oct (14 persons from Kańczuga and surrounding villages), 18 Oct (18) and autumn 1942 (25), but Szpytma warns the dates are unreliable; in November 1942 the fire brigade was ordered to search all buildings. After the war the bodies were moved to the Jewish cemetery in Michałówka near Radymno. The two sources differ on date and number: see conflicts file.

Event: 24 March 1944: German gendarmes from Łańcut (Eilert Dieken, Joseph Kokott, Michael Dziewulski, Erich Wilde) with Polish "blue" police went to the house of Józef and Wiktoria Ulma, who were hiding eight Jews of the Szall family from Łańcut and the Goldman family, and shot all eight Jews and then Józef, the pregnant Wiktoria and their six children: sixteen dead per Szpytma (Wikipedia also counts the unborn child). The Ulmas were betrayed, most probably by the blue policeman Włodzimierz Leś (Szpytma pp. 223-224: "much indicates"; Wikipedia states it as fact). Szpytma p. 219 (PDF p. 216): at least 17 Jews survived the occupation in Markowa in five Polish homes (Wikipedia now says at least 21). Józef and Wiktoria Ulma were recognised as Righteous Among the Nations in 1995 and the family was beatified in 2023.

Event: in 1687 the Opatów community went to the session of the Council of Four Lands because its ghetto, which covered one street, was too crowded after a large stream of refugees from all over Poland; there was fear that the Christian townspeople, who guarded against any widening of the ghetto, would turn on the Jews. The Council issued a proclamation favouring the permanent settlement of the passing Jews within the ghetto boundaries of Opatów (JewishGen translation of the Zamość memorial book, chapter on the Zamość rabbinate; the signatures include Rabbi Zvi Hirsch of Zamość). Lead: Hundert 1973, no. 8, 'Jews in Opatow at the Turn of the 17th and 18th Centuries' (Bursztyn, BFG 12, 1960). The map's Opatów rows for this period are the 1662-1698 and 1699-1754 population rows.

Event: host-desecration accusation. In 1689 two Jews of Opatow were imprisoned and accused of profaning a host and a crucifix (Lis, citing Kubicki 2007; Kubicki); to save them the kahal gave the collegiate chapter 1,000 zloty (Kubicki). A school-project text on the Jews of Opatow (rmg.zum.de) says Jews were falsely accused of violating the Catholic religion in 1689 and the kahal paid the chapter 1,000 zloty, which became an annual duty; Lis and Kubicki date the annual 1,000-zloty payment to the 1649 case, so that text probably merges the two cases. [Source detail: (A. Lis, "Żydzi w Opatowie w XVI-XVIII wieku", Roczniki Humanistyczne 58(2), 2010, p. 100); https://rmg.zum.de/images/3/31/Opatow_History_of_Jews.pdf; R. Kubicki, "Żydzi opatowscy od XVI do początku XIX wieku", in: Z przeszłości Żydów polskich..., ed. J. Wijaczka (Kraków 2005), p. 79 (PDF p. 76)]
According to a 17th-century census list, there were 2034 Jews in the Opatów kahal, which included 57 villages and 4 towns.

comment: Event: the building of a second (wooden) synagogue in 1708-1713 was challenged by the sub-dean of the collegiate church, who complained to the owner of the Opatow estate that it was being built without the consent of the Krakow bishop. Kubicki (citing Hundert p. 41) thinks it was probably left unfinished and never used, since the inventories from 1721 on list only one brick synagogue (plus the klojz), and the fire of 1714 may have finished it off. Lis (p. 105) instead states that a wooden synagogue from the early 18th century functioned alongside the brick one (see conflicts file). Year 1708 is the start of the range 1708-1713. No online source found for the sub-dean's complaint. No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish).

Event: in 1710 the Jews of Opatow were suspected of sorcery after a ram was found buried in their cemetery (Lis); Kubicki: Catholics accused the Jews of using witchcraft. Lis says that in these accusations (1689-1713) the kahal regularly ended the matter by paying high sums to church and secular dignitaries. [Source detail: (A. Lis, "Żydzi w Opatowie w XVI-XVIII wieku", Roczniki Humanistyczne 58(2), 2010, p. 101); R. Kubicki, "Żydzi opatowscy od XVI do początku XIX wieku", in: Z przeszłości Żydów polskich..., ed. J. Wijaczka (Kraków 2005), p. 79-80 (PDF p. 76-77)]

[Source detail: (A. Lis, "Żydzi w Opatowie w XVI-XVIII wieku", Roczniki Humanistyczne 58(2), 2010, p. 101); R. comment: Event: anti-Jewish riot during a sejmik. In 1713, at the sejmik of Sandomierz voivodeship held in Opatow, the servants of the assembled nobles plundered Jewish stalls and houses; a nobleman named Romer was killed in the rioting (Kubicki, citing Kriegseisen, Sejmiki Rzeczypospolitej szlacheckiej, p. 197). Kubicki says such disputes and anti-Jewish tumults were frequent during the Opatow sejmiks. Lis (p. 102) quotes a 1722 sejmik resolution admitting that servants and peasants habitually attacked and robbed the Opatow Jews during the sessions, and that the synagogue offered 40 zloty per sejmik for their security. No online source found for the 1713 riot itself. No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish).

Event: great fire of winter 1714. Kubicki (citing Horowitz): the whole Jewish part of Opatow burned down and, because of the winter, the Jews had to live in the villages around the town and in the suburbs (probably the start of Jewish settlement on the suburbs). Lis: the street inhabited by Jews was destroyed by a terrible fire and Catholic neighbours helped the victims. A school-project text (rmg.zum.de) adds that the kahal then forbade building Jewish houses or shops on the Polish street or the Christian market square, and that the Jewish street was rebuilt. A disaster, not persecution. [Source detail: (A. Lis, "Żydzi w Opatowie w XVI-XVIII wieku", Roczniki Humanistyczne 58(2), 2010, p. 101); https://rmg.zum.de/images/3/31/Opatow_History_of_Jews.pdf; R. Kubicki, "Żydzi opatowscy od XVI do początku XIX wieku", in: Z przeszłości Żydów polskich..., ed. J. Wijaczka (Kraków 2005), p. 70 (PDF p. 67)]

Lis gives 129 Catholic houses and 95 empty plots, which matches 233 - 104 = 129 for the whole town. Houses are not people, so Population is blank. [Source detail: (A. comment: Event: tumult in the Jewish quarter. In 1733 the servants and part of the nobility assembled at Opatow started a tumult and plundered the Jewish part of the town; the disturbance lasted a full day; the Voivode of Sandomierz, Jerzy Lubomirski, tried to suppress it by force and several Catholics, at least one of them a nobleman, were killed (Kubicki, citing Rzeczpospolita w dobie upadku 1700-1740, ed. Gierowski, pp. 131-136). Lis (p. 101) corroborates the context only: the Jews had to pay large sums for their safety during the confederation formed at Opatow after the death of Augustus II in 1733 (supporting Leszczynski's election). The details of the looting and deaths come from the paper alone; no online source found for them. No online source found; source is a scholarly conference article (Polish).

Event: protection payments. In 1752 the kahal of Opatow handed over about 1,700 zloty to secure the Jewish population during the sejmiks (Lis, citing Leszczynski 1986; Kubicki: the kahal spent almost 1,700 zloty to be safe during the sejmik sessions). In 1758 the estate owner ordered his governor to keep the sejmik servants from violence and robbery against Jews, and the kahal also made yearly gifts to the clergy (Kubicki: 1760, dean 90 zloty etc.) and to nobles, partly to keep the peace. [Source detail: (A. Lis, "Żydzi w Opatowie w XVI-XVIII wieku", Roczniki Humanistyczne 58(2), 2010, p. 103); R. Kubicki, "Żydzi opatowscy od XVI do początku XIX wieku", in: Z przeszłości Żydów polskich..., ed. J. Wijaczka (Kraków 2005), p. 84 (PDF p. 81)]
