Event: in 1759 a Catholic inquisitorial commission sat in Opatow to investigate an accusation that a Jewish woman had killed (Lis) or tried to kill (Kubicki) her own child. Kubicki's reading: it was not a criminal case but a custody dispute - the baptised father, with men 'from the Church', tried to take the child from his estranged Jewish wife, who hurt the child while escaping through a window; the kahal spent 5 zloty 26 groszy on the commission's officials and the child probably stayed with the mother. Possibly linked to the Frankist movement (two Opatow Jews converted in 1759-60). Weak item. [Source detail: (A. comment: Event: leaflets ordering Jews to leave Radom. Online (Destroyed Communities Interactive Learning Center, Radom page, fetched; image credited to the USHMM): a leaflet dated 29 July 1945 says "I recommend that all Jews remove themselves beyond the borders of the city and district of Radom by August 15, 1945", with a warning of punishment for those who stay or ask the government for help; the same page gives the estimated Jewish population of Radom in May 1945 as 400 (Population = that estimate). The paper (pp. 255-256) adds, from archival documents: leaflets, probably signed "D.O.W.S." (cryptonym of Lt S. Bembinski "Harnas-Sokol", Radom centre of the Armed Forces Delegation), spread in Radom and probably the whole county, justifying the order by alleged collaboration; on 14 July 1945 Jewish militia sergeant Boleslaw Gaut was shot in Radom; on 10 Aug 1945 four Jews and one "Red Army officer" were killed in Radom (the least clear case); Hersz and Abram Blumsztajn served in the PUBP Radom operational group in 1945. The author thinks the cases may be linked to the DSZ Radom centre and a reaction to perceived security-police collaboration. Only the leaflet and the May 1945 estimate have an online page; the killings are from the paper alone. Confidence high (leaflet), medium (killings).

comment: Event: liquidation of the HASAG camp. Paper: on 25 July 1944 the guards began registering every prisoner and marking each name for life or death; the picric-acid workers ('yellow people') were killed first, then the sick, and a further selection took place on 30 July; some days later SS officers announced transfers: part of the prisoners went to the HASAG works at Czestochowa (Pelcery), most deep into the Reich, among them 1,200 women to Leipzig; the camp was closed in the first half of August (Table 1: 1 Aug 1944). On 26 Oct 1949 the trial of eight Suchowola residents began before the Court of Appeal in Białystok. Charges: herding dozens of Jewish citizens and suspected Soviet sympathisers to the market square, killing some and imprisoning others in the ghetto or prison; drowning dozens of Jews in a pond and burning others alive in a building; beating Jews; guarding the ghetto. Four defendants got life, the rest 15 years; the Supreme Court sent the case back for procedural errors and at the retrial before the Voivodeship Court (25-27 June 1951; over 70 witnesses) the witnesses changed their testimony, saying the perpetrators came from outside the town, and all the accused were acquitted. The paper calls such outcomes typical of the 61 trials (1945-58) over pogroms in the western part of the voivodeship (source cited: A. Zbikowski, 2002). Near Myrtilis (Mértola): a small hoard of Roman coins of the 1st century AD found during the demolition of an old wall (now in the Belmonte Jewish Museum) includes coins minted in Jerusalem and Roman Palestine between 6 and 60 AD by King Agrippa and by procurators; Cravinho (2017), citing Centeno and Valladares Souto 1993/1997, calls it 'the earliest concrete evidence' for Jewish immigrants, presumably from Judaea, in the Iberian Peninsula. Year 60 is the end of the coin range; the hoard was buried later. WEAK ITEM: coins alone do not prove Jewish residents (they may have come with soldiers or traders); single scholarly source; the hoard was found 'near' Mértola. No population. No catalogue lead.

Myrtilis (Mértola): a fragmentary marble grave-slab with a Latin inscription dated 4 October 482 AD; the name of the deceased is lost, but a partly preserved Hebrew word and a schematic menorah with tripod base engraved below make his Jewish origin evident (Cravinho, Studies in Ancient Art and Civilization 21, 2017, introduction, summarising the Portuguese literature; she adds that of the several Jewish tomb inscriptions in Portugal some come from Mértola). English Wikipedia ('History of the Jews in Portugal') says an attested Jewish presence in Portuguese territory 'can be documented only since 482 CE', which agrees with this stone. No second page describing the stone itself was found, so confidence is medium. No population. No catalogue lead.

On March 30, 1543, a denunciation to the Lisbon Inquisition claimed that out of 50 inhabitants in the locality, only 3 or 4 were Old Christians and the rest were conversos who judaized in a secret synagogue (though the historian notes these numbers are hard to accept uncritically).

Earliest documented Jewish resident: Abraao, recorded in Viseu in January 1284 (Saraiva, Medievalista article). Coordinates checked: they point to Viseu (Beira Alta), correct. Existing marker only had a 15th-century synagogue row.
Abraao accused of charging more than double on a loan (4 June 1293); the king orders restitution if proven. In 1303-1305 he lived in Cimo de Vila near S. Domingos.

Event: Cortes of Elvas (Pedro I) require Jewish communities to organise in judiarias; c. 1359 a Jew Jacob is recorded near the Praca and Rua das Tendas, suggesting the community had moved from the arrabalde toward the centre.

First documented reference to the synagogue (1 Feb 1379), near the Praca and Triparia off Rua das Tendas; first reference to the Rua da Judiaria 13 Apr 1386; in 1384 John I granted the royal service paid by Viseu's Jews to a squire.
A fifteenth century residence stands with symbols revealing its past as the first Jewish synagogue in Viseu.

Event: the judiaria relocates 1415-1418 to a contiguous street between the Praca and Rua das Tendas (now Rua da Senhora da Piedade); from 1421 the old street is the Judiaria Velha; synagogue placed in the new judiaria 7 Aug 1433.
King Duarte confirms the community's privileges, foros, liberdades and costumes (26 Dec 1433).

M. J. Ferro Tavares, "Os judeus da Beira interior: a comuna de Trancoso e a entrada da Inquisicao", Sefarad 68:2 (2008) 369-411, pp. 374-380, p. 374: trade-contract letters granted by Afonso V in 1441-42 to Jews of the Beira interior: Lamego 75, Covilha 72, Guarda 62, Trancoso 44, Castelo Branco 30, Viseu 23, Celorico 22, Pinhel 17, Gouveia 6 (a count by default taken from the royal chancery only); here 23 adult Jews. Households x5 applied by the compiler (Ferro Tavares applies x5 only to Trancoso); minimum figure, weak.

Event: the Viseu council asks the Evora cortes (14 Feb 1444) to move the judiaria within the walls; never carried out. In 1468 (Santarem cortes) the council complains of Jewish doors and windows facing Christian property and Afonso V orders them closed. The article says the community grew 'exponentially' in the 15th century but gives no figures.

Event: Manuel I's decree orders Jews to convert or leave. In 1498 the Rua da Judiaria is renamed Rua Nova; on 13 Nov 1499 a house 'que foy Judaria' is leased to Diogo Henriques, son of Jewish parents.
,Rabbi Harold Khunivitch, originally from a Makow immigrant family, served as chief rabbi in San Juan.
When the island passed from Spanish to American rule at the end of the Spanish-American War in 1898, there were practically no Jews there.

Presence-only marker: sources document a few Jewish individuals or families here but give no city-level count, so population is set to 3 by convention. Practically no Jews at the 1898 change to US rule; refugees arrived from 1933. A 2014 estimate of ~3,000 covers the whole territory, not San Juan.
Passenger lists of vessels arriving at San Juan from October 7, 1901, to June 30, 1948, contain Jewish personal names indicating arrivals or transit.
Following the rise of Nazism in Europe, Jewish refugees made their way to Puerto Rico, with most settling in San Juan.
San Juan was designated as INS Naturalization District 26 for processing immigration records between 1933 and 1943.
The Jewish Community Center was founded. The Shaare Zedek Synagogue-Community Center was established in the Santurce neighborhood.

Presence-only marker: sources document an organized community or synagogue here but give no city-level count, so population is set to 20 by convention. Jewish Community Center, Shaare Zedek and Beth Shalom synagogues in San Juan.
In the 1950s and 1960s, the community was bolstered by the arrival of Jews from the United States and Cuba; most of the island's Jews resided in the capital, San Juan.

San Juan's Jewish community dates back to the mid-20th century. The city hosts the Reform Synagogue Beth Shalom, the Conservative Synagogue Shaare Tzedek, the Orthodox Chabad Synagogue (containing the island's only Mikvah), the Caribbean's largest Jewish library, and a Holocaust Memorial.

A 2014 study reported approximately 3,000 Jews in Puerto Rico; this figure is a regional aggregate for the entire territory rather than San Juan specifically, though most of the island's Jews reside in the capital.

Arrests began in September 1952 (37 people initially, including 17 Jews); on 13 January 1953 Pravda announced the accusation against nine Moscow doctors, six of them Jewish, of plotting to kill Soviet leaders. Stalin died on 5 March 1953; a decree of 31 March cleared the doctors and Pravda announced it on 6 April 1953. Historians dispute whether a mass deportation of Jews was planned (Wikipedia). comment: Chatschim "of Celje" (Cilli), with his brother Mosche of Maribor, was the Jewish creditor in the 2,613-florin surety of 13 November 1355 for Bishop Paul of Gurk (Wiedl p. 65 and n.43: brothers, sons of Scheblein, who resided in Maribor and Cilli/Celje). The regest of 1355 (Nr. 804) names "Mosche aus Marburg und seinem Bruder Chatschim" without a town for Chatschim; regest Nr. 863 (9 November 1357) calls Chatschim and Mosche "Söhne Schebleins aus Cilli", and a Hebrew signature of 1376 reads "Chaim son of Shabtai of Zil" (regest Nr. 1513, issued at Cilli). On 3 July 1362 Duke Rudolf IV enfeoffed Chatschim, with wife and son, to the Counts Ulrich and Hermann of Cilli for life, allowing them to settle him anywhere in their territory (regest Nr. 1027; Wiedl p. 68 n.56: Chatschim of Celje "had been given as a fief to the Counts of Celje in 1362"). Caveat: regest Nr. 966 (24 November 1360) says Chatschim "aus Cilli" was then living in Trieste, so "of Cilli" may name his family origin rather than his residence in a given year. The map has only century-level Celje rows (1000-1249, 1250). No population. Confidence medium. Wiedl calls the brothers two of the most prestigious Jewish moneylenders of the time, Mosche of Maribor and Chatschim of Celje; in n.43 she says they were sons of Scheblein who resided in Maribor and Cilli/Celje. It is the only documented Jewish credit of Paul; the "certain Jews" to whom he later pawned a mitre and a crozier (papal mandate of 1360) cannot be identified (p. 71). The map has Maribor rows for the Judengasse (1353) and the synagogue (1354) but no dated moneylender entry for the 1350s. No population. Confidence high. Mosche was a direct subject of the dukes, unlike Chatschim of Celje (a fief of the Counts of Cilli) and Abrech of Friesach (a subject of the archbishop of Salzburg) (Wiedl p. 68 n.56). The text states January 1908 (an apparent typo for 1808), noting that Jewish officer Jakob Szpot was dispatched to conquer Cuenca, successfully capturing it before being surrounded by Spanish forces.

After the reconquest of Daroca by Alfonso i of Aragon in 1122 Jews were granted the same rights as the Christian and Muslim residents in a fuero ("municipal charter"), endorsed by Count Ramon Berenguer iv in 1142.

Municipal fuero of Daroca (confirmed by Ramon Berenguer IV in 1142; Encyclopaedia Judaica also mentions Alfonso I retaking the town in 1122) gave Jews the same rights as Christian and Muslim residents.
Pedro II exempted the Jews of Daroca from certain tolls, including those on entering and leaving Moorish territory.
The Daroca community flourished during the 13th century. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)
The Daroca Jewish community paid an annual tax of 750 dineros (Jewish Encyclopedia).
James II halted sale of Jewish property seized for debt and banned arrests on the Sabbath and Jewish holidays.
Event: Daroca townspeople accused the Jews of poisoning wells.
Alfonso IV set rules for Jewish oaths, taken at the synagogue entrance with a Torah scroll before three Christian witnesses (evidence of a synagogue).
Event: peasants joined townspeople in attacking the Jews of Daroca and pressed them to convert; the king extended protection.
After the 1391 attacks only 27 taxpaying Jewish families remained (Encyclopaedia Judaica). Population = households x 5 (source count 27 families).
At the beginning of the 15th century the community of Daroca, like many others in the Crown of Aragon, was under great pressure from Christian society. (century-only date, round year 1400 used)

Rabbi Joseph Albo represented Daroca at the Tortosa disputation 1413-14; about 110 of the most prominent and wealthy members then converted (on 20 Aug 1414 Ferdinand I exempted converts from communal taxes).

Event: after April 1414 the aljama ceased to exist as a legal body; townspeople arrested all remaining Jews; of about 40 families (source states roughly 160-180 people - midpoint 170) only 9 or 10 remained, imprisoned; trial of the prisoners opened January 1426.

The amount is a levy, not population; the kind of levy is not stated, and the figures are well below the annual taxes recorded elsewhere for the larger communities. The same list gives 200 for Jaca and Fraga, 300 for Huesca and 350 for Monzon, amounts the Jewish Encyclopedia also quotes for those towns, which supports Depping's reading of the list. No online source found; source is the 1834 book (secondary, old). Confidence medium.
John II defined the limits of the Jewish quarter to separate Jews from Christians after an influx of Jewish immigrants.

Motis Dolader, "Poblacion, urbanismo y estructura politica de las aljamas judias aragonesas en la Edad Media", Hispania 56/3 no. 194 (1996) 885-944: in 1458 Juan II assigned the old quarter again; according to an Inquisition deposition (1492) "la primera oleada constó de seis o siete familias tan solo". Households x5 (6.5 families).

Various sources, including documents from the Cairo Genizah, tell about Jewish settlement in the town from the beginning of the 11th century, and it appears that in the middle of the century there was a substantial community there. (century-only date, round year 1000 used)
Jews are listed among the groups present in the Muslim statelet, or taifa, of Denia.

c. 1050: substantial community by mid-century trading by land and sea with Tunisia and Alexandria (merchant Nathan b. Naharai correspondence; Ibn al-Khatib family); court physician Isaac Ibn Yashush; scholars Samuel b. Joseph and poet Ibn Khazin (corresponded with Judah Halevi); R. Isaac b. Moses ibn Sikhri left for Babylonia to head R. Hai Gaon's yeshivah, succeeded by Isaac b. Reuben al-Bargeloni. Jews lived in a quarter of the alcazaba.

Event: Christian conquest (1244 per es.wikipedia: Muslim population largely removed; resettled under Fuero of Valencia); only a few Jewish families engaged in maritime trade remained (EJ; no conquest date given by EJ).
Tax: in 1274 the Jews of Dénia and Orembloy together paid an annual levy of 100 solidos Barcelona currency (joint levy, no population stated).
Event: 1391 anti-Jewish riots; EJ has no information on the community's fate afterwards.

Ferdinand III transferred to the Huelgas monastery of Burgos in 1221 the lands in Dueñas where Jews were settled; the first document naming the Jews of Dueñas is from 1225 (Encyclopaedia Judaica); es.wikipedia: a list drawn up about a decade later counted 23 Jews in the 'Puebla' quarter.
The first document referring to the Jews of Dueñas is from 1225.
Its Jewish community began to flourish in the 13th century. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)
In 1290 the Jewish community of Dueñas, one of the smallest in Castile, paid taxes of 2,427 maravedis; in 1352, impoverished by the Black Death, it paid only 300 maravedis.
The Jews of Dueñas owned land and vineyards; in 1346, the king's surgeon Don Judah, an inhabitant of Dueñas, leased several gardens belonging to the local church.
Event: The community was evidently impoverished by the Black Death (1348–49), since in 1352 it paid only 300 maravedis in tax.
Event: the Jewish quarter of Dueñas was attacked and sacked about 1368 during the Castilian civil war (chronicler Samuel Zarza).
Considering the tax paid, the community remained small in the 15th century. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)

Following the edict ordering Jews and Christians to live in separate quarters, Ferdinand and Isabella gave instructions in 1483 that the alcabalá ("indirect taxes") should not be collected from houses owned by Christians which were situated in the new Jewish quarter.

Event: in May 1492 the Jews of Dueñas complained they could not leave by the date fixed in the expulsion decree because they were hindered in selling property and collecting debts; the Jewish quarter lay near the castle and the new separate quarter dates from 1483.

c. 13th century: earliest record of Jews in Écija; after Fernando III's conquest the Jewish courtier Zulema received substantial property. Coordinates checked: they belong to Écija (Seville province).
The earliest information concerning Jews there dates from the 13th century. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)
Tax of the Jewish community: 5,000 maravedis (tax amount only; no population derived).
Yucaf (Joseph ha-Levi ibn Shabbat) de Écija, courtier of Alfonso XI, founded a yeshivah and paid stipends to its scholars.

Event: ritual-murder accusation in the reign of Alfonso (X or XI): a Jew was imprisoned on the eve of Passover and the populace rose; many Jews sought refuge in nobles' houses (date uncertain, c. 14th century).

source: Beinart, Atlas of Medieval Jewish History (Carta, Jerusalem 1992), map 57 p. 66

The map gives no year for the town; Year of Data 1366 is the conventional year of the civil war. No online source naming this town was found.
Event: synagogue destroyed in December 1390 on the order of archdeacon Ferrand Martinez, native of Écija (Jewish Encyclopedia corrects Jacobs's 1395).
Event: massacre spreading from Seville reached Écija; most Jews converted.
The archbishop of Toledo asked the vicar of Écija to account for the synagogue's destruction; the vicar said a mob had razed it.
Community tax assessment 6,800 maravedis in old coin (date of reconstitution of the community unknown). Tax amount only.
Event: Marranos cruelly treated until knights came to their rescue.
Organized group of conversos led by New Christian Fernando de Trujillo.

Pedro II of Aragon granted the Jews the Castillo de Ortes for resettlement (as stated in Spanish Wikipedia).

By 1271 the Jewish quarter, first in the Muslim alcazaba, had spread to Santa Maria de la Corona and neighbouring streets. Claims of one third Jewish population are undated and unsourced: not entered.

Jewish Encyclopedia (Elche): when James I of Aragon took Elche from the Moors he gave houses and land to the Jews he found there, as to the Jews of Valencia, and appointed a special street for them; in 1410 Vicente Ferrer came to Elche to convert the Jews and those who stayed faithful fled to Italy and Turkey; Abraham Rondi corresponded with Isaac b. Sheshet. Year 1263 is the date of the Aragonese conquest of Elche given in Encyclopaedia Judaica.

A Jewish scribe was in charge of the office registers and taxes of the Muslim community of Elche in 1308; in 1314 the scribe Abraham al-Behbehi wrote a Judeo-Arabic translation of a court record; Abraham b. Bahye farmed the taxes of Elche 1381-84.

Three Jewish households are counted in Elche in 1465 (Hinojosa Montalvo, cited by Motis Dolader; 3 households x 5 = estimate); unknown whether they persisted to 1492. Elche was one of the four Jewish settlements of the Alicante region of the Kingdom of Murcia.

es.wikipedia: at the 1492 expulsion the Jewish community of Entrena was important, constituting an aljama of roughly 50 families (count unattributed in the article, so no population given); Jews had moved to smaller villages for protection.

A document of 1397 refers to a 'sinoga biella que solia seer' (old synagogue no longer in use) beside the town wall in the barrio de las Herrerias, implying a newer synagogue by the late 14th century (Marin Padilla, Sefarad 55, 1995). Event: 16 Apr 1401 the Christian council ordered Jews, like Christians, not to work with open doors on Sunday, because Jews and Christians lived mixed without a Jewish quarter (Marin Padilla 1995).
Testamentary bequests from 1421 (and again 1425) were assigned to the repair of the synagogue (Marin Padilla 1995).

Motis Dolader (Hispania 1996) lists Epila at 170-190 Jews as a minimum 15th-century quantification (midpoint 180; year not stated, 1450 placeholder); he calls it a 'prospera colectividad' and notes Jews of Daroca migrated there after 1415.

Event: 1 Mar 1492 the king wrote to the count of Aranda ordering the expulsion edict proclaimed in Epila and Aranda. Among the last recorded acts in the synagogue, 12 Feb 1492: Zaragoza merchants Abraham Eli and son Juce swore the usury oath before the merino and the community's public crier Acach Abensenyor. Departures, sales and conversions in notarial acts of 1492 (Marin Padilla 1994-95).

According to an old history of Toledo, early Jewish settlers founded the town of Escalona four hundred years before the Christian era.

Jewish community existed in the Muslim period and stayed after the Christian conquest of 1083 (EJ). Coordinates are correct (Escalona, Toledo province). The -400 legend row in kehilot.csv comes from an old Toledo history and is not medieval evidence.
1130 municipal fuero gave Jews equal standing with Christians and Moors but barred them from judging Christian lawsuits.
Escalona's Jews were not named in the 1290 tax distribution among Jewish communities, probably because they were few.
Event: community destroyed in the persecutions of 1391; revived in the 15th century on a small scale.
1453: real estate given to R. Salamon, physician to Countess Juana Pimentel.
Aljama tax payments (maravedis, no population given): 1474 1000; 1482 2000; 1489 5040; 1490 6570; 1491 4000 (EJ citing Baer/Suarez Fernandez).
Jews segregated into a Jewish quarter (attested 1477-1489 in municipal archives); the mosque was included in the quarter. 1485 war levy against Granada: 38 gold castellanos.
The community paid 5,040 maravedis in 1489, 6,570 maravedis in 1490, and 4,000 maravedis in 1491.

Event: Jews are documented in Estella from the late 11th century (c. 1090), when the fuero of the Franks of San Pedro de la Rúa mentions their trade; the aljama (Elgacena) lay in the San Pedro de la Rúa quarter below the castle.
Origins of the Jewish community of Estella lie in the 12th century

Event: King Garcia Ramirez gave the synagogue to the bishop and it became the church of Santa Maria (Santa María Jus del Castillo); c. 20 years later the Jews' legal status was fixed by a favourable fuero.
Because of the privileges granted to the Jews there, the city attracted other Jews from many parts of Spain during the 12th century. (century-only date, round year 1150 used)
Event: Sancho VI allowed the bishop of Pamplona to admit Jews in Estella and Huarte with the same privileges as Estella's Jews.
A fuero ("municipal charter") granted to Estella in 1164 contained a series of articles regulating relations between Jews and Gentiles.
In 1265 there were 29 Jewish householders in Estella paying land tax and rent to the king. [Population: households x5, from 29 Jewish householders stated by EJ; estimate based on households.]

Event: Louis Hutin removed the seneschal who had arrested Jews, freed the prisoners and placed them under the seneschal of Pamplona; popular agitation against the Jews continued (tax collector Juan Garcia and the Franciscan Pedro Olligoyen).

Event: On the night of 5-6 March 1328 after the death of Charles IV the juderia was assaulted, burned and sacked; many were killed and only a few escaped (the family of Menahem ben Zerah died, he survived). Philip III ordered an inquiry and a fine of 10000 livres; in 1329 the community still paid an aid of 1600 libras. Before the attack the aljama was the third in the kingdom by tax contribution after Tudela and Pamplona (Carrasco; no victim count given).

Joseph ibn Bulat headed the aljama in 1358; the aljama had two directors and twenty regidores elected to replace retiring members, with power to fine and expel members; Jews were mainly in commerce and finance and several were tax farmers.

In 1365 Charles ii appointed Judah b. Samuel ha-Levi of Estella to act as high commissioner for the crown for collecting the money in services and taxes owed by Jews and in 1390 sent him on a diplomatic mission.
Population: households x 5. Jewish Encyclopedia gives 85 families in 1366 (source count 85 families).

Population: households x 5. Spanish Wikipedia gives 89 families in 1366 (source count 89 families), a different estimate from the Jewish Encyclopedia's 85; it also claims c. 110 families in the 13th century without citation (not used as a population).

Jews of Estella paid nearly 120 florins a month in taxes (119 florins per Carrasco, behind Tudela 521 and Pamplona 261); in 1377 the king seized their property to collect a disputed balance. In 1394 the pecha of the Estella aljama was 832 libras 7 s 3 d (Tudela 2476, Pamplona 988).
Abraham ben Isaac of Estella was sentenced to death and his goods confiscated in 1413; the 15th century brought increasing limits on Jewish trade and emigration.
Jews of Estella engaged in tax farming throughout the 15th century. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)

JE: King Pedro gave the taxes from the Gerona Jewry to his wife, Constanca.

Event: when Gerona prepared to defend itself against the French army, Spanish mercenaries forced their way into the Jewry, murdering and plundering; the old synagogue was destroyed with the rest of the Jewry (rebuilt some years later).

Event: From the end of the 13th century Jews were forced out of their positions in the local administration, as well as from various economic activities: no further mention is made of Jewish landowners cultivating their own land, and some Jews of Gerona settled in other cities under royal protection. (century-only date, round year 1290 used)

JE: tombstone of Enoch ben Shealtiel Saporta, who died in 1312, found in Gerona in 1873.

Event: the persecution of the Pastoureaux also affected the Jews of Gerona (JE gives no year in this article; Pastoureaux year 1320 as dated in the JE article Gaillac).

Jewish death toll from massacre in one day, described as comprising more than 1,500 Jewish families

The Castaño-del Rey Granell article also names Medina de Rioseco among the places of provenance of the Jews admitted at Villalón (within 45 km) and states that the tax of the Villalón aljama in the diocese of Palencia was exceeded only by the combined tax of the aljamas of Aguilar de Campoo and Medina de Rioseco (so Medina de Rioseco had an aljama). The volume (p. 329) says Alhanate left 'ten years later' (c. 1481); the article's 20 Sept 1482 date is used. Map had no marker for Medina de Rioseco. Population blank. Confidence high. Encyclopaedia Judaica: in the 14th century the community had between 50 and 100 householders (range, 250-500 persons at x5; Population left blank because a range).
Regulations of the Zamora council applied to Medina del Campo (badge, Christian servants, physicians, interest).
By the 14th century the community consisted of between 50 and 100 householders. (century-only date, round year 1350 used)

In 1290 the communities of Medinaceli and Sigüenza together paid annual taxes and services amounting to 34,217 maravedis, which indicates considerable prosperity.

The synagogue, which passed to the Church after the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492, was restored by the government.

Tax: the community paid 4000 maravedis in 1283 (tax amount only; no population derived).
Event: the Jews of Mérida suffered in the 1391 persecutions (EJ).

In 1290 the community numbered 15 families who paid an annual tax of 3,312 maravedis and 744 maravedis in services. [Population: households x5, from 15 families stated by EJ; estimate based on families.]
In 1304 Ferdinand iv confirmed that the Jews, Moors, and Christians in Miranda had equal rights, in particular as regards financial liabilities.

Event: The more friendly Peter showed himself toward the Jews, and the more he protected them, the more antagonistic became the attitude of his illegitimate half-brother, who, when he invaded Castile in 1360, murdered all the Jews living in Nájera and exposed those of Miranda de Ebro to robbery and death.

The map gives no year for the town; Year of Data 1366 is the conventional year of the civil war. No online source naming this town was found.

Synagogue: a document of the mid-15th century (c. 1450) mentions the Miranda synagogue, in the calle de la Puente near the Puerta de la Villa (today the 'calle de los Judíos' / calle de la Independencia); a nearby lane was the 'callejuela del Rabino'; by c. 1470 houses were built against the wall beside it (Cadiñanos Bardeci).

The privileges of Jews in Miranda, as enumerated to the authorities in Burgos in 1453, included the right to own synagogues, to participate in the tax apportionment, and to work on Sundays at home or in closed workshops, as well as exemption from paying dues to the cathedral.
By the system of taxation introduced by Jacob ibn Nuñez in 1474, several neighboring communities were joined with Miranda and their joint tax was fixed at 2,000 maravedis.

The council asked that neither synagogue nor fonsario (cemetery) be alienated; by royal order the synagogue went to the council as town hall (Cadiñanos dates the order 12 June 1493, the Spanish Wikipedia says June 1492).

The central facility for male foreign prisoners at Miranda de Ebro held variegated categories of prisoners, including a small number of foreign Jews.
Event: Moixent (lordship of Pero Maca de Lizana) is listed by Motis Dolader among the lordship places of the Kingdom of Valencia with a Jewish community in 1492.

Talmudist R. Yonatan b. Yaaqob was born in Molina in the first half of the 13th century (c. 1225) and later moved to Cuenca; aljama of some importance in Castilian Jewry in the 13th-14th centuries, closely tied to Cuenca and Daroca (Arenas Esteban and Castaño 2010).

Synagogue at Castil de Judíos probably built in the 13th century (c. 1275), then improved and decorated, reaching its excavated form by the late 14th century; excavations identify the building as a synagogue (Arenas Esteban and Castaño 2010).
Three of the ten Jews signing a 1326 agreement on credit between the Cuenca aljama and the Cuenca council bear the family name 'de Molina' (sign of ties between the aljamas).
Molina under the Crown of Aragon 1369-1375: rich documentation (register 1551 of Pedro IV's chancery) about the aljama and the Abolafia family.
Event: effects of the 1391 violence are not documented; the aljama possibly suffered serious disruption as at Cuenca, and the synagogue was apparently abandoned afterwards rather than converted.

The aljama disappeared abruptly after conversions and departures; e.g. Samuel Abenaya, Jewish lender of Molina, was temporarily in Aragon in 1412 and complained of robbery by men of Calatayud and Daroca villages.

c. 1460 there was no longer a synagogue; only a few Jews lived there temporarily (e.g. Mose Aben Xuxen) and celebrated Yom Kippur in a private house with conversos (Inquisition testimony). The Castil de Judíos quarter was still inhabited. Coordinates checked: they belong to Molina de Aragón (Guadalajara).

At the end of 1414 an official report found only fifteen Jewish houses remaining across Alcañiz, Caspe, Maella, Alcorisa, Castellote and Molinos; Jews of Molinos later emigrated to Monzon (monedaje 1397: 87 Jewish fuegos; 1451: 147).

Jews apparently lived in the fortress of Montclus and the adjacent area from the beginning of the 11th century. (century-only date, round year 1000 used) [Coordinates note: Monclus (Montclus) is a medieval fortress-town now a deserted village near the Mediano reservoir, La Fueva, Huesca; coordinates from es.wikipedia.]

The annual tax paid by the community in the 13th century was reduced by the king from 800 to 500 solidos in 1271, increased to 707 solidos and 3½ denarii in Jaca coin in 1304, and again reduced to 450 solidos in 1315.
In 1298 James ii ordered an investigation on the rate of interest charged by Jews on loans.
Event: The Montclus community helped to rehabilitate Jews expelled from France in 1306.
In 1307 the king authorized the community to absorb four families, including those of the physician Maestre Boninfante and Vitalis de Boulogne.
Event: However, between the end of June and the beginning of July 1320, the community was annihilated in the Pastoureaux (Shepherds) massacres.

In 1321 the king freed the remnant of the community from paying taxes and ordered that the walls of the fortress should be rebuilt, but by 1323 the Jews of Montclus had to pay taxes like the other Jews of the kingdom to finance the royal expedition to Sardinia.
Event: Nevertheless, when disorders broke out in 1333, the commander of the fortress, Garcia Bardaxi, did nothing to prevent the rioters from massacring the Jews and was pardoned.
His successor, Alfonso iv, in 1335 freed the community from paying taxes, as did Pedro iv in 1341–42.
With the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492, Montclus began to decline.

14th century (c. 1300 used as year): a Castilian chancery document addressed to Bishop Don Gonzalo of Mondoñedo mentions Jews (per Enrique Cal Pardo); several Jews lived under the bishop's protection. No judería or aljama located; location of a quarter unknown. Coordinates checked: Mondoñedo, Lugo province, correct.

In 1474 the Jews of Monforte, with those of Ourense, Ribadavia and Allariz, paid a combined annual tax of 2,000 maravedis (Encyclopaedia Judaica, Orense).

The aljama of Montalbán was founded by a cedula of James II in 1309 at the request of the commander Artal de Huerta (Motis Dolader, citing Sainz de la Maza's study of the aljama 1307-91).

Annual tax to the crown 4,000 sólidos (EJ); amount only, no population.

comment: Jewish presence in Monzón (Aragon) in 1461: the Jewish tailor Sento de Briviesca, originally from Briviesca (Castile), opened a workshop in Monzón in 1461 (Baer, Die Juden im christlichen Spanien I/1, p. 877 no. 548, cited by Castaño); an example of a Castilian Jew moving to Aragon. Castaño also records that the translator of philosophical treatises 'Eli Habillo' (identified with Eli Sarfati) worked in Monzón in about 1485 after studying at Aguilar de Campoo in 1464. Online: the Jewish Encyclopedia article on Monzón (source of the existing rows) confirms the community but does not mention the tailor; English Wikipedia 'Elijah ben Joseph Habillo' (from the Jewish Encyclopedia) confirms a philosopher-translator of that name active in Monzón in the second half of the 15th century (without the Aguilar or 1485 details). Existing Monzón rows 1414, 1463 (testament of Doña Oro) and 1465-1491: no conflict. No online source found for the tailor. Population blank. Confidence medium.
Bibliography mentions the 1463 testament of Doña Oro, wife of Samuel Rimok, a Jewish woman of Monzón, confirming Jewish presence
Notarial records 1465-78 name 44 Jewish householders (EJ); households x 5, source count 44.

Event: expulsion; Lascorz states that after the decree (given as 28 July 1492) 74 Monzón families went to Perpignan, others to Navarre, Morocco, Italy, Balkans. Households x 5, source count 74 (families leaving; single travel-magazine source, uncorroborated; EJ records no details of departure). Judería between Plaza San Juan, Santa María and calle Arriba.
es.wikipedia: two Hebrew tombstones were found, one inscribed with the burial of Rav Samuel son of Rabbi Shalthiel, dated 16 Elul 4857, which the article equates with 1097.
In 1290 the Jewish communities of Carrión de los Condes, Saldaña and Monzon (de Campos) together paid 91,987 maravedis in annual taxes and services (Encyclopaedia Judaica, Carrion article).
In 1489-91 the tax payable by the Jewish aljama of Monzón de Campos for the war of Granada was set.
Event: Mora de Rubielos (lordship of Joan Fernández de Heredia) is listed by Motis Dolader among the seigneurial places with a Jewish community in 1492.

Event: the Jewish aljama of Morella is listed among the Valencian-kingdom communities that disappeared after the 1391 repressions (so a community existed before 1391; no earlier date or size found; the page gives no Morella-specific figures). Coordinates checked: they belong to Morella (Castellon).
Event: Muniesa is listed among the Aragonese Jewish communities for which commissioners were appointed in 1492 to liquidate Jewish property (Motis Dolader).

Motis Dolader, "Poblacion, urbanismo y estructura politica de las aljamas judias aragonesas en la Edad Media", Hispania 56/3 no. 194 (1996) 885-944: "en 1492 tenemos constancia de nueve familias por las reuniones aljamales" (minimum; five heads of family attended in 1487). Households x5.

Coordinates correct (Murcia city). Event: Alfonso X (1252-84) assigns a separate quarter to the Jews of Murcia after the Castilian takeover (1243; reconquest by James I of Aragon 1265); late 13th c. each Jew paid 30 dinars yearly (Encyclopaedia Judaica).
Moses ibn Turiel of Castile held important administrative posts in Murcia in 1292; 1307 Isaac ibn Yaish, last Jew responsible for the kingdom Muslims (Encyclopaedia Judaica).
In 1307 jurisdiction over the Muslims of the kingdom of Murcia was entrusted to Don Isaac ibn Yaish, the last Jew to hold such a function.

Murcia juderia had a main synagogue and minor ones, an old cemetery near the Puerta Nueva, own butchery and oven (Martinez Carrillo 1993); she dates the acute decline of the aljama 1369-1492 and links it to the Manuel and Fajardo factions.

Toward the close of the 14th century, several Jewish tax farmers were active in the kingdom and in the town, among them Solomon ibn Lop, who settled in Majorca after 1378 and who was granted the special protection of the king of Aragon.

Event: 1391 persecutions in Spain; Murcia community survived (Encyclopaedia Judaica). Population: Torres Fontes (cited by Martinez Carrillo 1993) estimates about 1500 inhabitants in the juderia 1391-95 and 450 fewer from 1396 after the 1395-96 plague.
Valdeon estimate of about 1000 inhabitants of the Murcia juderia from the mid 14th century, as cited by Martinez Carrillo 1993 (basis not given there).
Encyclopaedia Judaica: late 14th and 15th centuries the community numbered some 2000 persons, many of them tax farmers (round figure without stated basis).
Martinez Carrillo (1993) hypothesis: about 700 Jews in Murcia in 1401, 900 in 1408 and 600 in 1411 (low point), always under 2000 in the early 15th century; no household count given.
Martinez Carrillo (1993) hypothesis: about 900 Jews in 1408 (see 1401 row).

Martinez Carrillo (1993): about 600 Jews in 1411, when the Jewish population of Murcia reached its lowest point (Vicente Ferrer preaching); she considers it unlikely the juderia held much more than 600 afterwards.

Event: attempted assault on the Murcia juderia in Feb 1413; 14 Mar 1414 Juan II protects the aljamas of Murcia and Cartagena against council pressure applying the ordinances of regent Catalina of Lancaster (Martinez Carrillo 1993; Ayaso 1997).
Throughout the 15th century, Jews of Murcia were often tax farmers, both in the kingdom of Murcia and in other towns near and distant. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)

Event: 1453 riot when townspeople demolished works by Rabbi Leon and Yucaf Abonafox on houses of the old mint being added to the juderia; further riots June 1460 and April 1461, Pedro Fajardo protecting Jews 1462 (Martinez Carrillo 1993). Aventuriel and Cohen families were prominent tax farmers.

Event: 1481 council orders closure of juderia side-gates facing the Christian quarter and doors on all new entrances, following the Cortes of Toledo 1480 (Martinez Carrillo 1993). 1485 Murcia aljama assessed 163930 maravedis for the Granada war castellanos tax, 83200 in 1489, 69610 in 1490 (Ladero Quesada via Ayaso 1997; tax amounts, not population).

J. Torres Fontes, "La juderia murciana en el siglo XV", Espacio, Tiempo y Forma, Serie III, Hist. Medieval 6 (1993) 177-228, pp. 220-221: a municipal levy of January 1481 at 30 maravedis per household assigned the aljama 5,000 maravedis (166 households); after the Jewish protest it was cut to 4,500, "lo que suponia asignarles un total de 150 vecinos, que ... resulta aceptable". Households x5 (the author also finds the factor 5 most acceptable).

J. Torres Fontes, "La juderia murciana en el siglo XV", Espacio, Tiempo y Forma, Serie III, Hist. Medieval 6 (1993) 177-228, pp. 220-221: "Resumiendo lo expuesto tenemos 150 vecinos o casas en 1481; 141 en 1484; 164-171 en 1488 y 143 en 1490". Households x5.
Samuel Abulafia received two years of royal protection in 1488 for services in the Granada war; 1490 Solomon b. Maimon Zalmati printed Hebrew books in Murcia (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

J. Torres Fontes, "La juderia murciana en el siglo XV", Espacio, Tiempo y Forma, Serie III, Hist. Medieval 6 (1993) 177-228, pp. 220-221: 164-171 Jewish households in 1488 (general padron of 1488: Jews and Moors together 204 households, split 164 and 20 by the proportion of taxable wealth); 171 Jews affected by the 1488 castellanos levy. Households x5 on 168; author: "Parece que el coeficiente 5 es el mas aceptable, lo que proporciona una poblacion total de la juderia en esta decada de 700 a 900 personas".
Conversos even used to come there in order to return to Judaism; one such case is mentioned in the La Guardia trial (1490).

J. Torres Fontes, "La juderia murciana en el siglo XV", Espacio, Tiempo y Forma, Serie III, Hist. Medieval 6 (1993) 177-228, pp. 220-221: 143 households paid in 1490 (47-96 split of the levy). Households x5.

Event: 1492 expulsion; Jews of the kingdom of Murcia left through Cartagena (Ayaso 1997, citing Torres Fontes); on 16 June 1492 the council still contracted meat supply with an Aventuriel (Martinez Carrillo 1993). A regional article claims about 150 families sailed 16 April 1492 but could not be fetched.

J. R. Ayaso Martinez, "Los judios en Cartagena en la Baja Edad Media", MEAH Hebreo 46 (1997) 137-160, note 26, quoting J. Torres Fontes (1993, p. 227): it is hard to count the Jews of Murcia who embarked at Cartagena in 1492, "aunque al aproximarnos al numero de familias que en estos anos se concentraban en la juderia, cabe deducir que podrian ser en torno a las 700 personas" (estimate by Torres Fontes, via Ayaso).

Event: Auto-da-fé at Murcia in 1562 (March 15; March 20). The Jewish Encyclopedia ('Auto da Fé') lists it among the autos 'in which it is positively known that Jews were concerned': "1562, March 15, Murcia / 1562, March 20, Murcia". Those tried were Judaizing conversos (crypto-Jews), not an open Jewish community. The LIST (p. 503, appendix list of auto-da-fés) gives 2 autos for 1562.

Event: auto-da-fé(s) at which Jews/Judaizers (New Christians tried as secret Jews) were involved, per JE's list of such autos (18th century): 1722, 1723, 1724, 1725, 1726; range 1722-1726. The list gives only date and city, no victim numbers. Book p. 325, ref 1700.1 (list entry).
Year rounded from a century-only statement. JE: "In the tenth century it had a prosperous Jewish community."

Following the 1076 incorporation of the city into Castile by Alfonso VI, an important Jewish community contributed to the rapid growth of the town

Event: Alfonso VII ratified the fuero including the Jewish provisions (blood-price equal to a knight or cleric); the charter later served as model for other localities (JVL). Jewish quarter near city wall and market in the south of town, synagogue remains found there.
Tax paid by the aljama in 1290: 24,106 maravedis (JE) or 30,318 maravedis (JVL, other source); a tax amount only, no population derived.
Event: during the civil war between Pedro I and Henry of Trastamara, Henry's soldiers attacked and massacred Jews of Nájera; the community suffered again in 1367 after Pedro's victory near Nájera.

The map gives no year for the town; Year of Data 1366 is the conventional year of the civil war. No online source naming this town was found.
The community suffered once more at the time of Peter's victory over Henry in 1367 near Nájera.

During the 15th century the position of the community in Nájera, as well as of the others in the kingdom, deteriorated, although at the beginning of the century some Jews still owned land and real estate in the old city. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)
Community taxes had fallen to 300 maravedis by 1474 (JE); decline through the 15th century. No details are known of its fate at the 1492 expulsion (JVL).
No details are known about the fate of the community at the time of the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492.
Event: Naval (lordship of Joan de Torrellas) is listed by Motis Dolader among the seigneurial places of Aragon with a Jewish community in 1492.

Sephardi communities inhabited Niebla during the Middle Ages. The city had a historic synagogue located in Real de Niebla street, whose frescoes point to it having been one of the most sumptuous synagogues in Andalusia.
According to tradition, an important mosque constructed by the Arabs was ceded to the Jewish community by King Alfonso X.
Following the reconquest of the city by Alfonso X the Wise in the mid-13th century, the site of a former important mosque was used as a Jewish Synagogue before later becoming a Christian church.

Coordinates correct (Ocaña, Toledo). Earliest documentary proof of Jews: Ferdinand IV ordered in 1296 that Ocaña residents pay their debts to the Jewish aljama. The aljama is absent from the 1290 Huete repartimiento because it paid taxes with Toledo.
Alfonso XI granted in 1313 to the master of Santiago, Diego Moniz, the tax the Ocaña Jews owed the crown (the town belonged to the Order of Santiago from 1182).
Aljama had a tax income (juro de heredad, 4,000 maravedis paid by Juan de Aponte) in 1386, the first clear sign of its economic standing.

Event: the aljama was sacked in the anti-Jewish riots of 1391 according to Solomon ibn Verga (Shebet Yehudah); Vinuales infers the community recovered and was strengthened by Jewish arrivals from harder-hit aljamas (1439 head tax almost 10,000 maravedis).
Event: Some of the Jews who were expelled from Andalusia in 1483 found refuge in Ocaña.

Peak of tax payments in 1485; 15th-century judería among the largest in Castile. In 1491 Ocaña with Yepes, Santa Cruz, La Guardia, Colmenar de Oreja, Lillo and Corral de Almaguer was the third highest payer of the servicio of castellanos de oro in Castile. Rabbi Isaac de Leon kept an academy there; Yehuda ibn Verga lived there 1487-1491. Judería around San Juan church (probably more than one synagogue, own butcher shop). Toledo Inquisition began trials of Ocaña conversos in 1485.
Among the refugees was Judah ibn Verga, one of the last Jewish tax-farmers, who lived in Ocaña from 1488 to 1491.

Event: Information is available on ten Inquisition trials held in Ocaña at the close of the 15th century and the beginning of the 16th; from this, close contact between the Jews of the town and the Conversos from the pre-Expulsion period can be inferred. (century-only date, round year 1490 used)
Population: Vinuales Ferreiro (1999) estimates about 1,500 Jews in Ocaña around 1492 ('se estima una poblacion judia ... en torno a las mil quinientas personas'), without naming a primary source.
Ocaña also attracted Conversos during the 16th and 17th centuries. (century-only date, round year 1550 used)

comment: Population/presence: Becker's footnote 4 (apparently after Leroy 1985, p. 17; footnote 4 is attached to the sentence 'some 3,000 individuals' in Navarre) gives 'some fifty in Olite, Los Arcos and Viana'. Read here as about 50 Jews in EACH of the three towns; the wording could also mean fifty in all three together (flagged for the owner). It is an estimate for the whole 13th-14th century period (the paper's period for Navarre's Jews), not for one year: Year of Data 1300 is the conventional midpoint. The Jewish Encyclopedia (Navarre article) separately lists Olite among the towns where Jews settled (presence only, no year, no number). Olite is not on the map yet (nearest marker Tafalla, 6 km). A Jewish community lived in the town during the Middle Ages.,https://kids.kiddle.co/Olmedo [UNVERIFIED: source URL not found among fetched pages]

Alfonso VI took Olmedo shortly before 1085; resettled and given a fuero in 1095 (no Jews named). Date of first Jewish settlement unknown (EJ); existing kehilot.csv year 1000 is unsupported. Coordinates checked: correct town (Valladolid province).
Jewish community grew significantly in the 13th century (EJ, c. 1200s); no information on the 14th century.
The community grew particularly during the 13th century. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)
No information is available on Olmedo Jewry throughout the 14th century. (century-only date, round year 1350 used)
Event: John II exempted the community from certain taxes and levies.
Event: battle of Olmedo (Henry IV vs infante Alfonso); community probably suffered, no details recorded.
Community taxes 500 maravedis in 1474 (EJ); amount only.

source: Castaño, "The Peninsula as a Borderless Space: Towards a Mobility 'Turn' in the Study of Fifteenth-Century Iberian Jewries", in: Jews and Christians in Medieval Europe: The Historiographical Legacy of Bernhard Blumenkranz, eds. Buc, Keil, Tolan (Brepols 2016), p. 327-328 n. 49
comment: Dispute over residence and taxes, 1485-1487: Jaco Levy and his family moved from Olmedo to Madrigal in late 1485 or early 1486; he kept some property in Olmedo and after almost a year and a half was still being assessed for tax there. He applied to the court of the chief judge of the Castilian aljamas, Abraham Seneor, who ruled in favour of Olmedo; he appealed to the royal corregidor, claiming the ruling lacked proper rabbinical advice, but his houses in Olmedo were confiscated and publicly auctioned by the local Jewish community; he then appealed to the royal court, which asked Seneor to review the case with the help of a halakhic authority (AGS, RGS, 27 March 1487, fol. 62, ed. Carrete Parrondo, El judaísmo español y la Inquisición, 1992, pp. 178-79 no. 12). Shows an organised Jewish community at Olmedo in 1485-1487. Existing Olmedo rows 1474, 1480, 1491, 1492: no conflict. No online source found. Population blank. Confidence medium.
Community taxes rose to 108,500 maravedis in 1491, probably through refugees from the south (EJ); amount only.
Event: expulsion; in March 1492 Luis de Alcalá and Fernán Núñez Coronel (Abraham Seneor) were authorized to collect debts owed by Christians to departed Jews.
A stone sign bearing the Hebrew date 4969 (1209) indicates that a wealthy Jew emigrated from Badresh to Olot and helped finance the synagogue.

es.wikipedia: the Jewish community of Oña built a synagogue in 1405, which passed to the local monastery after the 1492 expulsion.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Burriana): in 1278 Solomon Vidal, baile of La Plana, collected the rents of Burriana, Castellon and Onda; the communities of Burriana, Murviedro (Sagunto), Onda and Segorbe formed a single tax unit (collecta). es.wikipedia: Jews lived in a quarter around the Portal de Valencia and were expelled in 1492; the Plaza de la Sinagoga was the axis of the barrio.
Jewish nurses, most originally from Poland, were en route to a Belgian-run hospital in Ontinyent.

Coordinates checked: correct (Orihuela, Alicante province). First documented Jews: during the 1264 Mudejar revolt a Jew, Jacob Avendino, took refuge in Orihuela's fortress; soon after the Valencian Jew David Mascaran came to resettle the huerta under James I (Cabezuelo 2005-06).
Event: May 1296 James II regulates Jewish moneylending at four dineros per libra for the relief of the vecinos of Orihuela.

Early 14th century: the sources show a well-formed aljama in Orihuela (head of the governorate), assessed 6000 sueldos towards building/repairing the castrum Oriolet; in 1308 a Murcian Jew (Abbu) was received as settler by the royal bailiff Ferrer Descortell as part of a policy of attracting Jews (Cabezuelo).

Event: April 1312 James II asks the Jews of the Orihuela district for a 1000 sueldos subsidy; in 1311 Jews of Elche and Orihuela together paid 200 sueldos of questia (a fixed community tax; Cabezuelo says tax cannot be turned into population).

Accounts of 1316: Jews of Elche and Orihuela charged jointly 1050 sueldos, reduced to 800 (500 Orihuela, 300 Elche); 1321 the king addresses the aljamas of Elche and Orihuela; 1322 exemption from monedaje and permission to levy a sisa for the Sardinian expedition.
Event: 29 Aug 1329 royal order to prevent Christians living in the Orihuela judería, to avoid cohabitation; the governorate passes to the infante Fernando's lordship.

Orihuela was the most important of three Jewish communities in the infante Fernando's southern Valencian lordship: fixed tax 1100 sueldos (22 times Alicante's 50) in 1353 and 1356, plus 1500 sueldos for royal weddings in 1353 and 500 in 1356.

Event: during the Castilian war (War of the Two Pedros, 1356-66) Orihuela's Jews were obliged to give three sueldos per house as war aid and some lent money; after the war the Jewish quarters of Alicante, Elche and Orihuela were restored by royal and seigneurial favour (Cabezuelo). Year c. 1364, approximate.
Abraham ibn Bahya collected taxes in Orihuela and Elche 1381-1384 (Encyclopaedia Judaica); aljama accounts of 1384-85 record fines imposed by the aljama elders on its members.

Event: 1391 persecutions: Jews of Orihuela were baptized; Murcia's council demanded return of goods seized from its Jews in the Orihuela governorate; unlike many Crown of Aragon towns the main sources describe flight or conversion (Torres Fontes 1981: mass conversion of Orihuela's Jews).

About 1400 the converso Remir Alvarez denounced to the Orihuela council that Murcian Jews, sorry at the mass conversion of Orihuela's Jews, sent agents to pervert the converts (Torres Fontes). No Jewish population figure given by any fetched source for Orihuela.

Motis Dolader, "Poblacion, urbanismo y estructura politica de las aljamas judias aragonesas en la Edad Media", Hispania 56/3 no. 194 (1996) 885-944, p. 896 (footnote): "Orihuela acredita un maximo de 38 casas en el siglo xv" (J. Hinojosa Montalvo, En torno a los judios valencianos, 1990, p. 931; maximum of Jewish houses in the 15th century, year 1450 conventional). Households x5.
The movement led by Inés, "the Maiden of Herrera," in 1500 found adherents among the Conversos in Orihuela.

Stable Jewish community in Oviedo from the 13th century (Fernando III; round year 1250); Jews required to live inside the old walls; Huerto de los Judíos seized in 1492
Two letters of 1269 (cited by Juan Uria) give a tax roll of Oviedo with 900 households of which 40-50 were Jewish, i.e. about 200 persons (population as stated in the article).

Event: the municipal ordinances of 1274 confined the Jews to the Socastillo quarter (the Judería), fining those residing elsewhere 100 marbadas; the norm limited the community to about 500 persons and 50 dwellings; in 1286 Sancho IV ended the community's separate jurisdiction.

First documented Jews in Puigcerdà (1243); coordinates are correct (Puigcerdà, Cerdanya). Jaume I's 13th-c. privileges (market, fairs) favoured an aljama; Jews also came from Carcassonne, Toulouse and Nîmes fleeing French credit restrictions of 1246-1254.

Jews established in Puigcerdà by the mid-13th century and belonging to the Perpignan collecta (Pere Vidal study of the Jews of Roussillon and Cerdanya); Jews also paid tolls under the Puigcerdà lleuda of 1288.

Event: municipal ordinance of 1295 forbids gambling during Jewish festivals, especially at weddings, after disputes among Jews and with Christians. Jews then lived mixed with Christians in the Vila Vella.

Jewish occupations: cloth merchants, bookbinders, leatherworkers, dyers, gold-thread embroiderers, clockmakers and moneylenders (several women lenders); never more than about 10% of the local population (a share only, no count; Population blank). Lending reached Cerdanya, Roussillon, Languedoc, Garrotxa and Berguedà.

Jewish quarter (call) in the Vila Nova between plaça del Call and carrer de Sant Agustí; Franciscan convent built 1320-1333 over part of it (a fragment excavated). The call had a synagogue and school, hospital and charity house, mikveh near the lake and at Rigolisa; first cemetery in the 13th century at La Sèquia.

A town gate is first mentioned as 'del call dels jueus' c. 1325; in 1342 the Consolat regulated bringing water to the call (rec de Sant Agustí). A school or synagogue is mentioned in the second half of the 14th century. The community had a procurador dels jueus.
Event: Black Death year 1348: many Jews of Puigcerdà, frightened and threatened, left the town and took refuge in Llívia. The plague required a second cemetery (now within La Guingueta d'Ix).
In 1360 most royal revenues of Cerdanya were farmed to Jews of Puigcerdà; in 1370 Vidal Bonsenyor, Jew of Puigcerdà, leased the royal rent of Angostrina (Pere Vidal).

Event: persecution of the Jews in 1391; they sought refuge in the castle of Llívia (Enciclopèdia Catalana). Another source has no news of the 1391 riots but notes a fall in notarial protocols about Jews, perhaps because many left or converted.

Event: Roussillon and Cerdanya were French from 1462 to 1493, so the 1492 expulsion edict did not apply; Ferdinand recovered both counties in 1493 and applied the order of conversion or expulsion, ending the community.
On November 30, 1942, a Jewish refugee family of four (the author, his mother, sister Anna, and brother Willy) arrived at a tavern in Puigcerdà.

By the early 14th century, Sagunto (still known as Morvedre) had a growing Jewish population, resulting in the establishment of a Jewish cemetery under the castle walls in 1328.

Event: The Jewish quarter of Murviedro is one of the best preserved in Spain, probably because it did not suffer any attack in 1391.

In 1402 Queen Doña María authorized the Murviedro community to establish several societies for catering to communal needs: the Bikkur ?olim society, to care for the sick; a burial society; and a Talmud Torah society.
In 1416 Alfonso V dealt with the division of property of deceased Jews between the heirs who had remained Jews and those who had been converted.

In 1171, the superior gave the Jews of Sahagún land for a cemetery situated in a district of vines outside the town.
In the 13th century Sahagún was one of the thriving communities in the north. (century-only date, round year 1250 used)

Alfonso X on 12 April 1255 equates Sahagún's Jews with those of Carrión: Jewish judges appointed by the rabbis of Burgos and sworn before the abbot; Jews pay the abbot 18 dineros plus up to 100 maravedís a year.

Among other matters, the amount of ransom for the killing of a Jew was fixed at a total of 500 solidos payable to the head of the monastery, and in 1268 the king further prescribed a special oath for the Jews of Sahagún.
Tax: in 1290 the community paid a royal tax of 28,653 maravedís (Jewish Encyclopedia); a tax sum, so Population blank.

Few details are known about the Jews of Sahagún during the 14th century, but at its close it contained 30 heads of families occupied in agriculture and work for the monastery, around which the life of the town was concentrated. (century-only date, round year 1350 used)

Event: in 1399 a Burgos priest, Juan Martínez do Balves, tried to baptize the Jews forcibly and fled to the monastery after being attacked; Benedict XIII ruled for the abbot on 30 Aug 1403. In 1401 the king ordered the abbot to stop fining and jailing Jews, who said many had left the town.

Event: On Aug. 15, 1401 Henry III forbade the abbot to molest the Jews with fines or imprisonment (penalty 10,000 maravedis) after Jews had left the city because of his arbitrary procedure; the abbot disobeyed and imprisoned R. Abraham Obadiah, Maestro Yuce and others.
Despite this, Sahagún did not escape the impoverishment which befell the communities of Castile toward the middle of the 15th century. (century-only date, round year 1450 used)

Decline: in 1474 the taxes of Sahagún combined with those of the Jews of Monesterio totalled only 2,500 maravedís (Jewish Encyclopedia); a tax sum, Population blank. The community was insignificant before the 1492 expulsion.
The last information available about the Jews of Sahagún dates from June 7, 1492, a few weeks after the edict of expulsion.

Event: In 1335 the council forbade Christians to receive medical aid from Jew or Moor; it was forbidden for Jewish or Moorish wet nurses to tend Christian children; Christians were forbidden to serve in Jewish houses; Jews and Moors were forbidden to rent houses in the neighborhood of the Christian churches and cemeteries.

Four years later (1339) Alfonso xi confirmed the privilege of the Jews of the town, dispensing them from appearing before Christian judges, lay or ecclesiastic, in matters concerning the collection of debts owed them by Christians, though, in principle, they had to be judged by Christian judges in mixed lawsuits.
From the 14th century several resolutions of the town council regarding the affairs of its Jews are known. (century-only date, round year 1350 used)
In 1389 the Jews requested permission to erect a new synagogue, as one of their synagogues had been confiscated.
Event: Jews of Salamanca were not spared during the persecutions of 1391.
Jewish community expelled in 1492
Event: In 1412 Vicente Ferrer preached in Salamanca aiming at conversion of the Jews; converts called themselves Vicentinos; the large synagogue was turned into the church Vera Cruz.

He succeeded in persuading many to convert, and one of the synagogues was turned into a school named "The True Cross." In 1413 Juan ii conferred upon the University of Salamanca the bet midrash with its courts and all that belonged to it, most of the community having left Judaism by then.
Rabbi Menahem ben Hayyim ha-Aruk (Longo) lived in Salamanca (d. 1425); also Talmudist Moses ben Benjamin and his son Isaac.
Event: Ritual-murder accusation against the Jews of Salamanca in 1456; innocence established after royal investigation.
The Jews of Salamanca, "so numerous", together with those of Ciudad-Rodrigo paid 7,800 maravedis in taxes for the year 1474 (combined tax; not a population figure).

The origins of the Jewish community in Sangüesa lie in the 12th century, primarily along St. James' Way and in the Ebro valley.

Abraham de Tonneins, a Jew from France, enters Sangüesa; the pecha on his family was 40 marks of silver for four years from Christmas 1317, later five libras a year. About 30 French families (a quarter of those displaced to Navarre after 1328) were sheltered at Sangüesa.

Eleven local Jews were arrested, among them the surgeon Balavigny and a woman Belieta; Balavigny was questioned on 15 and 19 Sept and burned in early Oct 1348 (Kelly). Winkler adds: Balavigny said he had the poison from Rabbi Jacob of Chambery; the Jew Mussus allegedly put poison in a well at Chillon (a substance was found there); other accused named Iconetus, Mamson and Aquetus (at least three accused were called Aquetus); the castellan sent the interrogation record to Strasbourg. Archaeological records indicate a Jewish community existed in the city in the period immediately preceding the fall of the Second Temple in 70 CE.

דורה-אירופוס. Beneath the synagogue completed c. 244-245 CE the excavators found the remains of an earlier, smaller and more modest synagogue, dated by the Encyclopaedia Judaica to the last quarter of the 2nd century CE (c. 175-200; 190 is the mid-point). Adds an earlier phase to the existing 244/245/256 rows. EJ also reads the relative sizes of the temples and the synagogue as showing that the Jews were a small minority of the city and lived as an isolated group, about 400 km north of Nehardea.
The last phase of the Dura-Europos synagogue is dated by an Aramaic inscription to 244 CE; the Jewish community of Dura long preceded the synagogue. Town destroyed 256-257.

Greek tile inscription names Samuel son of Yedaya as founder and 'elder of the Jews', dated AD 245; the tabernacle mural is dated c. 245-256. The 58 surviving scenes are about 60 per cent of the original; no population figure.

Jewish Virtual Library: a Jewish community documented from the first century CE with friendly relations to Agrippa I and II, and the conversion may have encouraged proselytes; this is a royal conversion plus a general statement, not a city count. Hebrew-language sources (Hamichlol) mention a family of converts (Bar Ashthor) in Homs in the Yerushalmi (later, rabbinic period). Population: Arab (Emesene) city with a small Jewish element; no Jewish population estimate found. Earlier periods not covered by a fetched page. Population blank. In the 10th century BCE rulers of the Aramean kingdom of Bit Bahiani took their seat at Tell Halaf re-founded as Guzana (Wikipedia; Hebrew Wikipedia: King Kapara founded the city and built the Western Palace in the 10th-9th c.). Excavated by von Oppenheim 1911-1913 and 1929. People: Arameans. No population estimate.

Iron Age IIB (-900 to -722). Capital of Aramean Bit Bahiani under Kapara (Kapara 9th century monumental architecture per Hebrew Wikipedia; encyclopedia.com: Gozan on the Habor); reduced to an Assyrian province in 808 BCE, organized province by 793 BCE. People: Arameans then Assyrian administration. No population estimate.

Carthage was refounded by Julius Caesar as Colonia Junonia in 44 BCE and became capital of the province of Africa (Livius), so it was a Roman colonial city in this period. Jewish evidence: none for before 70 CE in the fetched pages. The Jewish Virtual Library says there is no evidence of Jewish settlement in the Punic period (before 146 BCE) and that substantial Jewish presence is documented only from the Roman Empire onward and grew after the disasters of 70 and 132-135 CE in Israel and 115-117 in Egypt; Wikipedia gives the 2nd century CE as the earliest documented evidence. Later evidence (outside this period): Gammarth necropolis (Delattre; early 3rd c. CE per Wikipedia; the Jewish Encyclopedia gives about 200 tombs with menorah and Hebrew inscription fragments but no date) and Tertullian's late 2nd c. remarks on Jewish fasting and veiling (TheTorah). Hypotheses of a Jewish presence in Punic Carthage (Josephus-based Djerba tradition; Yosippon's claim that Titus settled about 50000 Jews in North Africa, a regional figure and not a city population) rest on late tradition. Population blank: no estimate for Jews of Carthage in this period was found. Persian and Hellenistic periods: Punic Carthage was settled but no Jews are attested, so no rows; Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE and not refounded until 44 BCE. Identification not in doubt. Estimate: Carl Kraeling (as reported by the Antiochepedia blog) put the Jewish population at about 60000 at its peak (10-15 percent of the city); the date of the peak is not stated by the source (it places the city at its height in the first century CE) so the period assignment is uncertain. Other figures in Notes only: Josephus-based 20000-40000 (Keener; no specific scholar named). Brooten 2000 'The Jews of Ancient Antioch' is the key study (cited by Hamichlol; not read). Mixed Greek and Roman city with a large Jewish community. Jewish quarters not excavated (blog).

At the outbreak of the war the Antiochians spared the Jews who lived among them (Josephus War 2.479: Antioch, Sidon and Apamea 'spared those that dwelt with them'; the Jewish Encyclopedia cites B.J. ii.18 section 5). Josephus suggests the reason was that the Jews' own number was so great.

After the fall of Jerusalem the Antiochians repeatedly asked Titus to expel the Jews and destroy their bronze tablets of privileges; Titus refused, saying their homeland was destroyed and no other place would receive them (War 7.96-111), and the Jews kept their privileges. Earlier in the same book a Jew named Antiochus, son of the Jewish chief, denounced his people for plotting arson (War 7.41-62). Year c. 70-71: the fetched pages give no exact year (the Jewish Virtual Library says 66-70 CE).

Abba Judah of Antioch, a 2nd-century CE scholar, supported Palestinian scholars, many of whom visited Antioch (Jewish Virtual Library, Encyclopaedia Judaica text). Century-only date, conventional year 150.

The first Synod of Antioch forbade Christians to celebrate Easter on the day the Jews observed Passover (Jewish Encyclopedia and Jewish Virtual Library: 341). Church legislation held at Antioch; shows contact with a Jewish community, not a population.

John Chrysostom delivered six sermons (Jewish Encyclopedia) against the Jews of Antioch c. 366-387; Christians were attending synagogue services and using Jewish courts and oaths. The sources give only the range c. 366-387; 376 is its mid-year (conventional). The sermons are usually dated 386-387, which is not stated on the fetched pages.
Event: Antiochians deprived the Jews of their synagogue (destroyed after a Purim accusation); Theodosius II ordered it restored.
Event: anti-Jewish riots; Greens faction massacred local Jews (Malalas; 490 or 491), Asabiniani synagogue destroyed in one tradition.

Event: In 507 the Greens (a circus faction) led by the charioteer Porphyrius attacked a synagogue in Daphne, the suburb of Antioch, and many Jews were slaughtered (Wikipedia on Porphyrius the Charioteer; the underlying source is the chronicler Malalas). No victim count is given. The LIST (p. 97, ref 507.1) adds that the synagogue was plundered and burned and the site turned into a martyrium; that detail is not on the Wikipedia page. Marker coordinates are Antioch's; Daphne (Harbiye) lies about 9 km south. The map already has the earlier Antioch riot under Zeno (490); see conflicts file for the 489/490/491 dating.
Event: under Phocas Jews rebelled and killed Patriarch Anastasius; revolt suppressed and many Jews killed or exiled (Jewish Encyclopedia dates it 610). EJ: little further information afterwards.

Event: under Phocas an attempt to force the Jews of Antioch to be baptized led to a revolt in which Patriarch Anastasius was killed; governor Bonosus suppressed it, killing many Jews and expelling the rest (Jewish Encyclopedia, citing Malalas, Theophanes and the Chronicon Paschale: 610). The Jewish Virtual Library dates the same revolt 608 (already on the map): two dates for one event.

Benjamin of Tudela (c. 1165-71) found a handful of Jews engaged in glassmaking: the Gutenberg text says 'Ten Jews dwell here' (heads R. Mordecai, R. Chayim, R. Samuel) while Jewish Encyclopedia and EJ say ten families; unit unclear so Population left blank.

BCE; Jewish Encyclopedia names Apamea and Laodicea among the settlements; Jewish Virtual Library says Jewish community in Phrygia by end of 3rd c. BCE). Hasmonean (-167 to -63): settled Hellenistic city passing to Roman rule in the 2nd c. BCE (Attalid then Roman Asia; Wikipedia says Strabo ranks it next to Ephesus as a trade centre). Artichaeology says the Jewish community dated back to the founding; no source fetched gives a dated Hasmonean-period datum or number for Apamea's Jews specifically so continuity is inferred from that statement and the 62 BCE evidence. Population blank.

Early Roman / Herodian (-63 to 70): Cicero Pro Flacco 28 (delivered 59 BCE) reports about a hundredweight (c. 100 pounds / c. 45 kg) of gold seized at Apamea under Flaccus' edict in 62 BCE and weighed out in the forum; the context is the Jewish Temple tax (Jewish Virtual Library: sums gathered in Apamea and Laodicea for the Temple were confiscated 62-61 BCE; Jewish Encyclopedia: nearly 100 pounds). This shows a sizeable and wealthy Jewish community but no source fetched gives a head-count estimate; Population blank. City was Greek/Phrygian with Italian and Jewish merchants (mixed). Noah's-ark coins are 3rd c. CE (Severus to Trebonianus Gallus) so outside the period. Trebilco 1991 Jewish Communities in Asia Minor ch. 4 covers Apamea but only the abstract was readable (no estimate seen).
Under Flaccus about 45 kg of gold of Jewish Temple money was confiscated at Apamea (62 BC per Wikipedia); Antiochus the Great transplanted Jews there (Josephus, no year given).
After 200 CE a couple built a heroon whose inscription invokes the 'Laws of the Jews' in a curse against tomb reuse (c. 200 round year); Talmud mentions Apamea (probably this city).

Apamea issued coins showing Noah's ark under Septimius Severus (c. 202-205), long linked to a Jewish community; the Leu catalogue cautions the Noah imagery may reflect Christian rather than Jewish tradition and notes only one Jewish inscription is known from the necropolis.

Long Greek inscription (c. 210 CE per Tannenbaum; other scholars date it 4th-5th c.) lists 126 donors incl. 54 God-fearers (theosebeis) and a Jewish association; the page does not give an exact count of Jews. First documented Jewish presence at the site.

Seats in the Odeon (bouleuterion) reserved for 'the place of the Hebrews' and 'the Blues of the elder Hebrews' (IAph 2.6, 2.8, 2.18). Harland dates the seating inscriptions II-VI CE (basis not stated), so year 400 is only a round year inside a very wide range.

Indirect: the proconsul Publius Servilius Galba held a court at Tralles where a Milesian complained about Jewish Sabbath observance and ruled the Jews should not be prevented from following their customs (Josephus, Ant. 14.244-246), and the Trallians objected to Jewish rights before Rabirius (Ant. 14.242). Josephus does not say how many Jews lived at Tralles; Trebilco dates the Miletus document 46-44 BCE and concludes a Jewish community existed there.

Event: 13th-century Mongol conquests destroyed the town and impoverished the Jewish community (century round year).

The first Jew to arrive in the Buffalo area was Captain Mordechai Myers, assigned to the region during the War of 1812.
Mordechai Manuel Noah bought Grand Island just north of Buffalo and established it as 'Ararat,' a refuge for the Jewish people.
Mordecai Manuel Noah tried to launch a homeland for Jews called 'Ararat' on Grand Island.
After 1830, Polish Jewish peddlers supplied goods on the Niagara Frontier and prospered.
L. H. Flersheim, an immigrant from Frankfurt-am-Main, became the first Jew to settle in the city of Buffalo.
The town's first retail clothing store was opened in the 1840s by a nephew of Mordechai Noah.
The city's first synagogue, Congregation Beth El, was established by Polish and German Jews.
The first Jewish congregation in Buffalo was founded at a meeting of twelve men on May 9, 1847; they purchased a five-acre plot for a cemetery.
In June 1848, the congregation became known as Synagogue Beth El (or House of God). Polish Jews founded this first congregation.
In January 1849, the Jewish congregation voted to purchase a lot on Pearl Street to remodel into a synagogue.
Early German Jewish immigrants settled on the West Side in the mid-1800s.
Differences led the German Jews to form their own congregation, Beth Zion.
The Pearl Street synagogue building was dedicated on July 22, 1850. Well-educated German Jewish immigrants also organized an Orthodox congregation, Beth Zion.
Most of the Jewish settlers before 1860 worked in the clothing business.
Temple Beth Zion Pine Hill Cemetery was founded in the 1860s.
Nearly all the Polish families settling in Buffalo before 1865 were Jewish. In January 1865, a fire damaged the Synagogue Beth El building.
By 1870, commercial activity had encroached upon Synagogue Beth El, prompting a search for a new location.
Synagogue Beth El dedicated their second building on Elm Street on August 15, 1874.
A wave of Jewish immigration from the Russian Empire began in about 1880, shifting the center of Jewish life to the East Side.
In 1880, the first English sermon was preached at Synagogue Beth El.
By 1890, the Jewish population numbered 1,500.
Temple Beth Zion was erected.
By 1900, there were about twelve Orthodox synagogues in the area, as well as a Jewish library and a community house.
In 1906, under the leadership of Charles Polakoff, the search for a new synagogue location commenced.

City's first Jewish cemetery established 1852; B'nai Jeshurun organized as the first (Orthodox) congregation in 1851 per the Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Nineteen families split from B'nai Jeshurun to form the Reform congregation B'nai Israel (now Temple Israel) - a congregational subset (~95 persons if x5), not the Jewish population. Temple Israel's own history dates the Reform congregation's organization to spring 1868.
The first Agudas Achim minyan was held in a home on East Cherry Street in 1881; Agudas Achim is the oldest traditional congregation in central Ohio. Presence of an organized community.
Agudas Achim incorporated as an Orthodox congregation in 1889; Beth Jacob organized 1897 and Tifereth Israel (Hungarian immigrants) 1901 per the Encyclopaedia Judaica. Presence; no count.

Wikipedia states the city's first Jewish cemetery was established in 1854; this is contradicted by the Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia (which date the first organized institutions to 1870-1872), so treat as unverified. Presence only; no count.
Alex Simon owned a store in Dallas by 1858 before moving to Brenham in 1863; earliest named Jewish resident in the Encyclopedia of Southern Jewish Communities. Presence only (single individual).
Earliest Jewish settlement began in 1870 with the arrival of about 15 families, mostly retail merchants. Estimate based on families (15 x 5).
Moses Ullmann and Dr. E. M. Tillman took up residence in February 1871 and are described as the first Jewish settlers; Ullmann later moved to Galveston. Presence only (two individuals).
On July 1, 1872, 11 Jewish men including Alexander Sanger founded the Hebrew Benevolent Association, the community's first organization (founders only; not a population count).
Estimated 60 to 70 Jews in Dallas by 1872 (midpoint 65 used). Hebrew Benevolent Association founded the same year.
Congregation Emanu-El (Reform) founded in 1874 (first temple dedicated 1876 per the Jewish Encyclopedia; Wikipedia dates the first congregation to 1873). Organized community; no count in this source.
Shearith Israel, an Orthodox congregation, established in 1884 (12 founders per Hadassah; synagogue dedicated 1894 per Jewish Encyclopedia). Second organized congregation; no population count.
Tiferet Israel (Orthodox) founded in 1890 by eleven Orthodox Jews; 35 members in 1900 (organizational subset only).
