Simon Gabert, a German-born Jew, arrived in Fort Worth, marking the city's first Jewish settler.
Isadore Carb moved to Fort Worth.
"When newspaper editor Charles Wessolowsky visited Fort Worth in 1879, he found about 100 Jews, all of whom he claimed “are industrious, hardworking and energetic people."
Isaac Dahlman, an early Jewish entrepreneur, lived in Fort Worth.
A small Orthodox synagogue, Ahavath Sholom, was in existence by this year.
Beth-El, a Reform congregation, was chartered by 43 men in the fall.
Fort Worth Jews convened a mass meeting at Ahavath Sholom to protest the Kishinev massacres and collected funds for the Industrial Removal Office.
U. M. Simon was appointed as the local IRO liaison.
The Jewish population was estimated to be roughly between 500 and 800 people.
Paul Fisher (Fishel) Herman, son of Max Herman and Sarah Dricher, was born in Fort Worth.
Between 1903 and 1915, 72 IRO immigrant families (~360 individuals, estimate based on families) had been relocated to Fort Worth.

Event: blood libel. Four-year-old Barbara Griffiths went missing on 22 September 1928 (book dates the entry 23 September), two days before Yom Kippur; after a search by townspeople and state police a rumour spread that the town's Jews had kidnapped and killed her for a religious ritual. The state police questioned a Jewish resident the next day and then tried to question Rabbi Berel Brennglass, who told police and mayor they should be ashamed; the mayor may have led a boycott of Jewish-owned businesses. The girl was found unharmed in the woods about a mile from home (she had slept in the forest). The American Jewish Committee and Congress denounced the town's leaders, and the mayor and state police apologised. The article gives no figure for the town's Jewish population (the map already has 102 in 1927).

Orthodox group 'Sons of Israel' began gathering for daily services in Providence (origin of Temple Beth-El).

comment: The men's prayer hall of the Great Suburb Synagogue (Boznicza Street 16) was completed in 1632, the women's gallery in 1635; for many years it was the only masonry building in the Krakow Suburb and served as a refuge in sieges and disturbances (Piluk lists 1664). en.wikipedia: destroyed by fire in 1648, burnt by the Nazis on 14 August 1941. comment: Event: siege of Lviv by the Cossacks of Bohdan Khmelnytsky. The volume dates the attack 6 October 1648: to keep the enemy out of the centre the defenders shifted the main blow to the Krakow suburb and set it on fire, burning the Jewish suburb and its synagogue; Khmelnytsky demanded that Lviv hand over its Jews, the town refused (Encyclopaedia Judaica gives the same), and the Cossacks withdrew for a large ransom, a considerable part paid by the Jews (Jewish Encyclopedia, which says September 1648). Afterwards the suburb and city Jewish communities gradually merged (two kahals united in the 18th century). The map's 1648 row is only a population entry.

comment: Event: ritual-murder accusation against 15 Jews of Jampol (Yampil) in Volhynia in 1756 (Passover); the first investigation, by the Vilnius castellan M. K. Radziwiłł, found the body had been mutilated only after death and the Jews were acquitted, but on the order of the bishop of Łuck F. A. Kobielski the trial was reopened and confessions were obtained by torture. In 1758 one of the accused, Jakub Selek, escaped and was sent by the Council of Four Lands to Rome, where Cardinal Ganganelli (later Pope Clement XIV) reported against the ritual-murder charge. Online (fetched): "W 1756 w Jampolu oskarżono 15 Żydów o dokonanie morderstwa w celach rytualnych"; the Jewish Encyclopedia list has "1756 (Passover) Jampol, Poland". Guldon: "Po procesie o mord rytualny w Jampolu na Wołyniu Sejm Czterech Ziem wysłał w 1758 r. swego przedstawiciela do Stolicy Apostolskiej". Location: Volhynia places it at Yampil in Shepetivka district (the bishop of Łuck ruled Volhynia), not at the Podolian Yampil (Vinnytsia oblast) where the map currently holds a 1756 blood-libel row - see conflicts file. Confidence high for the event, medium for the location.

comment: Event: coin-clipping persecution of 1278-79. In November 1278 the Jews of England were seized overnight on charges of coin clipping and many were hanged; the Crown then had the chattels and property of condemned and sequestrated Jews collected and sold (thesis, PDF pp. 139-141; the persecution ran 1278-79 and the Year of Data is its start). Bedford is named in the account of money raised by the sale of ex-Jewish property (PRO C 47/9/50; thesis PDF p. 140). Online, the Encyclopaedia Judaica Bedford article says that three Jews were hanged for coin clipping in 1278 and that by 1290 the community seems to have been almost extinct. The map's Bedford rows have no entry for 1278-79. Population blank (victims, not a count).

comment: Event: Abraham of Berkhamsted, a wealthy Jewish financier who lived and had property at Berkhamsted and Wallingford and was 'granted' to Richard of Cornwall, was arrested in the 1250s and released on condition that he forfeit his chattels and keep away from the king for a year (Strickland p. 177, citing Langmuir 1972, p. 463). Matthew Paris (Chronica majora, entry for 1250; Luard ed. vol. 5, pp. 114-15) tells instead that Abraham defiled a statue of the Virgin and made his wife Floria do the same, and killed her when she repented. Online: medievalists.net ('Mary and the Jews in Anglo-Norman Monastic Culture') summarises the 1250 entry (Earl Richard of Cornwall intervened to save him from the gallows) and sees a kernel of truth; Patrick Comerford's blog adds that he was imprisoned in the Tower in 1250, lost his chattels and that Richard secured his release for a fine of 700 marks. The existing Berkhamsted 1250 row only says that Abraham lived in the town. Online year 1250 used (Strickland: 1250s). No population stated.

comment: Presence (a Jewish financier of Berkhamsted in 1255): a list of the debts owed to Abraham de Berkhamsted was drawn up in 1255 (Calendar of Close Rolls 1254-56 pp. 170-172, cited in Mundill's note 8); P. Elman used it in 1936, with the Cambridgeshire archa lists of 1240, 1262 and 1290, as a sample of Jewish debtors, describing Abraham as a man 'who had carried out his business all over the country' (Elman's words as quoted by Mundill, who spells the name Berkhamstead). Number of debts not given. Online: Patrick Comerford's blog says that in January 1255 Abraham was granted to Richard (of Cornwall), allowed to lend 'in the king's land like the king's demesne Jews' and exempted from tallage; the blog does not mention the debt list. The map already has a 1250 row for the same banker (a wealthy Jewish banker named Abraham of Berkhamsted lived in the town) and the atlas's 1242 expulsion. [confidence: medium]

R., The Jews in England 1272-1290 (PhD thesis, St Andrews 1987/88), pp. 230-232
comment: Presence: the 'Canterbury Treaty' (a Latin starrum) of autumn 1266. The Jewish community of Canterbury swore, through 17 signatories, that no Jew of any other town than Canterbury should live in the town (meaning liars, improper persons and slanderers); anyone who came by the king's writ would be disqualified at the community's expense, the sum to be set by Salle son of Jose, Abraham son of Leo and Vives of Winchester (Vives' seal is attached but his name is not among the 17 signatures). Samson 'presbiter' (le chapeleyn), the community's rabbi, appears for the first time. L. Rabinowitz called it probably the only extant document giving the formula of the communal ban on settlement by strangers (the herem, as Mundill calls it) known from France, Germany, Italy and eastern Europe; Adler called it a treaty of self-defence against an influx of refugees from other Jewries hit by the troubles of the early 1260s, Cohn-Sherbok an attempt to clean up the image of Jewish moneylending; there is no evidence that it was ever applied (Mundill, PDF pp. 230-232). It was signed two years after the sack of the Jewry in 1264. POPULATION 300 is Adler's ESTIMATE for the Canterbury Jewry in the period 1240-1266, derived from the records naming about 50 men and 8 women resident in those years, with their families ('about 300 souls'); it is not a count. Confidence: high for the treaty, medium for the population figure. [Source detail: (L. Rabinowitz, 'The Origin of the Canterbury Treaty of 1266', Jewish Historical Society of England, pp. 77-79)]

comment: Event: in 1274 the Crown vigorously enforced its claim to houses that had passed from Jews to Christians. The king sued Solomon de Campis and Christiana his wife for a house claimed through the trespass of Isaac son of Benedict and another through the death and trespass of Pictavin son of Isaac; the Priory of Holy Trinity for a house escheated on the death of Master Aaron; and three Canterbury citizens (William Talebot, Master Omer the clerk, Daniel le Draper) for houses of Isaac son of Salle, Deubeney of Canterbury and Josce of Kent. The defendants kept the houses only after paying fines, and Roger de Kinton, sergeant of the Exchequer of the Jews, was ordered to take inquests on all houses 'at any time in the hands of Jews and thereafter alienated' (Mundill, PDF pp. 237-238, fn 70-74 = Richardson PREJ 2 pp. 201-301). The Statute of the Jewry (1275) then forbade Jews to alienate houses without royal licence. Adler (p. 46) dates a similar seizure of the Canterbury houses of Jose and Isaac, sons of Salle, to 1275 (a different case). Shows Jewish-owned houses and the Crown's pressure on them before the Statute. Population blank. The 1274 suits themselves have no online page (Adler gives only the 1275 case); confidence: medium.

comment: Event: in 1278 Edward I ordered the arrest of all the Jews of England on charges of clipping the coin; the Jews of Canterbury were confined in the Castle (ruins near the Dane John, a few minutes' walk from the Jewry in St Mary Bredman) (Adler p. 53). Mundill (PDF pp. 230, 239): the royal escheators confiscated a further GBP 440 of movables from the Jews of Kent after the same allegations. comment: Event: after the expulsion of the Jews of England in 1290 the Crown surveyed the immovable property of the Canterbury Jewry (the 'Valor' of Jewish houses, PRO E 101/249/30 and BL Lansdowne MS 826). It consisted of the synagogue with a plot of land, houses in the High Street, Jewry Lane and All Saints Lane, and plots. Mundill (PDF pp. 237, 239-240): the best three properties were Elias of London's stone house with a solar (30s a year), Leo son of Elias's house (25s) and a house shared by Cok Hagin and Aaron son of Vives (40s); then Moses le Petyt (two properties, stone one 13s 4d), Joye widow of Vives of Winchester (two, 13s 4d and 16s 8d) and Sarra la Bele (15s); the synagogue with a plot and Abba de Doggestrete's house (6s 8d each); and small items (Sara la Petite 3s, Isaac Top 2s, a community plot of 4 by 15 feet 6d, Samson le Chapelyn 1s, Malkini 3d). Mundill thinks the Jews held less property than before 1275 because Christians had acquired the houses of dead Jews. Adler (pp. 55-57): synagogue with plot 66 by 15 feet, fifteen houses or parts of houses and three other plots. Differences between the two sources (synagogue value, number of houses) are in the conflicts file. Property of the community, not population: Population blank. Confidence: high for the survey, medium for the figures.

First documented Jews: c. 1181 a Jew (Piers Deulesaut / Delesalt) paid a fine (10 marks per Jewish Encyclopedia and Adler; one mark per Fonceca) for the king to take his bonds into custody. Fonceca notes Jews may have lived there earlier. Exeter was the most westerly Jewish community in England.

In 1188 an application (fine of one mark) was made for pleas before a Beth Din, suggesting an established community of several families (Adler; Fonceca). Adler also cites a 1177 law allowing a cemetery outside the city walls; Exeter Memories only dates the burial liberty to the reign of Henry II; the medieval cemetery site is lost.

Amiot was the only Exeter Jew named in the Northampton Donum (paid 1 pound 3s 3d towards the 5,000-mark levy). Exeter later became the seat of an archa with two Christian and two Jewish chirographers.

The Sheriff of Devon was expressly instructed to protect the Exeter Jews in 1218 (Fonceca); no massacre in Exeter is recorded in 1189-90 (Adler: Exeter apparently escaped). Deulecresse Episcopus appointed bailiff of the Jewry in 1218 (Adler).
Tax contributions: fifteen Exeter contributors gave 78 pounds 10s 6d in 1223 (Adler); in 1241 four Exeter delegates attended the Worcester assembly. Contributors, not a population count.

Estimate by Lipman: 'other communities like Exeter would probably have been within the 50 to 100 range'. Population = midpoint of 50-100. No date given; Year 1250 is a conventional mid-13th-century year. Lipman also says Exeter 'seems to have been virtually extinct as a community by the time of the Expulsion', which contradicts the 1290 household counts already on the map (see MWE_conflicts.csv).

comment: Event: aftermath of the 1290 expulsion at Hereford. Mundill (PDF pp. 322-325): the valuation of the Jews' property (writ delivered to the mayor on 12 September 1290 by the Bishop of Bath and Wells; letter of William de Marchia 4 October; inquisition by the sheriff and twelve bailiffs dated 29 October 1290) was made before the Jews were banished in November 1290. It records eleven properties, among them the synagogue with an adjoining shop in bad repair (4s a year), the dearest house, Aaron le Blund's (20s), and a messuage with shop of Cuntessa the Jewess (12s); there were no stone houses; the clear total was GBP 2 15s 6d (55s 6d in Abrahams' online edition of the return). The Jewry lay in the north-east of the town in Meliere (Maylord) Street or Jews Street, close to the Widemarsh Gate and the Bye Street Gate, with Christians living next door to Jews. In seven letters patent issued between 18 October and 2 November 1291, while the king was in Hereford, the property was granted to local Christians: Cok's house to John de la Felde, a chaplain; Aaron le Blund's house with the synagogue and two of Fauntekyn's shops to John Pedwardyn; the broken-down house pledged to Elias le Ardre to Nicholas Wyat; Hagin of Weobley's house and two more shops to Hugh Bade; Cuntessa's house in Jew Street to Hugh de la Hale; a house shared by Elias le Ardre and Aaron le Blund to Reginald Moniword; and a house in the Vicus Judeorum worth 12d a year that had belonged to Crespin, a Jew of Hereford hanged for felony and forfeited to the Crown, to Roger Younghusband (Rokeah's online table of Jews named in coinage cases has an entry 'Crispin (Hereford)', Exchequer reference E 370/2/19). Mundill concludes that the community had no cemetery (the nearest at Oxford or Bristol), was a border community on the periphery of Jewish activity and suffered less persecution than others, and that the expulsion was 'not quite so clear cut' there: a converted Jew, Absolon, formerly an officer of the city bailiff, received a pair of shoes for his services in 1291, and a Jewess, Floria Smallpurse, was killed by William son of William Younghusband and Robert, servant of Richard the Taylor, who fled; her goods (2s) were confiscated by the sheriff (date not given in the thesis; Rokeah, Hebrew Union College Annual 55, p. 130). The sum Hugh of Kendal received from the grantees is in the conflicts file. Population blank. Confidence: medium (valuation figures confirmed online; the 1291 grants, Absolon and Floria from the thesis only).

comment: Scrutiny of the Lincoln archa, 1240 (roll 'Debita Judeorum inventa in archa cirographorum apud Lincolniam', Monday before Michaelmas, 24 Henry III = autumn 1240; PRO E 101/249/4; Davis, Archaeological Journal 38, pp. 190-192, and Roth, as read in the thesis). Mundill (PDF pp. 343-345): the roll, probably drawn up as a result of the 'Worcester Parliament' of the Jews in summer 1240 (Lincoln's delegates were Judah le Fraunceys and Josce fil Moses), identifies approximately 156 Jews, of whom 133 held bonds in the archa (the footnote on PDF p. 406 says all 156 held bonds); 23 (or 25) are listed as having nothing ('de hiis qui nichil habent'); Leon fil Solomon held nearly 95 bonds worth about GBP 578 2s 10d. Davis's remark that the roll gives 'nearly all the Jews then residing in Lincoln' who 'must have been very numerous' is quoted. The roll also names Jews of other places holding bonds at Lincoln: two of York (Aaron fil Josce, Leon le Evesk), Elias fil Leon of Kirkton, Jacob genus Samson of Grimsby, Manser fil Benjamin staying at Cambridge, Bonefey of Oxford staying at Canterbury, twelve bonds of the London Jews Moses Crespin and Aaron le Blund, and Josce of Bungay, Abraham of Colchester, Moses of Grantham, Deulecresse and his daughter Avigaye of Grantham, Samuel of Grimsby, Pictavin of Hedon and Solomon of Stamford. Mundill calls it probably the most complete record of any thirteenth-century Anglo-Jewish community: an affluent cosmopolitan Jewry. The 156 includes Jews of other towns and is not a population count: Population blank. No online source found for the 1240 roll; source is a doctoral thesis. Confidence: medium.

Estimate by Lipman: a list, 'probably an assessment list', of 114 Jewish names in Lincoln in 1240 (80 males, 34 females) 'cannot have represented more than about 60 families at the outside. On this basis, one would get a total community of about 300'. Lipman adds that York and Lincoln, whose taxable capacity would suggest 300 to 600, were 'probably not in excess of 200 to 300'.

source: Mundill, R. R., The Jews in England 1272-1290 (PhD thesis, St Andrews 1987/88), PDF pp. 341-342
comment: Local restrictions on Jewish land dealings, c. 1240-1260 (Year of Data 1250 is the midpoint of that range). Mundill (PDF pp. 341-342, fn 46-54): Lincolnshire Jews worked with the local monasteries as 'real estate agents': the Jew lent, the monastery paid off the debt and took the land, and the Jew gave a quitclaim, sometimes written in Hebrew (Ursell son of Pucella and Kirkstead Abbey in the 1220s; Newhouse Abbey with Josce son of Elias in 1230 and 1232 and with Garcia son of Judah and others in 1236; Jacob son of Leon's Hebrew deed of 1240; Abraham son of Jacob and Bullington Priory, deed deposited in the Lincoln archa on 26 November 1264). The townspeople took fright, and between 1240 and 1260 a clause evolved that was written into various land transactions forbidding the recipient to alienate the land either to a Jew or to a religious institution (Registrum Antiquissimum, Lincoln Record Society 4, 6 and 7; Lincolnshire Archives Dean and Chapter deeds); in Lincoln itself the townspeople seem to have feared a Jewish takeover, especially in the area of St Martin's, the Strait, Brancegate and Michaelgate, areas that match the Jewish houses of the 1290 survey. The partnership continued until the Act passed by Walter of Merton in 1269 forbade Jews to take land on mortgage. Discrimination short of violence. No online source found (the Registrum Antiquissimum and the Newhouse cartulary are not online as text); source is a doctoral thesis. Population blank. Confidence: medium.

comment: Event: aftermath of the Libel of Little St Hugh, 1255-56 (the libel is already on the map). Mundill (PDF pp. 345-347): a Jew, Copin, was dragged by a horse and hanged at Canwick outside the city; 91 other Lincoln Jews were arrested; on 14 October 1255 the king ordered them taken to Westminster; on 22 November eighteen who refused the verdict of an all-Christian court were hanged in London; of the remaining 73 prisoners two were released (one converted; Rabbi Benedict son of Moses of London was cleared by the boy's mother Beatrice) and the other 71 were condemned again at a retrial on 3 February 1256, but the sentence was delayed after the intercession of the Franciscans, the Dominicans and Richard of Cornwall, and the Jews were released from the Tower in May 1256. Online (Historic Royal Palaces dataset, entry 56): 92 Jews brought to Westminster and imprisoned in the Tower on 22 November (Matthew Paris: 91), eighteen hanged, the other 71 released on 15 May 1256; JE: 92 carried to London, 18 executed. Property: on 26 November 1255 John de Wincle and Simon Passelawe were ordered to appraise the houses of the Lincoln Jews 'who had fled or were hanged or detained in prison'; in March 1256 an inquiry was ordered to identify the members of the synagogue of Peytevin Magnus who had fled Lincoln; in August 1256 the sheriff was ordered to sell the houses of the condemned: at least fourteen houses were sold, formerly of Jacob fil Leo, Vives of Northampton, Vives of Norwich, Leo fil Solomon and Elye fil Jacob (all 'suspensi', hanged) and of Peytevin Magnus (outlawed), mostly in the parishes of St Martin and St Michael and in Brancegate (Thomas de Bellofago and John Long paid GBP 48 for five houses and a rent in St Edward Wigford). Mundill: about a third of Lincoln's Jews arrested, at least 25 hanged, possibly more fled (the counts and the name of the first victim differ from the map and the online sources: conflicts file). The 1256 confiscation details are from the thesis only. Population blank. Confidence: medium. [Source detail: (entries 55-57)]

comment: Tallage of 1262: a list survives of the bonds that the Jews of Lincoln gave from the archa as their tallage contribution (PRO E 101/249/10; tables on PDF pp. 350-354). Ninety Lincoln Jews gave 151 bonds of face value GBP 405 14s 2d, plus small commodity debts (10.5 quarters of corn, a goose, two quarters of oats, a bushel of peas, a cart-load of wood and an annuity of GBP 2); the richest creditor was Benedict Crespin of London (15 bonds, GBP 54 1s 8d); 22 Jews gave bonds under GBP 1 and the mean bond was GBP 2 13s 8d. Many of the 90 were Jews of other towns (London, York, Canterbury, Rochester, Hereford, Exeter, Grimsby, Northampton, Colchester, Norwich, Stamford, Winchester, Wilton, Worcester, Luton, Kingston, Warwick and Bungay). Mundill reads the list as a recovery of Lincoln business after the 1255 libel, though lower than in 1240 (Leon fil Solomon alone held GBP 578 in 1240; the thesis footnote counts 90 Jews named in 1262, 156 in 1240, 93 in 1275 and 61 in 1290). Creditors, not population: blank. No online source found; source is a doctoral thesis. Confidence: medium.

comment: Event: consequences of the sack of the Lincoln Jewry by the Disinherited. The attack itself is already on the map (1266, from Wikipedia/JE). Mundill (PDF pp. 355-356) dates it 1265 (conflicts file) and adds: John Dayville, leader of the Disinherited sheltering in the Isle of Axholme, raided the city and besieged the castle; the rebels sacked the Jewry, entered the synagogue, tore up the scrolls of the Law, killed many Jews (Walter of Hemingburgh) and seized and burned all the bonds and charters; the king then ordered twenty-four citizens of Lincoln to protect the Jews and their goods (Calendar of Patent Rolls 1258-66, pp. 421-422). The loss of records led to disputes (Moses of Clare against Henry of Whaddon over a fee-rent of GBP 4 a year, Rigg, Select Pleas, p. 41); in July 1266 the king granted Benedict son of Master Moses and his brother Hagin a special dispensation that bonds in their hands or their debtors' hands be valid, and the same for other Lincoln Jews, Manser of Bradeworth, Isaac son of Benedict and Elias of Doncaster (CPR 1258-66, p. 617; CPR 1266-72, p. 95). Mundill: recovery was slow; by 1274 the Lincoln Jews paid only GBP 67 13s 3d of tallage (see MU2's Lincoln 1274 row; the text layer reads 5d, the scan 3d). Online: JE 'Lincoln': 'during the uprising of the barons in 1266 the Disinherited attacked the Jewry of Lincoln, mainly for the purpose of destroying the deeds of indebtedness'. No online source found for the protection order and the July 1266 dispensation; they are from a doctoral thesis. Population blank. Confidence: medium.

Mundill (PDF p. 485) calls it the 'Lincoln ketubbah' and gives the sum as GBP 13 6s 8d (= 20 marks); the online page calls it a premarital agreement. Evidence of a wealthy, literate Jewish family in Lincoln in 1271; no population. The map has no Lincoln row for 1271. [confidence: high] [Source detail: (Medieval Anglo-Jewish Women, ed. A. comment: Event: the Bishop of Lincoln has Christian servants of Jews arrested, 1278, and Lincoln Jews in the Tower. Mundill (PDF p. 363, fn 119-122): 'from 1273 to 1278 many Lincolnshire Jews were imprisoned in the Tower of London'; in 1278 Bishop Richard de Gravesend arrested Christians who worked for Jews in Lincoln and wrote to the king that he would excommunicate them, a purge in line with canon law (Fourth Lateran Council) that touched four areas of the city. Thirteen Christian women and men are named: from the Bail Cecilia, maid of Moses, and Eleanor, maid of Josce; from St Michael on the Mount Cecilia, nursemaid of Hakke, Emma, nursemaid of Hakke of Provincia, Alicia, maid of Josce Gubbay, Malcota, servant of Flekote, and Emma, maid of Marcote; from the Skin Market (St Cuthbert and St John Stanhaket) Robert, servant of Hagin, Matilda, nursemaid of Deulecresse, and Alice, servant of Samuel the Chaplain; from St Martin Becona, servant of Abraham of Stamford, and Matilda Belger and Marjorie Scott, servants of Manser (Lincolnshire Archives MCD.501, a copy of PRO C 85/99). Online (Historic Royal Palaces dataset, entries 207 and 173): from 13 June 1277 an unspecified number of Lincoln Jews paid the Tower sergeant 2 marks, and Hake son of Rose of Lincoln was held in the Tower, dates that coincide with the mass incarceration of the Jews for coin-clipping. No online source found for the bishop's action (a search for it found nothing); that part is from a doctoral thesis. Population blank. Confidence: medium. [Source detail: (entries 173, 207)]

comment: Event: coin-clipping prosecutions in Lincolnshire, 1279-81 (the national arrests of November 1278 are in the pending events). Mundill (PDF p. 364, fn 123-129, citing Rokeah, Bulletin of the Institute of Jewish Studies 1, pp. 21-22, 37-41, and J. Ross, Annales Lincolniae): in 1279 Hugh of Kendal was in charge of the confiscations and the sale of condemned goods in the Lincolnshire area, which brought the Crown over GBP 950; many Jews were accused and taken to London where they were hanged; a large amount of Jewish books and jewellery was sold; the only Jew known to have been fined and so to have escaped forfeiture was Manser son of Jacob of Brancegate (6s 8d); Christians fined included James de Scol, Philip de Stanburne, Hugh vicar of Coureby, Peter the Neven of Grimsby and William de Norton, and Roger de Leke (GBP 2), Thomas le Proctor of Boston and John Goddard of Spalding for pennies knowingly taken from a Jew in exchange; Stephen of Thorn, a canon of Lincoln, was amerced for the chattels of Moses son of Moses of Clare (CPR 1281, p. 452). Jewish property was quickly disposed of: on 12 May 1281 the houses in Wigford of Ursellus Levi (8s a year) went to Alexander of London (online, University of Lincoln Medieval Lincoln Jews Group: Ursell Levy 'was caught up in the coin-clipping trials at the end of 1278-9'; 'although not hanged, his property was forfeited and granted to Alexander of London on 12 May 1281', Charter Rolls p. 249; in 1286 he still paid 13s 4d 'for transgressions against the money'), and Hagin son of Master Moses, who died in 1280, may have been a victim (his property went to Queen Eleanor). Online (Rokeah's table): more than a dozen Jews styled 'Lincoln' appear in coinage cases, e.g. Abraham de London (accused clipper, 1281), Cok Luctor ('taken re money', 1281, 'later hanged'), Hake son of Abraham (clipper). The Lincoln house legend of Belaset of Wallingford is discussed under 1279 by Mundill, but online sources date her hanging to 1287-88 (conflicts file). Population blank. Confidence: medium (the sums and the Christian fines are from the thesis only). [Source detail: (Ursell Levy biography)]

MS Hunter fos. 48-49) lists ex-Jewish property in sixteen towns worth £1835 13s 4d in all; Lincoln is valued at £173 0s 0d. The Jewish community also owned a house adjoining the synagogue in the 'Street of the Synagogue' and two houses over the entrance to that house, which Mundill takes to be Jews' Court in St Cuthbert's parish. Hagin fil Benedict had a house in St Martin's parish worth 6s (he paid the king 1d and Adam Ack 9s a year, and rent to the Priory of St Katherine for the plot of his kitchen); Manser of Bradeworth a house in Brancegate worth 10s that he did not live in (John of Norwich lived there; 1d to the king and a pound of cummin to the Prioress of 'Heyming', as typed, probably Heynings); Floria of London a messuage worth 6s in St Cuthbert's parish; Solomon of London two small cottages in Brancegate worth 6s in all; Ursell Levi property in St Mark's parish in Wigford worth 8s; Elias Gabbay a small messuage (a cottage) worth 2s; Master Benedict of London two shops and two tenements in Brancegate worth 5s (15s paid to the Hospital of St Lazarus); Manser of Tickhill a small cottage in bad repair worth 3s. Mundill concludes from the whole Lincoln record that the Jews did not live in a closed ghetto and that some had diversified into property and trade. Online: B. L. Abrahams, 'The Condition of the Jews of England at the Time of their Expulsion in 1290' (Transactions of the Jewish Historical Society of England 2, 1894-95, pp. 95-96), prints the same 'Other Property' entries for these owners (from the Queen's Remembrancer rolls and Lansdowne MS 826): Hagin 6s with 9s to Adam Ack, Manser 10s with John de Norwich, Solomon 6s, Elias Gubbay 2s (1d to the king, 4s to John Stoyl), Ursell Levi 8s (1d to the king, 1d to Osbert le Lung), Master Benedict 5s and 15s to St Lazarus, Manser of Tickhill 3s; Abrahams does not give the parishes of Floria's second house or Ursell's, nor the community's house (only the thesis does). The larger houses are on PDF pp. 399-400 (another agent's page range); the 173 pounds total for Lincoln is in the Kendal row already on the map. [confidence: high for the values confirmed by Abrahams, medium for the parishes and the community's house]

Mundill (PDF pp. 365-376, fn 132-137): after the Expulsion edict the archa was sealed in October 1290 and early in 1291 the sheriff John Byre and the Christian chirographers John Cotty and Richard de Baud delivered it to Westminster in person, with a chest of 'nova debita' sealed by Robert of Caddeworth (a former sheriff), a small pyx of ten bonds brought by Alan of Trikenham and Richard of Bothelingthorp, the archa of the Jews of Stamford (contents lost) and a list of all Jewish domiciles in Lincoln supplied by the bailiffs. 252 bonds (242 in the Nova Cista and 10 in the pyx; the thesis table counts 250), 23 per cent of all surviving Jewish bonds in England, face value about GBP 2,500 (table: GBP 2,461 18s 6d), held by 61-62 Jewish creditors, the largest number of provincial moneylenders in any 1290 archa (against 156 named in 1240, 90 in 1262 and 93 in 1275; Mundill infers fewer Jews lending, and a parallel decline in population is only 'likely'). Bonds ran from 1278 (2) to 1290 (68), 136 were for wool (208.5 sacks and 8 stone, GBP 1,602 14s 8d), 73 for corn (2,122.5 quarters, GBP 552 13s 10d) and 41 for money (GBP 306 10s); the largest creditor was Jacob of Brancegate (32 bonds). The last money bond was made in June 1290, the month of the king's secret writs, and bonds were still being registered in August-September 1290 (see MU1's Lincoln row). Online: Abrahams (1894-95, pp. 94-96) prints the Lincoln list of 66 Jews and the community with bonds and houses, and JE counts 66 householders with deeds of GBP 423 15s (money), GBP 601 9s 4d (corn) and GBP 1,595 6s (wool): the figures differ from the thesis (conflicts file). The map's ~330 for 1290 is JE's 66 x 5. Population blank. Confidence: medium (counts from the thesis tables).

comment: Jewish property in Lincoln at the Expulsion, and the synagogue. Mundill (PDF pp. 399-400, fn 191-200): the return of summer 1290 by twelve 'probi homines' (and the inquisition of October 1290; Hugh of Kendal's sale of the twenty-three Jewish properties raised GBP 173, the figure in MU1's row) shows that the Jews of Lincoln did not live in a closed 'ghetto' but in an open Jewry among Christians. Online (Medieval Lincoln Jews Group): Hugh of Kendal was appointed on 20 December 1290 to value and sell the Jewish property and on 27 December 1290 listed Lincoln at GBP 173 (TNA E 101/249/1); the first Lincoln grant was issued on 15 January 1291, then one on 20 January, seven on 20 February, four on 27 March and one on 10 April 1291, so the Crown disposed of the Lincoln property in under six months; the group gives GBP 141 as the sum for all the former Jewish properties of Lincolnshire (Lincoln and Stamford) (conflicts file). Seven houses were worth more than 20s a year: Floria of London's 'best house with two shops and a fine exit' in St Martin's parish, 30s (occupied by a Christian, William le Welley; she lived in a 6s house in St Cuthbert's), Master Benedict of London's house in St Benedict's parish (Abrahams: three messuages in which he lived), 40s (3d land rent to the king and 21s 4d to the cathedral; also property in Brancegate), properties of Manser of Bradeworth and of Belaset (about 20s), and 'Le Gannok', two high, well-built tiled houses of Benedict de la Gannok, 20s; ten houses were between 10s and 16s 8d (Manser's in Brancegate 13s 4d, Josce of Colchester's 12s, Jude's in the Bail, Hagin son of Benedict's 13s 4d, Jacob of Brancegate's in St George Brancegate 15s, Benedict le Civitate's 11s in St John the Poor); and the 'Scola' or synagogue was worth 10s a year, for which the Jewish community of Lincoln paid the king a land rent of 1d (the thesis continues on PDF pp. 401-403 with the community's other house and the cheaper holdings, which MU6's Lincoln 1290 row covers). Online: the University of Lincoln Medieval Lincoln Jews Group counts the properties by parish (six in St George, three each in St Martin, St Cuthbert, St Michael and St John, two in St Benedict outside the walls), gives Benedict of London's 40s as the highest and Floria's as 28s (the thesis and Abrahams' no. 34 give 30s); Abrahams prints the same houses; JE: thirty houses, mostly in Brancegate and St Martin's parish, 'where indeed the ghetto seems to have been'. comment: Event: after the expulsion the Crown regranted the ex-Jewish properties of Lincoln (Valor of 1290 and BL Lansdowne MS 826 fos. 28-64, as used by Ross and Birch; Mundill's notes 194-209). The Jews' burial ground (valued 3s 6d), together with Elias Gabbay's small messuage (2s), was granted in 1291 to Walter of Carlisle. The synagogue (scola) in St Cuthbert's parish, one of at least two in Lincoln (the other in St Martin's parish near Hungate), was granted by a charter of 27 March 1291 to Robert de Leverton, with other property of Benedict son of Arabella, for a rent of 2d a year, although the roll values it at 20s a year; a later grant of the St Cuthbert scola is recorded in 1316 (online: Wikipedia 'Jews' Court, Lincoln' says a 1316 charter shows a Jewish scola or synagogue had stood to the west in the tenement behind the two houses). Belaset's house (St Cuthbert's parish, between the King's Street at the Corn Market and the Drapery, 'identified with the house still standing' by Ross) is not in the Valor; it was granted in 1291 to Walter le Ffeure of Foleteby and valued at 19s 6d, and Ross notes that Belaset was implicated in coin clipping and put to death, so the property had escheated earlier, 'but it is not stated when' (online: Abrahams, JHSE 2, p. 95, no. 2, lists Belaset of Wallingford, daughter of Solomon, with 'a house of the clear annual value of 19s. 6d.', from Lansdowne MS 826; the University of Lincoln Medieval Studies Research Group says Belaset of Wallingford was hanged for clipping the king's money, citing Lincolnshire Archives D&C A/1/8 fol. 107 no. 290, the record Mundill cites for this house; the map's Lincoln 1287 row gives the Jewish Encyclopedia's year for her execution). Other grants in the notes: Robert le Venour paid 26 pounds 13s 4d for Master Benedict of London's house and received Hagin fil Benedict's house in St Martin's parish and Benedict le Civitate's property; Floria of London's house with the fine passage (valued 28s-30s) went to William le Came, cordwainer (the name is spelled variously; the house reached the Dean and Chapter by 1310 and was demolished in 1324); Walter Bek received Jude the Jew's property, Peter of Coleby Jacob of Brancegate's, Simon le Ffeure Floria's second house, Adam Cokerel (a Lincoln bailiff in 1291) Ursell Levi's property. [confidence: medium; high for the 1316 charter and for Belaset's hanging]

At Stamford seventeen Jews gave 26 bonds from the archa, with a total face value of GBP 69 6s 10d and two quarters of corn, about one-sixth of the Lincoln figure (GBP 405 14s 2d, see the Lincoln 1262 row). Creditors, not population: blank. Evidence of an organised Jewish community with a working archa at Stamford in 1262, a gap on the map between 1245 and 1275. No online source found; source is a doctoral thesis. Confidence: medium.

source: https://www.hrp.org.uk/media/3082/dataset-of-jewish-prisoners-refugees-and-staff-at-the-tower.pdf | Mundill, R. R., The Jews in England 1272-1290 (PhD thesis, St Andrews 1987/88), PDF pp. 100, 103
comment: Event: Jews of Stamford held in the Tower of London for unpaid tallage during the Great Tallage of 1274-75. On 13 May 1275 the tallage commissioners were ordered to acquit Bateman of Stamford of his tallage because he had offered the king all his lands, goods and chattels if the king would have him delivered from the Tower, where he was imprisoned; on 10 July 1275 the Barons of the Exchequer were ordered to release from the Tower Sampson son of Master Miles of Stamford and Abraham son of Diey of Holme, together with Samuel son of Manasser of Lincoln, Elias son of Ursel of Lincoln, Vives son of Garsias and Abraham son of Samuel, their tallage to be levied from their better debts and the six to be re-imprisoned if it was still unpaid in September (thesis, PDF p. 103). The Stamford community also paid through a Christian official: the Prior of St Leonard's outside Stamford paid £60 7s 1½d for the 'commune of Stamford' in the Great Tallage roll (PDF p. 100). Online corroboration (not the same orders): Historic Royal Palaces dataset, entries 79-80 (CPREJ ii, iv): the two Jewish chirographers of the Stamford archa, Elias of Doncaster and Sampson son of Master Elias (probably imprisoned for arrears of the 1274 tallage), were held in the Tower by October/November 1274, and a search of the Stamford archa in January/February 1275 found 126 bonds. The patronymic of Sampson is 'Master Miles' in the thesis and 'Master Elias' in the dataset. Population blank. [Source detail: (entries 79-80)]

source: https://www.hrp.org.uk/media/3082/dataset-of-jewish-prisoners-refugees-and-staff-at-the-tower.pdf | Historic Royal Palaces, Dataset of Jewish prisoners, refugees and staff at the Tower (PDF) | Mundill, R. R., The Jews in England 1272-1290 (PhD thesis, St Andrews 1987/88), PDF pp. 357-358
comment: Scrutiny of the Stamford archa, early 1275 (Plea Rolls of the Exchequer of the Jews vol. 4, pp. 14, 62-65; PRO E 401/1568). Mundill (PDF pp. 357-358): 45 Jews are named, of whom 18 had bonds in the archa; the 18 had 126 bonds deposited; 55 of the 126 bonds that had been sent to Westminster were returned to Stamford and listed by an Exchequer scribe, for ten Stamford Jews with a face value of GBP 380 5s (business in lower Lincolnshire, Rutland, Cambridgeshire, Nottinghamshire and Northamptonshire). Tony son of Meir (who still owned property in Stamford in 1290) had all eleven of his bonds returned (face value GBP 43 13s 4d) after paying GBP 3 19s 11d to the Great Tallage; Diey of Holme (indicted for murder in 1276, see MU2's Stamford 1276 row) had 21 bonds returned (GBP 181 16s 8d) and paid just under GBP 10 in cash. Online (Historic Royal Palaces dataset, entry 79, the chirographer Elias of Doncaster, who lived in Stamford): 'In January/February 1275, a search of the Stamford archa found that Elias had the second-largest number of bonds, at 18 out of 126'. Creditors, not population: blank. Confidence: high for the 126 bonds (two sources), medium for the rest. [Source detail: (entry 79)]

source: Mundill, R. R., The Jews in England 1272-1290 (PhD thesis, St Andrews 1987/88), PDF pp. 109, 137
comment: In the tallage of 1276 the community of the Jews of Stamford yielded £24 (PRO E 401/1572; thesis PDF p. 109). Event: in April 1276 Diey of Holme, a Stamford Jew, was charged with the murder of Brother Richard of the priory of St Michael at Stamford and with killing a groom in the Earl of Warwick's wood outside Stratton; he was indicted for murder and receiving from thieves, his body was 'attached' and his goods in Stamford and elsewhere were seized, including money hidden in the walls of his house, which was seized as treasure trove and handed to Luke de Lucca, the king's merchant (CPR 1276, p. 137; thesis PDF p. 137). The outcome is not stated. The Diey of Holm page on majw.uvic.ca lists only a 1274 Stamford debt record and nothing on this case. No online source found; source is a doctoral thesis.

comment: Event: Stamford Jews in the coin-clipping prosecutions of 1277-79. Mundill (PDF p. 332, fn 10, citing J. Ross, Annales Lincolniae, and Rokeah, Bulletin of the Institute of Jewish Studies 1, p. 37): 'the Stamford Jews also suffered during the coin-clipping allegations of 1279'. Online corroboration: the Historic Royal Palaces Tower dataset (entry 200) records an unspecified number of Jews from Stamford who paid the Tower sergeant 50s from 13 June 1277 to be held by themselves, a date that coincides with the mass incarceration of England's Jews for coin-clipping; Rokeah's table of Jews named in coinage cases lists about ten Stamford Jews (e.g. Dyey of Hulme, who paid a fine for a 'money trespass' in 1275-6; the widows Blanche and Terta; Bateman; Isaac Motun; Elias son of Manser; Tony son of Aaron). comment: Jewish property at Stamford at the expulsion (Valor Judaismi). Mundill (PDF p. 332, fn 8-9): the Stamford archa was brought to Westminster in 1290 with Lincoln's, its contents are lost, but Jews lived in Stamford up to 1290: the Valor shows that Bellassez, a Jewess, owned two messuages in the parishes of St Michael and St John, Reyne, wife of David, one messuage in All Saints parish, and Tony son of Meir also one in All Saints; there was a synagogue at Stamford and, according to Peck's Annals of Stamford (18th century, not checked), a Jewish library forfeited in 1290 passed into the hands of a neighbouring abbey. Online: Abrahams (1894-95, p. 103, 'Stamford: 1. Belaset, 2. Reyne, who was wife of David, 3. Tony, son of Meyr') gives the same three owners, with Belaset's two messuages (St Michael's parish 3s 6d a year; the St John's messuage is valued in the same entry, the figure is garbled in the OCR) and the All Saints houses (2s each); Abrahams thought it doubtful that Stamford had an archa, which JE's list of 26 archa towns, the 1221 roll, the 1275 scrutiny and Mundill contradict (conflicts file). The sale of the Stamford property raised GBP 13 6s 8d (MU1 row). Population blank (three property owners are named, no count of Jews). Confidence: high for the three owners, medium for the synagogue and library (thesis only).

Jewish history in Bukhara stretches back at least 1,500 years from 2025 (approx. 525 CE), when Persian Jews migrated east after the Babylonian exile.

First mention of a Bukharan Jewish community, noted as being apparently small at the time.
Timur rebuilt the city and imported Persian Jews to work as dyers and weavers, establishing the makhallai yahudiyon (Jewish quarter) and building a synagogue used for 500 years.
Following the destruction of Samarkand, Jews migrated to Bukhara, which became the center of Central Asian Jewry.
Some gravestones in the Old Jewish Cemetery in Bukhara date to the 1500s.
Jews of Bukhara began to settle in a special quarter called Old Makhalla; they were subjected to restrictions such as a special tax and dress codes.
A formal Jewish quarter developed around the end of the 16th and beginning of the 17th centuries.
The Bukhara Synagogue was built, considered the oldest surviving synagogue in Central Asia.
Periods of forced conversion to Islam affected Jews; some outwardly practiced Islam while secretly retaining Jewish identity (Chala).
The mullahs of Bukhara began to institute forced conversions of the Jews toward the end of the 18th century, creating a separate anusim community known as chalas.
Joseph Maman arrived and remained as a religious leader, strengthening education and introducing the Sephardic prayer rite.

Joseph Mamon of Tetuan arrived to find the community in a desolate condition; he stayed to instruct local Jews, leading to a rise in ethnic and religious awareness and the creation of a second Jewish quarter (New Makhalla).
Rabbi Joseph Maman Maghribi arrived, beginning a revival of Bukharan religious and spiritual life; he served the community for thirty years.
Rabbi Yosef Maman traveled from Safed to Bukhara with prayerbooks, introducing Sephardi religious customs.
Rabbi Maman returned to Bukhara to settle permanently and helped establish a second synagogue, Ohel Itzhak.

Waronker, African Synagogues: the Jews of Luanshya built a single-storey brick synagogue (the 'Former Luanshya Chapel', completed 1953), the southernmost of the Copperbelt communities; EJ: Jewish mayors served in Luanshya before 1964.

Waronker, African Synagogues (Lusaka Hebrew Congregation): Lusaka's Jewish community 'dates to the 1910s, when they were able to form a minyan (quorum) by 1910 and procure a Sefer Torah in 1914'; prayers in a private home or at a cinema for four decades.

Wikipedia: of 110 Jews in Northern Rhodesia in 1921 most lived in Livingstone and Lusaka (110 is the national figure, not Lusaka's). By the mid-1950s the centre of Jewish life had moved to Lusaka; Council for Zambia Jewry created in Lusaka in 1978.
Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Zambia' (as reproduced on the ZJC Zambia page): 'In 1921, out of a total Jewish population of 110, 48 lived in Livingstone, 11 in Broken Hill, and 25 in Lusaka.'

Waronker, African Synagogues: the foundation stone of the Lusaka synagogue was laid on 20 July 1941 and the building was completed the next year (consecrated 8 March 1946); German Jewish refugees joined the Eastern European Jews already there.

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Bulawayo': 'In 1900, when there were 300 Jewish residents (76% of the total Jewish population of Rhodesia)' - wording is ambiguous whether the 300 is Bulawayo or all Rhodesia; Year Established = Hebrew congregation formed 1894

Rhodesian Jewry and its Story, Part Two: the Bulawayo Chovevi Zion set up the first Jewish Library in Rhodesia in 1901, 'from which offshoots were established in Salisbury, Gwanda, Gwelo and Selukwe' (offshoot libraries imply Jewish readers; year of the offshoots not stated; weak).

Wikipedia: 'A third congregation was established in Gwelo in 1901' (after Bulawayo 1894 and Salisbury 1895). Rhodesian Jewry history: the first service at Gwelo in 1901 gathered 15 people (attendees, not a population) who raised GBP 1.7.6 for Zion.

Rhodesian Jewry and its Story, Part Two (E. Rosenthal): 'when in 1901 the first service was held at Gwelo, it was possible from the 15 people to raise GBP 1.7.6' (15 = people present at the service, not the community size).

Kosmin, Majuta (1981), p.139: 'The Gwelo Hebrew Congregation was founded in 1901 when the town had a total population of only fifteen Jews.' Its first service coincided with the visit of the Revd M.I. Cohen of Bulawayo. Scanned book, page image viewed (PDF p.93).

Jewish Guild Journal (Bulawayo), Vol. I No. 3 (Pesach 5680, spring 1920), 'Gleanings from Gwelo': 'The Jewish community in this district numbers about 45.' District figure (Gwelo and surroundings); the paper adds that the community needed a Hebrew teacher. Scanned journal, page image viewed (PDF p.14).

Kosmin, Majuta (1981), p.139: until 1928 the New Year services took place at the Masonic Temple, 'until a synagogue was erected in 1928 on a site given by the Government'; Waronker's African Synagogues page dates the synagogue 1933 according to its stone inscription (separate row).

Waronker, African Synagogues (Gweru Hebrew Congregation, founded 1901): 'The synagogue, dedicated in 1933 according to its (now gone) stone inscription, went on to serve the Jewish community for about a half a century'; Kosmin (1981, p.139) gives 1928 for the building (separate row). Sold to a Pentecostal church in 2000.

ZJC Gweru page: 'The Gweru Community was established in the early 20th Century and the last member passed away in 2003' (a cemetery of about 50 graves remains); Waronker: the death in 2003 of the last Jewish resident ended a period of Jewish life of more than a century.

JVL Zimbabwe tour: 'The Harare (formerly Salisbury) Hebrew Congregation ... was founded on June 2, 1895, by twenty men and two women' (first leader Joe van Praagh); Encyclopaedia Judaica (JVL 'Salisbury'): a meeting of 20 men and two women founded the Salisbury Hebrew Congregation. The founders are not the town's population (Population blank).

JVL Zimbabwe tour: 'In 1901, the first synagogue was built on Rhodes Avenue with 70 members'; a new synagogue was erected on Salisbury Street in 1920 (the opening on 29 February 1920 is reported in the Jewish Guild Journal) after the community had outgrown the first by 1912; Joe van Praagh was Salisbury's first Jewish mayor (1900-01). Members, not population.

The Hon. A. E. Abrahamson, 'The Jewish Communities' Contribution to Rhodesia', Rhodesiana No. 34 (March 1976), pp. 45-46: 'Whereas in the earlier years of this century there were some 400 Jewish members in Bulawayo and only 17 in Salisbury, nowadays the Salisbury community is far larger than that of Bulawayo.' Undated ('earlier years of this century' set to 1905) and the unit is 'Jewish members' (of the community), not a census; weak row. Kosmin gives 1,289 Jews in all Rhodesia in 1921 and the Jewish Guild Journal 45 families in Salisbury in 1920.

ZJC Kadoma page: 'In 1956, the first Jewish Mayoral Service ever held in Gatooma took place when Mr Stemberg [Sternberg] became the first Jewish Mayor.'

JVL Zimbabwe tour: 'The last minyan with the Kadoma Congregation occurred in 1979.' Jews began to leave in the late 1950s and 1960s because of economic trouble; fewer than 20 Jews remained in the city (undated, 2000s), none of them children.
